name: California
title: Candidatos de California están dando instrucciones discretas sobre cómo atacar a sus oponentes. Así es como funciona
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Algunos candidatos a la Legislatura de California están utilizando cada vez más una táctica controvertida que, según expertos y organizaciones de vigilancia pública, parece contravenir las leyes estatales de financiación de campañas electorales.
Una revisión realizada por CalMatters a sitios web de campañas legislativas reveló que al menos 14 candidatos tienen mensajes electorales detallados y empaquetados en sus sitios web de manera que resulte fácil para los comités de gastos independientes utilizarlos en anuncios publicitarios.
Esta técnica, conocida como “marcaje en rojo” o “red boxing”, se utiliza cada vez más ante la falta de supervisión por parte de los organismos reguladores estatales.
 CalMatters encontró al menos tres casos en los que grupos externos crearon anuncios de campaña digitales que replicaban los mensajes predefinidos en los sitios web de los candidatos. Según las normas estatales de financiación de campañas , los anuncios realizados “a instancias” de campañas oficiales se presumen gastos “coordinados” —no gastos independientes— y pueden exceder ilegalmente los límites de contribución para la financiación de campañas.
 Por ejemplo, una sección en un recuadro rojo en el sitio web de la candidata a la Asamblea, Jessie Lopez, dice: “Los votantes demócratas y (sin afiliación partidista) deben saber” que su competidor, el también concejal de la ciudad de Santa Ana, David Penaloza, votó a favor de aprobar un contrato municipal con la empresa de cámaras de vigilancia Flock, que está financiado por intereses especiales y que Jessie Lopez “luchará por la gente trabajadora”.
El 14 de octubre, apareció un anuncio de 15 segundos en las redes sociales de los residentes de Santa Ana, en Facebook e Instagram, destacando la aprobación del contrato de Flock por parte de Peñaloza, su financiación por parte de “multimillonarios de las grandes tecnológicas” y el apoyo de enfermeras y educadores a López. El anuncio fue financiado por un grupo externo, Working People United, patrocinado por el Consejo Estatal de California del SEIU, que ha gastado al menos 1.4 millones de dólares en apoyo a López desde abril.
 López no respondió a un mensaje de texto solicitando comentarios, y su campaña tampoco respondió a las consultas enviadas por correo electrónico sobre si la información estaba destinada a un comité de gastos independientes. Working People United tampoco respondió a una solicitud de comentarios.
 Sin embargo, los estrategas de campaña y los grupos de vigilancia coinciden en que esta práctica se está generalizando en las reñidas contiendas electorales de California.
 “Después de Citizens United y todo eso, y con el dinero entrando en la política, la cosa se ha vuelto una locura, ¿verdad? Las cosas se han vuelto inmanejables”, dijo Jorge Contreras, director en California del Partido de las Familias Trabajadoras, que apoya a López.
 “Por eso, los candidatos están utilizando recuadros rojos para intentar comunicarse.” 
Qué es el “marcaje en rojo”
En California, los donantes, incluyendo corporaciones, sindicatos e individuos adinerados, tienen un límite en la cantidad que pueden donar a los candidatos. Según las normas de la Comisión de Prácticas Políticas Justas, el organismo estatal que supervisa la financiación de campañas, pueden donar hasta 5,900 dólares por elección.
 Sin embargo, quienes realizan grandes donaciones pueden aportar cantidades ilimitadas a los comités de gasto independiente que publican anuncios a favor o en contra de los candidatos. Las normas de la FPPC establecen que el gasto de estos comités puede ser ilimitado siempre y cuando los pagos “no se coordinen con el candidato ni se realicen a su petición”.
 Se aplican reglas similares a las contiendas para el Congreso federal. Sin embargo, en la última década, el uso de recuadros rojos se ha popularizado en las campañas para el Congreso. Los candidatos dejan instrucciones, generalmente resaltadas en un recuadro rojo, para que los anunciantes independientes las sigan al crear sus anuncios. En algunos casos, incluso especifican a qué grupos demográficos dirigirse.
 Según Patrick Llewellyn, director de financiación de campañas estatales del Campaign Legal Center, una organización sin ánimo de lucro que aboga por la reforma del financiamiento de campañas, las casillas rojas son una forma de eludir los límites de contribución. Llewellyn afirmó que esto puede generar la apariencia de corrupción, incluso si no existe un acuerdo explícito entre el candidato y el comité independiente.
 “Cuando un candidato utiliza recuadros rojos y luego se realizan gastos en respuesta a esos recuadros rojos, eso contradice cualquier comprensión de sentido común sobre la independencia”, dijo, y agregó que el fenómeno se ha extendido a las elecciones estatales y locales en todo el país, aunque los funcionarios en algunas áreas han tomado medidas enérgicas en los últimos años.
 La portavoz de la FPPC, Shery Yang, dijo que existen normas que regulan el boxeo rojo. 
 Una captura de pantalla del sitio web de la campaña de Jessie Lopez muestra un recuadro rojo titulado “Lo que los votantes deben saber”, con viñetas que contrastan las posturas de Lopez con las de su oponente David Penaloza sobre la aplicación de la ley de inmigración, las cámaras de vigilancia y las contribuciones de campaña. Captura de pantalla vía el sitio web de la campaña de Jessie Lopez
 En un correo electrónico, afirmó que “las formas comunes de recuadro rojo generalmente se presumirían como coordinación según las regulaciones vigentes de la FPPC”.
 La normativa establece que se presume que un gasto está coordinado si se basa en información sobre las necesidades de la campaña proporcionada “directa o indirectamente” o si difunde “en su totalidad o en gran parte, una comunicación, incluyendo material de vídeo, diseñada, producida, pagada o distribuida por el candidato o el comité”.
 Decenas de candidatos tienen varios minutos de metraje de archivo publicado en sus sitios web, que los comités de gastos independientes utilizan habitualmente en sus anuncios.
 Yang no respondió a las preguntas sobre si la comisión, conocida por su lentitud a la hora de investigar las quejas, ha aplicado alguna vez las normas relativas a la clasificación en rojo, o si está investigando algún caso este año.
 El estratega demócrata Steven Maviglio afirmó que esta práctica se ha “acelerado considerablemente” durante los dos últimos ciclos electorales, ya que las campañas han comprobado que la táctica funciona a nivel federal.
 Y las campañas no creen que las vayan a pillar, dijo Maviglio.
 “Nos guste o no, el organismo de control estatal no tiene la capacidad para hacer su trabajo”, dijo.
 El expresidente de la FPPC, Dan Schnur, afirmó que la inacción del organismo podría deberse a una falta de recursos.
 “El reto de la FPPC radica en que se financia con los fondos de los legisladores a quienes debe supervisar”, afirmó Schnur. “Los funcionarios electos no tienen muchos incentivos para proporcionarles la financiación o el personal suficientes para que realicen su trabajo de manera integral”. 
 Mantenerse fiel al mensaje
 En el Distrito 36 de la Asamblea, en la frontera sur, los demócratas tienen una ventaja de registro del 12% sobre los republicanos. Eso no impidió que el veterano de la Infantería de Marina, Jeff Gonzalez, arrebatara el escaño a los republicanos en 2024. Ahora, Gonzalez lucha por conservar el puesto frente a su rival demócrata, la alcaldesa de Imperial, Ida Obeso-Martinez.
Grupos externos, entre los que se incluyen compañías petroleras y de gas y un comité de acción política de la Cámara de Comercio de California, han gastado alrededor de 3.4 millones de dólares en apoyo a González y en contra de Obeso-Martínez.
 Hasta hace poco, el actual senador republicano tenía un mensaje para las “partes interesadas” en su sitio web. En un memorando, posteriormente eliminado, que se encontraba en una carpeta de Dropbox llamada “Lo que los votantes quieren saber” y a la que se accedía a través de la pestaña “FOTOS” de su sitio web, la campaña de González identificó tres posibles líneas de ataque contra Obeso-Martínez, bajo los títulos “AUMENTO SALARIAL”, “IMPUESTOS Y TARIFAS” y “PROGRESIS”.
 “Ida Obeso-Martínez es solo otra política que vela únicamente por sus propios intereses”, decía el memorándum. “En el Ayuntamiento, Ida votó a favor de duplicar su propio salario, financiado con los impuestos de los ciudadanos, y votó a favor de otorgarse a sí misma un nuevo paquete de beneficios financiado con los impuestos de los ciudadanos”.
 El Centro de Transparencia Publicitaria de Google muestra que el 9 de octubre, un grupo llamado “Familias por una Vida Asequible”, financiado principalmente por franquiciados de McDonald’s, empresas de servicios públicos y compañías de petróleo y gas , publicó un anuncio que destacaba el aumento salarial de los concejales. 
 Captura de pantalla de un memorándum en PDF titulado “Por qué Jeff Gonzalez gana el Distrito 36 de la Asamblea”, que describe la trayectoria militar del candidato y su mensaje de campaña sobre la reducción de costos y la mejora de la accesibilidad a la atención médica. Captura de pantalla del sitio web de la campaña de Jeff Gonzalez.
 “Como concejala, Obeso-Martínez votó a favor de duplicar su propio salario”, dice una voz mientras aparece una superposición de billetes cayendo sobre imágenes de la demócrata.
Maviglio afirmó que, en algunos casos, los gastos independientes se convierten en la “estrategia completa” de la campaña debido a la cantidad de dinero que los comités están dispuestos a invertir. Los registros de financiación de campaña muestran que la campaña de González ha gastado 1.04 millones de dólares desde las primarias, menos de un tercio de los 3.4 millones de dólares que los comités de gastos independientes han invertido en su nombre durante el mismo período.
 Sin embargo, el consultor demócrata Michael Trujillo afirma que el gasto ilimitado por parte de grupos externos puede ser peligroso si los gastos independientes no están “en consonancia con el mensaje”.
 “No quieres que tu mensaje sea secuestrado por ningún esfuerzo independiente, bueno o malo”, dijo Trujillo, y agregó que el uso de recuadros rojos puede ser una forma para que grupos externos comuniquen “cuál es la esencia de la campaña”.
 Recientemente, Obeso-Martínez se sumó a la contienda. El 19 de octubre, su campaña añadió una pestaña de “Comunicaciones” a su sitio web con el siguiente mensaje : “Los votantes de todo el distrito necesitan ver y escuchar comunicaciones negativas en televisión, radio, plataformas digitales y otros medios sobre la alianza de Jeff González con Donald Trump”.
 El asesor de campaña de Obeso-Martinez, Orrin Evans, declinó hacer comentarios. Ni el tesorero de “Families for Affordable Living” ni el principal financiador del comité, la Alianza de Empresas Familiares de California, respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios. 
 Una carrera armamentística de gasto
 Pocas contiendas electorales han recaudado más dinero externo que los casi 7 millones de dólares acumulados en la batalla en el norte del Área de la Bahía de San Francisco entre el demócrata moderado y supervisor del condado de Marin, Eric Lucan, y su oponente demócrata progresista, Jackie Elward, concejal de Rohnert Park.
Lucan se ha beneficiado de la mayor parte de ese gasto, más de 4.5 millones de dólares, provenientes en gran medida del grupo Grow California, respaldado por multimillonarios del sector de las criptomonedas. Los sindicatos han aportado alrededor de 2 millones de dólares a Elward.
 En la sección “Galería” del sitio web de Elward, un carrusel de fotos de alta resolución y grabaciones de archivo muestra al candidato paseando por un mercado de agricultores, una estación de bomberos, una plaza del centro y un campus universitario. Hasta esta semana, si los visitantes se desplazaban hasta el final, podían encontrar una guía con los puntos clave sobre las instrucciones para la comunicación de la campaña.
 Una de las frases hacía referencia a los anuncios de campaña de las primarias: “También hay que recordar a los votantes de dónde provienen los anuncios de ataque contra Jackie y los anuncios de apoyo a Eric: multimillonarios de fuera del distrito alineados con MAGA, grandes farmacéuticas y empresas de servicios públicos con fines de lucro”.
 El 18 de octubre, “Workers for Jackie Elward”, cuyos principales financiadores son Consumer Attorneys of California, California Labor Federation y SEIU California Council, comenzó a publicar anuncios en Facebook e Instagram. 
 Captura de pantalla de una guía de mensajes de campaña titulada “Lo que los votantes necesitan saber”, que describe las prioridades políticas de Jackie Elward y sus críticas a su oponente, Eric Lucan. Captura de pantalla vía el sitio web de la campaña de Jackie Elward.
 Sobre fotografías de los multimillonarios donantes de Grow California, Chris Larsen y Timothy Draper, una voz pregunta: “¿Por qué estos multimillonarios tecnológicos que apoyan a Trump están gastando tanto dinero para que (Lucan) sea su representante en la Asamblea?”
 En un comunicado, Doug Linney, asesor de la campaña de Elward, dijo: “Todo lo que aparece en el sitio web de una campaña es información pública que creemos que los votantes merecen conocer”.
 La campaña ya había eliminado la página.
 En septiembre, Lucan publicó mensajes en Instagram y Facebook pidiendo a los comités de gastos independientes que dejaran de gastar dinero en la campaña electoral.
 “Este dinero oscuro está engañando a los votantes sobre mí, así como sobre mi oponente, y todo ello está distorsionando y corrompiendo nuestra democracia; es todo lo que repugna a la gente de la política”, decía la publicación.
 Sin embargo, el sitio web de Lucan todavía tiene material de archivo disponible para que cualquiera lo use, el cual ha aparecido en muchos anuncios de campaña en apoyo del candidato, pagados por Grow California.
 «Imágenes de nuestras redes sociales, páginas de YouTube y sitio web han sido utilizadas por simpatizantes y medios locales», declaró Four Waters, portavoz de la campaña de Lucan (quien escribe su nombre en minúsculas). «Nunca hemos ejercido ningún control ni hemos tenido coordinación alguna con los medios de comunicación que trabajan a favor o en contra de nuestra campaña».
 Grow California no respondió a la solicitud de comentarios.
 Las campañas legislativas han cambiado significativamente en los últimos años debido al auge del gasto independiente, afirmó Mike Gatto, exmiembro de la Asamblea de Los Ángeles y miembro del Partido Demócrata.
 “Hace apenas 10 o 15 años, era bastante común que las elecciones legislativas se decidieran únicamente en función de los recursos que los propios candidatos planteaban”, afirmó. “Eso es cada vez más raro”.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Feds eye New England universities in push to reshore rare earth metal refining
text:
"We have to train the workforce, in the field and in factories and in mines, and also the high tech workforce and innovative workforce needed out of our universities," said Audrey Robertson (center), assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy, on a visit to an Exeter, New Hampshire, rare earth refinery Oct. 30, 2026. Robertson said a labor shortage was holding back U.S. mining of critical minerals and announced funding aimed at increasing mining training programs. From left: Curt Coccodrilli, U.S. Department of Energy acting assistant secretary and principal deputy assistant secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office, Robertson, and Phoenix Tailings CEO Nicholas Myers. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)U.S. Department of Energy officials came to the New Hampshire Seacoast on Friday to announce plans to distribute $70 million to universities across the U.S., a move they said was intended to boost training of mining engineers and other professionals of the domestic “critical minerals” workforce. 
But no university in New Hampshire, or in New England more broadly, has a mining program that would make them eligible for the awards, the officials said — so why make the announcement in Exeter?
“This is where the workforce is needed,” said Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy, in a conference room at the mineral refinery operated in the Seacoast town by rare earth startup Phoenix Tailings. “It’s actually indicative of the problem.”
The set of 17 elements known as rare earth metals are considered critical to manufacture a range of technologies, from electric vehicles to missiles, MRI machines, computer chips, and more. They are relatively common in the Earth’s crust but difficult to isolate. Globally, the mining and refinement of rare earth metals is linked to environmental destruction and the generation of toxic waste.
Phoenix Tailings, which is based in Massachusetts with locations in Burlington and Woburn in addition to Exeter, New Hampshire, is one of a limited number of domestic rare earth refining companies. The U.S. Department of Energy has used grant funding to try to incentivize domestic production; Phoenix Tailings received one such award totaling about $66 million dollars this summer.
But the U.S. industry is still comparatively small. Globally, the People’s Republic of China holds a disproportionate share of the rare earth refining industry. More than 90% of the rare earth metals refined globally are produced in China, according to the International Energy Agency. President Donald Trump has called for domestic production to increase.
On Friday, Robertson said the current state of the supply chain made the U.S. “100% reliant on foreign adversaries.” She credited Phoenix Tailings with playing an important role in strengthening the industry in the U.S.
The company’s Exeter facility can process 200 metric tons of rare earth metals annually, with plans for an expansion that could more than double that output, Head of Communications Max Fresen said Friday. But like the broader mining industry as a whole, they face a labor shortage.
Robertson said the funding announced on Friday would help address that by supporting efforts to train the mining workforce. The funds will be available to schools with accredited mining engineering programs, she said. An earlier phase of the funding announced on Monday went to 16 universities, including Pennsylvania State University and Columbia University in New York City.
Describing the jobs as well-paid and resistant to disruption from artificial intelligence, Robertson called on New England universities to bolster degree offerings in the field.
“We need to innovate, quickly, across the supply chain,” she said, “and then we need to have students who are educated in the way that those companies need, to continue to grow — and we don’t have enough of either.”

name: California
title: Cómo la Proposición 45 podría alterar las luchas en California contra los centros de datos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Los votantes de California que estén considerando la Proposición 45 decidirán el destino de una medida de infraestructura de gran alcance que, según advierten sus opositores, podría dejar prácticamente sin efecto las nuevas leyes estatales sobre centros de datos.
 Eso facilitaría enormemente que los promotores inmobiliarios impongan instalaciones no deseadas en las comunidades locales, lo que podría socavar una creciente ola de prohibiciones, moratorias y resoluciones contra los centros de datos a nivel municipal y de condado.
 Los defensores de los centros de datos insisten en que la medida electoral no les reportará ningún beneficio, incluso cuando algunos beneficiarios de los centros de datos están invirtiendo grandes sumas de dinero para respaldar la Proposición 45.
 Los partidarios de la Proposición 45 la han presentado como una herramienta para acelerar proyectos de infraestructura crítica , como viviendas y escuelas, y la medida no menciona directamente los centros de datos entre los tipos de proyectos que considera críticos. Sin embargo, algunos expertos legales y defensores del medio ambiente afirman que el lenguaje técnico de la proposición crea una laguna legal. Al agilizar las evaluaciones ambientales bajo la Ley de Calidad Ambiental de California para amplias categorías de proyectos —incluidas las instalaciones de internet de banda ancha y cualquier infraestructura adicional necesaria para su funcionamiento—, la medida podría permitir discretamente que los centros de datos eludan las recientes salvaguardias estatales y el escrutinio local.
 Julia Stein, experta en derecho y subdirectora del Instituto Emmett sobre Cambio Climático y Medio Ambiente de la Facultad de Derecho de UCLA, advierte que la medida actúa como un “instrumento de fuerza bruta en lo que respecta a la racionalización” debido a la amplitud de su ámbito de aplicación secundario.
 “Lo que hace la Proposición 45 es designar toda una categoría de proyectos que estarían sujetos a una simplificación, y también establece que los proyectos auxiliares a esos proyectos —es decir, algo que podría ser necesario hacer durante el desarrollo del proyecto que está exento— quedarían incluidos en esa misma simplificación”, dijo Stein.
 Los proyectos de telecomunicaciones se simplifican explícitamente según la propuesta, “y hay argumentos para considerar que el desarrollo de centros de datos podría ser necesario para proyectos de ese tipo”, añadió Stein.
 Otros proyectos, como el tren de alta velocidad, quedan explícitamente excluidos de la simplificación de trámites según la propuesta, pero los centros de datos tampoco figuran en esa lista. Stein y otros tres expertos en derecho ambiental declararon a CalMatters que esto abre la puerta a posibles impugnaciones legales.
 “El hecho de que hayan excluido algunos proyectos, pero no hayan excluido expresamente los centros de datos, probablemente un tribunal lo interpretaría no como un descuido involuntario, sino más bien como una intención de incluir los centros de datos en la iniciativa”, dijo Matt McKerley, abogado de Shute, Mihaly y Weinberger.
 Además, los opositores argumentan que la redacción de la propuesta, que incluye una cláusula que establece que prevalecería sobre otras leyes relacionadas, anularía medidas como el Proyecto de Ley 887 del Senado , aprobado recientemente, que dificultó la tramitación acelerada de la revisión ambiental para los centros de datos.
 Los representantes del sector afirman que estas objeciones a la Proposición 45 son infundadas. La Coalición de Centros de Datos, un grupo industrial que apoya la Proposición 45, insiste en que sus instalaciones quedan fuera del alcance de la iniciativa, que se centra principalmente en el desarrollo de viviendas y otras infraestructuras como carreteras y puentes.
 “La Coalición de Centros de Datos ha revisado la Proposición 45 y ha llegado a la conclusión de que los centros de datos no cumplen los requisitos para la simplificación que contempla la Proposición 45, ni son una entidad cubierta por ninguna parte de la medida”, dijo Khara Boender, Directora de Asuntos Gubernamentales para la Región Oeste de la coalición.
 Los representantes del sector también hacen referencia a un reciente dictamen jurídico de la Oficina de Asesoría Legislativa de California, que presta servicios legales a los miembros de la Legislatura. El dictámenes argumenta que las definiciones legales de la Proposición 45 no se aplican a los centros de datos.
 Amelia Matier, de la campaña “Sí a la Proposición 45”, se hizo eco de esa opinión, afirmando: “Los centros de datos no están incluidos en la Proposición 45”. Añadió: “Los defensores del inasequible statu quo de California están desesperados por distraer a los votantes con mentiras porque no pueden justificar las costosas demoras y la burocracia que elevan los precios para las familias trabajadoras “ .
 Entre los opositores a la medida se encuentran la Federación Laboral de California, el Centro Occidental de Derecho y Pobreza, y varios grupos de defensa del medio ambiente que han gastado más de 31 millones de dólares para oponerse a la medida.
A pesar de sostener que los centros de datos quedan fuera del alcance de la propuesta, los intereses tecnológicos y de servicios públicos que se benefician del auge informático de California están impulsando su aprobación con un enorme apoyo financiero . Los defensores han invertido más de 40 millones de dólares en la campaña a favor de la Proposición 45, incluyendo 3.05 millones de dólares del gigante de servicios públicos PG&E y 500,000 dólares del desarrollador de almacenes y centros de datos Prologis; una inyección de capital que, según los opositores, revela quién espera realmente beneficiarse si la medida se aprueba.
 El debate sobre el impacto de la Proposición 45 en los centros de datos surge en un momento crucial del auge de la infraestructura de IA en California. El gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó recientemente siete leyes históricas sobre centros de datos destinadas a obligar a los operadores a revelar su consumo de agua, financiar sus propias mejoras de la red eléctrica y someterse a una evaluación ambiental.
 Sin embargo, las comunidades locales no esperan a que entren en vigor las regulaciones estatales. Ante el creciente temor a las subidas de tarifas, la sobrecarga de la red eléctrica y el agotamiento del agua, ha surgido una fuerte oposición ciudadana en toda California. Al menos 26 ciudades y condados han propuesto o aprobado moratorias, prohibiciones o límites estrictos destinados a frenar la construcción de centros de datos en sus comunidades.
 Nina Robertson, abogada adjunta de la oficina regional de Earthjustice en California, afirmó que la ambigüedad del texto de la papeleta electoral desencadenaría de inmediato batallas legales sobre la autoridad local para otorgar permisos.
 “¿Y quién va a asumir el coste de ese litigio?”, preguntó Robertson. “Serán los gobiernos locales”.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Watchdog’s report urges Congress to take action on flood insurance
text:
A truck stands in water after Tropical Storm Arthur caused flooding in Avoyelles Parish in June 2026. (Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries)Almost 90% of U.S. properties facing high flood risk don’t have insurance to cover such a catastrophe, according to a government watchdog agency’s latest report. To address the problem, it’s calling upon Congress to confront large structural issues within the insurance industry to try and close the coverage gap.     
Officials from the U.S. Government Accountability Office spoke alongside flood insurance reform groups in a virtual meeting Thursday afternoon to discuss findings from its report, published Oct. 1. Its recommendations to Congress include increasing coverage limits under the National Flood Insurance Program, which the Federal Emergency Management Agency administers. 
NFIP coverage is available to property owners who can’t obtain policies elsewhere, though the increasing frequency of major floods has stretched the program’s capacity to cover damages. Congress has taken a kick-the-can approach in recent years, extending the program several times since 2017 for short stints while failing to come up with a permanent solvency solution. 
The NFIP’s current temporary reauthorization is set to expire Dec. 11, when it’s likely Republicans who are expected to lose control of at least one chamber in next week’s election would have to push through another extension.  
“It soon became clear that many of the program’s challenges were structural and required congressional action to fix,” GAO senior analyst Nathan Gottfried said about the analysis. 
Flood insurance is required by law on properties in zones that FEMA designates as a high flood risk. Mortgages backed through the federal government also must have the coverage, and most private lenders follow the same standard when a property is flood prone.
Louisiana has the highest rate of flood insurance policyholders, with 28% of properties covered where required. Despite this, data show there are still areas widely underinsured compared to their risk.
The GAO report recommends Congress require lenders offering federally backed mortgages to ensure homebuyers obtain a flood insurance quote before they purchase a home. Buyers would also have to sign documents that detail their flood risk. 
The report also suggests increasing NFIP coverage limits and adding a way for the program to adjust them periodically. Damage claim limits for single-family homes are $250,000 for the structure and $100,000 for contents under program policies.
The report also urges Congress to force FEMA to make flood risk information for individual properties available to the public. Gottfried said his office came up with this recommendation after interviews revealed property owners, insurance agents, real estate agents and lenders don’t have easy access to this data. 
“When consumers are more aware of this risk, they are more likely to purchase the coverage,” Gottfried said. 
FEMA sets premium rates for the National Flood Insurance Program, which private insurers often use as a benchmark for determining what they will charge policyholders. Officials in flood-prone regions have pushed for the NFIP to lower premiums, with hopes it would bring overall insurance prices down. 
FEMA’s Risk Rating 2.0 tool, put in place under the Biden administration, doesn’t accurately reflect infrastructure upgrades and other steps taken to reduce flood threats, according to critics who argue the agency isn’t transparent with how it comes up with its numbers.
Louisiana is the lead plaintiff in a lawsuit that then Attorney General Jeff Landry filed against the federal government in 2023 to block Risk Rating 2.0. The Trump administration has defended its use as part of its overall emphasis on shifting the federal government’s burden for disaster recovery onto states. In July, the Department of Justice filed a motion to dismiss the case, which remains active.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Father and son plead guilty to Montana poaching charges
text:
The Montana Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks logo. (Courtesy Montana FWP)A father-and-son duo pled guilty to multiple poaching violations this month according to Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks. 
The department conducted a yearlong investigation after reports of a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery-only season last September. 
Michael Letasky, of Billings, was identified by FWP game wardens and Wheatland County sheriff’s deputies during a traffic stop. 
During the investigation, game wardens discovered that Letasky also shot a raghorn bull elk in 2023 in the same area with a firearm during archery-only season, that Letasky was in possession of an unlawful black bear, and that his son, Kolton, had killed two animals without correct licenses in 2022 and 2024.  
In addition to charges for hunting during as closed season, the elder Letasky was charged with two counts of unlawful possession of a game animal and one count of wasted game animal. The bull elk also met the state’s trophy restitution requirements, an additional $8,000 cost. 
Letasky faces more than $12,000 in fines and will lose hunting privileges for 20 years in Montana and nearby states. 
His son, a Texan, also pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of a game animal and two counts of hunting without a license and faces $3,000 in fines and will lose hunting privileges for four years. 
Montana FWP officials say that reports and witness accounts from members of the public are key in opening up and carrying out poaching investigations. 
“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” said game warden Diego O’Brien, who led the investigation. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation.” 
Anyone with possible information about crimes against wildlife or state lands is asked to call the local game warden, 1-800-TIP-MONT, or visit tipmont.mt.gov to provide details. Those who report information may be eligible for a cash reward of up to $1,000.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Rising costs, protecting democracy: Santa Fe early voters discuss their reasons for casting ballots
text:
New Mexicans line up to vote early at the Greer Garson Theater in Santa Fe on Oct. 30, 2026, one of the early voting locations in Santa Fe County. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Some voters in Santa Fe County cited rising costs and protecting democracy as top issues after casting their ballots during New Mexico’s early voting period. The county’s top election official said that with early voting ending Saturday, the county is on pace to surpass final turnout from the 2022 General Election. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This general election, New Mexicans will elect a new governor for the first time in eight years, as well as vote in contested races for the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. Voters will also weigh in on several races for the state Legislature, along with constitutional amendments and ballot initiatives. 
As of Friday morning, nearly 42,000 absentee and early vote ballots had been cast in Santa Fe County, according to the New Mexico Secretary of State’s office, pushing voter turnout more than halfway toward surpassing its final turnout percentage in the previous general election, the Santa Fe County Clerk’s office said in a news release. 
Outside the Greer Garson Theater, one of the early voting locations in Santa Fe the clerk’s office said had been particularly busy, Liliana Diaz, 20, and her brother Anthony, 19, said rising costs and concern over the Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County brought them to cast their ballots. Liliana, now a student at the University of New Mexico, previously graduated from the New Mexico School of Arts high school in Santa Fe and told Source NM it would be “against her morals” to support Project Jupiter since A.I. is “against the artisticness of Santa Fe.” 
Anthony Diaz told Source NM that the Trump administration made “false promises” after launching the Iran War in February. With gas and grocery prices rising, Diaz, also a student at UNM and a math tutor, told Source NM he has to find ways just to get by.
“I end up donating plasma just so I can have a little money for rent and for groceries,” he told Source NM. Liliana added that her brother “almost passed out” a few days ago after donating plasma when the pair were set to go to a pumpkin patch. 
The siblings said they were most excited to vote in the gubernatorial race between Democrat Deb Haaland and Republican Gregg Hull. Both said they voted for Haaland, citing the candidate’s identity as a Native American woman,  which “would be really beneficial to New Mexico,” Liliana Diaz said.
Anthony Diaz, left, next to his sister Liliana Diaz, right, voted early at the Greer Garson Theater in Santa Fe on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Chloe Brennan brought her daughter to vote early at the Greer Garson Theater in Santa Fe on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Danielle Scott Taylor voted early at the Greer Garson Theater in Santa Fe on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Chloe Brennan and Danielle Scott Taylor, both early voters, also said they were most excited to vote in the gubernatorial race and both also voted for Haaland. For Brennan, who brought her baby daughter in a chest carrier to vote early, the most important issue was “voting rights and maintaining democracy as we know it.” 
Scott Taylor told Source NM that “keeping the momentum” for Democratic leadership in the state was her most important issue. She added that she also voted for U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) in both their races. 
“I voted every election,” Scott Taylor said, but the Trump administration made her “certainly more motivated to keep the leadership that we have and show support.”
One man at Greer Garson Theater said he voted for Republican gubernatorial candidate Gregg Hull, but declined to provide his name.
Registered Democrats make up 58.1% of registered voters in Santa Fe County, followed by 25% independent or Decline to State voters and 15.4% registered Republicans, according to the most recent Secretary of State registration data. 
Ahead of the end of early voting before Tuesday Election Day, Santa Fe County Clerk’s Office encouraged voters in a Thursday news release to use the county’s nine early voting locations, all open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. that day. 
“Make this final Saturday of early voting part of your Halloween plans,” Santa Fe County Clerk Katharine Clark said in a statement. “Check your polling location before you go and remember: earlier is easier.”

Becca Balint, D-Vermont, announce the winners of the Turnip Contest during the Gilfeather Turnip Festival in Wardsboro on Saturday, October 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDiggerTurnip sales are brisk during the Gilfeather Turnip Festival in Wardsboro on Saturday, October 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
WARDSBORO — Every year, Anita Rafael climbs a hill near downtown Wardsboro to place a turnip on John Gilfeather’s grave.
The slope is a short distance from the site of last Saturday’s Gilfeather Turnip Festival, an event featuring a turnip-judging contest, legendary turnip soup and “Turnip Talks” by Rafael herself.
At the festival, children wrapped in fleeces and sweatshirts wandered around, carrying chalkboard signs advertising raffle tickets. Clusters of festivalgoers traipsed up and down the street, showered in bright Vermont sunlight and bundled up against the chill. 
This year, they were blessed with blue skies. But the festival, one of the biggest annual celebrations in Wardsboro, goes on each year regardless of weather complications.
As sunset colors start to spread through Vermont’s foliage, fall festivals turn local traditions into reasons to gather and splurge. Visitors buy specialty foods and crafts, nonprofits raise money for local services, and communities celebrate the features that make them unique. Wardsboro’s Gilfeather Turnip Festival shows how those purposes intertwine.
In Wardsboro, the word “turnip” is synonymous with community.
The story begins with John Gilfeather, Rafael told the guests assembled for one of the “Turnip Talks” by the freelance writer and Wardsboro resident. Gilfeather was an enterprising farmer in Wardsboro in the late 1800s and early 1900s who claimed to have a turnip unique to his farm.
Sweetened by the first frosts of fall, these turnips seemed impervious to the bitter taste that plagued the rest of their species. The special turnips were jealously guarded by Gilfeather. Before selling them, he would cut the roots and tops off each vegetable so no one else could seed the plants.
Still, by the time of Gilfeather’s death, enough seeds had spread across Wardsboro’s community to continue his legacy. For decades, word of the turnip spread only by hearsay, until a Wardsboro couple named William and Mary Lou Schmidt worked with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the University of Vermont and the state to certify the vegetable as an “heirloom variety” and sell it under the name of the Gilfeather turnip. 
The Gilfeather turnip was officially declared the state vegetable in 2016 in an effort championed by Wardsboro schoolchildren.
In the early 2000s, Wardsboro residents realized that their turnip legacy could bring more than pride to their community. It could bring a source of revenue to keep their town library afloat.
Wardsboro isn’t the only town to see the benefits of festivals like these. Rutland is home to two annual Art in the Park festivals, which are the biggest fundraising opportunities to keep Rutland’s Chaffee Art Center going throughout the year.
The two festivals occur in August and October, with the October event dubbed the Art in the Park Fall Foliage Festival. The events attract people from all over the nation and even some international visitors, according to Sherri Birkheimer Rooker, executive director of the center. 
Festivals like these allow rural Vermont communities to connect with people from all over the map, she said.
“They’re beautiful towns, but they’re not, it’s not like New York City or Boston, right?” she said. “So I think the festivals are a way to bring in people, either a repeat because they had such a great time, right, or bring in people who are looking for fun things to do and have never been.”
Festivals are common across Vermont year-round, according to Susan Evans McClure, executive director of the Vermont Arts Council. But foliage season is a powerhouse, according to a 2024 study by the University of Vermont that analyzed the impact of a solar eclipse in April 2024 on Vermont tourism. Even though the eclipse attraction brought in $34.8 million, that amount was equal to less than 10% of Vermont’s visitor spending in the foliage season.
Jay is another town that found a way to capitalize on the beauty of Vermont’s autumn. It hosts the annual Jay Community Recreational Centre Oktoberfest, where proceeds go toward trail maintenance and development projects in the community. The event is very kid friendly, according to Sally Rivard, one of the coordinators. It includes pumpkin launching, alpaca petting, a haunted gingerbread house contest and the annual Pumpkin Pi(e) Run/Walk, so named because the race is exactly 3.14 kilometers.
“Oktoberfest brings people to town, they visit the local businesses and celebrate autumn beauty all while helping us raise funds for our trail maintenance and development projects,’’ Rivard wrote in a text to VTDigger. “Community supporting community.”
Wardsboro’s turnip festival has also brought in crucial funding for its host town. Revenue peaked before Covid-19 hit, Rafael said, after gradually growing for around two decades. It was bringing in upwards of $10,000, she estimated, and funding a massive portion of the library’s operations. But the festival’s momentum stalled during the pandemic, and now the town is working to bring it back.
Organizers have had successes through enlisting the Boy Scouts and the Wardsboro School Club, which receive portions of the funds as well, she added.
At this year’s festival, crowds gathered and vendors sold everything from gourmet salsa to silver jewelry spread out on black velvet displays. One tent sold homemade turnip hats with knitted leaves sprouting where a pompom would normally sit. 
Central to the event was the soup stand, where volunteers filled cups for a revolving line of customers. An old-fashioned cart with wooden wheels stood just a stone’s throw away, full to the brim with turnips for sale.
One trio — Jim and Leona Kee, from New Hampshire, and Mickey Goldman, from New York — stood near the town hall steps, scraping the sides of their soup cups to retrieve the creamy liquid. The turnip festival had been on Leona Kee’s bucket list for about a year, she said, after she fell in love with the Gilfeather turnip soup sold at Dutton’s in Brattleboro.
When a festival starts to appeal to out-of-town visitors, Evans McClure said, the economic payoffs get higher. Vermont participated in a national study in 2023 that found that while cultural event attendees in Vermont spent $34.53 per person on average, apart from admission fees, nonlocal guests spent an average of $51.69 per person.
“If you’re from out of the region, you stay at a hotel, you go out to lunch. You pay for parking,” Evans McClure said. “Maybe if it’s an evening event, you pay for a babysitter. There’s all of these associated expenditures.”
Later in the day, festivalgoers trooped to the town hall’s upstairs room for the much-anticipated turnip-judging contest. 
The vegetables competed in various categories, from the heaviest to the most creatively dressed. Rafael’s entry was swaddled in a blanket and placed in a bassinet like a baby.
Another costume sent a woman speeding down the town hall steps, shouting that someone had dressed up a turnip as Dolly Parton.
“As they should,” chuckled a woman seated on the porch.
Typically the festival ends with costumed turnips left behind, Rafael said, which organizers collect and donate to the local food pantry. But she has other plans for her turnip. She will take the vegetable out of its bassinet and carry it up to Gilfeather’s grave to leave her yearly tribute to his memory.

title: Trump continues rally spree in attempt to blunt Dem momentum in midterms lead-up
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump is rounding out his midterm travel blitz in the final sprint leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3. With just four days to go, the Republican Party is aiming to keep its narrow majority in the U.S. House and control of the Senate. But elections forecasters see a bleak outlook for the GOP, saying Democrats remain heavily favored to win the U.S. House, while Senate races continue to move in Democrats’ direction. Heading into Election Day, Trump faces anemic approval ratings amid the war in Iran and its impact on gas and diesel prices. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter on Friday shifted a dozen House races in Democrats’ favor.The elections forecaster has identified 18 toss-up races in congressional districts in California, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan, Montana, North Carolina, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia.  Republicans are defending all but four of those seats. The forecaster on Friday also moved Senate races in Florida and Nebraska away from Republicans and in the direction of Florida Democrat Angie Nixon and Nebraska independent Dan Osborn.  The Cook Political Report has declared seven toss-up Senate races in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.Pope among record early votersAs early voting continues across the country, total figures have eclipsed early voting totals in the 2022 midterms, according to data from the University of Florida Election Lab.As of Friday afternoon, more than 48.5 million people had cast a vote — whether in person at the polls or by mailing in their ballot — per the UF Election Lab. In the 2022 midterm elections, 45.9 million Americans voted early, the UF Election Lab found. Standing among American voters is Pope Leo XIV, who cast his ballot in the midterm elections, the Vatican announced Friday. This makes Leo the first pope to vote in a U.S. election. Leo — a U.S. citizen who grew up in Illinois — submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, according to the Vatican.    Home-state ralliesAs Trump’s midterm travel that began in early October hits its final stops, the president was slated to rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. The Sunshine State, where the president is a registered voter, features a Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Ashley Moody and progressive Nixon, a Florida state legislator.  The Cook Political Report moved the race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” on Friday.Vice President JD Vance is scheduled to rally in Swanton, Ohio, on Monday. The Buckeye State features a toss-up Senate race, according to the Cook Political Report, between Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance’s seat when he became vice president, and Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.Kansas, Iowa on scheduleTrump’s two previously canceled Midwestern rallies this weekend are back on. The president will hold back-to-back rallies Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, and  Salina, Kansas, while also holding nearly 20 telerallies in the last few days before the election. Iowa and Kansas are home to two Senate races the Cook Political Report has identified as toss-ups. Kansas GOP U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall is in a tight race against Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton. That race is now the most expensive election in Kansas history, according to Kansas Reflector. In Iowa, Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson is vying with Democratic state legislator Josh Turek to fill an open Senate seat.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Attorneys worry for asylum-seeking kids at last-minute hearing in Kansas City immigration court
text:
Immigration attorney Madelyn Cox-Guerra makes notes before an Oct. 29, 2026, hearing at Kansas City Immigration Court. She and other attorneys were concerned about rapid changes in hearing status that brought unaccompanied minors to court unexpectedly. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)KANSAS CITY, Mo. — A young boy with autism played with brightly colored sensory toys Thursday morning in the Kansas City Immigration Court, his wide grin standing out in a room full of grim expressions. 
The boy sat shoulder-to-shoulder with attorneys and other unaccompanied minors called unexpectedly into court by a Chicago judge with little time to understand what was happening. 
Attorney Kirby Tyrrell, an associate professor at Washburn Law School who represents clients pro bono, sat with the 13-year-old boy she represents, apprehensive about what the hearing might mean. 
“We were in court a few weeks ago, and everything went normal, and we were scheduled out for an appearance in March,” she said before the hearing. “Then last Thursday, I received a notice that the case had suddenly been transferred to an immigration judge based out of Chicago, and that we had a new hearing a week later.”
Tyrrell spoke to other immigration attorneys in the area and found out others had received the same notice, fast-tracking client dates to appear. The departure from typical processes concerned the attorneys and their young clients.
Immigration attorney Aly Englander, with Asylum Clinic Kansas City, said there has been an “indisputable” targeted effort to increase child deportations recently across the country. 
“The reason, in my opinion, is children are easier to deport,” she said. “They need to keep up their numbers.”
Englander referred to quotas set on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents regarding how many immigrants must be arrested. CNN reported earlier this month that the ICE quota for daily arrests had ramped up to 9,000. 
“These kids need time to access the benefits that Congress established for them,” Englander said.
A lawsuit filed Oct. 15 challenges the Trump administration on denying due process to unaccompanied minors. 
“A coalition of immigration advocates and legal aid providers say the administration has ignored federal law to create a ‘deportation assembly line’ for unaccompanied children and undocumented minors,” The Appeal reported. 
 
Chicago Judge
Their apprehension turned out to be unnecessary in the short term, as Chicago Judge Shawn Abraham mostly delayed the morning’s cases for another hearing in two weeks. He apologized to the attorneys several times throughout the proceeding that he couldn’t sign any orders or access the Kansas City docket to look at the files. 
Abraham, a former ICE attorney, was appointed as an immigration judge and began hearing cases in May, according to the Executive Office for Immigration Review.  
The unexpected reassignment of cases to Abraham’s docket led Englander to search online for more information. She found numerous articles about Abraham deporting six children who had pending immigration cases in Chicago, adding to her concerns that the Thursday hearing might end or delay her clients’ hopes to stay in the United States.
Tyrrell, Englander and other attorneys were worried ICE agents might be waiting for their clients outside the courtroom, as they can’t arrest immigrants at their court hearings. 
One young girl in a bright red sweater had been told she might be deported and came prepared to leave her family, Englander said. 
“It has been nonstop chaos,” she said. “Kids’ hearings have been advanced and then canceled and then advanced again.”
It makes it difficult for attorneys to prepare cases and represent them “in the way they deserve,” Englander said. 
“The emotional roller coaster that this puts them on is so unfair, especially when we don’t know why these specific kids were just pulled out of the Kansas City docket and put with this judge in Chicago,” she added. 
The uncertainty in the system is frustrating and adds to the trauma of children who are in the country through no fault of their own, she said after the hearing. Englander’s been working in the immigration system for five years, and many of the processes once considered “normal” have been changed. 
Englander represented five cases Thursday, including two girls she told the judge were “despondent” and scheduled for their asylum interviews, which would be “very, very difficult” because of the traumas they had to relive to make their case for asylum. 
She asked if they could appear next time virtually, as it was less stressful for them. Abraham agreed, as he did for most cases. Englander said they were told they had to be in court in person on Thursday, so she was relieved the judge was allowing virtual interviews in two weeks.  
 
The process
Unaccompanied minors can apply to stay in the United States through the Special Immigrant Juvenile Status program, and most of the children at the Thursday hearing have pending applications. 
“Congress created Special Immigrant Juvenile Status for the purpose of these kids who have been abused, abandoned, and neglected getting a green card,” Englander said. “In the past, judges have understood that and given them the time that they need to be able to apply for this green card that they are entitled to.”
In April, the Trump administration rescinded the policy that let judges defer children for deportation based on pending applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status.
The problem is that the United States approves only a certain number of green cards, so there’s a wait list for approval for those cards, Englander said. With deferred status off the table, the children are approved for the program but not able to actually get their green cards. That means they can be deported, she said. 
If the child is deported and not in the United States when the opportunity comes for them to get their green card — which is determined by a priority date that holds their place in line — then they no longer qualify for the green card, Englander said. 
Madelyn Cox-Guerra, attorney at Asylum Project Kansas City, said the child she represented Thursday was just a single judicial decision away from getting his green card. 
He needed the judge to terminate deportation proceedings because he has appropriately completed everything regarding the case and his place in line is ready for him to apply for a green card, she said. That can’t happen until the judge terminates the case, Cox-Guerra said. 
But Abraham continued the case for another two weeks. 
“I could apply for my client as soon as today, just getting all the documents ready,” she said. “And we’re not able to move forward until our hearing in November, and we could only hope that it’s going to get terminated, and we’ll have enough time (to apply for the green card).”
Englander wasn’t surprised. 
“There’s a lot of pressure from the top down to not give kids more time, not to terminate cases, not to administratively close cases,” Englander said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: As WA open enrollment begins, far fewer than expected have lost coverage
text:
U.S. Sen. Patty Murray hosts a roundtable on rising health insurance costs alongside Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer, center-right, small business owners and a local physician on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Starting Sunday, Washingtonians who need to buy health insurance through the state’s online marketplace can enroll in or change their plans, but they face another major cost increase to maintain coverage.
About 260,000 people are currently enrolled through the Washington Health Benefit Exchange. That number is far higher than state officials had expected amid rate hikes and the loss of some federal financial aid. 
State leaders originally feared 80,000 people could lose or drop their coverage after Republicans in Congress declined to extend federal subsidies despite a push from Democrats. The debate led to a lengthy federal government shutdown last year. The subsidies helped save enrollees, most of whom qualified for them, an average of more than $1,000 annually on premiums. 
Every state, except New Mexico, saw a drop in enrollment this year, according to an analysis by nonpartisan health research firm KFF.
At the end of September 2025, roughly 275,000 residents were enrolled through the individual market, with a drop of only about 15,000 a year later. That decrease is also far from what was seen earlier this year when 36,500 fewer enrollees were covered. More people, worn down with months of higher premiums, were expected to drop their coverage, but it went the other direction. People can enroll during the year if they have a qualifying life event, like changing jobs. 
State Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer attributed the better-than-expected news to an emergency rule out of her office to maximize other premium tax credits. Washington was one of the few states to take this step, she said. The state’s own premium assistance, known as Cascade Care Savings, also helped avert some of the more dire fears of the drops in coverage.
Residents who still get their health plans through the Affordable Care Act exchange face an average 22.2% increase in rates starting Jan. 1, as the cost of care increases and people need more robust care. Rates went up 21% this year. 
“People are once again making difficult decisions about whether to stay insured, and we know that the people who keep coverage despite the rising costs are the ones that need the coverage the most,” Kuderer said in a Thursday roundtable in Seattle with U.S. Sen. Patty Murray.
The state exchange is meant for people not covered through their work or government programs like Medicaid or Medicare, like those who are self-employed, work seasonally or retire early. It launched in 2013 under the Affordable Care Act. Meanwhile, upward of 200,000 residents could lose their Medicaid coverage due to new federal work requirements taking effect in January, officials expect.
Small businesses with fewer than 50 employees also use the exchange for their workers. Those insurance rates are rising by 16.7%. The increases are in line with national trends.
Since opening in June 2025, premiums for workers at PureGreen, a juice bar in Seattle, have gone up about 20%, said owner Alicia Anderson Pieri.
“That impacts obviously both me and my bottom line as a business owner, but it impacts all of my employees,” Anderson Pieri said. “It means that they have to work about an extra hour every two weeks in order to cover that premium increase.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
For coverage to start Jan. 1, residents have to enroll by Dec. 31. Applying by Jan. 15 means a plan would start Feb. 1.
If Democrats retake Congress in Tuesday’s midterms, healthcare policy is a top priority, with reinstating the expired subsidies high on the to-do list, though legislation would still be subject to President Donald Trump’s signature.
“It’s very clear to me that we have got to reinstate the ACA tax credits,” Murray said.

title: Community nurse programs are getting a lot of airtime this election. Here’s how they work.
text:
Hartford Community Nurse Katie Williams talks with Joan Ponzoni in Jan. 2025, at the Bugbee Senior Center in White River Junction. File photo by Jennifer Hauck/Valley News

Jodi Hoyt’s office is a nurse’s bag and an accordion file folder in a rainbow of colors.
She totes those items from house to house while checking on patients in her role as the community nurse for the towns of Chelsea and Tunbridge. 
It’s a role that’s gotten a fair amount of airtime recently as the Democratic/Progressive candidate for governor, Amanda Janoo, touts the virtue of community nurses and cites their work as a model for the type of publicly funded primary care she hopes to bring to Vermont.
In Vermont Public’s Oct. 21 debate, where Janoo and Republican Gov. Phil Scott pitched their competing visions for healthcare reform, Janoo specifically cited Hoyt’s job.
“In Tunbridge, for example,” Janoo said, “their community nurse is just a municipal employee, and that ensures that everybody has some sort of local healthcare. And I love that model, right?” she said. 
The shoutout came as a surprise. “Oh, I had no idea!” Hoyt said the next morning, smiling as she read a text from a friend letting her know about it.
Mostly she keeps her head down and focuses on the work. “I help everyone,” she said. “I’m trying to reach the demographic that doesn’t see a doctor regularly, whether that’s college students or the elderly, for whatever it may be.”
Hoyt said she started the program in Tunbridge in 2022 after refining her pitch to the town more than once. She’s since grown it to 12 hours a week, from the original five to eight hours. A year ago she expanded to Chelsea, where she grew up, and now works 10 hours a week there as well. 
Spending a college semester in Botswana first exposed Hoyt, then a young nursing student, to the idea of community nurses — a caretaker who is deeply embedded in the community. She loved the concept, which has now become her reality, that a nurse might be flagged down at the market or a soccer match to look at someone’s rash or address a concern about an elderly neighbor.
Coincidentally, the idea was already taking root around the same time in Vermont’s Upper Valley, where Hoyt grew up. Community Nurse Connection began as a project in 2010. The nonprofit network has evolved to now include 12 community nurse programs in Vermont and five in New Hampshire. 
Each community approaches the role a bit differently, said Kristin Barnum, the executive director of Community Nurse Connection. Some towns, such as Tunbridge, fund the position as a municipal employee, while others create a nonprofit fund. What’s important, Barnum said, is that the nurses’ services are free to patients and not billed to Medicare or any other insurer. 
“A lot of people will say to me, ‘Well, you know, this is such a great idea. Don’t you think it should be billable?’ and my quick answer is no,” Barnum said.
The salary model gives the community flexibility to administer care broadly. A nurse might sit and talk with a patient for half an hour about nutrition or help them sign up for food assistance. The nurse can develop a care plan according to the patient’s own goals, rather than seeing them for a set number of visits in a set number of weeks to meet goals defined by a doctor or insurer.
It also means that anyone can refer a patient to a community nurse, whether that’s another healthcare professional discharging a patient from the hospital, a person worried about their aging parent or someone recognizing a need for help themselves. 
But the funding model also limits the amount of direct care the nurses can give. Because they are not under any physician’s orders, community nurses cannot perform hands-on care the way a home health nurse billing Medicare would.
Katie Williams, Hartford’s community nurse, calls her approach “slow medicine.” 
The ability to tailor the care to patients’ needs over time enables relationships to build, “which allows for trust, which allows for really understanding the patient’s complexity,” Williams said. “What I like to say is (we get) the ecology of their whole health picture.”
On average, Williams spends an hour per visit with each of her patients, who normally number about 45. She supplements that work with daylong drop-in clinics at Hartford’s senior center. 
The town is able to connect with Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center to see patients’ records and medication lists and help coordinate ahead of medical appointments, Williams said.
“I like to say that the community nurse role is this hybrid between social care and personal health. The line between those two is so thin and perhaps even invisible,” she said. 
Hoyt sees her role as more directly clinical than a social worker’s. 
“I’m always evaluating. I can’t turn it off,” she said of her tendency to be attuned to symptoms no matter the context.  
Hoyt cites an example. While addressing the patient’s mobility issues in a home visit, Hoyt noticed that the woman’s husband had what looked like a large melanoma on his chest where his shirt was unbuttoned. When Hoyt asked about it, he brushed it off, she said. But with some persuading and his eventual permission, Hoyt sent a picture to a dermatologist friend, who confirmed Hoyt’s concern. He needs to get that removed as soon as possible, Hoyt remembers the friend saying. 
But the husband didn’t have a doctor to make the needed referral. So Hoyt helped him fill out the paperwork to establish a relationship with a primary care provider. The couple had no internet at their house, so when it was time for the husband’s virtual care visit, Hoyt set up her phone for him to take the call. She walked him through each step to eventually get the melanoma removed.
“I don’t think anyone else would have caught it,” she said. It was only because she was in the home and able to shift her responsibilities beyond the one patient that she was able to help, she said.
Catching cancers early can avert much more costly care later. Reducing the need for hospital care and 911 calls is one of the community nurse program’s biggest selling points.
“Many of these clients, especially if they live alone, if they fall, they call 911, even if there’s no physical injuries,” Barnum said. Medicare doesn’t reimburse emergency medical services if they do not take a patient to the hospital, so often the patient goes to the emergency room. Barnum said community nurses have averted those kinds of calls by removing fall risks — such as installing handrails or ramps. 
In Hartford, Williams’ job is housed within the fire department. The department connects her with residents who have had multiple nonreimbursed falls — usually people who are not taken to the hospital. The department also turns to Williams when staff respond to a call and see red flags in the home, such as a lack of heat or signs of dementia. 
Older patients sometimes call 911 because they’re lonely and scared, Barnum added. But knowing a visit with the nurse is on the calendar can lower their anxiety and avert calls. 
In Tunbridge, Town Clerk Bonnie McCrillis sees Hoyt’s role as invaluable. 
“To be honest with you, just here in Tunbridge, Jodi could be kept busy eight hours, 10 hours a day, six, seven days a week,” McCrillis said. “If she could clone herself three times, I think she would have a good start on being able to service the people like she would like to.”
Community Nurse Connection tracks outcomes across its programs each year and has found that the biggest impacts are in reducing falls, helping elderly people continue living independently at home and alleviating anxiety and isolation. 
Outcome metrics are not why Hoyt is in the game, though. 
“Most of the time, it’s not that life-saving,” she said of the care she provides. “I don’t think people realize the small things, all the little things are also life changing.” 
The work clearly invigorates Hoyt, who radiates spunky energy in her pink scrubs. She said she feels like she’s only just getting started. 
“I would like to see a community nurse in every town,” she said. “I want to keep my program successful, and I want to keep going.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: 2 Walgreens stores fined for negligence related to temporary closures
text:
Walgreens, 3245 Agency St., Burlington, Iowa.  (Photo via Google Earth)Two Walgreens pharmacies in Iowa have been sanctioned by the state for negligence with regard to temporary closures and customer service.
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy recently charged a Walgreens store in Burlington and a Walgreens store in Fort Madison with negligence in the practice of the profession and failure to engage in the business for which they are licensed.
With regard to the Burlington store, the board alleges the pharmacy temporarily closed on Oct. 23, 2025, due to a shortage of pharmacists needed to staff the business. The store allegedly steered all customers’ prescriptions to a Walgreens store in Fort Madison but failed to communicate that information to the public, the store’s customers or even the Walgreens staff.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the board, as late as Dec. 10, 2025, the Burlington store’s website indicated the store’s pharmacy was open for business although phone calls to the pharmacy at that time were answered with a message indicating it was closed. That message included no information as to where customers could have their prescriptions filled, the board alleges.
“No notice was given to anyone,” the board alleges, adding that this not only inconvenienced customers but also caused delays in customers receiving their medications.
Because some of the prescriptions had already been filled at, but not yet dispensed from, the Burlington store, customers who went to other pharmacies to obtain their medication were still unable to get their prescriptions filled, the board alleges.
According to the board, the exact same set of difficulties occurred when the Walgreens pharmacy in Fort Madison temporarily closed on Nov. 7, 2025, due to a purported lack of staff.
Each of the stores was fined $1,000 by the board and ordered to develop new policies that will supplement the existing policies the two stores allegedly ignored in 2025.
The publicly available board records identify the precise location of the two stores only by Walgreens’ internal store-numbering system. The company’s online records suggest the two stores are located at 2639 Avenue L in Fort Madison and 3245 Agency St. in Burlington.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Texas congresswoman campaigns to help SC Democrats, says she’s ‘not one of those’ 2028 contenders
text:
U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas rallies in the McGirt Auditorium at Emmett Scott Recreation Center in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)ROCK HILL — U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett distanced herself Thursday from other Democrats crisscrossing South Carolina ahead of the midterms as they test the waters for a potential 2028 presidential bid.
The Texas congresswoman rallied with state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, the Democratic nominee for governor, hours after President Donald Trump rallied less than 2 miles away in support of Republicans on the ballot.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

Potential White House hopefuls are already flocking to South Carolina, which will hold Democrats’ first-in-the-nation presidential nominating contest in 2028.
All have dismissed questions about 2028 and insist they’re here to help Democrats flip seats in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to statewide office in 20 years.
But Crockett, who’s gotten national attention for her fiery style, indicated everyone at the rally knew otherwise — even while saying she’s not in that group.
“Y’all already know all the eyes are going to be on you come 2028. You already know that part. That’s why y’all had a lot of visitors? I’m not one of those visitors. Y’all know which ones I’m talking about. Y’all know which ones. Don’t make me say the names,” Crockett said to laughter from a crowd of roughly a thousand people inside McGirt Auditorium.

Democratic governor candidate Jermaine Johnson rallies in the McGirt Auditorium at Emmett Scott Recreation Center in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

Crockett said South Carolina Democrats need to prove to the hopefuls they should be here not just to introduce themselves to January 2028 voters who can propel them to a nomination but that it’s possible to win South Carolina’s electoral votes too.
The last Democrat to do that was Jimmy Carter from neighboring Georgia in 1976.
“I want them to look and be running to South Carolina because they see not only an opportunity in the primary, but they know that South Carolina can do it again for them in the general,” she said to applause.
“What does this mean for you? It means that you are going to have to talk to any and everybody,” she continued. “I need you to call your exes and be like, you don’t like them like that. But the congresswoman said, I need to call him and tell you to do what you need to do.”
Crockett, first elected to the U.S. House in 2022, lost her primary bid for U.S. Senate earlier this year to Texas state Rep. James Talarico.
Potential contenders who have campaigned in South Carolina recently alongside Johnson include Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former White House adviser Rahm Emanuel, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, California Rep. Ro Khanna, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And on Tuesday evening, Vice President Kamala Harris joined Johnson for a virtual fundraiser.
Asked why she was in South Carolina on Thursday, Crockett told reporters the visit was about instilling hope in South Carolina Democrats.
“I need people to know that it’s possible, and I think that when you have somebody like me travel all the way from Texas, they say, ‘Well, at least she believes it’s possible.’ Even if it’s not, she believes it. A lot of this is about believing,” Crockett said.
Earlier Thursday, she was with Johnson for a “fireside chat” at Benedict College, a private historically Black college in Columbia. On Friday, she campaigned in Charlotte, North Carolina, to help Democrats in the presidential swing state, including a stop of Johnson C. Smith University, also a private HBCU.
Johnson and fellow Democratic nominees in South Carolina face an uphill battle in normally reliably Republican state.
While polls in the U.S. Senate race between three-month incumbent GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews indicate a close finish — within the margin of error — that’s not the case for other statewide offices.
SC Democrats rally with Georgia US senator ahead of early voting

Johnson believes he can prove those polls wrong.
“I don’t have to bring the momentum. The people are already fired up … people are ready,” he told the SC Daily Gazette ahead of the Rock Hill event. “I’m going to continue to go in here and talk about this new South Carolina, let people know that it’s time for a new South Carolina.”
He faces Republican Alan Wilson, the state’s attorney general since 2010, who spoke at Trump’s rally in Rock Hill hours earlier.
Wilson’s two-week bus tour around the state concludes Monday. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp joined him Friday for stops in Lexington and Aiken counties, after making his official endorsement.
“There’s no question that a Gov, Alan Wilson will mean more money in the pockets of the people of South Carolina and a brighter future for all who call the Palmetto State home,” Kemp said in a statement.
Early voting runs through Saturday. Election Day is on Tuesday.
