name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Civil Rights Act hasn’t sparked more lawsuits, police resignations, early study finds
text:
University of California, Los Angeles School of Law Professor Joanna Schwartz, left, and New Mexico Association of Counties Risk Management Director Grace Philips, right, speak to the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Oct. 29, 2026, about the impacts of the New Mexico Civil Rights Act. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)In the years since New Mexico adopted its own Civil Rights Act, the state has not seen a significant uptick in lawsuit settlement payments or police officer resignations, according to a new study presented to state lawmakers Thursday.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed the New Mexico Civil Rights Act, which lets residents allege that their civil rights under the state Constitution have been violated, into law in 2021. It also made New Mexico just the second state in the nation, behind Colorado, to eliminate qualified immunity — which completely shields public officials such as police officers from lawsuits — as a defense.
In the years since the law’s enactment, advocates for local government bodies and law enforcement agencies have argued it would lead to costly settlement payouts and difficulties in recruiting and retaining police officers. The new study presented at Thursday’s interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee, however, found that hasn’t been the case in the law’s first years.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The study, titled “Watching the Sky Not Fall: A Quantitative Study of the Impact of the NMCRA,” used public records requests to analyze law enforcement agency data from 2017 to 2023 in the two states that abolished qualified immunity — New Mexico and Colorado — and in two states that didn’t — Washington and Utah.
Joanna Schwartz, a University of California, Los Angeles School of Law professor who co-authored the study and presented it to state lawmakers, provided a disclaimer with her presentation: Some of New Mexico’s law enforcement agencies didn’t fulfill her records request, limiting her research team’s ability to fully analyze the law’s impact.
“The evolution of litigation under the Civil Rights Act will take years and will develop as lawyers write and defend cases and judges issue rulings,” Schwartz said, adding that researchers need more data before they can make “definitive conclusions” about the full impact of the law.
The data she did obtain, though, showed that New Mexico and Colorado did not see a significant increase in the number of lawsuits filed against law enforcement agencies. It also showed no marked increase in lawsuit payouts or in police officer resignations and retirements. Resignations and retirements peaked in all four surveyed states in 2021, which Schwartz said was likely due to the national protests and sentiment regarding law enforcement agencies in the aftermath of George Floyd’s murder.
Across all four surveyed states, the cost of insurance rates increased from 2017 to 2023 — with no indication that increases in New Mexico and Colorado were related to the civil rights laws.
Despite the preliminary findings, officials with the New Mexico Association of Counties speaking alongside Schwartz told lawmakers they want to see the civil rights law amended in the upcoming legislative session, which begins in January.
Grace Philips, the New Mexico Association of Counties’ risk management director, told lawmakers she thinks the law needs three amendments to cap how much money can be awarded in these cases; eliminate the practice of plaintiffs’ attorneys recovering money under both the New Mexico Civil Rights Act and other laws in the same case; and require that plaintiffs give government bodies advance notice when they intend to file a lawsuit under the law.
Philips said that limiting the amount of money that can be awarded in these cases will help insurance pools that government entities rely on to stay solvent. The New Mexico Civil Rights Act initially capped claims at $2 million, but a provision in the law says that the cap will increase annually based on cost-of-living metrics.
“Frankly, we’re terrified about the solvency piece,” Philips said, asking lawmakers to go back to the $2 million limit.
State Rep. Marianna Anaya (D-Albuquerque) asked Philips how many settlements under the state civil rights law have hit the maximum payout. Philips said she didn’t have the figure readily available.
Anaya told Philips that civil rights cases brought in federal court under the U.S. Constitution do not have a cap on damages.
“I believe it would be an incentive for us to just keep going with what we have, which seems like a good thing, comparatively,” she said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: District judge upholds convictions against notary for Nebraska medical cannabis petitions
text:
Hall County Attorney Marty Klein, standing, speaks to the jury during the first day of trial before Hall County Judge Alfred Corey, center, against a former notary public, Jacy Todd of York, at left, who is connected to two 2024 statewide medical cannabis ballot measures in Grand Island on Feb. 23, 2026. (Courtesy of Kasey Mintz-Pool/KSNB Local 4)GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — A Hall County District Court judge on Friday upheld 24 convictions and a nearly $4,000 fine against a former Nebraska notary for 2024 petitions to legalize and regulate medical cannabis.
Hall County District Judge Andrew Butler found that Hall County Judge Alfred Corey III, who presided over a three-day February trial, did not err in refusing to issue a directed verdict (a judge stepping in where the evidence is so clear that no reasonable jury could find otherwise) or grant a mistrial because of prosecutorial statements made in opening arguments.
Butler said that the evidence was sufficient for the jury to be able to consider the facts of the case and that Corey addressed the defense’s concerns about statements in opening arguments about knowledge to commit wrongdoing, including that attorneys’ statements are not evidence.
“The court finds that the Hall County Court did not err in denying the defendant/appellant’s motion for directed verdict and did not abuse its discretion in denying the defendant/appellant’s motion for mistrial,” Butler said in his 14-page order Friday.
Hall County District Judge Andrew C. Butler. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)
Butler is the same judge who overruled an initial November 2024 order from Corey to throw out the charges against Jacy Todd of York, a former notary. Todd would go on to run in the GOP primary for governor against Gov. Jim Pillen this spring.
Corey had said notaries were not “public servants,” a necessary element of “official misconduct.”
Much of Friday’s order affirms what Butler decided in April 2025: Notaries are public servants and can face criminal charges. That’s a continued point of contention in Todd’s appeal. His attorney, Mark Porto, has long maintained Todd is the first notary to be convicted in this way.
“A notary public is an officer, and that status supports the conclusion that a notary public may qualify as a public servant under the applicable statutory framework,” Butler wrote Friday.
Porto had pointed to an entire chapter of state law, Chapter 64, dedicated to notaries as a reason why notaries can face civil penalties, but not criminal ones. Butler and prosecutors disagreed.
“The court finds no language establishing that civil penalties are the exclusive remedies available or that criminal penalties are categorically precluded,” Butler wrote. “Nor does the court find language providing that Chapter 64 constitutes the exclusive statutory framework governing all misconduct by a notary public.”
Hall County Judge Alfred Corey presides over the first day of a criminal trial against a former notary connected to two statewide medical cannabis ballot measures in 2024 in Grand Island on Feb. 23, 2026. (Courtesy of Kasey Mintz-Pool/KSNB Local 4)
Porto did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Butler’s order or next steps. He could appeal to the Nebraska Court of Appeals.
A six-panel jury in February convicted Todd on all charges filed by the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office and Hall County Attorney Marty Klein in October 2024. Prosecutors said Michael K. Egbert, a paid Grand Island petition circulator, never appeared before Todd to notarize his petitions to legalize and regulate medical cannabis — a verification step required by law.
The jury found Todd guilty of 23 counts of official misconduct for improper notarizations (each a Class II misdemeanor) and one count of making a false statement under oath (a Class I misdemeanor). Corey assessed Todd a fine of $3,866.44, including court costs, but no jail time. 
Todd is required to pay the costs by April 17, 2027.
Jacy Todd, a GOP candidate for Nebraska governor, speaks to reporters at the Nebraska State Capitol Rotunda in Lincoln on Monday, March 2, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Despite allowing the charges to continue, Butler, in his April 2025 order, had also questioned the extent of resources being used to pursue such charges, and the number of them, “when looking at the current climate of the state and voice of its residents.”
Nearly 71% of voters voted to legalize medical cannabis, and about 67% approved regulating it.
“However, those decisions are left to another entity,” Butler wrote in his April 2025 order. “The court simply is tasked with applying the laws as written and, in this matter, the motion to quash should have been denied and the matter considered by a finder(s) of fact.”
Even without Todd’s valid signatures, the 2024 Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana campaign gathered enough signatures to have still qualified for the 2024 ballot. The Nebraska Supreme Court unanimously ruled against a separate challenge from the AG’s Office and a longtime marijuana opponent in September, upholding the validity of the voter-approved laws.
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission has continued to work toward regulations. The next commission meeting is Nov. 16.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Democrats have long hopes, and odds, in bid to oust Jeff Van Drew
text:
Democrats hope this is the year they oust Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R), but district lines and campaign spending heavily favor Van Drew. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]Democrats are hoping a voter enthusiasm gap in their favor will help them reclaim GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew’s seat in the 2nd Congressional District, but redrawn lines and the Republican’s entrenched brand make their path to victory steeper than the one Van Drew walked eight years ago.
In the 2nd District, a sprawling one that spans coastal communities in counties like Ocean and Cape May and inland ones in counties like Gloucester, Van Drew faces a challenge from Cape May City Mayor Zack Mullock, who hopes he can flip a seat Democrats have held for just about 12 months in the last three decades.
Michael Suleiman, a former Atlantic County Democratic chairman who is now seeking a South Jersey state Senate seat, said he is optimistic because of the early voting numbers coming out of Van Drew’s district.
“I still think there is a path to victory for Zack, and I’m hopeful for that,” Suleiman said.
New Jersey’s 12 House seats are on the ballot on Nov. 3, as is Sen. Cory Booker (D). As Democrats nationwide aim to reclaim control of Congress in a bid to serve as a check on the Trump administration, the party here thinks it could oust Van Drew as well as Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in the 7th District. The GOP controls three of the state’s House seats.
The Cook Political Report on Friday shifted its rating of the 2nd District from safe Republican to likely Republican.
Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock (D) is challenging Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) next week. (Photo courtesy of Mullock campaign)
Democrats have built commanding leads in preelection voting statewide, and as of Friday morning, more than twice as many Democrats had voted compared to Republicans. But the disparity in the 2nd District wasn’t quite so broad.
There, Republican preelection turnout was equal to about two-thirds of Democrats’ total, a gap of just over 14,000 votes, according to a New Jersey Monitor analysis.
That gap remains narrow enough that Republican leaders in the district are confident Van Drew will win a fifth term in the House next week, even if his margin of victory ends up being slimmer than in past years.
Cape May County GOP chair Mike Donohue said he doesn’t see a chance for Democrats to win.
“It would have to be a dramatic Republican sort of collapse across the district,” he said.
Democrats have won the 2nd District only once since Rep. William J. Hughes (D) forewent reelection in 1994. That was in 2018, and Van Drew was the Democrat who won it.
Then a right-of-center Democrat sitting in the state Senate, Van Drew was carried into Congress by the same Democratic wave that swept Mikie Sherrill and Andy Kim, among others, into the House. But he remained a Democrat for only a year after.
In early 2020, Van Drew swapped his party affiliation, a defection he marketed as an embrace of President Donald Trump and a repudiation of a party they said was too far gone.
When Van Drew, who had sat in the Statehouse as a Democrat for 18 years, sought reelection in 2020, he prevailed over Democrat Amy Kennedy by about six points. Fearing losses elsewhere on the congressional map, Democrats prioritized securing other ground rather than improving their odds in the 2nd District.
As a result, during redistricting in 2021, the district gained heavily Republican portions of Ocean County that once fell in the 3rd District, a change that Suleiman said “frustrated the hell out of us.”
“I definitely think in the next redistricting, whether that’s mid-cycle or in the next census, we’ve got to get District Two back to what it was historically, truthfully. It had less Ocean County in it. Somebody’s got to give for that. I don’t know who,” he said, adding he believed Democrats could still take the seat.
Van Drew won reelection in 2022 and 2024 with 58% of the vote. Trump won it by 12 points in 2024.
Van Drew’s long tenure in local and state politics also helped him build a brand. Unlike his challenger, who before his campaign was a low-profile local elected official, Van Drew doesn’t have to spend much to boost his name recognition, an advantage that compounds his already sizable cash lead, Donohue said.
Through Oct. 14, Van Drew had raised nearly $2.5 million, spent nearly $2.4 million, and had $894,792 banked, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission.
Mullock, by comparison, had raised $960,948, spent $855,389, and had just $105,400, and though the liberal super PAC Project 218 reported spending nearly $1.5 million for Mullock or against Van Drew, outside spending overall has fallen far short of the levels seen in districts that Democrats have made top targets.
Democratic Party organizations like the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee have steered clear of the race, preferring other districts across the country they view as more competitive.
“I thought that was a huge mistake, and my biggest fear is they’re going to lose this thing by two or three points, and it’s going to be ‘shoulda, coulda, woulda,’” Suleiman said. “When the president is playing defense in Alaska and South Carolina, why wouldn’t you take a swing at Two?”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump DOJ wants to give the Jackson Police Department millions, with strings attached
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Jackson is one of four cities that could get tens of millions of dollars under a new U.S. Department of Justice grant. 
City officials have said the federal money would be used to rebuild the city’s forensic laboratory, hire more officers and expand surveillance of violent crime, including using artificial intelligence to track potential criminals.
The Trump administration announced Friday that it has awarded its new Model Cities Initiative grant to Mississippi’s capital city and three others. The Jackson Police Department had applied for an award of up to $125 million over three years.
Next, the Jackson City Council will have to vote whether to accept the money. The new initiative has proved controversial in other Democratic-led cities, including Charlotte and New Orleans, as the grant requires municipalities to cooperate with certain Trump administration priorities, including immigration enforcement and a ban on people sleeping in public.
But in Jackson, which has some of the highest homicide rates in the nation and recently dealt with budget cuts, at least one council member said that JPD needs the money too much to turn the grant down. 
“I hope they get it because we’re going to reduce their budget,” Ward 2 Council Member Tina Clay told Mississippi Today before the grant was awarded.  
“I’m not concerned about anything other than them (JPD) solving crimes and reducing the crime rate,” she added. “I don’t care what style they use as long as it’s legal and ethical, and they get the results we need.” 
The budget issue is one reason Jackson’s new police chief, RaShall Brackney, has prioritized pursuing federal funding.
Unlike other federal law enforcement grants, the Model Cities Initiative will be administered through a “cooperative agreement,” giving the DOJ a more active role in implementation.
The city’s grant application was supported by letters from state and local law enforcement officials, including Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones, then-Capitol Police Chief Bo Luckey, Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell and Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch. 
Mayor John Horhn also wrote a letter of support in which he mischaracterized the city’s progress in reducing homicides.
“Under the leadership of Chief Brackney and the dedicated men and women of the Jackson Police Department, we have seen meaningful reductions in homicides and violent crimes,” Horhn wrote.
The letter presented to the city council was dated June 10. On that day, WLBT’s Homicide Tracker showed that Jackson had seen 32 homicides, equal to the number it had seen by that date last year. 
By Aug. 3, the date on the letter that Horhn submitted to the federal government, Jackson’s homicides had outpaced last year. 
In an interview earlier this week, Horhn said he was not aware of the inaccuracy until a reporter brought it to his attention.  
Jackson is poised to receive the grant alongside Baton Rouge, St. Louis and Jacksonville, Fla. 
JPD proposed to use most of the $125 million to create a specialized gun-crimes unit focused on “repeat shooters,” expanding its network of cameras housed at the Real Time Command Center, and creating a database that would link 911 calls to the addresses of burned-out homes, illegal dumping sites and other code enforcement complaints.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Ready for hard night Tuesday, GOP legislators look to life after Trump
text:
President Donald Trump will be vying with Richard M. Nixon on Tuesday for a dubious achievement in Connecticut politics: Which president’s midterm election will produce the smaller Republican minority in the General Assembly?
The broad bipartisan consensus among lawmakers is that Democrats will continue to hold comfortable majorities in the state’s Senate and House of Representatives when votes are counted Tuesday night.
Unresolved is the question of how much lower will Republicans fall on Tuesday, the 10th anniversary of their winning half the seats in the Senate and coming within five seats of a majority in the House. It was a high-water mark.
Democrats now have majorities of 102-49 in the House and 25-11 in the Senate. 
The post-Watergate election of 1974, a modern low point for GOP legislative races in Connecticut, yielded a legislature with Democratic advantages of 118-33 in the House and 29-7 in the Senate.
The results were stunning for two reasons: Not only were the GOP minorities tiny, but the party had been in the majority in 1973 and 1974. Republicans lost 60 seats in the House in 1974, going overnight from 93-58 majority to a 33-118 minority.
Comparatively, the GOP is facing an erosion of its minority status, not an upending of the status quo. Democrats say they expect to pick up three or four seats in the House and two in the Senate next week — though the ceiling is higher for Democrats in both chambers.
“It’s a question of those surprise seats,” said House Majority Leader Jason Rojas, D-East Hartford. “To what extent are there surprise seats? I don’t know that there’s a surprise loss [for Democrats] this year, as there has been in the past. But are there surprise wins?”
At least four Republican Senate seats are in play, including two swing districts in Fairfield County where GOP incumbents are not seeking reelection: the 28th, held by Sen. Tony Hwang of Fairfield, and the 36th, held by Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, the gubernatorial nominee.
Rob Blanchard, an advisor to Gov. Ned Lamont, is running for a second time as the Democratic nominee the 28th. In place of the moderate long-serving Hwang, Republicans have nominated a conservative, Amybeth Laroche. It is hard to find GOP optimism for holding the seat.
In the 36th, Republican Joe Kelly of Greenwich, a former school board chair and rugby coach, is trying replicate Fazio’s success in a district where Democratic voters have the edge and Trump has been a drag on down-ballot Republicans. He faces Jill Oberlander, a former chair of the town’s Board of Estimate and Taxation.
One of the incumbent Republicans in an unexpectedly competitive race is Sen. John Kissel of Enfield, who was elected in 1992 and is the longest-serving Republican in the Senate. His margins have shrunk in recent cycles, Democrats flipped local government in Enfield last year, and his opponent this year is a well-known Democrat, former Rep. David Kiner.
Another is Sen. Jeff Gordon of Woodstock, a physician who won the 13-town, east-of-the-river 35th District seat with less than 51% of the vote in 2022. His opponent is Ethan Werstler, also of Woodstock, a 26-year-old UConn graduate.
One of the endangered House Republicans also is from Enfield. Rep. Carol Hall, who won reelection two years ago in the 58th House District with just 50.7% of the vote, has a rematch with Democrat Rick LeBorious.
LeBorious is one of several Democrats who lost close races to try again in a cycle that polling shows is more favorable. In the 35th House, Republican Chris Aniskovich of Clinton is opposed again by Democrat Cinzia Lettieri, who lost with 49.5% of the vote in 2024.
In the shoreline 23rd House District of Lyme, Old Lyme, Old Saybrook and Westbrook, Democrat Jane Wisialowski is making another run after getting 48.5% of the vote in a close loss to Rep. Devin Carney, R-Old Saybrook. Carney is not running this year. The GOP nominee is Barbara Labriola.
Other open seats long-held by Republicans are in play, including the 8th House District, where Rep. Tim Ackert, R-Coventry, is quitting after an unsuccessful run for lieutenant governor. The GOP nominee is Will Gifford, a 21-year-old UConn journalism student who posted a video in December in which he nods in seeming agreement as a white Christian nationalist figure tells him Judaism is “evil.” His opponent is Democrat Francis Lombard.
The list of seats where Republicans hope to make a gain is short: Their prime target is Rep. Rebecca Martinez, D-Plainville, who flipped a Republican seat in the 22nd House District of Farmington, Plainville and Southington two years ago. They also have hopes for an unusual gain: The GOP has endorsed Rep. Jill Barry, D-Glastonbury, a conservative who lost the Democratic nomination to  Moise “Moses” Carelus.
Republicans failed this year to nominate candidates in six Senate districts, all of which had GOP candidates two years ago.
They include two with open seats — one in the 13th District of Cheshire, Meriden, Middlefield and Middletown. It was won by a Republican as recently as 2016, but the GOP is not contesting Democratic Jack Fazzino, who has only a minor-party opponent in his run to succeed Sen. Jan Hochadel of Meriden.
The Democratic incumbents guaranteed reelection are Derek Slap of West Hartford, Gary Winfield of New Haven, Heron Gaston of Bridgeport and Pat Billie Miller of Stamford. Like Fazzino, Al Paolillo of New Haven has a minor-party opponent in his bid to succeed Sen. Martin M. Looney.
In the House, 33 Democrats and six Republicans are unopposed, including the top leaders of either party: House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, and House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford.
In both parties, the conversation already has turned beyond Tuesday to speculation about how rapidly the political landscape will change as Trump begins the last two years of his final term.
“We have to regroup as a party,” said Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield. “I think both parties regroup after these election cycles.”
Trump, a uniquely dominant political force who has insisted voters make this election a referendum on him, has been an albatross for a Connecticut GOP and a godsend for Democrats when it comes to voter turnout.
“For Democrats, they are going to have to learn how to run without Trump,” Candelora said. “If you look at their messaging, it’s very hollow.”
Republicans are eager for the return of a political environment where they can bring the focus in Connecticut back to the high cost of living — a top concern of voters in public polling.
“I think that their challenge is when they’re going to have to be able to campaign on a platform that is going to be what they’re going to do in Hartford, as opposed to what’s going on in Washington D.C.,” Harding said. “I don’t think they have much to campaign on, and I think that’s where you’re going to see the Republican Party hopefully rejuvenated in the state.”
That was the successful GOP formula after the party retained only 37 state House seats in the Obama landslide of 2008. The party made steady gains after Democrat Dannel P. Malloy was elected governor in 2010, inheriting a budget shortfall met with tax increases, service cuts and demands for labor concessions.
Even if there is a blowout on Tuesday, Democrats are ready to caution against misreading the results as a mandate to the move the state dramatically to the left. In wave elections, the majority party tends to make advances they cannot hold.
“Once there is no longer a Trump factor in it, do we continue to hold on to the seats that we otherwise won because so many people turned out, not necessarily because of what Democrats did proactively, but because they’re so angry at Trump, right?” Rojas said. “That is a liability for us. And I’ve been talking about that on the fundraising circuit.”
Ritter noted the dissension in his party over Gov. Ned Lamont’s more centrist fiscal policies, relative to Democrats in the legislature. He already hears chatter about the party’s identity after Lamont, who is favored to win a third and final term on Tuesday.
Lamont was easily reelected four years ago, boosted by strong showings in suburbs that had favored the Republicans in his close win in 2018.
“I think Connecticut is moderate fiscally and liberal socially. And I think that defines the governor to a T,” Ritter said. “He’s been at the top of the ticket. It’s the third time, and we’ve done well all those times in those places like Avon, Simsbury and Fairfield. And he’s going to do very well again. If you know, if you run somebody a little more, a little more to the left in four years, I don’t know what happens.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Commentary: Epstein’s money left a record. New Mexico is right to demand it
text:
Maps of the Zorro Ranch from a New Mexico State Land Trust file and photos of the Santa Fe County residence once owned by convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Graphics courtesy of State Land Office/U.S. Department of Justice)Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes took more than one man. Someone had to manage the properties, handle the paperwork, move the money and keep quiet. New Mexico’s attorney general says those people were Epstein’s lawyer and his accountant, and he is asking a federal court to stop the estate from paying them tens of millions more.
The lawsuit against Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn, the first law enforcement action brought against either man, alleges they helped finance and conceal a trafficking operation that included the abuse of girls and young women at Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County. The state says Indyke received more than $16 million and Kahn more than $10 million from Epstein and his entities between 2011 and 2019. Through their attorney, both men deny any knowledge of or participation in the trafficking. The allegations have not been proven in court.
What strikes me is how ordinary the alleged mechanics are. According to the complaint, the two men held or managed at least 140 bank accounts tied to Epstein and his businesses by 2005. The state alleges some of those accounts moved money between entities, while others paid girls and young women who were abused or recruited. Epstein or people acting for him withdrew more than $6 million in cash between 2002 and 2013, the complaint says. It also alleges Indyke structured withdrawals to avoid federal reporting requirements, taking out more than $200,000 a year from Epstein’s Deutsche Bank accounts between 2013 and 2017. The state argues that these activities went beyond ordinary legal and accounting services.
I spent years as New Mexico state auditor tracing how money moves and who benefits when it moves the wrong way. I am also a Certified Fraud Examiner. That experience taught me to look beyond individual transactions and examine how they fit together. Bank accounts, corporate filings and property transfers can show how money moved between people and businesses, and whether those arrangements served a legitimate purpose or helped conceal wrongdoing. In this case, the records may help establish what Indyke and Kahn knew and what they did with that knowledge.
Zorro Ranch itself shows why those questions matter in New Mexico. According to the complaint, Indyke handled the 2011 transfer of Zorro Ranch’s title to Cypress Inc., an Epstein-controlled company where Kahn served as treasurer and a director. Another company, Zorro Development Corp., ran the property’s operations, and Indyke was its secretary and an authorized signatory on its bank account from 2016 to 2019. The state alleges that corporate structure helped conceal transactions tied to the trafficking. When the estate sold the ranch in 2023, Kahn oversaw the sale.
The questions for the court are what these men knew, what they should have known and what they did with that knowledge while they were being paid.
That is why the request to freeze payments matters. Indyke and Kahn are co-executors of the estate and administrators of the trust, and the complaint says they are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to available funds. The estate was valued at roughly $577.7 million after Epstein’s death in August 2019. As of June 30, 2026, probate records cited in the complaint put it above $107 million. The state named the trust as a defendant for a practical reason: It holds assets that could satisfy a judgment. Survivors have also objected publicly to an arrangement in which the men help oversee payments to survivors while standing to receive millions themselves.
This is a civil case, not a criminal prosecution, and the state’s separate criminal investigation continues. New Mexico seeks damages, restitution and the return of any profits tied to the alleged trafficking, along with limits on the men’s authority over estate distributions.
The case also raises a question about professional responsibility. Lawyers and accountants often have access to financial information that can reveal how a client operates. Professional status should not shield anyone from scrutiny when evidence suggests their work may have helped conceal exploitation. If the allegations are proven, the people who helped make the operation possible should be held accountable for their own conduct.
As Attorney General Raúl Torrez put it, “Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible.” Survivors have called for answers under oath. New Mexico should pursue the evidence to establish what happened at Zorro Ranch and whether the financial and corporate arrangements surrounding the property helped conceal the alleged abuse. The records may show who was involved and what role they played. The state is right to demand that accounting.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Stevens sets conditions for unity event with El-Sayed ahead of election
text:
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, left, and former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, right, participate in a U.S. Senate candidate debate during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)A reported joint rally ahead of the Nov. 3 election to unify supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham will more than likely be a visit to a Black church in Detroit and not an event widely open to the public or press, although El-Sayed is set to campaign with U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina on Sunday.
El-Sayed’s campaign announced Friday afternoon that Clyburn —  one of Stevens’ most prominent supporters in the August primary, which she ultimately lost to El-Sayed — will join the Democratic nominee for a Souls to the Polls event Sunday afternoon.
The Associated Press reported late Thursday evening that a rally would commence on Sunday featuring El-Sayed, Stevens and Clyburn together. As an icon of the civil rights movement, Clyburn’s appearance was seen as a way to shore up support from the Black community that preferred Stevens over El-Sayed in August.
AP also reported that the event would happen at a Detroit church.
Those plans were apparently still in flux on Friday, and the existence of two separate appearances with Clyburn was new information released Friday. 
When Michigan Advance inquired about the two separate stops, neither El-Sayed’s campaign nor Stevens’ press team would talk about the events on the record.
Described as more of a joint appearance than an actual rally, the stop bringing El-Sayed and Stevens together was placed in doubt after the congresswoman released a conditional statement in which she said she had been told El-Sayed would condemn an outside political ad that some found to be antisemitic.
El-Sayed’s campaign had no comment about Stevens’ response issued Friday morning, in which she also said she expected him to apologize for past statements made during the campaign. 

On the eve of the eve of the eve of our BIG and important election, a unifying moment has arrived, our democratic nominee for U.S Senate disavows the Rebellion PAC ad made by Hasan Piker’s uncle that claims Jews are responsible for America’s economic woes. We have learned from party leaders and emissaries, as reported in the news media that he has.
On Sunday I will join with the Great Democratic leader, Jim Clyburn and Dr El Sayed for a church service in the beautiful city of Detroit.
The political coalition of Black and Jewish voices that have carried Michigan and this country through so many storms to the righteous path of liberal democracy and equal opportunity for all will ring out. Full statement here:
— Haley Stevens (@HaleyforMI) October 30, 2026

CNN reported on Friday that the joint appearance’s status was “tenuous” and that it was negotiated in part by Michigan Democrats and Stevens’ fiance, Jason Turkish, who made headlines this week by saying he would vote for El-Sayed’s opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, instead.
That event was put into doubt on Friday following a statement from Stevens, which received immediate backlash among some Democrats because it demanded that El-Sayed condemn an advertisement paid for a group outside of El-Sayed’s campaign.
Stevens hailed the fact that the two former rivals were coming together soon in a show of unity, but positioned that appearance as having conditions. Stevens said she expected El-Sayed to forcefully condemn an ad from RebellionPAC, led by The Young Turks founder Cenk Uygur. Initially created for Uygur’s unsuccessful 2024 run for the White House, the ad attempts to connect high prices on things like groceries to defense spending for Israel. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Many Jewish Michiganders and their allies, who have been critical of El-Sayed’s rhetoric on Israel, pointed to the ad as invoking an antisemitic trope and called on El-Sayed to condemn it. Stevens and her fiance, Turkish, had been part of that wave of condemnation.
“For days, Abdul’s only answer to the Rebellion PAC advertisement … was that his campaign was ‘not affiliated’ with it,” Stevens wrote in her statement issued Friday. “The chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League called it ‘a case study in antisemitism.’ A disclaimer is not a condemnation and everyone in my community knows the difference. I have learned from Democratic Party leaders and emissaries, as reported in the news media, that Dr. El-Sayed has heard the deep concerns of the Jewish community and is now, for the first time in this campaign, formally condemning that ad for what it is. That is why I accepted Congressman Clyburn’s invitation to appear with Abdul on Sunday. I urge voters and the press to confirm it with Abdul directly.”
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina speaks at a meet and greet event for U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens just hours after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed her bid for the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination at a Teamsters hall in Detroit, Mich. July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Condemnation against the ad came from a wide swath of voices, including those in Democratic circles, such as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly), and also Rogers’ campaign.
El-Sayed’s team had previously said that no outside entity speaks for his campaign, not Uygur or Hasan Piker, a controversial pro-Palestinian Twitch streamer who has been the focus of criticism leveled at El-Sayed down the stretch. Uygur, who is Piker’s uncle, has since defended the ad.

This is a defining moment for national media. If you see any “reporter” saying @RebellionPac ad blames Jews for price of groceries, that person is lying to you on purpose. It’s about Israel and never blames anyone for the price of groceries. This is what propaganda looks like.
— Cenk Uygur (@cenkuygur) October 30, 2026

Stevens’ statement went on to say that the ad did not invent the argument Uygur was trying to make, and instead blamed it on comments El-Sayed “has made in his own words throughout the campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and childcare.”
“The standard here is simple. If those words are wrong when a Political Action Committee supporting his campaign says them, then they are equally wrong when Abdul says them, and Abdul has said them from the start,” Stevens wrote. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well. Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything that Michigan cannot afford. And it is my hope and expectation that, out of the same respect for Michigan’s Black community, he will take down his own advertisement featuring white Christian nationalist Tucker Carlson, an insult to the congregation that will welcome us on Sunday.”
Aside from the RebellionPAC ad, the El-Sayed campaign did release an ad featuring Carlson, but only in a clip from his show in which he said he “wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers at gunpoint.” Carlson did not appear in the ad as a surrogate of El-Sayed’s campaign. The ad also featured Fox News hosts including Jesse Watters complimenting El-Sayed as someone who “beat the machine.”
As reported by CNN, Clyburn and U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) had acted as diplomats between El-Sayed and Stevens to organize the church rally on Sunday. However, the Souls to the Polls event featuring Clyburn and El-Sayed was well in the works before the agreement to bring Stevens and El-Sayed together was reached. It was also reported that Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel was part of the negotiations with Stevens’ team and Turkish.
The party did not respond to a request for comment on Hertel’s involvement at the time of publication. This story will be updated if a response received.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: “Thriller” gets students into spooky season at New Haven arts school
text:
It was the tinny swell of 80s-style synth and the boom of a drum machine that tipped people off to something strange stirring in a first-floor hallway of Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy (BRADA) Friday morning.
In the lobby, 50 students pressed themselves against the walls and doorways, listening for what might come next. Down the hall, lockers began to shift and jiggle on their hinges. One by one, the metal doors swung open, zombies sliding out of them with their eyes locked on the humans ahead. 
Fearsome footwork filled the halls of BRADA that morning, as seventh and eighth grade students enrolled in the school’s dance emphasis emerged from lockers, extended their arms to perfect zombie length, slithered along the floor, and transformed the New Haven magnet school into a haunted house just in time for Halloween. For weeks, the young dancers have been meeting after-school to learn choreography to Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” with teacher Nikki Claxton, a veteran educator who has been at Betsy Ross for 26 years. 
At BRADA, which is in the process of turning itself into an arts high school after decades of teaching fifth through eighth grade, the dance has also been a chance for students to meet each other outside of their classes.
“This is the place where we’re looking to elevate what we’ve been doing and take it to the next level,” said Principal Jennifer Jenkins, whose daughter began dancing at BRADA, and is now a student choreographer at Vassar College. “We’re thinking of all the things we’ve kind of imagined over the years and making it happen. It’s things that we’ve talked about … we’re putting them into action, and taking it as far as we can.” 

Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy student Delia Ortiz pops out of a locker at the beginning of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” on October 30, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

The Thriller piece has been in the making since last year, when Halloween fell on a Friday. Claxton, a self-described Michael Jackson super fan, started thinking about how much fun it would be to bring the dance to life. As a longtime educator and the mom of a college freshman, she sees firsthand how much pressure her students are under — especially now that they have the internet at their fingertips for much of the day (although not during school hours thanks to a district-wide ban on cell phones). 
Normally, she’s not shy about bringing it into her classroom or onto the stage: her students have performed dances that address book bans, bullying, suicidality, Black history and the Black Lives Matter movement, and global conflict. Many of her students have followed her beyond the classroom, and work on technique at the Elements Dance and Movement Conservatory in Woodbridge, where she is the artistic director. 
But “I just wanted to do something fun with them,” she said in an interview in her classroom earlier this week, as a few students trickled in to talk about what the dance has meant to them. “Thriller,” she knew from years of watching the video and dancing herself, would give students a reason to get silly and a little strange.
So in September, shortly after the beginning of the school year, she put up a notice for rehearsals. “If you’re afraid to be creepy, this is not for you,” she wrote. Ultimately, 13 students helped put the dance together during weeks of after-school rehearsals. 

Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy (BRADA) students Kennedy Artis and Ralani Moody help each other with makeup before performing Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” for the school on October 30, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror


Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy student Nalia Nevin and teacher Ramzie Highsmith prepare for Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” on October 30, 2026. 

“I didn’t really know what I was getting into,” said Nalia Nevin, an eighth grader who plans to dress up as the large, furry turquoise creature Sulley from the film “Monsters, Inc.” for Halloween. “Like, I love to be creepy. I watch horror movies with my dad. I just feel like it’s the only time of year that you can do anything without judgement … sometimes you can just let yourself be that character.”   
“It keeps a lot of energy up and it gives me positive vibes,” she added of joining the “Thriller” ensemble. 
Eighth grader Destiny Trimble, who is still putting the final touches on a Mad Hatter costume that she plans to wear for Halloween, said she was especially grateful for the rehearsal process, because it gave her a chance to bond with fellow students outside of class. That, and she never thought she would finish middle school knowing how to fit herself into a locker, and then fling it open while preparing to dance down the hallway. 
As a longtime dancer, the newness of “Thriller” also surprised her, she said. For her, there’s something freeing about being weird, even for just four and a half minutes, at an age where her peers can feel judgemental. 
“And I get to be crazy,” she said with a mischievous smile. 

MJ was the inspiration behind Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy’s Halloween-themed “Thriller” performance on October 30, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Friday, that excitement was palpable by the time school started. Just shy of 8 a.m., students scurried up the school’s staircase to Claxton’s second-floor dance studio and slipped into their homemade costumes, a mix of ripped jeans, tights rubbed in dirt and makeup, old sweaters and time-softened T-shirts that had met their match with scissors and slasher-style red paint. If a person popped in unannounced, they might have thought they had found, at long last, a real-life version of “The Final Girl Support Group.” 
Ralani Moody, an eighth grader at the school, remembered tearing up an old blouse and short dress that were sitting unused in her closet, and then covering them with makeup that Claxton had brought in. Before leaving the room, she checked the costume on seventh grader Kennedy Artis, imagining how a ripped, oversized plaid shirt might look with brown-green grease paint and mussed-up hair. 
Around them, the school day had begun. Snippets from brass and woodwind instruments rose up from the open door of a band classroom downstairs. Administrators hurried around the office in matching back-and-rainbow BRADA t-shirts, half-unaware that a congress of the undead was about to take over the lobby. Drama teacher Daniel Sarnelli rolled in to discover that his classroom, the lights still off, had temporarily been taken over by a trio of zombies waiting on directions from their teacher. 
In the school’s green room, art teacher Ramzie Highsmith was waiting with eyeliner, grease paint, fake blood and creamy foundation to make the transformation complete. As he invited students into an artist’s chair — he’s taught visual arts in the district for three years, but worked as a certified makeup artist for almost a decade — peers hopped into action around him, pairing off with palettes and makeup brushes balanced in their hands. 

Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy (BRADA) students Oni David, Jules Sullivan Young and Anayjah Hopkins prepare for a performance of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” on October 30, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Eighth grader Oni David, who has danced with Claxton for three years, took a moment to try a back bend with seventh grader Jules Sullivan Young, the two dissolving into giggles as she lost her balance and slid backwards on the floor. Claxton appeared in the doorway and checked her watch. There were 12 minutes until 9:30 a.m., and two students still needed makeup. 
“Ghouls, get a move on,” she said, a smile dancing at the edges of her mouth even as she kept an eye on the clock. 
“Can we go outside and pick some leaves?” student Londyn Brockington asked Claxton, worried that she was still too recognizable in a ripped-up old dance costume that she’d painted over with mascara. 
She didn’t need to worry: a floppy babydoll collar, rubbed from white to reddish brown with makeup, made her look like she had walked straight out of the horror film 2022 “M3GAN,” about an evil animatronic doll.  
Claxton beamed at Brockington. “No.”
“Well can I go out and rub my jazz shoes on the ground?” 
Claxton smiled again, not needing to say anything at all. 

Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy student Phoenyx Bush, who is in the seventh grade, prepares for a dance to Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” on October 30, 2026.   Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Back at his chair, Highsmith scrunched his face for a moment, looking at a foundation palette opened on the counter. A range of beiges and browns stretched out across its surface in neat, identical squares. “This brown is too ashen,” he said. As he dipped a brush in white powder, he said he was happy to help. “Close your eyes and don’t breathe in,” he instructed a student. 
“We need to get more chances to integrate the arts together!” he said as he hustled to finish one student’s makeup, and invited another into the chair. “We kind of are seen as such separate entities, but in performance, they all connect.”   
Just after 9:30 a.m., those words came to life as a few classes filled the lobby, unaware of what they were about to see. As Claxton cued up the music to “Thriller,” the hallway was totally, eerily silent, save a teacher looking out periodically to see what was afoot. Then Delia Ortiz, who is in the eighth grade, swung her body out of a locker in which she had been crouching, and went into a full back bend, her hands holding the locker’s metal edge for support. 
As she began to crawl down the hallway, like something slippery, swampy thing, Moody opened another door, and lowered herself to the ground. Brockington, slipping to the front of the pack, moved from a locker into a full split. 
As their classmates followed, the group filled the space, peers gasping as they neared the lobby, and then flooded it in three lines of constant movement. 

Ralani Moody goes full zombie – with a balletic twist – in her performance of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” at Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy on October 30, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

“Ohmygod!” teaching fellow Jorhenzi Esquivel exclaimed in a single breath as students rounded the corner. He later said he wasn’t scared, so much as totally delighted and tickled by the performance. 
Those weeks of rehearsal really paid off. As Claxton watched, students took over the lobby, flinging themselves forward and hanging there for a moment before they rose, eyes turned up just slightly to reveal the whites. 
Shoulders rose and rolled in mechanical, syncopated motion as they added a head bob and a slow zombie walk forward. They extended their arms, moving back and forth across the floor as legs kicked up, slicing through the air, and braids and ponytails flew through the air. 

Londyn Brockington in a performance of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” at Betsy Ross Arts & Design Academy on October 30, 2026. A lifelong dancer, she said that she was “gonna have a lot of fun scaring people,” because “I’m normally so kind to everybody.” Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

“I’m gonna have a lot of fun scaring people,” Brockington had said earlier in the morning. “I’m normally so kind to everybody.”      
Following the performance Friday, the 13 students boarded a bus, en route to Benjamin Jepson Magnet School and Nathan Hale Elementary School, both in New Haven. That’s part of the hope as BRADA becomes a high school, said Assistant Principal Amy Migliore — to show other students in the district the work that these young artists are doing. 
“We want the art to be everywhere,” Migliore said. “Not just in the classrooms, but to show kids that we can perform in different spaces and different places.” 

        View this post on Instagram            

Watch the full dance in the embedded video above.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: 5 things to know about CT’s 2026 elections if you haven’t voted yet
text:
Nearly 400,000 people had cast ballots in Connecticut’s midterm elections as of Thursday, according to the secretary of the state’s office. That represents about 17% of the state’s roughly 2.2 million active registered voters. 
That means more than 80% of the state’s registered voters are either voting this weekend, voting on Election Day or sitting out the midterms. For those still deciding when to vote or who to vote for, here are five things to know.
What offices are up for election this year?
The state’s constitutional officers are all up for election this year. This includes the governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of the state, treasurer, comptroller and attorney general.
Also up for grabs are the state’s five seats in the U.S. House of Representatives, with incumbent Democrats seeking to fight off challenges from the GOP in all but the 1st District, which will have a new representative in Congress after incumbent Rep. John Larson lost his Democratic primary over the summer.
And all 151 state House seats and 36 Senate seats are on the ballot this year.
What do I need to know about these races?
The CT Mirror has you covered. Check out our 2026 voter guide for more information about those running, including those seeking a constitutional office.
And check out the reporting Capitol Bureau Chief Mark Pazniokas has done on the debates between gubernatorial candidates Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, Sen. Ryan Fazio, here and here and on the state legislative races here. 
Or read Federal Policy Reporter Lisa Hagen’s breakdown of each of the congressional races here:

1st District: Bronin vs. Chai
2nd District: Courtney vs. Austin
3rd District: DeLauro vs. Lancia
4th District: Himes vs. Goldstein
5th District: Hayes vs. Shea

What is the breakdown of who has voted so far this year?
Of the 394,407 people who had voted as of Thursday, most — 347,279 to be exact — went in person to early voting locations throughout the state, with polls in West Hartford, Norwalk and Milford reporting the most ballots cast.
More than 47,000 votes had also been cast by absentee, or mail-in, ballot.
The vast majority of voters have been Democrats, with 193,901 ballots cast. Unaffiliated voters are the next biggest voting bloc so far, with 119,476 ballots cast. Republicans, meanwhile, had cast 75,819 votes between early and absentee ballots.
That represents almost 22% of the more than 880,000 Democrats registered in Connecticut, about 11% of the more than 1 million unaffiliated voters and roughly 14% of the more than 520,000 registered Republicans.
What are my options for casting my vote at this point?
Early voting ends on Sunday. Those polls are open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Absentee ballots, meanwhile, must be requested by Monday, Nov. 2 and be received by 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3 to be counted. Anyone eligible to vote can request an absentee ballot.
Election Day voting begins at 6 a.m. Tuesday and ends at 8 p.m.
What do I do if my questions weren’t answered here?
Still have questions about things like same-day voter registration or how to request and send in an absentee ballot? 
The CT Mirror’s 2026 voter guide has answers to election-related questions and more information on the constitutional office candidates running this year.
The secretary of the state’s website also has a wealth of information about voting, elections and more, including a look at how to find your polling location, a look at sample ballots in each town and regular updates on the early voting turnout.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Sledgehammers for you, pillows for me: the politics of selective morality in Tennessee
text:
State Sen. Brent Taylor of Shelby County has cultivated an image of toughness and has not been characterized by showing mercy to those he criticizes. At a moment of political crisis days before the midterm elections, he now wants mercy. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)There is something almost theological about watching a politician suddenly discover grace.
State Sen. Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee for Tennessee’s newly redrawn 9th Congressional District, is now asking voters to extend him something he has rarely seemed eager to extend to the people he criticizes: mercy. 
The Nashville Scene reported this week that Taylor acknowledged sending nude photographs of himself in the past, while one source told the publication that an unsolicited picture was sent as recently as 2021, when Taylor was 53. Taylor called the conduct “youthful indiscretions,” said his wife and God had forgiven him, and suggested others should consider doing the same.
And I believe in forgiveness. I am a Black preacher. Grace, mercy, redemption, reconciliation and restoration are not foreign concepts to me. But neither is accountability or consistency. And that is precisely where this situation becomes larger than Brent Taylor’s private behavior.
The issue is not simply that Taylor wants grace. The issue is that he appears to have discovered a softer, gentler moral vocabulary at the exact moment he needs it himself.
Tennessee congressional candidate responds to allegations he sent unsolicited nude pics

This is the same Brent Taylor whose public rhetoric has often been anything but gentle. He once described people working on a Memphis hotel-tax measure as “working harder than an ugly stripper.” During debate over state intervention in Memphis-Shelby County Schools, he said students were “hanging in there like a crackhead’s last tooth.” 
Taylor’s political persona has not generally been built around ambiguity, tenderness or restraint. He has cultivated an image of toughness, certainty, law and order, punishment and accountability. He has supported aggressive state intervention in Memphis institutions and policies, and Democratic lawmakers who have dealt with him have publicly described his style as bullying and crass.
But now the hammer has become a pillow.
Suddenly we are invited to consider context. Suddenly the past should not define a person. Suddenly a family’s private process of forgiveness matters. Suddenly we should recognize human frailty and complexity. Suddenly judgment should be tempered by grace.
Again, I agree with every one of those principles.
I simply want them applied consistently. 
Because too much of contemporary conservative politics has operated according to a remarkably convenient moral formula: a sledgehammer for your failures and a pillow for mine. 
Hypocrisy is their superpower
That hypocrisy shows up whenever politicians and commentators try to wrap themselves in a kind of moral superiority while applying radically different standards depending on whose conduct is being examined. At the state and local level, politicians like Taylor use similar language to condemn protesters, immigrants, Black elected officials, public institutions and communities they believe have fallen short.
Many political voices that once built entire brands around “character,” “family values,” “personal responsibility” and Christian morality have demonstrated extraordinary flexibility when those standards collide with partisan power. Conduct that would disqualify an opponent becomes irrelevant, exaggerated, old news or evidence of persecution when committed by someone on their side.
That is not moral consistency. It is tribalism dressed up in moral language.
And that is what makes the Taylor situation important beyond the salacious details. I do not believe an election should turn solely on someone’s failures. I do not know everything that happened inside Taylor’s marriage, and I have no desire to know. His wife’s decision to forgive him belongs to her. His relationship with God belongs to him. Human beings fail. People change. People deserve opportunities for redemption.



				 I believe in forgiveness. Grace, mercy, redemption, reconciliation and restoration are not foreign concepts to me. But neither is accountability or consistency. And that is precisely where this situation becomes larger than Brent Taylor’s private behavior.			


But public hypocrisy belongs to all of us.
If Taylor believes his Democratic congressional opponent, state Rep. Justin J.Pearson should be judged harshly for his behavior at the Tennessee Capitol when state troopers arrested Pearson’s brother for not leaving his seat in legislative session, then Taylor cannot suddenly insist that his own behavior should be understood primarily through forgiveness and context. 
If he believes immigrants should face severe consequences for breaking rules, then consequences cannot suddenly become unfair when he is the one under scrutiny. If he believes Memphis institutions deserve aggressive intervention when he concludes they have failed, then he cannot reasonably expect scrutiny of his own failures to arrive wrapped in bubble wrap.
You cannot spend years carrying a sledgehammer for everybody else and then demand a pillow when it is your turn to lie down.
This is why the moment should matter to voters even if they could not care less about Taylor’s personal life. The larger question is whether we are going to continue rewarding politicians and political movements that weaponize morality against others while privatizing grace for themselves.
There are no perfect candidates. There never have been. Voting is not canonization. We are not electing saints, bishops, prophets or messiahs. Morality cannot be legislated into perfection, and no political party possesses a monopoly on virtue or vice.
But voters can demand consistency.
We can reject the notion that accountability is only for the people we dislike. We can refuse to accept political movements that preach personal responsibility downward while practicing endless rationalization upward. We can insist that if grace is a principle, it must be available to everybody. If accountability is a principle, it must apply to everybody. If dignity is a principle, it cannot disappear simply because the person being discussed is poor, Black, undocumented, politically inconvenient or unpopular.
And then we can vote accordingly.

name: VTDigger
title: Tax the rich to spare the rest of us
text:
Dear Editor,
There is one single, fundamental issue underlying the election next week, and many people speak a partial truth about it: Our taxes are too high. Agreed; for most Vermonters, they are.  
But some people’s taxes are too low. The wealthiest among us have not paid their fair share to properly support our society in generations, if ever. Not in Vermont, and not in the U.S.  
According to data from the Vermont Department of Taxes, the number of Vermont income tax filers earning more than $300,000 in 2015 was 3,519, just under 1% of all taxpayers. By 2024, this fortunate group had grown to 9,788, constituting just over 2.5% of taxpayers. In 2015, they collectively paid 6.93% of their income to the state, and in 2024 they paid 6.73%. During that time, their collective income nearly tripled. 
By my calculation, if this wealthiest cohort paid just 2% more, that would be about half what it would take to render taxes on anyone earning under $100,000 unnecessary. If they paid 6.2% more, no one making under $150,000 would need to pay taxes. That’s about 90% of us.
Is anyone proposing to tax the rich so hard they worry about affording heat this winter? Or keeping their cars running? Or even taxing them enough that they might worry about affording a vacation? No, of course not. 
Why, then, is it fair to tax any Vermonters to the point that any of us must have such fears?

READ MORE

Let’s compromise and consider taxing the rich just enough so their increased payments let us lower everyone else’s taxes and relieve everyone of such fears. In the process, we would fund our schools, roads and social services to a level where all Vermonters can start to feel that we live in a healthy state where everyone shares in the work.
We should each pay, within our means, toward the well-being of Vermont and its people. There is obviously a deep unfairness in our system when hardworking people are taxed so hard that it hurts, while wealthy people are not. 
If you want change, don’t get distracted by the implementation details. We will only get the chance for change if we elect people willing to effect change. The wealthy and comfortable buy our land and our houses; they vacation here and, yes, many make tax-deductible contributions to the nonprofits trying to provide a safety net. The wealthy own the TV and radio stations and social media platforms. They fund political parties and pay for political ads that overwhelm our thinking with the drumbeat that we need to cut “our” high taxes and that we must forever keep finding ways to do less with less. 
If you’re eligible to vote but not sure you are registered, call your friendly town clerk and find out. It’s a miracle of Vermont law that you can register and vote even on Election Day — though your hardworking clerk will appreciate you not waiting that long. Don’t miss this chance to change the failing status quo.
Alan Turnbull
Craftsbury, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tax the rich to spare the rest of us.

title: Pranks, parties and prognostication: The history of Halloween in Vermont
text:
A postcard postmarked Oct. 31, 1921, in Burlington. The reverse side includes a woman’s note to a friend, reminiscing about the Halloween pranks they’d done the year before. Courtesy of Elizabeth A. Allen

This story by Kyle Neece was first published by Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship, on Oct. 29, 2026.
On Halloween, Vermonters will don costumes and hand out candy as the phrase “Trick or treat!” will be repeated many times over.
But decades ago, typical Halloween celebrations looked a bit different. A recent paper published by the Vermont Historical Society chronicles the history of the holiday in the Green Mountain State from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century. It documents the pranks, parties and fortune-telling trends that made for spooky seasons past.
The paper’s author, Elizabeth A. Allen, began researching the topic after finding a 1922 newspaper clipping of her grandmother at a Halloween party.
“I realized that small-town Vermont newspapers really liked to report what people were doing for Halloween,” Allen said. “I found a rich vein of information that people haven’t really looked into.”
Pranks
Mischief-making has always been a part of Halloween, and between 1870 and 1940, some of the more notable pranks were documented in local newspapers. Allen found stories about cast-iron lion sculptures being knocked over, youngsters ringing doorbells and then fleeing, “and many other annoyances too numerous to mention,” one newspaper reported.
But some Halloween pranks weren’t so light-hearted. Allen found numerous articles about pranks gone bad, with their subjects spraining shoulders, crashing cars and nearly suffocating. Vermonters debated how far these pranks should go.
In one infamous prank in 1933, University of Vermont students stole a cart of apples. Two police officers stopped the group of students, who threw the fruit at the police. One officer fired his gun into the air, and the other shot four times into the crowd. A bullet pierced the arm of Ray Collins Jr., of Colchester, causing minor injury. Mayor James Burke also supported the use of tear gas for crowd control.
The officers’ response reflected a larger societal shift, Allen said. Before World War I, tear gas had been used on the battlefield. But after the war, in the 1920s, police began using it domestically, according to Allen.
She connects the escalating violence of Halloween to postwar social assumptions and implications.
“It made me think that maybe World War I somehow made some people think there was a confusion between the home front and the theater of war, and some people, at least, Burke included, seemed to think they were under siege by these apple-throwing UVM students. So he considered chemical weapons an appropriate response,” Allen said.
By the 1940s and 1950s, Halloween celebrations became more controlled. Tricksters were more likely to be arrested or fined if they were caught being disruptive, Allen wrote.
As such, communities began organizing parades, parties and other events, which served as spaces where children could gather and prevented them from committing mischief. Allen said that trend has continued to today.
“I’ve seen a shift away from trick-or-treating towards trunk-or-treating, with kids going around to the trunks of various cars in a parking lot in the daytime, so the parents can monitor them,” she said. “It’s a smaller trek that the kids make, so that the observance of the holiday is made safer for the kids involved.”

This 1913 postcard shows a young woman hoping to see her future husband’s reflection in her mirror — one of many Halloween fortune-telling practices. Courtesy of Elizabeth A. Allen

Telling fortunes
In decades past, Halloween celebrations were somewhat gendered: Boys pulled pranks, and girls participated in fortune telling, Allen wrote.
Halloween fortune telling links to Scottish romantic rites and practices. These rites involved examining cabbages’ health and shape, displaying pairs of nuts on hearths to represent lovers, and looking into mirrors by candlelight to see the visages of future spouses.
According to Allen’s research, Vermonters didn’t start these rites and practices until the latter half of the 19th century. They gave Halloween a romantic characteristic that is not really seen today.
At the time, women were being afforded greater civic opportunities, but they still couldn’t vote and were expected to have families. Fortune telling gave them an outlet for anxieties, Allen said.
“The consideration of who to marry and what their economic future would look like was a significant crossroads for them,” she said.
Zoe Senecal, a history lecturer at UVM who specializes in the histories of magic and witchcraft, agreed that these fortune-telling activities were an important practice for women.
“Love magic is more than just frivolous, ‘Oh, I wonder who I’ll end up with,’ historically,” Senecal said. “And I think that accounts for its popularity today, too.”
In the 1900s, fortune telling grew into a more commercial enterprise. At parties, costumed seers surrounded by props would hold booths and, for a fee, reveal their subjects’ past, present and future.
But while the business of fortune telling became popular during this era, the practice had existed for centuries, dating back to medieval times, Senecal said. The practitioners of such magic were called “cunning folk.”
“All of these cottage-industry cunning folk would use combinations of spells and prayers to help people with their everyday problems,” Senecal said. “And usually they would do this in exchange for money.”
Today, fortune telling is seen as more of a carnival amusement than a Halloween pastime. And although it was more popular among women in the past, men now practice it, too.

Advertisements for Halloween parties were printed in major newspapers, including this edition of the Burlington Free Press on Oct. 31, 1930. Courtesy of Elizabeth A. Allen

Parties and costumes
One of the first recorded Halloween parties in Vermont dates back to 1884 and was in Island Pond.
Masquerade balls, in which guests wore masks, became popular soon after. Reports of these parties would appear in newspapers but were not generally advertised. 
“The food for Halloween parties in this era was simple and, down to the ice cream and candy, homemade,” Allen wrote.
Like the pranks, Halloween parties escalated in the 1900s. The number of guests at parties grew to triple digits, and newspapers began advertising parties to reach larger crowds, according to Allen’s research.
The costumes at these parties sometimes reflected the prevailing stereotypes of the day. Newspaper accounts included descriptions of costumes that appropriated East Asian and Indigenous cultures and those that romanticized the image of the South under slavery.
“The assumptions that underpin Halloween have a long life, and unfortunately, in this case, it’s negative stereotypes that are still seen as valid costumes by some people even over a century after they first appeared in newspapers,” Allen said.
Racist costumes were not the only stereotypes celebrated on Halloween. Senecal said witch costumes reinforce a lot of the features, characteristics and props that are associated with the trials of witches as “spiritual criminals” in the 16th and 17th centuries, who were tried and prosecuted by churchmen.
Senecal, however, still encourages people to get into the Halloween spirit.
“I think it’s always worth dipping into the history, both to find interesting and fun things to celebrate, but also to be aware of what you should be sensitive about as you’re dressing up, what tropes you’re invoking,” she said.
Allen agreed that revelers should be sensitive to how they dress on Halloween, while still encouraging them to have fun.
“Whether you’re going to bob for a McIntosh apple, or wear a mask, or just look up at the sky and say, ‘Wow, I see the stars out; something might happen tonight’ — those seem like wonderful ways to catch a bit of the Halloween spirit to me,” she said.
