title: Grizzly bear deaths in Yellowstone region climb to modern record high for third straight year
text:
With weeks left to go before many grizzly bears den up, it’s already the bruins’ deadliest year in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in modern times, surpassing records set in 2024 and 2025. 
Historically, regional grizzly bear death counts have been higher. For example, biologist Frank Craighead tallied 120 of the large carnivores that perished in 1972, the year after Yellowstone National Park closed the last of its garbage dumps that scores of bruins depended on for food. 
Over the decades that followed, wildlife managers and landowners went to great lengths to reduce conflicts. At the same time, grizzly mortality rates plummeted as the population recovered and bears spread out geographically — expanding their range until 2021 when it began to slowly recede.  
Wildlife managers call the uptick in bear fatalities somewhat predictable and not a cause for alarm, but the numbers of grizzlies that have died the last three years have each set a modern record. As of Oct. 21, 81 known grizzly bears died in the calendar year, according to a database maintained by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team. And there’s at least one additional mortality that hasn’t been logged yet, bringing the count to 82, according to Wyoming Game and Fish Department Large Carnivore Supervisor Dan Thompson. 




(Graph by Tennessee Watson/WyoFile, with assistance from AI)
This year’s total mortality tops past highs set in 2025 (74), 2024 (72) and 2021 (70). Although this year was a record, the surge in conflicts and related deaths for grizzly bears paled in comparison to the “unprecedented” conflict-ridden year for black bears in Wyoming and neighboring Rocky Mountain states. 
“I don’t have conflict numbers yet, but it was just a more prominent [year] with black bear conflicts, definitely, than grizzly bears,” Thompson said. 
In 2026, grizzly bears in the Yellowstone region predictably died from the full spectrum of causes. The majority, about 65% of the 81 deaths logged so far were human-caused — a dynamic that is the norm. 
Grizzly bear managers break causes of death into nine categories, Higher-than-average causes in 2026 are listed below: 

Cattle/livestock depredation: 27 grizzlies (1.6X higher than average)
Accidental: 12 grizzlies (2X average)
Natural: 11 grizzlies (3.6X average)
Illegal poaching: 6 (3X average)

Remaining causes — those that are undetermined, from human-bear site conflicts and “human removal,” self-defense killings or mistaken ID incidents from black bear hunters — either occurred at below average rates this year or haven’t yet been calculated. 
Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team leader Matt Gould told WyoFile in an email that the variations in causes of death occur every year and are “natural and often substantial.” 
“Drawing major conclusions from a single year is difficult,” Gould said. “That’s why the long-term monitoring conducted by [the study team] is essential for understanding drivers of population dynamics as they relate to sources of mortality.” 
Grizzly bear 399 and her four yearling cubs emerge from their den, walking from Jackson Lake Lodge to Signal Mountain Lodge under the watchful eyes of a park ranger and countless photographers April 15, 2021, in Grand Teton National Park. (Ryan Dorgan)
Wyoming Game and Fish’s Thompson noted some silver linings to the rough year for grizzly bears. For one, he said, adult female bears — the reproducers and important drivers of the population — fared relatively well, especially in the ecosystem interior zone known as the “demographic monitoring area.”
“Literally one female had been killed in an agency action in the DMA,” Thompson said. “I think that’s relevant because people think we’re just murdering bears left and right, but that’s not necessarily the case.” 
Still, it was a rough year overall for grizzlies inside the 19,278-square-mile DMA, which is the area where wildlife managers estimate the population. The deadliest year for grizzlies inside that interior zone took place in 2025, when 54 known bruins perished. But this year isn’t far off, with 48 mortalities so far. 
Another bright spot, according to Thompson: The grizzly bear population has so far absorbed the deaths without declining.
“There’s enough recruitment in the population going on that it compensates for this level of mortality,” he said. “We forget that there are over 300 bears born in the ecosystem every year.” 
The now-record counts of grizzly deaths might end up becoming the norm as grizzly densities grow along the ecosystem periphery, Thompson said, though it’s too early to say. 
“Maybe this is kind of where we’re at proportionally,” Thompson said. “I still am not worried about the population, whatsoever.” 
Former Grizzly Bear Recovery Coordinator Chris Servheen agreed. The nearly 400% occurrence of natural bear-on-bear deaths in the Yellowstone region this year is “interesting,” he said. 
“Grizzly bears are self-regulating,” Servheen said. “At higher densities, they tend to have lower subadult survival rates, because males are killing them. Over time, as the population increases in density, the growth of the population will slow because of those adult males and that higher mortality rate among subadults. That’s probably what we’re seeing.” 

A grizzly bear killed by hunter gunfire in the Aspen Creek drainage west of Cody in 2014. Grizzly bears have died at a high rate so far in 2024. Some 16 deaths are being investigated, which means the bears were likely killed in self-defense. (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

High mortality numbers alone don’t mean much in regards to the health of the population, he said. 
“The key is the trajectory of the population,” Servheen said. “If we saw the trajectory change and start to decline, then I would be really worried about these numbers.” 
So far, that’s not the case. 
Grizzlies have recovered enough since hitting a low a half-century ago that the ecosystem’s tri-state managers in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho are anticipating a third attempt at “delisting” bears from their threatened status under the Endangered Species Act. In the meantime, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is finalizing a rule that gives the states more management latitude. 
Courts have reversed past attempts to delist grizzlies. In 2007, a ruling rejecting delisting hinged on how the decline of whitebark pine — its seeds are a major grizzly food source — would impact the species. In 2017, state jurisdiction was overturned days before the first hunting season in four-plus decades. The court cited concerns about genetic diversity and what happens when population numbers are “recalibrated” by scientists changing the way they count bears.
Recent high grizzly bear mortality figures likely won’t factor much into the delisting decision. Nevertheless, it “doesn’t benefit” states’ argument for more control, said Servheen, who’s been a leading voice against delisting. His chief concern is that anti-predator state politicians influence grizzly bear management, putting the species at risk.

title: High schoolers start podcast to center young transgender Vermonters
text:
Rafaela Botti, second from right, host of the “Transmission of Truth”  podcast, speaks during a podcast release celebration at Outright Vermont in Burlington on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — The voice of Ace, a 15-year-old transgender Vermonter, broadcasted through a large speaker to a room of about 40 people gathered to listen to a group rarely heard from: trans youth. 
“In middle school I would be scared to go to school every day. I would be worried something was going to happen to me,” Ace said. 
In the first episode of a new podcast started by other high schoolers, Ace described being targeted in school and bullied for being transgender and disabled. “I really just wish people understood that it’s not like something that you could just brush off, it’s not something you could just ignore because it really is unsafe,” they said. 
Ace’s voice carried through the room of people gathered Wednesday night to celebrate the first episode’s release at the office of Outright Vermont, an LGBTQ+ youth advocacy organization. The podcast, called “Transmission of Truth,” was created and produced by high schoolers to feature the perspectives of transgender youth.
During a time when trans people have had their healthcare, protections against discrimination and participation in sports threatened during President Donald Trump’s recent administration, the podcast episode encourages queer youth to be given a say on policies that impact them at the state level.
Before playing the podcast for the room, Dana Kaplan, Outright’s executive director, took the mic. 
“Young people need to have the ability to shape their own future,” he said, and trans voices are too often left behind. Letting trans youth share their own stories “feels pretty radical,” he said. 
Over half of LGBTQ+ youth age 13-17 have experienced bullying and those who did reported much higher rates of attempting suicide compared to their peers, according to a report from the Trevor Project, a national advocacy group for LGBTQ+ youth. According to the report, 40% of transgender or nonbinary young people have considered attempting suicide in the past year. 
The podcast was the brainchild of Rafaela Botti, a homeschooled high school senior who lives in Middlebury. Botti said in an interview that she created the podcast as a response to “a really nasty rhetoric right now surrounding queer and trans youth.” 
“We really wanted to destigmatize that and make sure that there was an accessible way for people to learn about the trans community, especially young people here in Vermont,” Botti said. 

Max Van Dyne listens to the first episode of the “Transmission of Truth” during a podcast release celebration at Outright Vermont in Burlington on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

In the first episode, Botti talked with Ace, lobbyist Meg Larraine Fuerst and Sen. Ruth Hardy, D-Addison, about how youth can advocate for themselves in the Statehouse, an environment they said can be intimidating for kids and marginalized communities. 
Too often, education policy gets rewritten without any input from kids themselves, Ace said in the podcast. Last year, they took part in youth leadership day at the Statehouse, an annual event in which kids testify in front of committees, which allowed them to talk to legislators about their experiences in school. 
In the episode, Ace and Botti celebrated the proposed equal rights amendment to the Vermont Constitution, or PR. 4, which is up for voter approval on Nov. 3. The youth also condemned statements that Sen. Steve Heffernan, R-Addison, made on the Senate floor in May about the proposed amendment.
While senators were discussing a bill with harsher punishments for animal cruelty, Heffernan said, “in these crazy times, what happens if the individual identifies as an animal having intercourse with an animal?” 
Heffernan then said he was concerned that the equal rights amendment to the state constitution would offer protections for people who “identify as a dog” and have sex with dogs. 
In the podcast, Botti called Heffernan’s comments “degrading and transphobic.” 
An hour into the event — and after the podcast mentioned him — Heffernan walked into the room and sat down front and center. Hardy, who sat at an adjacent table, shook her head. 
In an interview after the event, Heffernan said he attended because he was invited by the organizers. He said he wasn’t aware of the comments made about him in the podcast and said he supports the rights of gay and transgender youth.
“My uncle was gay. My cousins are gay. I got a brother-in-law that’s gay. I got trans that I know. It’s like, I accept people for who they are,” Heffernan said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: What happened with threatened lawsuit over secretary of state’s race ad?
text:
Indiana secretary of state candidates, from left, Democrat Beau Bayh and Republican Max Engling. (Photos provided by campaigns)Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling’s campaign says it will wait until after the election before filing a threatened lawsuit against Democrat Beau Bayh over a TV ad.
Engling said in a televised debate, a news conference and news releases last week that he would sue for what he called defamation over references in the ad that he had been convicted of reckless driving.
His campaign said that prominent conservative lawyer Jim Bopp was preparing the lawsuit, but no court filing has occurred after more than a week.
“With four days until the election, we will have to file after Nov. 3,” campaign spokeswoman Chloe Anagnos told the Capital Chronicle on Friday. “We will hold Beau Bayh accountable for his lies.”
The Bayh ad features a uniformed sheriff’s deputy saying Engling “has been convicted and investigated at least eight times for reckless driving and reckless behavior.” It ran on Indianapolis TV stations for at least a week beginning Oct. 17.
Engling’s campaign acknowledged that his driving record includes eight speeding tickets from more than a decade ago “all traffic infractions, not misdemeanor charges or convictions.”
Bayh has defended the ad and his campaign provided the Capital Chronicle with a timeline supporting its contentions that included an expunged misdemeanor criminal reckless case from 2007 in which Engling, who was then 20, threw eggs at passing vehicles from a U.S. 31 overpass in Carmel.
That timeline includes no “reckless driving” criminal charges against Engling.
Bayh’s campaign did not immediately reply Friday to a request for comment.
During a debate last week, Bayh criticized Engling’s actions.
“It seems to me that going 87 miles an hour in a 60 would be reckless. Seems to me that speeding through a construction zone is also reckless,” he said. “It seems to me that throwing projectiles off of an overpass into oncoming traffic, where you could have killed someone, would also be reckless.”
Engling has countered by pointing to Bayh being initially charged in 2018 at age 22 in Brunswick County, Virginia, with misdemeanor reckless driving for driving faster than 85 mph. That charge was reduced to an infraction for defective or unsafe equipment and Bayh was fined, according to Virginia online court records.
“Unfortunately, there’s only one person on this stage that has been charged with reckless driving, and that’s my opponent, not me,” he said during last week’s debate.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Déjà vu in some Alaska House districts as voters decide the outcome of rematches
text:
Nome's Anvil City Square, with a giant gold pan and statues of the "Three Lucky Swedes" whose discovery kicked off the 1899 Gold Rush, is seen on Sept. 5, 2021. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Voters in some of Alaska’s state House districts might feel a sense of déjà vu when they go to the polls this year.
From the Arctic to South Anchorage, several races for House seats are rematches from 2024 and, in some cases, elections in earlier years.
One of those rematches is a contest in the farthest-north House district between two Democratic women. Rep. Robyn Niayuq Burke Frier of Utqiagvik is defending her seat against Kotzebue Mayor Saima Chase in District 40. Both women ran in 2024, as did incumbent Republican Thomas Baker of Kotzebue, who finished in third place.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
In House District 39, which encompasses the Bering Strait region and a slice of Lower Yukon River territory, incumbent Democratic Rep. Neal Foster of Nome again faces Tyler Ivanoff of Shishmaref.
Ivanoff ran against Foster in 2020, 2022 and 2024 under different party labels — as a Democrat who narrowly lost the primary in 2020 and as an Alaskan Independence Party member in the next two elections. This year, he is running as a nonpartisan, as is a third candidate in the race, Reynold Okitkun of Kotlik.
In South Anchorage, incumbent Republican Mia Costello and Democrat Denny Wells are facing each other for the second time in District 15. The district encompasses the West Dimond Boulevard, Jewel Lake and Campbell Lake areas. For Wells, it is his third attempt to win the seat.
District 40: Arctic rematch
In the nation’s farthest-north state legislative district, each of the Democratic candidates on the ballot have deep public-service experience.
Frier, who is finishing her first two-year term, has a background in education. Before being elected to the legislature, she served for four years on the North Slope Borough School District board, which she chaired for two years. She was the secretary/treasurer of the Association of Alaska School Boards Board of Directors and has held other leadership positions.
 

Snow-dusted Copter Peak, at the northern edge of Noatak National Preserve in Arctic Alaska, is seen from a valley. Nunaviksak Creek runs along the base of the mountain. The area straddles the North Slope and Northwest Arctic regions. The two regions make up Alaska House District 40, the nation’s northernmost state legislative district.(Photo provided by National Park Service)
 

	Chase has a career in emergency response and public safety.
Before being elected as mayor of the hub city in the Northwest Arctic region, she served as the Northwest Arctic Borough’s fire chief and search and rescue coordinator. Her current day job, aside from her position of mayor, is as the emergency manager for the local tribe. She has served in other public safety organizations as well.
In 2024, Frier — then using the last name Burke, which she changed upon her recent marriage — topped Chase in a three-way general election, with results counted through ranked-choice voting. In the primary that year, however, Chase wound up on top by three votes.
In this year’s Aug. 18 primary, Frier received 61.8% of the vote to Chase’s 38.2%.
Frier and Chase are both Inupiat, and they have common positions on issues. The main point of separation is their place of residence — the North Slope for Frier and Northwest Arctic for Chase.
Earlier in Alaska history, the North Slope and Northwest Arctic were in separate House districts. Though both regions are majority Inupiat, they have some contrasts, some stemming from a wealth gap.
The North Slope holds Alaska’s major oil fields, which generate significant revenue for local governments. The Northwest Arctic does not have oil fields. Its main industrial activity is at the Red Dog mine, one of the world’s largest zinc producers. The mine provides local government revenue and jobs — but not at the high level that that North Slope oil activity provides.
Over past election cycles, House District representation has seesawed between the two regions.
Representing both sides of the district requires understanding both the differences and similarities between the regions, Frier said by email.
“For example, modern and reliable water infrastructure is an acute need for the Northwest Arctic, where erosion and freeze-ups can damage pipe systems,” she said. 
 

Rep. Robyn Niayuq Frier, D-Utqiagvik, speaks on the House floor on the last day of the regular legislative session on May 20, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

	When extreme cold hit Northwest Arctic villages last March, she worked with Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s office to ensure a disaster declaration and deployment of needed resources, she said. “I saw firsthand during trips into Ambler how broken water systems in these communities can make basic wellness, bathing, and fire response nearly impossible. No Alaskan should live like that, and it’s these fundamental, human challenges that ground my perspective as a legislator,” she said.
Shared needs between the two regions include a well-funded school system; strong, safe communities; lower energy costs, protection of voting rights “and the preservation of Inupiaq traditions and practices,” she said.
“These shared priorities are reflected in over 50 years of cooperation between our region’s respective school districts, regional corporations and local governments to better coordinate priorities, land claims and disaster response effort,” she said.
Chase, also responding to questions by email, said the regions share a culture, language and a lot of family ties, but they have some different needs.
“The North Slope Borough has a strong local tax base, so it can fund many of its own services. The Northwest Arctic doesn’t have that, and our communities depend much more on the State for basic services like public safety, school funding, roads and airports, health care, and help after storms and erosion,” she said. That means when the state cuts services, those cuts are felt first and hardest in the Northwest Arctic, she said.
Like Frier, she said it is important to consider sometimes contrasting conditions in the two sides of the district.
“Representing both means listening to each region on its own terms and not assuming one size fits all,” Chase said.
“Where our interests line up, on subsistence, energy costs, and protecting our coastlines, I’ll make sure the North Slope and Northwest Arctic speak with one strong voice in Juneau. Where the Northwest Arctic needs the State to step up, I’ll fight for that without apology. Our elders taught us atautchikun, working together as one, and that’s how I’ll represent every community in HD 40,” she said.
 

Kotzebue Mayor Saima Chase is a Democratic candidate for Alaska House District 40. (Photo provided by Saima Chase)
 

	Whether separate House districts or joined together, the North Slope and Northwest Arctic have produced prominent legislators who played significant roles in Alaska history.
They include Eben Hopson, who was the first mayor of the North Slope Borough and the founder of the Inuit Circumpolar Council, in addition to serving in the territorial legislature and later in the state Senate. Hopson is a towering figure in Alaska and Arctic history and credited with protecting Indigenous culture and political rights.
Also from the North Slope was Brenda Itta-Lee of Barrow, as Utqiagvik was officially named then. In the 1970s she became the first Alaska Native woman elected to the state House.  
Legislative leaders from the Northwest Arctic included Willie Hensley, who was one of the architects of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act and one of the founders of the Alaska Federation of Natives, in addition to serving terms in the state House and Senate and numerous other accomplishments.
Frier and Chase say those historic leaders inspire them.
Frier named Hopson, “a true monument of a man,” and called Itta-Lee and former Rep. Reggie Joule, D-Kotzebue, as inspiration. Joule, a Native Olympics star prior to his political service and a Northwest Arctic Borough mayor after his legislative service, was “a personal role model and has helped guide me and ground me in the needs of our entire region,” Frier said.
Chase cited Hensley as “someone I’ve looked up to my whole life.” She cited his numerous accomplishments, which she said continue to shape the Northwest Arctic. “He showed that one person from our region can change the direction of the whole state,” she said.
 

Longtime Native leader Willie Hensley, sesated in the front and wearing a blue parka, poses for photos on Oct. 22, 2026, with several other past and present leaders of the Alaska Federation of Natives. The photos were taken after a panel discussion with Hensley and others at the AFN confention that reflected on the organization’s 60-year history. (Photo byYereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Chase also listed former Rep. Eileen Panigeo MacLean, D-Barrow, as a leader she admires. “She wasn’t afraid to stand up to the big urban caucuses in Juneau, but she worked well with everyone and got things done for rural Alaska. She also had roots in both the North Slope and the Northwest Arctic, which is exactly the kind of bridge HD 40 needs,” Chase said.
District 39: A Bering Strait rematch
Foster is a legislative veteran with a very familiar name to district voters. His father, Democrat Richard Foster, held the seat from 1989 to the time of his death in 2009. Neal Foster was appointed to the seat after his father died and has been returned to office since then.
He has served since 2017 as co-chair of the powerful House Finance Committee, that body’s gatekeeper for all budget matters. The House and Senate finance committees hammer out the budgets that the legislature must pass each year. That gives committee members clout, and committee chairs even more clout.
There is little difference between him and Ivanoff on policy stances and goals, though Foster said he does not know much about Okitkun in an Oct. 23 interview at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention.
The big difference is the seniority and experience he offers as a contrast to his competitors, he said.
“What I’ve really focused on for me is the fact that I will be ranked number one in the House next year because Bryce is moving to the Senate,” he said, referring to House Speaker Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham. “If we get a new person in, they’re going to be ranked number 40 or somewhere down at the very bottom, which is not necessarily good for our district.”
 

Rep. Neal Foster, D-Nome, stands a lobby of the Dena’ina Civic and Conventon Center in Anchorage on Oct. 23, 2026, during the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	An example of the policy similarities is the desire for a “full” Alaska Permanent Fund dividend, the annual payout from the state’s oil-wealth fund. Whether Alaskans get a big dividend depends on action to raise revenues, Foster said, citing a curtailment of oil tax credits as an important step. Foster has also favored the elimination of an income tax exemption for S corporations, which are known as pass-through corporations because their profits flow to private owners rather than public shareholders so they do not pay corporate income tax in Alaska. The main company benefitting from that tax exemption in Alaska is Hilcorp, the privately held Texas-based company that is now one of the state’s major oil producers and operators.
Foster said that having seniority and clout helps not just District 39 but all of rural Alaska. He cited as one example his protection of the state’s Power Cost Equalization fund, which helps cover rural electricity costs so that they are closer to urban Alaska costs.
“I’ve literally had people come to me over the years and say, ‘Neal, to balance the budget, you’ve got a billion dollars in this PCE fund. We’re going to need to start chipping away at that,’ and I say, ‘No, no, no, we will not,’” he said.
To Ivanoff, who is mounting his fourth run against Foster, legislative seniority is not necessarily an asset.
In his responses to the candidate questionnaire published in the Alaska Beacon and elsewhere, Ivanoff said some new approaches will be needed to raise state revenues. “Right now the incumbents who have been in office for many have their minds set,” he said in the questionnaire.
Ivanoff came close to Foster in the Democratic primary in 2020, finishing 100 votes behind, or 5 percentage points. In the next two elections, Ivanoff ran as an Alaskan Independence Party member and lost in the general election by wider margins — by 16.5 percentage points in 2024. The Alaskan Independence Party disbanded earlier this year.
The third candidate is Reynold Okitkun of Kotlik, a former mayor and city council member in that village. Okitkun, whose nickname “Papa Joe” appears on the ballot, is also a former member of the local tribal council.
This year, Ivanoff and Okitkun have also teamed up to support each other through Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system.
 

Tyler Ivanoff of Shishmaref is an independent candidate challenging Rep. Neal Foster. (Photo provided by Tyler Ivanoff)
 

	“Reynold Okitkun and I are both candidates from small rural communities in our district. We have lived the lifestyle of rural Alaska our entire lives. We have hunted for our food, gathered from the land and sea, and supported our communities throughout our lives,” Ivanoff said in a Facebook post.
“We understand the challenges of living in rural Alaska because we live them ourselves. We know what it means to depend on our subsistence way of life, support our families, and look out for our neighbors.”
“Even though Reynold and I are running for the same seat, I respect him and believe we can put our communities first. We are both nonpartisan candidates, and I believe our region deserves a leader who understands the people and the challenges we face every day,” Ivanoff wrote.
In the Aug. 18 open primary, Foster won 52.2% of the vote to Ivanoff’s 29.2% and Okitkun’s 18.6%.
Politics aside, Foster and Ivanoff have some ties to each other, and possibly to Okitkun as well.
Foster and Ivanoff are distant cousins, sharing a pair a great-great-grandparents, the incumbent said.
Okitkun may be a cousin, too, Foster said.
The Fosters are related to the Okitkon families in Koyuk and Elim, he said. This summer, when he was in Koyuk, he got another hint of family ties. “Some of my cousins said, ‘Oh, we are related to the Okitkuns in Kotlik, too, even though the name’s spelled a little bit differently,” Foster said. 
The spelling difference is in the last vowel: O for the Koyuk family and U for the candidate’s family.
Potential flip in South Anchorage
Another rematch is getting attention in South Anchorage. That is because Democrat Wells, now making his third attempt and in his second matchup against Republican incumbent Costello, has the potential to flip the seat and expand the now-slim House majority.
Wells’ first race, in 2022, was against former Rep. Tom McKay, a Republican. It was the first year that Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system was in effect. When the rankings were fully calculated, McKay won in a squeaker, by just nine votes.
In 2024, he lost by a wider margin to Costello, a legislative veteran who served previously in the state Senate. Costello had 51.5% of the vote to Wells’ 45.5%.
But in this year’s Aug. 18 open primary, Wells finished ahead of Costello, with 52.7% to her 47.3%.
Unlike the Arctic and Bering Strait races, the contest for District 15 has a decidedly suburban flavor.
Wells is making a pitch for increased education funding — and citing the close 2022 election, in which he lost by nine votes, to make the point that every vote matters.
“Those nine votes elected a representative who was the deciding member to uphold vetoes that cost our schools tens of millions of dollars,” Wells says in one of his Facebook videos showing him riding an electric scooter as he goes door-to-door in the neighborhood.
He bought the scooter specifically for the campaign, he said by email, and it has been helpful. He knocked on doors all along Jodhpur Road and West Dimond Boulevard between Sand Lake Road and Kincaid Park in a single day, he said. Without the scooter, the task would have taken two or three days, he said.
But it has also added a fun twist to the campaign, he said. “The scooter makes a great conversation piece — people often smile and comment about it when they see it at the end of the driveway while we are chatting at their door,” he said.
Costello, a former teacher, is also emphasizing education, though not explicitly supporting increased funding.
“Mia Costello supports responsible funding for education by funding Alaska’s schools early, putting more education dollars directly into the classroom – not administration – and lowering class sizes. Investing in children today helps build Alaska’s future tomorrow,” her campaign’s Facebook page says.
Like Wells, Costello is campaigning with a neighborly flair. Her Facebook page features a video of her walking a neighborhood street, photos of her with voters at their homes and even a video from a Dimond High School swim and dive team carwash fundraiser. Costello was a star swimmer herself, at West Anchorage High School and Harvard University.
Although the race has statewide implications, the candidates appear to be focused locally.
“I suppose political pundits or party insiders may be paying more attention, but in my social circles I’m still just the guy at church who volunteers and has photos on the wall or the bass singer in my theater performance groups or the real estate photographer or my kids’ dad at their schools,” Wells said in his email.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, and early voting is available before then at numerous sites in the state.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: After five years, Providence Superintendent Montañez to leave post
text:
Providence superintendent Javier Montañez speaks with reporters on Aug. 29, 2024. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Providence Public Schools Superintendent Javier Montañez is stepping down from his post after leading Rhode Island’s largest school district for five years.  
Montañez announced his departure on Friday, just shy of the four-month anniversary of the district regaining local control of its schools. 
“After laying the foundation, it’s now time for me to move on and allow the next generation of leaders to take Providence Public Schools to the next level,” Montañez said in a statement provided by the district.
District spokesperson Alex Torres-Perez said Friday afternoon that the official resignation date hasn’t been set yet, as Montañez is still in discussions with the School Board to finalize his departure. In the meantime, Montañez will continue overseeing the district. 
“The decision for the superintendent to resign was entirely his,” Torres-Perez said. “He notified District leadership and the School Board this morning.” 
Financial details about Montañez’s departure, such as possible severance or continued benefits, were not disclosed by the district Friday, but the superintendent’s current contract runs through June 2027.
Except for the last few months, Montañez’s tenure took place entirely during the seven years the Rhode Island Department of Education had control over the capital city’s schools. His exit follows continued disputes and several shakeups in the upper echelons of Providence schools leadership, including a recent attempt to oust the school board’s president and the resignation of several senior administrators.
“It is my hope that no matter the circumstances and challenges, district leaders continue to put students first in all their decisions,” Montañez said in his statement. 
A job posting for the interim superintendent position is expected to go live early next week, according to a letter sent out Friday by board President Ty’Relle Stephens, who said the board will seek out qualified internal candidates first before searching outside the district, if necessary. 
Montañez is a product of the Providence school system himself. He experienced homelessness as a youth and struggled with illiteracy and dyslexia as a teenager, and would sometimes attend school only for the meals it provided. He dropped out of Hope High School, but later obtained his GED and went on to get a master’s degree in education from Rhode Island College and a doctorate in educational leadership from Johnson & Wales University. 
Montañez began working in the Providence school system in 1996 as a bilingual teacher at what was then Laurel Hill Elementary School, now known as Spaziano Elementary School. He climbed the ranks to eventually serve as the school’s assistant principal and then principal, before heading to Leviton Dual Language School to serve as its principal for a decade. 
In 2021, two years after Commissioner of Elementary and Secondary Education Angélica Infante-Green took control of the struggling school district in 2019, Montañez became superintendent.
In his letter Friday, Stephens thanked Montañez for his decades of service to the district.
“His commitment to our students, our schools, and our community has not gone unnoticed,” Stephens wrote. “And his historic leadership as the first Hispanic male to serve as Superintendent of our district represents an important milestone in our city’s history.”
Stephens noted the board has recently and consciously tried to “strengthen communication, set aside our differences, and renew our focus on the responsibilities we share. I remain confident in our Board’s ability to find common ground, move forward together, and get back to work on behalf of the students of Providence while ensuring a smooth transition.”
Infante-Green issued her own statement Friday on Montañez’s departure, noting that it left her “deeply saddened” to see him go. 
The commissioner credited Montañez’s leadership with improved graduation rates, reductions in chronic absenteeism and the betterment of school facilities in the district.
Providence’s four-year graduation rate rose from 73.6% in 2019 to 79.4% in 2024, although it dipped back down to 77% for the class of 2025, according to recent education department data. 
The district’s chronic absenteeism rate fell from a pandemic-era peak of 57.1% in the 2021-2022 school year to 25.3% in the 2025-2026 school year. At least six new or significantly renovated school buildings — part of districtwide facilities investment of around $1 billion — opened during the takeover and Montañez’s tenure. 
“None of these accomplishments came easily, but Dr. Montañez not only believed in the potential of Providence students, he worked tirelessly to help make the district a destination for education,” Infante-Green wrote.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gov. Laura Kelly says blocking Medicaid expansion the ‘dumbest thing Kansas has ever done’
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly, who completes her second term in January, speaks with journalist Jim McLean about the joy and despair of being governor for eight years. Her remarks came during an Oct. 29, 2026, economic conference at the University of Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly said the biggest disappointment of nearly eight years in office was the Kansas Legislature’s refusal to expand Medicaid health coverage to the working poor.
Kelly repeatedly urged the Republican-led Legislature to broaden eligibility standards to include as many as 150,000 working adults who earned too much for traditional government-sponsored Medicaid and too little to qualify private-insurance subsidies. Political opponents of expansion argued extending benefits to adults 19 to 64 years of age making no more than $21,600 per year was too costly for the state or clashed with philosophical objections to deepening entitlement programs.
“I think it’s the dumbest thing Kansas has ever done,” Kelly said Thursday during an economic conference at University of Kansas. “Not only has it hurt the people who would have been eligible for insurance under the Medicaid program, but just financially we have left over $8 billion in Washington, D.C. We’ve seen it play out in the closure of some of our rural hospitals and certainly with so many of them today on the brink of it.”
Kansas stands among 10 states that turned aside expansion options within the federal Affordable Care Act. All states bordering Kansas embraced Medicaid expansion to improve health care service options.
Kelly said her administration could have hammered out a Medicaid expansion deal with the Kansas Senate led by President Ty Masterson, the Andover Republican running for governor. The problem, she said, was opposition by Kansas House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican campaigning to become the state’s insurance commissioner.
“There’s one person in the state really responsible for the fact that Medicaid has not been expanded and that would be the current speaker of the House,” she said. “We got so close so many times, but he was absolutely determined not to allow Medicaid expansion to come to a vote because he knew it would pass. For his own reasons, he did not want Medicaid expansion. That’s why we don’t have it.”
In response, Hawkins said the governor was entitled to her opinion.
“Calling people names and assigning blame doesn’t change the facts,” he said. “Medicaid expansion would create significant new obligations for Kansas taxpayers based on hopes and dreams that the federal government will maintain their share of the burden. I’ve never believed that adding more people to a government program is automatically the same thing as improving access to health care.”
Kelly spoke for an hour with participants in the 2026 Kansas Economic Policy Conference about policy issues ranging from water resources to data centers, economic development and property taxes.
She expressed gratitude for her sustained popularity among Kansans as well as cherished and disliked aspects of being governor. She was frustrated by time spent on the campaign trail in 2022 as she sought reelection. Interacting with voters was never an issue, she said, but road trips drew her away from day-to-day responsibilities of the job. On the upside, Kelly welcomed opportunities to delve into details of the state budget.
“The budget is where everything happens,” Kelly said. “I love numbers. I really love math.”
 
Data centers and AI
Kelly said she followed ongoing debate in Kansas about proposals to build data centers and was comfortable decisions on those projects remained with municipal government officials. She said the Kansas Department of Commerce shared information on benefits and drawbacks of data centers, but the state wouldn’t be offering supplemental incentives to draw developers to Kansas.
A 2025 state law granted a 20-year state and local sales tax exemption for data centers tied to a minimum investment of $250 million. The Kansas Corporation Commission mandated new businesses, including data centers, using more than 75 megawatts of peak energy load per month to pay higher utility rates.
Advocates of data centers champion the potential of local economic growth as well as new property tax revenue. Critics say the state didn’t adopt sufficient safeguards against electricity cost surges or impose proper environmental regulations in terms of shielding the water supply.
“I know there’s a lot of noise out there,” Kelly said. “There are legitimate concerns about data centers. Water, particularly for rural Kansas, is a huge issue. Obviously, electricity and energy. Kansas has got their arms around that. It’s really become much more of a political issue than anything else. Once we get through this election cycle, we may see some of that die down.”
She said data centers were needed to drive the Kansas economy. Some of opposition to data centers resembled the community response to wind and solar farms, she said.
“Remember when wind wanted to come in and people were flipping out completely?” said Kelly, who urged data center developers to be transparent about their plans. “Stop just coming in and announcing you’re opening your doors. Work with these communities, just like they ended up doing with wind. They started going to the county commissioners and they started going to the people and having conversations.”
Kelly said she joined many Kansans who were uneasy with rapid development of artificial intelligence. She said Congress should take the lead in regulating AI.
“People are absolutely petrified of AI because nobody knows what it really means. You know, it’s scary,” the governor said. “I’m hoping with a new Congress that we will have some serious people there who will recognize that you can’t fool around with this stuff.”
 
Water, tax policy
Kelly said she was disappointed, but not surprised, the Legislature declined to embrace her recommendation to create a rolling 10-year strategic investment program for water resources. She said the plan should have a dedicated funding source just like the state’s 10-year highway program, which guaranteed annual investment in high-priority projects.
If the Legislature didn’t set aside funding, she said, issues with the quantity and quality of water would remain the state’s biggest challenge.
“We had wonderful water plans in the past,” Kelly said. “I would even say that my predecessor, Sam Brownback, put together a really, really comprehensive and good 50-year water plan that ended up sitting on the shelf because it’s not free. You’ve got to pay for it.”
She said the Legislature’s opposition to sustained funding could be personal.
“I’m hoping that’s exactly what it is. That they’re just waiting until I’m out of here,” she said.
Kelly said the Legislature’s debate on property tax reform was unproductive, because Republican bills were unfair to local units of government heavily reliant on property tax revenue. She said the solution would require a partnership between state and local government.
“It would have to be a trusted partnership,” Kelly said. “The way it could work is that the state pick up the burden of some of the things that our local units of government are paying for right now.”
The options could include corrections or mental health services, she said.
“There has to be some structure there that there’s a burden on the state but also a responsibility on the local units of government to actually flatten out if not decrease property taxes,” Kelly said.
Kelly said it would be reasonable, but politically challenging, for townships, cities, counties and other units of government to form regional coalitions to pool resources to better fund public services.
She said obstacles to consolidating schools ranged from parochial ideas about sports to unwillingness of state legislators to take risk.
“Consolidation has always been like a swear word, you know, in Kansas. It’s very, very difficult,” the governor said. “We’ve got what 700 cemetery districts or something ridiculous? It is crazy. It’s going to take some guts and willingness to spend some political capital and recognize you’re going to have to do some very unpopular things in order to keep the state moving forward.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Court suspends attorney’s law license, citing client fund issues and case neglect
text:
(Main photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus; seal courtesy State of Iowa)The Iowa Supreme Court has suspended the law license of a northern Iowa attorney who was the subject of five separate disciplinary complaints.
Court records indicate that between October 2024 and September 2025, the Iowa Supreme Court’s Attorney Disciplinary Board initiated an investigation into five complaints against attorney Elizabeth M. Wayne of Parkersburg.
The complaints alleged Wayne was neglectful in her handling of court proceedings and client funds, and the board charged Wayne with failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing her clients.
In one of the five cases, according to board documents, Wayne allegedly failed to respond to the opposing counsel’s emails for several months, only answering after a motion for contempt was filed against her client. In two other cases, the board alleged, Wayne missed court-imposed deadlines, resulting in default notices, and she was ultimately removed as legal counsel in both matters.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the two remaining court cases, Wayne allegedly missed court hearings, which the board alleged represented a “conscious disregard” for the duty owed to her clients. In three of the five cases, she also failed to adequately communicate with her clients, the board alleged.
In addition, the board alleged that in three of the five cases, Wayne failed respond to the board’s notice that she was the focus of disciplinary complaints, and that she “improperly commingled her own earned funds with client funds” and then failed to promptly return to her clients $1,636 in unearned money she had collected. In one instance, the board alleged, Wayne waited seven years before returning a client’s money.
As mitigating factors, the board noted that Wayne expressed remorse for her actions and that the unexpected death of her mother in 2025 had caused her grief, depression and anxiety — although, the board added, her misconduct occurred both before and after the death.
The board also noted that in 2022, Wayne had been reprimanded for her dilatory handling of a client’s estate, which raised some of the same issues as in her 2026 disciplinary proceedings. “Wayne has not heeded the warnings her prior discipline delivered,” the board told the Iowa Supreme Court in recommending a 90-day suspension of Wayne’s law license.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Wayne for comment, but in court filings related to her disciplinary case, she admitted each of the allegations against her and consented to a 90-day suspension. In her filings, Wayne stated, “I do not anticipate at this time returning to the practice of law but would like to have the option in the future.”
Wayne told the Iowa Supreme Court that while practicing law, she had handled a large number of cases where she acted as the court-appointed attorney in northern Iowa counties that are underserved by attorneys. Wayne also said she regretted not seeking treatment for her grief and depression and that “it took the suspension of my law license to get to that point.”
On Friday, the Iowa Supreme Court imposed a 90-day suspension of Wayne’s law license.

name: VTDigger
title: Voter voices from Milton’s Bombardier Park
text:
Bombardier Park in Milton as seen on Oct. 29, 2026. Photo by Charlotte Oliver/VTDigger.

MILTON — Troves of adults clutching soccer balls and sporting T-shirts came and went from Bombardier Park on a warm Sunday afternoon. Ahead of the Nov. 3 election, those out for a stroll or showing up for a game shared how they plan to vote. 
Shosawna Mastin, 43, of Milton, said she plans to vote in person next week because she doesn’t believe in mail-in voting. Mastin, who works doing highway construction, said that affordability and the quality of education is top of mind when deciding how to vote. 
“Education in Milton is a huge thing I’m concerned about,” she said. 
The mother of four only has one kid left in school, and she said she thinks the quality of education in town has declined over the years. Mastin declined to say who she supported for governor, but she said she plans to vote Republican across the ticket. 
Jim Lambert, of Milton, who walked along a gravel path with his four dogs, said he already cast his vote for incumbent Republican Gov. Phil Scott with his mail-in ballot. He plans on voting for Republicans in every race, he said. 
Scott, Lambert said, has done a “fair job” at keeping spending and taxes down over the years.
The 67-year-old said he’s worried that military veterans aren’t getting as much support from the government as immigrants, namely for resources like housing. He’s also concerned about the rising cost of living in Vermont, he said, especially for young people looking to buy a house in Milton. 
Calvin Mabie, 32, was heading to a soccer game. He said he voted by mail for Democrat Amanda Janoo for governor. 
Affordable housing is the most important issue to Mabie, he said, and he supports Janoo’s platform on housing. Janoo has said she supports raising property taxes on second homes and vacation rentals with the intent of lowering housing costs and rising property taxes for primary homeowners. 
“I think it’s time for a change,” Mabie said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Clinton Math and Science School senior vying in national Super Kid contest
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
High school senior and Clinton resident Jeremy Burwell is on track to go from being a fan of comics to starring in his own.
He is one of 840 quarterfinalists in Stan Lee’s Super Kid contest. If he wins the national contest, he’ll get a $25,000 honorarium, four VIP passes to Los Angeles Comic Con 2027 and a comic book character based on himself.
Parents must submit an entry form on their child’s behalf. LaToya Clarke-Horne, Burwell’s mother, nominated him to the competition. However, knowing her son can be pessimistic, she waited until he garnered positive results to tell him about the contest. 
“I’m not really sure how to feel…surprised, definitely,” said Burwell, when asked how he felt about the support he’s received.
Clark-Horne describes her son as kind and intelligent. 
“His heart is unmatched,” she said.
“He loves the Lord, he loves people, he loves his family, he loves annoying his sister.”
Jeremy Burwell, left, and his mother LaTonya Clarke-Horne, right, at Harvard University in June 2024. Credit: Courtesy photo
At the time of publication, the contest is in the quarterfinals. Contestants, who must be between the ages of 5 and 17, are divided into groups. To advance in the competition, a contestant must get the most votes out of his or her group. Supporters can cast one vote per day, or donate to the Stan Lee Foundation to cast multiple votes at once.
During the final round, the votes will be reset, and a single winner will be chosen. One quarterfinalist will be the “Critic’s Pick” winner and appear in the comic book along with the Grand Prize winner.
According to Burwell’s profile, he got into comics when his mother was a high school librarian.
His mother said on the profile page, “He would read everything he could get his hands on, and he gravitated to superheroes because of the core values they taught. He often talked about fighting for those who couldn’t help themselves, and I think it just took root. That’s part of the reason why he does his best to help others.”
His favorite heroes are Iron Man and Black Panther, and his preferred super power is healing. Reading is one of his favorite hobbies, along with video games, napping and more.
If he wins, Burwell wants to donate the prize money to local charities and his high school, the Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science in Columbus.
At school, he’s in the Model Security Council, Tales from the Crypt, is an English peer tutor, a senator in Student Government Association and more. He also does tutoring and manages the livestream at his church, Faith Christian Center Ministries in Utica.
Outside of school, he’s part of the Mississippi Department of Education’s State Superintendent Student Advisory Council.
Voting ends on Nov. 19, and the grand prize winner will be announced on Dec. 17.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: As millions pour into Idaho’s US Senate race, Achilles raises more than Risch’s recent challengers
text:
Independent candidate Todd Achilles, left, and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch. (Photos courtesy of the candidates) Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles has collected more than $1.8 in his campaign against incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch — the most of any federal election challenger in recent years. 
Risch’s campaign has collected a total of around $4.1 million since the beginning of 2025, according to the most recent federal election campaign finance data reported by candidates on Oct. 14. Since 2021, the Risch campaign has garnered more than $5 million total. 
Achilles’ fundraising has surpassed former Democratic candidate Paulette Jordan, whose campaign for U.S. Senate in 2020 raised over $1.1 million. Jordan lost to Risch in that race.
“We are proud that so many people have put their trust in this campaign,” Achilles campaign spokesperson Crispin Gravatt said in an emailed statement. “The fact that we have raised the most of any Senate challenger in Idaho history without either party’s support. This is proof positive that Idahoans are truly independent- and excited for Todd!” 
Former Democratic Idaho Congressman Larry LaRocco raised more than $1.4 million in 2008 as he unsuccessfully sought to unseat Risch. In 1992, Democrat and former Idaho Congressman Richard Stallings raised more than $1.2 million in his unsuccessful run against Republican Dirk Kempthorne for U.S. Senate, according to FEC data. 
The Achilles campaign this election cycle has spent more than $1.7 million, and Risch’s campaign has spent over $4.7 million, according to federal campaign finance data. 
Risch will face challengers Achilles, Libertarian Matt Loesby and independent Natalie Fleming in the Nov. 3 general election. Loesby and Fleming did not file federal campaign finance reports.
The Risch campaign could not immediately be reached.

Political Action Committees, or PACs, have contributed a total of $33,000 to his campaign, according to the most recently reported data.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Republicans say they’re not sweating early voter turnout — not yet, anyway
text:
Signs outside of a polling location in St. Petersburg on Oct 21, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Although Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded the alarm about Republican voter turnout earlier this week, other Florida GOP officials insist they’ve little to worry about as Democrats turned out in bigger numbers than they did four years ago in early in-person and mail voting.
Little to worry about yet, anyway.
Anthony Pedicini, a Republican strategist, predicts the Republicans will dominate on Election Day and that everything will turn out just fine for the party in power.
Democrats have already cashed their chips,” he said in an email to the Phoenix. “Their most reliable voters have voted. Ours haven’t yet, because Republican super-voters show up on Election Day. Anyone calling this race before Tuesday is reading half a tea leaf.”
He added: “We’ve heard it at the door, on the phone, and in the surveys: ‘I’m voting Tuesday.’ No one should be celebrating anything in Florida until 7 p.m. Tuesday.”
(Getty Images)
Early voting in Florida ends on Saturday in many counties. Some counties will extend early voting until Sunday, Nov. 1.
In traditionally red Polk County, as of Friday morning, registered Republicans had cast just 468 more votes than registered Democrats. That’s in a county where Republicans have a 13-point registration advantage.
“We’re doing a campaign of trying to get people to go out and vote early because a lot of people, they’re just used to doing it on Election Day, so that’s why the numbers look like they do right now,” said Kat Gates-Skipper, a Polk County GOP state committeewoman. “So, we’re contacting people and telling them, ‘Don’t wait until Tuesday.’”
 Banking on Election Day
Hillsborough County was one of the bluest spots on the map for Democrats during the 2010s, but Republicans overtook them in party registration there in early 2025. The GOP has nearly 20,000 more registered Republicans than Democrats in the county, but Democrats held an 18,312-vote lead as of Thursday afternoon.
“What I’m seeing on the ground, it appears that the Democrats have been able to create or develop more enthusiasm for their top of the ticket than what we’re seeing from Republicans,” said Hillsborough County state GOP committeewoman April Schiff. “I’m not sure why that is, but it is what it is.”
Republicans in recent election cycles have voted in greater numbers than Democrats on Election Day in Florida, and that is what the GOP is counting on. In the August primary, Republican election day turnout was double the number for Democrats (60%-30%).
More than 4.4 million Floridians had voted as of Friday afternoon. Registered Republicans had cast 40.4% of all votes. Democrats had cast 38.4% of votes, a 2% margin. Non-party-affiliated and third-party voters made up 21.2% of the vote. That’s according to the University of Florida Election Lab tracker.
“We have seen Republicans turn out in force on Election Day in the last couple of cycles,” Democratic strategist Jackson McMillan acknowledged. “However, I’m confident at this point that they need to increase their turn-out lead to around R + 25 to be comfortable. And right now we’re in an R+2 environment. So, they need to dramatically increase their lead to be comfortable.”
“Republicans are clearly counting on Election Day to save them, but if I were them I’d be concerned about the combination of increased Democratic turnout and NPAs appearing to break heavily our way,” added Democratic strategist Chris Mitchell. “The enthusiasm is clearly on our side, but this is far from over.”
 Enthusiasm gap
Some Republicans acknowledge dissatisfaction with the Iran war and the attendant high gas prices have hurt the economy and their popularity. They also attribute the sluggish early turnout to the fact that it’s a midterm election.
“It’s just more the traditional reduction in enthusiasm during an off-year election, I think,” said John Roberts, chair of the Escambia County Republican Party. “A presidential election is just going to draw in more people.”
Jack Brill, chair of the Republican Executive Committee in Sarasota County, predicts this year’s midterm elections in Florida will see closer margins than the past two election cycles.
“This will be a closer race like 2018 versus 2022, the governor’s race, where you’re seeing the same polling we’re all seeing,” he said. “It’s going to be a tight race, and it’s going to be a race where Byron [Donalds] will win, but it’s going to be much closer to 2018 than 2022.”
In 2018, the margin of victory for DeSantis, Scott, and Democratic Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried were all within 0.5 percent, triggering statutorily required-machine recounts.
By contrast, DeSantis defeated Democrat Charlie Crist in the 2022 gubernatorial race by 19 points and Republican Marco Rubio won the U.S. Senate seat by 16 points over Democrat Val Demings.
“In ’22, when I was running four years ago, I mean like, you could put hot coals in front of the polling place and our people were going to walk over those barefoot. They wanted to vote, right?” DeSantis said this week during a press conference in Crystal River. “Just a different time.”
Kevin J. Cooper, chair of the Miami-Dade County Republican Party, is confident Trump’s appeal to Republican voters has not waned. The president was the first Republican to carry Miami-Dade in more than three decades when he won there in 2024.
 Toxic’

Cooper believes the Democrats caused themselves a big problem by nominating Angie Nixon as their standard-bearer for Senate, noting her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America.
Any association with socialism can be toxic in Hispanic precincts in South Florida, home to hundreds of thousands of immigrants, refugees, and exiles from authoritarian governments in Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua.
That taints all Democrats running in Miami-Dade, Cooper said, noting the kerfuffle that took place last week when Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries appeared with Democratic Congressional District 27 candidate Eliott Rodriguez at a Cuban bakery in Miami.
While both Democrats have denounced socialism, some social media users criticized the bakery for hosting the two men, accusing it of association with that ideology.
“They go in there, they chitchat, they do whatever they do, and then everyone has to condemn socialism,” Cooper said.
“It just shows you that it’s a great case study as to the way that people are thinking and the way that people are feeling, that these folks go to a Cuban bakery and the bakery has to condemn socialism. When socialism wasn’t even discussed at the event,” he said.
“That just shows you how toxic this issue is from a leadership perspective from the top, that they come to South Florida with this message, and everyone recoils at it. There is no difference between the Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists Party. They’ve basically merged.”
Some observers warn the governor’s race, at least, could prove more competitive than was expected at the beginning of this year. Matt Towery, a pollster with InsiderAdvantage, said his team had been analyzing the early vote in Florida and “it is entirely possible that the race for governor will be very close.”
“While the GOP has a slight advantage in the early vote, there is a large segment of independent voters in the mix … and in our surveys they are breaking more for Democrats this cycle,” he wrote on X.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Lawsuit seeks to block TN from denying driver’s licenses to immigrants legally allowed to work
text:
An immigrant advocacy organization has filed a legal challenge to new state rules denying licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in the United States, placing them at risk for losing jobs without transportation or for arrest, detention and deportation for driving without a license. Pictured: a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer and a Homeland Security Investigations officer searched a vehicle during a traffic stop in Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 7, 2025. (Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)An immigrant advocacy organization filed a legal challenge on Friday to new Tennessee rules that deny driver’s licenses to immigrants who are legally authorized to work in the United States, arguing the state failed to follow its own rules by abruptly shifting long-standing license requirements.
The Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition is seeking an immediate court order to temporarily block the state from denying licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in Tennessee, among them thousands of state residents who have been able to legally hold and renew state licenses for nearly two decades.
The organization is joined in filing suit by six individuals, identified only by their initials, who were recently denied licenses and license renewals, or face being denied a license or license renewal in the future.
The legal challenge, filed in Davidson County Chancery Court, also seeks a finding that new rules, implemented in recent weeks without public input, are invalid. 
Tennessee Gov. Lee questions state rules denying licenses to immigrants legally able to work in U.S.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, legal deputy director of the National Immigration Law Center, among the groups representing the plaintiffs. 
Tennessee “issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them.”  
For many years, the Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security routinely accepted an “employment authorization document” issued by the federal government to immigrants legally allowed to work and live in the United States as sufficient proof of immigration status for the purposes of obtaining a license.
In recent weeks, the department began rejecting individuals seeking new or renewed licenses who presented the federal work permit. For many immigrants who are not permanent residents — such as asylum seekers and so-called Dreamers who were brought to the U.S. as children and are now protected from deportation — the document is among the only valid proof they have of their immigration status. 
On Wednesday, Gov. Bill Lee said he had just learned of the rule change and was in the process of determining “ what impact it actually does have and are there changes we need to make.” 
A spokesperson for the state Department of Safety and Homeland Security on Friday cited longstanding practice in declining to comment on pending litigation.
Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits

Immigrant advocates said the denial of licenses could impact potentially thousands of Tennessee immigrants with legal authorization to be in the country. Without a valid license, they said, immigrants face an impossible choice: stop driving and risk losing their jobs or risk driving and be subject to arrest, detention and subsequent deportation if caught.
Among those recently denied a license is an East Tennessee registered nurse who asked to be identified only by his initials, L.R., who is not a party to the lawsuit.
Speaking at a virtual news conference on Friday, L.R. said he is legally allowed to work and live in the United States as a recipient of DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. DACA recipients were brought to the United States without legal authorization as children and have since been granted the right to legally live and work in the country.
He went to multiple county driver’s centers earlier this month to renew the temporary license that has previously been made available to DACA recipients who are able to produce the credit-card-sized federal work permit cards. He was turned away at each one, he said.
After 20 years in Tennessee, he is considering leaving despite an acute statewide nursing shortage. There is no public transportation in the rural community where he lives, and finding a ride to his job at a Level 1 trauma center at 4 a.m. to begin his shift is impractical, he said.  
“I hate the idea of having to uproot my entire life due to being gatekept (by) a piece of plastic just to survive,” he said. “I’m holding strong to the belief that change can be made, but if I have no other choice then I will relocate and put my knowledge and skills to use in a new place.”
The legal challenge argues the Department of Safety & Homeland Security is violating its own regulations and state law in imposing new rules that limit acceptable forms of immigration status. 
It also challenges the decision as exceeding the department’s authority. 
“Under its new rules, the Department is determining — in place of the federal government — who is authorized to be present in the United States, for what purpose, and for how long,” in violation of state law. 
The lawsuit alleges that in addition to rejecting work permits, the department is no longer verifying license applicants’ status through the federal S.A.V.E. system, an online system administered by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that states use to verify immigration and citizenship status for those seeking “benefits or licenses.”
No court date has yet been set in the legal challenge, which was brought by attorneys with the Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, Nashville law firm Bass, Berry & Simms and the National Immigration Law Center.
