name: Delaware
title: Halloween Weekend in Delaware: 10 Things to Do Across the First State
text:
Photo: Here are 10 events worth considering this weekend. Image created on 10/30 with AI.
From trick-or-treating and haunted attractions to live music, community walks and a major film festival, Delaware offers a full weekend of activities Oct. 30-Nov. 1.
DELAWARE — Halloween falls on a Saturday this year, giving Delaware residents a full weekend to enjoy fall festivals, community celebrations, outdoor activities and live entertainment.
From Wilmington’s Trolley Square to the beaches of Sussex County, events scheduled for Oct. 30 through Nov. 1 offer something for nearly every age and interest.
Families can spend Saturday collecting treats from Hockessin businesses, exploring Fifer Orchards or celebrating Halloween in Milford. Those looking to support a good cause can participate in Wilmington’s Walk to End Alzheimer’s or Milford’s Run for the Arts.
For evening entertainment, Frightland brings Halloween scares to Middletown, while singer-songwriter Suzanne Vega closes the weekend with a Sunday performance at The Queen in Wilmington.
Here are 10 events worth considering this weekend.
1. Walk to End Alzheimer’s — Wilmington
Hundreds of walkers, families and supporters are expected to gather along the Wilmington Riverfront for the annual Walk to End Alzheimer’s, supporting research, care and services for people living with Alzheimer’s disease and their caregivers.
The morning includes a Promise Garden ceremony recognizing people affected by the disease, followed by a 2-mile community walk. Registration is free, although donations and fundraising are encouraged.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31. Registration at 8 a.m.; Promise Garden ceremony at 9 a.m.; walk at 9:15 a.m. Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park, Rosa Parks Drive, Wilmington. Information and registration: Alzheimer’s Association.
2. Halloween in Hockessin: Candy Corn Trail — Hockessin
Hockessin businesses are turning Halloween into a townwide celebration, with 48 local shops, restaurants and organizations participating in a daytime trick-or-treat event.
Organized by the Hockessin Business Association, the Candy Corn Trail invites costumed children and their families to visit participating businesses throughout the community. Locations include Lantana Square, Valley Road, Old Lancaster Pike and Lancaster Pike.
The free event gives families an opportunity to enjoy Halloween while supporting neighborhood businesses.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31, 11 a.m.-3 p.m. Participating businesses throughout Hockessin. Information and participating-business map: Town Square Delaware LIVE.
3. Ladybug Dark Bloom Music Festival — Wilmington
Wilmington’s Trolley Square neighborhood will host the inaugural Ladybug Dark Bloom Music Festival, a free Halloween celebration combining live music, art and seasonal entertainment.
The all-ages event features women-led musical performances, local artists, vendors and a creative atmosphere inspired by autumn, Halloween and Día de los Muertos.
The afternoon festival offers a family-friendly alternative to traditional Halloween activities.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31, noon-6 p.m. Trolley Square, Wilmington. Free admission. Information: Town Square Delaware LIVE.
4. Run for the Arts 5K — Milford
Runners and walkers can combine fitness, Halloween fun and support for the arts during the ninth annual Run for the Arts 5K and 1-mile fun walk in downtown Milford.
Organized by the Mispillion Art League and Seashore Striders, the event benefits local arts programming, including exhibitions, classes and community events. Halloween costumes are encouraged.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31, 9 a.m., with race-day registration beginning at 7:30 a.m. Bicentennial Park, 206-218 NE Front St., Milford. Registration is $25 in advance through 10 p.m. Friday or $30 on race day. Information: RunSignup.
5. Fifer Orchards Fall Fest — Camden-Wyoming
Families looking for traditional fall activities can visit Fifer Orchards for pumpkins, apple picking, a corn maze and outdoor farm attractions.
The festival also features seasonal favorites such as apple cider, cider doughnuts, kettle corn and farm-fresh food. Saturday is the final Halloween-weekend opportunity to enjoy the festivities.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31, 10 a.m.-4:30 p.m., with visitors exiting by 5 p.m. Fifer Orchards, 1919 Allabands Mill Road, Camden-Wyoming. Admission is $18 online or $24 at the gate; some activities cost extra. The festival is closed Sunday. Information: Fifer Orchards.
6. Frightland Haunted Attractions — Middletown
One of Delaware’s best-known Halloween attractions continues its season with haunted houses, a haunted hayride and other spooky experiences.
Frightland offers multiple themed attractions, including Zombie Town, and is geared toward visitors seeking a more intense Halloween experience. The haunted attraction remains open into early November, but Halloween night is likely to be a popular time to visit.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31, beginning at 6 p.m. Frightland, 309 Port Penn Road, Middletown. Saturday ticket booth hours and admission deadlines vary by schedule. Tickets are approximately $55 for Saturday admission. Information: Frightland.
7. Haunted Dover Lantern Tour — Dover
History and Halloween come together during the Haunted Dover Lantern Tour at First State Heritage Park.
Participants follow interpreters through the historic Dover Green while hearing stories of ghostly encounters, local legends and unexplained events connected to Delaware’s capital city.
The lantern-lit walking tour lasts approximately one hour and offers a different way to experience Dover’s historic district after dark.
TO GO: Friday, Oct. 30, 7:30-8:30 p.m. First State Heritage Park, 43 The Green, Dover. Tickets are $15 per person, and advance registration is required. For last-minute availability, call 302-739-9194. Information: Visit Central Delaware.
8. Milford Halloween Trick-or-Treat and Community Activities — Milford
Milford families have several opportunities to celebrate Halloween, including traditional neighborhood trick-or-treating and activities organized by local community groups.
The Carlisle Fire Company is hosting an open house during the day and a Truck or Treat event in the evening, featuring fire department vehicles and treats for children.
Milford’s official trick-or-treat hours are scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m. Saturday, giving families a designated time to visit participating homes.
TO GO: Saturday, Oct. 31. Carlisle Fire Company open house, 11 a.m.-3 p.m.; Truck or Treat, 6-8 p.m. Citywide trick-or-treating, 6-8 p.m. Locations throughout Milford. Information: City of Milford.
9. Rehoboth Beach International Film Festival — Lewes and Rehoboth Beach Area
Film lovers can begin a week of international cinema as the 28th annual Rehoboth Beach International Film Festival opens Sunday.
The festival, running Nov. 1-8, features 113 films representing more than 32 countries, including documentaries, international features, short films and special presentations.
Screenings take place at several venues in the Lewes area, and the festival offers opportunities to see films that may not receive wide commercial theatrical releases.
TO GO: Sunday, Nov. 1, through Sunday, Nov. 8. Screening times vary. Venues include Cinema Art Theater, 17701 Dartmouth Drive, Lewes, and other nearby locations. Individual tickets are $15 for members and $18 for general audiences. Information, showtimes and tickets: Rehoboth Beach Film Society.
10. Suzanne Vega at The Queen — Wilmington
Acclaimed singer-songwriter Suzanne Vega closes the weekend with a Sunday evening concert at The Queen in downtown Wilmington.
Known for songs including “Luka” and “Tom’s Diner,” Vega will perform material spanning her career, along with songs from her 2025 album, “Flying With Angels.”
The performance features longtime guitarist Gerry Leonard and cellist Stephanie Winters.
TO GO: Sunday, Nov. 1, 7:30 p.m. The Queen, 500 N. Market St., Wilmington. Tickets and information: The Queen Wilmington.
Plan Your Weekend
With activities spread across New Castle, Kent and Sussex counties, Delaware residents have plenty of opportunities to enjoy the final weekend of October.
Many Saturday events are outdoors, and several offer free admission. Visitors should check event websites for last-minute schedule changes, ticket availability and weather-related updates before leaving home.
Whether the weekend plans involve raising money for a community cause, taking children trick-or-treating, exploring a haunted attraction or enjoying a night of music, Delaware’s Halloween weekend offers a range of ways to celebrate the season.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ most populous county votes to bar DOJ monitors from entering polling sites
text:
Signs for several candidates line the street outside the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on the first day of early voting on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Officials in Arkansas’ most populous county voted Thursday not to allow monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice inside polling sites on Election Day.
The Pulaski County Election Commission’s 2-1 vote came three days after Washington County’s panel made the same decision unanimously.
Residents of both counties urged the commissioners to reject the election monitors, which the Justice Department is sending to all 50 states. The department informed both counties of its decision on Oct. 20.
Pulaski County Clerk Terri Hollingsworth was among those who spoke against the election monitors Thursday. She cited similar reasons the Washington County commission rejected them: short notice and the Justice Department not explaining why it chose Pulaski County.
Hollingsworth and several others also said the presence of election monitors could intimidate voters. Little Rock Branch NAACP President Marie Hollowell reminded the commission that the city is home to a large proportion of Black voters.
“Black Americans have faced poll taxes, literacy tests, threats and violence simply for trying to vote and let their voices be heard,” Hollowell said. “That history is why we cannot dismiss concerns about intimidation.”

DOJ confirms it’s sending election monitors to Louisiana — and all 50 states

 

Opponents of the monitors also voiced concerns that their presence would intimidate Latino voters, especially following the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement. Washington County also has a significant Marshallese population.
Unlike in Washington County, more Pulaski County citizens at the meeting spoke in favor of election monitors than against them.
“This is certainly not a racial issue,” said Jackie Kaufman, who unsuccessfully ran as a Republican for a quorum court seat in 2024. “If Pulaski County believes that it operates secure elections, then transparency is a non-issue because there’s nothing to hide.”
Marianne Harrington, one of two Republican commissioners, said she supported the presence of election monitors because rejecting them “invites public skepticism.”
Raymond Jarvis, the commission’s chairman and other Republican, said his belief that the county has nothing to hide motivated his vote against election monitors.
Steve Harrelson, the commission’s sole Democrat, and several audience members noted that Republican Secretary of State Cole Jester has touted Arkansas’ elections as the most secure in the nation.
Harrelson, a former state representative, also said he believes “people are for smaller government” and do not want federal officials involved in local administration of elections.
“We rank dead last in [voter] turnout, and everybody’s going to have their opinions over this, but it’s my belief that this is designed to hinder turnout even further,” Harrelson said.
Both candidates for Pulaski County judge spoke at the meeting. Democrat Wendell Griffen, who ousted incumbent County Judge Barry Hyde in the March primary, said he opposed election monitors while Republican Michael Rushin said he was “indifferent” to their presence but wanted more information about where they would be stationed.
With 2 weeks until midterms, analysts say Dems still on track to win US House majority

The election monitors will be in plainclothes and stationed 100 feet outside the polling place, Pulaski County Election Coordinator Amanda Dickens said.
Republican President Donald Trump’s administration has spent the past week trying to assert authority over election officials in multiple states. These actions come on the heels of projections that Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress.
Some Republican-held U.S. House seats are considered competitive, including Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, which includes part of Pulaski County. The Almanac of American Politics moved Arkansas’ U.S. Senate race from safe to “likely” Republican, though other forecasters have labeled the race as safely Republican.
More than 280,000 Arkansans have cast a ballot since early voting began Oct. 19. More than 76,000 Pulaski County residents have voted as of Thursday, the election commission posted on Facebook.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Commentary: Handing out ballots and counting them up
text:
Voters enter a Davidson County early voting site. (Photo: Phoebe Zerwick/Down from DC)“Low visibility ahead,” a Google Maps alert read one recent morning as I drove west on U.S. 421 toward Yadkin County for a meeting of the county board of elections.
And sure enough, when I hit the bridge to cross the muddy Yadkin, a soft fog hung over the river, the effect of cool morning air meeting water that still held the summer’s heat.
A coalition of voting rights groups is sending hundreds volunteers like me across the state to monitor local election officials when they open mail-in ballots and count up votes after Election Day. I’ve also been observing polling places and will continue through Election Day, all part of a nationwide effort to monitor this year’s midterm.
At 8:30 a.m. sharp, the three board members present of the five appointed bowed for a brief prayer and got down to the tedious business of opening absentee ballots. There were 28 total. One ballot was missing the required photo ID, but the voter had filed an exception form. Another ballot came in from the online portal used by military and other voters living overseas.
The board meets in the county warehouse behind its regular office space, which it uses as the only early voting place for Yadkin’s 25,784 registered voters. In 2024, voters here gave President Trump an 80 percent margin, one of highest in the state.
The elections supervisor told the board she had already rejected three ballots because the envelope was missing required signatures, then had spoken with the voters and issued clean ballots. Poll workers would soon be collecting ballots from a local nursing home, well before the Election Day deadline. Then it was time for the board to formally accept all 28 ballots, feed them into the voting machine to be tabulated, and get on with the day.
Not exactly headline-worthy, but it’s these details and the integrity of local officials like the ones in Yadkin County that make for a free and fair election.



An early voting site in Davidson County (Photo: Phoebe Zerwick/Down from DC))




Until the election of 2020, when President Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden, I never worried much about election integrity. But then Trump pressured local election officials across the country to falsify results in his favor, and when that failed, he rallied his supporters who stormed the Capitol to prevent Congress from certifying Biden’s win. He still calls it a rigged election.
Trump’s not on the ballot this year, but his party is, and he’s made it clear he is willing to interfere again if things don’t go his way.
The Department of Justice, at Trump’s urging, has filed a preemptive challenge against the election in Alaska and another suit to stop election officials in California from counting 20,000 mail-in ballots the suit alleges are fraudulent. Trump has not ruled out sending federal agents to polling places and promises a $1 million reward for information on electron fraud. And he has been relentless in spreading lies about widespread cheating, casting doubt about the integrity of our election system and the people who run it.
That’s just not the way elections are supposed to happen. So along with more than 800 other North Carolinians, I signed up for online training in “voter protection,” taught by lawyers from such nonpartisan voting rights groups as Common Cause, Democracy Now, the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, the NC Black Alliance and more.
My husband and I also went through training with the N.C. Democratic Party so that we can observe inside polling places, a role only available to volunteers appointed by the local Republican and Democratic parties. State law does not provide for nonpartisan observers inside the polls.
The state Republican Party is also training poll observers, with a focus on fraud, according to its website: “We must protect the ballot from any form of tampering, fraud or manipulation,” something that multiple studies have shown rarely happens.
To accept or reject
Local boards of election are meeting weekly until Election Day to open mail-in ballots one at a time, checking required signatures, that photo ID’s are present, and that the outer and inner envelopes are both sealed. It’s up to officials in all 100 counties to accept or reject each of these ballots.
The work requires patience and attention to detail. In Davidson County, the board reviewed 361 ballots on Tuesday afternoon, among them 22 cast online from voters living overseas. Two board members, a Democrat from Lexington and a Republican from Denton, transcribed these by hand onto paper ballots so that they could be fed into the vote-counting machines. In the end, the board accepted all but 14 ballots, which they rejected unanimously for several reasons, among them missing signatures or a required photo ID or ballots returned loose inside the outer envelope instead of sealed inside an inner envelope.
Davidson officials said they had sent letters to the 14 voters whose ballots were rejected, with the expectation that they would arrive in time for the voters to correct the error or fill out a clean ballot.
Statewide, the rate of rejected ballots is up from 2.6 percent in 2022 to 3.1 percent, according to figures released last week by the State Board of Elections. The data doesn’t list the reason for rejections. New rules require officials to reject ballots if the inner and outer envelopes are unsealed, and volunteer observers in 27 counties reported that many rejections were related to an unsealed inner envelope.
“Potentially thousands of votes could be spoiled by this new guidance,” Sailor Jones, the state director of Common Cause North Carolina, told The New York Times. “This is a huge deal for North Carolina.” That’s because we’ve had close races here decided by a few hundred votes.
An analysis by Common Cause of state data found that problems with mail-in ballots vary significantly by county. In counties where people of color make up a large share of registered voters, more than 7 percent of mail-in ballots were rejected, reissued or corrected by voters.
An inside view
I also observed election officials inside two polling places in Forsyth County, where I live, without a single instance of potential abuses to report back to the Democratic Party’s “voter protection” program.
Instead, I saw dedicated, knowledgeable election officials doing their best to make sure that eligible voters were able to cast their ballots.
Sometimes that meant trying various spellings of a voter’s name if it didn’t show up right away in the electronic voter rolls. Or if a voter forgot a picture ID, giving them a chance to file a form explaining the missing ID and to cast a “provisional” ballot, which are counted later by local election boards. They also did their best to make voters feel welcome. One worker in Kernersville told corny jokes all afternoon – most voters laughed – and he and his colleagues cheered every time a first-time voter cast a ballot.
And I saw lots and lots of voters: elderly voters with canes; disabled voters in wheelchairs; people dressed in church clothes, patriotic ball caps, sparkly shoes or Doc Martens; parents with their children in tow; first-time voters who barely looked 18; and a woman who had never voted relying on her adult daughter for help both to register and to vote.
The enthusiasm I observed shows up in the data. By Friday morning, more than 2.3 million of 7.8 million registered voters in North Carolina had cast ballots, an increase of 34 percent from the last midterm in 2022. The largest share of these voters have been Democrats and unaffiliated voters.







The president wants us to think that all this is rigged.
The most detailed account of Trump’s effort to cast doubt on the integrity of election officials and of voters was published this week by The New York Times. The report tracked the president’s comments throughout the 456 days of his second term and found that he routinely refers to elections as rigged, crooked, stolen or corrupt – without any evidence to support these claims.
I don’t believe him, and according to recent polling that found widespread confidence across the state in our election officials, neither do most North Carolinians.
I’m headed back to the polls Saturday for the final day of early voting and again on Election Day. If voters get turned away, machines break down or worse, I’ll be there taking notes.
I hope it’s as uneventful as it has been, a bland but powerful record that will hold up against claims that the election was anything but free and fair.
Still, after Election Day, when it’s time for local officials to accept the rest of the absentee ballots and provisional ones and to certify the final vote count, volunteers like me will be back to watch – just in case.
This column was first published in Down From DC, a substack newsletter by Phoebe Zerwick and Natalie Jennings. It’s reprinted here with permission.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana GOP pushing for Republicans to vote — and not stray from the party
text:
The Indiana Federation of Republican Women has launched a digital billboard ad buy urging Hoosiers to vote Republican on Tuesday, November 3. (Photo courtesy of IFRW)Indiana’s Republicans are working to ensure their base comes out for the midterm elections.
Signs of Republican jitters have popped up in turnout texts and social media posts as voters are deciding a hotly contested secretary of state’s race and the GOP works to fend off challenges to its control of congressional and legislative seats.
A letter circulated this week from the Republican chair for northeastern Indiana’s 3rd congressional district warning party members that they can’t openly support non-GOP candidates and remain a “Republican in good standing under party rules.”
“These expectations are fundamental to the trust we place in those who seek office and/or serve in any capacity under the Republican banner,” said the letter from Patricia Brown, who is also the LaGrange County GOP chair.
Similar calls for party action against wandering Republicans have emerged — especially as secretary of state candidates tout GOP supporters who are going against Republican nominee Max Engling.
Former Lt. Govs. Sue Ellspermann and John Mutz, both longtime Republicans, are both supporting Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard — the former GOP mayor of Indianapolis. 
Democrat Beau Bayh, meanwhile, has featured Republican state Sen. Greg Walker (who lost in May’s GOP primary) in a TV ad and this week promoted online an endorsement of Republican Union County Commissioner Tim Williams.
A state Republican spokeswoman didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment Friday about the calls for party sanctions.
Former GOP state party chairman Kyle Hupfer even took to Facebook recently to encourage voting and remind Republicans to stay in line.
“We need all Republicans to get out and vote and come home for Max Engling for Secretary of State, then cast votes for their congressional, state legislative and local Republican candidates,” he posted.
“If you are an elected Republican or hold a party position, I believe that there is no wiggle room. Support the Republican nominee,” Hupfer added.
The Indiana Federation of Republican Women put out a blunt message this past week with some highway billboards saying “Republicans who stay home elect Democrats.”
“Elections are decided by the people who show up,” said Chloe Anagnos Pierce, the group’s president who is also the Engling campaign spokeswoman. “This is the first time our organization has made an ad buy like this, and it reflects just how committed our members are to turning out Republican voters.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Advocates ask lawmakers to close gaps in New Mexico state law regarding domestic violence
text:
Advocates urged lawmakers on Oct. 29, 2026, to amend the state’s family violence law to close domestic violence and animal abuse gaps, such as those governing weapons. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Advocates pitched proposals to New Mexico lawmakers this week to close what they describe as gaps in state law regarding domestic violence and animal abuse. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico’s Family Violence Protection Act allows victims of domestic violence to secure an order of protection — which prohibits a person from hurting, threatening or harassing another person — against their abuser.
Under the current statute, a judge must make a finding of a “credible threat” in order to have the abuser relinquish firearms to authorities within 48 hours of the order being issued. This creates issues with sometimes deadly consequences, Miranda Viscoli, co-president of New Mexicans to Prevent Gun Violence, told lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee during their Wednesday meeting. 
“The last thing you want is somebody who is a domestic violence abuser to have 48 hours to get rid of their firearm,” Viscoli said. “You want that immediately taken.”
Viscoli highlighted the 2023 murder of Aeriel Gallegos after she received a 20-year order of protection against her abuser, Manuel Weahkee. But just two months later, Weahkee shot and killed Gallegos in Farmington before taking his own life. Even though Gallegos received the order of protection, Viscoli said, the box for the judge to indicate that Weahkee was a credible threat — and therefore must give up his firearms — was unchecked. 
State Rep. Joy Garratt (D-Albuquerque) sat beside Viscoli to repropose House Bill 67, which died in the Legislature last session, and would force the domestic abuser identified in a protection order to surrender their firearms immediately, not within 48 hours, and eliminate the requirement that a judge deem a “credible threat” before authorities could seize firearms. 
The bill “is closing a gap in domestic violence protection orders,” Garratt said. 
Committee Chair Rep. Christine Chandler (D-Los Alamos) expressed support for the proposal, adding that “the intent is to mirror” some of the changes found in House Bill 12, passed in the 2025 legislative session, which eliminated the 48-hour period a person flagged by the state’s “red flag” law had to turn over firearms. The “red flag” law allows law enforcement or a district attorney to file a petition to seize a firearm from a person deemed a threat.
As for Garratt’s effort to amend the state’s law on a victim of abuse’s petition, Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez (D-Albuquerque) expressed concern that eliminating the credible threat requirement might create “Second Amendment scrutiny.” Garratt pointed to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in United States v. Rahimi, in which the court ruled that federal law can temporarily ban people under domestic violence restraining orders from having guns. 
Lawmakers also heard from animal advocates who said the Family Violence Protection Act does not include animals in its definition of abuse or provide any provision allowing animals in protection orders. 
“Acts of violence or threats to harm an animal are forms of psychological abuse that abusers will use to control survivors,” Grace Montaño Irwin, government affairs director of Animal Protection Voters, told lawmakers. Between 18% and 48% of domestic violence victims either delayed leaving an abusive situation or returned to their abuser “out of fear” for their pets’ welfare, according to an American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals study. 
As a solution, Montaño Irwin recommended that lawmakers add “harm or threats to harm an animal” to the statutory definition of abuse and require courts to include animals in orders of protection. She noted that New Mexico is one of eight states nationwide lacking these legislative protections.
“For many individuals experiencing abuse, animals are more than companions,” Montaño Irwin said. “They offer comfort, support and security.”
Sedillo Lopez said she plans to introduce a bill incorporating the animal advocates’ recommendations in next year’s legislative session that starts in January, saying, “This bill, I think, is going to be the most popular and probably draw bipartisan support. Data and experience show that if somebody is abusing animals, they’re likely abusing humans as well.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Listen again: All of Searchlight Report’s candidate and ballot-question interviews
text:
Recent episodes of the Searchlight Report podcast have featured interviews with candidates and people involved in ballot-question campaigns. That includes, from top left, South Dakota State Treasurer Josh Haeder, state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, state Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls; from middle left, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, independent U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs, state Rep. John Hughes, R-Sioux Falls, Dakota Rural Action Organizer Chase Jensen; and from bottom left, South Dakota Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley, Democratic U.S. House candidate Nikki Gronli, Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, and Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight; Chase Jensen photo courtesy of Dakota Rural Action)Throughout this campaign season, Searchlight Report podcast episodes have featured interviews with candidates for major statewide offices and people from each side of the four statewide ballot questions.
With Election Day looming on Tuesday, see below for all of those interviews with candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, and pro and con voices on Amendments I, J, K and L.
For more information on other statewide and legislative races, see South Dakota Searchlight’s online Voter Guide.
Governor race
Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden is seeking his own full term in the state’s top office after being elevated from lieutenant governor when then-Gov. Kristi Noem resigned early last year to serve in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden was one of four Republicans running for his party’s nomination during a primary election earlier this year, which was when he was interviewed for Searchlight Report. The primary race resulted in a top-two runoff election, which Rhoden won.
Rhoden is facing Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a businessman and former legislator from Dell Rapids.
Check out these episodes of Searchlight Report to learn more about Ahlers’ and Rhoden’s policy priorities, and to hear a recap of their debate hosted by South Dakota Public Broadcasting and South Dakota News Watch.


 
U.S. Senate
Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds is seeking reelection to a third term as one of two of South Dakota’s U.S. senators. He faces independent Brian Bengs, who previously ran unsuccessfully as a Democrat against Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota.
Rounds spoke to Searchlight about some of his priorities in the Senate, and Bengs spoke to Searchlight about the issues he’s focusing on during his campaign.


 
U.S. House
South Dakota’s lone member of the U.S. House of Representatives, Rep. Dusty Johnson, unsuccessfully sought the Republican nomination for governor earlier this year. That leaves the state’s seat in the House up for grabs.
Democrat Nikki Gronli is a former U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development state director for South Dakota under then-President Joe Biden. Republican Marty Jackley is the state’s attorney general and has also been U.S. attorney for South Dakota.
Senior Reporter John Hult and Searchlight Report Host Meghan O’Brien asked Gronli and Jackley the same set of policy-focused questions.


 
Ballot questions
Voters are deciding on four ballot questions this year. All four are proposed state constitutional amendments placed on the ballot by state lawmakers.
Amendment I would repeal the expanded Medicaid eligibility requirement in the state constitution if the federal government’s share of funding for the expansion drops below 90%. There’s also a dispute about whether the amendment would trigger an immediate termination of expanded Medicaid under that scenario, or whether the amendment would merely give lawmakers the opportunity to consider eliminating the expansion in the event of reduced federal funding.
Amendment J would add language to the state constitution specifying that people who are not U.S. citizens are disqualified from voting. The state constitution already includes citizenship as a voting eligibility requirement.
Amendment K would put unclaimed property — including proceeds from abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and more — in a higher-earning trust fund managed by the state Investment Council, like other funds such as the retirement pool for public employees. Much of that money has previously gone into the state budget, because not all of the rightful owners come forward to claim their property. Yet they could come forward at any time, leading state lawmakers to put the money in a trust fund available to pay claims, while the fund also generates interest for the state budget. Now they’re asking for permission to let the Investment Council manage the fund for higher returns.
Amendment L would raise the bar for passing state constitutional amendments. If it passes, future amendments would need 60% support from voters for approval, rather than a simple majority.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Women’s History House celebrates 25 years in Laramie
text:
Twenty-five years ago, the Wyoming Women’s History House opened in downtown Laramie to celebrate how the state led the nation in women’s suffrage. 
This month, the Louisa Swain Foundation rededicated the house’s courtyard to U.S. Senator Cynthia Lummis, Jon Johnson and Ray Hunkins — three of the house’s original supporters. The foundation also dedicated the courtyard’s two new gardens to Diana Enzi, wife of the late Sen. Mike Enzi, and in memory of Bobbi Barrasso, the wife of Sen. John Barrasso. 
Wyoming’s congressional delegation attended the ceremony alongside state and local officials, and the many volunteers, donors and community members who have made the house possible throughout the decades. 
“Together, this courtyard and these gardens reflect the women we celebrate: rooted in Wyoming, built to endure and open to all,” Jennifer Thomson, foundation chair, said in a press release. “We are grateful for our honorees, our donors and everyone who made today possible, and we look forward to the next 25 years.” 
With community support, the foundation hopes to bring Wyoming women’s history into classrooms across the state through virtual field trips to the house, and renovate the house’s interior for in-person visitors. It’s also aiming to add more drought-tolerant plants to the courtyard, update its irrigation system and create a “trailblazers timeline” along the central walkway that would feature more than 20 Wyoming women who have led the way since statehood.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware’s Business Superstars Honored for Leadership, Innovation and Community Impact
text:
Food Bank of Delaware, Synergy Consultants, First Ascent Design and GGA Construction receive top honors, while retired VanDemark & Lynch President Stephan Lehm earns the prestigious Marvin S. Gilman Bowl for more than 50 years of leadership and community service.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Four Delaware organizations were celebrated for business excellence Thursday, Oct. 29, but one of the most memorable moments at the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce’s annual awards luncheon came when a longtime business leader received an unexpected honor.
Stephan “Steve” Lehm, retired president of VanDemark & Lynch, was surprised with the prestigious Marvin S. Gilman Bowl, recognizing more than five decades of contributions to Delaware’s business community and his commitment to philanthropy.
The presentation was part of the Chamber’s 28th annual Marvin S. Gilman Superstars in Business Awards luncheon at the Chase Center on the Riverfront in Wilmington.
The event also honored four organizations representing different sectors of Delaware’s economy: the Food Bank of Delaware, Synergy Consultants & Psychotherapy Practice, First Ascent Design and GGA Construction.
Each was recognized for business leadership, strong management practices and contributions to the communities they serve.
Lehm honored for a lifetime of leadership and service
For more than 50 years, Lehm has helped shape Delaware through his professional work in civil engineering and his commitment to community service.
As president of VanDemark & Lynch, a Delaware engineering firm, Lehm built a career connected to the state’s development and growth.
His contributions, however, have extended well beyond his professional responsibilities.
The Marvin S. Gilman Bowl, established in 2008, honors individuals who have made exceptional contributions to Delaware’s small-business and nonprofit communities.
Unlike the annual Superstars awards, the recipient of the Gilman Bowl is kept secret until the presentation, making Lehm’s recognition a surprise during Thursday’s luncheon.
“From civil engineering to philanthropy, Stephan Lehm’s work is everywhere in Delaware, even if most people never see his name on it,” said Brett Smith, Marvin S. Gilman’s grandson. “He has spent more than 50 years building this state and giving back to it, leading with the kind of quiet generosity my grandfather admired most.”
The award reflects the values associated with Gilman, a respected Delaware homebuilder whose business philosophy emphasized integrity, innovation and giving back to the community.
Lehm joins a distinguished group of previous recipients whose leadership has helped strengthen Delaware’s economy and nonprofit organizations.
Previous honorees include Charles S. McDowell in 2025, Lawrence J. DiSabatino in 2024, Pamela W. Cornforth in 2023 and Timothy U. Boulden in 2022.
The award recognizes individuals whose influence extends beyond their businesses and whose service has created lasting benefits for Delaware.
The Chamber’s announcement honoring Lehm provides additional information about the recognition.
Four organizations earn Superstar honors
The Chamber presented its 2026 Superstars in Business Awards to four organizations selected from different employee-size categories and the nonprofit sector.
Food Bank of Delaware: Fighting hunger and creating opportunity
The Food Bank of Delaware received the Superstar award in the nonprofit category for its statewide efforts to fight hunger while helping residents achieve greater financial stability.
Working with more than 600 community partners, the organization distributes millions of pounds of food annually to Delaware families and individuals facing food insecurity.
Its work extends beyond emergency food assistance through workforce development programs that provide job training and opportunities for economic independence.
The award recognizes the Food Bank’s combination of direct community assistance and long-term efforts to address the underlying causes of poverty.
Synergy Consultants: Making mental health services more accessible
Synergy Consultants & Psychotherapy Practice received the Superstar award for businesses with one to 10 employees.
The outpatient mental health practice provides therapy and support to individuals, couples and families dealing with anxiety, depression, trauma, grief and significant life changes.
The organization also helps train future mental health professionals and participates in wellness and community outreach programs.
Its recognition demonstrates how smaller organizations can make important contributions to health care and the quality of life in Delaware communities.
First Ascent Design: Helping organizations grow
Wilmington-based First Ascent Design was honored in the category for businesses with 11 to 40 employees.
The digital marketing agency provides branding, website development, digital advertising, search engine optimization and content marketing services.
During its 11 years in business, First Ascent has worked with nearly 300 businesses, nonprofits and educational institutions.
Its work helps organizations strengthen their brands, reach customers and compete in an increasingly digital marketplace.
GGA Construction: Building Delaware’s future
GGA Construction received the Superstar award in the category for businesses with 41 to 150 employees.
With offices in Middletown and Rehoboth Beach, GGA specializes in commercial construction projects throughout Delaware and the surrounding region.
Its portfolio includes health care facilities, educational institutions, hotels, restaurants, senior living communities, multifamily housing and recreational facilities.
The company was recognized for its management practices, leadership and contributions to an industry that plays an important role in Delaware’s economic development.
Four more organizations recognized for excellence
In addition to the Superstar winners, the Chamber honored four organizations with Awards of Excellence for demonstrating notable performance and leadership.
The recipients were:




Sunday Breakfast Mission — Nonprofit category, recognizing its work assisting people experiencing homelessness and other hardships.






Integrity Nursing LLC — Businesses with one to 10 employees, recognizing its work in health care services.






Delmarva Central Railroad — Businesses with 11 to 40 employees, recognizing its role in regional transportation and commerce.






AKA Advisory — Businesses with 41 to 150 employees, recognizing its professional services and business leadership.




The additional awards highlight the diversity of Delaware’s small-business community, from health care and professional services to transportation and nonprofit assistance.
An award rooted in Delaware’s business heritage
Established in 1998, the Marvin S. Gilman Superstars in Business Awards honor the legacy of a respected Delaware entrepreneur who believed that successful businesses should combine sound management with ethical leadership and community involvement.
As president of Gilman Development Company, Marvin Gilman led one of Wilmington’s respected homebuilding firms.
The annual awards program recognizes businesses and nonprofit organizations that have operated for at least three consecutive years and have 150 or fewer employees.
In 2008, the Chamber’s Small Business Alliance expanded the program by establishing the Marvin S. Gilman Bowl to recognize individuals whose professional leadership and community involvement reflect Gilman’s principles.
Together, the awards celebrate both organizational achievement and individual contributions to Delaware’s business community.
Celebrating the people behind Delaware’s economy
The luncheon brought together organizations with different missions but a shared commitment to leadership and service.
For the Food Bank of Delaware, that mission is helping families overcome hunger and poverty. For Synergy Consultants, it is expanding access to mental health services. For First Ascent Design, it is helping businesses and nonprofits strengthen their presence in the marketplace. And for GGA Construction, it is building the facilities that support Delaware’s economic and community growth.
Lehm’s recognition added a personal dimension to those achievements.
His more than 50 years of professional contributions and philanthropy underscore a central message of the Superstars program: Business leadership can have an impact far beyond an organization’s daily operations.
Whether through creating jobs, providing essential services, developing infrastructure or supporting charitable causes, this year’s honorees demonstrate the many ways Delaware businesses and their leaders contribute to the First State.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: More than 135,000 Kentuckians cast ballots on first day of early voting, upping numbers since 2022
text:
A car moves through a drive-through Jefferson County Elections Center at the Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)LEXINGTON — Fred Vickers said he waited more than an hour to vote at the Tates Creek library in Lexington Thursday afternoon. 
“Once you get inside, there’s nothing to it,” Vickers added. He waited to cast his ballot because he felt like it was his “civic duty.” The line at the library stretched out the front door to the road. 
Fayette County, which is in the middle of Kentucky’s most competitive U.S. House race this year, had nearly 7,300 ballots cast during the first day of early voting, according to the State Board of Elections. 
Throughout the state, 135,901 voters participated in the first day of early voting. More than 66,000 of them were Democrats and nearly 61,000 of them were Republicans. That’s about a 65% percent increase compared to the first day of voting in 2022.
Secretary of State Michael Adams, a Republican, said on X during the last midterm election in 2022, about 82,000 Kentuckians voted on the first day of early voting. Ahead of the 2024 general election, which was a presidential year, more than 656,000 Kentuckians voted early. The process is officially called “no-excuse in-person voting.” 
For this year, more than 13,000 voters used excused in-person voting as of Thursday and nearly 43,000 absentee ballots have been returned, or 66% of all absentee ballots issued. 
Early voting is popping nationwide. The University of Florida’s Election Lab said more than 46 million Americans had cast ballots ahead of Election Day this year, eclipsing the early voting turnout of the 2022 midterms. 
An American flag waves in the wind outside a Jefferson County voting center in Louisville. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Adams told the Kentucky Lantern Friday morning that early voting was going well statewide. 
“I think this is the first day of voting since I’ve been in office where I haven’t had my phone going off all day. It’s been very smooth,” Adams said. He added that there have been “rinky-dink micro things” but no “macro issues.” 
Since introducing early voting during 2020, Kentucky has three days of early voting. Whether the state needs to expand that time frame is a question to come, Adams said. 
“If we do see a strong turnout of the early vote, then we have a question to answer, which is: Is it that we need more locations for early voting, or is it that we need more days for early voting, or is it both? Most counties don’t have all their polls open for early voting,” Adams said. 
One county that is trying something new this election cycle is Jefferson County, the state’s most populous county. Clerk David Yates urged the idea of a drive-through voting location this year as a pilot program, said Troy LeBlanc, the chief operating officer of the Clerk’s office. Throughout early voting and Election Day, voters can stay in their car to vote at the Kentucky Expo Center. 
Anderson County was the first in Kentucky to have such a location in 2020, LeBlanc added. Other county clerks have inquired about the program. LeBlanc predicted it will probably be discussed at a future county clerks meeting later in November. 
Jefferson had about 25,000 votes cast Thursday. The clerk’s office said about 1100 were cast at the expo center, which also has a walk-up option for voters. 
“Obviously, it was very overwhelming at first, but once we got into it and to the design and him pushing us as a team to do it, we found that it was actually very achievable,” LeBlanc said. 
Jefferson County’s drive-through location will also be open to all county voters on Election Day. Outside of the expo center, voters must vote in their local precinct, LeBlanc said. 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting in Kentucky lasts through Saturday. To find polling locations by county, visit the Kentucky State Board of Elections website.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Since Civil War, the law has prevented federal agents, including ICE, from polls, voting experts argue
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

During the presidential election of 1863, at the height of the Civil War, federal troops reportedly descended on polling places in Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland and Missouri and prevented people they deemed disloyal from voting. This prompted a fierce national debate that culminated in Congress passing an 1865 law barring federal “troops or armed men” from “any place” where an election is being held.
The central goal of this law, according to its proponents, was “to prevent the president and his officers from interfering in elections,” which are run by the states. Keeping armed federal officers away from the polls, they argued, was necessary to preserve democracy, even in the midst of civil war.
This has been the clear law, and the respected policy of every presidential administration, for over a century.
Until now.
Ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election, top Trump Administration officials have publicly refused to rule out the possibility of sending federal agents to the polls. In September, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that immigration officers could be sent to polling places to “serve a warrant” as part of immigration enforcement operations or if “there is a threat” to those polling places, adding “we’ll be where we need to be.”
“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” hedged Mullin. “We’re there to enforce specific threats.”
Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel similarly said, “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t.”
It is clear to us, and to legal experts, that barring extreme circumstances, sending ICE or FBI agents to the polls for Tueaday’s midterm election would be flatly illegal under the 1865 law, and several others. As Daniel Caine, chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, pointedly said this August, any request to send military troops to election sites would be an “unlawful order.” The same holds true for any other armed federal agents.
Voting spaces for voters Tuesday, Nov. 4, 2025 at Fondren Presbyterian Church in Jackson, Miss. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The only exception to the prohibition is to “repel armed enemies of the United States.” The Congress of 1865 originally included a second exception, allowing armed federal agents to “keep the peace at the polls.” But Congress repealed that exception in 1909 because lawmakers feared that federal authorities could point to any kind of disturbance as a pretext to deploy federal forces.
In other words, unless a hostile foreign power attacks voting sites using weapons, it is a crime for any armed federal agents to go to those sites, even to quell a disruption. And they are certainly not allowed to show up for routine policing or immigration actions.
If sending ICE to the polls is so plainly illegal, then why do top administration officials keep refusing to rule it out?
Context is important. The federal government has been conducting indiscriminate and often violent immigration enforcement actions in communities across the country. At the same time, the administration has been peddling conspiracy theories about widespread illegal voting, often targeting communities of color. The administration has redirected thousands of homeland security agents away from critical transnational security threats to hunt for elusive noncitizen voters.
These efforts are not uncovering any significant problems. Federal and state laws already bar noncitizens from voting in federal and state elections, and our election system does a terrific job of ensuring that only eligible citizens vote, with vanishingly rare exception as dozens of studies, election reviews and painstaking investigations have already confirmed.
This intimidation campaign is taking a toll. According to a University of California, San Diego poll conducted last month, a staggering 40% of voting-age American citizens expect ICE agents to be at the polls this November. Black, Hispanic and Asian American voters are three to four times more likely than white voters to worry that they will be questioned by ICE at polls or that members of their racial or ethnic groups will face intimidation at the polls. This fear is real.
But despite all the administration’s threats, voters should not be intimidated. The law protecting election sites from federal forces is ironclad. Anyone who violates that would be committing a federal crime. Federal and state laws also prohibit any effort to intimidate voters, wherever it occurs.
A broad array of civil rights groups and labor unions have already filed lawsuits to hold the federal government accountable for its intimidation effort – including The Brennan Center, where we work. Other lawyers across the country are poised to run to court to protect elections if federal agents do unlawfully show up to polls.
Outside court, election officials, state government officials, law enforcement and voter protection organizations are prepared to respond to any instance of voter intimidation. That includes de-escalation and backup plans, including changing voting sites if needed, to ensure that all Americans can continue to vote safely. Voters are determined and undeterred, as millions so far have already cast their ballot voting early and by mail.
Our advice to concerned voters: make a plan to vote as early as you can. Voters have multiple options to vote with confidence. In addition to voting at the polls on election day, they can vote early in person or vote by mail ballot, dropping it off in secure ballot drop boxes, at an election office or by mail. In Mississippi, people 65 and over, the disabled and those who will be away from home on election day, can vote until noon Saturday at the circuit clerk’s office or by mail, but the ballot must be postmarked by election day on Tuesday.
You can also go vote with a trusted group of loved ones or neighbors.
It is an outrage that the federal government has refused to rule out the idea of federal agents at the polls. In our view, it is part of a campaign to intimidate voters and undermine our elections.
The only way it will succeed is if voters don’t show up.

Wendy Weiser is vice president for democracy at the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School, a nonpartisan think tank and public interest law center that works to revitalize, reform and defend our systems of democracy and justice. She oversees the center’s work on voting rights and elections, redistricting and representation, federal reform, abuse of power and the courts.
Jasleen Singh is a senior counsel and manager in the Brennan Center’s Democracy Program, where she focuses on voting rights and elections. She previously served as deputy attorney general in the Civil Rights Enforcement Section of the California Attorney General’s Office. Her work has been cited in outlets including the New York Times, Los Angeles Times and CNN.

name: Delaware
title: Kirkwood’s $10M makeover aims to put Delaware on sports-tourism map
text:
BPG Sports officially unveiled Sprinturf Performance Park on Thursday, Oct. 29, the new name for the former Kirkwood Sports Complex at 1220 River Road.
Newly renamed Sprinturf Performance Park combines state investment and BPG Sports management as Delaware looks to attract more regional and national tournaments
NEW CASTLE, Del. — For generations of Delaware soccer players and families, it has simply been Kirkwood.
Now, a $10 million investment is transforming the longtime youth sports complex south of New Castle into a centerpiece of Delaware’s growing effort to attract tournaments, athletes and sports-tourism dollars from across the region.
BPG Sports officially unveiled Sprinturf Performance Park on Thursday, Oct. 29, the new name for the former Kirkwood Sports Complex at 1220 River Road.
The 65-acre, county-owned complex has undergone significant improvements, including the conversion of four natural-grass fields to synthetic turf and the addition of lighting. The broader capital program also includes renovations to the facility’s indoor turf arena.
The complex now advertises five lighted synthetic-turf fields and seven natural-grass fields, providing space for soccer, lacrosse, field hockey and other sports.
But the changes represent more than a facelift for a 34-year-old soccer complex.
They are also part of a larger effort by Delaware and private sports operators to turn the state’s athletic facilities into economic-development engines capable of bringing thousands of traveling athletes and their families to Delaware.
$4 million in state funding
Of the approximately $10 million investment at the Kirkwood property, $4 million came from Delaware’s Sports Tourism Investment Fund, according to reporting surrounding Thursday’s unveiling.
The fund was established to support capital projects that can attract sporting events and visitors to Delaware. State budgets have allocated $10 million annually to the Sports Tourism Capital Investment Fund in recent years.
Gov. Matt Meyer used Thursday’s event to argue that developing facilities on this scale requires cooperation between government and private operators.
“The reality is, with public funding alone, there’s no way we can do things like this across our county,” Meyer said at the event, according to WDEL. “It takes a strong, private partner.”
The state’s rationale is economic development.
Delaware tourism officials estimate that out-of-state visitors attending sporting events generated $231.4 million in spending at venues, hotels, restaurants and entertainment businesses, according to information presented at the unveiling.
The idea is straightforward: A weekend soccer, baseball or lacrosse tournament can bring hundreds or thousands of families into Delaware, many of whom need hotel rooms, meals, gasoline and entertainment during their stay.
BPG building a statewide sports network
The Kirkwood project also highlights the increasingly large role of Wilmington-based BPG Sports in Delaware’s youth and amateur sports business.
BPG Sports, an affiliate of the Buccini/Pollin Group, manages or operates a growing portfolio of sports facilities that includes Chase Fieldhouse in Wilmington, DE Turf in Frederica, Sprinturf Performance Park, WSFS Bank Sportsplex, Sports at the Beach near Georgetown and the planned Delaware Indoor Track facility.
That makes the Kirkwood investment part of a broader statewide network rather than a standalone project.
BPG describes itself as a full-service sports management company involved in athletic facilities, clubs and sporting events. Its facilities stretch from New Castle County through Sussex County.
The Sprinturf agreement adds another component.
Sprinturf entered into a multiyear agreement with BPG Sports to become the naming-rights partner for the New Castle complex and the official turf partner across BPG Sports’ portfolio.
Stephen Cavalier, senior vice president and general manager of BPG Sports, said the company had previously used Sprinturf products and viewed the broader partnership as a way to maintain consistent standards across its facilities.
Kirkwood soccer remains
For families who have spent years playing recreational soccer at Kirkwood, perhaps the most important part of the announcement is what is not changing.
The Kirkwood recreational soccer program is expected to remain at the complex.
Cavalier said during the unveiling that the existing Kirkwood Soccer Complex recreational league will continue to have a home at the facility.
Cavalier also has personal ties to Kirkwood, having played youth soccer at the complex himself.
But youth sports have changed significantly since Kirkwood opened more than three decades ago.
Travel sports, rankings and increasingly large regional tournaments have created greater demand for facilities that can host multiple games regardless of weather and continue competition into the evening.
“It has moved into a more competitive format,” Cavalier said during Thursday’s event. “These large-scale events are really what drive tournaments, and rankings, and things like that. Having facilities like this, we can host them.”
Sprinturf says the New Castle facility attracts more than 1.5 million visitors annually and hosts 15 large-scale tournaments each year, in addition to recreational programs, travel clubs, adult leagues and school teams. Those attendance figures come from the company and have not been independently verified.
A new experience for families
Families returning to the complex will notice more than artificial turf.
Two former fields were removed to make room for expanded parking as the facility prepares for larger events.
Tournament parking also represents a change for users. BPG Sports has introduced paid parking through ParkMobile, with parking enforcement at the site during applicable events.
Those changes illustrate the balancing act facing the revamped facility: maintaining Kirkwood’s traditional role as a community sports complex while developing the infrastructure needed to compete for larger tournaments.
More sports-tourism investment coming
The strategy is unlikely to end at Kirkwood.
Delaware Tourism Director Jessica Welch said during Thursday’s event that officials are particularly interested in indoor sports facilities that can attract visitors during months when outdoor tournaments are less practical.
“We want people to come here in January, February, and March, in those off-season, shoulder-season months,” Welch said. “So the indoor facilities are the ones that we are looking at.”
That could make the Kirkwood transformation an early chapter in a much larger Delaware sports-tourism buildout.
For local soccer families, however, the change is more immediate.
The Kirkwood name may no longer be on the entrance, but soccer will continue to be played on River Road — now on a complex designed to bring considerably more of the sports world to Delaware.

Sports: Soccer, lacrosse, field hockey and other field sports
Formerly known as: Kirkwood Sports Complex

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Unenrolled candidates are on the rise in Maine. So are questions about their party ties.
text:
Among the independent candidates running for Maine Legislature are (starting from top left) Clinton Collamore in House District 45, incumbent Rep. Sharon Frost of House District 58, Jason Litalien in Senate District 32 and Eryne Soule in Senate District 21. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]When Maine Rep. Sharon Frost was knocking doors as part of her re-election campaign, she said she frequently heard voters say, “‘I’ll vote for you because you’re independent, I’m sick of both parties.’”
Frost is the only incumbent independent running for Maine Legislature, but across the state, there are 25 more unenrolled candidates — 19 vying for the Maine House of Representatives and seven for Maine Senate. That is the highest number of independent candidates running in a decade, according to previous years’ of election data. 
Last session there were only four independents serving in the Legislature, three state representatives and Sen. Rick Bennett, who unenrolled from the Republican Party in 2025 before he announced his bid for governor.
In a state where almost a third of voters were unenrolled as of November 2024, the number of independent candidates may sway control of Augusta, which the Democrats have held for eight years. 
Maine Morning Star spoke with almost a dozen legislative incumbents, former lawmakers, political science experts and others about the influx of independent candidates, their alliance with either party and the history of independence among their constituencies. 
“I think Maine is a state that really values individualism and being an independent —a true independent — and I think we have a long history of respecting people as well as politicians who do that,” said Shanna Cox, a Democrat running against an independent candidate in Lewiston.
“But,” she added, “I think doing it as a strategy to shoehorn conservative ideology into a left-leaning district or vice versa, liberal ideology into a right-leaning district … it’s been in the playbook for a long time.” 
Another reason several unenrolled candidates cited for running as independents is the increasing polarization among both parties, and voters’ desires to distance themselves from it. But despite the message they’re campaigning on, not all independents are truly unaffiliated. 
“I’m encouraged by people who are truly independent, but I’m discouraged by people who are just you know shedding the label of the parties to run,” Frost said. “I would like to see more actual independence.” 
Influx of independents 
According to a Maine Morning Star analysis of the past 10 years of election results, more independents are running in this election than any other in the past decade. The next closest was in 2018, when 24 independents ran. Every other election, fewer than 20 unenrolled candidates have run. Rob Glover, a political science professor at the University of Maine, said in his 16 years teaching politics, he has not observed this many independent candidates vying for state office in one year. 
“Seems to be more people who were very, very recently Republicans and are continuing to be supported by Republican donors and the Republican organizing apparatus running as independents,” he said.
Outside groups spending millions to oust state lawmakers up for reelection

President Donald Trump’s low approval rating might be driving Republicans to leave the party and run unenrolled.  
“Midterm elections are often kind of a referendum on who’s held power and how things are going, and right now things are pretty challenging,” Glover said.
If enough independents win, it may actually shift the power dynamics in Augusta. “You could imagine a situation whereby if you have legitimate independents who are not affiliated with a party, that they kind of use that leverage and it deprives one side or the other of a majority,” Glover said. “They kind of become their own independent caucus and can work with both sides and encourage compromise, but that presupposes that they are in fact legitimate independents.”
Despite the lack of party ties, state parties and outside groups — which do not coordinate with campaigns or have to disclose their donors — are actively supporting some of the independent candidates based on their previous affiliations or positions. 
Frost, who caucuses with Democrats, has received $32,000 from left-leaning groups, according to data from the Maine Ethics Commission website, as of Thursday.
Her race is the second most expensive of the 151 Maine House districts this year,  despite representing fewer than 10,000 people in the Belgrade area. She is facing off against Republican Dexter “Buzz” Bridges for a swing seat that over the last decade has been held by both Republicans and Democrats.
A political flyer paid for by outside groups opposing independent Rep. Sharon Frost. (Photo Courtesy Sharon Frost)
Bridges, who did not respond to requests for comment, has been backed by almost $60,000 in spending by outside groups.
“I wish that that money would have gone to other things,” Frost said. Instead, she said a lot of the opposition’s spending has been directed to negative ads and flyers against her.
While Frost’s race is against a Republican, the majority of independent candidates — 16 of 26 — are challenging Democrats this election cycle, many of whom are incumbents in reliably Democratic districts. 
 Southern Maine independents challenging Democrats
Three of these races are in York County, where incumbent Sen. Henry Ingwersen, along with Reps. Marc Malon of Biddeford and Traci Gere of Kennebunkport, are all running against independents.
Malon said while their challengers are all unenrolled, they represent an array of views. His opponent, Marc Lessard, is a moderate city councilor, based on his responses at a candidate forum hosted by the Biddeford Buzz. He also has a record of supporting some Democrat-led initiatives, such as a local ordinance prohibiting city cooperation with federal immigration agents, which Malon pointed to as an issue on which they agree. 
Lessard did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
“In my race the choice is between someone who holds Democratic values, which is me, or someone who is more conservative and is also kind of a lone wolf and I would not think would be particularly effective,” Malon said.
But Ingwersen’s opponent, Jason Litalien, is being accused of hiding his partisanship. . Malon said he’d argue Litalien is an example of “Republicans masquerading as independents, no matter what they might say on the record.”
Litalien told Maine Morning Star local Democrats were attempting to bad-mouth him, adding that he has voted for “independents, Democrats, and Republicans at all levels of government.”
He said if elected, he would not caucus with either party. 
On his campaign website, social media and in his responses to Maine Morning Star, he appears to hold many typically Republican positions, including a desire to audit the Maine health department, opposing transgender athletes’ rights to play on teams aligning with their gender identity and opposing syringe service programs.
In an email to Maine Morning Star, he said the harm reduction policy of allowing intravenous drug users to exchange old syringes for 100 clean ones goes against common sense.
”Not only is it counterintuitive to give someone using a needle to kill themselves 100 more chances to do so,” he wrote, “but it also ignores the working Mainers that are having to pay for their needles just to survive and go to work to pay taxes to provide drug users with free needles.”
Sen. Henry Ingwersen at protests in Biddeford against federal immigration agents this summer. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
He also criticized Ingwersen’s attendance at a local protest opposing federal immigration enforcement in Maine following the fatal shooting of Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. He said, “Henry ran to Mechanic’s Park to protest without any facts or evidence to support his claims, but when the (the Department of Health and Human Services’) website shows child fatalities he ignores them,” referring to legislative oversight of child protective services. 

Ingwersen is running under the Maine Clean Elections Act and receives no outside spending.  According to campaign finance disclosures, Litalien has received $24,000 from conservative-leaning PACs.
Litalien said he disagrees with some of the rhetoric and negative content of the mailers paid for by Common Sense for Maine, which has backed several Republican legislative candidates this election cycle. But, he noted that candidates are not allowed to coordinate with PACs, “so I have absolutely no control over what their free speech produces and I have no idea what they are planning on sending out.”
Ingwersen, who first served in the House and has been in the Senate since 2022, said the reason several independents are backed by conservatives in the Biddeford area might be strategic. 
“If they remove the Republican label and run the candidate as unenrolled or independent, they’re hoping to gain votes and run candidates whose views are just as conservative or extreme as it would be if they were Republicans,” he said. “But if candidates are going to declare themselves as unenrolled, they also need to be independent from any influence from either party.”
Lewiston race heats up 
A similar race is unfolding in Lewiston, where Cox, who’s running against independent Eryn Soule to replace outgoing Democratic Sen. Peggy Rotundo, has noticed a recent uptick in negative ads against her.
Cox, who stepped down as head of the regional Chamber of Commerce to run for office, said voters consider her a moderate and that she plans to work across the aisle. She said she doesn’t often discuss her opponent on the campaign trail, but will clarify for voters that Soule recently unenrolled from the Republican Party. 
Independent candidate Eryn Soule’s sign displayed on the side of the road. (Photo by Emma Davis/Maine Morning Star)
“I think the thing that I hear most commonly is folks saying, ‘I don’t know if she’s actually independent. I only ever see her yard signs with other Republicans,’” Cox added. “I think that is one of the most visible ways that people identify ideology alignment, if not registered party alignment.” 
Soule admitted that she’s been a Republican for years, and only recently unenrolled to run for state office because it wasn’t a consideration as a nonpartisan Lewiston city councilor. She described herself as fiscally conservative, highlighting her vote several years ago in favor of a low-barrier shelter in Lewiston, but said she was opposed to the city funding it.  
She said her motivation for leaving her party was not to distance herself from President Donald Trump’s administration, though she did vote for him, nor was it a campaign ploy.
“I’ve lived here for long enough to know that Republicans are not well loved here in Lewiston … but that is not why I unenrolled,” she said. 
Soule has not determined whether she will caucus with Republicans, though said the party has reached out while she said she’s been “blacklisted” by the Democratic Party.
“I think the parties worked while they worked, and they clearly are no longer working,” she said. “When people won’t even speak together or work together, that’s not good for Maine.”
Soule, like Litalien, is backed by Common Sense for Maine, but Democrat-leaning PACs including the Maine Democratic State Committee have spent more than $11,000 to oppose her. 
While left-leaning political action committees have also spent more than $23,000 to support Cox, she said, “none of my ads that I’ve personally authorized or that have come from my campaign or that I’ve approved have been negative, or have mentioned my opponent.”
“I think you’ll find that that’s not true in reverse,” she added. 
Focus on local issues in Lincoln County 
In House District 45, both Republican Becky Stephens and independent Clinton Collamore disavowed the influence of national politics on local elections, saying they are focused on what their Waldoboro-area constituents need from their representatives.
“National politics seems to seep into some of these local races, in my opinion, in a really strange way,” Stephens said. 
“We’re worried about the rhetoric about what’s happening nationally … instead of just focusing on the people that live in the districts.” 
Stephens has been a Republican her whole life, but told Maine Morning Star she isn’t afraid to disagree with her party if it benefits her constituents. 
Three conservative PACs have spent more than $32,000 to support Stephens in the race, but the only flyer she has sent out was to invite voters to an event where she served ice cream sundaes and talked about local issues such as high electric and heating bills.
But the outside groups sending out flyers on her behalf, one of which opposed Collamore, used her full first name, which she does not go by. 
“Which would let you know why these mailers didn’t come from me because they all say Rebecca on them, and all my stuff says Becky,” she said. “They obviously didn’t check out my website beckyformaine.com,because they just looked at what registration looked like I guess.”
Collamore is a former Democratic state representative who resigned after being charged with campaign violations and is now running as an independent. He said he unenrolled from the party soon after he left the Legislature in 2023.
“I just kind of think that it’s a group of people that’s overlooked, and it might be the independents that can maybe bring people together,” he said.
“People don’t want petty bickering, they want issues resolved.”
Like Stephens, he said he’s running to focus on problems his local constituents have told him about. 
“This isn’t Washington D.C., that’s where you expect it,” he added. “For me, it’s local. These races will come and go but after this is over, all of us here still have to live together in this community.”
