name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Long before the Salem witch trials, Connecticut executed its own
text:
In 1648, Wethersfield’s Mary Johnson claimed the devil helped round up her hogs. She was then executed for witchcraft.
“I think the devil had bigger fish to fry than rounding up hogs,” Martha Smart, a volunteer librarian with the Wethersfield Historical Society, said.  
Johnson was the second of 11 known people executed for witchcraft in Connecticut in the 1600s. In fact, Connecticut was the site of the first known witchcraft executions in America — decades before the infamous Salem witch trials.
Alice, or Alse, Young of Windsor was tried, convicted and executed a year before Johnson. These two women went through the first of 27 documented witchcraft trials and 14 convictions in Connecticut. In total, there were 49 documented witchcraft cases in nine towns across the state according to the Wethersfield Historical Society and John Demos’ “Entertaining Satan: Witchcraft and the Culture of Early New England.”
Despite being the first witchcraft execution in the country, little is known about Young’s case. But in 1647, the same year Young was executed, there was an influenza outbreak in the Connecticut and Massachusetts colonies. Around 90 people died — including prominent leaders in the settlements.
“Puritans thought things didn’t just happen,” Smart said. “There was a reason for them.”
Many settlers believed these deaths were the work of the devil, according to Smart. So, they began searching for the “agent of the devil” within their own communities — witches.
“Thou hast entertained familiarity with Satan, the great enemy of God and Mankind; and by his help has done works above the course of nature,” reads the indictment of Joan Carrington, a Connecticut woman tried and executed for witchcraft in 1651. “According to the laws of God and the established laws of this commonwealth thou deservest to Dye.”
This type of indictment — accusing the indicted of familiarity with Satan — was common for those accused of witchcraft, Smart said. Joan Carrington and her husband, John, were both tried, convicted and executed for witchcraft in 1651.

Of the 11 people executed, nine were women and two were men. Some people had cases brought against them multiple times, and some people escaped before their punishment or trial. Others had their sentences reprieved.
In 2023, the state House of Representatives offered absolution, though not exoneration, to the nine women and two men hanged for witchcraft.
The trials are closely related to documented spread of disease in the colonies. The first trials and executions came during the flu outbreak. In 1662, a second group of trials, coined the “Hartford Witch Panic of 1662,” began after the death of a young girl who was believed to have been bewitched. Dozens of people during these two periods were put on trial.
For the next 24 years, there were no trials, convictions, indictments or executions on the basis of witchcraft. But in 1692, more people fell ill, and seven more people were indicted within the year. 
The last two trials were held in Connecticut in 1697 — the same year as another flu outbreak in the state.

name: Delaware
title: Wilmington Woman Identified as Victim in Fatal New Castle Crash
text:
POLICE LOG – October 30, 2026
NEW CASTLE, DE — Delaware State Police have identified 30-year-old Elizabeth Ramirez Tellez of Wilmington as the woman who died following a two-vehicle crash Wednesday morning in New Castle.
The crash occurred October 28, 2026, at approximately 8:45 a.m. at the intersection of West Basin Road and Washington Avenue.
According to investigators, Ramirez Tellez was driving a Hyundai Elantra southbound on West Basin Road in the left-turn lane approaching Washington Avenue.
At the same time, a Chevrolet Tahoe driven by a 21-year-old man from New Castle was traveling northbound on West Basin Road in the right lane.
Police said both vehicles entered the intersection at the same time for reasons that remain under investigation.
The front of the Chevrolet Tahoe struck the passenger side of the Hyundai, causing the Hyundai to crash into a traffic signal pole.
Ramirez Tellez was transported to an area hospital, where she died from her injuries.
The driver of the Tahoe was also taken to an area hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
The roadway was closed for approximately four hours while investigators examined the crash scene and crews cleared the wreckage.
Delaware State Police have not released additional information about what caused the collision.
The Delaware State Police Troop 2 Collision Reconstruction Unit continues to investigate.
Anyone who witnessed the crash or has video footage of the collision is asked to contact Master Corporal R. Kunicki at 302-365-8417.
Information may also be provided through Delaware Crime Stoppers at 800-847-3333 or by sending a private Facebook message to Delaware State Police.

title: Early voting sets midterms record, breaking 2022 mark
text: WASHINGTON — As of early Friday, more than 46 million Americans had cast ballots ahead of Election Day, eclipsing the early voting turnout of the 2022 midterms, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab.In the 2022 midterm elections, 45.9 million Americans voted early, according to the UF Election Lab. It’s still unclear if this year’s midterm elections will break the overall record voter turnout of 2018. The 53% turnout that year was the highest rate in a midterm since 1914.UF political science Professor Michael McDonald, who leads the election lab, said in an interview this week that based on the incoming early voting data, overall turnout is shaping up to match 2018 participation. Of the early voting participants up to Friday, 43.9% are registered Democrats, 31.3% are registered Republicans and 24.8% have no party affiliation, according to the UF Election Lab.Republicans are vying to maintain their majority in both chambers amid anemic presidential approval ratings that stem from an unpopular war in Iran and an aggressive immigration crackdown. Democrats are favored to win back the majority in the House, which presidents often lose in midterm elections, and potentially the Senate, according to elections forecasters. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted 12 House races in the direction of Democrats on Oct. 30. The elections forecaster lists 18 House races as toss-ups.In the Senate, the Cook Political Report identified seven toss-up races, in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A developer’s warning: Question 7 is not an affordable housing plan
text:
LONG BEFORE I became a residential land developer, my father was fighting development. 
I grew up in Westwood, where he was involved in efforts to protect forested land from clear-cutting and development. After a decade-long battle, much of that land remains preserved through Hale Reservation and Westwood Land Trust. 
There is some irony in the fact that I ultimately made a career out of residential land development. 
But I like to think I inherited part of his perspective. My work is pro-housing and pro-development, but I also believe responsible development means balancing growth with open space, mature trees, environmental constraints, and the existing character of a place—not simply maximizing lot count. 
That is one reason Question 7 concerns me. Another is practical: I know what I would do with it. 
In fact, if Question 7 passes, I may be almost obligated to start shopping for deals in Massachusetts. That probably tells you something about how developers will view it. 
Question 7 would establish a statewide right to build a single-family home on a lot of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of frontage where public water and sewer are available. Local governments could retain “reasonable” regulations, including setbacks, height, bulk, open space, and parking, but could not prohibit, unreasonably restrict, or require discretionary zoning approval for that use. 
The argument is intuitive: Smaller lots reduce land cost, so they should produce less expensive homes. 
Sometimes they do. But smaller lots do not require cheaper homes. That distinction matters because zoning does more than regulate what can be built. It affects what land is worth. 
If an older $600,000 house sits on land that can suddenly support two more valuable homes, that property is no longer competing only as a $600,000 residence. It is competing as redevelopment land. A builder can pay more for it because the development rights are worth more. The existing house may become more valuable to demolish than to preserve. 
I have watched this happen in Nashville. 
Across much of East Nashville, modest older homes have been demolished and replaced with pairs of narrow detached houses commonly called “tall-skinnies.” A house that might have sold for $600,000 can disappear and be replaced by two homes selling for approximately $1.2 million each. 
That is housing production. But it is not affordable housing. 
It is gentrification. It is capitalism. It is the market doing what markets do: making the most profitable use of a development opportunity. 
Question 7 would certainly increase housing production. It does not ensure that the homes produced will be affordable. 
The scale of the zoning change also matters. Massachusetts communities were not all planned around the same development pattern. Across suburban towns, conventional single-family zoning can range from relatively compact lots to one-, two-, and even three-acre minimums. A 5,000 SF threshold may be familiar in an urban neighborhood designed around tight setbacks, compact blocks, alleys, and infrastructure that supports smaller lots. In a community built around acre-plus lots, it represents something very different. 
That does not mean 5,000 SF lots are inherently bad. They are not. Smaller lots and greater density can be useful tools for addressing housing supply. The question is whether those additional development rights should be granted statewide without requiring the housing outcome being used to justify them. 
Question 7 does not require the resulting home to be affordable, modest, or small. There is no statewide sales-price restriction, affordability requirement, owner-occupancy requirement, or cap on house size. 
Yet Massachusetts already has a policy aimed more precisely at the starter-home problem. 
Chapter 40Y allows municipalities to create Starter Home Zoning Districts where qualifying homes are permitted as of right at a minimum density of four homes per acre. Homes are capped at 1,850 square feet, at least half must have three or more bedrooms, and developments of more than 12 homes must make at least 10 percent affordable to households earning up to 110 percent of area median income. 
Just as importantly, 40Y allows communities to pair that density with reasonable design standards and open-space planning. In other words, it recognizes that housing production, affordability, neighborhood form, and conservation do not have to be treated as mutually exclusive goals. 
That is the model worth strengthening. 
Allow smaller lots. Allow meaningful density. Make approvals predictable and by right. But do it alongside thoughtful open-space, environmental, and neighborhood-character standards. Make it easier and more profitable for developers to build the modest, family-oriented homes Massachusetts needs. 
The economics matter. Additional development rights are valuable. When government increases what can be built on a piece of land, we as developers run the numbers, determine the highest and best use, and compete for that opportunity. That is not a criticism of developers; it is how the market works. 
If the public is granting valuable new development rights in the name of affordability, it should expect affordability in return. 
Smaller lots can produce more housing. 
They do not, by themselves, produce affordability. 
Alex Becker is a partner and land development specialist at EcoTerra, a Tennessee firm focused on development that designs projects around the natural character and contours of sites.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Republicans pull ahead in early voting, lagging in battleground districts in West Virginia
text:
An early voting sign sits outside of the Girl Scouts of Black Diamond Council building at 321 Virginia St. W in Charleston, West Virginia, on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Republicans have edged out Democrats in casting early in-person ballots, but are lagging behind in key battleground districts, according to data released by the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office on Thursday. 
Overall, 115,855 votes have been cast, 30% higher than during the same period of the 2022 midterms, according to a news release. 
Data shows as of Wednesday, 45,333 Democrats have either voted in person or returned absentee ballots, while 47,153 registered Republicans have done the same. 
Voters registered as no party, or other party — meaning not a member of one of the recognized minor parties in the state — accounted for 22,845 of early ballots cast in person or through the mail. 
However, in counties with tough state house races, the Democrats appear to be outnumbering Republicans in early and absentee voting. 
In Cabell and Wayne counties, where an open state Senate seat is up for grabs, 3,807 Democrats have either voted early or returned an absentee ballot, compared to 3,337 Republicans. 
In the Northern Panhandle, where a one-term incumbent Republican is facing a challenge from the House minority whip, there’s similar margins in Ohio, Brooke, Hancock and Marshall counties. 
So far, 2,943 Democrats have either early voted or returned an absentee ballot, while 2,715 Republicans have done the same. 
In the Morgantown-Fairmont area, where two seasoned politicians are vying for state Senate, the margins are even wider. So far, 6,448 Democrats have cast a ballot in Marion and Monongalia counties, while only 4,054 Republicans have done so. 
Early voting concludes on Saturday, Oct. 31. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: California
title: Departamento de Justicia cita a declarar a funcionarios electorales de California a pesar de la orden del juez de que dejen de amenazarlos
authors: Jeanne Kuang, Ryan Sabalow, and Sergio Olmos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El miércoles, un juez federal emitió una orden contundente advirtiendo a los fiscales federales que dejen de amenazar con delitos a los funcionarios electorales de California.
 Un día después, los fiscales federales continuaron con el proceso.
 Al menos cuatro trabajadores electorales en California han recibido citaciones del gran jurado federal durante la última semana, y al menos una de ellas fue entregada el jueves tras la orden judicial.
 En esa citación judicial, emitida a la oficina del Registro de Votantes del Condado de Orange, agentes federales del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional solicitan los registros de votantes sin censurar de 60 personas, según documentos obtenidos por CalMatters.
 Las citaciones judiciales señalan una intensificación de la vigilancia sin precedentes del gobierno federal sobre las elecciones de California, lo que podría derivar en un enfrentamiento sobre los fundamentos de la democracia estadounidense en torno a las elecciones de mitad de mandato del próximo martes.
 Entre los fiscales se encuentran miembros de la oficina del fiscal federal principal de Los Ángeles, Bill Essayli, un asesor destacado en la campaña del presidente Donald Trump para encontrar pruebas que respalden las antiguas afirmaciones —nunca probadas— de que las elecciones de California están amañadas a favor de los demócratas debido a los votos de personas que no son ciudadanas.
 Bloomberg Law informó el jueves que los líderes del Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos habían ordenado a los principales fiscales federales que solicitaran citaciones judiciales a funcionarios estatales y locales para investigar si se permitía votar a personas no ciudadanas. El medio citó a dos fuentes anónimas familiarizadas con la situación.
Este mes, Essayli demandó a California y al condado de Los Ángeles, exigiendo que anularan las papeletas de 20,000 votantes registrados a quienes acusó de no ser ciudadanos estadounidenses, y la semana pasada el Departamento de Justicia envió cartas amenazando a los funcionarios electorales locales con cargos penales si no hacían lo mismo con las listas de votantes de sus respectivos condados.
 Funcionarios electorales de varios condados de California han declarado que las verificaciones aleatorias revelaron que la lista de nombres del gobierno era inexacta y han cuestionado la legalidad de las solicitudes. Hasta el momento, solo los funcionarios de un condado, San Luis Obispo, han anunciado que investigarán a los votantes mencionados en las cartas de requerimiento del Departamento de Justicia. 
 Lo que dicen las citaciones
 En el condado de Los Ángeles, los fiscales federales citaron la semana pasada a tres empleados de la Oficina del Registrador Electoral, ordenándoles que testificaran ante un gran jurado en una investigación penal el 4 de noviembre, un día después de las elecciones.
 Los fiscales exigieron que los empleados del condado presentaran registros sobre cómo su departamento impide que los no ciudadanos voten y “registros relacionados con pruebas recopiladas por su agencia que tiendan a indicar que un extranjero ha votado en una elección federal”.
 En un comunicado, el registrador del condado de Los Ángeles, Dean Logan, afirmó que los fiscales estaban adoptando un enfoque “confrontativo y hostil”. Añadió que la advertencia del juez federal de que cesaran las amenazas contra los funcionarios electorales “fue oportuna y se agradeció”.
 “Las amenazas y la intimidación no tienen cabida en las elecciones”, declaró Logan. “Tomaremos todas las medidas necesarias para garantizar la seguridad de nuestros empleados y para seguir centrados en servir a los votantes del condado de Los Ángeles, para que puedan ejercer su derecho al voto”.
 En el condado de Orange, los agentes federales obtuvieron la nueva citación del gran jurado la semana pasada, pero los funcionarios electorales la recibieron el jueves. Es similar a las solicitudes de información previas de los fiscales federales. En septiembre, los funcionarios electorales habían entregado registros de 20 votantes registrados en respuesta a las citaciones. El jueves, el registrador de votantes, Bob Page, declaró a CalMatters que tres de esos nombres aparecían nuevamente en la nueva citación.
 El gobierno federal restó importancia a las citaciones y sugirió que los funcionarios electorales no eran el objetivo de su investigación.
 “Recibir una citación judicial no significa que uno sea un objetivo”, declaró Kiersten Pels, portavoz del Departamento de Justicia, en un comunicado enviado por correo electrónico. “De hecho, por lo general, el Departamento de Justicia no cita a personas que son objeto de investigación”. 
El juez afirma que “estas amenazas deben cesar”
 El martes, en su sala de audiencias, el juez de distrito estadounidense David O. Carter dejó claro que el gobierno federal debía dejar de amenazar a los trabajadores electorales con cargos penales si no cumplían con las exigencias de los fiscales.
 “Este tribunal considera que sería prudente que cesaran de inmediato todas las amenazas contra los empleados estatales o del condado (en materia electoral)”, dijo Carter ante la sala del tribunal.
 Formuló la advertencia de manera formal en su resolución escrita emitida el miércoles por la noche.
 “Nunca antes en la historia de Estados Unidos el gobierno federal, en vísperas de unas elecciones, había intentado coaccionar a un gobierno estatal y local para que abandonara sus propios procedimientos electorales constitucionales y se doblegara ante la voluntad del Poder Ejecutivo”, escribió Carter.
 “El tribunal reitera lo que dijo ayer: estas amenazas deben cesar”, escribió.
 El Departamento de Justicia ha apelado la decisión de Carter ante el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Noveno Circuito. Pels afirmó que los fiscales simplemente están haciendo lo que Carter les ordenó: procesar los casos de votación ilegal si se detectan.
 Al expresar su escepticismo sobre las afirmaciones de la administración Trump, Carter le dijo a Essayli en el tribunal el martes que si los no ciudadanos realmente están votando en cantidades tan grandes como afirma la administración Trump, no hay nada que impida a los fiscales federales encontrarlos y acusarlos sin el riesgo de impedir que se cuenten los votos de los electores legales.
 La semana pasada, fiscales federales de California acusaron a 28 personas de registrarse para votar sin ser ciudadanos. No todas habían votado en elecciones anteriores; los acusados representan el 0,0001% de los 23 millones de votantes registrados del estado.
 “Si es tan grave, por Dios, tienes una solución”, le dijo Carter a Essayli durante la audiencia. “Sal y presenta una acusación formal”.
 “Para que quede claro, el juez del tribunal de distrito explicó que votar ilegalmente conlleva responsabilidad penal”, escribió Pels en su declaración. “En consonancia con esto, California también indicó en su escrito que la vía para sancionar el voto ilegal es el enjuiciamiento penal. Por lo tanto, si bien el Departamento de Justicia sostiene que aún existe una vía civil, todos coinciden en que el voto de personas no ciudadanas debe abordarse mediante el derecho penal”.
 Justin Levitt, experto en derecho electoral de la Facultad de Derecho de Loyola, afirmó que los fiscales federales pueden argumentar que están llevando a cabo una investigación criminal legítima, pero en ese caso, no debería haber prisa por citar a declarar a los funcionarios en plena campaña electoral. Señaló que el plazo de prescripción para los delitos electorales federales es de cinco años.
 «Dado que no tienen ninguna influencia en los resultados electorales, no hay motivo alguno para que exijan esta información ahora», declaró Levitt. «No contraviene directamente la orden del juez… pero sin duda no le agradará».
 El senador californiano Tom Umberg, demócrata y exfiscal federal que representaba la zona de Santa Ana, dijo estar consternado de que su antiguo empleador estuviera intentando claramente “intimidar a los funcionarios públicos en el ejercicio de sus funciones juramentadas”. “Me avergüenza y me indigna que estén intentando interferir en las elecciones”, dijo. Essalyi no respondió a un mensaje de texto que se le envió el jueves para solicitar comentarios. El profesor Michael Vitiello, experto en derecho penal de la Facultad de Derecho McGeorge de la Universidad del Pacífico, coincidió en que el gobierno federal está intentando generar “inseguridad y miedo” entre los funcionarios electorales.
 “Tal vez, técnicamente, estén tratando de evitar un conflicto directo con la orden del juez, pero sin duda están dando a entender que… los funcionarios electorales deberían perder dinero, perder el sueño y tal vez incluso consultar con abogados”, dijo Vitiello.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas official says DOJ election monitors won’t hinder voting
text:
Election monitors are expected in Kansas on November 3, but state officials say they cannot interfere in the election  The state is reporting high numbers of early voters and in Shawnee County, they can take a selfie to share online. (hPhoto by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Department of Justice election monitors will be in Kansas on Tuesday but won’t interfere in the voting process, says a spokeswoman for the secretary of state.
“The voter experience should be unchanged compared to previous elections,” said Whitney Tempel. “Any monitors or observers will be clearly marked as such and are only allowed to observe. They will not be permitted to obstruct or hinder any voter in casting a ballot.”
Tempel said voters should follow their usual procedures at the polls, including bringing a government-issued photo identification.
“No voter will be turned away without being offered a chance to vote, at minimum, a provisional ballot,” she said. “Electioneering is prohibited inside the voting place as well as a 250-foot radius from the entrance. Do not sign your ballot or put your name on your ballot.”
Anyone who has questions or concerns should contact the supervisor at the polling place, she said.
President Donald Trump’s administration said it would increase the number of election monitors over past years to 1,000 and said they would be in all 50 states. The NAACP and Advancement Project, a civil rights organization, filed a lawsuit to stop the administration from sending FBI agents and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling places because of concerns about voter intimidation. 
The Justice Department said Wednesday during that lawsuit that monitors will be staff from the Drug Enforcement Administration; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms; and the Federal Bureau of Prisons, according to a news release from Vote Safe, a voter protection organization.
“Just days before Election Day, this administration is unveiling what appears to be its largest election monitoring operation in history, staffed by people from agencies that run federal prisons and conduct drug and firearms raids,” the Vote Safe news release said. “The DOJ still won’t say which polling places they’re headed to. This is yet another effort to keep eligible Americans from exercising their rights.”
The ACLU encouraged anyone who sees anything concerning on Election Day to report issues to its election protection hotline, 866-OUR-VOTE.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s U.S. House election includes a last-days push against a candidate in federal prison
text:
Independent candidate Bill Hill, who is challenging U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, speaks at a campaign event held Oct. 22, 2026, at Fire Island Bakery in downtown Anchorage, a few blocks from the Dena'ina Civic and Convention Center, site of the Alaska Federation of Natives annual convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)In the last days before Election Day, the Alaska Democratic Party is making a request: Don’t vote for the Democratic candidate in the U.S. House race.
Eric Hafner, the lone Democrat in the four-candidate House election, is in federal prison for threatening federal officials and isn’t expected to be released until 2036.
Since July, the Democratic Party has been supporting independent candidate Bill Hill, who is now the lead challenger to incumbent Republican Rep. Nick Begich III. 
“The Democratic Party has enthusiastically endorsed Bill Hill,” said Eric Croft, chair of the state party. 
As Hill campaigns across the state, Democratic officials have been working with him, trying to tell voters that they believe Hafner’s candidacy is a Republican-backed sham.
Yellow signs emblazoned with the words “Don’t be tricked! Eric Hafner: In Prison in New York” dot lawns across the state. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“I think Bill wants to bring a kind of that independent coalition spirit that we have in the (state) legislature here,” Croft said.
Despite the fact that Hafner would be ineligible to serve — the U.S. Constitution requires a member of the House to live in the state when they are elected — he’s nonetheless polling in the high single digits, near the margin between Begich and Hill. Libertarian Jim McDermott is the fourth candidate in the race.
Hill, who has never run for statewide public office before, has been trying to campaign on two levels — introducing himself to voters who have never heard of him before, and informing them about Hafner. 
“I think there are a lot of people who are doing the groundwork for us, and our campaign’s doing everything we can to ensure that when we send messages to voters, that we make a clear distinction between Nick Begich and myself, and also add that Eric Hafner is not a true Democrat. He’s really there to help out a Republican campaign,” Hill said on Thursday before an event in Juneau.
Third-party groups have also spent more than $450,000 against Hafner, according to Federal Elections Commission filings tallied by the website OpenSecrets.
Hafner has never lived in Alaska and ran unsuccessfully for Alaska’s House seat in 2024. The Democratic Party sued, trying to get him off the ballot, and the Alaska Republican Party fought to keep him on it, putting him in position to act as a spoiler against then-Rep. Mary Peltola’s re-election campaign.
The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in Hafner’s favor, and Begich defeated Peltola. Hafner, who was backed by advertising from a national Republican campaign group, was not decisive in that defeat. He earned a little over 1% of the vote. 
The next year, Hafner ran in a special U.S. House election in Florida.
Now, he’s running again in Alaska. 
Reports filed with the Federal Elections Commission show he hasn’t raised or spent any money on his campaign, but third-party groups appear to be working in support of him.
Ahead of the August primary election, some Alaska voters received anonymous pro-Hafner text messages that contained none of the disclosure language required by federal law. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Similar messages have popped up again in the past week, as early voting takes place ahead of the general election. 
“I think the reason you’re seeing so much money behind Hafner is (opponents are) belatedly realizing Bill Hill, a real independent, progressive independent, if you will, can win,” Croft said.
Alaska’s U.S. Senate race was rocked by a New York Times article this week that revealed independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan had been recruited by Democratic campaigners who wanted him to act as a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election campaign.
The Beacon asked Begich by text message on Thursday: Did he or anyone he knows encourage Hafner to run?
“Absolutely not,” Begich said. “No one on my campaign team has ever even made contact with him or would even know how to.”
Earlier this month, Begich and Hill participated in a televised debate that illustrated the differences between the two men.
Begich promoted his success in Congress. He’s set a record for the most legislation enacted by a freshman legislator in the history of the U.S. House of Representatives.
He also highlighted his support for increased oil and gas drilling on federal land in the state and an amendment to federal law that will steer more revenue from that drilling to the state.
“The nation needs these resources as well. Not just because it lowers the cost of energy, but it also helps to reduce the pressure that’s being applied to us down in Juneau for an income tax or a statewide sales tax. A huge portion of our state revenue comes directly from oil and gas royalties and production taxes, the more we produce, the better our state does,” Begich said.
During the debate and again on Thursday in Juneau, Hill criticized Begich’s votes in favor of the Iran war, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
“We need somebody who understands what the cost of fuel is doing to Alaskans, the loss of health care, and the fact that Nick has continued to vote for the Iranian war and tariffs and against our healthcare in this state, and Alaskans just need to know that,” Hill said on Thursday.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Sandy Hook families urge Supreme Court to uphold bans on AR-15-style rifles
text:
Relatives whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are making an impassioned plea to the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on certain semiautomatic rifles, citing the high body counts and devastating injuries the weapons can inflict.
The parents of five of the 20 first-graders killed in the 2012 Connecticut shooting and relatives of one of six educators who died filed a “friend of the court” brief on Wednesday, weighing in on two cases challenging bans in Connecticut and the Chicago area. Justices are scheduled to hear oral arguments in both cases on Dec. 2.
“The assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School, carried out by an untrained, 112-pound youth armed with an AR-15-style rifle, is graphic proof of the unusual and extreme lethality of that firearm and the harm it is capable of inflicting on American communities,” the relatives’ filing says. They added that they “seek to protect other American families from becoming casualties in another AR-15 killing spree.”
Gun rights advocates and groups whose lawsuits led to the two Supreme Court cases are arguing that it’s unconstitutional under the Second Amendment to ban semiautomatic rifles, which are legally owned by millions of Americans. Supporters of the bans say such rifles were designed for military use, are too dangerous for civilians and should be regulated like machine guns.
More than 40 other people and groups — most in favor of the rifle bans — also filed “amicus curiae” briefs on Wednesday. Such filings are submitted by parties who are not directly involved in the litigation.
Sandy Hook shooter killed 26 people with AR-15-style rifle
The 20-year-old Sandy Hook gunman, Adam Lanza, shot his way into the locked school in Newtown, Connecticut, and unleashed a fury of more than 150 bullets in about four minutes with a Bushmaster AR-15-style rifle fueled by high-capacity ammunition magazines. The massacre led Connecticut to ban such rifles in 2013 — the same law now before the Supreme Court.
Jennifer Hensel, whose 6-year-old daughter Avielle Richman was killed in the shooting, was quoted in the relatives’ brief saying Avielle was shot multiple times in the face and authorities told her that she would not recognize her daughter if she saw her body.
“A moral imperative is truly at hand,” Hensel said in supporting weapons bans. “Please, do not allow more blood to soak our Connecticut soil from assault-style weapons. A fundamental duty to protect all in Connecticut is at stake.”
A similar brief filed Wednesday by Sandy Hook Promise, the gun violence prevention group started by Newtown families, said another victim, 6-year-old Dylan Hockley, was shot five times — “his body destroyed so completely, his mother was told not to touch him to say goodbye as he lay in his coffin.”
[RELATED: Sandy Hook Promise’s ‘Start With Hello’ enlists teens to end gun violence]
“The effects of these weapons on children’s bodies are catastrophic and obscene,” the filing said.
Dylan’s mother, Nicole Hockley, a co-founder of Sandy Hook Promise, urged the Supreme Court to consider children’s safety.
“I know firsthand the devastation a semiautomatic rifle can inflict in minutes on the bodies, hearts, and minds of children — and the families who love them,” she said in a statement. “No family should have to live with that pain. As the Court considers this case, the consequences being experienced by children and communities cannot be an afterthought.”
Gun rights advocates filed suit to block rifle bans
Gun rights supporters say that while they sympathize with gun violence victims’ families and condemn mass shootings, the solution isn’t to curtail Second Amendment rights. They say school shootings happen despite bans on so-called “assault weapons.”
“Solving or at least mitigating school shootings is not about banning a type of gun,” said Konstadinos Moros, director of legal research and education for the Second Amendment Foundation, a plaintiff in the challenges to both the Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, bans.
“While some guns are obviously more capable than others, school shooters inflict harm not because of the capability of their firearms, but because of the helplessness of their targets,” he said in an email to The Associated Press. “The real solution lies in proper school security, which can both more quickly respond to shootings, and deter attacks from happening in the first place, given that the depraved individuals who commit these sorts of crimes tend to pick ‘soft targets.’”
Justices to weigh whether bans violate Second Amendment
The current Supreme Court, which has expanded gun rights, announced in June that it would hear appeals challenging bans on the AR-15 and similar semiautomatic firearms in Connecticut and the Chicago area. The ban in Cook County was first passed in 1993. Lower courts have upheld both laws.
Similar laws are in place in about a dozen states, covering major cities like New York, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Congress allowed a national assault weapons ban to expire in 2004, but Democrats have supported renewing it in response to mass shootings. States have also continued to pass their own laws, including recent measures in Virginia and Rhode Island.
It is the latest high-profile dispute over guns to reach the court since its conservative majority handed down a landmark ruling in 2022 that expanded Second Amendment rights and spawned challenges to firearm laws around the country. The court said that any gun laws must have a strong grounding in the nation’s historical traditions.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi has 23 public colleges and universities. Can the state sustain them?
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
When Rep. Trey Lamar, a Republican from Senatobia, introduced House Bill 1284 in January to merge six community college districts, college leaders and students quickly launched a petition to shut it down. 
The bill died in committee, but the question behind it did not: Does Mississippi still need 23 public colleges and universities? 
“I wanted to start a conversation,” said Lamar, who is also a member of the House Select Committee on Consolidation. “What worked for our colleges decades ago doesn’t always work today.” 
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Trey Lamar, R-Senatobia, speaks in the House chamber during legislative session on Wednesday, Feb. 25, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
House Bill 1284 would have merged Coahoma Community College with Mississippi Delta Community College; Meridian with East Mississippi; and Southwest Mississippi with Copiah-Lincoln. The mergers would not have closed any campuses but were meant to reduce administrative costs by consolidating college districts from 15 to 12. Any money saved from merging would have been put back into the community college system, Lamar said. 
Lamar’s bill intensified discussions about college mergers, said Rep. Donnie Scoggin, a Republican from Ellisville who co-chairs the House consolidation committee. Scoggin also chairs the House Colleges and Universities Committee, which he said allowed the bill to die because there wasn’t enough time to study the issue. 
“We didn’t want to do anything that was rushed and just start closing colleges,” Scoggin said. “But now we’re taking time to examine all factors to make informed and better decisions.” 
Rep. Donnie Scoggin, left, and Rep. Trey Lamar have a conversation during legislative session at the Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, March 23, 2023. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Mississippi’s public universities and community colleges are funded through a mix of state appropriations, federal funds, student tuition and local tax revenue. Overlapping districts can leave some property owners paying more in taxes to support multiple colleges — a situation Lamar said is unfair. 
Meridian Community College serves Lauderdale County, which is also part of East Mississippi Community College’s six-county district. Merging the two districts could reduce duplicative administrative costs, he said. 
Dips in population across the districts are also driving the move to consolidate. Over the past decade, thousands fewer residents have lived within the Coahoma and Mississippi Delta community college districts. In 2010, there were 26,000 residents in Coahoma County; a decade later, there were 21,000 residents, according to Census data. In Sunflower County, home to Mississippi Delta Community College, the population dropped by 4,000 people over the same period. 
For Cole Cooksey, a sophomore studying pre-political science at Southwest Community College, attending the school was the next logical step after high school graduation. He received scholarships that covered his first year of tuition, and the campus’ proximity to his parents’ home in McComb made college more affordable and accessible, he said. 
When Lamar’s bill threatened to merge Southwest with Copiah-Lincoln Community College, rumors of closure began circulating online. Cooksey said he wanted to raise awareness about the importance of the state’s oldest public college system and its benefits to students in rural and underserved communities. 
A student walks the campus at Copiah-Lincoln Community College on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
So, Cooksey launched an online petition to “Stop The Progression of House Bill 1284,” on Jan. 23 which received more than 330 supporters in its first day. When the bill died in the House committee, the petition had attracted the support of 750 people.  
“Community colleges help fill in the gaps of support and education that high schools are not able to do and they fill in the gaps that universities refuse too,” Cooksey said. “The more conversations we have about their benefits and services, the more we are able to open other people’s eyes to the good community colleges do within our state.” 
The state should not have to maintain separate community college boards  in areas serving fewer people, Lamar said. 
Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Mississippi Community College Board operates as the statewide coordinating board for each of the 15 colleges. Each college also maintains its own local board of trustees, which works with the college board. The local boards are responsible for the day-to-day operations, local administration, facilities, personnel decisions and local tax support for their respective campuses, according to state law. 
Legislators’ consolidation discussions have also questioned if colleges in overlapping communities have duplicate academic programs or services and whether students are earning college credentials that lead to jobs, he said. 
Legislators are asking similar questions about the state’s eight public universities.
Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford, is pushing trustees overseeing the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning to tie state funding to graduation rates, job placement and earnings.
The state college board’s new performance-based funding formula  would aim for universities to meet the state’s workforce and education attainment priorities. 
In June, IHL trustees took a step toward adopting a proposed public university funding formula that would tie a portion of state money to graduation rates, student retention and workforce outcomes. As of October, the college board is still working to define specific metrics and goals for the universities. It is also unclear when it will be fully implemented. 
Sen. Nicole Boyd, R-Oxford, asks a question about a bill in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In 2024, Boyd introduced Senate Bill 2725, which would have created a 10-member task force to examine funding formulas as Mississippi approached a looming enrollment cliff because of a predicted sharp decline in high school graduates. That same year, former Sen. John Polk, a Republican from Hattiesburg, also authored Senate Bill 2726, which would have required college board trustees to close three universities based on  similar factors such as graduation rates, enrollment and student retention outcomes.  
An enrollment dropoff could put pressure on the state’s regional universities, particularly Mississippi University for Women, Delta State, Alcorn and Mississippi Valley State by forcing them to compete with the state’s flagship universities, University of Mississippi and Mississippi State University, for a shrinking pool of students.  
The conversations around university funding are about more than finances, Boyd said. It’s about centering students. 
Copiah-Lincoln Community College is pictured in Wesson on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“These conversations are a cultural shift for Mississippi,” Boyd said. “We just want to make sure students aren’t leaving school saddled with debt and now worse off because of it.” 
Consolidating the state’s smaller colleges and universities could hurt rural students’ access to higher education, said Pernell Goodwin, vice president of Copiah-Lincoln Community College’s Natchez campus. Having to travel further for college would make it more difficult for students to visit campuses and increase their overall college costs, he said.
Accessibility was the goal behind the creation of Mississippi’s community college system, Goodwin said.
“It was to ensure that no matter where a student attends college, he is at least within a certain distance from his home to get to campus and access education.” 
Bruce Hanson, who was a state representative in the 1980s, has pushed back against closing or consolidating universities. 
A student sits on the steps of a campus building at Southwest Mississippi Community College is pictured in Summit on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
As chair of the Citizens Coalition for MUW and Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science, Hanson has sought to protect the two campuses from consolidation proposals seeking to close schools that enroll fewer students. He said smaller public universities play a crucial role in providing affordable tuition and easy access to higher education for Mississippi students.
They nevertheless generate millions of dollars and produce graduates who are essential to the state’s economy and workforce, Hanson said.
“If these institutions disappear, where will the children in our community go?”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Final pitch over Missouri abortion ban turns to fight over voter power
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway speaks at a Yes on 3 rally hosted by Her Health, Her Future, on Tues. Oct. 27 at Encounter Church in Arnold (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).As Missouri voters prepare to decide whether to reinstate the state’s abortion ban, the final arguments over Amendment 3 are reaching beyond abortion itself.
The campaigns are linking the measure to other questions on Tuesday’s ballot and framing the election as a fight over who holds power in Missouri — voters, politicians or wealthy outside interests.
To supporters of Amendment 3, which aims to repeal the state’s 2024 reproductive rights amendment, the threat comes from wealthy out-of-state liberals trying to turn Missouri into a haven for abortion.
“No on 6. Tell billionaires keep their paws off our laws,” read signs at a Yes on 3 rally Tuesday in Arnold.
To opponents of Amendment 3 who are aiming to keep abortion legal, the threat comes from Republican politicians trying to overturn the will of Missouri voters.
“Vote No on 3. Vote No on A. Voters decide. Not politicians,” read signs at a Stop the Ban rally Saturday in St. Louis.
Proposition A is a referendum on a gerrymandered congressional map drawn last year by Republicans. Amendment 6 would require support from at least 80% of both legislative chambers for lawmakers to put a change to a voter-approved initiative back on the ballot. 
Both measures appear on the Nov. 3 ballot alongside Amendment 3.  
If Amendment 3 fails and Amendment 6 passes, it would be nearly impossible for the Republican-led statehouse to put another measure with abortion restrictions before voters.
Amber Jones, program manager with the nonprofit LeadMO, said tying Proposition A to Amendment 3 is about protecting the people’s power. It’s a message she said resonated with voters as she helped collect signatures from Missourians across the state to put the gerrymandered map on the ballot.
“A handful of powerful people shouldn’t be able to rig the rules to protect themselves,” Jones said. “That is what this fight is about. They want to divide communities, manipulate who gets represented together and make it harder for voters to hold politicians accountable.” 
More than 600 volunteers with abortion-rights groups, labor unions and voter advocacy groups knocked on 14,000 doors across the state Saturday, urging voters to oppose Proposition A and Amendment 3, according to a press release from Abortion Action Missouri.
Leaders with Missouri abortion rights and labor groups gather for a canvassing event on oct. 24 in St. Louis (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
On Tuesday, Tim Jones, a Republican radio host and former speaker of the Missouri House, said the initiative petition process has become “an abhorrent abomination to our constitution.” He accused out-of-state donors of deceiving Missourians by pouring millions of dollars into progressive campaigns. 
The 2024 campaign to legalize abortion, and the 2026 campaign to keep it legal, have been backed by small donations from thousands of Missourians. But most of the more than $27 million raised by Stop the Ban this year has come from large out-of-state donors and progressive nonprofits that aren’t required to disclose their donors. 
Her Health, Her Future, the campaign supporting the abortion ban, has drawn far fewer donors, with significant financial backing from Missouri-based contributors, including a newly formed nonprofit that does not have to disclose its donors. As of Thursday, the campaign had raised more than $7 million.
Amendment 3 would reinstate an abortion ban with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and rape or incest within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
It would also allow the state to reinstate dozens of regulations on abortion providers struck down this summer by Jackson County Circuit Judge Jerri Zhang, who ruled they were unconstitutional under the reproductive rights amendment voters approved in 2024. Those included a 72-hour waiting period, special licensing requirements for abortion providers and hospital admitting privileges.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway criticized the ruling at Tuesday’s rally in Arnold, asking supporters if they would protect women and “stand up to that judge who overruled every single safety protection for women.”
But Zhang did not strike down every regulation. She upheld requirements that medication abortion be administered in person and that only doctors can perform abortions or prescribe abortion medication. She also wrote that several safeguards remained in place even without the regulations she overturned.
Amendment 3 would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors. State law prohibits gender-transition surgery for minors and bars minors from beginning cross-sex hormones or puberty blockers. The restrictions on hormones and puberty blockers are set to expire in August 2027, though lawmakers have discussed making the ban permanent. 
Former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who recently stepped down as co-deputy director of the FBI, speaks at a Yes on 3 rally hosted by Her Health, Her Future, on  Tuesday at Encounter Church in Arnold (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
Former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who recently stepped down from the FBI, also made an appearance in Arnold as part of what he called an effort to barnstorm Missouri for Amendment 3. 
He recently teamed up with U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley to launch a political action committee called Vote Yes on Amendment 3. An Oct. 26 report filed with the Missouri Ethics Commission showed the campaign had received one donation — for $1 million — from America Next Inc., a conservative Louisiana-based nonprofit launched by former Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal.
America Next does not disclose its donors. 
Bailey told the Arnold crowd that “voters were deceived by the lie behind reproductive freedom a few years back.” 
The 2024 reproductive rights amendment passed with 51.6% of the vote. Polling shows the potential for another very close race.
Those rallying in opposition to Amendment 3 reject the suggestion that voters were deceived when they approved abortion rights two years ago. 
“Powerful politicians think they know better. They say we didn’t know what we were doing when we voted to legalize abortion,” Nancy O’Brian, a volunteer with Abortion Action Missouri, said at a rally Saturday in St. Louis. “They say that we didn’t mean it when we kicked politicians and lawyers out of private medical decisions between families and doctors. But they don’t know Missouri like we do. We know how Missourians feel about abortion because we already asked them.” 
O’Brian, who had an abortion when she was a young woman after she said she was targeted by an older man who became abusive, said access to that care allowed her to have her current career and family, which includes two children.
Knocking on doors, she said, has shown her that Missourians have nuanced feelings about abortion. 
“But I also know that no matter how we personally feel about abortion, Missourians agree that politicians should never get to decide for us and our families,” she told a cheering crowd. “They certainly shouldn’t get to just overturn any vote of the people just because they don’t like it. Politicians don’t get the final say. We get the final say.”

name: California
title: Jane Kim and Ben Allen squabble over state-run wildfire insurance
text:
Insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim speaks to the press at the Curran Theater in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters




How do you distinguish between the two Democrats running for insurance commissioner? Well, one of them wants state-backed public insurance. We have more on that, as well as details on a move campaigns are using to dodge spending limits this fall.
But we have more than election news in your inbox today. California employers scored a big win in federal court against a new state law that would limit anti-union messaging in workplaces. More on that below.
Insurance commissioner candidates Jane Kim and state Sen. Ben Allen have attacked each other over their main plans to improve California’s property insurance market: A public option and broad wildfire mitigation, respectively. 
Their latest back-and-forth is around what Kim’s plan to create a public wildfire insurer — a proposal that critics say would shift big risks to the state — might cost homeowners.
Kim recently released a policy brief that lays out how such a plan could work. Funding the program would involve having a two-part wildfire premium, collected by private insurers and diverted to the state, which would be based on each home’s wildfire risk, plus a “small, capped share that every home in the state contributes to cover the bad wildfire seasons.”
Her brief cited a proposal included in a California Earthquake Authority report that could serve as a model. It estimated that such a program would need about $25 billion for a very bad wildfire year. The program would buy reinsurance for that risk, which would cost $2 billion to $3 billion a year, or about $150 to $230 a policy. Without reinsurance, a “once-in-a-century fire” would mean a charge of $1,900 to $2,000 per policy over several years, the report said. 
On social media and elsewhere, Allen’s campaign is using Kim’s brief to say her plan would cost policyholders “$230 a year added to every homeowner’s policy” and “$2,000 or more in assessments on every policyholder.”
That’s not the case, Kim told reporters this week.

Kim: “Either he is being intellectually disingenuous, or he doesn’t know how to read a policy brief … we were referring to a study that if we do not buy reinsurance that it would cost homeowners, on average, $2,000 more.”

CalMatters contacted Allen’s campaign about Kim’s pushback. Allen spokesperson Joe Arellano repeated his campaign’s claim. 
The two Democratic candidates have also tussled over campaign finance, including their promises not to take money from the insurance industry.
For the record: The Oct. 8 WhatMatters newsletter contained an error about what the Public Interest Legal Foundation agreed to in a confidential 2019 settlement of a lawsuit by plaintiffs who claimed they were falsely accused of voting improprieties. 
The foundation’s president, J. Christian Adams, says the foundation did not admit to falsely accusing thousands of Virginia voters of being noncitizens, as an earlier version of this newsletter stated. The foundation apologized to the three plaintiffs for relying on what he said were inaccurate government records, when the foundation falsely labeled them as noncitizens in its reports. 
The newsletter and article have been updated to provide corrected and additional details about the settlement.



We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners: Local news organizations, colleges and nonprofits. Our next event is today at 12 p.m. in Fresno at Fresno State University.

Other Stories You Should Know


How candidates dodge spending rules


Assemblymember Jeff Gonzalez speaks during a floor session at the state Capitol in Sacramento on June 30, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




More would-be California lawmakers are employing a controversial tactic that sidesteps campaign finance laws to spread their influence on potential voters, write CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe and Nadia Lathan. 
Donors in state elections are only allowed to give candidates as much as $5,900 per election. But independent expenditure committees, which can run ads supporting or opposing candidates, do not have a spending limit. 
These groups cannot directly coordinate with campaigns. But over the past decade, candidates have been using a method known as “red boxing” to leave instructions on their campaign sites, typically outlined in a red box, for independent spenders to follow when creating ads. 
Critics say the tactic can create the appearance of corruption. But the California Fair Political Practices Commission is unlikely to rein in the behavior soon. 

Steven Maviglio, Democratic strategist: “Like it or not, the state watchdog doesn’t have the capacity to do their job.”

Read more.



CA employers win in challenge to workplace meeting law


A waitress sets tables at a restaurant in Alturas on Sept. 3, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




A federal court handed California business groups a win Thursday in their fight to stop a pro-labor law limiting so-called captive audience meetings.
In 2024 the state passed a law banning employers from punishing workers who refuse to attend workplace meetings about political, anti-union or religious matters. Three major industry groups — California Chamber of Commerce, the California Restaurant Association and the Western Growers Association — sued the state, arguing that the measure violated their First Amendment rights.
A district court issued a preliminary injunction last year preventing the law from taking effect. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the ruling on free speech grounds, agreeing with the industry groups’ argument. 

Judge Richard C. Tallman, in his opinion: “The potential for any employee to expose an employer to liability for damages (including punitive damages) based on the employee’s perception of the workplace’s history and culture surrounding meetings ‘creates its own chilling effect’ on the employer’s ability to speak on political matters in the workplace.”

In a joint statement, the industry groups praised the ruling, saying that “the state cannot limit the speech of any business owner simply because the contents of that speech might differ from the political viewpoint of elected officials or outside interest groups.”
The office of the California attorney general said it was reviewing the ruling but did not comment on whether it plans to appeal.



And lastly: What does Prop. 45 mean for data centers?


An Amazon Web Services data center under construction in Gilroy on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Opponents of Proposition 45, which would lift some restrictions on the state’s environmental review law, say the measure would make it easier for developers to build data centers. Data center backers say the proposal doesn’t do that, but that hasn’t stopped the beneficiaries of such centers from pouring millions of dollars into supporting the measure. Read more from CalMatters’ Katherine Ortiz.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: Though there were plenty of chaotic events for political junkies to savor this California election season, candidates did not meaningfully address the many challenges facing California, including its budget deficits, homelessness or rising living costs.
Prop. 13 was sold in 1978 as a way to save families from unpredictable property tax bills, but it also became a permanent discount for wealthy, corporate property owners that has resulted in billions of dollars in lost tax revenue, writes John Kim, president and CEO of Catalyst California.
