name: Michigan Advance
title: Majority or bust: Michigan parties make final push for legislative control
text:
The statue of former Gov. Austin Blair at the Michigan Capitol | Susan J. DemasMuch of the 2026 election attention has been on Michigan’s must-watch U.S. Senate and congressional races, but the battle for control of the state Legislature has emerged as another major contest.
In a highly favorable year for Michigan Democrats, the party is hoping that President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, pegged at 57% in a recent Marist poll, and stagnant economy on his watch will help the party retake the Michigan House, hold the state Senate and retain the governor’s office. 
“Our candidates have worked hard this cycle to build strong campaigns that highlight the issues Michiganders care about,” state Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) said in a statement. “We are looking forward to returning to the Senate in January with an expanded majority to continue our work in building a Michigan where everyone can live and thrive.”
But the state’s Republicans, despite warning signs the GOP might have a bad year, are aiming to retain their current House majority and retake the Senate. That hope is at least partly based on the potential to exploit the controversies connected to U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
“With El-Sayed at the top of the ticket, the Senate Republicans are on offense, and the Senate Democrats know it,” Sen. Roger Hauck, R-Mount Pleasant (R-Mount Pleasant) said in a statement. “They’re so desperate that they’re spending $1.3 million they don’t have. Every target district’s early and absentee voting is more Republican than it was in 2022, when Republicans lost shared control of the chamber by 400 votes. The Democratic majority ends Nov. 3.”
The Senate Republican Campaign Committee has made a final round of ad purchases to try and make that goal a reality.
State Sens. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) and Chedrick Greene (D-Saginaw) take questions from reporters. June 10, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Democrats like their chances to expand Senate majority
For the Senate’s Democrats, who currently control the chamber, the most favorable scenario on Nov. 3 would be to hold what seats they have while also expanding their majority by flipping three long-sought after Republican districts.
“The momentum is clearly behind Democrats this election, and across the board, Senate Democrats have strong, passionate candidates who are ready to fight for working families,” Olivia Bradish, spokesperson for the Michigan Senate Democrats said. Bradish added that they have “heavily invested to ensure Democrats defend and expand” their Senate Majority.
At the top of that list is the 9th District held by Republican Sen. Michael Webber of Rochester Hills. He faces Democratic nominee Dr. Theresa Brooks of Troy. Democrats are hoping to defeat Webber, a longtime legislator and a leader in the Senate Republican caucus, and said that Brooks has been knocking on doors almost every day since she won a tough three-way primary. 
Brooks has also outraised Webber, picking up a little more than $320,000 in the latest reporting period, while  Webber raised just under $220,000.
While protecting Webber’s seat is a major priority for the GOP, Democrats are confident that Brooks has the resources, community support and motivation to win.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines, Michigan Senate candidate Theresa Brooks and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/ Michigan Advance)
Next on the list of hoped-for Democratic pickups is the 30th District, held by GOP Sen. Mark Huizenga of Walker. He faces Democratic challenger state Rep. Carol Glanville, also of Walker. Democrats believe Glanville is in a comfortable position and that West Michigan is showing signs of shifting toward greater support for their party and candidates — a trend the party has noticed over the last few years. 
While her roots in the community were helping Glanville, the party noted she’s also outraised Huizenga in the latest period. Huizenga raised just north of $100,000 during the latest reporting period, whereas Glanville raised a little more than $300,000.
Regardless, Republicans also feel good about Huizenga’s chances, touting his bipartisan voting record — which the party said was among the most bipartisan records of any sitting state senator — and the fact that he’s worked hard for the district as its senator over the past four years.
The third pickup opportunity being eyed by Democrats is West Michigan’s 32nd District. Republican state Sen. Jon Bumstead of North Muskegon cannot seek reelection due to term limits, setting up a fight between Democrat Rebecca Amidon and Republican Mason County Sheriff Kim Cole. Although Cole is well established in the district, having served as sheriff since 2013, Democrats believe Amidon is a strong enough candidate to be spending heavily on TV advertising in the district deep into the election cycle.
While winning the district will be a challenge for Amidon given its history as a safe seat for Republicans, Democrats said her message aimed at working families was resonating amid Trump’s economic woes.
That said, the GOP is confident Cole will put the race away early on election night, noting that the seat is still trending toward the Republican Party despite changes in West Michigan demographics that have trended toward Democrats.
State Sens. Sylvia Santana (D-Detroit) and Mark Huizenga (R-Walker) discuss legislation creating a framework for behavioral health transport in the state. May 13, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Hertel legislative legacy included in must hold seats for Senate Dems
Tops on the list of must-hold Senate seats are Sen. Kevin Hertel’s 12th District and the open 13th District race to replace retiring Sen. Rosemary Bayer. 
Republicans have made defeating Hertel a priority, with a barrage of recent ads highlighting his family’s political dynasty as reason to reject him in favor of Republican John Goldwater. Democrats said this will be a tough seat to hold onto, as Hertel won in 2022 by just more than 400 votes, but the positive environment for the party has them optimistic about Hertel’s chances. 
Republicans, meanwhile, are all in on Goldwater’s prospects to flip in Hertel’s seat. They’ve highlighted not only Hertel’s family political dynasty, but also his voting record aligning with Democrats in what was a +7.5 Trump district in 2024.
In the 13th District, Democrat Sean Carlson has similarly been working hard, with more than 5,000 doors knocked in his race against Republican former state Rep. Ryan Berman of Commerce Township. Berman previously sought and lost the GOP nomination for attorney general in 2022. Democrats were optimistic after Carlson outraised Berman nearly 10-to-1 in the last reporting period, gaining more than $364,000 to Berman’s approximately $38,000.
Senate Republicans, however, believe the newly drawn district allows a better chance for Berman to pick up the seat. They’re also banking on Berman’s district having a high population of Jewish voters, who might end up breaking for Republicans due to issues with El-Sayed.
Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores) discusses a slate of proposed regulations on data centers at a press conference. June 18, 2025 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
56 seats is the goal for House Democrats this year
The Michigan House Democratic caucus currently holds 52 seats and just needs four more to hold a majority in the lower chamber of the Legislature, which they lost control of in 2024. The party is eyeing nine potential winnable seats out of the 12 that it has targeted, and campaign operatives said that the other three offer some cautious optimism.
“We feel very good about our chances of taking back the House on Nov. 3,” Sam Lundry, executive director of the Michigan House Democratic Fund, said. “We have excellent candidates who know their communities and hear every day from people who need some relief from rising costs. Matt Hall and House Republicans are stuck defending the GOP record of corruption and higher costs, and that’s a tough sell to families watching their bills go up. We have multiple paths to a majority, and we’re taking nothing for granted.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Among the top targets for a flip is the 27th House District, where state Rep. Rylee Linting (R-Wyandotte) is seeking reelection to the seat she won in 2024 against its former incumbent, Jamie Churches, also of Wyandotte. Democrats feel good about the race for Churches, due to her reputation as one of the House campaign arm’s hardest working candidates, along with hopes that the Trump effect puts the seat back into play. They’ve backed that optimism with cash, as Gongwer reported Thursday on a $200,000 television ad buy to support Churches.
Another key rematch for the House this cycle is state Rep. Steve Frisbie (R-Battle Creek) versus Democratic former state Rep. Jim Haadsma in the 44th District. Haadsma lost the district to Frisbie in 2024 by just 79 votes and Democrats like their chances of surmounting that small gap this cycle..
Another chance for Democrats to gain a House seat is in Oakland County, where state Rep. Donni Steele (R-Orion Township) is not seeking reelection to the 54th District, instead seeking election to the state Senate in the 23rd district. 
Sarah Pounds is the Democratic nominee, while Roman Gaskey was nominated by the GOP. The signs are positive for Pounds, who has been supported by national Democrats, with both California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigning for her. Additionally, Pounds polled more than 12,000 votes in the August primary, where she ran unopposed, which was almost 3,000 more votes than Gaskey and his primary opponent received.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (at left) campaigns Sunday in Oakland County with Michigan House candidates Sarah Pounds and Alex Hawkins. Aug. 9, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance
State Rep. Mark Tisdel (R-Rochester Hills), the incumbent in the adjacent 55th District, is seeking reelection and faces Democrat Alexander Hawkins, a military veteran whose job with the Michigan National Guard was defusing bombs. Party operatives believe his military ties can buck the narrative that Democrats running in this cycle are El-Sayed or William Lawrence-style progressives with some baggage.
Other targets for potential Democratic seat expansion include the 68th, 86th and 109th House Districts. Although these seats, on paper, appear harder to flip, the Democrats are cautiously optimistic.
State Rep. David Martin (R-Davison) is the incumbent in the 68th District, Rep. Nancy DeBoer (R-Holland) currently holds the 86th District, and Rep. Karl Bohnak (R-Deerton) represents the 109th District. Each is seeking reelection in what are typically safe Republican seats.
The anti-incumbent environment has Democrats feeling good about their chances, especially in the West Michigan seat held by DeBoer, who is facing Democratic challenger Joseph McClusky, and the Upper Peninsula seat held by Bohnak, who is fending off a strong challenge by Democrat Anna Aho Rink. 
The trend line showing West Michigan becoming bluer over the past few cycles and the fact that El-Sayed drew big crowds up north during his campaign swings puts those two seats, in particular, in the potential pickup category for Democrats.
As both parties target a handful of competitive races to try and tip the scales, control of the Legislature will  ultimately depend on whether Democrats can translate a favorable political environment into gains in districts that have long eluded them, while Republicans are betting that incumbency and the divisions surrounding El-Sayed can blunt Democratic momentum.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: It’s time to end Boston’s unique status of being exempt from the state zoning code
text:
IN AUGUST 1960, amid catastrophic population loss and the prospect of vast amounts of federal aid, State House leaders and then-Mayor John Collins struck a deal exempting Boston from most Massachusetts zoning laws. Sixty-six years later, the post-war urban crisis and the era of federally funded urban renewal are long over, but that deal is still the foundation of Boston’s development process. So why does Boston still operate under real estate development processes built for that bygone era?   
The case for maintaining the archaic status quo grows weaker with every statewide housing reform. Because of that 1960 deal, Boston is exempt from the MBTA Communities Act, statewide legalization of accessory dwelling units (ADU), and the proposed Legalize Starter Homes ballot question. These laws are some of the highest profile legislation Beacon Hill has passed in the last decade, but do not apply to the state’s own capital and largest city.   
The idea that housing reform is needed in Boston has been endorsed by Boston’s most powerful leaders. Both Michelle Wu and Marty Walsh won their first races for mayor on platforms to reform the city’s development process, but both failed to make more than cosmetic changes.  
If Boston’s mayor, the most powerful local elected official in Massachusetts, can’t change the system, what can? The answer is simple: End Boston’s 66-year experiment in DIY development policy and make Boston subject to Chapter 40A. That would legalize ADUs citywide, more than two years after Mayor Wu promised to do so in the 2024 “State of the City” address and help solve Massachusetts’s statewide housing crisis.   
Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would also ensure the city’s elected and appointed officials and larger real estate ecosystem face the same housing rules, incentives, and consequences as the rest of Massachusetts.   
There is no better time than now: Speaker-in-waiting Aaron Michlewitz and House Majority Leader Mike Moran are both Boston residents. Both face the prospect of forcing their House colleagues to take difficult votes on important housing legislation that their districts are not subject to. Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would end that contradiction.  
The greatest impact of this change would be in Boston, where the switch to Chapter 40A would require reconciling decades of DIY planning with state standards. The chief site of those changes would be the city’s notoriously long and complex zoning code. This switch would be an opportunity for politicians and activists who routinely criticize the city’s zoning to burnish their pro-housing bona fides to turn that rhetoric into action.   
Benefits would extend well beyond Boston. Massachusetts ranks near the bottom nationally in housing construction per capita. An often overlooked reason is that the state’s largest city not only has a different zoning code, but operates under an entirely different development process. Today, Brookline and Great Barrington, towns on opposite ends of the state, have more similar development processes than neighboring Brookline and Boston.  
Housing is the top issue in Boston and across Massachusetts. Bringing Boston under Chapter 40A would empower elected officials at City Hall and on Beacon Hill with the same tools and incentives as the rest of the state.  
If solving the crisis requires “all hands on deck,” everyone needs to be in the same boat.  
Gregory Maynard is senior fellow at Pioneer City Initiative, a newly launched program at Pioneer Institute.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC’s abortion ban has ‘serious problems,’ federal judge says
text:
South Carolina's abortion ban could be vague enough to be unconstitutional, a federal judge said Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, during a trial in Charleston, S.C. (File/Photo by Getty Images)CHARLESTON — South Carolina’s abortion ban has clear issues, potentially making it unconstitutional, a federal judge said Friday.
U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel, speaking at the end of a three-day trial in Charleston, didn’t give any official verdict on a case challenging the state’s ban on most abortions past six weeks of pregnancy. But he did have major concerns with the law as written, which he said makes its exceptions too vague to follow or enforce.
“I think the statute has serious problems, but frankly, I think the General Assembly can fix it,” Gergel said.
The lawsuit, filed last year, argued the state’s abortion ban was vague enough to violate the U.S. Constitution’s guarantee of due process. Over three days, doctors testified they’re afraid to provide abortions even when the law might allow them.
The law, passed in 2023, prohibits most abortions after a fetal heartbeat is detectable, which the state Supreme Court has set as six weeks. It threatens violating doctors with up to two years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000 and the possibility of losing a medical license.
The trial focused on when, exactly, medical exceptions to the ban apply: abortions needed to save the mother’s life or prevent lifelong impairment or diagnosis of an anomaly so severe the fetus isn’t expected to survive after birth.
The plaintiffs argued that its wording can lead different doctors to reach different conclusions.
The law allows doctors to use “reasonable medical judgment,” but doctors challenging it questioned how a prosecutor would decide that.
Doctors should understand what’s reasonable and what isn’t, attorneys for the governor and attorney general’s office said. Four doctors who testified for the defense said they found the law easy to understand and implement.
“If you are being reasonable, you are not violating the law,” said Grayson Lambert, attorney for the governor.
“That’s a subjective standard,” Gergel replied.
None of the defense’s doctors performed abortions before the law passed because of religious objections, they testified. That means they have no reason to fear the law, unlike the doctors challenging the law, who previously performed abortions as a routine part of their care, their attorneys said.
Gergel repeatedly called the law vague and said he had serious problems with it.
He also questioned how wide his ruling should be, including whether it should apply only to the doctors who sued. He’s unlikely to issue an order halting the law entirely, he said.
If Gergel finds the law unconstitutional, an appeal is certain, Lambert told him.
‘Good faith’ clause
Gergel said there’s a relatively easy fix to the problems he saw: If legislators added a clause protecting doctors acting in good faith, Gergel would consider the law constitutional, he said.
That wording would fall in line with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1992 decision in Planned Parenthood v. Casey, which redefined the guaranteed right to an abortion nationally and allowed more state regulation.
Pennsylvania’s law, which the case challenged, included similar phrases to those contested in South Carolina. But the blanket “good faith” clause made it clear doctors wouldn’t face prosecution if they misunderstood, Gergel said.
The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that returned the legality of abortions back to the states overturned both Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey.
As written, the state’s 2023 law has no mention of a doctor’s intention. Other criminal laws require proof that a person intended to harm someone. The abortion law requires only proof that doctors intended to provide an abortion, even if they thought they were following the law, Gergel said.
Doctors don’t have the power of hindsight, he said.
Sometimes, a doctor has to make a call in the moment that another doctor might not agree with, or even that the doctor might not have done in retrospect, Gergel said.
Whether legislators would make that change is another question. Trying to tweak the law would reopen debates on even stricter abortion restrictions.
Gergel can’t change the law. And he probably couldn’t strike only the exceptions, he said, though Lambert tried to argue Gergel could legally get rid of the exception for fatal fetal anomalies.
Legislators clearly intended for abortions to remain legal in certain cases, Gergel said.
Otherwise, he noted, they would have passed a law with no exceptions. Proposals of that sort have failed repeatedly.
Unconstitutionally vague
Doctors who testified during the trial disagreed about when the exceptions applied.
Even the state’s witnesses, chosen to speak about how they found the law clear, disagreed about when an abortion would be legal under the exceptions.
“I think the only thing we can agree on here is none of them agree with each other,” Gergel said.
For instance, one doctor interpreted a requirement that an abortion could be performed only if the fetus had an abnormality “incompatible with sustaining life after birth” to mean the baby would live no more than six months. Another drew the cutoff at a year. And both said they thought chromosomal abnormalities that kill most babies at birth would qualify, even though other doctors pointed out some rare cases when those children lived for years.
“Can we figure out what is ‘reasonable medical judgment’ when there’s such a diversity of opinion?” Gergel said.
Being ambiguous doesn’t necessarily make a law unconstitutional, Gergel said. But when the punishment might mean prison time or the end of a person’s professional career, people need clarity, he said.
That’s especially true in a complicated medical case, Gergel said.
Doctors need to feel certain about which procedures they can perform without wondering whether they’ll go to prison. And police need to understand what’s allowed so they don’t make arbitrary arrests, he said.
“The statute is sort of written like (legislators) are playing checkers and doctors are playing three-level chess,” Gergel said.
None of the doctors who testified during the trial were investigated or charged with a crime for performing an abortion. But those who did offer abortions erred on the side of caution, often sending patients with ambiguous cases out of state, they said.
“Had they kept them in (state), who knows what would’ve happened?” Gergel said.
Some cases are clearly defined, Gergel said. If a woman is in active kidney failure, “a Boy Scout can figure” out she qualifies for the exception, he said.
“I’m trying to figure out, for the not-easy cases, is there some fixed meaning so physicians are not put in jeopardy?” Gergel said.
Without it, the state will continue losing OB-GYNs afraid to practice in the state, Gergel said.
“There won’t be any OB-GYNs left,” he said.
