name: Nevada Current
title: Microplastics found in freshly fallen snow in Sierra Nevada
text:
Aleksandra Karapetrov collecting fresh snowfall to measure microplastics. (Sonya Maple/CDFW)Microplastics are everywhere — including in Nevada’s snowpack.
After years of skiing on freshly fallen snow in remote locations across the Sierra Nevada, Aleksandra Karapetrov — an environmental toxicologist at the University of California, Riverside — wondered how pristine the snow really was. 
Over six months, Karapetrov and a team of University of California, Riverside scientists tested fresh snowfall at seven sites across the Sierra Nevada and found something they did not expect: a steady delivery of tiny plastic fibers, even in the most remote locations.
“It was surprising the consistency at which we found microplastics everywhere,” Karapetrov said. “It’s kind of disrupting this narrative of pristineness. I hope it brings awareness to the circularity and widespreadness of pollution. There’s this boomerang effect, and it’s important we recognize that.”
The study, published this month in the journal Environmental Science and Technology, found significant amounts of microplastics in fresh snowfall at both remote and populated sites across the Sierra Nevada, which supplies about 60% of freshwater in northern Nevada. 
While populated sites had roughly three times as many microplastics as more remote locations, all sites tested contained microscopic bits of the plastic commonly used in clothing and packaging. 
The remote location of the sites revealed that airborne plastic from the atmosphere is being carried into the Sierra Nevada snowpack from communities miles away, rather than directly deposited by human activity.
Microplastics enter the air when plastic products shed fibers or wear down into small fragments, said Karapetrov.  Those fibers and fragments are eventually blown by winds and then – through mechanisms which are not fully understood – transported long distances through the atmosphere.
Snowflakes collect tiny plastic particles suspended in the air through a process called scavenging, which they deposit on the ground as they fall.
“Snowflakes have such a big surface area, it’s well known that they’re good for scavenging particles in general, like dust particles and minerals, from the atmosphere,” Karapetrov said.
A majority of the storms tracked by the researchers (70%) traveled over the San Joaquin Valley in central California, suggesting the region may be contributing these particles. However, finding the exact origin of the microplastics would take further study, said Karapetrov.
“For the sizes of microplastics that we were detecting there was local transport, so coming from nearby towns within a 10 to 20 mile radius. There was also regional transport. Regional meaning, less than 50 miles,” Karapetrov said. 
The University of California, Riverside study specifically examined how much microplastics are being deposited on the ground during individual storms, allowing researchers to connect measurements with particular weather events.
“We’re reporting the amount of microplastics coming out in a single storm, and that’s like what the novelty here is,” Karapetrov said. “We can calculate the rate of microplastics that were deposited in a storm, and so that time point resolution is what’s really unique.”
The study found that longer dry periods were associated with higher concentrations of microplastics following storms, possibly reflecting atmospheric buildup, said Karapetrov.
The study did not measure how much plastic ultimately reaches Nevada’s drinking water, but the findings could be significant as the Sierra Nevada snowpack supplies about 60% of freshwater in northern Nevada. 
Microplastics research is still in its infancy, said Karapetrov. It’s still unclear how widespread microplastics in drinking water and snowpacks really are, and there’s no standardized method to test for them either. But a 2019 World Health Organization metastudy found the microplastics were widespread in water supplies and wastewater effluent.
Limited research also makes it unclear how microplastic pollution in air and water impacts human health. But researchers have found that some chemicals used in plastics have documented health effects including hormone disruption, inflammation, and cellular damage.
The issue is likely widespread. Earlier research has already established that microplastics occur in snowpack across the west and globally.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Worrisome domestic violence statistics aren’t declining in NC
text:
(Graphic: NC Criminal Justice Analysis Center)October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month. But a new report this month shows North Carolina isn’t making much headway on the problem. 
In 2025, more than 63,000 people in North Carolina reported being victims of a crime committed by current or former spouses, partners or family members, according to a report released this week by the state’s Criminal Justice Analysis Center.
The report shows that domestic and family violence rates are holding steady in North Carolina even as overall violent crime is declining. Women, Black people and adults 25 to 34 were most frequently identified as victims in domestic violence reports, the report said.
The analysis center defines domestic and family violence as any crime against a person — homicide, assault or intimidation, sex offenses, kidnapping or human trafficking — in which at least one offender is either a current or former intimate partner or a family member. 
The report examines trends in these offenses, looking at changes over the past six years and patterns in victimization in the past three years and comparing them against other crimes against persons.
Rose Werth, director of the N.C. Criminal Justice Analysis Center (Courtesy photo)
Domestic and family violence in 2025 accounted for the majority of murders of women and girls in the state, and more than half of reported kidnappings and simple assaults, according to the report. 
Rose Werth, director of the analysis center, said that trend stood out to her because that wasn’t necessarily the case two years ago.
“It was from a variety of different causes” in the past, Werth said. “That increase in the last couple of years is something that I’ll be keeping my eye on.”
The report also shows that incidents of domestic and family violence are more prevalent in urban parts of the state. In rural parts of North Carolina, there were 518 incidents of domestic and family violence per 100,000 residents. That’s compared to 555 per 100,000 in suburban areas, and 729 per 100,000 in urban areas, the report shows.
Caroline Farmer, executive director of the Governor’s Crime Commission, says the data helps to inform funding decisions every year.
Caroline Farmer, director of the N.C. Governor’s Crime Commission (Courtesy photo)
“It’s incredibly helpful for the Governor’s Crime Commission and for our commissioners to understand what the trends are, where things are happening, so we can make sure that we are addressing those trends and making sure that we are putting our grant funds where they need to be,” Farmer said. 
But the available grant funding is dropping. Federal funding to support crime victims and the organizations that provide services to them is on the decline. 
Established by the Victims of Crime Act of 1984, the federal Crime Victims Fund is financed by fines and penalties from convictions in federal cases, not from tax dollars. Fewer prosecutions of federal criminal cases and white-collar crimes have meant fewer deposits into the fund.
North Carolina received $41.5 million to distribute to service providers this year. That was down from a peak of $103 million in 2018, the report said.
“When resources become constrained, we remain focused on gathering information and working with our partners to support informed decisions that improve public safety,” North Carolina Department of Public Safety Interim Secretary Casandra Hoekstra said in a statement.
Elizabeth Sager, director of evaluation at the N.C. Coalition Against Domestic Violence, said the reduced funding has caused several domestic violence organizations to close over the last three years.
NC victim service providers urge lawmakers for increased funding

“Other agencies have had to take on neighboring counties to cover that population, and there’s one right now that just launched a GoFundMe campaign so that they can try to keep their doors open,” Sager said. 
Sager was referring to Greenville’s Center for Family Violence Prevention. The agency, which serves Pitt, Martin and Washington counties, launched a campaign in September to raise $28,000 to help keep its doors open. It had only raised $3,220 as of Oct. 29.
“Right now, the organization is facing an approximately $160,000 deficit and could be forced to close its doors within the next few months,” the GoFundMe page says.
Sager said agencies can’t generate enough money through community fundraising to cover the costs of 24-hour shelters, hotlines and other services. 
“Right now, staff are working overtime to keep everything open and running smoothly as possible,” Sager said. “But the funding – there really is no way to make up the shortfall by just fundraising during Domestic Violence Awareness Month to try to cover that.”
She noted that the increase on divorce filing fees to help agencies that address domestic violence will help. The fee increase is expected to generate about $1.3 million a year for the state’s Domestic Violence Center Fund.
“It just got passed in this latest budget,” Sager said. “That’ll provide a little bit, but it’s definitely not covering the amount of loss that we got from the decreases from the Victims of Crime Act money.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Young adults are stepping up, and not just at the polls
text:
Michael King, a Grand Valley State University Student and organizer for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters addresses a crowd on the Capitol steps on Sept. 26, 2023. | Kyle Davidson937,461 young adults are living in Michigan. They’re studying, working, caring for families and taking on leadership roles in communities around the state. They’re also showing up for democracy.
Young adults have typically voted at lower rates than older adults, mainly due to busy schedules, confusing registration rules, apathy, more frequent moves and other barriers. But Michigan has been doing a great job of removing some of those barriers, which is part of the reason our state has one of the highest voter turnout rates for young adults in the nation.
Over half of Michigan’s young adults ages 18-24 voted in 2024, a significant increase over previous presidential elections. And among the youngest voters, those ages 18 and 19, Michigan saw the biggest jump in voter registration of any state in the country between 2020 and 2024. Our future voters are ready to engage, too. Since 2024, eligible 16- and 17-year-olds have been able to pre-register to vote in Michigan, and in the first year alone, more than 114,000 teens signed up, so they’ll be able to cast a ballot in the first election after they turn 18.
The Michigan League for Public Policy’s latest Kids Count report explores this data and more, pointing to the fact that Michigan’s voting reforms have made voting more accessible for young adults. Proposal 18-3 brought automatic voter registration, same-day registration and no-reason absentee voting. Proposal 22-2 strengthened absentee voting and added early voting.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
These changes benefit all Michiganders (I was able to vote early this week because it worked better with my schedule), but they’re especially effective for young adults.
It’s definitely a point of pride to see our young people turning out to vote, but that’s just one area where they’re excelling.
A first job helps build communication, technical and problem-solving skills that young people will use throughout their lives. Right now, Michigan’s labor force participation rate among people ages 16-24 is 62%, above the national rate of 56%. Our young adults are also learning. Nearly half of them are enrolled in or have completed college despite rising tuition costs, and programs like the Michigan Achievement Scholarship and Community College Guarantee can help make college more affordable.
Michigan is home to 10,000 young adult apprentices, most of whom are training to become skilled workers like electricians, pipefitters and carpenters. These apprentices are making a median wage of $17.54 an hour, keeping young people out of debt and putting them on a path to a well-paying career.
Michiganders ages 18-24 also reflect the way Michigan is evolving. They are the most diverse generation we’ve had, bringing new perspectives and experience into our workplaces, campuses and neighborhoods.
For those of us who are older than 24, we have some work to do. We all remember that it’s not easy coming up in the world, and it’s up to us to give the newest generation of adults the support they need. With our state population continuing to decline, we need to make sure Michigan is a place where flourishing young people want to put down roots.
You can learn more about how we can do that by checking out the recommendations in the latest report. You can also follow the lead of our youngest adults by getting out there to vote between now and Tuesday!
For those of you who are younger, thank you for being part of some monumental changes. Your generation is working, learning, and voting for a better tomorrow, and we appreciate you.

name: California
title: California’s campaign drama entices political junkies, but serious issues get short shrift
text:
This year’s political campaigns gave California’s political junkies plenty of chaotic events to savor: gerrymandered congressional districts; the sudden, scandalous downfall of a frontrunner for governor, and running feuds with President Donald Trump over voting.
However, for those of us who just want effective governance that addresses the multitude of challenges arising from California’s socioeconomic complexity, the campaign season has been drearily disappointing.
Few, if any, office seekers have even mentioned such serious issues as unstable water supplies, budget deficits, homelessness or rising living costs, much less offered voters clear-eyed approaches to them.
The Democratic playbook has often been to blame Trump for everything negative, even though those important issues afflicted California long before he appeared on the political scene.
Meanwhile Republicans, with very slim chances of making gains in such a blue state, have pinned every unresolved problem on outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, even though he inherited many of them when he took office in 2019.
Polls tell us that Californians are in a sour mood. They’re worried about soaring living costs and the economy in general and are unhappy with the status quo. Yet they seem unwilling to make big political changes — preferring the known to taking a chance on the unknown.
That contradictory attitude is particularly evident in the campaigns for the two most important offices being filled this year, the governor and mayor of Los Angeles.
Despite having served in public offices for decades, including a stint as attorney general, Xavier Becerra’s support for governor in polls last spring was in the low single digits. Back then the odds-on favorite, Congressmember Eric Swalwell, self-destructed as multiple women accused him of sexual harassment or even assault.
Swalwell not only dropped out of the race but resigned his congressional seat. The only other candidates with double-digit support were left-leaning billionaire Democrat Tom Steyer and Republicans Steve Hilton and Chad Bianco. 
But they were unacceptable to Democratic leaders and their labor union allies, who immediately chose Becerra as a known quantity and therefore the most acceptable of the single-digit candidates. With Democrats holding a massive edge in voter registration, that made Becerra the likely next governor, and he still is.
Becerra’s campaign has consisted almost entirely of blaming Trump and refusing to offer any tangible approaches to the multiple issues he’ll likely inherit from Newsom. He knows he can win without committing himself publicly, so he doesn’t.
While Becerra represents the don’t-rock-the-boat stance at the state level, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, another veteran of multiple offices, is his counterpart in the state’s largest city. 
But she, unlike Becerra, cannot coast into victory. Bass is carrying heavy baggage from her sloppy handling of the wildfires that swept through Los Angeles and its suburbs early last year.
Bass was junketing in Ghana when the fires erupted, even though there had been forecasts that hot winter winds could create wildfire conditions. She tried to blame others for the miscue, fired the L.A. fire chief and later attempted to alter an official report on how the fires were handled.
Bass is highly unpopular but offers herself as a known quantity, while her left-leaning opponent, city councilmember Nithya Raman, represents the potentially disruptive unknown. The outcome could go either way.
Thank goodness the cacophony of shrieking TV spots making promises that cannot be kept or portraying rivals as devils incarnate — and the fliers filling our mailboxes — will all end soon.
Sometime after the polls close Tuesday — maybe weeks later in some close contests — we’ll learn who survived. The losers will be disappointed, the winners will be jubilant and once again we will hope that they’ll do more than plot how to climb the next rung on the political ladder.

name: California
title: Candidates are giving lowkey instructions on how to attack their opponents. Here’s how it works
text:
In summary
A CalMatters investigation found more than a dozen legislative candidates appear to be providing campaign materials for outside special interest groups to use on their behalf.


Some candidates for the California Legislature are increasingly using a controversial tactic that experts and watchdog organizations say appears to flout the state’s campaign finance laws.
A CalMatters’ survey of legislative race websites found at least 14 candidates have detailed campaign messaging packaged on their websites in ways that make it easy for independent expenditure committees to use in advertisements.
The technique, known as “red boxing,” is being increasingly used in the absence of oversight from state regulators. 
CalMatters found at least three instances in which outside groups made digital campaign ads that mirrored the packaged messaging on candidate websites. Under state campaign rules, ads made “at the behest” of official campaigns are presumed to be “coordinated” spending — not independent expenditures — and may illegally exceed campaign finance contribution limits. 
In one example, a section in a red box on Assembly candidate Jessie Lopez’s website says “Democratic and (No Party Preference) voters should know” that her competitor, fellow Santa Ana city councilmember David Penaloza, voted to approve a city contract with the surveillance camera company Flock, that he is funded by special interests, and that Jessie Lopez will “fight for working people.” 
On Oct. 14, a 15-second ad popped up on the Facebook and Instagram feeds of Santa Ana residents highlighting Penaloza’s approval of the Flock contract, his funding from “big tech billionaires,” and nurses’ and educators’ support for Lopez. It was paid for by an outside group, Working People United sponsored by SEIU California State Council, which has spent at least $1.4 million in support of Lopez since April. 
Lopez did not respond to a text message requesting comment, and her campaign did not respond to emailed inquiries about whether the information was intended for an independent expenditure committee. Working People United also did not respond to a request for comment.
But campaign strategists and watchdog groups agree the practice is becoming widespread in competitive California races.
“After Citizens United and all of that, and big money getting into politics, it’s gotten crazy, right? Things have just gotten unwieldy,” said Jorge Contreras, California Director of the Working Families Party, which supports Lopez. 
“Because of that, the candidates are using red boxes to try to communicate.”
“Red boxing” explained
Donors in California elections, including corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals, are limited in how much they’re allowed to give to candidates running for office. Under rules from the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, they can give candidates up to $5,900 per election. 
However, big spenders can give unlimited amounts to independent expenditure committees that run ads supporting or opposing candidates. FPPC rules say the committees’ spending can be unlimited as long as the payments “are not coordinated with or made at the behest of the candidate.” 
Similar rules exist for federal congressional contests. However, over the past decade, red boxing has cropped up in congressional races. Candidates leave instructions, typically outlined in a red box, for independent spenders to follow when creating the ads. In some cases, they are even specific about which demographic groups to target.
The red boxes are a way to “sidestep” contribution limits, according to Patrick Llewellyn, the director of state campaign finance at the Campaign Legal Center, a nonprofit that advocates for campaign finance reform. He said it can create the appearance of corruption, even if there is no explicit agreement between the candidate and the independent committee. 
“When a candidate red boxes and spending is then done in response to that red box, it just belies any commonsense understanding of independence,” he said, adding that the phenomenon has spread across state and local races nationwide, although officials in some areas have cracked down in recent years.
FPPC spokeswoman Shery Yang said there are rules on the books regulating red boxing.
A screenshot from Jessie Lopez’s campaign website shows a red box titled “What Voters Should Know,” with bullet points contrasting Lopez’s positions with those of opponent David Penaloza on immigration enforcement, surveillance cameras and campaign contributions. Screenshot via Jessie Lopez’s campaign website
In an email, she said “common forms of red boxing would generally be presumed to constitute coordination under existing FPPC regulations.” 
The regulations say an expenditure is presumed to be coordinated if it is either based on information about the campaign’s needs provided “directly or indirectly” or if it disseminates “in whole or in substantial part, a communication, including video footage, designed, produced, paid for or distributed by the candidate or committee.”
Dozens of candidates have several minutes of B-roll footage posted on their sites that is routinely used by independent expenditure committees in their ads.
Yang did not respond to questions about whether the commission, which is notoriously slow in investigating complaints, has ever enforced the rules around red boxing, or if it is investigating any cases this year. 
Democratic strategist Steven Maviglio said the practice has “really accelerated” during the last two election cycles as campaigns have seen the tactic work on the federal level. 
And campaigns don’t think they’ll get caught, Maviglio said. 
“Like it or not, the state watchdog doesn’t have the capacity to do their job,” he said. 
Former FPPC Chairman Dan Schnur said the agency’s lack of action may boil down to a lack of resources. 
“The FPPC’s challenge is that it’s funded by the legislators who they’re required to oversee,” Schnur said. “There’s not much of an incentive for an elected official to give them enough funding or staff to do their job in a comprehensive way.”
Staying “on message”
In Assembly District 36 on the southern border, Democrats have a 12% registration advantage over Republicans. That didn’t stop Marine veteran Jeff Gonzalez from flipping the seat red in 2024. Now, Gonzalez is fighting to protect the seat from his Democratic challenger, Imperial Mayor Ida Obeso-Martinez.
Outside groups including oil and gas companies and a California Chamber of Commerce PAC have spent around $3.4 million supporting Gonzalez and opposing Obeso-Martinez. 
Until recently, the Republican incumbent had a message for “interested parties” on his website. In a since-deleted memo within a Dropbox folder called “What Voters Want to Know” accessed through the ‘PHOTOS’ tab on his website, Gonzalez’s campaign identified three potential lines of attack against Obeso-Martinez, under the headings “PAY RAISE,” “TAXES & FEES,” and “WOKE.” 
“Ida Obeso-Martinez is just another politician who only looks out for herself,” the memo read. “On the City Council, Ida voted to double her own taxpayer-funded salary and voted to give herself a new taxpayer-funded benefits package.”
Google’s Ad Transparency Center shows that on Oct. 9, a group called “Families for Affordable Living,” funded mostly by McDonald’s franchise operators, utilities and oil and gas companies released an ad that highlighted the city council pay raise.
A screenshot of a PDF memorandum titled “Why Jeff Gonzalez Wins AD-36,” outlining the Assembly candidate’s military background and campaign messaging on lowering costs and improving health care affordability. Screenshot via Jeff Gonzalez’s campaign website
“As a city councilmember, Obeso-Martinez voted to double her own salary,” a voice says as an overlay of money falling appears over images of the Democrat. 
Maviglio said in some instances, independent expenditures become the campaign’s “entire strategy” because of how much money the committees are willing to spend. Campaign finance records show Gonzalez’s campaign has spent $1.04 million since the primary, less than one-third of the $3.4 million independent expenditure committees have spent on his behalf in the same period.
However, Democratic consultant Michael Trujillo says unlimited spending by outside groups can be dangerous if the independent expenditures aren’t “on message.” 
“You don’t want your message to be hijacked by any independent effort out there, good or bad,” Trujillo said, adding that red boxing can be a way for outside groups to communicate “what the campaign’s heart is about.” 
Recently, Obeso-Martinez jumped into the game herself. On Oct. 19, her campaign added a “Communications” tab to her website with a message: “Voters across the district need to see and hear negative communications on broadcast, radio, streaming and digital about Jeff Gonzalez’s alignment with Donald Trump.” 
Obeso-Martinez’s campaign consultant, Orrin Evans, declined to comment. Neither the listed treasurer for “Families for Affordable Living,” nor the committee’s primary funder, the California Alliance of Family-Owned Businesses, replied to requests for comment.
A spending arms race
Few races have garnered more outside money than the nearly $7 million racked up in a north San Francisco Bay Area battle between moderate Democrat and Marin County Supervisor Eric Lucan and his progressive Democratic challenger, Jackie Elward, a Rohnert Park councilmember.
Lucan has been the beneficiary of most of that spending, more than $4.5 million, largely from crypto billionaire-backed group Grow California. Labor unions have contributed about $2 million to Elward.
On the “gallery” tab of Elward’s website, a carousel of high resolution photos and B-roll footage shows the candidate strolling through a farmers market, fire station, downtown plaza and college campus. Until this week, if visitors scrolled to the bottom, they could find a “need to know” guide to campaign messaging instructions.
One line referenced the campaign ads from the primary: “Voters also need to be reminded where the attack ads against Jackie and the support ads for Eric are coming from: out-of-district MAGA-aligned billionaires, big pharma, and for-profit utility companies.”
On Oct. 18, “Workers for Jackie Elward,” whose top funders are the Consumer Attorneys of California, California Labor Federation and SEIU California Council, started running an ad on Facebook and Instagram. 
A screenshot of a campaign messaging guide titled “What Voters Need to Know,” outlining Jackie Elward’s policy priorities and criticism of her opponent Eric Lucan. Screenshot via Jackie Elward’s campaign website
Over photos of billionaire Grow California donors Chris Larsen and Timothy Draper, a voice asks: “Why are these Trump-lovin’ tech billionaires spending so much money to make (Lucan) your assemblyman?”
In a statement, Elward campaign consultant Doug Linney said “Everything on a campaign website is public information that we feel voters deserve to know.”
The campaign had already deleted the page. 
In September, Lucan posted on Instagram and Facebook calling on the independent expenditure committees to stop spending in the race.
“This dark money is misleading voters about me, as well as my opponent, and all of it is distorting and corrupting our democracy — it’s everything that disgusts people about politics,” the post read.
However, Lucan’s website still has B-roll footage available for anyone to use, which has appeared in many campaign ads supporting the candidate paid for by Grow California.
“Images from our social media, YouTube pages and website have been used by supporters and local media,” said four waters, a spokesperson for Lucan’s campaign who uses lowercase spelling. “We have never exerted any control or had any coordination with IEs working either in support of, or against, our campaign.”
Grow California did not respond to a request for comment. 
Legislative campaigns have changed significantly in recent years as independent spending has exploded, said former Los Angeles Assemblymember Mike Gatto, a Democrat.
“It was actually quite common just 10, 15 years ago for entire legislative races to be decided just based on what the candidates themselves raised,” he said. “That is increasingly becoming very rare.”

name: California
title: Google and Meta spent big this election cycle. Is Big Tech trying to ‘buy the legislature’?
text:
In summary
Tech interests have spent tens of millions of dollars this year on state legislative races alone. Industry advocates say they want to protect innovation from overregulation.



Big Tech has proven a big spender in this year’s election cycle.
Google, Meta, and other tech interests account for at least 20% of all the contributions made to outside groups spending on legislative races, according to a CalMatters analysis of campaign finance disclosures.
Tech companies are looking to push back at a growing volume of state regulations they say could stifle the industry. Some companies, like Facebook owner Meta, spent record sums on lobbying last year as tech interests looked to temper regulation on artificial intelligence and shape a half dozen data center bills. 
Tech money substantially or in part funded half of the top 10 spenders among political action committees that have sought to influence the state’s legislative races. Big donors to the largest independent expenditure groups include Google, Meta, Uber, cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Critics argue the tech spending is an attempt to buy the California Legislature. The industry says tech companies are just advocating for themselves like any other interest group. 
The total amount spent on California Assembly and Senate races rose to more than $128 million this year, as of Oct. 29, compared to $74.2 million in 2022, the last non-presidential election year, and nearly $100 million in 2024.
Independent expenditures for things like advertising and direct mail flyers have become a key source of political spending because they are not subject to state spending limits like candidate donations are. Individuals can give up to $5,900 per election to a candidate running for the Legislature. Independent expenditures are not allowed to coordinate with candidates’ campaigns on advertising.
Nationwide, pro-AI super PACs have spent more than $50 million to influence 46 congressional races this year, supporting Democrats and Republicans alike, according to the New York Times. Tesla founder Elon Musk alone has reportedly spent more than $350 million to support Republicans in the midterm elections, more than any other donor.
Big spenders
An independent expenditure group created by cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen and venture capitalist Tim Draper spent more than any other on California legislative races this year. Larsen speaks with Marisa Lagos on Political Breakdown at KQED in San Francisco on Oct. 15, 2026. Photo by Martin do Nascimento, KQED
CalMatters found the independent committee spending the most on legislative races in California so far this year is  from tech investor Tim Draper and Larsen. The committee, GROW California, has spent more than $23 million trying to offset the influence of labor unions, who last month saw seven laws from a package of nine bills they backed to protect workers from AI signed into law. The group’s stated goal is to influence California politics for the next decade.
The second-largest funder of such groups is California Leads, a committee bankrolled primarily by Google and Meta, which has spent nearly $152 million this year in races including the reelection campaign of Republican Inland Empire Assemblymember Greg Wallis.
The two groups have also backed a Democratic Assembly candidate in Marin County, Eric Lucan; a Democratic Senate candidate in Los Angeles, Sara Hernandez; and another Democratic Senate candidate in Los Angeles, Brian Goldsmith. Lucan and Hernandez both defeated union-backed candidates in the primary. Hernandez was criticized by her general election opponent Sarah Rascón, who is endorsed by Democratic Socialists, for taking money from tech billionaires as part of what Rascón said is a plan to buy an Assembly seat. Hernandez did not respond to a request for comment.
Goldsmith told CalMatters he has no idea why tech interests are supporting his campaign. Asked about tech’s independent expenditures this year in general, he endorsed campaign finance reform “to get special interest money out of politics.”
“Because Trump has abdicated responsibility, it’s up to individual states to responsibly regulate tech — and California should lead the way,” Goldsmith said. “I don’t want to push these companies and jobs to Texas or Tennessee, but I will hold them to high standards. I strongly believe we can do both.”
Other major spenders are groups backed by Meta and Uber.
Meta’s group, Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (META) California, spent $1.3 million backing Democratic former Palantir executive Scott Sakakihara in a Senate district near Silicon Valley.
Two committees funded largely by Meta and Google spent more than 90% of the independent expenditures that went to support Democrat Andrae Gonzales, who is running for Assembly in Kern County. Gonzalez is running for an open seat in a district that is still blue but had the biggest swing to the right of any Assembly district in California in the 2024 presidential election, according to California Target Book. His primary opponent, Ana Palacio, a Democrat supported by unions, saw nearly $800,000 in opposition spending, more than 40% of which came from tech interests.

The two tech-giant-funded committees also accounted for 63% of the independent expenditures that went to support Democrat Annalisa Perea in an open Fresno Assembly district. In the primary she defeated Sandra Celedon, a Democrat supported by healthcare unions and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. 
Perea and Gonzalez did not respond to questions from CalMatters. 
Sakakihara, the former Palantir executive, did not respond to questions about how he speaks to voters about tech companies that support his candidacy, but said in a statement that tech has both created incredible economic growth and serious consequences across society that warrant stricter scrutiny and government action.
JOBSPAC, an independent expenditure group organized by the California Chamber of Commerce, has received $3 million from Brin, $2.5 million from Meta, nearly $1 million from Google, and hundreds of thousands of dollars from companies including Amazon, and Airbnb. Landlords, major consulting firms and McDonald’s also gave money to JOBSPAC.
Legislative Action PAC, whose mission is to elect Republicans, received more than $500,000 from business interests including Airbnb, Amazon, DoorDash, Meta and Uber.
What tech wants
In some ways, the tech industry’s campaign spending is comparable to those of other interest groups, just bigger.
Stephen Aguilar, who studies AI in education at the University of Southern California, said that tech is to California what oil is to Texas. To Aguilar, tech companies spending big to protect their interests is “what every industry does, and for better or worse, that’s how our political system is settled since Citizens United,” the 2010 Supreme Court ruling that opened the door for unlimited independent expenditures.
Industry advocates have a similar take. Robert Singleton, director of policy and public affairs for national tech policy lobby Chamber of Progress, said Silicon Valley is just playing catch up.
“Unless we start spending money we’re going to continue to get hundreds of bills every year taking aim at new industries.”Robert Singleton, Chamber of Progress, a national tech policy lobby
“Folks in the industry are realizing that unless we start spending money we’re going to continue to get hundreds of bills every year taking aim at new industries,” he said.
Tech interests, he said, want to support moderate and pragmatic candidates who, in an overwhelmingly Democratic state, understand the benefits of the industry to the California economy, innovation and tax revenue.
“New technologies need some breathing room,” Singleton added. “If California lawmakers keep piling new rules onto companies before they’ve even had a chance to get off the ground, they risk overregulation, which could be a loss for California’s competitive edge, and thus tax revenue and jobs.”
Tech’s focus on California may be especially intense because Congress has proven reluctant to regulate the industry at the federal level. “State legislatures are realistically the only place where AI policy is going to get made over the next two to three years,” said Catherine Bracy, executive director of Tech Equity Action, a group that tracks tech money flowing into campaigns. California continues to pass more AI regulation than any other state.
Critics like Bracy and Long Beach Democratic Assemblymember Josh Lowenthal think the industry is trying to essentially buy the Legislature.
But some also say the industry has stirred up such a fierce public backlash that its spending could be counterproductive.
Jeremy Mack, executive director of Phoenix Project, which tracks and criticizes the influence of tech money in San Francisco Bay Area politics, noted that GROW California has had strong initial results, with 11 out of 12 of its candidates successfully advancing to the general election. But citing the souring of public attitudes about groups like GROW SF in San Francisco, Mack said the tide is bound to turn.
“The shelf life for these organizations is not long as they become more toxic and reviled for their egregious spending,” he said.
One group, Guardrails Alliance, is actively trying to spark the backlash. Last week the group invested nearly $2 million in ads to shame candidates who took money from pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, including Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a Los Angeles-area Democrat. 
“The tech industry has just never seen a problem that they didn’t think they could solve by throwing more money at it,” said Guardrails Alliance’s political director, Charlie Blaettler.
Lowenthal, the Long Beach assemblymember, said the tech industry is throwing around its money to build a broad influence base that he sees as pernicious.
“I saw money being doled out in the primaries for state legislative races to candidates that have never taken positions on tech, and it sure feels like there’s a concerted effort to buy the Legislature,” he said.
Lowenthal has good reason to keep an eye on the industry’s efforts: He has coauthored bills to strengthen digital privacy laws and penalize social media companies that injure children.
In February Lowenthal said that “we have one, two, three years before this money gets so deeply entrenched with the current crop of elected officials that it can be devastating to an entire generation.”
Earlier this month, Lowenthal warned that California will be a state controlled by tech companies in a few years.
“That amount of money dwarfs any other sector or special interest by a long shot, and I think it’s just the beginning,” he said of the industry’s spending.
Reporters Natasha Uzcátegui-Liggett and Kate Li contributed to this reporting.

name: California
title: How Prop 45 could reshape California’s fight over data centers
text:
In summary
Prop. 45, billed as a pro-housing development measure, may have the unintended consequence of making it easier to build data centers, opponents say.




California voters considering Proposition 45 will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless.
That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions at the city and county level.
Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45.
Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects, like housing and schools and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny.
Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends.
“What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. 
Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added.
Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges.
“The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. 
Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887, which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers.
Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development.
“The Data Center Coalition has reviewed Proposition 45 and concluded that data centers are not eligible for Prop. 45’s streamlining, nor are they a covered entity under any part of the measure,” said Khara Boender, the coalition’s Director of Government Affairs—West.
Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers.
Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight behind its passage. Corporate backers have poured over $10 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. 
The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review.
Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development in their communities.
Nina Robertson, a deputy managing attorney in Earthjustice’s California regional office, said the ambiguity written into the ballot text would trigger immediate legal battles over local permitting authority.
“And who’s going to bear the cost of that litigation?” Robertson asked. “It’s going to be the local governments.”

name: California
title: California can’t afford to keep Prop 13 loopholes open when billions of dollars are on the line
text:
Guest Commentary written by

John Kim
John Kim is the president and CEO of Catalyst California.


I have fond memories of growing up in the suburbs of Los Angeles in the 1970s. The weather felt perfect. Yes, there were hot days, but you could look forward to perfect summer nights. Public schools felt relatively new, which they were, and there were open spaces yet to be explored. 
Though there was a new danger every week on the news, I somehow felt safe tumbling around, untethered, in the back of my parents’ station wagon. 
The state’s transformation over the last 50 years has been mind boggling. You likely would have been laughed out of most rooms in the ‘70s for predicting that California would become the fourth-largest economy on earth, behind only the United States, China and Germany. 
Innovations forged here reshaped how the world works. And yet, state and local governments failed to keep up.
The population nearly doubled, but we did too little to house these new Californians. We made some gains in public schools after short-sighted disinvestment during the 1980s and ‘90s, but we still struggle with achievement gaps across race and class.
We set conditions for technological invention but do too little to mitigate an exploding wealth gap that would make the Gilded Age blush. And we’re nowhere near ready to manage an AI-driven economic transition, let alone the increasing severity and cadence of climate catastrophes. 
The favorite bogeyman, though, is bureaucratic intransigence, sometimes called one-party rule. But we should be clear the problem isn’t partisanship or a lack of imagination — it’s structural and goes back to the 1970s. 
Proposition 13 was sold in 1978 as a way to save grandma’s house from unpredictable property tax bills. It also became a permanent discount for wealthy, corporate property owners. 
Under the proposition, homeowners pay taxes based on market value when they bought their homes, rather than on current values. And that’s fine. But since Prop 13 passed, high-priced tax attorneys have leveraged loopholes in Prop. 13 to let commercial and industrial property owners avoid property reassessments and higher taxes when their property changes hands. 
The result: billions of dollars in lost tax revenue.
USC researchers recently estimated that as much as $25.1 billion more could be collected per year by state and local governments if California closes Prop. 13’s commercial and industrial loophole and those properties are assessed at their current fair-market values.
Think of all we could do with those resources if we told wealthy corporations, after 50 years, that the party’s over.
California is about to need every dollar it can raise. 
President Donald Trump’s signature legislation, dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill, takes healthcare and food aid from working families and hands the money to the wealthiest Americans.
Roughly 2 million Californians will fall off Medi-Cal by 2028, and nearly half a million are now being shoved off CalFresh. The state now has to cover a deficit of more than $20 billion a year.
And again public school districts up and down the state are struggling with empty coffers and potential layoffs.
Often big wins get lost in a bureaucratic wilderness, and cynicism rises among voters who are legitimately hurting.
But when we focus, we can get it right — like when the state offered all 4-year-olds an extra year of education by adding transitional kindergarten to public schools. This is a concrete, visionary program that protects the pocketbooks of California families while increasing trust in government.  
Now the Legislature and next governor have a rare political window. They can refill the federal breach and create a version of government we all want and need. The goal is not to restore California to 1970, but to build what will get us to 2070.
Until they seize this chance, the whole state is like me as a kid in the back of that station wagon: No seat belt. No headrest. Nothing to hold on to. 
Just sliding around, bracing for whatever comes next.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Longtime homeless cleanup nonprofit shuts down, leaving 125 unemployed
text:
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick, Max Loveridge, and Trevor Howell, left to right, clean out bins of abandoned property at the Transitional Storage Program  in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Despite efforts to save about 125 jobs, most of which were held by people experiencing homelessness and other challenges, the longtime Utah social enterprise nonprofit Advantage Services is shutting down amid financial struggles. 
“With heavy hearts, we announce that Advantage Services will be closing its doors and ceasing all services” effective Saturday, the nonprofit’s CEO Rob Ferris wrote in an email to customers and other community partners sent Thursday. 
He told Utah News Dispatch he and his team were in “shock” after receiving an email from the state Office of Homeless Services on Thursday that sank their last hope for a solution to save the social enterprise that’s existed for more than 34 years or the jobs it provides to vulnerable people. 
Rob Ferris, CEO of Advantage Services, Inc., poses for a photograph at their facility in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“We didn’t think that we were too big to fail, but we thought we were too important to let go,” he said. “The services that we provide are vital to the unsheltered community, to our community partners.” 
Ferris said over the next 30 days he’ll be working on liquidating the company’s assets, which includes a fleet of vehicles, in hopes he can use the money to pay out employees’ unused vacation time as severance. 
He’s also encouraging any current customers or members of Utah’s homeless services network interested in hiring his former employees to reach out to him. 
Why is Advantage Services shutting down?
Utah News Dispatch reported in August that Advantage Services had been facing financial woes due to several issues: unexpected cost increases, higher insurance premiums, and scaled-back contracts from various customers. But one of the biggest reasons was its largest contract with Salt Lake City’s Urban Services Division was slashed in half from roughly $2 million to less than $1 million. 
Longtime Utah homeless cleanup nonprofit on brink of bankruptcy, issues ‘urgent’ call for help

Since then Ferris has been trying to expand Advantage Services’ contracts or merge with another nonprofit to preserve its jobs so that the people who rely on the nonprofit for work aren’t left unemployed. Earlier this month, he furloughed about 110 employees as a last-ditch effort to keep the company afloat after not being able to make payroll. 
Earlier this month Advantage Services’ situation caught the attention of the Utah Homeless Services Board, the powerful body that oversees the state’s homeless system and distributes state funding to homeless service providers. State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy expressed a willingness to explore solutions, but none came before the clock ran out. 
In response to Ferris’ request for “emergency bridge funding” to keep Advantage Services afloat, an Office of Homeless Services staffer told Ferris in an email Thursday “OHS will not be able to provide funding for the requested purpose.”
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge, Anthony Tarchick and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Ferris said the social enterprise nonprofit’s slide toward closure has been “devastating” to his employees. He also worries that the loss of Advantage Service will leave a “void” in Utah’s homeless services network — not just because of their now canceled clean-up contracts on city streets, state highways and more, plus transportation services to and from homeless resource centers, but also because of the people that relied on the work. 
“I have some of my homeless employees, or people who’ve just come off the streets and got apartments, now concerned that they’re going to be homeless again because nobody’s going to hire them because of their criminal record,” Ferris said. “Each person that is employed by Advantage Services has some sort of barrier to employment.” 
‘We need help’: Homeless cleanup nonprofit furloughs employees, faces full shutdown

Since it was formed in 1992, Advantage Services has employed people who are disadvantaged, whether they have disabilities, are currently or formerly homeless, leaving jail or prison, are refugees, or are living in poverty. 
The nonprofit doesn’t function like a typical employer, but rather provides “supportive employment,” offering job coaching, mentoring, and other resources to help meet employees’ needs so they can not only work, but “thrive.”
The work Advantage Services employees do isn’t glamorous. They pick up garbage, clean up homeless encampments, power wash streets of biohazards, shuttle people to and from homeless shelters, and more, depending on the contract. But the opportunity to work can be life-changing for people building their resumes and developing life skills. 
‘I feel betrayed’
Megan Belagam, who worked as Advantage Services’ office manager, was in tears after she learned that her employer would be shutting down and she’d be out of a job. 
“My heart stopped,” she said. 
Belagam said she’s worked in various roles for Advantage Services since 2013, when Ferris gave her a job during a time when she struggled to find employment. She said she was diagnosed with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, which affects ligaments, tendons and muscles in her feet, arms and wrists, creating mobility challenges. 
Ferris gave her a chance, Belagam said, and the job gave her “independence,” enabling her to get off Supplemental Security Income, federal assistance that’s offered to people with disabilities and older adults with little or no income. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The idea of possibly having to go back to that is paralyzing,” she said, choking back tears. “That’s what I’m looking at. Rob and his team saw past my hands and what I could do. They gave me a chance. And so having that taken away from me, I feel very robbed.” 
Belagam also grieved for her fellow employees, who she called “family.” 
“They don’t have anywhere else to go, either,” she said. But she said she’s urging her coworkers to “not give up hope, to keep moving forward. … I’m very scared right now and I know that I do not know what my future holds, but I’m going to keep trying.” 
Belagam said she’s devastated but also angry, especially because of the slashed Salt Lake City contract that in large part led to Advantage Services’ failure. 
“I feel betrayed,” she said, not just for herself but for the other employees. “I am damn mad that they took away their opportunity. I am damn mad at that.”
What angers her the most, Belagam said, is “this shutdown has dehumanized” Advantage Services’ workers, “and nobody cares.”
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
