name: Maryland Matters
title: Howard lawmakers’ bill would set higher tax rates on propose ICE facility in Elkridge
text:
Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Howard and Anne Arundel) and Del. Gabriel Marone (D-Howard) unveiled their bill Thursday that would let the county set higher property tax and transfer tax rates for a proposed immigration detention facility in Elkridge. (Photo by Pera Onal/Maryland Matters)After Howard County officials lost the first round of a court fight to block a proposed immigration facility in Elkridge, state lawmakers Thursday unveiled legislation that would let the county instead set special, higher property taxes on any such property.
The tax proposal comes after a federal court rejected county emergency legislation that would have withdrawn the permit for the proposed 29,000-square-foot Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Elkridge office park. The facility would include a holding cell for immigrant detainees.
The bill, sponsored by Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Howard and Anne Arundel) and Del. Gabriel Moreno (D-Howard), would give county officials the authority to assess the impact of the facility on county services, and set a higher property tax rate and a hither transfer tax to compensate.
“ICE’s facility is not something that we asked for…. We never wanted it here, and we will all pay a price,” Lam said at a Thursday press conference in Ellicott City. “We don’t believe that Howard County taxpayers should be footing the bill for their unwanted presence.”
The bill would apply the higher taxes to any property leased as a “secure confinement facility.” Moreno said the bill aims to combat the direct and indirect fiscal effects of the facility, such as additional traffic management and public safety concerns, that the county is unprepared to take on. 
Howard County community members rally Thursday in support of a proposal to hinder a proposed ICE facility in Elkridge. (Photo by Pera Onal/Maryland Matters)
“Our responsibility is not simply to respond to the presence of detention facilities, but to ensure that public costs and human consequences of its operations are not ignored,” Moreno said.
Lam added that the county aims to be a diverse space, and the “out-of-control agency” that ICE has become runs against community values.
Dozens of community leaders and members from organizations like We Are CASA, Indivisible Howard County and St. John’s Episcopal Church in Ellicott City joined Lam and Moreno in support of their efforts.
We Are CASA Maryland’s policy manager, Ninfa Amador-Hernandez, said the legislation is a necessary way for the community to ensure it has the resources to push back against the federal administration’s actions.
“The federal government plans to continue burdening our community, not just with their hatred and their infrastructure for their mass deportation and family separation agenda, but it will be hyper-able to do this with this detention center right here in our backyard,” she said.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email Thursday that “no tax will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make Maryland safe again.”
The bill would first have to be approved the county’s delegation in Annapolis of eight delegates and three senators, before going to the full General Assembly for consideration this spring. If passed and signed into law, the next step would be for county to pass legislation to set the specific rate, Lam said.
“We recognize that there is still a heavy lift coming up to make sure that we get it across the General Assembly and pass it into state law,” Lam said. “I feel fairly confident that our new county council, as well as our incoming county executive … will allow this to go into law.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In February, the council passed and current County Executive Calvin Ball signed emergency legislation that would have revoked the permit that had been granted to the developer for the property. The bill, which was rushed through in less than a week, would also have established that local government was the only operator of a detention facility.
County officials at the time justified the permit revocation by saying the project failed to post notice and hold necessary public hearings, while also being too close to schools, parks and shopping centers.
The same day the county bill was signed, Gov. Wes Moore sent a two-page letter to Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem criticizing a potential ICE facility in Hagerstown, writing that he had “grave concerns” about the project’s implications on that community’s public safety.
Project developer Genesis Strategic One LLC sued Howard County in March, claiming the county interfered with federal authority by attempting legislation to ban privately owned detention centers.
Hundreds rally against ICE as judge agrees to block detention center construction

U.S. District Judge Adam Abelson ruled in August that Howard County’s attempts to block the facility had overstepped its authority. He ruled that the county’s blockage of the project, which was almost complete when the permit was yanked, was pushing Genesis Strategic One into bankruptcy, and the county had to let the project continue while the court case proceeded.
The county has appealed that ruling, but it’s unclear when an appeal might be heard.
Lawmakers and community leaders maintained Thursday that the development runs counter to what they stand for. As the county braces for potential federal retaliation on the legislation and its efforts to block the development, Lam said they will continue fighting.
“Were it not for this facility, the extra burden would not be borne by Howard County,” Lam said. “This legislation is about accountability. That if you are using our resources, you do not get a free ride. You should foot the bill.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Rehabilitation, reduction in repeat offenses will require ongoing investment, task force says
text:
South Dakota's Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force meets on Oct. 29, 2026, in Sioux Falls. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)It would cost at least $1.9 million a year to begin addressing shortcomings in rehabilitation within South Dakota’s prison system, according to the consultants hired to assess the system and recommend fixes.
That money’s needed to pay rehabilitation-focused staff members at a market rate, fund housing and transportation support for people after their release, and to pay community partners to offer ongoing support to parolees after release.
“You have to look at all parts of the elephant,” said David D’Amora, a senior policy adviser for the Council of State Governments Justice Center. “You have to look at what happens on the way out, and what happens when they are out.”
The $1.9 million annual figure is a floor. It’s the ongoing price of recommended changes before factoring in the cost to hire additional staff — which the consultant also said is necessary immediately, but did not offer cost estimates for — or any additional operational costs associated with the $650 million men’s prison under construction in Sioux Falls.
The state’s Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force heard the consultant’s final recommendations on Thursday at the Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls. 
Gov. Larry Rhoden convened the task force after lawmakers greenlit the prison project, which will replace the oldest parts of the 144-year-old state penitentiary in Sioux Falls.
Its goal has been to study ways to reduce repeat offenses in a state where half of former inmates commit a new crime within three years of release.
The group will meet one more time to sign off on a final report that’s meant to incorporate the consultant’s recommendations and those penned by four subcommittees of task force members that labored between public task force meetings. The document is meant to guide discussions on prison budgeting and policy change when the legislative session begins in January. 
Sara Friedman, the program director for the Justice Center, lauded the efforts of the group and the Department of Corrections thus far, but also said the state is unlikely to see repeat offense rates decline quickly.
“Making big shifts inside prison always takes time, more time than we want it to, frankly,” Friedman said. “You all are starting a yearslong process.”
Costs for staff, quality assurance, community partnerships
Salaries represented the largest single ongoing expense in the consultant’s document. It would cost $821,720 a year to bring pay for the Department of Corrections’ program director and its behavioral health staff up to market rates.
“Those are the folks that particularly find other employment at much better rates,” D’Amora said.
The state also needs to spend around $700,000 a year for “peer support” contracts with community organizations to help people leaving prison do things like find work, set and get to appointments and manage the stressors of life on the outside, the consultants said.
Work, housing and staffing: How South Dakota’s corrections chief aims to keep inmates from returning

They said the state should also spend $150,000 a year for a “landlord liability fund,” which would compensate landlords for housing people with felony convictions if those people are unable to pay rent, and $250,000 a year in transportation support, which could include bus passes for parolees.
Rich Merkouris, who’s on both the task force and the Sioux Falls City Council, said the city already has a landlord liability fund, but needs program managers to help connect people to housing. 
“The issue is there’s not case managers in place for the individuals that qualify for the fund,” said Merkouris, adding that he’d rather see the state help connect people to existing programs.
Merkouris also said the city would happily give 90-day bus passes to people leaving prison, but it doesn’t have anyone to run such a program.
D’Amora said the idea is to set aside funding for housing and transportation that could be used to fill gaps statewide, like in cities where there are no buses and no source of funding to encourage landlords to rent to ex-felons.
The state needs more program, parole agent and correctional officer staff, the report says, but the state would have to decide how many.
That frustrated Tesa Schwans, a task force member and Republican state representative from Hartford.
“My question goes back to, and it’s pretty simple, pretty blunt: How many correctional officers do we need? How many parole officers do we need? And how many instructors are needed? Do we have any of that data?” Schwans asked. 
Brent Fluke, deputy secretary for the Department of Corrections, said the state’s still working through its programs to decide which will stay and which will go as it makes organizational changes to trim its waiting list and move inmates through them more efficiently. The department is also trying to decide whether to add parole officers after moving some experienced officers into an enhanced compliance unit that monitors parolees on nights and weekends.
The state will need more staff to do what’s needed, but “I would say that’s a work in progress,” Fluke said.
The department is looking at a quality assurance officer for programming, however, and at adding a correctional officer duty post at the penitentiary to make sure it has enough security staff to move inmates safely to and from class, and to monitor them during class.
Officers are sometimes pulled away from programming duty to work in other parts of the prison with higher security needs, effectively shutting down rehabilitative programming until enough officers are available to oversee it.
Final recommendations coming next month
The task force first heard the consultant’s recommendations, then approved a 34-point document that referenced the consultant’s findings and the work of subcommittees on education, faith-based rehabilitation, tribal concerns and behavioral health.
Each point was discussed and voted on for inclusion in the final report, due for review at the task force’s Nov. 30 meeting. 
Poor coordination, missing documents, mismatched training: Report analyzes prison releases in SD

The addition of a duty post for programming earned support, as did recommendations to prioritize literacy programming, GED classes, partnerships with technical schools, the pursuit of a tribal liaison to help parole officers work with “willing” tribes, adding tribal-specific programming and a tribal cultural liaison inside prison walls, and adding evening volunteer hours to support those who visit and train inmates through nonprofit or religious organizations.
One religious program, a prison seminary program that trains inmates to act as moral guides inside the walls, was formally endorsed, although it had been in the works already. The first seminary class will begin in January.
The group also endorsed “full funding” and appropriate staffing for the new men’s prison. Ryan Brunner, a policy adviser for Gov. Rhoden, said the estimated annual operational cost for the new facility is $44.6 million, about $20 million more than the cost to run the current Sioux Falls-based prison operations.
Rep. Greg Jamison, R-Sioux Falls, said he was pleased with the task force’s work, but he’s concerned about what happens when the work is done. Rhoden’s executive order disbands the group in January.
The next crop of lawmakers might not go for the task force’s ideas, particularly the ones that require long-term commitments.
“Who is going to hold all of this together?” Jamison said.
There’s little the task force can do on its own to make sure anyone does, said Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen, who leads the group. 
“The best we can do is set things in the right direction and hope that our successors follow through,” Venhuizen said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Turek criticizes Hinson’s ‘Save Our Bacon Act,’ calls for supporting small farmers
text:
Rep. Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate, met with Megan and Vance Veldboom at Raffety Farms in Grinnell Oct. 29, 2026 to discuss Iowa's agriculture economy. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)GRINNELL — With five days left until Election Day, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek visited a farm Thursday to discuss his plans to support Iowa farmers if elected to Congress — a plan he said will not include the “Save Our Bacon” act proposed by his opponent, Republican Ashley Hinson.
Farmers Lance and Megan Veldboom, who own Raffety Farms, a family farm on the outskirts of Grinnell, gave Turek a tour of their property and equipment while telling the candidate about some of the problems they have faced with high input costs and volatile markets over the past year.
Megan Veldboom told Turek, a state representative, that she and many farmers are feeling “uncertainty” about the future. “I mean, certainty that expenses are going up, and uncertainty of what the future holds,” she said.
Turek and other Democrats on the campaign trail have highlighted the impacts of President Donald Trump’s tariff policies and high fuel and fertilizer prices caused by the Iran war. The Veldbooms said these were issues contributing to high costs, and there are other long-term impacts on Iowa markets that could hurt the state’s economy, like the loss of international markets for pork.
Hinson, who currently represents Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, has championed the “Save Our Bacon Act” — a proposal she introduced that would block block individual states from enforcing conditions on livestock products sold across state lines. The legislation was introduced specifically in response to California’s Proposition 12 that enacts certain standards for growing conditions of livestock like hogs.
While Hinson and farmers supporting the measure say the Save Our Bacon Act will help local Iowa hog farmers, Turek said he believed the measure benefits large, international companies like JBS Foods and Smithfield Foods more than it helps small Iowa farmers.
“When I’m out there talking to small providers, most of them have already updated themselves to the standard,” Turek said. “… Certainly, California shouldn’t be telling Iowa farmers what to do. But … when I’m talking to small pork providers, they’re telling me this doesn’t benefit them. This doesn’t help them. This only helps foreign ownership.”
He said he would instead advocate for legislation that would provide more help to small pork and beef producers, like mandatory of country of origin labeling.
But Linda Schroeder,  a hog farmer in northwest Iowa with her husband and two sons, says Hinson’s proposal helps small Iowa producers because many family farms are not able to pay for the costs necessary to upgrade their facilities to comply with California’s Proposition 12.
“Small family farmers can’t possibly basically shell out the (roughly) $3,000 per sale that it would cost to comply with Prop 12,” Schoeder said. “I guess that means a lot of family farms would have to close for good, and that would be more consolidation in the ag industry.”
Schroeder also said the proposal would help shield Iowa farmers from other state initiatives regulating agricultural products coming into their states.
Billy Fuerst, Hinson campaign communications director, said in a statement, “When it comes to agriculture and more specifically Prop 12, Josh Turek has no idea what he’s talking about.”
“Farmers don’t trust a liberal like him who supports Prop 12, wants a 50% tax rate on many Iowa farms, and voted to let fake meat be labeled as real,” Fuerst said.
Turek has stated he does not support California’s Proposition 12. Opponents of Hinson’s proposal, including some local farmers and groups like the American Meat Producers Association, have argued the measure allows Chinese companies to override state and U.S. laws.
Turek called for Iowa farmers to support him over his opponent because “I’m going to look out actually for our small family farms. I think what Ashley Hinson has fought for is just big ag.”
“Farmers can see what she’s done,” Turek said. “Five times voted in favor of the tariffs. That has decimated rural communities and small family farms. It’s led to a loss of markets. It’s led to commodities prices being upside down. Seven times she’s voted in favor of this war. It’s led to gas prices going up here in Iowa more than almost any other state. Diesel prices at an all-time high, and fertilizer prices skyrocketing. She’s not looked out for farmers. She’s looked out for herself. She’s looked out for China.”

name: WyoFile
title: University of Wyoming grad student accused of poisoning peer now faces second-degree murder charge
text:
A University of Wyoming graduate student accused of poisoning her colleague now faces an additional charge for attempted second-degree murder, according to a new court document filed Thursday. 
Aili Wang, 32, originally faced one felony charge for aggravated assault and battery after she allegedly put acrylamide, a neurotoxin, in the tea of a fellow graduate student. The additional second-degree murder charge carries the possibility of 20 years to life in prison. 
Police began investigating after the victim, identified in court records as “K.T.,” started having symptoms. A chemistry professor tested water from the alleged victim’s coffee maker, which he used to make tea, and found acrylamide, a police affidavit states. 
According to the police account, Wang, who was a microbiology student, used her university email over the summer to buy acrylamide two times on eBay and later requested the site to delete her order history and account. 
Wang was recorded Sept. 27 on a surveillance camera going through the victim’s desk, the affidavit states. She was also recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug.
On Oct. 6, authorities arrested Wang at the Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she was attempting to flee the country and return to China, court records show. 
While the court originally set a $200,000 bond for Wang, Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford subsequently granted prosecutors’ request to increase the amount to $1.5 million cash-only. 
Wang is scheduled to appear in court Monday for her preliminary hearing.

name: WyoFile
title: Election complaints allege donors to Bextel, Bien and Degenfelder exceeded campaign finance limits
authors: Maggie Mullen and Jasmine Hall, Jackson Hole News&Guide
text:
The Wyoming Secretary of State’s office is reviewing multiple complaints filed by a Teton County lawmaker Wednesday regarding contributions to several gubernatorial campaigns allegedly exceeding the legal limit an individual can give to a statewide candidate per election. 
Jackson Democratic Rep. Mike Yin filed three separate complaints against the Constitution Party’s Rebecca Bextel, as well as Brent Bien and Megan Degenfelder, two Republicans defeated in August’s primary election. 
Wyoming state law limits individuals from giving more than $2,500 — including in-kind donations like services or campaign assistance — to a statewide candidate per an election. The primary and general are considered separate elections. Yin alleges that Bextel, Bien and Degenfelder all filed campaign finance reports with the Secretary of State’s office that include contributions from individuals that exceed that limit. 
“For Ms. Bextel, whose election is still ahead, I ask for the fix the law allows: give the extra money back, and correct the report before people finish voting,” Yin said in a statement. “For Mr. Bien and Ms. Degenfelder, the primary is over, and a refund cannot take back the advantage those campaigns carried into it over candidates who followed the rules. In those cases, I asked the Secretary of State to refer the largest entries to the Attorney General, who decides whether a penalty is warranted.”
Secretary of State Chuck Gray confirmed his office had received the complaints and is currently evaluating them according to Wyoming law. 
“Secretary Gray has said that election integrity is the core mission of his office,” Yin said in a statement. “Under the law, these complaints land on his desk first, and he decides whether they go to the Attorney General. Campaign finance limits are part of that mission, and I trust his office will act on these before Tuesday.”
Degenfelder denied any wrongdoing, while Bien said he was reviewing his campaign finances. Both say that donations may have been inadvertently duplicated in the state’s campaign finance reporting system. Bextel did not respond to multiple requests for comment by publishing time.
The reports are filed and available to the public, but they are not reviewed unless an election complaint is filed. That’s because the secretary of state’s office does not automatically audit campaign finance reports. Errors are not uncommon. 
Bextel complaint
According to the campaign finance report Bextel filed Tuesday, Susan Gore of Cheyenne contributed $4,000 across four donations while John Warren of Cordova, Alabama gave $3,000 across six donations. 
Reached by phone Thursday, Warren told a reporter he is Bextel’s father and was under the impression that Wyoming law does not limit how much a candidate’s immediate family can give to their campaign. Warren’s understanding is correct, though Bextel did not include her father’s donations in the immediate family portion of her report. 
Bextel, who reported raising a total of $89,000, reportedly told Cowboy State Daily this week she would “soon be filing an amended report reflecting a much higher fundraising figure, at about $500,000.” 
Tuesday marked the deadline for candidates to file their campaign finance reports ahead of Tuesday’s general election. State law allows for amendments in instances where additional contributions or expenditures occur after filing, or if inaccuracies are found. 
“Additional statements shall be filed within a reasonable time not to exceed 30 days from the time the inaccuracies or additional contributions or expenditures became known,” according to the election code.  
Bextel amended her report Thursday, according to the secretary of state’s website. However, the amendment did not add contributions, but instead deleted a $500 donation from Warren. The secretary of state’s website did not show additional amendments by publishing time. 
Gore, a conservative donor and Gore-Tex heiress, could not be reached by publishing time. 
Bien complaint
Yin flagged donations to Bien’s campaign from 10 individuals, according to his complaint. 
Four contributions were listed from Wheatland resident Jill Kaufman, totaling $6,700, according to Bien’s amended primary election campaign finance report. 
Bien’s campaign reported $4,900 across three donations, as well as an in-kind donation of $1,800 for campaign outreach, administrative support, supplies, catering and a venue. Kaufman didn’t respond to a request for comment before press time.
Wheatland resident Mark Kaufman contributed $2,000 and made an in-kind donation of $2,500, according to the primary report. That in-kind donation was for the same services as Jill Kaufman. He didn’t respond to a request for comment before press time. 
Retired Jackson physician Richard Sugden reportedly gave two $2,500 donations, both on March 16, according to the primary election campaign finance filing. He didn’t respond to a request for comment before press time. 
Albany County GOP state committeeman Jerry Gruber gave $3,200 across two donations, as well as $1,300 in-kind donation for campaign outreach, administrative support, supplies and catering, according to the finance report. Gruber didn’t respond to a request to comment before press time.
Gillette resident Wanda Lieneman gave $400 across three donations, as well as $2,300 in-kind contribution for campaign outreach, administrative support, supplies and catering, according to the primary election campaign finance report. She didn’t respond to a request for comment before press time. 
Cheyenne resident Don Odom, who ran for House District 61 in 2022, gave a $700 contribution, as well as two in-kind contributions: one for $150 for a venue fee and another $1,800 for campaign outreach, administrative support and supplies, according to campaign finance records.
When asked about the complaint, Odom said in an email Thursday that, “Those figures are incorrect.” 
“I talked to Brent and they are getting it straightened out,” he said. 
Ron Smart of Rock Springs reportedly gave $900 across two donations and a $1,700 in-kind donation for campaign outreach, administrative support, supplies and catering, according to the primary election campaign finance report. He couldn’t be reached before press time.
Bob Aguiar, a Hot Springs county commissioner, contributed $180 across three separate donations, as well as made a $2,340 in-kind contribution for campaign outreach, according to the campaign finance records. He didn’t respond to a request for comment before press time. 
Yin also said in his complaints that two other entries were over the limit, “but may be duplicates: Elena Campbell of Sheridan reportedly gave $3,200, including two identical $700 donations on July 11, and Cheryl Aguiar from Thermopolis, who has worked on Bien’s campaign, donated $2,500 in 2026, plus two $60 in-kind contributions in 2025. 
“If any entry in this letter is a duplicate or a spouse’s gift entered under the wrong name, the cure is an amendment that says so,” Yin said. 
Yin raised one more issue with the report.
“It shows a cash balance of negative $18,067.47 at the end of the primary period, and negative $26,209.03 after the General Report filed October 27, with no loan reported,” he wrote. “Whoever covered those bills, and in what amounts, belongs on the report.”
Bien said he called the Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office on Thursday morning and that they are reviewing the campaign finance records. He was concerned about duplicate donations of the same amount for certain contributors in the finance reporting system. He said his team is also looking at in-kind donations and what the value of certain services or assistance were for the grassroots campaign, as well as cross-checking with explicit monetary contributions. 
“I just got off the phone with the bank to potentially set up a teller to go down line-by-line,” Bien said Thursday. “But it’s going to take awhile because unfortunately you can’t go in on an app or on your computer. You actually have to go to the bank to figure out what exactly the donation was.” 
Degenfelder complaint
Yin flagged contributions from four individuals to Degenfelder’s campaign in his complaint. 
According to campaign finance reports Degenfelder filed in August, Ty Jenkins of Ten Sleep gave $7,500 across two donations and Debbie Jenkins of Ten Sleep gave $5,000 across two donations. Neither responded to a request for comment by publishing time.
Yin also named Tiffany and Blake Gamble of Casper in the complaint. According to campaign finance reports, Tiffany gave $2,500 to Degenfelder’s superintendent campaign committee in December and $2,500 to her gubernatorial campaign in January, while Blake made identical contributions. Yin argues that “still violates the statute.”
Tiffany Gamble, who hosted Degenfelder’s campaign kick-off event in Casper, told a reporter she is aware of the legal limit, and wondered if donations from her and her husband got mixed up somehow. Blake declined to comment. 
“The committee has not accepted any contributions in excess of campaign finance limits, and the complaint is frivolous,” Charlotte Jones, Degenfelder’s campaign manager, said a statement. “The contributions from the Gamble’s were made to two independent committees, one that existed prior to Megan’s decision to run for Governor and formation of a new committee to seek that office. The Jenkins’ also did not make contributions in excess of limits, rather these contributions were double reported. The campaign’s treasurer has notified the Secretary of State of the clerical error, which requires deletion by the Secretary’s office.”
In both Yin’s complaints about Degenfelder and Bien, he requested the Secretary of State’s Office refer them to the attorney general to determine whether a civil penalty was warranted, as well as to direct the campaign committee to refund the excess and file an amended primary election report and “confirm to me in writing when the referral is made and when the amendment is on file.” 
He added in Bien’s complaint that he would like the office to “direct the committee to amend the report to identify the source of the funds covering its negative balance, or to explain in writing why it cannot.” 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Governor releases Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force recommendations
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)Finalized recommendations from the Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task force include suggested legislative changes to increase penalties for Medicaid fraud, give investigators more authority and add anti-kickback and civil penalty laws. 
The task force, which was initiated by Gov. Kim Reynolds over the summer, submitted its recommendations Tuesday and Reynolds released the finalized document Thursday. 
The task force evaluated Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and found that the unit was significantly smaller in size compared to states with similar Medicaid programs and laws. While Iowa’s unit “produces results far beyond its size,” the task force recommended more than doubling staff.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Increasing the staff from nine to 24 would cost roughly $3.3 million annually, but according to the recommendations, the federal government would cover 75% of the cost, leaving Iowa to come up with $550,000 for the unit. 
“That increase—especially accompanying civil fraud enforcement—will create an enormous return on investment for Iowans,” the report stated. “Going forward, the unit’s budget should grow with Medicaid spending rather than stand still.” 
According to the report, Iowa’s Medicaid program grew 129% since 2013 but the unit budget grew only 31%, meaning each staff member “polices nearly $1 billion in Medicaid spending.”
The task force also recommended that part of the staff serve under the attorney general, as it said is common with many other states. Those staff could pursue civil fraud enforcement under the Iowa False Claims Act, while other investigators pursue criminal enforcement. 
“Civil enforcement is where the money is, and the Iowa False Claims Act makes it far easier to reach,” the report said. 
The report said Iowa “leaves civil money on the table” because it has no “civil litigators to recover money under the Iowa False Claims Act.”
A group of former state officials who have criticized the task force as being politically motivated have argued that the attorney general could have dedicated staff to this effort without the task force’s recommendation to do so.
Many of these recommendations would require statutory changes, which the report said “could be accompanied by Executive action” to start the process. 
Greater authority and punishment 
The task force also recommended changes to Iowa law that would make Medicaid fraud a Class D felony, similar to insurance fraud, and a Class C felony for instances over $10,000. 
The evaluation of Iowa’s current system concluded that the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s legal tools “are weaker than its mission requires.” 
To address that issue, the task force recommends giving unit investigators the ability to execute their own warrants and allow investigators with proper certifications to carry firearms. 
It also recommends the unit have investigative subpoena authority and a formalized partnership with U.S. Attorneys’ offices. 
When compared to other states, the report said Iowa “lacks” a Medicaid-specific anti-kickback statute and a state civil monetary penalties law, which are “tools nearly every peer state has.” 
The task force recommended legislative action for these regulations that would prohibit parties from offering or accepting kickbacks to generate health care business and give the state the authority to seek civil monetary penalties.
“If the Legislature enacted those laws, it would let the State penalize referral schemes in managed care, laboratories, and medical equipment that fall below federal enforcement thresholds,” the report stated.
The report also noted a need for better data management and case litigation tools, and called for AI-assisted analytics software within the unit. 
These recommendations comprised the first and largest section of the report. 
Other sections detail recommendations to improve public knowledge and reporting of Medicaid fraud, to strengthen the quality and oversight of high-risk Medicaid services, to improve data resources and to encourage managed care organizations to oversee their networks to ensure billings are coming from real providers for appropriate services.  
In a news release, Reynolds said the recommendations will help to make Iowa’s Medicaid system “one of the most accountable and secure in the nation.” 
“While we work to protect Iowa taxpayers’ investment in these programs, we’re equally focused on ensuring that quality care and services are available for every eligible Iowan who relies on them,” Reynolds said. “The recommendations put forth by the task force help advance these goals and will support the system’s long-term sustainability.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Republican officials order investigations of Peltola and other Democrats after New York Times report
text:
Carmella Warfield, chair of the Alaska Republican Party, and Gov. Mike Dunleavy listen to JD Vance deliver a speech at an Oct. 5, 2026, campaign rally in Fairbanks. Vance was in Alaska to campaign for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska’s governor said late Wednesday that he is ordering the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, her campaign or national Democratic groups violated state law by recruiting independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan to run in this year’s election.
Sullivan’s recruitment was first reported Wednesday by the New York Times, which said Democratic campaigners worked through an intermediary to convince Sullivan to run for office and act as a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election campaign.
State law does not prohibit the recruitment of spoiler candidates, and it is a tactic that has been used by both Republicans and Democrats in statewide races within Alaska.
Alaska’s Senate race is thought to be among a handful of elections that may decide whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate.
Following Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s announcement, a Republican member of the U.S. House said he would also investigate, and the Associated Press reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has expanded an ongoing criminal investigation.
Speaking Thursday on Fox News, Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the state investigated Sullivan’s candidacy before ruling him ineligible, a ruling that was overturned by the Alaska Supreme Court in June.
“With these new revelations in the New York Times article, we’re more than compelled to follow up on the investigation, and we are starting that diligently here today,” Dunleavy said.
Trump calls for Peltola to be criminally charged, removed from Alaska’s U.S. Senate race

On Thursday morning, the head of the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. James Comer, R-Kentucky, said he would seek to interview two of the sources cited by the Times.
He asked Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager and a source for the Times’ reporting, to sit for a voluntary interview after Election Day. If she does not agree, he said in a letter, “we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process.”
Comer sent a similar letter to Jerid Kurtz, a person whom the Times article said acted as an intermediary between Democratic campaign groups and Dan J. Sullivan.
The U.S. Department of Justice is pursuing a criminal investigation into Dan J. Sullivan and the Peltola campaign, and the Associated Press — citing an unidentified source — said the DOJ issued more subpoenas related to the investigation on Thursday.
In addition, the DOJ is pursuing a civil lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections. 
President Donald Trump said last week that he ordered the lawsuit, which asks a federal judge to prohibit anyone but Dan S. Sullivan from being declared the winner of the Senate election.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed an amended legal complaint that puts the Times article at the center of the issue. 
Judge Sharon Gleason — an appointee of President Barack Obama — had been expected to rule by Monday on motions seeking to dismiss the DOJ lawsuit, but hours after its filing, the DOJ argued that the amended complaint means she should push back her deadline.
That could mean a ruling on or after Election Day.

title: In a blizzard of lawsuits, Trump’s DOJ battles across the US over midterm elections
text: The Trump administration’s sweeping efforts to combat noncitizen voting and assert authority over elections came under intense scrutiny in courtrooms across the country on Thursday, as Democrats and voting rights groups alleged federal election interference.A federal judge in Washington, D.C., ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to either reveal by midday Friday all states where it has demanded election officials pull aside or not count ballots — or else promise it won’t direct election officials to refuse ballots from some voters.On the West Coast, an appeals court appeared skeptical of a Trump administration request to allow the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to resume election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens.In California, the Justice Department vowed to keep fighting to require election officials there to set aside the ballots of some 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are suspected noncitizens and not count their votes unless they can prove their citizenship. On Thursday, Los Angeles County disclosed it had received federal grand jury subpoenas last week for election-related records.  And in Alaska, the DOJ kept up pressure on election officials over its U.S. Senate race.The bevy of lawsuits and hearings underscore the high stakes of the midterm elections to determine control of Congress. Amid sagging approval ratings, President Donald Trump faces investigations and a thwarted legislative agenda during his final two years in office if Democrats retake the House or Senate.Final days before midterm electionsFor the past year, Trump has sought power over elections. The Justice Department unsuccessfully sued dozens of states in an attempt to force them to turn over sensitive voter data, including driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The president also tried to use the U.S. Postal Service to impose restrictions on mail ballots, but was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court.Now, in the final days before Election Day, the Trump administration and its allies have launched a new effort to influence elections that pits it against state and local officials who say the federal government is overstepping its authority. A growing number of federal judges agree, and have handed Trump a series of court losses over the past two weeks.At the heart of several of these cases is what power, if any, the Trump administration has over federal elections. The elections clause of the U.S. Constitution gives states the authority to run their own elections, though Congress can override state rules and regulations.“The DOJ’s actions are indicative of a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials,” U.S. District Judge David Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton in the Central District of California, wrote in an order released late Wednesday that blasted the Trump administration’s efforts in California.But the legal challenges continue to multiply.The Republican National Committee on Thursday sued an election official in Black Hawk County, Iowa — home to Cedar Falls and Waterloo — alleging public records had been withheld related to the security of ballot tabulators. A day earlier, the Potter County, Texas, Republican Party sued to force a hand count of ballots in the state.“We gotta be careful with the cheating vote counters,” Trump said during a rally in Michigan on Sunday, adding that “bad things happen with the vote counters, so we gotta be careful.”In DC: Judge wants DOJ to identify targeted statesDuring a Thursday hearing, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg directed the Justice Department to provide more information on its efforts to require states to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters.California and Washington state have so far publicly disclosed that they have received letters demanding that they segregate ballots. The Justice Department provided California officials a list of 20,000 voters and about 400 voters in Washington. While the DOJ has sued California in an effort to force officials to comply, as of Thursday afternoon Washington hadn’t been sued.House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who’s in line to become speaker if his party retakes the House, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, along with other Democratic groups and a California voter, alleged in a lawsuit this month that the Trump administration has engaged in a pattern of intimidation intended to frighten officials into complying with unlawful demands to thwart voting.The Democrats asked for a temporary restraining order, citing the Trump administration’s expanding campaign to pressure state and local election officials. Boasberg, an appointee of President Barack Obama in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, ordered the Justice Department by noon Eastern on Friday to identify all states where the Trump administration has demanded ballots be set aside since July 1.But the judge also offered the Trump administration a way out.“Defendants may moot this process at any time by filing a notice indicating that they will not engage in the conduct sought to be enjoined in connection with the upcoming election,” Boasberg wrote in a brief order.At the 9th Circuit: Homeland Security limits weighedAt the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, a three-judge panel appeared unpersuaded by Trump administration arguments that Homeland Security needs limits lifted on election-related field operations less than a week before Election Day.“What do you need in the next four days? What are you prevented from doing in the next four days?” Appellate Judge Sidney Thomas, a Clinton appointee, asked a DOJ lawyer during oral arguments on Thursday.Earlier this month, a federal judge in California prohibited DHS from conducting operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens. The prohibition applies in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin until polls close on Election Day.A Homeland Security Investigations internal memo dated Aug. 31 describes a “surge initiative” beginning Sept. 1 that includes conducting field interviews. The memo, which was filed in court, identifies those states as targets of the surge during September. Additional locations are redacted in the document.Justice Department lawyer Gabriel Schonfeld said he couldn’t speak to the specifics of any particular investigation. He called the injunction entered by the lower court judge vague, making it difficult for federal officials to know exactly what is and isn’t allowed.“The government is being chilled,” Schonfeld said.The original lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. They alleged voters, especially naturalized citizens, are at risk of intimidation and fear they could be wrongly targeted.“Those folks have a civic duty they want to perform and they shouldn’t have to do it under this cloud of fear,” Hayden Johnson, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, told the appeals court.California and Alaska: What’s next?The Justice Department immediately filed a notice that it would appeal a ruling by Carter denying its request that California election officials be forced to segregate the ballots of 20,000 voters.The 9th Circuit already denied a previous, preemptive appeal brought by the Justice Department — a signal the appeals court would likely once again rule against the Trump administration.But the case is set to continue past Election Day. While Carter has denied the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order, the underlying lawsuit remains.On Thursday, Carter appointed a special master to aid him and scheduled a hearing for Nov. 13 where witnesses may be called to testify about the list of suspected noncitizens.In California, county election officials must certify results by Dec. 3.The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office on Thursday disclosed federal grand jury subpoenas it received for a range of election and voting-related documents and information.The disclosure came after Carter warned Justice Department officials to drop threats of prosecution against election officials. The subpoenas don’t make clear the target of the grand jury investigation.In Alaska, the DOJ sued Alaska election officials last week in a preemptive attempt to stop the state from certifying the results of its Senate election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting method, the Republican incumbent loses by a smaller margin than the votes earned by another candidate of the same name. Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his supporters have cast Dan J. Sullivan, another candidate, as a spoiler in a competitive race against Democrat Mary Peltola. State officials initially kept Dan J. Sullivan off the August primary ballot but the Alaska Supreme Court overturned the decision.The case drew fresh attention after The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign helped recruit Dan J. Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has ordered an investigation, while Trump has called for Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan to be kicked out of the race.The Justice Department on Thursday amended its lawsuit to highlight the Times reporting.The Trump administration “brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the complaint says.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: The census is a count, not a loyalty test
text:
Two people walk on the Tony Knowles Coastal Trail on Sept. 23, 2023, with the downtown Anchorage skyline and snowcapped peaks in the background. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On Nov. 2 the U.S. Census Bureau will close the public comment period on a proposed Trump Administration regulation to redefine who counts in America. It is his latest effort to erase immigrants from their collective participation in the American experiment. The proposed changes are several-fold: they would not only remove undocumented immigrants from the census count, but also immigrants who are in the United States legally, but have yet to receive their green cards or citizenship. They would bar questions about race, ethnicity and gender identity. Trump’s proposed actions reflect a fundamental disregard for the role the decennial census plays in our democracy.
The Enumeration Clause — Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 of the U.S. Constitution — was to serve as the objective mathematical engine for political power and taxation. It mandated that an “actual Enumeration” of the population take place within three years of the first meeting of Congress and every ten years thereafter. It was intended to resolve power-sharing among the states in the House of Representatives, every state being guaranteed at least one seat regardless of its size, but proportionally rewarding additional seats based on actual counts. Because the census would both determine the number of delegates and each state’s share of federal taxes, there was a premium on accuracy — no state wanted to pay more to the federal government than required.
Requiring a decennial census guaranteed that shifts in population could be accounted for over time. Following the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment set the norm that has prevailed until Trump’s arrival on the scene by requiring counting of the “whole number of persons in each State,” thus establishing the constitutional precedent that everyone physically living in a community counts toward its representation, regardless of citizenship.
Late in his first term, Trump issued a presidential memorandum to exclude undocumented immigrants from the population totals used for congressional apportionment. Federal courts in New York, California and Maryland all enjoined the order, finding that he had exceeded his authority since federal law requires the Secretary of Commerce to tabulate the “total population.”  They noted that undocumented immigrants qualify as “persons” and that physical “usual residence,”  that is, where a person sleeps and eats most of the time, must be counted regardless of legal status. And they observed that since the founding of the Republic, the government has systematically counted all residents—non-citizens, temporary inhabitants and undocumented individuals. The Supreme Court vacated the New York order, concluding it was not yet “ripe” for decision.  Trump’s term came to an end before he could pursue the matter further and President Biden revoked the Trump memorandum on his first day in office. Now Trump not only renews his previously failed attack on who to exclude, but actually expands its reach to bar any foreigner who is not a permanent resident or a citizen.  
His proposal to eliminate collection of data regarding race, ethnicity and gender identity is equally misguided. Today, census data directly governs the annual distribution of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funding for healthcare, infrastructure, schools and public safety.  The change would have major implications for civil rights enforcement, particularly regarding fair housing and voting rights. The data being collected is essential for state and local governments, non-profits and businesses to make critical decisions about how resources should be allocated, where services are needed, and where to make investments.
Alaska’s Foraker Group has observed that in FY2020, $8.26 billion flowed into Alaska as a result of census data—more than 11 times the economic impact of the 2025 Permanent Fund Dividend. It notes that by removing questions about race and ethnicity, the census eliminates important demographic data about Alaskans, data that aids in securing federal resources.  “Without this information, it will be harder for communities to identify and redress longstanding disparities or to serve underserved communities, or appropriately distribute federal funding across the country—including Alaska,” the report states.
Unfortunately, this Trump initiative, like a similar failed one in the 2020 census to include a question about citizenship, may have the effect of discouraging immigrants, including immigrant citizens, from cooperating with census takers for fear that the information will be used for enforcement purposes despite federal law that expressly prohibits the bureau from sharing individually identifiable information with any other agency.
Alaskans have until Nov. 2 to tell the Census Bureau what they think about this proposal. Our neighbors do not disappear when Washington D.C. refuses to count them. Neither do their children’s classrooms, their need for health care or their contributions to our communities. The census should measure the country we are—not manufacture the country a President wishes to see.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Trump OKs individual FEMA assistance for eight Florida counties hit by Isaias
text:
Isaias made landfall in Destin as a powerful Category 2 Hurricane on Oct. 9 (Photo by Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)President Donald Trump has approved the DeSantis administration’s request that the Federal Emergency Management Agency provide individual assistance to eight counties in the Florida Panhandle that suffered damage from Hurricane Iasias.
Trump approved the request for individual FEMA assistance for people in Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Holmes, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton, and Washington counties, according to a statement released by the federal agency.
Individuals who sustained losses in those counties should file claims with their insurance carriers before applying for federal assistance, according to the FEMA press statement.
To that end, Florida Office of Insurance Regulation data show that as of Tuesday, 62,295 claims totaling more than $652.2 million had been filed with insurers following the Oct. 9 landfall of Isaias, a Category 2 hurricane that made landfall in Destin.
Claims stemming from residential property losses account for the majority, or $599.9 million. Residential property is a broad umbrella category that includes homeowners, mobile homeowners, and commercial residential.
Claims for damage to commercial properties total $19.1 million. Private passenger automobile insurance claims also are accounted for in the OIR information, constituting $21.7 million.
Inside look at the insurance claims
Of the 62,295 filed claims, 4,292 were open and the policyholders had received some form of payment from their insurance carriers. A far greater number of claims, 33,368, remained open and no payment had been made.
Another 9,293 claims had been closed by the insurer after some payment had been made, and 15,342 claims were closed by the insurance company without payment.
OIR indicates that “common reasons” claims are closed without a payment include those in which the  total damage doesn’t exceed the policy deductible, or claims for flood coverage not included in standard homeowners’ coverage. Claims can also be closed without payment, the OIR website says, if the insurance company cannot contact the insured and the adjudication process cannot be completed.
In all, the OIR website shows that 39.5% of the claims have been closed, a figure that represents those closed without any payment and those closed with payments.
Trump approves Hurricane Isaias disaster relief 12 days after it was made

Meanwhile, Santa Rosa County leads the state among counties with the most Isaias-related claims, with 29,463 filed, followed by Escambia (19,274), Okaloosa (5,859), Walton (2,3490), and Bay (2,259) counties.
The president earlier in the week approved for FEMA to provide assistance to repair public roads, bridges, buildings, and other infrastructure to 15 counties.
The release didn’t say how much Trump had approved for FEMA public assistance but the DeSantis administration submitted a request for $237 million.

name: VTDigger
title: Bennington Battle Monument dig reveals possible historic tavern, artifacts
text:
Researchers think these stones may mark the threshold into the former tavern. Photo by Jeff McRae/Bennington Banner

This story by Jeff McRae was first published in the Bennington Banner on Oct. 27, 2026.
OLD BENNINGTON — The archeological dig at the Bennington Battle Monument State Historic Site in Old Bennington was open Monday, Oct. 26 for tours, with members of the Vermont Division of Historic Preservation on hand to make the pits and their thought-provoking revelations meaningful to visiting community members.
Visitors had the chance to view foundation outlines, partial brick walls and a spectacular set of flagstones researchers think may have marked the entrance to a long-gone tavern. At the other end of the green, a table was set up to display an array of small artifacts the recent excavations produced.
In addition to the familiar antique square nails and pottery fragments, researchers also uncovered objects more suggestive of life in Ye Olde Bennington.
“We have some really amazing finds,” said Joshua Bell of the Division of Historic Preservation.
“The pipe pieces actually had the mason symbol on it, which was kind of cool. That King George III coin speaks to the life that was happening here.
“We’re really excited for this archaeology to be done,” Bell said, “and for it to be open to the public. And we hope to find new ways to use what we have learned to enhance our interpretation here at the site.”
Discussions are underway as to what to do with the objects the team uncovers and where they’ll be kept.
“We are looking at having them go to our central location in Barre,” said Bell. “Jess Robinson, our state archaeologist, has a collection there. But we want to make sure that we’re able to use these everywhere. So we can check them out and show people.”
Bell thinks there is much more the site can reveal, but said the dig will be winding down by the end of the week.
“We are going to start slowing down here a little bit, and at the end of the week, start covering things back up. We originally anticipated having to go down 6 to 8 feet,” he said. “We were very pleasantly surprised that most of it was right near the surface.”
On Monday, visitors were allowed inside those areas for a close encounter with the distant past.
“We’re very excited by the turnout today,” said State Archaeologist and Director of the Vermont Archaeology Heritage Center Jess Robinson. “We certainly got a lucky day with the weather and the temperature,” he said, indicating the blue sky and the more than two-dozen people touring the site. 
“It’s a testament to the interest in the greater Bennington area in the history of this place and everyone’s part in it. People (in the Division for Historic Preservation) are really, really excited not only by the turnout, but the (community) enthusiasm has been really remarkable. And it really excites us and makes us glad that we’re doing this stewardship project.” 
Robinson described a multi-step process he and his team followed.
“The first step was sort of some basic archival research, getting into some more advanced stuff about the history of this area prior to the construction of the monument in the green,” he said. “And then (we conducted) a ground-penetrating radar survey that, combined with where we thought buildings would be based upon the archival research, revealed some tangible deposits, although their outlines and parameters were still pretty vague.
“We thought something might be still intact here, but we were very surprised with the degree of integrity and interpretability that we’re seeing here.”
Visitors, both local and from farther afield, slowly circulated through the site that, as previously reported, researchers need to first assess before repair work to the monument begins so artifacts and structures, where possible, can be avoided during future construction.
The project is federally funded through congressionally directed spending administered by the National Park Service.
Cynthia McGuire and her family came over from Cambridge, New York, to enjoy time together with husband Jim and their two adult sons, Dan and Gavin, the latter home on leave following an “extra-long stint” aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln. He also holds a degree in anthropology with a focus in archaeology.
“So, we’re here to take a look,” she said.
Among the many interesting things to see, none is more interesting, perhaps, than what Robinson and his team think might be the threshold of the former tavern and, in what would have been the rear of the building, a round, stone-lined structure they initially thought looked like it might have been a well or cistern.
“But it doesn’t appear to be,” he said. “It actually shallows out and comes to a stone base. And if you go look at it, there’s an interior circle of brick, and then bricks protruding from the outside.”
“Now the thought is it might be some sort of brewing vat or tank or even a large storage tank for barrels. So that would probably indicate that that’s more the back-end kitchen brewery side of (the possible tavern).”

Site visitors were exposed to a slate of evocative reminders of the town’s former inhabitants. Photo by Jeff McRae/Bennington Banner

He and his team will soon be busy trying to assemble the narrative of the site from the artifacts they’ve found and what structural elements they’ve uncovered.
“A lot of this isn’t going to be teased out until we look at what artifacts were found where within the structure which will give an indication of use,” he said. “If we find kitchenware and things, we’ll be able to say, ‘Oh, OK, this was either the dining room portion or perhaps the kitchen area.’ Other artifacts will tell other stories, so a lot of this is (yet) to be determined until the synthesis and analysis (is complete).”
Visitors will have only a few more days to see what has turned up at the evocative site before the archeological and preservation crew begins the process of filling the pits back in with Bennington earth.
“We don’t want to leave it exposed for too terribly long, particularly when the bad weather starts coming in, which it will. If we get a big, heavy stretch of rain, this will turn into a swimming pool, which we don’t want,” Robinson explained. 
“We’re going to lay down geotextile fabric over all these important site components. And that will basically protect it. Then, the plan now — and it might change, we are actually in active discussions — but the plan now is to take a lot of the rubble out of this fill, fill (the pits) in carefully, and then it’ll be intact here for future research education.”
Eventually Robinson and his team will make available a report that will tie together everything.
“The town will certainly be privy to the final report that comes out of this and any other publications we’re going to share widely,” he said. 
“The only concern we ever have with sharing archaeological materials is that locations might be compromised. But there’s no hiding this. We don’t want to. We want to make it as public as possible. And so all the literature and products that come out of this archaeological work are going to be shared broadly and widely.”
The monument site will remain open to visitors through Oct. 31.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa lawmakers call for board of regents policy barring DEI in all required courses
text:
State lawmakers are asking the Iowa Board of Regents to craft a policy prohibiting DEI and "related ideological frameworks" in all required curriculum. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)State lawmakers are once again calling upon the Iowa Board of Regents to tighten its restrictions on diversity, equity and inclusion content in required courses after a University of Iowa official was secretly recorded discussing the topic.
Rep. Taylor Collins, chair of the Iowa House Committee on Higher Education, and Sen. Lynn Evans, chair of the Senate Committee on Education, have sent a letter to the Iowa Board of Regents requesting the governing body develop a policy barring any “DEI content and related ideological frameworks” from all required courses, whether through core curriculum or major-specific courses.
The letter comes after Accuracy in Media, a conservative media company with a history of recording university officials and posting the videos online, published an edited video appearing to include UI Senior Academic Advisor of Elementary Education Carter Burks.
“The public’s trust in Iowa’s universities depends on concrete action that demonstrates our institutions of higher education exist to educate, not to indoctrinate,” the letter stated. “As the governing body charged with oversight of the state’s public universities, the Board of Regents bears primary responsibility for ensuring that students encounter a genuine marketplace of ideas and remain free to complete their degrees without being required to take courses steeped in divisive ideology.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the video, posted by Accuracy in Media Oct. 27, said there is “a lot going on politically in the state” but the college’s “core values haven’t changed a lot,” adding that there is room for learning about “African American culture, native peoples” and other “wide-ranging history” topics.
“We obviously, as a program, we believe in educating all students about everything they need to know about all this stuff, right,” Burks said in the video. “Different professors take that differently.”
He described Iowa City as “very forward-thinking” in a “conservative state,” and he didn’t believe that students would come to the UI and get a “very right-wing” education. Burks asked in the video if he was being recorded, which the recorder denied, and he mentioned staff had been fired for mentioning diversity and inclusion in the past.
Burks is still employed by the UI and is not on leave, UI Assistant Vice President for External Relations Jeneane Beck said in an email. Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach Burks for comment.
Iowa Board of Regents Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman said in an email the board is aware of the video and has received the letter, both of which the body is reviewing.
The UI has dealt with other employees being recorded and publicized for their comments previously, with one complaint dismissed and the other having led to disciplinary proceedings in February. Board President Robert Cramer at the time instructed the firm that handled the investigation to conduct an audit of all three state universities for their compliance with state and federal laws relating to DEI, which Lehman said in his email is still ongoing.
The Iowa Legislature and Gov. Kim Reynolds have enacted laws barring taxpayer money from funding “DEI initiatives that prioritize group identity over individual merit,” the letter stated, including prohibiting DEI offices and activities at universities, to “restore public confidence” in higher education, keep taxpayer dollars from “political activism” and protect students.
“The continued presence of DEI-aligned content in courses required to complete a degree undermines those goals,” the letter stated. “It also raises serious questions about whether the Board of Regents and the universities under its governance are fully committed to changing the culture of higher education in Iowa, or whether they intend to preserve the status quo.”
Evans and Collins said in the letter that it is the responsibility of the board of regents to ensure “students encounter a genuine marketplace of ideas and remain free to complete their degrees without being required to take courses steeped in divisive ideology,” and it will take more than “boilerplate affirmations of academic freedom” to make that happen.
Policy manual revisions approved by the board this and last year include a biannual review of general education courses for DEI and critical race theory content and the clarification that instructors can teach controversial topics relating to course content but it must avoid indoctrination and feature different views on the topic.
Changes to required courses themselves are necessary to stop students from having to “choose between completing a degree and avoiding mandatory exposure to divisive ideology,” the letter stated, and lawmakers are prepared to help the board in creating a new policy and outlining their steps to implement it.
“The integrity of Iowa’s higher education system and the confidence of the citizens who fund it depends on decisive leadership that protects every student’s freedom from mandatory ideological instruction,” the letter stated.

name: WyoFile
title: Trump and Freedom Caucus approval, election confidence: Three takeaways from a Wyoming survey ahead of the general election
text:
From approval of the president to confidence in elections, the Wyoming Survey and Analysis Center’s 2026 election survey, which was published Wednesday, takes the state’s pulse on a wide swath of political and policy issues. 
Here are three takeaways from the survey. 
More Wyomingites disapprove than approve of Trump. 
In a state where 72% of voters chose Trump in the 2024 general election, about 49% of respondents disapprove or strongly disapprove of the way the president is handling his job, while roughly 39% approve or strongly approve. Another 12% are neutral. 
The survey asked about Trump differently in previous years, so it doesn’t provide a direct comparison to see how approval of the president has changed in Wyoming over time. Nationally, Trump’s approval rating has fallen from roughly 48% when he began his second term in 2025 to 34% this month, a historic low, according to CNN Poll of Polls. 
Wyomingites aren’t happy with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, but it’s a slim majority.
In line with Wyomingites’ rejection of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus in the primary elections, the survey indicates that a majority of respondents aren’t happy with the group. 
But it’s a slim majority. About 51% of respondents said they disapprove or strongly disapprove of the caucus, while roughly 21% approve or strongly approve of the group. A decent chunk of people — about 28% — are neutral. 
Those results contrast with the caucus’ overwhelming losses in the state Legislature during the August primaries. After the caucus gained majority control of the state House in 2024, it lost most of its House seats this year and also fell behind in the Senate. 
Most Wyomingites feel confident in the state’s elections. 
Amid Trump’s ongoing claims that America’s voting system is not to be trusted, about 56% of Wyoming respondents said they believe vote counts across the state will be very reliable, while another 28% expect counts will be somewhat reliable. Roughly 16% are neutral, or believe vote counts will be somewhat or very unreliable. 
The numbers indicating confidence in Wyoming’s elections are similar to 2024 survey results, which asked about Wyoming vote counts specifically for the presidential race. But the percentages of people who indicated that they think the vote counts will be neither reliable nor unreliable, somewhat reliable or very unreliable are slightly higher this year than in 2024. 
In both years, Wyomingites indicated that they were much more confident in the state’s elections than they were in vote counts across the country.
