name: Michigan Advance
title: As Huizenga hosts US Energy Secretary, McCann campaigns with Whitmer and Slotkin
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) take questions from reporters during a canvass launch in Kalamazoo on Oct. 29, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)A hotly competitive U.S. House district in Southwest Michigan saw a flurry of activity from two opposing candidates on Thursday.
In the morning, U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) joined U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright for a press conference at the Palisades nuclear plant, a once shuttered facility in Covert, Michigan, which could be the first nuclear plant in the country to resume operations following a $1.5 billion loan announced under President Joe Biden’s administration.
In the afternoon, state Sen. Sean McCann’s (D-Kalamazoo) campaign hosted Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) in Kalamazoo for a canvassing launch in support of Democrats at the state and federal level.
Over the past year, Huizenga’s 4th Congressional District has shifted from a likely win for Republicans to a complete toss-up, according to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. 
During the visit, MLive reports that Wright praised Huizenga and other Republicans who have embraced the Trump administration’s policies, while Huizenga spoke out against state efforts to transition to 100% clean energy resources by 2040.
While there were no new announcements from the Trump administration Thursday, Huizenga defended the visit to reporters as one focused on policy rather than politics when asked whether the secretary’s visit was related to the upcoming election.
In Kalamazoo, Slotkin reflected on the 2022 election, in which Democrats successfully flipped the 3rd Congressional District, centered on Grand Rapids, previously considered to be a Republican stronghold.
If Democrats are able to turn Huizenga’s district blue, Slotkin said, that sends the message that “when Democrats compete, they win.”
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) speaks to reporters during a canvass launch in Kalamazoo on Oct. 29, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)
Whitmer also praised McCann, who served in the state House of Representatives for four years and has served in the state Senate for nearly eight years.
“I love Sean McCann,” Whitmer said. “He has been a phenomenal partner, and this community is lucky to have him.”
While Whitmer reflected on the gains Democrats made in Lansing on issues like reproductive freedom, LGBTQ+ rights and expanding access to early childhood education and community college, McCann said there’s more work to be done at the federal level.
McCann’s campaign noted that the money which was funding the restart of the Palisades plant came from 2022’s Inflation Reduction Act, which Huizenga voted against.
“Bill Huizenga voted against the federal financing helping reopen Palisades. Now he’s showing up for the cameras to celebrate the very investment he opposed. You can’t vote no on Michigan jobs and then take a victory lap when those jobs come back, McCann said in a news release.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state senator also criticized Huizenga for his votes against congressional war powers resolutions to end the war in Iran, his support for the president’s tariff policies and his refusal to request congressional spending for projects within the district.
Huizenga spokesman Calvin Moore hit back in a statement to Michigan Advance.
“Gretchen Whitmer wanted a 45-cent gas tax hike and pushed extreme energy mandates that are doubling energy bills across Michigan, so of course ‘Tax Man’ Sean McCann is campaigning by her side,” Moore said in a statement. “Tax Man McCann has spent his entire career raising taxes and making life more expensive for Michigan families. Now he wants to go to Washington so he can do it all over again.”
The Michigan Public Service Commission, which regulates energy companies and their rates, has pushed back on arguments that clean energy is raising energy prices, calling them a myth. 
“The growth of renewable energy in Michigan has saved more than $948 million in fuel costs — primarily for natural gas and coal — over the last 20 years because a majority of renewable energy produced in Michigan is from wind and solar, which have zero fuel costs,” the commission’s website states, noting that the main driver of energy costs in the state, is the need for upgrades to improve grid reliability.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico US Rep. Leger Fernández’s bill would require mining companies to pay royalties
text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) announced Oct. 29, 2026, legislation that would impose royalties on companies seeking to extract hardrock minerals like uranium, which is what a Canadian company is seeking to do in Canjilon, N.M., pictured above. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) on Thursday announced legislation that would require companies extracting hardrock minerals like gold, silver and uranium to pay up to 10% in royalties, as well as crack down on foreign adversaries’ extraction of valuable minerals from the United States.
In announcing the Minerals Royalty and Investment Act, Leger Fernández released a video featuring her standing on Carson National Forest land near Canjilon, where a Canadian company recently sought exploratory permits to mine uranium. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposal by Gamma Resources, Ltd., — which remains pending before state and federal regulators — has drawn widespread outrage from communities around the site since Source NM first reported on it in March. Leger Fernandez and other members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation have a separate bill pending that would ban uranium mining in the Chama Watershed outright. 
“It could pollute the water. It could destroy the land,” she said of the proposal in the video released Thursday. “And foreign mining corporations aren’t required to pay a single dime in royalties. I have a bill to change that.”
Leger Fernández noted that the General Mining Act of 1872 has allowed firms to mine hardrock minerals on public lands for more than a century without paying royalties, unlike companies that extract oil, natural gas and coal. 
The bill would impose fees of between 5% and 10% on gross income that companies receive from mineral extraction and allocate those funds to states and tribes. Funds also could go toward remediating abandoned mines that continue polluting public lands across the West, as well as to a newly established financial assistance program aimed at building domestic critical mineral processing facilities.
The bill text notes that no revenues from the newly imposed royalties can benefit coal or uranium processing facilities. 
Separate from the royalties, the bill would prohibit “foreign entities of concern”  — which Leger Fernández named Thursday as adversaries like China and Russia — or their subsidiaries from hardrock mining activities in the United States. 
Canadian uranium firm says lack of outreach in northern New Mexico a ‘mistake,’ vows future candor 

“We should not let foreign mining corporations take our precious resources and not pay a dime. Let’s invest it,” Leger Fernández said in the video. “Let’s invest it in things that our public lands need.”
The congresswoman noted that U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, co-sponsored the bill, as did five other House Democrats. National environmentalist groups like the Wilderness Society and New Mexico Wild also endorsed it. 
“New Mexicans and American taxpayers continue to be on the hook for legacy hardrock mining cleanup across the state, and new claims keep coming,” Mark Allison, executive director of New Mexico Wild, said in a statement. “Adding insult to injury, under existing law, mining companies — including foreign based ones — pay the public no royalty for what they take from the public estate. The American Minerals Royalty and Investment Act provides a long overdue remedy.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Focus groups highlight gaps in Arkansas’ family and medical leave policies
text:
(Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)A study of five focus groups found insufficient paid family and medical leave policies in Arkansas workplaces, according to a nonprofit organization’s report published Thursday.
The 35 Arkansans who participated in the focus groups conducted by Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families agreed that paid leave policies exist on paper but are difficult to access in practice. 
Many participants said they encountered “confusing deadlines, paperwork requirements and institutional barriers” in their workplaces. Their ability to take time off work to care for themselves and others had profound impacts on their mental health, according to the report.
Arkansas does not have a statewide paid family and medical leave requirement, and the report urges lawmakers to make it a priority in the legislative session that starts in January.
More GOP states embrace paid parental leave for teachers, public employees

Nationally, only about 1 in 4 employed Americans receive paid family and medical leave.
The District of Columbia and several Democrat-led states have paid family and medical leave policies, covering about one-third of the nation’s private-sector workers as of this year.
Arkansas is among several Republican-led states that have adopted paid leave policies for state and public school employees. Since 2023, Arkansas has required 12 weeks of paid maternity leave for state workers, and a 2025 law extended this policy to public school employees. Both laws exclusively cover new mothers.
The report recommends that Arkansas create policies covering not only new fathers but also adoptive and foster parents.
Two of the report’s five focus groups were exclusive to teachers and nurses. Both said they regularly delayed medical care, used up all their paid time off or returned to work before recovering from illness or childbirth.
“The nurses repeatedly argued that paid leave is not just good for workers and families; it is necessary for patient outcomes and the stability of Arkansas’s healthcare workforce,” the report states.

AACF.PFML_.webfinal.10.27.26 
The other three focus groups included residents of Fayetteville, Texarkana and Helena-West Helena.
All five groups agreed that paid leave is “an equity issue” that generates “enhanced recruitment, deeper morale, higher workforce participation, reduced employer costs, and greater productivity,” according to the report.
Little Rock and Fayetteville both instituted paid parental leave for city employees earlier this year, with costs covered by existing city budgets instead of tax increases.
The report recommends that state policymakers account for rural Arkansans’ long drives to healthcare providers and the resulting need to take more time off work to receive care.
Arkansas hospitals have been scaling back services due to low reimbursement rates from Medicaid and from private insurers.
Starting Jan. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025’s sweeping budget overhaul is expected to cut rural Medicaid spending by $15.5 billion per year for the next decade. In mostly rural Arkansas, more than 800,000 low-income or disabled residents rely on Medicaid.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont to receive $4.5M settlement from General Motors following data privacy investigation
text:
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark and members of her staff addressed the press on Thursday afternoon. Photo by Theo Wells-Spackman/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
MONTPELIER — Roughly two years ago, Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark and James Layman, who leads Clark’s consumer protection unit, read a New York Times journalist’s coverage of worrying data sharing practices at car manufacturing giant General Motors.
The account, which laid bare the auto maker’s practice of sharing data about customers’ driving habits — such as seat belt use and speeds — with insurance companies, led the Vermont officials to initiate what became a joint effort between 35 states and the District of Columbia to investigate the company’s handling of consumer information. The resulting $220 million nationwide settlement leaves the state with a $4.5 million payout and a host of new privacy guarantees from General Motors, according to Clark.
At a press conference Thursday, Clark said the investigation found the company’s use of data had clear impacts in Vermont between 2016 and 2024, allegedly violating the state’s Consumer Protection Act through unfair or deceptive practices.
“GM collected data from tens of thousands of Vermonters and sold that data to insurance companies and data brokers without obtaining consent from drivers,” she said. Auto insurers, she added, then “charged some drivers higher rates based on the data.”
The settlement, which was reached before the multistate coalition formally filed a lawsuit, expressly states that the company does not admit to having broken any law.
A spokesperson for General Motors told VTDigger that the company had discontinued its “Smart Driver” program in 2024 in an emailed statement Thursday, and added that the company had already taken steps to strengthen its privacy practices. 
“GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson said.
The practices in question related to data collected by a digital program offered by General Motors that tracks drivers’ behavior to promote safer driving. Clark said the company failed to be transparent about where that data was shared, and to ensure that buyers were able to give informed consent before opting into the program.
“Not only did consumers not know that their data would be used this way, many consumers reported that they didn’t even know they were enrolled in the ‘Smart Driver’ program to begin with,” she said.
Settlement terms laid out in a Thursday court filing include standards for customer consent General Motors must abide by, and place limits on the collection of driver data, among other agreements.
The company has recently faced scrutiny on several other related fronts: The Federal Trade Commission issued an order in January restricting the company’s data-sharing practices, and a class-action lawsuit leveling similar charges against the company by customers is ongoing.
The payout announced Thursday will ultimately rest in the state’s General Fund, which is controlled by the Legislature, Clark said. Because of Vermont’s work at the very outset of the investigation, the state is receiving substantially more money than it would ordinarily have been allocated based on population, she added.
Data privacy has been a hot-button issue among Vermont lawmakers in recent years, and Gov. Phil Scott signed into law a bill designed to help secure residents’ control over their personal information earlier this year. Clark said she was grateful for a number of the bill’s protections but was concerned that it limited individual Vermonters’ ability to sue companies on their own.
Clark, who also recently announced a large settlement with tech giant Meta, said her focus on consumer protection in relation to data privacy and the internet would continue. She recently requested that lawmakers fund a new staff position in her office to focus on large tech companies, she said.
“The internet is paid for with our data,” Clark said. “We have to always be mindful of ways that we need to be enforcing the law, and protecting people.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Federal prosecutors announce more indictments in NC for illegal voting
text:
American flags hang alongside the official agency flag at the U.S. Department of Justice building in Washington, D.C., in August. The Justice Department is sharing state voter roll data with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
(Photo by Jonathan Shorman/Stateline)The U.S. Department of Justice on Thursday announced it has indicted 18 more people living in North Carolina with voting illegally in 2024.  
Two weeks ago, on the first day of early voting, the Justice Department announced the indictments of 10 people on charges of voting illegally in the state. 
Seventeen of the people indicted Thursday are legal permanent residents, according to the Justice Department. The other is in the country without permanent legal status, according to the DOJ. 
The indictments allege that the defendants falsely claimed to be U.S. citizens to register and vote in past elections. The charges, which carry a penalty of up to five years in prison, are part of the Trump administration’s nationwide campaign to uncover voting by noncitizens. 
Federal prosecutors announced Thursday’s indictments less than a week before Election Day and as the state’s early voting period is winding down. 
The Southern Coalition for Social Justice said in a press release that the timing of the indictments during an ongoing election is concerning. 
Studies have found that noncitizen voting is rare. More than 5.7 million people voted in North Carolina’s general election in 2024. 
The indictments represent a “miniscule percentage” of the more than 7.9 million people registered to vote in North Carolina, the Southern Coalition said. 
But federal prosecutors said finding illegal voters is important to protecting the integrity of elections. 
“In our most recent elections in North Carolina — the 2025 municipal elections — there were 14 races decided by 2 votes; 15 races decided by 1 vote; and 7 races that were tied,”  U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson for the Western District of North Carolina, said in a statement. “Every vote matters.  And the public must have confidence that our elections are conducted fairly and that every ballot cast is a lawful one.”

name: VTDigger
title: Let the wealthy help keep Vermont rural
text:
Dear Editor,
I very much appreciate Megan Durling’s recent commentary advocating for Vermont’s education policies to better include rural areas. Local schools are the heartbeat of small communities. They wither when they lose their schools. Though they need tax relief, most rural residents still resist school consolidation. 
Much of the current debate about Vermont’s future turns on whether we choose to remain a mostly rural state or become more urbanized. Most of us who choose to be here love our culture of neighborliness, our natural beauty, our relative freedom from industrial pollution and the sense of spaciousness and ease that contrasts so strongly with the crowded, tense, anonymous atmosphere of cities. Few want to lose what makes Vermont so special. Those who work the land have longstanding cultural traditions they wish to preserve and hand down to their children. And the wealthy who make their homes here value the beauty and peace that the land-based occupations have created and maintained over generations. 

READ MORE

Vermont attracts urban tourists precisely because those qualities embody a longed-for human scale. But the high cost of that character — a luxury in the modern world — creates pressure to lower property taxes. Competing visions for how to do so are to either broaden the tax base by urbanizing — attracting more people and employers — or strengthen existing small communities by asking the wealthiest among us to pay their fair share, so all can thrive. 
The fear that raising taxes on the wealthy few would drive them to leave the state seems baseless. My sense is that the wealthiest Vermonters, who could afford to live anywhere, choose Vermont out of love for the qualities I’ve listed, and most would willingly pay to preserve what they cherish. The same fear of flight accompanied New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign, yet since he won, not only have the city’s elite stayed put, but it’s my understanding that many more very wealthy people have moved there. What New York City offers is what they value, and they’re willing to pay for their chosen amenities. I believe the same is true for most wealthy Vermonters. They value what Vermont offers and want to preserve it. 
I fully agree with Durling’s quote from the late Wendell Berry that teaching children to abandon their authentic local culture leaves rural communities and lands “open to exploitation, and ultimately destruction, from the center.” She goes on to connect the dots between local issues and the bigger picture: “The industrial habits and priorities of a modernized educational model exacerbate our modern social and ecological crises. We need a radically different understanding of what educational equity looks like for rural people; our communities have been sacrificed at an urban-mandated altar for too long. The gods of the valleys are not the gods of the hills.”
Amen to that. 
Barbara McKay 
North Ferrisburgh, Vt.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State’s $2.6 million share of General Motors settlement will go to Consumer Protection Fund
text:
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley speaks during a press conference on Dec. 19, 2025, in Sioux Falls. Jackley announced a settlement this week involving allegations against General Motors. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Consumer Protection Fund will get a $2.6 million boost after General Motors agreed to settle allegations of selling private driver data to third parties.
South Dakota Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley announced the settlement in a press release Thursday. He was one of 36 attorneys general involved in the settlement.
The company collected drivers’ behavior and location data and sold it to data brokers, who sold that data to insurance companies, according to the release. Insurance companies used that data, in part, to set insurance rates, the release said.
“Protecting South Dakotans’ privacy is a priority,” Jackley said. “Our settlement guards privacy by requiring express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data.”
General Motors is required to provide customers with options to request a copy of their collected data, delete it and disable the collection of exact location and driving behavior data.
Money received from the settlement will go to the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Fund, to pay for litigation and investigation costs and future consumer protection efforts.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Eastern NC congressional race is most expensive in US history
text:
Republican Laurie Buckhout challenging Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis in North Carolina’s First District. (Photos by Lynn Bonner) The 2026 race for North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District has broken records to become the most expensive U.S. House general election in history, according to new ad spending data. 
In a district that Republican state lawmakers redrew last year to favor their party, GOP Army veteran Laurie Buckhout is challenging Democratic incumbent Don Davis. 
Inside Elections shifted the race from “toss up” to “tilt Democratic” on Thursday.
A mammoth $52.9 million has poured into ad spending for the district, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The number includes spending on aired ads and future ads reserved as of Oct. 27. 
Democrats have spent $29.6 million to support Davis, and Republicans have deployed $23.3 million to back Buckhout. 
The pair faced off in 2024, when Davis defeated Buckhout by 6,307 votes. It was the most competitive congressional race in North Carolina that election cycle. 
In 2024, Democrats bought $23 million in ads for the district, compared to $15.5 million for Republicans, according to AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance visited Kinston on Wednesday to rally support for Buckhout, U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, and other Republicans on the ballot. 
With five days remaining until the general election, Democrats are making pushes across the map. 
Where are the tightest races for US House control right now? Here’s the rundown.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is placing a coordinated ad buy with Richard Ojeda in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District. The ad, titled “Corrupt,” begins airing in the Greensboro media market on Friday. 
Ojeda, also an Army veteran, is seeking to unseat Republican incumbent Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Hudson has represented the district since 2013, and President Donald Trump won the district by nearly 16 points in 2024. 
While only $16,000 in ad buys have been reserved as of Thursday, the total buy will reach into the six figures, DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus confirmed to NC Newsline.
The buy will boost ad spending in the 9th District, which so far has totaled $571,000 for Republicans and $351,000 for Democrats, according to AdImpact. 
Inside Elections moved its rating for the 9th District contest from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” on Thursday.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Half of Maryland schools earn four or five stars out of five on latest report card
text:
Baltimore County Superintendent Bill Heiser, left, and state Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) students at Arbutus Elementary on Aug. 31, the first day of school. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Half of the slightly more than 1,300 public schools in Maryland earned four or five stars out of five on the state’s annual report card of individual school performance, an increase from last year, according to data released Thursday.
Performance on the 2026 report card was up slightly from the year before, when 43% of schools earned the top two marks, improvement that was attributed in part to improvements in attendance in recent years and in comprehensive test scores.
Statewide, nearly 89% of public schools statewide received at least a three-star rating on this year’s report card, compared to about 86% that got three, four or five stars last year.
Schools that earn a score of at least 75% on a formula that measures overall school performance get give stars under the star-rating system. From 60% to 74%, schools get four stars and scores between 45% and 59% earn three stars.
Geoff Sanderson, deputy state superintendent of accountability for the state Department of Education, said there remains “continuous improvement” in student achievement.
Sanderson said one reason for the improvement is a decrease in student chronic absenteeism, which decreased from nearly 23% during the 2025-26 school year from 31% in the 2021-22 school year. State officials also attribute minimal gains on test scores.

But this will be the last year for the star-rating system. State officials have said the current assessment does not take into account academic progress a school can make annually.
While he was pleased by the gains the latest report, State Board of Education President Joshua Michael said Thursday the current system is “flawed.” A school that showed a 12-point gain in a year, for example, could still be at three stars, its improvements not recognized or properly rewarded.
Michael has also said the new system would show a better outlook on student achievement in schools, especially those with a high population of low-income families.
The change to the school rating system comes as the state prepares to phase out its current Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program, a standardized student assessment on which the school ratings are partly based on, to use the newly designed Maryland System of Testing Academic Readiness (MSTAR).
The new test is slated to be used this spring for students in grades 3 through 8 for English and math tests. It is expected to be about 25% shorter than the MCAP, provide accessible features for students with special needs and an online portal for families to review student progress.
“What are we willing to do for children who are not our own?” Michael said during opening remarks Thursday morning. “We are increasingly becoming a state whose public schools reflect the expectations we hold for our own children. We are not there yet … but I will say we are just getting started as it relates to improving public education in our state.”
School improvement
Some of the criteria schools are measured on the report card include academic achievement, progress in English language proficiency and school quality and student success. High schools are specifically assessed on graduation rates and post-secondary readiness.
Based on state data, 74%, or 964, of the schools saw no change in their star status this year.
About 19%, or 252 schools, increased by one star. Some of the schools that increased from four to five stars were South Shore Elementary in Anne Arundel County, Huntingtown High School in Calvert County, Herbert Hoover Middle School in Montgomery County, Chapel District Elementary in Talbot County and Williamsport Elementary in Washington County.
Pocomoke Elementary in Worcester County increased from four stars to five stars on the 2026 Maryland School Report Card. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Worcester County, which has achieved the highest level of proficiency on the state’s standardized tests in English for the last three years, had 10 of its 11 schools — 91% — earn four or five stars.
Once again, Pocomoke and Snow Hill high schools received five stars. Pocomoke Elementary, a Title 1 school that receives additional resources due to the number of economically disadvantaged students there, joined the five-star club this year after getting four stars last year.
Several schools maintained a five-star status for at least a third straight years, including the Academy of Health and Sciences at Prince George’s Community College. It came in second place with 88 points, one point down from last year’s score.
Eastern Technical High School in Baltimore County recorded the highest number of points earned at 94, two points higher than last year.
Baltimore County recorded the second-highest number of five-star schools at 25, behind Montgomery County with 36.
“BCPS staff have worked relentlessly to advance excellence for all students, and we are seeing the positive results of our collective efforts to provide the highest-quality instruction and programs for students,” Baltimore County Superintendent Bill Heiser wrote in a letter to the school community. “We will continue to build on this momentum and strive for excellence in all our schools.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Judge grants restraining order in attorney general subpoena case
text:
(Greenleaf123/Getty Images)A US District Court Judge ruled Thursday to block investigatory subpoenas filed in September against environmental groups. 
US District Court Judge Joseph R. Goodwin granted a temporary restraining order Thursday afternoon against the West Virginia Attorney General Office to prevent it from enforcing subpoenas sent to the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org, an environmental group that advocates against the use of fossil fuels. 
The West Virginia Attorney General’s Office issued subpoenas to at least six environmental groups, pursuant to an investigation into suspected violations of the West Virginia Consumer and Credit Protection Act. The investigation came to light after the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org filed for a temporary restraining order in federal court. 
The groups contended their First and Fourth Amendment rights were being violated. 
In a strongly worded 27-page opinion, Goodwin agreed. 
“What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia’s waters and climate,” Goodwin wrote, “The State’s chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them. The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.” 
“The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives,” Goodwin added. 
The restraining order remains in effect until Nov. 12. Goodwin will set a hearing for a preliminary injunction – which would last the entire time the case is being litigated – at a later date. 
What happened in court 
Prior to arguments, Zachary Viglianco, the director of strategic litigation for the Attorney General’s Office, offered to cut down the scope of the subpoenas and to not enforce them until a more robust hearing in the future. 
“I appreciate your goodwill, but I have to go with what’s in front of me,” Goodwin said. “Informal offers that are amorphous are not of interest to me.” 
Amanda Demmerle, representing the two environmental groups, said she was ready to proceed. 
Earlier this week, Attorney General JB McCuskey’s office argued in a brief earlier this week that under the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act allows the state attorney general to investigate any “false or materially misleading speech” that affects West Virginia’s economy. 
“And the production of energy — including the mining of coal, extraction of natural gas and the use of those fuels to generate electricity — is both a critical part of West Virginia’s economy and a market sector that impacts the affordability of daily life of every West Virginian,” the brief stated. 
In her arguments in court, Demmerele said the groups she represented do not engage in commerce, therefore their speech would not fall under the Consumer Credit and Protection Act. 
“There can’t be probable cause to issue a subpoena if the act doesn’t cover the conduct someone is engaging in,” she told the judge. 
She said the subpoenas are meant to chill free speech — for example, she said the West Virginia Rivers Coalition did not want to publish a map of projects it is doing with community members for fear that McCuskey would target them. 
Demmerele said under McCuskey’s interpretation of the state statute, “a bad Yelp review could be investigated.” 
“The Credit and Consumer Protection Act is broad, but it is not unbridled,” Demmerele said. 
The Attorney General’s office contended both groups used out-dated climate models to harm the coal and natural gas industry in West Virginia. 
“It is the willful or knowing use of or reliance upon such a model, theory, or assumption,
with the aim of “directly or indirectly” affecting trade or commerce in West Virginia, that the
Attorney General’s subpoenas seek to investigate,” the brief stated. “These industries generate hundreds of millions of dollars in severance tax revenue and support tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.” 
However, in court, attorney Ryan Donovan, a private counsel representing the Attorney General’s Office, appeared to change courses. Instead of focusing on the effect of climate change information on the fossil fuel industry, he argued that the groups could be falsely using the outdated model to solicit donations. 
“I don’t see the donation stuff in your response,” Goodwin observed. 
Donovan stressed that years of revision and eventual retirement of the model meant the groups should have been aware, thus giving McCuskey reason to launch the investigation. Donovan also took issue with 350.org attributing extreme weather events to climate change. 
“How accurately do you want people to talk?” Goodwin asked. 
“That’s a great question,” Donovan said. “I think under the CCPA (Consumer and Credit Protection Act) you have to be accurate in knowingly making claims while engaging in commerce.” 
In her rebuttal to Donovan’s arguments, Demmerele warned that the Attorney General’s Office is engaging in unconstitutional overreach. 
“It appears the attorney general wants to be the arbiter of what is true and what is not,” she said. “This shouldn’t be argued in court. This is something that should be argued in scientific journals, in public debate.” 
After the hearing, Dave McMahon, a lobbyist and attorney, said he showed up to watch because he’s concerned about how the attorney general’s subpoenas affect those outside the organizations. 
“I am not a party, I do not represent a party, but I have worked with these groups over the years and I deeply resent the idea of my correspondence being subpoenaed,” he said. “This is unlawful and abusive.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court declines to hear GOP appeal in case challenging mail-in voting guidance
text:
Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty ImagesThe Michigan Supreme Court issued an order Thursday declining to hear an appeal by the Republican National Convention, the Michigan Republican Party and Chesterfield Township Clerk Cindy Berry in their lawsuit challenging election guidance from Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson on how to handle mail-in ballots with mismatched numbers.
The order did not come with a written opinion or statement from the justices in the majority, but noted that the appeal was denied because they were “not persuaded that the questions presented should be reviewed by this Court.”
However, Justice Brian K. Zahra, the high court’s sole Republican, wrote a dissent on the order, concluding that a decision not to hear the case “cheapens the role of this Court and fails to recognize the importance of the right to vote in our state.”
Zahra added that the case has particular prominence because of Michigan’s role as a swing state with competitive local and statewide elections. 
“As Michigan’s court of last resort we owe it to the people of Michigan to explain why ballots with mismatched or missing ballot numbers are tabulated when our Legislature has plainly stated that ‘[i]f the ballot numbers match, the board of election inspectors shall . . . prepare the ballot for tabulation’,” Zahra continued.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Justice Richard H. Bernstein also indicated that he would grant leave to appeal, but did not include a further dissent.
Benson’s guidance had said that ballots returned with mismatched numbers between the ballot stub and the envelope should be counted as a “challenged ballot,” something that Berry and the national and state Republican Party organizations had challenged.
Court of Claims Judge Brock A. Swartzle ruled in December 2025 that if the numbers do not match, the vote cannot be counted, but a panel of judges on the Court of Appeals overturned that decision in June 2026, ruling that because Michigan law, “does not prohibit the tabulation of those ballots and because the Court of Claims granted permanent mandatory injunctive relief without making the required findings, we reverse and vacate the final order and judgment.”
While in the Court of Claims, Benson’s lawyers had argued that because there was no specific instruction in the law about what to do with a ballot if it was returned with mismatching numbers, it fell within her realm to make a decision on. 
Swartzle disagreed with that argument, writing that though there is no specific guidance on what to do in that situation, the law is clear that such a ballot should not count, and issued a permanent injunction on the matter. 
But in a Court of Appeals opinion authored by Judge Michelle Rick and joined by Judges Mariam Bazzi and Alli Maldonado, they argue that the state law in question “does not prohibit election inspectors from tabulating absent-voter ballots with missing or mismatched stubs as challenged ballots under the Secretary’s guidance. The Court of Claims erred by declaring that such ballots cannot be tabulated.”
Rick added that the Court of Claims “abused its discretion by imposing plaintiffs’ 10-step cure procedure” as a permanent injunction, writing that such an injunction is an “extraordinary remedy.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Two Alabama cannabis dispensaries expected to open next week
text:
Mock medical cannabis tinctures in a display case at Callie's Apothecary in Montgomery, Alabama, on May 14, 2026. Two more dispensaries are expected to open next week, state officials announced Thursday, bringing the total so far to five. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Two medical cannabis dispensaries are expected to open next week, bringing the total to five statewide, state officials announced Thursday.
Justin Aday, general counsel for the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission, said one of the dispensaries will open in Bessemer and will be the third location of Callie’s Apothecary, the first medical cannabis dispensary to open in the state. It has operating locations in Montgomery and Talladega. 
Aday said the other dispensary is expected to open in Birmingham next week, the second location of Bama Bloom. It has an operating location in Athens and a third planned in Etowah County.
“Altogether we have those two dispensary licensees that are operating. We have five cultivators who are operating, two processors are operating, two secure transporters, and then of course the one state testing lab that we have,” Aday said. 
He projected the three open dispensaries would generate $130,000 to $140,000 in revenue in October. 
“The past two months, we’ve had a little over $120,000 monthly revenue, which is pretty good for a new market,” Sam Blakemore, chair of the commission said. 
The commission has awarded dispensary licenses to three companies, who can have three locations each. One license has yet to be awarded due to litigation, but there will be twelve dispensaries across the state under that license once all are awarded and operational.  
The third dispensary licensee, RJK Holdings, has locations planned in Oxford, Mobile, and Daphne.
“It’s been fully briefed. It’s before the court of civil appeals, and the court could issue a ruling on merits at any time,” said Mark Wilkerson, an attorney with the commission.
At the program’s full capacity, it can also award five integrated facility licenses – businesses that can cultivate, process and dispense medical cannabis – which will bring the dispensary count up to 37. 
Litigation is still pending for those licensees, and the commission is far from awarding those licenses, Wilkerson said. 
The Alabama medical cannabis law, enacted in 2021, allows registered physicians to recommend cannabis for about 15 medical conditions, including cancer, depression, Parkinson’s Disease, PTSD, sickle-cell anemia, chronic pain, and terminal diseases. 
People who suffer from the qualifying conditions must get approval from their physician and enter the patient registry in order to buy products at a dispensary.
The approved product forms are restricted to tablets, tinctures, patches, oils, and gel cubes (only peach flavor), with raw plant material and smokable forms remaining prohibited.
As of Thursday, there are 83 physicians certified to recommend medical cannabis to patients in Alabama, according to the Alabama Board of Medical Examiners. Aday said 62 are registered with the AMCC, and the commission is “making contact” with the remaining physicians to ensure they get registered. 
“We’ve also been doing some other educational work with the physicians, and we will have another webinar next week for the physicians that the Board of Medical Examiners has approved, going through just the process, making sure that they’re comfortable with the patient registry and the different requirements under the law,” Aday said. 
He said more than 2,300 medical cannabis cards have been issued.
John McMillan, director of the commission, also announced his intent to retire. Blakemore appointed several commissioners, and himself, to a transition committee to search for a replacement.
“I think we’re going to open it up to all resumes from wherever we can find them, and we’re going to work with the personnel department to narrow it down,” Blakemore said.
The transition committee will report its progress at the commission’s December meeting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Reynolds pauses driver regulations to improve fuel transportation in Iowa
text:
The state of Iowa is temporarily easing driver hour regulations to help improve access to fuel in the state. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gov. Kim Reynolds announced Thursday a temporary suspension of regulations on the number of hours that drivers carrying fuel, diesel and biofuels within the state of Iowa can operate. 
The proclamation comes in the midst of record high diesel prices across the country and fuel supply shortages in Iowa as farmers work to bring in a delayed harvest. 
John Maynes, the president of government affairs for FUELIowa, said suspending hours of service regulations is “a lever the government can pull” to help improve access to fuel in the state, by allowing drivers more flexibility as they face long drive and wait times to deliver fuel.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Maynes said the issue started in western Iowa and along the Nebraska and South Dakota borders Oct. 19, when fuel terminals experienced supply shortages. He said when this happens, it causes a “snowball” effect as demand migrates to other terminals. 
“Where previously they’re maybe able to run four, five loads of fuel to customers in a day, now maybe they’re only able to do one, and we don’t have like a backfill of drivers,” Maynes said. 
For example, if a driver who normally picks up fuel in Council Bluffs to deliver it to stations in western Iowa has to go to a terminal in Des Moines to get fuel, they now have to spend more time in the truck and waiting in line to fill up at the terminal that has extra traffic. 
That time adds up and makes it difficult for drivers to complete a job, or to be able to drive home after their deliveries and comply with the state laws limiting the number of hours a driver can be on duty and driving. 
Maynes said Reynolds’ proclamation, which doesn’t happen every season but he said is not unprecedented, doesn’t mean that drivers will be “operating 24 hours a day.” 
“It allows them to finish their last load and go home for the night,” Maynes said. 
The proclamation specifies that motor carriers cannot require or allow fatigued drivers to operate, even with the suspension of the hours of service regulations. 
Maynes said the fuel shortages in certain regions are due largely to spikes in demand from farm equipment after a rainy September delayed the start to harvest. 
The war in Iran and global trade disruptions that have caused fuel prices to rise, have created a “cascading effect” to the demand, according to Maynes. With diesel at more than $6 a gallon, he said many producers have not wanted to “maximize the usage of their storage space” to fill up on the pricey fuel. 
The demand from the farm sector has created “inefficiency” in fuel deliveries, which have in turn caused some retail fuel stations to be temporarily out of fuel as their deliveries are delayed. 
“This isn’t going to solve the problem, but it helps to address the inefficiency created for drivers being able to move product freely from terminal to customer location,” Maynes said. 
The proclamation, which declared a state of disaster emergency, is in effect for 30 days.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmakers revisit proposals to curb high levels of firearm crimes, trafficking
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice said guns, pictured here, were seized in Albuquerque, New Mexico in the country's largest ever fentanyl bust in April, 2025 (Photo courtesy U.S. District Attorney's Office, District of New Mexico)New Mexico state lawmakers on Thursday revisited legislative proposals to curb the state’s high rates of shootings and gun trafficking.
A bill in this year’s legislative session would have required firearm dealers to train their employees to recognize signs of gun trafficking, would have raised the minimum age of employment at gun stores to 21 and would require gun stores to keep detailed records of each sale. It died, though, after some lawmakers criticized a provision that would have banned the sale of certain types of firearms.
Leaders from the advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety, which was involved in crafting this year’s failed bill, spoke before the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee again on Thursday. While they stopped short of endorsing a specific bill for the upcoming lawmaking session, which begins in January, they stressed the need for the Legislature to address New Mexico’s persistently high levels of gun crimes.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Retailers need to be trained to recognize the signs of trafficking, such as a customer who routinely buys guns in bulk and “straw purchases,” in which someone buys a gun and then later sells it to someone who is not legally allowed to purchase a firearm.
Lawmakers pitched the previous bill after a report from Everytown for Gun Safety found that New Mexico has an outsized problem with gun trafficking. It ranked New Mexico fifth in the nation for the highest rate of firearm homicides.
Police find the vast majority of guns used in crimes — 89% — in possession of someone other than the person who originally bought it at a store, Everytown for Gun Safety Senior Industry Advisor Marianna Mitchem said Thursday, adding that such statistics constitute clear signs of trafficking. Trafficking at that scale enables guns to quickly move across city, county and state lines, she said.
“When people engage in firearm trafficking activity, they don’t say, ‘Well, I bought this gun in Rio Rancho, so I’m only going to sell to people in Rio Rancho,’” Mitchem, a former Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives official, said.
Mitchell credited the New Mexico Department of Justice with equipping police departments across the state with technology that can accurately trace guns and spent shell casings found at crime scenes. In August, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez announced that the initiative identified more than 500 crimes since it launched last year, including one gun that was used in 17 different crimes.
Nationally, gunfire is the leading cause of death for children and teenagers. New Mexico’s firearm mortality rate of 26.6 per 100,000 residents is among the highest in the nation, according to U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.
Ryan Burt, the CEO of Calibers, an Albuquerque-based indoor shooting range, presented alongside Mitchell and pushed back that her report was meant to “scare people.”
He said that he subjects his employees to rigorous background checks and trains them to spot the signs of straw purchases and trafficking. He said he believes raising the cost to secure a federal firearm dealer license — which is $200 and then $90 to renew every three years — would be a more effective way to weed out bad actors.
“Make it $5,000. You’re going to get rid of half, if not more” of gun dealers, he said.
Burt also sits on the National Shooting Sports Foundation’s Range and Retail Advisory Council. The foundation joined the Second Amendment Foundation earlier this month in suing New Mexico over its weeklong waiting period for gun sales. A federal judge in August found that the state couldn’t enforce the waiting period on two people who challenged the rule in 2024. 
State lawmakers on Thursday were split on the broader issue along party lines.
Rep. Stefani Lord (R-Sandia Park) said she believes business owners such as Burt are “very careful” in making sure they don’t sell to traffickers, because they could face stiff penalties if they don’t.
“There’s millions of us in New Mexico with firearms who are doing nothing wrong,” she said.
Democrats, including Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) who co-sponsored the anti-gun trafficking bill in this year’s legislative session, said the state ought to more closely regulate “the most deadly weapons in our society.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Powell and Harding make final pitches in Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District
text:
Denise Powell with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (left) and Brinker Harding  with Rep. Don Bacon (right) in Omaha on Oct, 29. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — The leading candidates in Nebraska’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district are making their final pitches as Election Day approaches. 
Denise Powell is looking to be the first Democrat to represent the district in about a decade. Brinker Harding is trying to defend the House seat for Republicans as Rep. Don Bacon decided not to seek another term. 
At his west Omaha campaign office, Harding held a press conference Wednesday with Bacon to hammer home the message he’s repeated throughout the campaign, saying Powell is an outsider and too extreme for the district, and voters can’t let Powell’s “ideology represent Nebraska.”  
“Denise Powell is too radical for Nebraska. She’s bought and paid for” by the Democratic Socialists of America, Harding said. “She’s given to AOC (Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez) twice. She’s on record that she would have voted for the largest tax increase since World War II. That’s not a benefit to this district.” 
Rep. Don Bacon speaks in Omaha on Oct. 29. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
He then repeated attacks on Powell alleging support for “sex education” for kindergartners and “transgender surgeries” for minors — during one of their debates, Powell said that wasn’t true. 
In North Omaha, Powell, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries by her side, focused less on her opponent. Jeffries looked ahead to Democrats’ plans to “address the affordability crisis” in his stump speech for Powell. 
“Our job today and every day from now until Nov. 3 and beyond that is to remind them that there’s still hope,” Powell said. “That there are people who are going to keep fighting for them. That we are never going to roll over and surrender.”
The two camps have been trying to paint each other as extreme throughout the campaign. In the last few weeks of the race, the two candidates have attacked each other over benefiting from PAC spending and making late tax payments. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The slightly red-leaning 2nd District is a swing district that typically draws national attention. Notable Democrats and Republicans have campaigned there. Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned for Powell; House Speaker Mike Johnson visited the district for Harding. 
Nebraska as a whole has seen former President Joe Biden, President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton this election cycle. 
While the spotlight on the Omaha area district remains, it has dimmed as the national political environment has worsened for Republicans across the country. The D.C. outlet Punchbowl News reported last month that “operatives in both parties” feel NE-02 is one of the races Republicans will struggle to win this cycle. 
Both super PACs for national Republicans and Democrats have pulled scheduled ad buys from the race — through Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters recently told News Channel Nebraska that “just because we reallocate dollars doesn’t mean it’s a lost seat; it just means that we’re focused on the seats where we know we have to win.”
The House Majority PAC, the main super PAC for House Democrats, is now spending $1 million to support Democrat Chris Backemeyer for Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District as the race is now viewed as more competitive than initially thought. 
Cook Political Report shifted the 2nd District race from “lean Democrat” to “likely Democrat” earlier this month. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, another notable election analyst group, also has the race as “likely Democratic.”
Harding and Bacon, in their Wednesday dual press conference, pushed back on the notion that this race is a foregone conclusion. Bacon said this race is tight and general congressional polls for this year’s midterms “are off to a bit.” He pointed to his performances outrunning the political environment during his five terms in office, something he said Harding can do. 
“I would say a Reagan-type Republican,” Bacon said of Harding. “He works with city councilmen that are Democrats. … He’s worked with Republican and Democrat business leaders to grow this city. He’s independent-minded. He’s going to do what’s right for this district.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks in North Omaha on Oct. 29. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Harding also pointed to his experience on the Omaha City Council and his time working as former Omaha Mayor Hal Daub’s economic development director and chief of staff. Bacon said Powell would be a “rubber stamp” for Jeffries.  
In a short press gaggle after the stump speech, Powell said Jeffries “knows that Nebraska is not Brooklyn.” 
“I’ve said this before: I will go toe to toe with anybody who’s trying to push anything that is going to hurt Nebraskans,” Powell told the press. “I think that’s one of the reasons why Leader Jeffries is here to support me, because they’re not looking for rubber stamps; they’re looking for people who really care about, understand and are connected to their district and will show up for them in that way.” 
Jeffries added that Powell is committed to finding common ground, whether with Democrats, independents or Republicans, and that he believes she’ll disagree with Democratic House members at times.
“She’s demonstrated the ability and willingness to do it by always putting the people in Nebraska first; she’s exactly the type of leader that we want in Washington,” Jeffries said. “We don’t need more rubber stamps for anyone. We need people who are going to put hardworking American taxpayers first.” 
Early voting has already begun. The general election is Nov. 3.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Assembly approves higher penalties for underage tobacco sales
text:
Legislation approved on the Assembly floor Thursday would triple fines for retailers that sell tobacco products to underage users. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images)Assembly lawmakers moved to triple penalties for underage tobacco sales in a bid to stop teenagers from using electronic cigarettes lawmakers say have proliferated in recent years.
The bill, which passed the chamber’s floor in a 66-7 vote with four abstentions from Republicans, would triple progressive fines for retailers who sell any tobacco product to anyone below the age of 21 and lower the bar for the state to strip violators of their tobacco licenses.
Bill sponsor Assemblyman Michael Venezia (D-Essex) said the changes are meant to help local authorities enforce tobacco age limits amid a proliferation of vape shops.
“It’s hard because there was not a lot of funding put in place for them to enforce it,” Venezia said. “The fine was only $250, so most vape shops are happy to pay that $250 fine, so what we’re doing is we’re increasing the fine. We’re putting some teeth to it.”
NJ Assembly OKs bills expanding human trafficking protections and enforcement

Under existing law, retailers who sell tobacco products to underage customers face a $250 fine for the first offense, a $500 fine for the second, and a $1,000 fine for third and subsequent violations.
The bill would triple those fines at every level, to $750, $1,500, and $3,000, respectively.
It would also require the state’s taxation division to suspend a retailer’s tobacco license at the host municipality’s request following a local hearing. After a second violation, the division would be required to revoke the license if the municipality requests it to do so.
Current law gives the division discretion in both circumstances.
Eric Blomgren, executive director of the New Jersey Energy Marketers Group, which represents convenience stores and others that sell tobacco products, said his organization backs the measure to help weed out bad apples.
“We support full enforcement of the law. We support full compliance of the law,” Blomgren said. “Generally, we find the type of business owner that joins a trade association really is the cut above, and if anything, they get kind of victimized by the people who break the law.”
Less scrupulous competitors could draw business away from retailers that follow the law, Blomgren said.
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex), who abstained on the bill, questioned why lawmakers were not applying similar restrictions to alcohol retailers.
“I’m not here advocating that we should loosen restrictions and let’s sell a bunch of these things — alcohol, cigarettes, tobacco — to kids. That’s not the point at all,” she said. “What I’m saying is why does the liquor retailer get more flexibility than the convenience store or the bodega owner down the street?”
Fines under the bill would flow into the host municipality’s coffers, though 5% of the penalties would go to the state Department of Health for educational and outreach programs on the dangers of nicotine vaping products and the consequences of selling them to underage users.
The bill has not yet moved in the Senate.
Sen. Joe Vitale (D-Middlesex), who chairs the Senate Health Committee and is the bill’s sponsor in the chamber, said its movement is a matter of timing. Opposition hadn’t appeared let alone blocked the legislation, he said,

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Winner of Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate race next week could take office next month, AG rules
text:
The U.S. Capitol on Oct. 9, 2024. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)OKLAHOMA CITY – The winner of the U.S. Senate race can take office once the Nov. 3 election results are certified, according to an Oklahoma Attorney General’s opinion released Thursday.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond’s decision means the winner of Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate race will likely take his or her oath of office well before Jan. 3 when the current U.S. Senate term ends. 
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt and Alan Armstrong pose for a photo after the governor held a press conference announcing Armstrong as his appointment to the U.S. Senate on March 24, 2026 at the state Capitol. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
That means current U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong’s term would immediately end. 
Gov. Kevin Stitt in late March appointed Armstrong, a Republican, to fill the remainder of former U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s term. Mullin resigned March 23 to serve as President Donald Trump’s Secretary of Homeland Security.
NPR affiliate KOSU reported in September that Armstrong wanted to continue serving until January, but U.S. Rep. Kevin Hern, R-Tulsa, wanted the winner of  Tuesday’s election to take office as soon as the election results were certified. 
Hern, who is widely favored to win, is running for Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate seat against Democrat N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, Libertarian Sevier White and independents Ron Meinhardt and Curtis Stinnett.
Stitt and Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, asked Drummond to determine whether state law allows Armstrong to finish the term or if the newly elected senator can assume office once the State Election Board certifies the results of Tuesday’s general election.
Because the seat was already on this year’s ballot for a full six-year term, state law does not call for a separate special election, according to the opinion.
Instead, the winner is considered elected to both the remainder of the current term and the new term, the opinion said.
“Oklahoma law and the U.S. Constitution point to the same answer: the voters fill this seat,” Drummond said. “Oklahomans will choose their next senator at the polls Nov. 3, and that person will be eligible to take office once the election is certified.”
If the election is uncontested, the State Election Board will meet at 5 p.m. Nov. 10 to certify the results.
An opinion from the state Attorney General’s Office has the force of law unless challenged in court.
Hern’s campaign issued a statement that said the opinion confirms that Stitt’s appointment ends when a successor is elected.
“This is consistent with the clear language of the statute and ensures Oklahoma will have an elected voice in the Senate without delay,” the statement said.
Armstrong’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New campaign aims to help NC Medicaid recipients keep coverage under new rules
text:
Congresswoman Deborah Ross (left) sat on a panel with Nicole Jorwic, Kirk Adams (center), Rep. Sarah Crawford, D-Wake, and Jamie Richmond (right) in Raleigh on Oct. 29, 2006. (Photo: Keep Your Care)A new campaign launching in North Carolina aims to help Medicaid recipients navigate upcoming federal requirements and avoid losing coverage because of confusing paperwork or reporting rules. 
Keep Your Care, a national campaign focused on helping people maintain Medicaid coverage, launched its North Carolina effort Thursday at a Raleigh roundtable with recipients, caregivers and lawmakers. 
“No one should lose health coverage because of confusing paperwork or red tape,” said Nicole Jorwic, a co-lead of Keep Your Care.
Beginning Jan. 2027, most adults covered through Medicaid expansion will need to document at least 80 hours of work a month, education or community service or qualify for an exemption. States will also be required to check eligibility at least twice a year, rather than annually. 
The Keep Your Care campaign plans to use digital advertising, community outreach and partnerships with local organizations to help people understand the rules, identify exemptions and meet deadlines. Enrollees and caregivers can sign up through the website to find information and get the latest updates on rule changes. 
More than 700,000 North Carolinians enrolled through Medicaid expansion will be subject to the new rules. Gov. Josh Stein’s office estimated that more than 250,000 people could lose coverage under the changes. 
Stein says NC counties will shoulder costs of new Medicaid rules, urges Congress to reverse cuts

Even as the deadline approaches, the rules are still in flux. On Thursday, a federal court ruling narrowed how the requirements can be applied to some very ill patients. 
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson announced that a judge has struck down a federal rule that would have required patients with cancer and other serious illnesses to prove their conditions prevented them from meeting the work requirements. The state estimated the restriction threatened coverage for 64,000 North Carolinians.
Although the ruling blocks enforcement of that restriction, the other Medicaid work and reporting requirements will remain in place for now, though another legal challenge is underway in Maryland. 
At Thursday’s roundtable, caregivers and advocates described how losing Medicaid coverage could affect families already struggling to afford care and disability services. 
Jamie Richmond, a family navigator at the Tammy Lynn Center, described balancing her work supporting families with care for her 7-year-old son, who has autism, and her mother, who lives in Florida and relies on Medicaid. 
She said her son’s speech, music and other therapies cost about $1,400 a month out of pocket. Medicaid also helps families access services like respite care, she said. 
“Families need help before they reach a crisis,” she said. “And it looks like the crisis is coming faster.” 
Campaign organizers said they want to reach people before the new requirements take effect, including those who may qualify for coverage but struggle to understand or comply with the reporting process. 
Congresswoman Deborah Ross, a Raleigh Democrat who participated in the roundtable, said outreach and education will be important as the state prepares to implement the requirements. 
Ross said Democrats could pursue changes to the law if they regain control of Congress, though she did not outline any specific proposals.  
“One good thing about some of these changes is that they don’t go into effect immediately,” she said. “People are terrified, but we can reverse it. We can extend some of the deadlines, and we can change things around.”
The federal requirement applies specifically to Medicaid expansion enrollees. However, advocates at the event raised concerns about additional funding cuts to the Medicaid program that could also affect people with disabilities, seniors and the families who care for them.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Idled WA coal power plant generates a natural gas fight
text:
The steam plume from the TransAlta coal power plant outside Centralia, Wash. could formerly be seen from 30 miles away on cold, clear days. But it’s been absent since mid-December when the plant shut down for conversion to natural gas. (Photo by Tom Banse)
The owner of the only remaining coal power plant in the Pacific Northwest is doggedly proceeding with a plan to extend its life by converting to natural gas fuel over the next two years. TransAlta Corporation got political support, signed a utility to take the electricity and is accumulating the necessary permits to remodel the currently idled power station near Centralia. 
But the coal-to-natural gas conversion is coming into question after a coalition of environmental groups challenged the energy production contract. Now the future of the hulking Centralia coal plant – a generous employer in Lewis County – is wrapped up in a contentious Puget Sound Energy rate increase case. It will be dissected beginning Tuesday, Nov. 3, with expert testimony and cross-examination in front of the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission in Lacey.
The saga of the big power station matters far beyond Centralia because it encapsulates many themes bedeviling policymakers, ordinary ratepayers and utility managers these days: How to control rising electricity rates; where to get the juice to serve a growing population and attract new industry; and, does natural gas belong on the menu anymore?
TransAlta and its utility customer Puget Sound Energy assert that their contract for natural gas-fired generation is necessary to meet surging electricity demand and fill resource gaps. But the environmental coalition contends the 17-year power deal flies in the face of Washington’s goals to move beyond fossil fuels.
“There are far more less expensive, more efficient and cleaner resources to meet the demand that PSE is anticipating that they have written off,” Earthjustice Senior Attorney Victor Zertuche said in an interview.
Zertuche didn’t name specific alternative projects, but spoke about renewables being cheaper. Besides solar, wind and large-scale battery storage, the green groups also favor giving customers incentives to cut back during times of peak demand. PSE already does this to a degree.
Zertuche represents five groups in this case: Washington Conservation Action, NW Energy Coalition, Sierra Club, Front and Centered and Climate Solutions. Together, the challengers want state utility regulators to throw out PSE’s proposed contract for gas-fired electric generation.
The argument for conversion
Puget Sound Energy’s argument to state utility regulators reiterates that it needs to rapidly address forecasted shortfalls in electricity supplies. The utility said it is aggressively pursuing new clean energy projects, but that is not enough to assemble a balanced portfolio of resources. 
PSE testified that local electric demand is surging from wider adoption of air conditioning, heat pumps, electric vehicles and data centers. At the same time, the utility said it is facing increasing competition from data center developers when it seeks to put new wind and solar farms under contract to meet the forecast demand.

PSE is Washington’s largest utility, with 1.2 million electric customers and nearly 900,000 natural gas customers. PSE’s rates and generation asset selection have to pass scrutiny from state regulators since it is a private company with a monopoly in its service territory. During the current rate case, legions of upset customers demanded that the state utilities commission comb through PSE’s books to reduce proposed rate increases.
PSE Senior Vice President (and Chief Development Officer) Craig Pospisil told the regulatory panel that restarting the Centralia power station with natural gas would provide a vital and dependable backstop during periods of high demand such as summer heat waves and winter cold snaps. He said the remodeled plant would not run continuously. 
“Its value lies in providing necessary firm capacity using existing infrastructure, avoiding greenfield development risk, and supporting reliability during periods when renewable resources and storage may not be sufficient,” Pospisil said in written testimony.
PSE’s long-term deal with TransAlta runs from 2028 to the end of 2044. Then it’s curtains for the Centralia power station. That’s because beginning in 2045, Washington’s power grid is supposed to be 100% non-polluting under the state’s energy transition law.
A three-member independent panel will decide whether the coal-to-gas conversion is a prudent investment. Those state utility commissioners gave no indication of their leanings during two public hearings a month ago. The commissioners were variously appointed by Govs. Jay Inslee or Bob Ferguson and subsequently confirmed with bipartisan votes of the state Senate.
The Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission is expected to make a final decision in January to accept, reject or modify PSE’s proposed rates and generation plans.
Opinions and analysis aplenty
A staff analysis of the competing arguments concluded with a recommendation that the commissioners disallow the PSE plan to buy natural-gas fired electricity from TransAlta. If the commissioners don’t want to go that far, the staff suggested they at least demand more proof from PSE that natural gas generation was the lowest reasonable cost option available.
After reviewing the testimony of PSE critics, the Public Counsel inside the Office of the State Attorney General recently came around to the same position of recommending the commission reject the Centralia power contract.
Adding to the pile-on, a trade association for large commercial and industrial electricity users filed skeptical testimony. The Alliance of Western Energy Consumers cited its own consultant’s analysis that power to be supplied from the converted Centralia generating plant ”does not appear to be cost-effective.”
PSE filed rebuttal testimony with confidential financial data that it said showed gas-fired generation was cost-effective once the reliability value of the resource was factored in.
No one testified in favor of the Centralia plant’s coal-to-gas conversion during more than seven hours of spoken comments the utilities commission accepted over two nights in late September/early October.
“It is absurd that anyone would be trying to add fossil fuel capacity now when the early effects of climate change are already apparent and will continue getting worse,” said electric ratepayer Eddy Donofrio of Thurston County when it was his turn to speak at the commission hearing.
A broader range of opinions in favor and against appears in the public comment file of the state Department of Ecology. That state agency accepted comments separately as it prepares to finalize an environmental permit for natural gas-fired power generation by TransAlta.
The Centralia-Chehalis Chamber of Commerce said the planned coal plant conversion would preserve jobs and economic activity, “rather than prematurely abandoning a major piece of existing regional infrastructure.”
“We know we are short on generation. The natural gas plant would help make up for the shortage until sources of clean energy come on line for the grid,” retired IBEW Local 77 lobbyist Bob Guenther added in his comment to the Ecology Department.
TransAlta has generally kept a low public profile in Washington state this year as other parties vigorously debate the future of its coal plant.
“We’re continuing to work through the permitting and regulatory approval processes required for the conversion project to move forward,” a spokesperson for the Canadian company said in an emailed response to questions.
In a September presentation to stock market investors, Calgary-based TransAlta reported that it had completed the preliminary engineering and cost estimating for the Centralia project. The company’s board is holding off on making a final investment decision until sometime in early 2027.
The 730-megawatt Centralia plant hasn’t operated since last December, in accordance with a long-standing agreement with Washington state to phase out coal power. But the big facility is required by order of the Trump Administration to remain on standby in case of extreme power demand.
TransAlta’s Centralia operation is one of at least six coal-burning power plants around the nation that the Trump administration is trying to keep open past their planned retirement dates. However, the thrice-renewed emergency orders to TransAlta are being challenged as unjustified by the Washington State Attorney General and allied environmental groups.
The most recent order issued to TransAlta by Energy Secretary Chris Wright indicated the department is aware of the plan to convert the coal plant. Wright’s order directed the company to provide his department written notice when it receives the required permits to transition to natural gas. Pospisil said TransAlta informed PSE that it did not expect the series of Energy Department orders to delay the planned plant conversion.
The saga of the aging coal plant has become something akin to a three-ring circus for people interested in tracking the outcome, such as Earthjustice’s Victor Zertuche.
“With the rate case and the permits that are involved, there are just so many angles related to this,” he said.
“As we’re getting closer and closer, there is much more suspense,” Zertuche said. “Optimism, a lot of that as well. We’ll see.”
