name: Maine Morning Star
title: Outside groups spending millions to oust state lawmakers up for reelection
text:
Senate District 20, where Republican incumbent Bruce Bickford is being challenged by Democrat Michael Scott, has seen the most outside spending of any legislative race, with more than $392,000 spent by PACs so far this year. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]With Maine’s entire state Legislature up for election in November, even incumbent lawmakers aren’t safe in their reelection bids. With outside groups — that don’t have to disclose their donors — increasing their involvement in state elections, the legislative districts with the most outside spending feature lawmakers up for reelection. 
According to data from the Maine Ethics Commission as of Thursday, Oct. 29, outside groups spent roughly $4.6 million in state races. And hanging in the balance is which party will claim a majority in Augusta for the new legislative session. 
Democrats currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers. The Maine Senate has 20 Democrats, 14 Republicans and one independent, Rick Bennett, a former Republican who still caucused with the party this session. In the Maine House of Representatives, Democrats hold 75 seats to Republicans’ 73, with one independent and two unenrolled members.
The nonpartisan newsletter Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics released its final analysis of state legislative races earlier this month. Senior columnist Louis Jacobson marked the Maine Senate as likely Democratic while the Maine House is considered leaning Democratic, with Jacobson naming it one of the 15 most competitive legislative chambers in the country. 
Data from the Maine Ethics Commission on independent expenditures, or spending in a candidate’s favor but not coordinated with the campaign, shows that outside groups are taking note and pouring hundreds of thousands of dollars in several State House races. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nicholas Jacobs, associate professor of government at Colby College, said the rise of this sort of spending in Maine follows national trends. 
“A lot of that is just the general nationalization of our politics,” Jacobs said. “Maine had been immune for many election cycles from that nationalization.” Jacobs said that 2020 was probably the inflection point, or “the last hurrah for the ‘all politics is local’ mentality here in Maine.”
The major shift in campaign spending is broadly understood to be 2010, when the U.S. Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling sided against campaign rules on First Amendment grounds, opening the door to unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions. 
But Jacobs said other, larger states soon after saw an influx of outside spending in state races, while the trend is just now reaching Maine, with many of the partisan groups now working  across several states.
“One of the things we know is that they sort of run very similar-looking campaigns in multiple states,” Jacobs said, noting that this helps groups scale their investment with the aim of a better return. 
“Mainers are going to see the same sort of advertisements in Maine as they’re going to be seeing in Virginia, as they’re going to be seeing in Iowa,” Jacobs said. This will ultimately impact what Maine voters see and hear about those running for local office.
“Especially for something as near and dear to the local as a state legislative contest,” he added, “I think this shapes people’s impressions about what the race is about, what their state government does.” 
Follow the money
Across the state, the bulk of the outside spending in legislative races is coming from a few political action committees. 
The biggest group not affiliated with a campaign participating in this election cycle is the Maine Democratic State Committee, the Maine Democratic Party’s political action committee, which has spent nearly $1.9 million on independent expenditures in state house races. 
The vast majority of Democratic spending is from that single PAC, while Republican support comes from several organizations.
Lead Maine Action, a political action committee run by outgoing Rep. Laurel Libby’s (R-Auburn), has spent more than $364,000 and Prosper Maine PAC, another conservative group, has spent just over $401,000. 
The PACs directly associated with the Maine Republican Party, the House Republican Fund and Maine Senate Republicans, have spent only $193,000 and $217,000, respectively. 
See who is running for Maine Legislature in your district

And much of that money is focused on a few key races. The Senate races are drawing more outside dollars than the House races, but most of the costliest races in both chambers feature a sitting lawmaker running for reelection, suggesting the opposing party sees an opportunity to flip the seat and oust the incumbent. 
That’s the case in Senate District 20 in Androscoggin County. The district has seen the most outside spending of any legislative race, with more than $392,000 spent by PACs this year. 
Republican Sen. Bruce Bickford currently holds the seat, and is running for reelection against Democrat Michael Scott. Bickford was elected to the seat in 2024, and prior to that it was held by Republican Eric Brakey. 
But the Maine Democratic State Committee has bet big on flipping the seat, spending more than $182,000 to oppose Bickford and another $126,000 to support Scott. 
On the other side, Lead Maine Action has spent almost $5,000 to support Bickford and more than $38,000 to oppose Scott. 
Not far behind is Senate District 16 in Kennebec County, where $319,000 has been spent by political action committees. It’s another seat with a Republican incumbent, this time Sen. Scott Cyrway, who is facing off against Democrat Patric Moore. 
Cyrway was first elected to the state Senate in 2014, and represented the district until 2022. Because of term limits, he served the next two years in the Maine House and returned to the Senate in 2024. 
But during the two-year period that Cyrway was in the House, Democrat David LaFountain narrowly won the Senate District 16 seat over Republican Michael Perkins. 
The Maine Democratic State Committee has now spent $61,000 to support Moore, and $177,000 to oppose Cyrway. There hasn’t been any spending from PACs to oppose Moore, but Cyrway has gotten a boost from Maine Senate Republicans, which spent more than $24,000 in support. 
House districts are smaller, and independent expenditures are generally lower than in Senate races, but the majority of outside spending is still coming from a few key groups. 
House District 58 in Sagadahoc County has seen the most outside spending for that chamber, with outside groups spending more than $98,000. Rep. Sally Cluchey (D-Bowdoinham) has held the seat since 2022, and is facing off against Republican David Guilmette. 
The Maine Democratic State Committee has spent just over $16,000 to support Cluchey. Meanwhile, the Prosper Maine PAC, a conservative group, has spent nearly $18,000 to support Guilmette. 
Even independent incumbent Rep. Sharon Frost of Belgrade is not immune to outside spending. Her race in House District 58 is second in most outside spending in the chamber, with more than $95,000 from outside groups. 
Close behind in third place is House District 98, made up of Bowdoin, Durham, Lisbon, Pownal and Topsham, with more than $94,000 in outside spending. 
Incumbent Rep. Kilton Webb (D-Durham) is running against Republican William St. Michel. Webb won the seat in 2024, and before that it was held by Republican Joseph Galletta. 
The Maine Democratic State Committee has spent nearly $14,000 to support Webb and $3,000 to oppose St. Michel. While Prosper Maine PAC has spent nearly $19,000 supporting St. Michel and $2,000 opposing Webb. 
One open race drawing lots of monied interest is Senate District 15, another in Kennebec County. Sen. Dick Bradstreet (R-Kennebec) currently holds the seat, but isn’t running for reelection. Bradstreet won the district in 2024 following Republican Matthew Pouliot in 2022. 
Even though it’s an open race held by Republicans for several terms, more than $306,000 has been spent by outside groups. 
The Maine Democratic State Committee is again the biggest spender in the district, with more than $156,000 supporting Democrat Amanda Heath and $75,000 opposing Republican Kati McCormick while Maine Senate Republicans have spent $27,000 to support McCormick.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: ‘Ambitious’ timeline means DeSantis could pass new vax rules before he leaves office
text:
State administrative judge will consider arguments in a challenge to the Florida Department of Health's proposed new vaccine rules for entry into schools and daycare. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)Gov. Ron DeSantis’s efforts to pare back the number of vaccines children must receive to enter school or daycare could pay off for him before he leaves office on Jan. 5 in light of a state administrative judge’ agreement Thursday to expedite a hearing on challenges to them.
Florida Division of Administrative Hearings Judge David Watkins consolidated two separate challenges to the proposed new rules and set the week of Dec. 14 to hear arguments.
Albeit a tight timeframe, the schedule could allow the DeSantis administration to implement the changes if Watkins recommends in favor of the Florida Department of Health, Jacksonville healthcare attorney Chris Nuland said.
“It’s ambitious, but not impossible. The judge would have to be diligent in preparing an order during the Christmas and the New Year holidays,” Nuland told the Phoenix.
 But “if the department wins prior to inauguration day, then the rule can go into effect without any action by the new administration.”
If Watkins issues an order against the DOH before DeSantis is term limited out of office, the DOH could file an appeal before the next governor is sworn in and takes office, Nuland said.
To pursue any such appeal, though, would be a decision for the next administration, Nuland said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Florida law requires children at a minimum to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, and tetanus to attend school and daycare.  A religious exemption to shots exists, plus exemptions for any parent if the child cannot be fully immunized for medical reasons.
Beyond what is legislatively mandated, the DOH is authorized to pass rules requiring vaccines for  “other communicable diseases as determined.” Under that authority, the DOH has required through its regulations for children to be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
Ladapo: Eliminating vaccine mandates isn’t about science, it’s about parents’ rights

The new proposed rules would eliminate those four vaccines.
The DOH held a workshop on the proposed rule changes in Lake Mary outside Orlando earlier this month. While there, Ladapo told the crowd that the changes were being pursued to ensure parents remain in charge of their children’s healthcare decisions.
“You know, this isn’t about the scientific effectiveness of one vaccine or the other, the safety of one vaccine or the other,” Ladapo said at the time, noting that the DOH would be “open to hearing about that.”
One of the challenges to the proposed rule comes from the Florida Academy of Family Physicians, physician Danielle Carter, and three individuals identified only by their initials. The second challenge was filed by Kimberly Thorpe and her two minor children, plus Genevieve Rahmouni and her minor son. Both cases involve medically fragile children.
Both challenges argue the DeSantis administration didn’t follow proper rulemaking procedures and that the DOH overstepped its legislative authority.
The Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians Services and the Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Family Pediatrics have filed motions to intervene in the now-consolidated cases. Nuland represents both groups.
DOH legal counsel told Watkins Thursday the agency would file motions opposing allowing the groups to join as intervenors. Watkins has given the DOH until Monday to file its motions against allow the two groups to join the challenge.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Blue Coats Begin 2026-2027 G League Season with Weekend Homestand
text:
The Delaware Blue Coats home stadium, the Chase Fieldhouse. Photo Courtesy of the Greater Wilmington Convention & Visitors Bureau and Moonloop Photography
The Delaware Blue Coats will start their 2026-2027 season with two home games on November 6 and 7, during the NBA G League Tip-Off Tournament.
 
WILMINGTON, Del — The NBA season has just begun and, for many fans in Delaware who support the Philadelphia 76ers, it’s shaping up as an exciting year. Lebron James and Jaylen Brown joined the team in the offseason creating an incredible starting five alongside former NBA MVP Joel Embiid, two-time All-Star Tyrese Maxey and All-Rookie first teamer VJ Edgecombe. 
As much as that core will carry the lionshare of production, the team’s depth will be critical to supporting the teams’ superstars. That’s where the Delaware Blue Coats play their role. 
Last season, five players that appeared in a game for the Blue Coats also appeared in a game with the 76ers. Players like Justin Edwards and Marjon Beauchamp even started for the 76ers and made significant contributions helping the team reach the playoffs and defeat the Boston Celtics in the first round. 
This year the Blue Coats roster features three two-way players — two-way players are players signed to two-way contracts meaning they can spend a certain amount of time with the NBA affiliate before having to return to the G League team — Caleb Love, Rayan Rupert and Tacko Fall in addition to a couple returners from last season, forwards Saint Thomas and Marcus Bagley. Former University of Delaware standout Jameer Nelson Jr. is also on the Blue Coats roster after spending time with the G Leagues’ Stockton Kings and Austin Spurs in recent seasons.
The Blue Coats season opener is also their home opener, welcoming the Capital City Go-Go (Washington Wizards affiliate) into Wilmington for a two-game, weekend homestand on November 6 and 7. The Blue Coats stay at home to host the Maine Celtics (Boston Celtics affiliate) the next weekend, before beginning their first road trip to play two games against the Long Island Nets (Brooklyn Nets affiliate) on November 16. 
All of these games are a part of the league’s G League Tip-Off Tournament which lasts from November 6 until December 18. The tournament acts as an introduction to a new season of G League basketball and breaks the teams into four different regions. The teams within the regions play each other and the team with the best winning percentage in the region advances. The other four teams that make up the eight team field will be the four teams with the highest winning percentage regardless of region, according to the NBA G League website. The teams that advance will play at-least two games at the 2026 NBA G League Winter Showcase before a champion is decided.
The Blue Coats will play in the East region and host seven G League Tip-Off Tournament games. The 2026 NBA G League Winter Showcase will take place in Orlando. The Salt Lake City Stars (Utah Jazz affiliate) were the champions last season.
Following the showcase, the Blue Coats will begin their 36-game regular season slate with a two-game homestand against the Wisconsin Herd (Milwaukee Bucks affiliate) December 27 and 29. Their regular season concludes on March 26, at home against the Long Island Nets. The Blue Coats finished the 2025-2026 season with an 18-18 record in the regular season.
The Blue Coats will host multiple promotional nights throughout the season, including two Education Day games on February 17 and 25. These nights welcome students from local elementary schools to experience a Blue Coats gameday. Last season, the Blue Coats set an attendance record during an Education Day event, according to a Blue Coats press release. The team will also host a Trading Card Night during their February 27 game against Cleveland Charge (Cleveland Cavaliers affiliate). 
The full promotional schedule for the 2026-2027 season can be found on the team’s Facebook account.
To learn more about the team or how to purchase tickets to a game click here to check out the team’s official website.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Marshall-Hamilton showdown becomes most expensive election in Kansas history
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, right, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participate in a debate at WDAF TV on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Pool photo by Charlie Riedel/Associated Pressl)TOPEKA — Ad spending on the U.S. Senate race in Kansas has exceeded $84.5 million between the two major-party candidates, creating the most expensive election in state history. 
Spending has exceeded the state’s previous record of $49.1 million in 2020, when U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall first ran for senate, according to AdImpact, an ad tracking and analysis company.
Marshall faces the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor in the Kansas City-area, and Libertarian candidate David Graham in the Tuesday election, which has attracted national attention as the parties battle for Senate control. The 2026 election cycle also has been the most expensive on record nationwide.
Following the August primary, Marshall and Hamilton have run relentless campaigns. Marshall dug into Hamilton’s old sermons and highlighted a child sex abuse incident at the church’s youth camp two decades ago. Hamilton lambasted Marshall for his ties to Florida and spread the word about Marshall’s medical debt collection practices while an OB-GYN in central Kansas.
The Hamilton campaign has spent more than $16 million this election season while Marshall’s campaign has spent just more than $6 million, according to federal campaign finance records as of Oct. 14.
Meanwhile, outside groups have made up a majority of the spending on the two campaigns. Spending is up by 3,332% compared with the 2022 Kansas Senate election, according to AdImpact.
Groups have spent more than $27 million on ads supporting Marshall, with at least $8.5 million more in the pipeline, and more than $34 million backing Hamilton, with $14 million more expected.
The Senate Leadership Fund has been the most significant spender for Marshall, spending at least $11 million in the state after it redirected money from North Carolina to Kansas earlier this month. It has aired anti-Hamilton and pro-Marshall ads.
A Kansas-based super PAC, the People over Politics Action Fund, has been the largest spender against Marshall, spending more than $11 million. The PAC has ties to former independent U.S. Senate candidate Greg Orman, who attempted to unseat Republican U.S. Sen. Pat Roberts in 2014. Orman contributed $50,000 to the anti-Marshall PAC in July as one of its first donors. 
Roberts, like Marshall, faced residency questions and got a late start on campaigning for a tougher-than-expected general election. Orman, like Hamilton, performed well in polls ahead of the general election and worked to distance himself from national Democrats.
Lower Costs Now, a Democratic super PAC spending against Republicans and for Democrats in key Senate races across the country, has spent nearly $6 million against Marshall and $4.5 for Hamilton, according to PaidForPolitics, which scrapes federal campaign finance reports.
Main Street Fund, a Republican-affiliated super PAC formed on Kansas’ primary election day, has spent nearly $4.6 million against Hamilton as of Oct. 21. The PAC’s funding came from other Republican-affiliated and pro-Trump PACs, according to campaign finance records.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Supreme Court rules in favor of Mantoloking in public records dispute
text:
Justice Douglas M. Fasciale wrote Thursday’s decision blocking the release of the name of an attorney who emailed advice to a municipal prosecutor in Ocean County. (Photo by Amanda Brown/New Jersey Monitor)Mantoloking can shield the identity of a private attorney who emailed advice to a government lawyer on how to handle a case, the New Jersey Supreme Court ruled Thursday in a divided decision.
The email, sought in a local dispute over traffic violations, is indeed subject to disclosure under the state Open Public Records Act, but the sender’s privacy interests and two balancing tests still weigh against releasing the private attorney’s name, the high court ruled.
“It is the sender’s reasonable expectation of privacy, which outweighs any interest in disclosure here, that protects the sender’s identity,” Justice Douglas Fasciale wrote for the majority in the 5-2 decision.
The conflict began when Jakob Weingroff, a former state trooper, filed a civilian complaint for alleged traffic violations against Donald Burke Sr., who sought Weingroff’s criminal and disciplinary history in response, suspecting Weingroff had previously falsified records.
A municipal court denied the request, and while the case was on appeal, Elizabeth Leahy, the municipal prosecutor appointed to oversee the proceedings due to a conflict of interest with the regular prosecutor, revealed a letter where she asked a colleague for advice about the admissibility of expunged records.
The colleague, whose name Leahy redacted in the letter provided in court, told her the expunged records were not admissible, citing statute. The trial court denied Burke’s request, but an appeals court said the circumstances entitled him to Weingroff’s expunged records.
Prosecutors dropped the charges against Burke after that ruling, but the case persisted because a separate group, the Association for Governmental Responsibility, Ethics, and Transparency, sued to reveal the colleague’s identity. Burke represented the group.
A trial court judge denied the request, ruling the email was a private communication on a private server and therefore exempt from disclosure. A divided appeals court affirmed the ruling, adding that even if it weren’t exempt, the sender’s identity would be shielded from disclosure that guards lawyers’ work product.
The Supreme Court’s majority ruled the email between the municipal prosecutor and her friend is disclosable under the Open Public Records Act because it was sent in the course of her official business. That it was sent on a private server was irrelevant and would not shield the email, the court said.
But when considering a balancing test weighing the sender’s privacy interests against the public’s right of access, the high court ruled the lawyer’s privacy won out.
“Attorneys might be discouraged from reaching out to their colleagues to discuss legal issues — and their colleagues may be reluctant to respond — if they believe personal identifying information might be released as a result,” Fasciale wrote for five members of the court, adding, “This is especially concerning to the extent it chills constructive attorney communications such as those here.”
With the case dismissed, the sender’s identity was irrelevant anyway, the high court ruled.
Donald Burke Jr., who represented his father and the association, did not immediately return a request for comment, nor did Robin La Bue, who argued the case for Mantoloking.
New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Michael Noriega (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
The dissent, by Justice Michael Noriega and joined by Chief Justice Stuart Rabner, said the email is a government record and that a balancing test favors disclosing the sender’s name.
Any reasonable expectation of privacy the sender had evaporated when Leahy introduced the letter in open court, Noriega wrote.
“A government actor cannot voluntarily disclose the substance of a government record in a public court proceeding and then continue to claim a reasonable expectation of privacy in the record’s sender,” he wrote.
Leahy had waived her interest by sharing the email instead of just reading the statute it cited, he added.
The majority’s ruling “turns accepted practice regarding reasonable expectations of privacy on its head,” Noriega said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: What races to watch in Pennsylvania on Election Day
authors: Peter Hall, Ian Karbal, Whitney Downard
text:
A sign directs voters to where they can cast their ballots at Allegheny County Election office in Pittsburgh on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The airwaves, streaming services and your mailbox will be politics-free after voters finish casting their ballots on Nov. 3.
With nearly 250 races across Pennsylvania that will determine party control of the governor’s office, General Assembly and, potentially, the U.S. House, the commonwealth is back in the national spotlight this election season. 
The majority of state and federal legislative seats are considered to be safely Democratic or Republican. But flipping just a few in any chamber could change the balance of power, and midterm elections traditionally favor the minority party. Combined with low presidential approval ratings and economic concerns, some experts theorize there could be a “blue wave” next week.
So what are the top races to watch in the state on election night?
 Garrity challenges Shapiro

At the top of the ticket, Gov. Josh Shapiro is pitching his vision for a state government led by Democrats as he seeks a second term and tries to help his party expand its footprint in both Harrisburg and Washington, D.C. 
He’s pitching himself as a moderate who knows how to “get stuff done,” even when that involves working with the Trump administration or the GOP majority in the state Senate.
Governor Josh Shapiro visits a Bucks County middle school to ceremoniously sign a school cellphone ban into law on Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo from PACast)
And he’s tried to tie his opponent, Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, to the unpopular decisions of President Donald Trump, who she has staunchly supported since his first term in office.
Garrity, however, is telling a different story. Shapiro, according to her campaign, is more focused on his presidential ambitions than the state of Pennsylvania, and has become too cozy with special interests like data center developers.
When it comes to data centers in particular, she’s repeatedly accused Shapiro of flip-flopping on the issue and called an executive order he signed aimed at reining in new development too little, too late. Garrity herself used to support increased data center development, but has since called for an indefinite pause.
She’s also sought to remind voters about the governor’s past controversies, like a settlement paid out to one of his top advisers after allegations of sexual misconduct surfaced in 2023.
But it’s not clear if her message is getting through. Shapiro, whose relatively high approval rating has held throughout his first term, has maintained a wide lead in the polls, and massively out-fundraised his opponent to boot.
Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity at a Sept. 29, 2026 event returning a collection of historical artifacts. (Photo from PACast)
As he campaigns for reelection, Shapiro has also been criss-crossing the state in an attempt to boost Democrats running for both state and federal seats. His big-picture goals include expanding the state’s Democratic congressional coalition, and flipping the state Senate, which has long been held by Republicans.
Since this race is atop the ballot, Democrats are hoping a Shapiro win could impact downballot races. They note the bigger the margin, the better night it would be for their candidates. Shapiro defeated Republican state Sen. Doug Mastriano by nearly 15 points four years ago. 
 Shapiro dreams of a trifecta

Shapiro’s popularity has emboldened Democrats to pursue what was once unheard of: flipping the Senate, which Republicans have controlled continuously since 1994. A unified legislature which would be more agreeable to his agenda could bolster Shapiro’s credentials if he runs for president in 2028. 
Republicans control the upper chamber with 27 seats. In the case of a 50-50 split, Lt. Gov. Austin Davis, a Democrat, would be the tiebreaker. 
Half the chamber’s seats are up for election this year, but only a handful are considered to be competitive. Closely watched races are almost all located in the eastern half of the state.
Democrat opportunities:

Senate District 6 (Bucks): incumbent Sen. Frank Farry, a Republican, is fending off a challenge from Bucks County Clerk of Courts Eileen Hartnett Albillar. 
Senate District 16 (Bucks and Lehigh): In a rematch from 2022, Sen. Jarrett Coleman, A Republican, will face Lehigh County Controller Mark Pinsley. 
Senate District 24 (Berks and Montgomery): Chris Thomas, a former middle school teacher and construction worker, hopes to knock out incumbent Sen. Tracy Pennycuick.
Senate District 40 (Lackawanna, Monroe and Wayne): Brian Wrightson, a small business owner, is challenging incumbent Sen. Rosemary Brown. 

But Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) told reporters in September that he believed Republicans would grow their majority by one member, likely referring to Lancaster County’s Senate District 36.
Sen. James Malone, a Democrat, won the seat in a 2025 special election by 529 votes, and will have to defend it again this year. The slim margin of victory one year ago and the district’s large number of registered Republicans make the seat one of the best opportunities for a Republican pick-up.
Also on the radar for the GOP: Senate District 14 (Lehigh and Northampton), where Omy Maldonado is challenging incumbent Sen. Nick Miller; and Senate District 38 (Allegheny), where incumbent Sen. Lindsey Williams is fending off Thomas West. 
The nonpartisan Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics put the Pennsylvania Senate as a toss up, meaning both parties have a shot at keeping — or taking — control. Previously, the chamber was considered to be leaning Republican.
With all 203 state House seats up for grabs, and a three-seat Democrat majority following a special election, the parties are eying two dozen seats as potential flips. Sabato’s, however, doesn’t rank the lower chamber as competitive as the Senate, putting it in the “likely Democratic” category. 
Three of those races are without an incumbent due to retirements. House District 45 (Allegheny) and House District 121 (Luzerne) are currently held by Democrats, while House District 88 (Cumberland) is currently occupied by a Republican.
In addition to open seats, races on priority lists for both the Republican State Leadership Committee and the House Democratic Campaign Committee include:

House District 18 (Bucks): Held by Republican Rep. K.C. Tomlinson, with a challenge from Democrat Bryan Allen.
House District 44 (Allegheny): Held by Republican Rep. Valerie Gaydos, with a challenge from Democrat Hadley Haas. 
House District 72 (Cambria): Held by Democrat Rep. Frank Burns, with a challenge from Republican Phil Rice.
House District 137 (Northampton): Held by Republican Rep. Joe Emrick, with a challenge from Democrat Jeff Warren. 
House District 142 (Bucks): Held by Republican Rep. Joe Hogan, with a challenge from Democrat Kristin Egan.
House District 160 (Chester and Delaware): Held by Republican Rep. Craig Williams, with a challenge from Democrat Elizabeth Moro. 

 Control of the U.S. House may well go through the Keystone State

Just 21 of the nation’s 435 U.S. House districts are considered competitive, and four of those seats are in Pennsylvania. Republicans currently hold a four-seat edge over Democrats in Congress’ lower chamber and a 10-7 edge in the commonwealth’s delegation. 
Congressional District 1:
Fifth-term Republican U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who was elected after his brother Mike Fitzpatrick retired in 2017, won his last reelection bid two years ago by a roughly 13% margin. 
The 1st Congressional District includes all of Bucks County and a sliver of Montgomery County in the Philadelphia suburbs. It’s the lone Republican holdout, whereas other suburban Philly districts have gone blue in the last decade and are considered safe for Democratic incumbents this election.
That means Democratic challenger Bob Harvie is a long shot to flip the seat this year. Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner, has criticized Fitzpatrick for supporting the Trump administration’s policies and for taking contributions from corporate PACs, while pledging not to accept any himself. 
Fitzpatrick, meanwhile, has cast himself as an independent voter; he was one of two GOP representatives to vote against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). And he touts his role in a bipartisan Problem Solving Caucus that has tackled election reform and accountability in Congress. 
His campaign has attacked Harvie as “divisive” and a “hack,” while a PAC aligned with Fitzpatrick ran ads alleging Harvie is the subject of an FBI investigation. Harvie’s campaign sent a cease and desist letter to Fitzpatrick in July stating that the claims are false and defamatory. The following month, Harvie sued the Defending America PAC and Chris Pack, a Republican consultant, for defamation.  
The most recent New York Times/Sienna University poll gives Harvie a 2-point advantage after trailing Fitzpatrick most of the year. That’s despite Fitzpatrick’s significant fundraising edge with nearly $8 million collected compared with Harvie’s $3.1 million.
Cook Political Report rates the race as “Leans Republican” and Sabato’s Crystal Ball calls it a toss up.
Congressional District 7:
After ousting Democratic incumbent Susan Wild by a 1% margin in 2024, U.S. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie is running to keep his seat. He’s challenged by Democrat Bob Brooks, a former firefighter and president of the state professional firefighters union.
The 7th District lies in eastern Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, encompassing Carbon, Lehigh and Northampton counties. The latter two counties have been described by political observers as among the most swingy in the nation in the last several presidential elections.
Mackenzie touts his support for the OBBBA and the tax cuts it included as demonstrating his support for working families. He also cites housing initiatives and the House’s passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which is designed to insulate consumers from data center costs.
Brooks has attacked Mackenzie as “a career politician who has voted with Trump nearly 100% of the time in Washington” and tells voters it’s time to “send one of us” to Washington to “shake things up.” He says his experience as a union leader will help him hold corporations accountable for high prices and fight corruption.
Polls give Brooks a 4- to 5-point advantage over Mackenzie. And Brooks holds a slight fundraising edge, with nearly $5.3 million raised against Mackenzie’s $5.2 million.
Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “leaning Democratic.”
Congressional District 8:
U.S. Rep. Rob Bresnahan, a first-term Republican congressman, flipped the Scranton-area seat in 2024, snagging the seat from longtime former U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright, a Democrat. 
But he won with less than 51% of the vote, providing an opening for Democratic challenger Paige Cognetti. She won Scranton’s mayoral special election in 2019 as an independent, later changing her party affiliation. 
Throughout his freshman term, critics of Bresnahan have hammered him over stock trading, which tracker Quiver Quantitative puts at $8.74 million. The multimillionaire now says he has “consistently” supported banning such activities and appears to have halted the money-making moves.
Bresnahan touts his deep, local roots and business connections., criticizing her ties to Wall Street and actions as mayor that he says threaten local police safety and increased taxes. 
Cognetti has raised more than $7.5 million since Jan. 1, 2025, compared to Bresnahan’s $6.5 million. Candidates and outside groups have bought more than $28 million in advertising, making it one of the most expensive national contests.
Cook Political Report ranks the race as a toss up, while Sabato’s Crystal ball changed its rating to “leans Democratic” on Tuesday. The latest New York Times/ Sienna University poll sponsored by the Philadelphia Inquirer gives Cognetti a four-point advantage over Bresnahan. 


Congressional District 10:
The race to represent the 10th Congressional District is one of the most competitive in the state. Six-term incumbent Republican Rep. Scott Perry is facing Democrat Janelle Stelson, a former WGAL news anchor.
The race is a rematch. In 2024, a year when Democrats underperformed up and down the ballot. But, while Stelson came within striking distance of unseating Perry, she lost to the incumbent by just over 1% of the vote.
Democrats are hopeful that the momentum on their party’s side driven by Trump’s cratering approval ratings — along with Stelson’s fundraising advantage — can push her over the top this year.
But recent polling has the race locked in a virtual tie. It’s also become the most expensive congressional contest in the state, with nearly $16 million raised between the two campaigns to date.
Stelson has highlighted Perry’s support of unpopular Trump administration policies, like his votes to authorize the war in Iran and cut funding for Medicaid. She’s also sought to remind voters of his role in efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. After Trump’s loss to Joe Biden in 2020, Perry was a key ally in Congress as the president fought to block the certification of the election
Perry’s campaign, on the other hand, has largely cast him in advertisements and campaign mailers as a principled conservative focused on cutting government waste, highlighting his multi-decade military record. He’s also tried to paint Stelson, a former Republican, as too liberal for the central Pennsylvania district.
Nearly one million Pennsylvanians have already voted via mail-in and absentee ballots as of Oct. 29, but millions will likely vote in-person on Election Day. State law prevents counties from starting their counts until polls open at 7 a.m. on Nov. 3, so the winner in some races may not be declared on election night.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Oopsie: PAC linked to Morrisey sends election mailers to wrong parts of West Virginia
text:
Election mailers from Black Bear PAC were mistakenly sent to voters in West Virginia's Northern Panhandle and Kanawha County in support of Sen. Anne Charnock, R-Kanawha, and Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio. (Photo illustration by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)A super political action committee linked to Gov. Patrick Morrisey sent election mailers backing governor-friendly senators. That’s not abnormal. The problem is the PAC sent the mailers to voters in the wrong parts of West Virginia.
Black Bear PAC sent a mailer in support of Sen. Anne Charnock, R-Kanawha, to the Northern Panhandle. It was meant for Kanawha County voters.
A mailer in support of Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, from the PAC was sent to Kanawha County instead of Northern Panhandle residents. 
Whoops. 
Black Bear PAC spent nearly $20,000 on the mailers on Oct. 26, according to a filing with the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office.
An email account listed on the PAC’s registration didn’t respond to an inquiry from West Virginia Watch. Its mailing address is listed as Beverly, Massachusetts.
Sen. Anne B. Charnock, R-Kanwawha
Morrisey appointed Charnock to the District 17 Senate seat in early 2025 after Eric Nelson resigned from the seat after being named Secretary of Revenue.
Richie Robb
Charnock faces a significant challenge from her Democratic opponent Richie Robb, a South Charleston politician, due to national political winds shifting Democrat and Charleston’s strong Blue voting base. 
Chapman’s Senate race in District 1 is one of this cycle’s most competitive races due to Democratic challenger Shawn Fluharty’s favorable odds to perform well in the area, including with President Trump backers. 
Chapman has held the Senate seat since 2022, and this is her first reelection bid. 
Fluharty currently serves in the House of Delegates and vocally opposes Morrisey, billing the race as him versus the governor. 
In District 1, incumbent Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, faces a challenge from Democratic candidate Shawn Fluharty, who currently serves in the House of Delegates. (West Virginia Legislative Photography photos)
Morrisey endorsed Chapman and Charnock in the May primary. The governor was heavily involved in endorsements and campaigning against some Republicans challenging pro-Morrisey candidates in the spring — an unusual move for a governor in the same political party. 
On Wednesday, Morrisey said he has been very active this campaign cycle ahead of Election Day, Nov. 3. 
“We’re trying to help a lot of people,” Morrisey said in response to a question from WOWK reporter Maddy Sperling during a press conference. “I think I made it clear I support our Republican ticket from the top to the bottom, and I think that’s important. I think it’s really critical that people make educated decisions about who to get out and vote for.”
“I want to be in a position to work closely with the Legislature to get a lot done next year, regardless what the makeup is in the House and Senate, that’s my duty as governor, and we’re going to continue to do that,” he added.
Polling from State Navigate showed that a Morrisey endorsement this election could be “toxic,” though the potential negative effect wasn’t as high in Districts 1 or 17 compared to other parts of the state. In Senate District 1, Morrisey’s approval rating was an even 45-45, according to recent State Navigate polling.
Black Bear PAC was active ahead of the May primary election in the Supreme Court races to back Morrisey’s preferred judicial candidates. Both judicial candidates, Gerald Titus and Tom Ewing, lost in the spring election. 
Super PACs like Black Bear can’t donate directly to candidates but can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to run advertisements, both in support or in opposition to candidates. 
Early voting continues in West Virginia through Oct. 31.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Weddle request to move his case to Franklin County is denied
text:
London Mayor Randall Weddle exits the courtroom at the Laurel County Judicial Center in London on April 15, 2026. Weddle was there to be arraigned on four felony counts of campaign finance violations. He entered pleas of not guilty. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Morgan Hornsby)Laurel Circuit Judge Michael Caperton has denied former London Mayor Randall Weddle’s motion to move his case – that alleges excess campaign contributions to help Gov. Andy Beshear win reelection in 2023 – from Laurel County to Franklin County.
The order, issued on Oct. 15, is the first significant pre-trial order in the case since Weddle was indicted by a Laurel County grand jury on March 31 on four counts of violating the state law that limits the amount a person can give to a political committee.
At the time, the law limited that amount to $2,000 per election to a candidate for state office and $15,000 per year to a political party.
The indictment charges that Weddle shattered those limits by giving $18,000 to Beshear’s campaign, and $130,000 to the Kentucky Democratic Party in the names of his family members, friends and employees in a series of credit card transactions made during the final days of 2022.
Each of the four counts is a Class D felony  which carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Weddle has pleaded not guilty.
Weddle’s attorney, Guthrie True of Frankfort, argued in a motion filed in April, and at a hearing in London in July, that the trial should be moved to Franklin County. True argued none of the alleged illegal behavior occurred in Laurel County. He said that the contributions were solicited from Franklin County and accepted in Franklin County, and that they were made by Weddle when he was on a family vacation in the Bahamas.
The case is being prosecuted by the office of Attorney General Russell Coleman, which argued that Laurel is a proper venue because Weddle’s credit card has a Laurel County address and that the actions of Weddle, which occurred just days before he assumed the office of mayor, “had a greater effect on the citizens of Laurel County than the citizens of any other county.”
CourtNet, the website for Kentucky court records, lists that Caperton issued the order on Oct. 15, but the order itself is not accessible on CourtNet.
True did not return phone calls from the Kentucky Lantern. A spokesman for Coleman’s office declined comment.
The Lantern first raised questions about the Weddle contributions in an April, 2023 story. The story said that reports filed by Beshear and the Kentucky Democratic Party listed contributions totaling at least $305,500 from Weddle family members, employees and friends. It further identified another $385,162 in other contributions to Beshear and the party from Weddle business associates from across the country.
Beshear initially defended the contributions. But when Weddle later told Beshear that many of the contributions were made on his credit card, the Beshear campaign and the KDP refunded $202,000 in contributions to Weddle.
The Kentucky Registry of Election Finance launched an investigation of the matter, but the registry later stepped aside when Coleman began investigating the matter.
In documents filed by Weddle during the registry’s investigation and in the ongoing criminal case, True has said that a series of more than 80 text messages between Weddle and Beshear’s chief fundraiser, James Lucas Johnson, in late 2022 show that the fundraiser initially gave Weddle the green light for initially putting campaign contributions of others on his own credit card.
Weddle’s tumultuous term as mayor ended prematurely in July when he resigned after the Kentucky Court of Appeals reaffirmed the city council’s decision in 2025 to remove him from office for reasons that include the mayor’s signing of a $5 million mortgage for the city without council’s approval.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Early voting ends Friday. Idahoans can still register at the polls on Election Day.
text:
A "Vote Here" sign is on display during the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Lowell Elementary School in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Across Idaho, in-person early voting ends at 5 p.m. local time Friday.
Check with your local county clerk’s office for a list of early voting locations near you. Ada County, Idaho’s largest, has more than a half dozen spots. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
If you miss early voting, the last chance to vote in Idaho’s general election will be in-person at the polls on Tuesday. Polls will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Idaho offers same day voter registration.
By the time polls close on Election Day, absentee ballots are due to election offices. If you haven’t mailed your ballot yet, election officials encourage you to physically drop off your absentee ballot in-person at an election office or drop box. 
Even though the president isn’t on the ballot this year, it’s still a big election year for Idaho.
All statewide offices — such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state controller and state treasurer — are up for grabs, along with three congressional seats in the U.S. House and Senate, and all 105 state legislative seats. So are local races like for county commissioners, highway district officials and even a runoff election for an Ada County judge. 
But perhaps the biggest race this year is Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights. That’s one of several ballot measures that voters can decide on, along with a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow only the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun.
 



 How to prepare for Idaho’s general election

Visit VoteIdaho.gov, a website run by the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, to verify your voter registration status, find your polling place and preview what your ballot will look like.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: Editor’s note: I’m retiring, April’s going to take over
text:
From left: Dana Gentry, Jeniffer Solis, Hugh Jackson, April Corbin Girnus, Michael Lyle.Early in October I informed the Nevada Current staff and States Newsroom, our parent nonprofit, that I’m retiring, and Friday, Nov. 20, will be my last day with the Current. 
States Newsroom sensibly did the obvious thing and quickly asked April Corbin Girnus, the Current’s deputy editor, to accept the job as editor. To everyone’s delight, April said yes.
When we first started working with each other in the late spring of 2018, I had no way of knowing that all five members of the original team would still be together more than eight years later. 
(Nor did I imagine I would end up editing the Current longer than I held any other job over the course of my sometimes bumpy but mostly pretty lucky career.)
All of us — senior reporter Dana Gentry, reporters Michael Lyle and Jeniffer Solis, April, and myself — each in our own way but also in collaboration with each other have made the Current a unique and indispensable space on the Nevada media landscape.
I’m proud to have been a part of it.
And I’m excited to see what April does with the joint.

name: VTDigger
title: Bringing flood reporting from VTDigger and FRONTLINE (PBS) to more Vermonters
text:
Photo by Taylor Haynes/VTDigger
After 17 years as an all-digital newsroom, VTDigger is trying something new: our first printed project.
“In an era where screens are everywhere, I think even our most die-hard readers appreciate an analog experience where they can take their time and form a stronger connection with what they’re holding in their hands,” said VTDigger CEO Brendan Kinney.
VTDigger has partnered with FRONTLINE (PBS) to report on Vermont’s capacity to recover from flooding. The Coming Storm, a three-part series, exposes gaps in the systems meant to support communities in the months and years after the water recedes.
Why we printed it
We wanted The Coming Storm to reach as many people as possible, including Vermonters who don’t regularly read VTDigger online. In this case, making our journalism accessible meant considering readers’ access to internet and cell service, reading preferences and how people encounter news in their daily lives. That led us to think beyond our digital reach and explore new ways for people to discover our reporting.
The answer was a special 12-page VTDigger print edition, distributed in partnership with Seven Days inside its Oct. 28 paper. The insert brings the first story in the series, reported by Emma Cotton with photography by Glenn Russell, to print. The second and third stories will be available online.
Who is helping us distribute this work
Seven Days’ distribution network carries the print edition to communities across the state. We’re extending that reach with help from partners so that more people will encounter the reporting in places like grocery stores, libraries and coffee shops.
Community ambassadors who worked with us on Dirt Road News, a community listening project, are returning to help distribute copies, along with local businesses and community organizations. Together, they’ll help spread the reporting even farther.
We’re grateful to Seven Days (here’s publisher Paula Routly on why they said yes), our community ambassadors and the local businesses and partners helping put this reporting in more hands.
Listening through print
Pick up a copy of the print edition and you’ll find an invitation to tell us how flooding has affected you, in writing or by recording a short audio message. We’re grateful for whatever people feel comfortable sharing, and it will help inform future reporting.

READ MORE

“Our series is called ‘The Coming Storm,’ in part, because scientists expect the flooding problem to worsen in Vermont,” said Emma Cotton, who reported the series for VTDigger. “We’re committed to covering this topic beyond the series, and it’s important to us that Vermonters help guide that reporting.”
Don’t have a copy? Seven Days is available free at locations across Vermont. You can also share your experience or a tip with our newsroom at tips@vtdigger.org or through our tip drop.
Help us build something useful
There is one thing every Vermonter can help with. We’re building a flood resource guide, but we want to build it from what you tell us would help you most.
What information would have helped you before, during or after a flood? What was hard to find? What is your community doing to prepare or respond that others should know about?
You can respond whether or not you pick up the print edition.

Help shape the flood resource guide

Why we’re calling this an experiment
VTDigger is a digital newsroom, and printing our journalism is new territory for us. We’re treating it as a test, and we’ll be honest about what we learn.
Here’s what we’re watching:

How many people find the series through the print edition, and where they’re located in the state
How many readers respond to our questions, and what they share with us
Whether print reaches people who don’t already read VTDigger

What we learn will shape how we approach future projects, including whether and how we print again. We look forward to sharing what we heard and what we’re doing with it in 2027.
Pick up this week’s Seven Days to find the print edition and read The Coming Storm online. Thank you to everyone helping bring this reporting to more Vermonters, and to everyone willing to tell us what would make our work more useful.
You can always share your feedback about our reporting by emailing contact@vtdigger.org.

We’re grateful to the American Journalism Project and Google News Initiative for supporting the printing, distribution and community listening efforts connected to this project.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Bringing flood reporting from VTDigger and FRONTLINE (PBS) to more Vermonters.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico educators lay out proposals to improve student job prospects
text:
Photo caption: From left to right: Sen. Bill Soules (D-Las Cruces), KYVA Analytics President Scott Secamiglio, Pacific Fusion External Relations Lead Matt Pahl and New Mexico School Counselor of the Year Teach Robert Wiebelhaus at Teach Plus New Mexico’s Statewide Economic Mobility Summit in Albuquerque on Oct. 26, 2026, where three recommendations to address student economic opportunity and mobility were announced. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)A group of New Mexico educators presented policy recommendations this week to improve student job prospects.
The recommendations, presented Monday in Albuquerque at Teach Plus New Mexico’s third Statewide Economic Mobility Summit, build on feedback the nonprofit gathered at conferences in Hobbs and Santa Fe last year and include creating more workforce opportunities for students, boosting the student-counselor ratio and improving workforce data collection. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hope Morales, Teach Plus New Mexico executive director, told Source NM that middle and high school students at both previous conferences expressed the desire for more hands-on learning through internships and more information about job opportunities. The group also recommends boosting the number of school counselors to help students learn about and find those opportunities.
“If counselors have too high a caseload, we’re stretched too thin and not able to guide students in emotional coping strategies and career readiness,” Robert Wiebelhaus, New Mexico’s 2026 school counselor of the year, told Source NM. Teach NM recommended focusing first on schools and communities with the greatest caseloads and opportunity gaps.
According to the American School Counselors Association, New Mexico has a 406-to-1 student-to-counselor ratio. The association recommends a 250-to-1 ratio.
State Sen. William Soules (D-Las Cruces), chair of the Senate Education Committee, attended the summit and told Source NM that New Mexico is “short hundreds of counselors” and the state “ought to be actively recruiting counselors from other states to come to New Mexico while we’re building our counselor program at our schools.” 
The organization also wants New Mexico to make its current state student data program, called Rise NM, more accessible and usable by educators in the classroom. Rise NM links records from the Public Education Department, Higher Education Department, Workforce Solutions, Early Childhood Education and Care Department and the Department of Vocational Rehabilitation to track student outcomes from K-12 to the workforce. 
The group said the program’s information can be fragmented because of limited teacher and counselor input, particularly in historically underserved communities, making it difficult for educators, policymakers and communities to understand what is working. 
Source NM has a pending request for comment with the Public Education Department.
“We’re not recommending that we start over,” Morales said. “We’re recommending that we strengthen what exists and ensure that the information that we are collecting is accessible, meaningful and actually used to improve decisions and student outcomes.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Abortion stance a ‘tell’ for candidates, Slotkin says in pre-election podcast
text:
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, record a live taping of the My Body, My Pod podcast in Detroit on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, agreed that a candidate’s stance on abortion can signal a candidate’s beliefs more broadly, with Slotkin calling it a “shorthand for extremism” if a candidate supports an abortion ban, especially one without exceptions.
“I think a woman’s right to choose that one for me is usually a good tell on what people think is the role of government in our lives,” Slotkin (D-Holly) said. “Ironically, the people who claim they believe in small government when it comes to controlling women’s bodies and their health, they become big government champions, and I think it’s a tell on what kind of legislator they will be.”
During a live taping of Reproductive Freedom for All’s My Body, My Pod podcast in Detroit Tuesday, Timmaraju similarly said that the issue is a “signal to voters on how extreme they are” and “an immediate way to disqualify candidates.”
The full podcast is set to air on Nov. 2, the day before the general election.
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) discusses abortion and dynamics within the Democratic Party with Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, during a live podcast taping in Detroit on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
The issue of reproductive rights is still salient, even in Michigan, Slotkin emphasized — telling reporters after the podcast recording that the continued conversation about the issue in competitive races, including her former congressional district in mid-Michigan, shows just how much voters still care about it. 
“I think it’s interesting that Abdul just put out an abortion ad, and I think that you don’t do paid media at the end of a campaign, a tough campaign like this, without that being a deeply salient issue,” she said of another highly competitive statewide race, the U.S. Senate race between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers. “He’s in the closest race I think in the state, and that’s one of his closing messages.”
Slotkin was also critical of what she called an attempt by Rogers to “cover up” his voting record on reproductive rights in response to public opinion. 
“Just own your record, dude. Just own it,” she said. “You ran on it, and you fundraised off of it, and the whole thing. I think that’s what’s happening now for him, on a whole bunch of issues — tariffs and Canada and gas and the war in Iran and all these things that literally six weeks ago he was championing, he’s now flipped on, which again is part of that character issue.”
Recorded a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress as well as Michigan’s executive and legislative branches, Slotkin also discussed the importance of discussing abortion even in extremely conservative areas — and how her experience running in Michigan and in a swing congressional district taught her that.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“In Michigan we understand that you can’t just win by going to really blue places, okay? You have to go to the Upper Peninsula. You have to go to the west side of the state. You have to go to the Thumb of Michigan,” Slotkin said. “You have to go everywhere and compete for people’s votes. And if you don’t show up in those places, like don’t be surprised when they don’t vote for you.”
Slotkin emphasized to Timmaraju that, though some Democrats may feel demoralized by the state of the country, she has seen in visits to more conservative states, including Kansas, Indiana and Idaho, the need to engage with swing voters and independents, and to encourage Democrats taking risks by running in red states. 
She spoke about Idaho specifically in relation to its upcoming ballot proposal vote on whether or not to retain the state’s abortion ban — one of four states that will vote on the legality of abortion in 2026.
Michigan is also facing a referendum in 2026 that advocates have warned could impact reproductive freedoms in the state, which were enshrined in the state constitution in 2022 — a vote on a constitutional convention. 
Slotkin and Timmaraju did not address that ballot measure during the podcast taping, but speaking with reporters afterward did note that in conversations with voters leading up to the election, Reproductive Freedom for All members are encouraging Michiganders to vote against the constitutional convention.
“I think it’s just really important for us to remind folks to again fill out the whole ballot, and to make sure we’re protecting our democratic institutions,” Timmaraju said. “Making the connection to the integrity of their prior votes, every state that’s tried to change the rules midstream has faced political consequences. Voters do not like that.”
Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, records a live taping of the My Body, My Pod podcast in Detroit on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Shanay Watson-Whittaker, Reproductive Freedom for All’s director of Michigan campaigns, also referenced past comments from Republican lieutenant governor candidate and state Rep. Jay DeBoyer suggesting that a constitutional convention might be used to roll back reproductive freedoms, as well as the recent closures of Planned Parenthood locations, as reasons to vote against that ballot measure when talking to reporters.
“We have a problem with access right now in the state, as a result of the big ugly bill, and if we continue to have someone who talks like that and money that’s spent to actually do that, we’re in trouble,” she said. “What we did in 2022 will be for naught, and we don’t want to do that. So we don’t want to go backwards. We don’t want to pass Proposal One.”
The Democratic divide: ‘team fight’ vs. ‘team flight’
Outside of the issue on abortion, Slotkin reiterated her idea of division in the Democratic Party — not along ideological lines of progressive versus moderate, which she called “very 2019,” but instead about “team fight versus team flight.”
“For this country to be the country we know it can be, you have to fight for it, right? Because this guy’s trying to tear down our democracy, ruin our economy,” Slotkin said, referring to President Donald Trump. “Or are you like a lot of you know Democrats I serve with who are kind of like ‘Elissa, just wait, politics is cyclical.’”
Slotkin discussed this divide in relation to Michigan’s U.S. Senate race and her own relationship with El-Sayed, and the need for a new generation of Democrats in Congress.
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, record a live taping of the My Body, My Pod podcast in Detroit on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
“I’m interested in working with anyone who is interested in thinking about new ways of exerting pressure and oversight and accountability,” she said. “Because the strongly worded letter that worked 30 years ago, that might have meant something 30 years ago, when a ton of senators wrote a strongly worded letter to the president. It doesn’t work. Let’s stop repeating, rinsing, and repeating the things that don’t work, and let’s think about new models of accountability.”
She also told Timmaraju that she sees two visions of America emerging in politics right now — an inclusive vision based around decency and ensuring that everyone has a right to participate, and a “dark vision of corruption” embodied by Trump where there is not a belief that America can be a good and decent place. 
“When you have leaders, up and down the ballot, there is no law that says you have to agree with everything they say,” Slotkin said. “You’re not looking for perfection in the people on the ballot. You’re looking for who stands up for that vision of America, integrity, and who’s going to fight. That, to me, is more important than any one difference you may have with an elected leader.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former school administrator challenges think tank founder for SC superintendent
text:
State Superintendent Ellen Weaver, left, is vying against Democratic challenger Sylvia wright, right, to lead the state's public school system. (Photos provided by candidate campaigns)COLUMBIA — Voters’ choice to run the state’s Department of Education could determine agency support for a taxpayer-funded education voucher program over the next four years.
Democrat Sylvia Wright is challenging Republican Ellen Weaver for the position overseeing policy for the state’s 72 public school districts. While both want to continue improving students’ test scores, they differ in their opinions of a program giving students funds for education-related expenses, including private school tuition.
Weaver, who’s seeking a second term, previously led Palmetto Promise Institute, a conservative education-focused think tank she co-founded in 2013 with her former boss, U.S. Sen. Jim DeMint, after he left office.
Wright most recently worked as a district coordinator for Dorchester 4, where she oversaw curriculum, reviewed testing data and helped train teachers. She resigned last fall to focus full-time on her campaign.
The last time voters chose a Democrat as state superintendent was in 2006, when Jim Rex won with fewer than 500 votes.
Still, Wright said she’s optimistic, pointing to polls showing significant support for Democratic candidates even in traditionally safe Republican areas during the midterm.
“This is a unique election cycle,” Wright said.
The job is also getting less attention this round. In 2022, the superintendent’s race was the most crowded field on South Carolina’s primary ballots, with six Republicans and three Democrats competing to replace retiring Superintendent Molly Spearman. Four years later, Weaver had no GOP opposition, and Wright became the Democratic nominee in June by defeating the party’s last nominee for the job.
Education Scholarship Trust Fund program
The place where Wright and Weaver vary most starkly is on whether to support the Education Scholarship Trust Fund, which provides money to pay for children’s K-12 educational needs, including private school tuition.
No money is sent directly to parents. Rather, quarterly installments are deposited into online accounts controlled by parents, who direct where the dollars go.
Since the program is written into state law and uses taxpayer dollars, the Department of Education must award scholarships to at least 15,000 students, no matter who wins.
By law, the scholarship amount adjusts yearly based on per-student funding to public schools. This year, that calculation provided roughly $7,600 each to parents earning up to 500% of the federal poverty limit.
Providing less would require a Legislature-approved change in state law.
The state superintendent can ask for more money through the agency’s annual budgeting process to open up more slots in the program. The decision of whether to fund those spaces is ultimately up to legislators.
Weaver has long advocated for a broader program, including as head of Palmetto Promise Institute, the state’s leading proponent of school choice legislation since she launched it. The think tank wants the K-12 scholarships to be “universal,” which means available to all parents.
K-12 scholarships through federal tax credits start in January. Nonprofits will oversee spending.

A federal tax credit program set to start in January could end up dwarfing the state’s numbers, without oversight by the state’s K-12 agency.
In an emailed statement to the SC Daily Gazette, Weaver said she wants to enroll more students in the state’s program. This year, roughly 20,000 families applied for 15,000 slots, leaving thousands of students on the waitlist, she said. She asked legislators to expand enrollment to 20,000 students this year, but the state budget kept the cap at 15,000.
“My commitment is to continue to implement the law faithfully, strengthen accountability and program operations, preserve meaningful flexibility for eligible families, and work with lawmakers to responsibly expand access,” Weaver said.
Wright wouldn’t ask legislators for more slots, she said. She has concerns about how the program has worked so far.
Officials have no idea how well students who used the money to pay for private school are performing, she said.
Schools submitted inconsistent and incomplete data for the program’s first year, making it impossible to analyze or give legislators results as required by law, according to an Education Oversight Committee report. A report on the second year’s results is expected in December.
Questions over whether homeschooled students should receive state funds also rankled legislators this year.
When legislators passed the law, both in its original form in 2023 and to reinstate funding for private school tuition in 2025, senators made it clear they didn’t want the money going toward homeschooling. That came at the request of homeschooling parents, who worried about government oversight.
Yet, the Department of Education awarded roughly 1,000 students money for homeschooling expenses, Weaver told senators earlier this year. Since the program excludes students homeschooled under the three methods allowed under state law, the education department essentially created a fourth option in which the agency oversees learning.
Senators, including the Senate’s majority leader and chairman of the education committee, accused Weaver of exploiting a loophole in the law and betraying their trust. Weaver told them she was just following the law as written.
“On matters of implementation, I have always believed that the law — not political pressure — must guide the department’s decisions,” Weaver said. “Reasonable people can disagree about policy, and the General Assembly has every right to clarify or change the law. My responsibility is to administer the law as written, communicate openly, and continuously improve how we serve South Carolina families.”
The questions over whether the law was implemented correctly raised concerns for voters, Wright said.
“That lack of transparency, the dishonesty as far as the homeschoolers receiving those vouchers — people are mad about that, and not just Democrats,” Wright said.
If she were superintendent, she would make sure money went where it was supposed to go, she said. That also means making sure low-income students get priority, as legislators said they intended, she said.
Applications for the funds open in windows, with lower-income students coming ahead of their more affluent peers. Wright wants more data on how many low-income students the program is actually helping, she said.
Instead of putting more money toward vouchers, Wright said, she’d rather put those funds toward improving public schools.
“My focus is going to be more on fully funding our public schools and making them a viable option,” she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Test scores and teacher retention
When it comes to improving students’ test scores and keeping teachers in classrooms, Weaver wants to stay the course, she said, pointing to improvements in both areas in recent years.
“Four years ago, I promised South Carolinians that we would raise expectations, support our teachers, strengthen our schools, and put students first,” Weaver said. “We have delivered on those promises, working shoulder to shoulder with the governor, General Assembly, and educators across our state.”
This year, more schools than ever received top scores on the state’s revamped report cards, which measure test scores, classroom surveys and student progress, following years of upward trends. At the same time, the number of schools in the lowest possible category declined.
More SC schools get top scores than ever, but education leaders say there’s still work to do

More students are reading and doing math on grade level in recent years, with both reaching their highest scores since the SC READY tests began in 2015. Just over 61% of all students tested in the spring could read on grade level, while nearly 48% could do math as expected for their grade.
Meanwhile, the number of vacant teacher positions has dropped since a record high during the 2023-24 school year. At the start of last school year in 2025, schools reported 706 open positions, the lowest number in at least five years, according to an annual survey.
“These are real results, earned through the hard work of South Carolina’s teachers, students, and families,” Weaver said.
Teachers’ advocates and state leaders credited changes in how students learn to read as a big reason for improvements in English scores. A similar program for math began this spring, with hopes of similar advancements in math.
Weaver has backed initiatives to keep teachers in classrooms. She asked for money to give certain teachers performance-based bonuses in an effort to reward student progress. And she’s supported the governor’s push to get base salaries for first-year teachers over $50,000, which legislators did this year.
If reelected, Weaver would keep building on that success, she said, without giving specifics.
“Our next chapter is about going further and faster — strengthening early literacy and math instruction, better preparing and rewarding excellent teachers, modernizing school facilities, and continuing to expand educational opportunity,” Weaver said.
Wright would want to look at other creative ways of continuing that progress if elected, she said.
Student success should start with early education, Wright said. She wants to push for universal pre-kindergarten for 4-year-olds and work more closely with First Steps, the agency overseeing state-paid preschool in private daycares.
Gov. Henry McMaster recommended legislators pay to expand eligibility for state-funded preschool to every 4-year-old in the state, but that didn’t make it into the final budget. Wright would look for other funding sources, potentially using local grant money, she said.
“There are so many issues that we’re seeing in K-12 because they’re not being addressed in the early, pre-K, birth-to-5 realm,” she said.
Along with continuing to push for higher teacher salaries, Wright would like to put in place a statewide training program for administrators. For a lot of teachers, the quality of their principals and superintendents can be a deciding factor in whether they want to continue teaching, she said.
Having a statewide training program could create more consistency in school environments, she said. Teachers who want to become administrators might also be more encouraged to stay in their local districts with more support from the state, she said.
“For me, it goes beyond just the incentives and the pay,” Wright said. “We have a leadership problem in South Carolina. As superintendent, I want to strengthen our leadership pipeline.”
