title: Dartmouth provost resigns after review finds undisclosed AI use
text:
Santiago Schnell, the Dean of the College of Science at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, has been named the next provost of Dartmouth, the college announced Tuesday. Photo credit: University of Notre Dame – Barbara Johnston

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Oct. 28, 2026.HANOVER — Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell has resigned and is leaving the university after a faculty-led committee found he used artificial intelligence in his writing without properly disclosing it.
President Sian Leah Beilock announced the resignation Wednesday afternoon in an email to the campus community.
“Out of respect for his colleagues and the institution, Santiago has resigned as provost and is leaving the university,” Beilock wrote. “This was his decision.”
Beilock formed the committee on Sept. 25, after news reports questioned Schnell’s use of AI, including an August Semafor article about AI-written opinion pieces that named his Washington Post column.
In its report, dated Oct. 27, the committee found that Schnell “used AI to meaningfully alter his writing in violation of at least one publication’s AI use and/or disclosure requirement, failed to disclose his use of AI in clear violation of a national newspaper’s stated policy, was not forthcoming about his AI use,” and fell short of Dartmouth’s ethics and professionalism standards.
The committee said it did not use AI detection tools. Instead, it reviewed Schnell’s logs from Dartmouth’s enterprise AI tool, Claude, along with his emails. It also noted that it was not recommending any disciplinary action.
Schnell has published at least 30 pieces since joining Dartmouth in July 2025, according to the report. Given the short timeline, the committee focused on a handful of them.
In one journal paper, the committee found Schnell used Claude to “substantially edit his research manuscript, troubleshoot errors in computer code, and generate figures.” The journal required that kind of use to be disclosed, and Schnell did not disclose it. He told Beilock in a Sept. 22 email that he had relied on older author instructions.
“This wasn’t the case, but a disclosure would have been the best approach,” Schnell wrote, according to the report.
The committee said the publisher has required AI disclosure since at least 2023.
Schnell told Semafor he used ChatGPT “to refine a few arguments, check for grammatical errors, and submit it to the Washington Post.” The committee said that was a “clear violation” of the Post’s policy.
According to the committee, in a forthcoming article, Schnell uploaded his manuscript to Claude and asked, “Are there many signatures of AI writing in this article?” He later submitted a version with the kinds of changes Claude suggested. When the journal’s editor asked about AI use, Schnell said he “did not understand that this type of AI-assisted editing required disclosure.” The committee said his description “understates the nature of the Provost’s actual AI use.”
The committee found no violation in a fourth paper, which Schnell co-authored.
The report also says Schnell did not fully cooperate.
“Although he did provide his Dartmouth-issued laptop for inspection, the Provost did not, upon request, provide logs of his use of personal LLM accounts that he used for his academic and public writings,” the committee wrote.
Former provost and computer science professor David Kotz led the committee. Its other members were computer science professor Hany Farid, English professor Peter Orner, linguistics professor Lindsay Whaley and trustee Odette Harris.
Schnell did not respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, and Dartmouth Director of Media Relations & Communications Strategy Jana Barnello did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
History professor Matthew Delmont will serve as interim provost through June 2028.
In her letter, Beilock said leaders must “model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars.” Dartmouth hosts its “AI at 70: What Must Remain Human?” conference later this week.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Commentary: The New Mexico Reforestation Center is a key part of rebuilding New Mexico’s forests
text:
General Obligation Bond 3 on the Nov. 3, 2026, ballot includes $17.65 million in funding for a third greenhouse at the New Mexico Reforestation Center, which is growing seedlings to reseed New Mexico's burn scars. (Nina Riggio for the New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission)Have you ever wondered what happens to forests after a wildfire, long after the flames go out? We’ve all driven through old burn scars that remain littered with black, peeling tree trunks. Will those forests ever look like they used to?
New Mexicans know — too well — that burn scars lead to persistent erosion and devastating floods, taking out our roads and homes, damaging our rivers and water quality, and uprooting even more of our trees. New Mexico is no stranger to extreme wildfires, and the scale of tree loss today is outpacing forests’ natural ability to recover. But in the Nov. 3 election, New Mexicans can vote on General Obligation Bond 3, a large package that includes $17.65 million in funding for a new tree nursery — The New Mexico Reforestation Center.
Historically, fire has been a natural and even necessary part of New Mexico’s forests. But catastrophic wildfires, like those that impacted Mora and Ruidoso, are not the same low-intensity fires evolved over millennia. New research conducted in our state shows that wildfires today are burning more severely and at higher temperatures, due to a hotter and drier climate.
Intense burns make it harder for forests to recover because they scorch all the way down to the seed source, destroying forests’ natural reserve that they rely on to regenerate and start anew. Without regrowth after a burn, there are no trees or roots to help filter water or hold soil in place when heavy monsoon rains return, resulting in a chain of natural disasters that pummel our communities. That’s where the New Mexico Reforestation Center comes in.
Under the leadership of State Forester Laura McCarthy, New Mexico is at the forefront of post-fire forest restoration with the proposed expansion of the reforestation center in Mora, set to be the largest science-based tree nursery in the country. Here, local researchers are growing drought-hardened seedlings that are more resilient to our hotter and drier climate. These native trees will be used to replant and restore burned areas across the state to help our forests get started again after catastrophic wildfires.
Right now, the Reforestation Center can grow up to 300,000 seedlings annually. That isn’t enough to reseed our existing burn scars, which on their own require an estimated 385 million new trees, let alone prepare for future disasters New Mexico will face.
If approved by voters this November, General Obligation Bond 3 would fund the addition of a third greenhouse to the tree nursery, ensuring we help our forests when they need us without increasing tax rates. As the Reforestation Center builds capacity, it will help supply the needed seedlings to meet that call, nurturing up to five million trees annually to make our forests healthy once more.

title: New Mexico outdoor recreation officials seek more funding to meet demand for youth programs
text:
Officials from the New Mexico Outdoor Equity Fund requested additional funds during an interim legislative committee hearing on Oct. 27, 2026, saying that high demand and limited funds left nearly half of program applicants without funding. Above: Mesa Prieta Petroglyph Project summer youth interns build archaeology skills alongside traditional skills and knowledge. (Photo courtesy of New Mexico Outdoor Recreation Division)Officials for New Mexico’s outdoor youth grant program told lawmakers this week that at its current budget level, the program could only fund approximately half of the proposals during a recent grant cycle. They hope to receive more funding during next year’s legislative session to meet growing demand. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Outdoor Equity Fund, a program of the state’s Outdoor Recreation Division, has awarded $12.8 million in grants for various outdoor youth programs across 25 of the state’s 33 counties since it began in 2019. 
Originally, the program capped grants at $40,000, but in May began awarding up to $100,000 to larger programs. In September, the program announced eight $100,000 awards in the first round of FY27 grants spread among 54 total recipients — totaling $2.2 million. Some examples of those awards include $100,000 to Friends of Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks in Doña Ana County for outdoor education, afterschool mountain biking and other youth programs; to just over $30,000 to Adaptive Sports Program New Mexico in Sandoval County to provide adaptive ski and snowboard instruction to students with disabilities; and $15,000 to the Northern NM R.O.C Foundation in Rio Arriba County for The Fly With Me program to connect Chama Valley middle school students with free fly-fishing lessons and other types of outdoor education.
However, demand has outpaced available funding, Outdoor Recreation Division Grants Coordinator Evan Pilling told lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee during its Tuesday meeting, with applications increasing more than 140% in FY26. In total, the program received $7.8 million in requests but had only $4.2 million in funding, Pilling said, leaving 48% of applicant requests unmet. 
“We do the best we can to provide funding to the highest quality and highest impact programs,” Pilling said, “while also taking into account factors like rural and tribal communities.”
Chas Robles, executive director of Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps, presented the Coalition of Outdoor Equity Fund New Mexico’s request to increase program funding to $10 million annually for the next three years. Robles said the proposed increase would make outdoor programs more “visible and accessible, rather than leaving a young person to figure it out alone.”   
One of the existing grant-funded programs is Sugar Hill Pathways in Mescalero, which offers bike mechanic training and a cycling program for Mescalero Apache Tribe youth. Sugar Hill Pathways received a $40,000 grant from the program last year. 
Leerae Lester, a 17-year old member of the Mescalero Apache Tribe, told lawmakers that while his peers spend their time “on their phones and gaming,” he recently started bike mechanic training with Sugar Hill, which has taught him “how to use tools, solve problems and work with other people.” He added that he and seven other Sugar Hill members now hope to open their own community-run bike shop when they are older.
“When New Mexico invests in programs like this, you’re not only paying for an outdoor experience — you’re investing in young people who could become the mechanics, guides, business owners, trail workers and community leaders of the future,” Lester said. 
Sen. Linda López (D-Albuquerque) praised Lester, calling him a “leader” and said she “looks forward to seeing what we can do to make sure that $10 million is recurring” during the next legislative session.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Hotline available to help NH voters with disabilities access ballots on Election Day
text:
Accessible voting machines are required in in all New Hampshire elections. (Photo by Bruce Bennett/Getty Images)By law, New Hampshire polling locations are required to take certain measures to make voting accessible to people with disabilities.
In an effort to help ensure those measures are taken, the Disability Rights Center of New Hampshire has created a hotline for people with disabilities who encounter problems while attempting to cast their ballots.
Most notably, the locations are required to let people use accessible machines specifically designed for blind people who can’t see a paper ballot or people with physical disabilities that prevent them from filling in the ballot or getting into a polling booth.
“Voting is a fundamental right, and our hotline is here to make sure that voters with disabilities can exercise that right,” James Ziegra, a DRC staff attorney, said in a press release.
On Election Day, Nov. 3, disabled voters in New Hampshire can reach the organization’s Election Day Hotline by calling 603-410-5200. Callers can ask questions or seek legal support on a range of voting issues, the DRC said, including:

Using the accessible voting system
What to do if a polling place isn’t accessible
How to request accommodations
Reporting unfair treatment or voter intimidation at the polls
Understanding and exercising rights under laws like the 2002 Help America Votes Act or the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act.

Voters across New Hampshire will cast ballots for governor, Congress and State House positions on an Election Day that could tip the balance of power in both Washington, D.C., and Concord.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Friends’ Snapchat messages surged with worries about Nolan Wells
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Over 200 pages of Snapchat messages pulled from the cellphone of Nolan Xavier Wells have only fueled questions surrounding what led to his death on Horn Island. 
The forensic phone extraction by Garrett Discovery covers messages sent within nearly 30 group chats between July 4 and July 26. The 18-year-old and his friends communicated primarily on Snapchat and other social media apps like Instagram, which is why investigators focused on the app. Wells’ body was discovered July 6.  
The recovered Snapchat messages provide a glimpse into how Wells’ friends tried to reconstruct where he was and who he was with. Some also mention the presence of what they described as “sketchy” characters on the island that day. 
After Wells died, messages in the groups turned from words of support to anger over social media speculation and criticism directed at lawyers representing Wells’ parents. Some of the national and online attention led some group chat members to express concerns about their own safety. 
The release of the Snapchat messages and GPS from Wells’ phone came days after a Jackson County grand jury declined to indict anyone for the Ocean Springs native’s death, concluding the condition of his body was consistent with drowning despite the lack of water found in his lungs, stomach and throat. 
National civil rights attorney Ben Crump and team members have presented more information such as an independent autopsy that highlighted injuries that the state noted but did not explain. They have also called for federal investigators to step in. 
In the report, Garrett redacted phone numbers and Snapchat usernames that identify senders in the group chats, but forensic investigators identified at least 200 distinct users. 
Mississippi Today reviewed the messages and organized them chronologically across all groups rather than individual group chats. Below is the start of messages friends sent directly to Wells checking in on him and asking if he needed help, which continued through the early morning of July 5. 
Wells was not able to read any of the messages because his phone was left on the boat that headed from the barrier island back to the Coast on the afternoon of July 4. His parents reclaimed the phone from his friends and later turned it over to the forensic investigators. 
‘You scaring me dude’
Wells told his friends he would get a ride back to the mainland on a different boat. He was reported missing the night of July 4, and the next day law enforcement, his family, volunteers and others began their search by water, land and air. 
Direct messages sent through Snapchat show how people began to worry. Some showed anger toward the people who took Wells to the island but did not return with him.
“If (you) bring someone on boat (you) make sure they fucking get back on,” wrote one person wrote in “thevapersofgtv” group text, which did not appear to include anyone from the boat.
The messages continued throughout the early morning of July 5, showing a mix of worry and best wishes. 
People asked Wells to text or call them back and offered prayers of safety. They told him to tell them where he was so they could come get him. Others told Wells they loved him. 
The messages picked up later in the morning with people mentioning that Wells had been reported missing, and they were more insistent about needing to hear back from him. 
“You scaring me dude I’m seeing and hearing a lot of stuff about you going missing can’t (lose) you bro,” one person wrote just before 10 a.m. 
Next are the group messages members traded July 5, the day after Wells was last seen. 
‘Has anyone seen Nolan yet’
One of the earliest messages about Wells was in the “Supa Senior Guyz” group chat at 6:15 a.m. As the morning progressed, other group chat members began to ask similar questions, including whether Wells got a ride off the island and who he interacted with throughout the day. 
Just before noon, people from multiple group chats said things seemed suspicious, but they also held out hope. Wells wasn’t the type of person “to get left,” someone wrote from the “WCBIA” group chat. Another person from “thevapersofgtv” chat said if he were on land he would’ve called someone. 
“(He’s) gotta be shlumped somewhere (right now) hopefully,” someone wrote in the “Supa Seniors” group. 
People from at least two groups chats wondered why Wells’ phone was left on the boat that departed without him. 
Group messengers told each other to look at their Snapchat memories and phone camera roll to see if Wells was in the background or if there was anything they could glean. 
Several people across different group chats asked about a girl Wells was seen with, which is in line with what his friends reported to law enforcement. 
The “Supa Seniors” group members traded messages about two “sketchy looking” people nearby at Horn Island who they believed were ex-felons. One said their father had to walk a woman who knew the men to her boat. Another responded that sheriff’s deputies told their dad that the men were people “you wouldn’t want to be left alone with,” especially if alcohol was involved.
By the afternoon of July 5, people in a few group chats said they had been contacted by law enforcement about Wells’ disappearance. They encouraged each other to “stick to what you know” and share what they could.
“(The police) are just trying to help Nolan, so be as cooperative as possible,” someone wrote in the “Supa Senior Guyz” group.
‘We’ll get through this together’
The morning of July 6, the Jackson County Sheriff’s Department said a body was found around Horn Island by a National Park Service ranger matching Wells’ description, leading to messages in the group chat expressing anxiety and, again, hope that it wasn’t Wells. 
Members of the group chats told others they loved them and that Wells loved them, too. They offered each other support and spoke highly about their friend. A few shared Bible verses or prayers. 
“Nolan was the most nice and caring guy we knew. He’s in a better place now and we’ll get through this together,” said one message sent July 6 in the “Supa Seniors” group around 10:15 a.m., before the body had been identified. 
“I wish I could help his family (right now),” a person in “thevapersofgtv” group wrote around 11:30 a.m.
Seconds later, in the same group, someone wrote: “I feel so bad bro.”
By noon, Wells’ parents announced that the body found on the island was his. 
As news spread across the state, nation and online, public discussion and social media chatter ramped up. The tone of some of the group chat messages took a turn. 
Members of multiple group chats had already complained about social media attention on Wells’ disappearance and death, calling the speculation lies and slander meant to provoke them. 
Through Snapchat, people in the group chats shared clips, posts and other information about Wells’ death that they found problematic. One member of the “thevapersofgtv” said people online were “(just) stirring up mess” and another person replied that “anything along that topic is dividing everyone.”
Intertwined with that displeasure were comments about race. Members from different group chats noted a focus on how Wells was Black and only his white friends made it home, and the idea was circulating on social media that white people in Ocean Springs were racist. 
“If they knew how much we love him, they wouldn’t say that,” one sender wrote in the “OS + BTown” chat the evening of July 5.
Several of the group chat participants criticized how Wells’ parents were working with Crump. A week after his death, members of the “Supa Seniors Guyz” called Crump someone who “does his job for the wrong reasons” and “hides behind the wall of being an ‘activist.’”
“It’s almost like their brainwashing Nolan’s parents and taking advantage of them while (they’re) overwhelmed with grief,” a member of that chat said about the legal team on July 14, a week after Wells’ parents hired Crump and joined them in several news conferences. 
Some also talked about taking precautions, such as limiting communication beyond friends and law enforcement and digital safety by turning off locations, blocking calls and ignoring messages on various social media apps. 
To date, some who have accused Wells’ friends of playing a role in his disappearance and death have been threatened with legal action. Three of Wells’ friends filed a federal defamation lawsuit against NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens over a social media post. Those making death threats to people linked to Wells’ death investigation are facing charges in federal court. 
One said in “thevapersofgtv” group chat that Wells’ case had grown bigger than that of Aubreigh Wyatt, another case that put Ocean Springs in the center of online and social media conversation. In 2023, Wyatt, 13, committed suicide after years of alleged bullying by classmates. Her mother took to social media to share her daughter’s story and pursue legal action that is still active.
Weeks after Wells died, some of the members of the group chat continued to talk among themselves, following updates including Wells’ funeral and news conferences hosted by Crump. 
“Supa Seniors” group members discussed whether they should attend the funeral with their Black friends “to send a message to the media.” 
It’s not clear whether they attended, but the day of the funeral, one group member called the offer of the $150,000 reward announced during Wells’ service “a disservice … and so ignorant.”
Wells’ direct messages also captured longer, thoughtful words recounting memories, his impact on their lives and wishes for him to rest in peace. One person went further and called for justice. 
“(You) and your family deserve justice. I’m praying you get everything you deserve that wrong will be shown and that if anyone did something to hurt you that they will be accounted for and punished,” they wrote July 7. “You deserve everything good out of this situation and I pray that God will reveal that.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Bird flu detected in Iowa commercial flock for first time nearly a year
text:
Bird flu has been detected in a Sac County, Iowa, commercial turkey flock. (Photo by Stephen Ausmus/USDA)A case of highly pathogenic avian influenza has been detected in a commercial turkey flock of approximately 44,400 birds in Sac County, according to the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship. 
While the HPAI H5N1 outbreak has been ongoing since February 2022, Iowa has not reported an outbreak of the bird flu in a commercial flock since December 2025. The state has reported seven outbreaks of the virus in backyard, mixed species or game bird flocks in 2026. 
Iowa has had more total birds affected by the bird flu than any other state since the start of the outbreak, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for Sac County Wednesday after IDALS’s announcement. The disaster proclamation allows state and department resources to be more easily deployed to help contain and monitor the outbreak, which typically requires dispatching the affected flock and disposing of the dead birds. 
IDALS is encouraging producers and backyard flock owners to “continue bolstering” biosecurity measures to protect their flocks. HPAI is a viral disease that can travel in wild birds and infect wild and domestic birds. Instances of the virus typically rise during bird migration seasons. 
Poultry producers must report possible cases of the bird flu to IDALS and should contact their veterinarians if they suspect birds with the virus. Some clinical signs include a sudden increase in bird deaths, lethargy, decreased egg production, swelling of head, difficulty breathing, thin-shelled or misshapen eggs and diarrhea. 
Poultry and egg products remain safe to eat and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, continue to rate the public health risk of bird flu as low as there is no known person-to-person spread.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Small Business Administration loan program available to WV residents affected by August flood
text:
Many streets on Charleston, West Virginia's West Side, including Greendale Drive, experienced severe flooding on Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)West Virginians affected by severe storms and flooding in August still have time to apply for federal assistance through the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Disaster Recovery.
The federal government approved a disaster declaration for Kanawha, Fayette and Harrison counties in West Virginia after severe storms Aug. 14 through 18 caused flooding and damage. 
The Office of Disaster Recovery works alongside the Federal Emergency Management Agency to offer low-interest loans to those affected after a presidential disaster declaration. 
“What that means is those people, whether they’re residents, business owners, renters or nonprofits, are eligible for the full breadth of SBA’s disaster relief program or disaster assistance program,” said Patty Hartman, a public affairs officer for the Office of Disaster Recovery.
SBA’s program differs from FEMA in that it’s a loan program. Loans start at 3% for homeowners and 4% for business owners, and can be carried for up to 30 years, Hartman said. 
“The purpose is so that it’s not a heavy burden,” Hartman said. “If you’re trying to put your home or your business back together from the physical damage that was suffered from a disaster, and your insurance company won’t cover it, or won’t cover all of it, or maybe you don’t have insurance, this allows you to try to put the pieces back together without it being too heavy of a burden.”
In the three counties with a disaster declaration, affected residents are eligible for physical damage loans and economic injury disaster loans.
Counties that are adjacent to Kanawha, Fayette and Harrison counties are eligible for the SBA’s economic injury disaster loan program. Those counties include: Barbour, Boone, Clay, Doddridge,  Greenbrier, Jackson, Lewis, Lincoln, Marion, Nicholas, Putnam, Raleigh, Roane, Summers, Taylor,  Upshur and Wetzel.
The economic injury disaster loan program is for small businesses, agricultural cooperatives, and nonprofits that had economic injury from the storms but weren’t directly hit. 
“(For instance if) they couldn’t get their product to or from a primary county, or they couldn’t get their staff to or from a primary county, and they suffered business losses as a result of that, and they need to recoup that money, they can apply for an economic injury disaster loan,” Hartman said. 
Applications can be completed online at sba.gov/disaster. People can call the SBA at 800-659-2955 or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for assistance.
For in-person help, residents and businesses can stop by or make an appointment at the Business Recovery Center, 1116 Smith Street in Charleston. The Recovery Center is open from 9 a.m. until 6 p.m. Monday through Friday.
Affected businesses and homeowners in primary counties have until Dec. 7 to apply for help with physical damage. The deadline for the economic injury program is July 7.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri marijuana businesses await IRS rules on promised federal tax relief
text:
Flora Farms Stateline dispensary in Pineville (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).Missouri marijuana businesses had reason to celebrate in April when the federal officials moved medical marijuana into a less restrictive category of controlled substances.
The federal order could also set marijuana companies on a path to substantial federal tax savings. For years, federal law has prevented many cannabis businesses from deducting ordinary expenses — including employee salaries, rent and other costs — when calculating their federal taxes.
But months after the change, Missouri businesses still don’t know exactly how to claim those savings, especially if they sell both medical and recreational marijuana.
That uncertainty was a key topic this month on the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation’s DCR OutLoud podcast, where leaders of the Missouri Cannabis Trade Association said they’re waiting for federal tax officials to explain how the new rules will work.
“Not only is the cannabis industry here in Missouri one of the most regulated industries, but it’s also one of the most taxed,” said Andrew Mullins, executive director of the association.  
The federal tax rule at the center of the debate is known as Section 280E. It generally prevents businesses that sell certain federally prohibited drugs from deducting everyday business expenses. This prohibition results in an effective income tax rate on marijuana businesses of as high as 80%, compared to the standard federal corporate rate of 21%. 
Missouri already allows licensed marijuana businesses to deduct those expenses on their state income tax returns, but the federal restriction has remained in place.
The April order moved marijuana regulated under state medical licenses into Schedule III but left recreational marijuana in Schedule I. That leaves businesses that sell both types of cannabis with a difficult question: How much of their spending can they deduct?
“Certainly they’re all very anxious to see if relief is on the way and if we’re going to see that guidance from the IRS that basically directs what they can do…” Mullins said. 
In late September, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and Internal Revenue Service listed Section 280E guidance among their priorities for the coming fiscal year, which runs through September 2027. But the list includes more than 100 other tasks.
Amy Moore, director of the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation, said the federal order creates a particular challenge for states such as Missouri, where many businesses handle medical and recreational sales under the same license.
“In our state, the difference between medical and just adult-use consumer product really only comes into play at that moment of sale when a particular tax rate is applied,” Moore said on the podcast. “But that [Department of Justice] order seems to be really organized around medical marijuana.”
Drew Lammert, chair of the trade association’s government affairs committee, said businesses may have to make their own decisions about how to divide expenses between medical and recreational sales while they wait for federal guidance.
Lammert is also the co-founder of High Fidelity Brands, where he says medical marijuana sales make up only 10% of the company’s business. 
“We are excited, but there’s also those questions of the unknowns,” he said, “and what does that mean for the 90% of adult use sales out there.”
 Separating the weed

Missouri issues what it calls “comprehensive licenses,” allowing businesses to serve both medical marijuana patients and recreational customers.
At cultivation facilities, plants also aren’t separated into medical and recreational categories as they grow.
“That is the beauty of the comprehensive license,” Lammert said. “There’s a lot of burden taken away with trying to track two separate systems, medical versus adult use.”
That arrangement makes operating a business simpler. But it could make the new federal tax rules harder to apply.
If a company grows the same plants, uses the same staff and operates out of the same buildings to supply both medical patients and recreational customers, it must determine which costs belong to its medical business — the part that may qualify for federal tax deductions.
“At retail, it’s simple,” Lammert said. “The person is either purchasing as a medical patient or purchasing as an adult-use consumer. But it gets a little more complicated when you go upstream to manufacturers and cultivators.”
Illicit Farms manufacturing and cultivation facility in Kansas City (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).
Lammert said his team has considered using the percentage of dispensary sales made to medical patients to estimate how much of the company’s growing and manufacturing costs should count toward its medical business.
“These are just some of the things that I think we’re going to have to figure out if we don’t get any further distinction or guidance as to how comprehensive licenses are going to be handled under this new rescheduling order,” he said. 
Moore said she had heard another possible approach: using the medical share of sales across Missouri’s entire cannabis market to determine how much of each company’s expenses qualify.
“I imagine that some licensees that have a higher percentage of medical would not be particularly satisfied with that,” she said. “I certainly don’t have any answers on how this is going to go.”
The financial stakes could be substantial, Lammert said. 
“If all of a sudden our businesses are allowed to take those standard business deductions,” he said, “I can write off the 30 people we have at our corporate headquarters and all those salaries. The lease on our corporate office, all that now becomes deductible.”
 Preparing for tax season without answers

The Treasury Department and IRS said in April that they expect the rescheduling order to have “significant positive tax consequences” for medical marijuana businesses.
But Kevin Jednachowski, chief value officer of the Denver-based Mindtrix Accounting firm, told The Independent this month that companies need more than the federal order to file their tax returns – and it’s unclear when the IRS will get to the items on its to-do list.
“Items slip,” Jednachowski wrote in a blog post on his website. “Some never get issued. The guidance, when it comes, may be narrower than the statements that preceded it.”
Until federal officials explain how the new rules work, cannabis companies must decide how to plan for their tax bills.
“Here is where the uncertainty turns into dollars,” he said. “If you are a C corporation, your last 2026 estimated payment is due Dec. 15.”
If companies underpay, they’ll owe penalties and interest on top of the tax. But if they overpay, they might not see that money back from the IRS for a while. 
“There is no clean answer, and we are not going to pretend there is one,” Jednachowski said. “The position most operators can defend is to pay estimates on a basis you can support today, and document why.” 
Jednachowski recommends that businesses prepare three estimates of what they might owe in 2026.
The first would assume nothing has changed and that the business receives no tax relief. The second would estimate the savings from medical marijuana sales, using a reasonable method to divide costs between medical and recreational operations. The third would calculate the largest tax savings the company could reasonably justify.
Comparing those estimates would help companies understand how much money they might owe under different outcomes.
“For many operators that gap is large enough to affect payroll, vendor terms, or a planned build-out,” he said. “Know how big the gap is today. Do not discover it in March.”
He also recommends that companies start keeping detailed records of the costs tied to their medical operations, including employee time, facilities, inventory and fees. They should document how they divide shared expenses and keep the information supporting those decisions.
That way, if federal officials eventually set different rules, businesses can adjust their calculations and explain how they arrived at their original figures.
“If new guidance prescribes a different approach, you can adjust and show why,” he said. “If it doesn’t, you already have a documented position. Almost every scenario depends on being able to say which dollars belong to which side of the business.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Mass deportation is diverting money that could be used for healthcare, other needs
text:
Over a hundred demonstrators gather outside of Minneapolis-St. Paul Airport to protest deportation flights that regularly fly out of MSP Wednesday, Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)We work quickly on our feet every day as parents to keep our children protected and healthy. So I’ll never forget the day I stood speechless in my kitchen, holding the letter declaring my daughter with Type 1 diabetes no longer had health insurance. My heart sank. I had no idea how we would pay for the daily medications she needed to survive. 
Too many families like mine carry the burden of financial hardship. While these challenges are hard to overcome, the economic policies we’ve seen during the second term of Donald Trump’s presidency don’t make it any easier. These policies have made life unaffordable — from feeding our families and putting gas in the tank to paying for doctor’s visits and medicine. Instead of helping lower costs, Trump is helping billionaires make their next billion, while forcing taxpayers to fund a mass deportation plan that sent shockwaves through our state and worsened the fear that so many were already experiencing. 
Policies that cut healthcare funding while raising gas and grocery prices put more Minnesotans in danger of financial ruin. Watching federal leaders prioritize unwanted mass deportations sickens me, especially because I know firsthand the importance of affordable health insurance. 
My daughter was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes in the early 2000s. When my daughter got her diagnosis, our family did not have health insurance. It was a horrific trifecta: My husband at the time made too much for state healthcare, his employer did not provide a group plan and we could not afford to buy private insurance. For the first year, we were lucky to enroll in a state program that helped pay for prescriptions for children with chronic diseases. 
About a year later, I found myself in the kitchen reading that letter: The state program had shut down, and they had no resources or recommendations on what to do next. Despite living in Rochester, which is home to some of the world’s best doctors, I worried about how we would now access her lifesaving medications without insurance. 
People with diabetes know that medical treatment is not optional. This was before Minnesota instituted price caps on insulin. We had no choice but to empty our savings as we fought to cover the exorbitant costs of insulin, supplies and doctor’s visits. The accumulating cost of medical bills and prescriptions meant that other bills came second. Years later, I found a new job that provided insurance for our family, but it was too late to recover. We lost our house and went bankrupt. 
Given the many needs of our people and after what I’ve gone through, I was infuriated to discover that across Minnesota, over $4.4 billion of our taxes, or $2,050 per taxpayer, is going to fund mass deportations that have devastated our communities, according to a new calculator by the Economic Policy Institute. The tool determines how much each state is contributing to the over $268 billion we’re spending to separate families and take people from their productive, tax-paying jobs. 
I can’t stomach that parents are working extra shifts while their taxes go directly from their paychecks to fuel these operations. Mass deportations have an incalculable human toll, and we stand to lose $4.4 billion in taxpayer money that could be spent saving lives by keeping rural hospitals open, families fed and insured, and more. 
To give you some idea of the cost of mass deportation policies, the same money could fund 11,600 Minnesota nurses, medical care to 82,000 Minnesota veterans and Medicaid for 130,000 Minnesotans. 
These numbers are particularly alarming after Trump’s “One Big, Beautiful Bill” slashed the budget for lifesaving programs like Medicaid, the Affordable Care Act and SNAP to provide massive tax cuts for billionaires and large corporations. 
To the elected officials who have supported this, let our message ring clear: Our taxes should not foot the bill for mass deportation.
We have a responsibility to speak up when leaders have betrayed our trust. My daughter and my family deserved better, and now, many others are in similar shoes while our taxes fund ICE. I encourage everyone to speak to their friends and family about how Trump will always be in the business of helping the ultra-wealthy, while making us pay for it: with our homes, our health and our lives.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Anti-tax pledges — never a good idea
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Minnesota State Fair. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)During a recent debate, both U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and GOP House Speaker Lisa Demuth ruled out raising taxes if elected governor. 
Demuth said, “Tax hikes are absolutely off the table for me,” while Klobuchar added, “I have made clear I’m not going to increase taxes, and I would actually like to lower taxes.” 
In comments reminiscent of President George H.W. Bush’s infamously broken “read my lips” pledge, the candidates took a stance that current budget realities and recent history suggest is unrealistic. 
Just to begin with, the state tax code changes nearly every year, as lawmakers adjust rates, credits and exemptions, and some of those changes raise taxes. Just six months ago, conservative Lisa Demuth voted for tax increases included in the 2026 tax bill, which will raise $353 million in 2028-29 through conformity to federal tax changes.
More substantively, blanket anti-tax pledges overlook the foundational role that taxes play in shaping a fair and functional society. Taxes are how we pay for the schools, roads, hospitals and other public goods that every community relies on. Minnesota does have higher taxes than many other states, but we also get less revenue from fees and other non-tax sources, which is easier on working families because progressive taxes ask more of those who earn more, while flat fees cost everyone the same.
Anti-tax soundbites may work on a debate stage, but the Legislature has to pass a budget in the upcoming session, and the next governor shouldn’t take policy options off the table before it starts. 
The allure of an anti-tax message is understandable given both candidates’ desire to deliver on the broad promise of affordability, but the reality is that most pro-affordability policies would require more revenue, not less. 
The state government can’t set the price of groceries, but it can address rising costs in healthcare, housing, childcare and other areas through proactive public investment. With a looming $2 billion deficit, the state can scarcely balance its budget without additional revenue, let alone invest in new affordability initiatives.
Two unaffordable visions of affordability 
Demuth’s “Affordability Agenda” would cut taxes on property, car tabs, income, gas, Social Security benefits, tips and overtime. Four of those cuts alone — Social Security, overtime, tips and gas — would cost more than $1.5 billion in the 2028-29 budget, according to Department of Revenue estimates of similar bills. 
To offset those cuts, Demuth promises to direct her commissioners to find $1 billion in savings, plus another $1 billion from cracking down on fraud. That will be easier said than done, especially considering that her calculations are based on an unproven estimate of total fraud in Minnesota. 
Demuth’s cuts would put money back in taxpayers’ pockets in the short run, but they would erode public services like K-12 education, rural healthcare and basic infrastructure that lie at the foundation of functional communities. 
Klobuchar would aim to lower costs through direct investment in the needs of Minnesotans. Her plans include expanding the state’s reinsurance program that’s aimed at making health insurance cheaper, building more child care centers and creating a rural housing loan fund.
These investments could have substantial impacts on the cost of living, but they all cost money. Klobuchar says economic growth and a top-to-bottom audit of state government would help pay for them, but the immediate savings are unlikely to be enough to balance the budget while also making meaningful investments in these new programs. 
The cost of tax cuts
Apart from the vilification of taxation, one essential problem here is the separation of taxes from what they pay for. A tax cut may add a little to your paycheck, but the money comes out of the public services that we all rely on, and the costs will be felt elsewhere.
President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for example, will cut federal tax revenue by more than $5 trillion from 2025 to 2034. This cut is partially offset by more than $900 billion in Medicaid spending reductions that will result in as many as 140,000 Minnesotans losing coverage. This will endanger human lives and community welfare, and the costs will simply be felt elsewhere.
Minnesotans kicked off Medicaid will still receive care, only now they will get it in emergency departments rather than primary care clinics, with the cost passed on to the rest of us. One-quarter of the state’s hospitals are financially distressed, and many are already cutting services, leaving patients with longer trips and longer waits for care. Hospital leaders warn that the federal Medicaid cuts could push small-town hospitals to close.
There are direct costs as well. When the state cuts taxes or suppresses needed funding, as both Klobuchar and Demuth’s approach would require, local governments pick up the slack in the form of property taxes.
Cities today rely far more on property taxes than they did 30 years ago when state revenues and aid were both larger as a share of our state’s economy. General-purpose state aid has fallen from 27% of city budgets in 1996 to 9% in 2026, while the share from property taxes has risen from 32% to 52%. The trend continued this year, as local property tax levies across the state increased $873 million or 6.8%, from 2025. 
On top of worse public services and higher property taxes, anti-tax pledges rule out the investments that could bring costs down for everyone.
Change requires revenue 
Economic anxiety has become a top issue this fall. To address it, policymakers need to consider what is driving it and where state government has meaningful power to intervene. 
For most families, the pressure comes from a few large bills: housing, childcare, and healthcare. A tax cut doesn’t make a rent check, a day care bill or an insurance premium any smaller, and pushes the costs further down the line, onto property tax bills and the services families rely on.
What would significantly reduce this anxiety is better access to those basic needs. That is what Klobuchar’s agenda is driving at, but a pledge not to raise taxes leaves little room to deliver the results she wants.
In a more recent second debate, both candidates make a second pledge: To part ways with a broken status quo. Leaving it behind will cost money, and the next governor will need to be willing to raise it.

name: California
title: El director de la agencia ferroviaria de alta velocidad de California renuncia en medio de un escándalo por gastos de viaje
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El director ejecutivo de la autoridad ferroviaria de alta velocidad de California renunció el miércoles por la noche, alegando que necesita centrarse en “prioridades personales y familiares importantes”, según una copia de la renuncia enviada por correo electrónico y obtenida por CalMatters.
 “Esta no ha sido una decisión fácil, ya que dirigir la Autoridad ha sido uno de los capítulos más significativos y gratificantes de mi vida profesional”, escribió el director ejecutivo Ian Choudri.
El anuncio repentino se produce en medio de una reunión de dos días de la junta que supervisa el proyecto, la cual continúa el jueves. Se produce tras la turbulenta gestión de dos años de Choudri, marcada por problemas presupuestarios, retrasos en el proyecto, inquietudes sobre la transparencia y diversos escándalos, incluido el uso indebido de casi 600,000 dólares de dinero de los contribuyentes para viajes cuestionables de consultores de la autoridad ferroviaria.
 Bajo la dirección de Choudri, la autoridad también perdió 4 mil millones de dólares en fondos federales durante la administración del presidente Donald Trump, después de que la agencia incumpliera repetidamente los plazos estipulados en el acuerdo de financiación para la compra de trenes. Inicialmente, el estado demandó a Trump por la falta de fondos, pero retiró abruptamente la demanda en diciembre de 2025, alegando que Trump no era un socio fiable y recurriendo en su lugar a inversores privados.
 Choudri no respondió a un correo electrónico ni a un mensaje de texto de CalMatters solicitando comentarios el miércoles por la noche. Se desconoce cuándo será su último día de trabajo.
 El mes pasado, los investigadores estatales descubrieron que los consultores de la agencia ferroviaria viajaban en primera clase, solicitaban servicios de transporte premium y frecuentaban clubes nocturnos, salones de puros y restaurantes a costa de los contribuyentes, a veces a petición de Choudri. Muchos de estos viajes implicaban desplazarse a Folsom, el suburbio de Sacramento donde Choudri tiene una casa, en ocasiones fuera del horario laboral.
 A principios de este mes, la junta votó a favor de limitar la autoridad contractual de Choudri tras la investigación, exigiendo que el asesor legal interno dé su aprobación previa a los contratos inferiores a 25 millones de dólares.
 Según una fuente con autoridad que habló bajo condición de anonimato porque no estaba autorizada a hablar sobre el asunto, la junta ha estado sopesando medidas disciplinarias adicionales contra Choudri durante semanas, incluyendo un posible despido.
En 2008, los votantes de California aprobaron una emisión de bonos de 10,000 millones de dólares para construir un tren de alta velocidad que conectara San Francisco con Los Ángeles para el año 2020, con un costo proyectado de 45,000 millones de dólares. Sin embargo, el proyecto se estancó debido al aumento de los costos, las disputas legales y la incertidumbre en la financiación.
Según el último plan de negocios de la autoridad, el proyecto podría costar ahora entre 126,000 y 231,000 millones de dólares, con el tramo actual de 171 millas entre Merced y Bakersfield en construcción, y se espera que esté completamente terminado para 2040.
Según declaró Micah Flores, portavoz de la agencia, a CalMatters el mes pasado, la junta debía decidir en la reunión de esta semana si Choudri reunía los requisitos para recibir una posible bonificación de 25,000 dólares en función de su desempeño este año.
Según la portavoz de la agencia, Annie Parker, la remuneración de Choudri este año supera los 534,000 dólares.
 Sobrecostos, retrasos en los proyectos, desafíos legales
 Choudri fue contratado en agosto de 2024 tras décadas de experiencia en ingeniería de transporte, con proyectos de construcción de trenes de alta velocidad en Francia y España . Según Tom Richards, entonces presidente de la junta directiva, la contratación se debió en parte a su “sólido conocimiento de proyectos de transporte complejos”.
 Bajo la dirección de Choudri, la agencia ha continuado la construcción del tramo del Valle Central y está a punto de obtener la autorización ambiental del estado para los 800 kilómetros (500 millas) de ferrocarril planificados entre San Francisco y el sur de California. Newsom, un gran defensor del proyecto ferroviario, ha comprometido mil millones de dólares anuales del fondo estatal para el clima destinados al proyecto hasta 2045.
 Choudri también ha liderado los esfuerzos para reducir los costos de los contratos de consultoría, atraer inversiones privadas y agilizar la contratación, según declaró Mark Tollefson, jefe de gabinete de la autoridad ferroviaria, durante una presentación el miércoles en la que destacó los logros de Choudri. 
 Ian Choudri, director ejecutivo de California High Speed Rail, habla durante una conferencia de prensa sobre el proyecto de tren de alta velocidad en las instalaciones de Wasco Rail Yard en Wasco el 3 de febrero de 2026. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
El miércoles, la junta aprobó por unanimidad un contrato de 772.1 millones de dólares con la empresa alemana Siemens Mobility, Inc. para el diseño, la construcción y las pruebas de tres trenes bala de alta velocidad de siete vagones para el año 2030. La autoridad también pagará hasta 63.7 millones de dólares en aranceles e impuestos de importación, ya que los trenes se diseñarán y construirán en Alemania.
La votación se produce tres años después de que la agencia abriera por primera vez la licitación para seis trenes en agosto de 2023 para optar a más de 3,000 millones de dólares en subvenciones federales, antes de perder finalmente la financiación por incumplimiento de los plazos.
 En su carta de renuncia, Choudri afirmó sentirse orgulloso de haber transformado el proyecto.
 “Asumí un proyecto que enfrentaba desafíos importantes y serias dudas sobre sus perspectivas de éxito, y lideré su transformación en un programa exitoso”, escribió.
 Pero el proyecto ha seguido enfrentándose a importantes sobrecostes, retrasos en el cronograma y demandas judiciales.
 La agencia ferroviaria podría quedarse sin fondos para diciembre de 2027, advirtió la oficina del inspector general en julio. Mientras tanto, la autoridad no dejó claro en su último plan de negocios que ahora se espera que el segmento del Valle Central esté terminado para 2034 a un costo que probablemente supere los 40 mil millones de dólares, dijo el inspector general.
 La autoridad también basó su cronograma del proyecto en el supuesto de que lograría aprobar las propuestas legislativas que no consiguió impulsar este año.
 Para ahorrar dinero, la autoridad propuso reducir el tramo entre Merced y Bakersfield en 9 millas y trasladar la estación del centro de Merced a South Merced, en aparente violación de la ley estatal . También solicitó una exención de las regulaciones ambientales y buscó contratistas para la nueva ubicación, lo que provocó una demanda este mes por parte de la coalición del Valle Central, Community Alliance for a Sustainable Economy.
 “Esta impugnación se enmarca dentro de un patrón de comportamiento ilegal por parte de la HSRA: proponer la reubicación de la estación del centro de Merced y luego actuar como si dicha reubicación hubiera sido aprobada cuando no lo ha sido”, dice la denuncia. 
Los viajes cuestionables plagan a la autoridad
 Entre 2024 y 2026, empleados de cuatro empresas consultoras que trabajaban para la agencia de Choudri facturaron al estado viajes cuestionables a lugares como gimnasios, una discoteca, una sala de escape, un bar tiki y un salón de puros, según la investigación realizada el mes pasado por la oficina del inspector general que supervisa la agencia ferroviaria.
 Según el inspector general, muchos viajes estaban mal justificados, pero la agencia los reembolsaba sistemáticamente sin la debida verificación.
Un asesor legal viajó entre Denver y Sacramento 30 veces en un año, lo que le costó al estado 86,500 dólares en concepto de “tiempo de viaje” y 40,800 dólares adicionales en reembolsos.
 En una tensa reunión a principios de este mes, la junta los acusó de utilizar la agencia como una “alcancía”.
El miércoles , el personal de la autoridad informó que las empresas consultoras han pagado casi 1.3 millones de dólares en reembolsos a la agencia.
 El mes pasado, CalMatters solicitó acceso a la información pública para obtener las facturas de viaje cuestionables de la oficina del inspector general. La agencia solo proporcionó los registros de una empresa, Nossaman, argumentando que los registros de otros consultores están relacionados con auditorías o investigaciones y, por lo tanto, no es necesario divulgarlos públicamente según una ley reciente firmada por el gobernador Gavin Newsom.
 Los documentos publicados fueron censurados en gran medida tanto por la oficina del inspector general como por la agencia ferroviaria, que argumentaron que gran parte de la información está protegida por el privilegio de confidencialidad entre abogado y cliente.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Western Alaska voters asked to weigh familiar state House candidates with similar stances
text:
The Yukon-Kuskokwim hub of Bethel is seen from the air on July 13, 2015. It is the biggest community in sprawling Alaska House District 38, where voters are deciding whether to keep the current incumbent or return a previous lawmaker to office. (Photo by Rachel Loehman/USGS Alaska Science Center)In a tightly fought Alaska legislative race, voters in one of the state’s most rural districts will be choosing between familiar candidates in a contest unlikely to change the balance of power in the state House.
The leading candidates are current Rep. Nellie Jimmie of Toksook Bay and the incumbent she beat two years ago, former Rep. CJ McCormick of Bethel. Both are Democrats, so a victory by either is unlikely to change the balance of power in the legislature.
In the Aug. 18 primary, McCormick edged Jimmie, winning 32% of the vote to her 29%.
Also in the race is another familiar candidate, Willy Keppel of Quinhagak, running as a Republican. He has mounted legislative campaigns since 2002, and in the last election ran as a member of the Veterans Party of Alaska. He took 24% of the primary vote.
A fourth candidate, Joseph Amik of Napaskiak, ended his campaign on Monday, citing health reasons, and endorsed Jimmie. Another Democrat, he had won 14.7% of the primary vote.
Jimmie and McCormick have similar views on issues like fishery management, public safety, infrastructure needs and fiscal policy.
The one issue that differentiated the candidates in the last election — their positions on the controversial Donlin Gold mine proposed for the region’s uplands — no longer distinguishes them.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The project would be one of the largest open-pit gold mines in the world, providing revenues and jobs in what is currently one of the lowest-income regions in Alaska. It would also be an economic boon to Alaska Native corporations; the site is on land with surface rights owned by the village Kuskokwim Corporation and mineral rights owned by the regional Calista Corporation. Both corporations are owned by the region’s Yup’ik people.
But there is deep opposition to the mine among many in the region because of potential environmental harm, affecting salmon and natural resources at the heart of people’s diets, lifestyles and Indigenous cultures.
McCormick said he has always opposed the mine and that opposition seems to be growing in the region. That is a contrast to Jimmie’s position of neutrality in 2024.
“I think people want someone who will stick up against Donlin,” McCormick said during an interview last week at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. “I think there is a difference between saying you’re neutral and saying you’re against something, especially when, you know, there’s kind of momentum in one direction.”
Jimmie, in an interview during the AFN convention, said she is no longer neutral and now opposes the mine, as well. Her experience in the devastating storms in Western Alaska around ex-Typhoon Halong was the catalyst that changed her mind, she said.
“After Halong, we’re not the boss of the water. The water says how much it comes. The storms say when they’re going to come,” she said. “I can’t support a mine that doesn’t have a guaranteed 100% that it’s safe. Mining jobs cannot protect our fish, you know.”
Along with the ex-typhoon, a new supplemental environmental impact statement issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers helped turn her opinion against Donlin, she said. That environmental study, ordered by a federal court, described the potential damages of a large though unlikely breach of the 471-foot dam that Donlin’s developers propose to build to contain mine waste.
 

State Rep. Nellie Jimmie, D-Toksook Bay, stands in a corridor at the Dena’ina Civic and Convention Center in Anchorage on Oct. 24, 2026, during the ALaska Federation of Natives convention. She is dressed in a traditional kuspuk and wearing a scarf she knitted from qiviut, the soft and ultra-warm hair found on muskoxen. She hunted the musk ox as well, she said. The Arctic fox jewelry necklace she is wearing was made by a niece, she said. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The new supplemental environmental impact statement was released in draft form last month,  “which to me is so last minute,” Jimmie said. The Corps and U.S. Bureau of Land Management issued key construction permits to the mine in 2018.
Keppel, the Republican candidate, is also against the Donlin project.
“The first time I ran for office was in 2002 against Senator Lyman Hoffman, and I ran because I was opposed to Donlin mine. I’m still opposed to the Donlin mine. I’ll always be opposed to the Donlin mine,” he said at a Sept. 30 candidate forum broadcast on public radio station KYUK.
A non-Native, he has repeatedly criticized Calista and its leaders for supporting the Donlin project.
Gubernatorial candidates
While the Donlin mine controversy is a top issue in House District 38, it has not gotten much attention in the statewide campaign.
A rare mention came during an Oct. 19 forum in Anchorage, when a question about Donlin was posed to the two candidates attending the event: former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, D-Sika, and former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, a Republican.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he will defer to whatever is the consensus of the people in the region, where there are currently deep divides over Donlin.
“I can’t say I know the answer right now,” he said in a response to the Donlin question, posed at a Justice Organizing Interfaith Network candidates event held at St. Anthony Catholic Church in Anchorage.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he has had conversations with people both in favor and opposed and will continue those conversations. “Basically, my commitment would be to spend time in the region and hear the voices of the people in the region and get a sense of where they are. And that is a major variable for how I would respond as governor,” he said.
Bronson said he supports the mine “as long as it’s done correctly.”
“I think the mine is a good idea,” Bronson said at the forum. “We’re in a situation where we’re short on money. And the single best way to create wealth in the state is to extract. That’s going to create wealth.”
Another gubernatorial candidate, former Attorney General Treg Taylor, a Republican, is a strong supporter of the Donlin project, according to his campaign.
“Treg Taylor is definitely in favor of the Donlin Gold Mine. He believes it will provide good paying jobs in an area that needs these opportunities. It will benefit the area and Alaska greatly!” April Gettys, Taylor’s campaign manager, said by email.
A query to Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson about her position on Donlin did not receive a response. However, she has generally favored resource-extraction proposals in the state.
 

Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Dave Briondon at the Justice Organizing Interfaith Network (JOIN) gubernatorial candidate forum on Oct. 19, 2026, at St. Anthony Catholic Church in Anchorage. The candidates were asked about their positions on the Donlin Gold mine, a subject that has not been much discussed in the gubernatorial campaign. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Aside from the Donlin controversy, a top issue for the Yukon-Kuskokwim candidates and voters is heightened awareness of the challenges posed by natural disasters like Halong.
Jimmy said the region “went through one of the toughest times (with) the Halong disaster displacing 1,700 of my people — my cousins, my relatives, my friends I grew up playing sports with,” she said. Beyond the villages that were evacuated, other communities suffered severe damages, she said.
“My office has been working around the clock with our constituents, you know, making sure they get the right help,” she said.
McCormick said he supports a proposal by the Association of Village Council Presidents to set up what it has called a Western Alaska Public Safety Emergency Response System, an idea that grew out of the 2022 ex-Typhoon Merbok disaster and has now become more prominent in the wake of ex-Typhoon Halong.
“It is really top of mind for both people responding to that disaster, but I think also really being equipped when they inevitably come again, because I think it’s just part of the life out there,” he said.
Keppel, 72, differs sharply from his Democratic competitors on almost all issues except for the Donlin Gold mine.
He has spent much of his campaign attacking Democrats in general and Jimmie in particular. He claims legislative Democrats killed hopes for a massive natural gas pipeline project because they did not approve Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s plan to provide tax breaks to project sponsor Glenfarne.
He has criticized Democrats’ environmental policies. “The Democrats’ platform is they want to do away with oil and gas in Alaska,” he said in the KYUK forum. “I don’t know how the heck they plan on heating their houses. Fairy dust and solar panels are not going to cut it in Alaska.”
And he has hurled personal accusations against Jimmie, including a claim he made during the KYUK forum that she “had an emotional breakdown” at one point.
That statement drew a rebuke from moderator Evan Erickson of KYUK.
“That’s a derogatory comment, Willy, can you please just rein it in on that?” Erickson said.
It was not the first time Keppel, who is not Native, has made a questionable comment. Last year, in comments on a conservative talk radio program, Keppel said he would “counter” the Native voice in a district that is overwhelmingly Yup’ik.
“I really believe it’s going to take somebody from out here to be able to go in and counter the Native voice from Western Alaska that wants to continue what we have going,” he told Michael Dukes, the talk-show host.
Different personalities
For Yukon-Kuskokwim voters who can no longer distinguish candidates by their Donlin stances, decisions may come down to personalities.
 

CJ McCormick, a former state House member who is seeking to return to his seat, stands on the patio of the Dena’ina Civic and Convention Center on Oct. 22, 2016, during the Alaska Federation of Natives convention. McCormick, of Bethel, is a Democrat. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	McCormick, though only 29 years old, has several years of government experience. He served on the Bethel City Council, including as vice mayor, before becoming a state House representative in 2023.
Though not Native himself, he has experience working for tribal organizations, both the Yukon-Kuskokwim Health Corp. and the Association of Village Council Presidents.
Born and raised in Bethel, the region’s hub community, he does not believe his non-Native heritage will be a minus, he said.
“I don’t really think it’s about identity. I think it’s about who supports you and who is that you are,” he said. “I’m doing this because I know people that I respect want me to do this, not because of who I am.”
Jimmie, 47, had never served in elected office before becoming the region’s House member over the past two years. Her previous public service experience was as a local representative for the Alaska Village Electric Cooperative.
However, in the legislature she secured a position on the powerful House Finance Committee. The last Yup’ik representative on that committee, she noted, was Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, a former state legislator.
Of Yup’ik, Ojibwa and Lakota heritage, Jimmy practices a traditional Indigenous lifestyle. She is an accomplished artist and artisan, and she often wears traditional clothing and jewelry that she made herself or that relatives made.  
Amik, whose name will remain on the ballot, highlighted Jimmie’s Indigenous heritage when he endorsed her.
“I will be voting for Nellie Jimmie. We need a Yup’ik voice. And I endorse Nellie Jimmie for District 38,” he said in a Facebook message posted Monday.
Beyond policies and personalities, the campaign in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region is colored by rural Alaska conditions and culture.
Traveling around by plane is expensive, so alternatives are employed, such as river travel by boat, McCormick said.
On one boat trip from Bethel to the nearby village of Napakiak, McCormick brought along 200 burritos to serve to the locals.
“Thankfully, my mom knows some catering tricks, and so we were able to keep them warm,” he said.
Jimmie faces similar cost challenges, but she has also made some fun discoveries in her travels.
“The one thing I love about campaigning is when I go to any of the communities, the villages, it’s like I end up finding out somebody’s my relative. Like, ‘You’re my aunt. You’re my cousin,’” she said. “It’s just beautiful.”
The Donlin Gold mine camp site is seen from the air on June 23, 2025. The question of whether to build the huge mine and bring it into production is a hot-button issue in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
