title: Dolores Huerta “se mantuvo en la lucha” durante siete décadas, inspirando a generaciones de californianos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
En casi todas las etapas del movimiento de los trabajadores agrícolas, desde sus inicios organizándose en la huelga de la uva de Delano en 1965 hasta la ley de 1986 que concedió amnistía a casi 3 millones de inmigrantes indocumentados, Dolores Huerta estuvo presente.
 Huerta, de 96 años, falleció el miércoles en su casa en Bakersfield. Tan solo dos meses antes, había participado en una manifestación en las escalinatas del Capitolio estatal.
Los líderes políticos y sindicales de California la recuerdan como una incansable defensora de los derechos de los trabajadores agrícolas, quien acuñó el lema y grito de guerra de la Unión de Trabajadores Agrícolas: “Sí, se puede”. Cada año, el 10 de abril, California honra sus contribuciones declarando ese día como el Día de Dolores Huerta.
 “El liderazgo de Dolores en la lucha por un sindicato para los trabajadores agrícolas de California, la UFW, es solo una parte de su historia”, dijo Lorena González, presidenta de la Federación Laboral de California. “Dolores se mantuvo en la lucha por los trabajadores durante décadas”.
 Ella “demostró a generaciones de mujeres que tenían un lugar en este movimiento obrero”. 
 La líder de los Trabajadores Agrícolas Unidos (UFW), Dolores Huerta, en el centro, encabeza una manifestación junto a Howard Wallace, presidente de la sección de San Francisco de la UFW, a la izquierda, y María Elena Chávez, de 16 años, hija de César Chávez, a la derecha, en el distrito Mission de San Francisco, como parte de un boicot nacional en protesta por lo que la UFW describe como el uso peligroso de pesticidas en las uvas de mesa, el 19 de noviembre de 1988. Foto de Court Mast, AP.
 Su influencia aún se hace evidente en la forma en que California recuerda su propia historia: mientras el nombre de César Chávez se retira de los edificios universitarios y las calles de las ciudades de California tras las acusaciones surgidas a principios de este año de que Chávez agredió y violó a varias mujeres, incluida Huerta, activistas en Los Ángeles pidieron que el nombre de Huerta sustituyera al suyo.
 “No puedo imaginar por lo que ha pasado en los últimos meses”, dijo el gobernador Gavin Newsom a un grupo de periodistas el miércoles. “Las revelaciones sobre César y lo difícil que debe haber sido para ella en estos últimos cuatro meses… Simplemente tenemos que reconocer sus contribuciones, su energía, su pasión y su aporte a este mundo”.
 Incluso en sus últimos meses, Huerta siguió adelante.
 “En agosto, se unió al Centro de Políticas para Inmigrantes de California y a nuestros socios en las escalinatas del Capitolio estatal para luchar contra los recortes federales que privan de alimentos a familias, niños y jóvenes inmigrantes”, declaró Masih Fouladi, directora ejecutiva del Centro de Políticas para Inmigrantes de California. “Alzó la voz en defensa de los trabajadores agrícolas, quienes serían los más perjudicados, las mismas personas que alimentan a este estado”. 
 Dolores Huerta interviene en el evento de CalMatters titulado “Salud de los trabajadores agrícolas: ¿Cómo puede California proteger a sus trabajadores esenciales?”, celebrado en Bakersfield el 22 de febrero de 2024. Fotografía de Jules Hotz para CalMatters.
 Huerta desempeñó un papel fundamental en la finalización del programa Bracero en la década de 1960, que otorgaba a los trabajadores agrícolas mexicanos un estatus temporal en los Estados Unidos, descontándoles la comida y el alojamiento de su escaso salario y exponiéndolos además a productos químicos mortales.
 “Su labor de toda la vida fue empoderar a su comunidad para enfrentar y superar las injusticias, y ha dejado a los trabajadores agrícolas y a toda la comunidad latina más fuertes y organizados de lo que los encontró”, dijo la presidenta de la UFW, Teresa Romero. “El trabajo de Dolores sigue siendo tan importante ahora como siempre, y continúa con su ejemplo e inspiración. El mayor homenaje posible a su vida es que su labor de organización continúe”.
 La familia de Huerta dijo que seguirán adelante con los planes para reconocer y celebrar su increíble vida y legado.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In three-way Kansas secretary of state race, deep disagreements over election administration
text:
From left, secretary of state candidates Jennifer Day, Scott Morgan and Pat Proctor speak at a Sept. 24, 2026, candidate forum in Salina. (Photos by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — In the race to become the state’s top elections officer, Kansas voters can pick from a Democrat who spent five months in the Legislature five years ago, a former Republican who is trying to establish an alternative party, and a Republican legislator whose campaign focuses on the fear of noncitizens voting.
The three are running to replace Secretary of State Scott Schwab, who pursued the GOP nomination for governor rather than seek a third term.
There’s Jennifer Day, a Johnson County Democrat, and Scott Morgan, director of the United Kansas party, who both said in interviews that Kansas elections are secure and that a constitutional amendment requiring voters be citizens is redundant because the requirement is already in the constitution.
And there’s Rep. Pat Proctor, a Leavenworth Republican who tilts against an imaginary and undefined “axis of ballot harvesting,” led the charge to put the constitutional amendment on the November ballot, and refuses to engage with Kansas Reflector reporters when questioned at campaign events or contacted by phone or email.
“There’s not a chance in hell I’m answering questions for your paper,” he said when approached at a September forum in Salina.
 
Jennifer Day, the Democratic nominee for Secretary of States, answers questions during an Oct. 22, 2026, interview. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Day’s background
Day said she came to Kansas to visit family, fell in love and decided to stay.
She has lived here for 30 years. She said she worked as an executive assistant before opening her own business in 2013 for real estate investment and interior design.
In 2020, she won election to the Kansa House by 62 votes. She then left the seat after her first legislative session when she moved out of the district.
She said she was motivated to run for secretary of state because of concerns about Proctor’s initiatives as chair of the House Elections Committee to restrict voting rights — some of which have landed the state in court. The Secretary of State’s Office should be “quiet and boring,” she said.
“The majority of Kansans really appreciate leaders that are not looking to make headlines and are really just wanting to do the job,” she said.
She said her “hands-on experience” of working elections will help her connect with county clerks across the state.
“I think it’s important that we elect someone to this position who has that disposition that is able to listen and connect well with legislators, voters, our elected officials across the state, and to collaborate in a way that is going to be impactful and not lead to litigation for the state in Kansas,” she said.
 
Scott Morgan, the executive director of United Kansas, the Free State Party, says the merger of two centrist political organizes will give voters an alternative to the Republican and Democratic parties in Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
Morgan’s background
Morgan is a fifth-generation Kansan who worked for U.S. Sens. Nancy Kassebaum and Bob Dole, and was Dole’s chief counsel when he ran for president in 1988. He also served as chief counsel for Gov. Mike Hayden.
In 1990, he was the GOP nominee for the 2nd District congressional seat, losing to Democratic U.S. Rep. Jim Slattery with 37% of the vote. He also challenged then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach in the 2014 GOP primary and received 35% of the vote. As his campaign website says: “Sure, he lost that one too. He is consistent.”
He managed to win two terms on the Lawrence school board along the way.
In recent years, Morgan said, he has been working to find a political home for those who aren’t being served by either of the major parties. He hopes to win enough of the vote to gain recognition for the fledgling United Kansas party.
“It’s just providing a choice is all it really is,” Morgan said. “We are an alternative. We’re trying to be the center-left and center-right, forming a coalition, instead of with the extremes.”
He said there is a “genuine hunger” among voters for “something different.”
As for the complaint typically lobbed at third-party candidates: “I’ve grown very wary of the whole ‘you’re a spoiler’ thing,” Morgan said. “I get that from hardcore Democrats a lot, and I think they really misunderstand the math in this thing. It’s not fair, because you’re not a spoiler. You’re a choice.”
He said a lot of the people who vote for him either would not have cast ballots for the office or picked the Republican, based on his background.
 
Kansas Rep. Pat Proctor prepares to speak ahead of President Donald Trump’s rally Oct. 19, 2026, at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Constitutional amendment
Proctor said during a recent Statehouse news conference, to which Kansas Reflector was not invited, that when people vote, they exercise the “political power that used to be exercised by a gun.”
“We’re all endowed by our creator — not government, by our creator — with the inalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness,” he said. “But we’re all so darn different, and that’s why it’s never worked before. That’s why no nation has ever been able to organize under principles.”
He continued: “Our founders found the secret sauce. They created the social contract that we still adhere to today that says, ‘Hey, every couple years we’re going to get together and we’re going to pick our leaders.’ Before 1776, the way people picked leaders is they picked up guns and they shot the other side until one side won and that person was in charge. The founders rediscovered the idea of the ballot box.”


The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787, and governments since at least ancient Greece have conducted elections.
“If we throw open the gates and let anybody exercise that political power, whether they have sworn to those principles or not, we’re not going to have a country anymore,” Proctor said. “We’re going to fly apart.”
Proctor said he started hearing concerns about noncitizen voting a couple of years ago and decided to look into the matter.
“You could have knocked me over when I found out that nowhere in our Kansas Constitution does it actually say you must be a citizen to vote,” Proctor said. “The way our constitution is written, it says ‘every citizen can vote,’ which is not ‘only citizens can vote.’ And so I thought, hey, that’s low-hanging fruit. We can fix that right now.”
Here’s what the state constitution currently says: “Every citizen of the United States who has attained the age of eighteen years and who resides in the voting area in which he or she seeks to vote shall be deemed a qualified elector.”
Here’s the proposed change on the November ballot: “No person shall be deemed a qualified elector unless such person: (1) Is a citizen of the United States; (2) has attained the age of eighteen years; and who (3) except as provided in subsection (b) or (c), resides in the voting area in which he or she such person seeks to vote.”
Amii Castle, who teaches constitutional law at the University of Kansas, wrote in a column for Kansas Reflector that the constitutional already requires voters to be citizens. She also warned that the proposed amendment could give Republicans a basis to reopen the legal fight over a state law that required people to produce a birth certificate or otherwise prove their citizenship before they could register to vote.
Federal courts determined the law was unconstitutional following a years-long legal battle. Kobach failed to prove his bogus claims about widespread voter fraud or show how the proof of citizenship requirement would solve a hypothetical problem. By requiring people to produce a birth certificate, the law blocked more than 35,000 eligible voters from registering.
Proctor pointed to the federal ruling as he complained about Castle’s column during his news conference.
“Nothing that we can do in the Kansas Constitution will, in any way, allow us to implement documentary proof of citizenship,” Proctor said.
He dismissed the argument that illegal voting is extraordinarily rare. He pointed to the conviction this year of the Republican mayor of Coldwater, who had a green card but wasn’t a citizen, as proof that immigrants sometimes vote. He said Kobach, now the attorney general, is prosecuting three additional noncitizens for voting.
“People will say, ‘Well, golly, it’s only four.’ I would just ask, ‘How many is too many?’ I would contend that one is too many because every time a noncitizen votes, they are canceling out the vote of a valid Kansas voter,” Proctor said.
Morgan said he was unimpressed with Proctor’s argument for the amendment.
“We know that thousands of actual citizens were denied the right to vote because they didn’t have the right paperwork, and all of that was to protect against a supposed threat of noncitizens voting, of which there are a minuscule amount,” Morgan said.
 
Rep. Pat Proctor, chair of the House Elections Committee, listen to testimony during a Jan. 27, 2026, hearing on legislation that adds restrictions to delivering advance ballots. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Election security
Morgan scoffed at Republicans who complain about election security, as many have since Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election fair and square.
In Kansas, Morgan pointed out, Republicans have won every election but one — in 1948, for a two-year term — for secretary of state since 1898.
He said the office needs to provide technical advice to county officials, especially smaller ones that don’t have the budget. He said the state could improve its election audits, and add risk assessment audits. The biggest vulnerability, he said, would be the list of registered voters, known as the “voter roll.”
“It’s just a gaping back door to the whole thing, and that is what really needs to be strengthened and can be strengthened,” Morgan said. “That is a solvable problem. It just requires will. But everybody’s worried about security, so I assume they’re willing to put a little bit of money toward that. Otherwise, you’re really just blowing hot wind.”
He said “ballot harvesting” — Proctor’s term for volunteers who deliver mail-in ballots — isn’t a real problem.
“It sounds scary,” he said, but it is really Kansans “just trying to help” their older friends and neighbors.
Day said she has heard concerns that people could somehow print ballots, randomly fill them out and turn them in.
“As I explained to my neighbor, you would have to know their driver’s license number. You would have to know how they sign their name,” she said.
“Harvesting — quote unquote — it just is not a thing,” she added.
Others have suggested, without evidence, that people who collect ballots on behalf of voters could throw them away instead of delivering them to the election office.
Proctor supported legislation that limited the number of ballots an individual could turn in to 10, and he proposed further restrictions earlier this year.
“There’s always these conspiracies, but I’ve just never seen them,” Morgan said. “Conspiracies are a lousy thing to make public policy on.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 7 is fair because it spreads the burden of building housing
text:
ON THE FIRST day of my undergraduate housing policy class, I show my students a headline from the satirical website McSweeney’s that encapsulates the problem at the heart of the Commonwealth’s affordability crisis. “Housing should be affordable,” it reads, “except when I sell my house for a million dollars.” 
Nobody wants denser housing built only near them, so no city or town wants to be the only one that builds. Spread McSweeney’s logic across all 351 cities and towns in Massachusetts, and you get a statewide housing shortage. The only way to break the zoning logjam is a statewide mandate, and Question 7 is a good first step. Anyone concerned about housing affordability should vote for it. 
Economists broadly agree that housing in “superstar cities” and regions like Greater Boston is unaffordable primarily because we have not built enough. Demand for living in thriving, dynamic, and innovative places like Massachusetts far outstrips supply. The shortage shows up as a gap between the cost of a house and the cost of building it, implying that house prices and rents are high because regulations have made buildable land artificially scarce. 
One such regulation is particularly notorious: minimum lot sizes. Localities have used large-lot requirements for over a century to limit density and keep the riffraff out. Among areas zoned for single-family homes, 66 percent nationwide have minimum lot requirements above 5,000 square feet and 7 percent require more than half an acre. These regulations are more common in affluent areas with fewer minorities. By limiting land supply, they drive up housing costs for everyone. 
Question 7 would require that single-family homes be allowed on any lot of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and access to public water and sewer. This would let market forces gradually densify cities and towns as developers subdivide large lots, pushing down housing costs. Both nationwide analyses and local policy studies provide strong evidence that rolling back minimum lot sizes reduces house prices and rents over time. Houston, for instance, cut minimums in 1998, leading to a boom in townhomes that added thousands of homes to supply. 
Opponents of Question 7, led by the Massachusetts Municipal Association, cry foul because it limits the autonomy of local governments, which they argue are best positioned to enact thoughtful zoning laws. They also claim that towns will voluntarily implement other, better policies. 
This is exactly the thinking that has led to our affordability crisis: We have failed to build because the balance has tipped too far toward local control. Cities and towns limit construction to free-ride on housing and density built elsewhere, so nobody builds enough housing.  
The resistance to the MBTA Communities Act shows that municipalities will not meaningfully relax zoning on their own, even with significant carrots and sticks. And when a law leaves wiggle room, towns exploit it: Marblehead complied with the law by rezoning a golf course that will never be redeveloped.  
The best way to overcome this is a simple bright-line policy that spreads the burden of density statewide through an across-the-board limit on lot sizes. This approach has gained momentum in recent years, with several states adopting similar limits. 
Question 7 is a modest step in this direction. It will not build a monstrous ziggurat next door. Instead, it will subtly change neighborhood character by allowing a few smaller single-family homes on land that would otherwise hold one large house.  
Some may argue that the 5,000-square-foot limit is too small and too one-size-fits-all. But any bright line is imperfect, and one that spares more towns would build far less of the housing we need and would not spread the burden. Furthermore, the water and sewer requirement means that Question 7 will not affect rural areas. Finally, the towns where Question 7 would have the greatest impact are precisely those that have used minimum lot sizes to avoid doing their share. They should not get a pass for their past resistance. 
Massachusetts needs more housing if we want to remain a place where smart, talented people want to move. Question 7 is a simple way to stop the zoning race to the bottom among cities and towns and force everyone to take on a bit more density for the Commonwealth’s greater good. Everyone worried about rising house prices and rents should support it. 
Adam Guren is an associate professor of economics at Boston University, where he teaches courses on housing policy.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: We’re retired law enforcement officers. Don’t turn back the clock on cannabis reform.
text:
TEN YEARS AGO, Massachusetts voters made a clear choice about how the state should approach marijuana. After decades of policy defined by prohibition, their 2016 vote on a ballot question created a legal, regulated retail market for cannabis. 
For those of us in law enforcement, the vote prompted serious reflection. Many of us had spent our careers enforcing cannabis laws. But to what end? The question was not simply whether marijuana carried risks, but whether prohibition was an effective or appropriate response to those risks. We also had to consider the consequences of criminalizing conduct involving consenting adults. 
A hard look at the evidence and our own experience pointed toward a different approach. Legalization provided an alternative to prohibition, allowing adults to obtain cannabis through lawful businesses while reducing the need for criminal enforcement. With fewer resources devoted to low-level cannabis offenses, police could concentrate on more serious threats to public safety. 
In the decade since, Massachusetts has established a regulated market that provides adults with legal access to cannabis, subject to testing and consumer safeguards. But now voters are being asked to revisit that decision through Question 8, a ballot measure that would repeal the state’s adult-use cannabis retail system and move policy back toward prohibition. 
There appears to be little appetite among many in law enforcement for returning to the enforcement practices of the past. In conversations with current and former officers, we’ve heard a consistent concern: Police already face considerable demands on their time and resources, and renewed cannabis enforcement would add to that burden. 
That isn’t to say law enforcement has no concerns about cannabis use or the current market. Impaired driving, sales to minors, and unsafe products are legitimate public safety issues. But criminalizing cannabis commerce is not the same as addressing those harms. Renewed enforcement of cannabis prohibition could divert already limited law-enforcement resources from investigating violent crime, combating human trafficking, and protecting vulnerable members of our communities. 
A regulated retail market provides consumers with information and safeguards that can be difficult to ensure when transactions occur outside an established oversight system. According to figures cited by the campaign, 84 percent of Massachusetts cannabis consumers obtained their cannabis through legal channels in 2023, compared with approximately 61 percent in 2019. This shift suggests that many consumers have chosen the regulated market when given the opportunity. 
Three issues deserve particular attention in this debate: youth use, impaired driving, and product safety. Each presents genuine challenges, and each calls for thoughtful public policy rather than a return to blanket prohibition. 
When it comes to protecting young people, Massachusetts has seen a substantial decline in reported cannabis use among public high school students. According to figures attributed to the state’s Youth Health Survey, past-30-day use fell from 30.2 percent in 2019 to 13 percent in 2025. Although this decline cannot necessarily be attributed to legalization, it challenges the assumption that a legal adult-use market inevitably leads to increased adolescent consumption. 
Licensed retailers are required to verify government-issued identification, providing one means of limiting sales to minors. Education, prevention, and treatment remain essential, and revenue from legal cannabis sales helps support public health initiatives. Eliminating that revenue would create additional funding challenges. 
Impaired driving is also a serious concern. Cannabis can impair judgment and driving ability, and operating a vehicle while impaired remains illegal regardless of how marijuana is obtained. Repealing legal retail sales would not eliminate consumption or the possibility of impaired driving. Regulation currently provides opportunities for consumer warnings, public awareness campaigns, and law enforcement training. Massachusetts has dedicated nearly $5 million to campaigns addressing responsible consumption, impaired driving, and related safety concerns. 
Product safety offers another reason to preserve effective consumer protections. Licensed cannabis products are subject to testing, potency and ingredient labeling, child-resistant packaging, and tracking requirements. When a problem arises, regulators can trace products, investigate concerns, and take corrective action. These protections help consumers make informed choices and provide mechanisms for responding to unsafe products. The challenge is to maintain appropriate standards without relying unnecessarily on criminal penalties. 
The work isn’t finished. We can continue improving consumer protections, public education, and efforts to prevent impaired driving. But criminalizing cannabis commerce is not the same as protecting the public. Law enforcement resources are better directed toward conduct that causes genuine harm rather than consensual transactions between adults. 
A decade ago, Massachusetts voters chose a different approach to cannabis policy. Whatever improvements may still be needed, returning to prohibition would raise serious questions about enforcement priorities, consumer safety, and the effective use of public resources. Those are questions voters deserve to consider carefully as they approach Question 8. 
Dianne Goldstein is a retired California police lieutenant and executive director of the Law Enforcement Action Partnership. Karen Hawkes is a retired Massachusetts state trooper.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Yale labor unions push for AI protections
text:
Helen Helpwell smiles at you as she speaks. She enunciates every word. She is “performing correctly,” according to a note on her personal webpage, when she responds to questions in a “concise, confident, warm, and policy-aligned” manner.“Think of me as your shortcut to the right person, the right process, and the right place to start,” she says, explaining her role as a “research administration concierge” at the Yale School of Public Health (YSPH) — a job she’s had for about a year.Helen doesn’t have the training to take over the former job of Dana Greene, who retired in May after 32 years as a senior administrative assistant at YSPH.Still, Greene is worried about her former employer’s decision to work with Helen. Unlike Greene, Helen doesn’t decorate her desk with union buttons. Helen is always available, and she never asks for a raise.That’s because Helen isn’t human.
She — it — is an artificially intelligent chatbot, accompanied by an AI-generated video of a young white woman, not a hair out of place in her shiny brown bob.“Helen” is just one example of how Yale has been delegating work to AI-powered chatbots.
According to Yale officials, AI is not intended to replace or reduce the number of human staff employed at the university. “Yale has not reduced positions in favor of AI tools but instead is focused on ways to make more time for staff to do human-centered work or to increase external access to Yale’s resources,” an unidentified university spokesperson wrote in an email to the Independent.
“The contributions of Yale’s staff are essential to the university’s mission, and AI is intended to support their expertise, judgment, and service to the community, not replace them.”
Even so, Yale’s approach to AI has raised alarm within Yale unions about the future of human labor at the university. The number of unionized clerical and technical workers at the university has reportedly declined by 179 in the last year and a half.
Concerns about job security in an AI-saturated future have become a flash point in the ongoing contract negotiations between Yale and its clerical and technical workers union, Local 34. In early October, the union released a report lambasting Yale’s rollout of AI technology.
Local 34’s report claims that “AI has led to profound changes in the fields of grant writing, memo writing, email outreach, customer service, information retrieval, and many other tasks that Local 34-UNITE HERE members do on a regular basis,” without input from the unions themselves. According to union spokesperson Ian Dunn, the report was produced entirely by human labor. (Side note: so was this article.)
The report includes personal narratives from a number of current and former union members, including Greene, describing how they were asked to incorporate AI into their work. One administrative assistant, Carolyn Kyrtopolous, described how generative AI cut the time it took her to produce scholar biographies by three quarters. Another assistant, Jennifer Ongley, wrote that the technology would produce a “confusing jumble of word salad” with errors that ended up taking extra time to fix.A key claim in the union’s report, which Yale refutes, is that the university is reducing human labor by way of “passive automation” or “passive replacement” — using AI to replace or redistribute the labor of employees who quit or retire from their positions.
The report cites a recent hiring freeze and retirement incentive as examples of how Yale has “cut the total amount of union workers across departments and units.” It argues that “by supplementing a smaller workforce with AI, the University can simply avoid hiring workers to replace those who have retired or have quit, thereby reducing the amount of union work needed to fulfill the same amount of work that was done previously.”
Local 34 is calling for the university to work with unions on a “responsible transition” to an AI-assisted workplace, as well as to protect existing jobs, bolster layoff benefits, and raise the salaries of people trained to incorporate AI into their work.
According to the report, the number of Local 34 members has declined from 4,112 in April 2025 to about 3,933 now.
Meanwhile, Yale appears to be hiring for at least 17 administrative assistant positions, according to its public job postings.
Since August 2024, Yale has been rolling out an internal proprietary platform called Clarity, which provides Yale employees access to versions of Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini that are designed to adhere to certain security standards.
Yale’s website states that the platform, among other tools, “enables Yale faculty, staff, and sponsored students to utilize secure and scalable API offerings allowing AI capabilities to be built into applications and workflows.” The website also outlines how Clarity allows “Yale faculty, staff, and sponsored students to create and manage Custom Agents at no cost.”A few Yale departments have launched custom agents, some designed for public use and others intended to assist staff. In addition to “Helen,” there’s “Harvey” at Yale’s medical library, which can “search across the catalog, PubMed, and our website.” There’s “Reggie” at the Registrar’s Office along with a nameless advising chatbot, which can each search for information posted to the university’s website. And there’s Yale Finance Chatbot, an internal agent described as “the best source for answers to most self-service Finance-related questions, including information about Yale’s finance-related policies, procedures, processes, forms, reporting, and other finance-related content.”Greene said that starting in the winter before her retirement in May, her supervisors began to repeatedly encourage her and her colleagues to make use of Clarity.At team meetings, she said, she was told to ask questions to a chatbot before coming to a manager. Her takeaway from the announcements, she said, was that “it’ll be learning from you, the answers you give. It will get stronger as it learns from you.”“Just because they were strongly encouraging it, I said all right, let me see what this is all about,” she recalled. Part of her job involved booking travel arrangements for faculty and students; she recalled asking the chatbot about “government rules related to travel.” She said that the chatbot would cite Yale’s official policies and procedures, the same resource that Greene would have otherwise consulted. “I guess the promise was that it gives it back to you faster,” Greene said.Greene worked as one of two administrative assistants at the Yale School of Public Health’s Chronic Disease Epidemiology department. She worked with about 15 faculty members, in addition to a rotating pool of postdocs, students, and study collaborators.On a day-to-day basis as a senior administrative assistant, Greene would coordinate events, reconcile university credit card expenses, help faculty plan for course logistics, and generally respond to “any needs of the department” as they come up.So far, Yale’s public-facing chatbots have comparatively narrow roles. As “Helen” explains in the pre-set welcome video, “My role is to help you and other faculty and staff find quick, accurate answers about pre- and post-award administration — things like budgets, hiring, or policies.”
The chatbot doesn’t have access to Workday, the university’s billing and personnel platform. It can rattle off travel policies, but it can’t actually book a flight. Not yet, at least.Greene emphasized that technical limitations are not the only way in which AI cannot replace her former job. “Helping to make the school run, you can’t do that behind a screen,” she said. “You have to connect with people.”She described often turning to her colleagues in other departments to brainstorm solutions to tricky situations not covered in any procedural handbook. “You can’t get that online, the tips and the strategizing and the figuring out another way,” Greene said.When Greene retired, she recalled that a group of YSPH students brought her a card — “this huge card that I still have in my house” — thanking her for things she didn’t realize they had noticed.“They loved the way I ordered a variety of lunches. I heard them when they said I want more of this, I want less of this,” Greene said.She put in effort, she added, “just to be able to put a smile on somebody’s face.” In the office kitchen, she would frequently post wellness and mental health tips. On her desk, she arranged faux sunflowers alongside “my union gear,” buttons and pins from Local 34. She would print out quotes that moved her and post them on a board titled “Words of Wisdom.”Over 32 years, she became a source of institutional memory, from “seeing things change for good and not so good.”The Yale spokesperson argued that AI might actually enable employees to “focus more on human-centered work that is personally fulfilling,” by making other tasks “more efficient.”“Because AI is transforming many parts of the professional workforce and jobs nationwide, we have observed a strong interest in hands-on workshops and other training opportunities,” the spokesperson wrote. Individual schools and teams have the leeway to implement AI according to their particular needs, they wrote. “Part of this strategy involves careful attention to the human aspects of our mission and the very essential social fabric of a residential university.”AI has clearly emerged as a point of tension, however, between the university’s leaders and its unions. According to Local 34’s report, Yale’s approach to AI has “made current negotiations more challenging” as the union seeks a new contract. The report calls on Yale to “agree to maintain at least its current level of 3,933 Clerical and Technical positions over the next five years” as a means to “give workers more confidence that innovative AI use will augment University operations instead of eliminating jobs.”Greene said she worries about what a more automated version of her workplace might look like in a decade. “I’m really, really concerned about the coworkers, the colleagues I left behind,” said Greene. She worries that new employees might be trained by robots, that people might generally work in increased isolation from other humans. “What kind of atmosphere would that be?” she asked.“I’m not totally against technology,” Greene added. “You gotta have it. And it has done wonders for us… But to do a job like our job, that human connection cannot go away. It cannot be replaced and should not.”“It was a sense of pride for me,” she said — “just the relationships and with the staff and faculty there. You can’t measure that.”
This story was first published Oct. 28, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Prediction markets diverge from traditional polls in NC races as Election Day nears
text:
A growing number of state officials fear prediction markets are opening the door to a new era of gambling on elections — a practice many states have long prohibited. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)With Election Day less than a week away, prediction markets are signaling strong chances for some North Carolina congressional candidates, even as some traditional polling remains uncertain. 
In North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, polls have consistently shown Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis and Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout within the margin of error. 
The Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up. But prediction markets give Davis a roughly 80% chance of winning reelection, making him a four-to-one favorite.
Do the markets know better than the pollsters? We won’t know until the election is over. 
Prediction markets allow traders to buy options on election outcomes for a profit. Traditional betting on elections is illegal throughout the U.S. But market owners say the trades are investments, not bets, and are therefore not subject to gambling laws.
Those markets are also less representative and less scientific than polls. They don’t require traders to live in the state or to be registered voters, and there’s no way to sample them to ensure a cross-section of likely voters from all parties.
But research suggests prediction markets may influence how voters perceive candidates’ chances of winning. 
A study published this month by the Brennan Center for Justice found that prediction market odds can influence voters’ perceptions of which candidate was likely to win, even when those odds conflicted with polling. 
Researchers surveyed about 2,000 registered voters using hypothetical races. The respondents were 10 to 20 percentage points more likely to view a candidate as the likely winner when prediction markets gave that candidate better odds. 
Election betting is booming as the midterms near. Do states have the power to curb it?

Only 19% said election prediction markets were accurate compared with 37% who said the same about traditional polls, according to the study. 
In the 1st Congressional District, about $27,000 has traded in the market for the race, with nearly 96% of the total coming this month. 
AJ Francia, head of product at Prediction.com, combines data from platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, which let users place bets on elections. 
Francia said the markets initially only gave Davis around a 25% chance of winning reelection after redistricting made his district more challenging for a Democrat. But the odds have now climbed to above 80%.
“Inflation, gas prices and geopolitics concerning the Iran war have led to a general shift toward Democrats winning these midterm elections,” he said. 
That shift has also occurred in the 11th Congressional District. Democratic candidate Jamie Ager’s implied chance of winning rose above 85% earlier this month, about two weeks before Cook changed its rating of the formerly deep-red district to “Lean D.”
About $42,000 has been traded in the 11th District market, with 79% coming in this month. 
The U.S. Senate race between Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley has drawn significantly more trading activity. 
About $4.9 million has been traded on Kalshi and Polymarket combined, with prediction markets giving Cooper a 96% chance of winning and Whatley 3%.
Francia said the markets can react quickly to new information, including economic developments and candidates’ public performances. But he said the track record of today’s large prediction markets is limited. 
Nonetheless, North Carolina Democrats say they’re seeing similar signs of momentum in the state and believe it could put more congressional seats in play. 
At a press conference Wednesday, North Carolina Democratic Party Chair Anderson Clayton said early voting numbers had put as many as 10 congressional districts in play, including those drawn to be safe GOP seats by Republican lawmakers. 
Democrat Richard Ojeda, who’s challenging Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District, said he believed Democrats are gaining support from unaffiliated voters and some Republicans. 
“We’re on the verge of flipping the seats,” he said.

name: California
title: Head of California high-speed rail agency resigns amid travel expenses scandal
text:
In summary
Ian Choudri, who has led the train agency since 2024, leaves a troublesome legacy marked by budget woes, project delays and various scandals, including questionable taxpayer-funded trips by consultants.


The CEO of California’s high-speed rail authority resigned late Wednesday, saying he needs to focus on “important personal and family priorities,” according to a copy of the emailed resignation obtained by CalMatters.
“This has not been an easy decision, as leading the Authority has been one of the most meaningful and rewarding chapters of my professional life,” wrote Chief Executive Ian Choudri.
The abrupt announcement comes in the midst of a two-day meeting of the board that oversees the project, which continues Thursday. It follows Choudri’s tumultuous two-year tenure, which has been troubled by budget woes, project delays, transparency concerns and various scandals including the misuse of nearly $600,000 in taxpayer money for questionable trips by rail authority consultants.
Under Choudri, the authority also lost $4 billion in federal funding under President Donald Trump’s administration, after the agency repeatedly missed deadlines required by the funding agreement to buy trains. The state initially sued Trump for the funding but abruptly dropped the lawsuit in December 2025, blaming Trump as “not a reliable partner” and turning to private investors instead.
Choudri did not respond to an email or text from CalMatters requesting comment Wednesday night.  It is unclear when his last day will be.
State investigators last month found the rail agency’s consultants flew first class, hailed premium rides and traveled to a nightclub, cigar lounge and restaurants on taxpayers’ dime, sometimes at Choudri’s request. Many of the trips involved traveling to Folsom, the Sacramento suburb where Choudri has a home, sometimes after hours. 
The board voted earlier this month to limit Choudri’s contracting authority following the probe, requiring the in-house legal counsel to sign off first on contracts under $25 million.
The board has been weighing additional disciplinary action against Choudri for weeks, including possible termination, according to a source with the authority who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the matter.
California voters in 2008 approved a $10 billion bond to build a bullet train connecting San Francisco to Los Angeles by 2020, with a projected cost of $45 billion. But progress stalled amid rising costs, legal fights and funding uncertainties. 
The authority’s latest business plan said the project could now cost between $126 billion and $231 billion, with the current 171-mile leg between Merced and Bakersfield under construction, and a full buildout expected by 2040.
The board was supposed to decide at the meeting this week if Choudri qualified for a potential $25,000 bonus based on his performance this year, agency spokesperson Micah Flores told CalMatters last month. 
Choudri’s compensation this year is more than $534,000, according to agency spokesperson Annie Parker.
Cost overruns, project delays, legal challenges
Choudri was hired in August 2024 after spending decades in transportation engineering, with experience building high-speed rail in France and Spain. The board hired him in part due to his “strong understanding of complex transportation projects,” according to then-board chair Tom Richards.
Under Choudri, the agency has continued construction of the Central Valley segment and is on the cusp of getting environmental clearance from the state for all 500 miles of planned railway between San Francisco and Southern California. Newsom, a big supporter of the rail project, has committed $1 billion a year from the state’s climate fund toward the rail project until 2045. 
Choudri has also led efforts to cut consultant contract costs, attract private investments and speed up contracting, rail authority chief of staff Mark Tollefson said during a Wednesday presentation touting Choudri’s achievements.  
Ian Choudri, CEO of California High Speed Rail, speaks during a press conference on the high-speed rail project at the Wasco Rail Yard facility in Wasco on Feb. 3, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters
On Wednesday, the board unanimously approved a $772.1 million contract to Germany-based Siemens Mobility, Inc. to design, build and test three seven-car high-speed bullet trains by 2030. The authority will also pay up to $63.7 million in import duties and tariffs, because the trains will be designed and built in Germany.
The vote comes three years after the agency first opened bidding for six trainsets in August 2023 to qualify for more than $3 billion in federal grants, before ultimately losing the funding following missed deadlines. 
In his resignation letter, Choudri said he was proud to have transformed the project.
“I took on a project facing significant challenges and serious questions about its prospects for success, and led its turnaround into a successful program,” he wrote. 
But the project has continued to face significant cost overruns, schedule delays and lawsuits. 
The train agency could run out of cash by December 2027, the office of inspector general warned in July. Meanwhile, the authority failed to make clear in its latest business plan that the Central Valley segment is now expected to be completed by 2034 at a cost likely exceeding $40 billion, the inspector general said. 
The authority also based its project schedule on the assumption it would achieve legislative proposals it failed to push through this year.
To save money, the authority proposed shrinking the Merced-to-Bakersfield segment by 9 miles and moving the downtown Merced station to South Merced, in apparent violation of state law. It also requested an exemption from environmental regulations and solicited contractors for the new location, prompting a lawsuit this month from the Central Valley coalition Community Alliance for a Sustainable Economy. 
“This challenge follows an unlawful pattern of behavior by the HSRA — proposing to relocate the downtown Merced station, then acting as if that move has been approved when it has not,” the complaint said.
Questionable trips plague the authority
Between 2024 and 2026, employees from four consulting firms working for Choudri’s agency billed the state for questionable trips to locations including gyms, a nightclub, an escape room, a tiki bar and a cigar lounge, according to last month’s probe by the inspector general’s office overseeing the rail agency.
Many trips were poorly justified, yet the agency routinely reimbursed them without sufficient vetting, the inspector general said.
One legal consultant traveled between Denver and Sacramento 30 times in a year, charging the state $86,500 in “travel time” payments and an additional $40,800 in reimbursements. 
In a testy meeting earlier this month, the board accused them of using the agency as a “piggy bank.” 
On Wednesday, authority staff reported that the consulting firms have paid nearly $1.3 million in reimbursements to the agency.
CalMatters filed a public records request last month seeking the questionable travel invoices from the inspector general’s office. The agency provided records only from one firm, Nossaman, arguing that the records for other consultants are related to audits or investigations and therefore are not required to be publicly disclosed under a recent law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. 
The records that were released were heavily redacted by both the inspector general’s office and the rail agency, which argued much of the information is protected by attorney-client privilege.

name: California
title: Bass-Raman mayoral race has avoided the identity politics that dominate LA’s history
text:
The race for mayor of Los Angeles has largely focused on the decision voters face between a liberal incumbent with four years of mixed success and a democratic socialist who might advance a more progressive agenda.
If that’s the choice in this election between Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman, it is also worth noting what it has not been: In the ethnic and national stew that is Los Angeles, this year’s race has avoided the theater of identity politics that has often shaped its mayoral contests.
With one exception, this campaign has not been marked by racial divisions or differences over issues relating to immigration, assimilation or cultural hegemony. That represents a break from much of this city’s recent political history.
Tom Bradley, the city’s first Black mayor, held office for five terms. Before moving to politics, Bradley had served as a police officer at the LAPD, navigating one of the most racially entrenched institutions of its time. He never forgot those experiences, and his mayoralty marked and solidified the place of African Americans in Los Angeles leadership, as well as fusing an alliance between Jewish and Black voters.
The mayors who have followed often have risen to office against a backdrop of racial divide. Richard Riordan won the support of white voters and many Latinos but never found much support in Black communities. His successor, Jim Hahn, rejiggered the Riordan majority and won by drawing support from Black and moderate-to-conservative white voters — only to lose both when he dumped Police Chief Bernard Parks and opposed San Fernando Valley secession. 
Antonio Villaraigosa was the first Latino to lead Los Angeles in the modern era, and his election was a triumph for the Latino-labor coalition that united behind him. Eric Garcetti looked like a white guy, but his mother was Mexican; he spoke fluent Spanish and he was popular with many of those who had supported Villaraigosa. And Bass, the mayor now fighting to keep her job, defeated a white, self-financed businessman in the Riordan mold by consolidating support from Black voters and building energy around electing the city’s first woman.
That marks a half-century of shifting identity politics, which is natural, perhaps, in a city whose demographics have been fast-evolving over that same period — from a mostly white and Republican anti-labor alternative to San Francisco, to a plurality-Latino metropolis where organized labor is a powerful political force.
And yet, there’s been barely a whiff of those tensions or that history in this campaign. Both Bass and Raman enjoy support across ethnic lines, with notably large chunks of the electorate undecided going into the campaign’s final days. 
The city’s Black voters, of whom there has not been much serious polling, appear to remain firmly in Bass’ camp. Even in that shrinking segment of the L.A. electorate, however, there are signs of younger Black voters coalescing around Raman.
Indeed, the only real nod to identity politics in this runoff campaign was telling. During a debate, Raman made a clumsy reference to former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates and the “gold standard” of the police department’s refusal to cooperate with immigration authorities.
Her comment, a reference to the department’s Special Order 40, was clipped. It was also historically suspect since LAPD has long turned over suspects found to be in the country illegally to federal authorities. What Gates did decades ago was prohibit officers from stopping people based solely on suspicion of their immigration status. But Raman’s remark roiled up old antipathies toward the police department and the racial dimensions of that history.
In some ways, that was just campaign noise. I did not hear it as suggesting that Gates represented any kind of “gold standard” for policing, and I say that as someone who had issues with Gates, who once challenged me to a fistfight for reporting that he had retired “in disgrace.” It sounded to me like Raman was trying to say that even in the Gates era, the LAPD understood the value of distancing itself from immigration enforcement.
Nevertheless, it’s not great politics to insert “Daryl Gates” and “gold standard” into the same sentence, and the words touched a nerve in a certain slice of the electorate. In short, it angered many Black voters who too-often were on the receiving end of racist policing.
After the debate, an impromptu community gathering rallied around Bass and demanded that Raman walk back her remark. It featured, for me, friendly and familiar faces. Carl Douglas, the great lawyer who defended O.J. Simpson at Johnnie Cochran’s side, spoke in his trademark stentorian eloquence. Danny Bakewell, the now-graying activist, was gritty and forceful. The crowd chanted “four more years.” All of it felt reminiscent of the 1990s.
To her credit, Raman did pull back the comment, however it was initially intended. 
But the episode felt out of character with this mayoral election. It stands out in this cycle precisely because the campaign has not been built on such flare-ups, the kind that refresh memories of the deep, destructive racial divisions that once plunged Los Angeles into riots, that threatened the city’s sense of itself as a place of welcome and refuge.
That’s not to say that the campaign has avoided division. All campaigns divide. The goal, after all, is to get more voters than the other side, to produce a winner and therefore a loser.
In this race, though, the lines of division are not primarily racial and certainly not of gender — not with two women of color contending for the office. Rather, the most palpable divide and predictor has been age, or someone’s time living in Los Angeles.
For those who were here when Gates was the chief, when LAPD was regarded as an “occupying army,” when more than 1,000 people a year were being murdered in Los Angeles, the urgency of Raman’s campaign may feel manufactured. It is hard to identify with the idea that the city is in crisis when it seems so much better than it once did.
But for newer arrivals, those who have come to the city in recent years in search of its age-old promise, it may feel bleaker. The cost of rent and gas and groceries, the dismaying presence of homeless encampments and the dark threat of immigration raids all seem to block the fulfillment of that dream. Those newer arrivals — Raman herself moved here in 2013 — are more open to the notion that something here is terribly off, that only a fresh take on leadership can bring the city to its fullest potential.
Is division by age or length of residence any better than division by race or gender? Probably. All of us were young at some point, and most of us get old, so generational divides have a built-in mechanism for healing in a way that gender and racial divides do not.
In the short run, they may decide this race for mayor. And the campaign’s defining divide is also what may keep it competitive. For while Raman is leading in every reputable poll, her support relies on those younger, newer voters, while Bass’ is built on those who have been here longer and have a greater stake in the city’s history.
Traditionally, those voters are more dependable, so Raman’s lead, while significant, is not dispositive. A poll of likely voters released this week had the candidates evenly split.
This election remains competitive, right to the finish.

name: California
title: California turf war between universities and community colleges needs a rational resolution
text:
California being what it is — an infinitely complex socioeconomic matrix — even the seemingly simplest political issues can become a whirlpool of competing special interests.
So it was in the final hours of the Legislature’s 2026 session two months ago, when the chancellor of California’s community college system sent a letter opposing two bills that expanded community colleges’ authority to offer bachelor’s degrees, something they had been seeking for years.
The bills, Senate Bill 960 and Assembly Bill 2694, passed anyway and were signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who had previously rejected such an expansion.
Chancellor Sonya Christian’s letter was prompted by a raft of last-minute amendments imposing an ultra-complex formula to calculate what kinds of degrees and how many degrees community colleges could offer.
“The cumulative effect of the recent amendments moves us too far from the original objective,” she wrote. “California should be making it easier, not harder, for community colleges to respond when there is a demonstrated workforce need, insufficient public baccalaureate capacity, and students who lack realistic access to a bachelor’s degree.”
That is true, but in California nothing in legislative politics is simply true. It is always subject to what’s necessary to placate myriad stakeholders, no matter how nonsensical or even corrosive the additional verbiage may be.
In this case, it reflects the transformation of the 1960 California Master Plan for Higher Education’s vision of seamless cooperation among community colleges, the California State University system and the University of California into a three-way battle over academic turf.
The plan spelled out how the three systems would meet the demand for low-cost, post-high-school education: The University of California would sponsor research and award four-year degrees, master’s degrees and doctorates in a vast array of fields; the state universities would concentrate on bachelor’s and master’s degrees in professional fields such as education and engineering, and community colleges would provide vocational training and lower-division academic classes, to prepare students for transfers to the two other systems.
In the decades following the master plan’s adoption, though, this tripartite vision developed cracks as California experienced vast cultural, ethnic, economic and political change and massive population growth.
Community colleges, especially those located far from UC or Cal State campuses, began exploring the possibility of providing baccalaureate degrees. That drew immediate opposition from Cal State, which saw it as poaching. 
But Cal State’s system also began pushing for authority to offer doctorates, which drew opposition from UC for the same reason.
Advocates for all three systems muscled up to pursue their aims in the Legislature, which responded with a series of pilot programs in community colleges and Cal State campuses. All were fashioned to supposedly bend — but not break — the master plan’s demarcation of academic turf.
The community colleges achieved very limited authority for bachelor’s degrees in 2014, followed by a modest expansion in 2021. Today they offer more than 50 programs in such fields as health care, industrial technology and public safety.
This year’s version of the turf war launched in February, when the community college chancellor’s office approved programs at three colleges over the objections of Cal State, which claimed they duplicate its offerings. Legislation was introduced to widen the scope of community college offerings and reduce some jurisdictional barriers, particular the ability of Cal State campuses to claim duplication.
What happened to the two bills in the final hours of the legislative session was a partial win for the community colleges. But a complex set of hurdles were added to the bills to placate Cal State, drawing Chancellor Christian’s opposition.
It’s obvious the three-way turf war will continue and become even more byzantine, unless rationality rears its head with a complete overhaul of the 66-year-old higher education plan, which has become hopelessly outdated.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Mirror hires new Hartford community engagement reporter, engagement manager
text:
The Connecticut Mirror has hired a new community engagement reporter to cover Hartford and a manager of engagement who will grow CT Mirror’s audience across several platforms.
Sandy Battulga, Hartford Community Engagement Reporter
Hartford Community Engagement Reporter Sandy Battulga will build relationships with the city’s residents and institutions through community outreach, listening sessions and other events, a text line, and social media.
She will crowdsource questions from residents on everything from city happenings to how to access public resources, then research answers and push that information out via text, social media and events.
She will also write about what’s working in Hartford’s communities and will seek out information and story tips to bring back to the CT Mirror newsroom.
Her work is part of the Raising Voices Lab, an initiative designed to take a more holistic approach to engaging with Connecticut residents and fulfill information needs in some of the state’s historically underserved communities.
Battulga comes to CT Mirror from Colorado Public Radio, where she gained experience in everything from daily news reporting to long-form radio production as a Max Wycisk News Fellow. She has also held internships at the TV news station WCVB in Boston and the Spanish language fact-checking organization Factchequeado. She is a graduate of New York University, where she did a yearlong stint at its campus in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
“We are thrilled to welcome Sandy to the CT Mirror,” said Keila Torres Ocasio, the CT Mirror’s enterprise editor, who leads the Raising Voices Lab. “Her experiences covering a broad range of issues in her home state of Colorado and building connections and engagement during her time reporting in Buenos Aires will inform her work in Hartford and help build on the connections we’ve already made in the city through our community engagement initiative.”
Kat Struhar, Manager of Engagement
As Manager of Engagement, Kat Struhar will be responsible for growing CT Mirror’s audience and deepening engagement with readers across the website, newsletters and social media platforms.
Her role will involve producing newsletters, managing CT Mirror’s mobile app and social media presence, and conducting audience listening to better understand how CT Mirror can show up for Connecticut residents.
Struhar is a former CT Mirror intern who has since interned at The Arizona Republic, American Journalism Project and The Washington Post. Originally from Maryland, she holds a bachelor’s degree from Wesleyan University and a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.
“It is so thrilling to welcome Kat back to CT Mirror after her time at The Washington Post,” said Chief Growth Officer Clare Dignan. “As an intern, Kat was creative, innovative, and excited to engage with our audience. She’s bringing all that again, with a new focus on listening and responding to our readers and their interests.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah files criminal charges against Kalshi over operations within the state
text:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New felony charges against Kalshi and a new federal lawsuit against Utah joined the litigation maze between the prediction market platform and the state this week.
Kalshi and its co-founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, are now facing 12 online gambling promotion felony charges, one count of pattern of unlawful activity, also a felony, and a misdemeanor charge for general gambling promotion, according to charging documents filed by Utah Attorney General Derek Brown on Wednesday.
“Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Brown said in a statement about the charges. “A federal court has already ruled that Utah’s gambling laws apply to Kalshi. Kalshi kept taking bets from Utahns anyway. That is illegal, and we’re putting a stop to it.”


Let us know what you think...


 

However, Kalshi is ready to fight the state on the challenge, Jacki McGavick, a spokesperson for the company said on Wednesday.
“This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” McGavick said in a statement referring to similar charges the company has avoided in Arizona courts.
At the same time, officials in Washington, D.C., argue that prediction markets should exclusively be regulated by the federal government. 
Utah sues Kalshi for ‘brazen pattern’ of violating state’s gambling ban

Just days after Brown filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi, accusing the company of a “brazen pattern of unlawful conduct,” the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, filed a legal challenge against Utah, aiming to block the state’s ban of derivatives markets.
“Utah’s efforts to prevent a CFTC-regulated (designated contract market) from offering CFTC-approved financial products intrude on the exclusive federal scheme Congress designed to oversee United States commodity derivatives markets,” the commission said in its complaint.
“Utah, however, is attempting to block the operation of exchanges that the Commission has expressly approved, as well as event contracts that have been self-certified to the Commission and that the Commission has permitted to be listed,” the complaint says. “These consequences directly harm the federal government’s sovereign, legally protected interest in enforcing federal law.”
Utah has anti-gambling provisions ingrained in its constitution and this year passed legislation to ensure that prediction markets were explicitly banned in the state. The issue has unleashed a series of legal and social media clashes between state and federal leaders, with Gov. Spencer Cox sending public messages via social media to CTFC chair Mike Selig. 
“These prediction markets you are breathlessly defending are gambling — pure and simple. They are destroying the lives of families and countless Americans, especially young men. They have no place in Utah,” Cox said in February. “Let me be clear, I will use every resource within my disposal as governor of the sovereign state of Utah, and under the Constitution of the United States to beat you in court.”
Kalshi is subject to Utah’s anti-gambling law, judge rules

The state prevailed in a federal lawsuit Kalshi filed challenging a 2026 state law that included  proposition bets in the definition of banned gambling, allowing state officials to prohibit prediction market companies’ operations within state limits. The platform appealed, and while its emergency request for an injunction also failed, that litigation isn’t over. 
According to Utah’s charging documents against Kalshi, despite the court decision allowing the state to enforce its anti-gambling laws, an undercover agent with Utah geolocations was able to place wagers on multiple sports events.
But criminal charges against the platform haven’t done well in the past. Another federal judge permanently blocked Arizona from criminally prosecuting Kalshi, deciding that federal law preempts the state from enforcing anti-gambling laws against prediction market companies because they are exclusively regulated by the CFTC. The state is seeking to revive the case.
