name: Mississippi Today
title: The false promise of consolidation in West Bolivar schools: ‘It takes a toll’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SHAW — Cassandra Phillips hates to see the old Ray Brooks School building rotting off Highway 1. 
To local lawmakers and residents, it was the best maintained public schoolhouse in Bolivar County. The one structure connected to a gymnasium with a vaulted ceiling and glossy wooden floors and a cafeteria with cushioned booths in maraschino red.
Now, vines hang where school banners did. Shelves and desks lie rusted and mangled in the abandoned breezeway, and wires stripped of their copper lay limp from behind shattered doors and windows.
Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Ray Brooks School, which served grades K-12, was a casualty of a 2014 consolidation between Benoit’s school district and those in Rosedale and Shaw. 
But the community lost more than a school. Families had gathered at the building for repasts, impromptu kickball tournaments and youth mentoring. They could attend a football game or pick up a child without making a 20-minute drive — the typical amount of time it takes now to get to school in Shaw. 
Now, former Ray Brooks Tigers, including Phillips, cheer for the Shaw Warriors, their pre-consolidation rivals. But that harmony that took six years to achieve is at risk again.
Ja’khyria Williams, from left, Zalia Sanders and Cassandra Phillips talk about Shaw High School during the school’s football game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
State lawmakers are considering another consolidation in Bolivar County, which has three districts: North Bolivar, West Bolivar and Cleveland. The details of lawmakers’ new consolidation plans are not yet clear, and  the promises of cost savings and better schools from the last one have fallen far short of expectations. Schools have closed, buildings have deteriorated and turmoil has plagued the resulting district. 
“Benoit has lost so much,” Phillips said.
Taking the fight against consolidation to Jackson
In January 2012, Beverly Culley, Benoit’s superintendent, addressed lawmakers to argue against consolidation. She handed packets detailing district budgets and student test scores.
She brought students, too. They sang a hymn. She made an impassioned speech and listed off the district’s high test scores relative to its neighbors. Benoit was one of the best performing school districts in the Mississippi Delta. The district had minimal debt. The community needed its schools.
“They didn’t listen,” Culley said. “They had all the data. But none of that mattered because they were going to do what they were going to do.”
Evelyn Henry, who served on the Shaw school board before the consolidation, was also present that session, but with a different pitch. She presented a binder with the total cost of unaddressed maintenance issues in Shaw schools, which was steep, she recalled. 
Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayThe old library at Ray Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRay Brooks School is pictured in Benoit on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
She hoped if lawmakers did go through with consolidation, they would consider consolidation with Cleveland, which had a larger tax base and was closer in distance.
“We had to realize something was going to happen,” Henry said of the board’s attempt to negotiate. “I just wish we could have had somebody to help us before we went to Jackson so we looked like a unified front.”
Neither Culley or Henry’s wishes were honored, both now saying their fears were realized.
‘We just couldn’t sit down and just make it work’
The consolidated West Bolivar school board would be tasked with fixing crumbling infrastructure in Rosedale and Shaw with little money. Lawmakers chose three communities with some of the lowest tax bases in the state to combine, which Henry felt set them up for failure.
The consolidated districts saved roughly $400,000 in administrative costs, much less than lawmakers’ claims the move would save up to  $1.6 million.
Jackie Lloyd, who has represented Rosedale schools on the West Bolivar board since consolidation, recalled getting little technical assistance from the state Education Department after the districts merged. She said pooling the different schools’ resources and then dispersing them equitably was particularly challenging.
Joyce Brown, left, and Shelia Ratliff prepare for Leland and Shaw high schools’ football game at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The districts had a combined $1.48 million in debt coming into the consolidation. West Bolivar School District, based in Rosedale, owed more than $1 million. Benoit’s district only owed $40,000.
Henry, who represented Shaw on the consolidated school board until 2020, had the same observation as Lloyd. She felt each community’s representatives were only interested in measures that would benefit their schools. The board increasingly failed to reach consensus, and gridlock on votes became common.
Five years and four superintendents later, Henry observed a more aggressive school board whose actions were fueled by the increasing polarization. According to a 2020 lawsuit Culley filed against the district and board members, board members aggressively bullied and harassed her. She alleged the behavior started soon after she was appointed superintendent of the consolidated district in 2017.
The district settled out of court in 2020 for an undisclosed amount for alleged behavior that U.S. District Court Judge Michal P. Mills called “distasteful.”
In Shaw, district consolidation meant no high school, no band
While videos of board members’ quarrels reached viewers on Facebook, district infrastructure continued to crumble. Two district high school buildings were eventually condemned: Shaw in 2018 and West Bolivar in Rosedale in 2020. As a result, Shaw High students attend classes at the elementary school building.
For Shelia Ratliffe, a Shaw alum, budget cuts at the school mean her children missed out on extracurriculars. 
At the Sept. 14 football game, Ratliffe pointed to the old Shaw High school gym, where she remembered majorette and band practices took place. She remembered the pride the community felt for Shaw’s band, when they had one.
The old gymnasium at the former Shaw High School is pictured in Shaw on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Failing infrastructure and fewer extracurricular offerings weren’t inevitable, Henry said. The Shaw school board received a grant from the Mississippi Department of Archives and History to renovate the high school building prior to consolidation. A crew from Jackson provided an on-site inspection along with a project overview in 2013, she recalled.
Later, the consolidated school board and a series of superintendents never prioritized the project. Instead, they abandoned the historic high school and relocated its students to the McEvans Elementary building.
Karmenisha Moore, left, and Jarquez Moore talk about school consolidation and the football game between Shaw and Leland in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson talks about Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora sits at a table at Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayDebbie Brooks talks about her efforts while working with Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson gives a tour of Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayDonated computers are in place at Delta Hands for Hope in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayCora Jackson talks about the books donated to Delta Hands for Hope while giving a tour of the nonprofit organization in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayKarmenisha Moore, left, and Jarquez Moore talk about school consolidation and the football game between Shaw and Leland in Shaw on Friday, September 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In 2020, the West Bolivar Consolidated school board, now dominated by representatives from Shaw and Rosedale — and one from Benoit — voted to close Ray Brooks, too.
“It made no sense,” Culley, the former Benoit superintendent, recalled. 
The district installed two portable toilets by the concession stand for spectators and players alike in lieu of a field house at Shaw High’s football field. 
Portable toilets are in place for Leland and Shaw high schools’ football game at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Our community, Shaw, just really started feeling like the ugly child,” said Henry of upkeep projects that went ignored at her alma mater. She said she paid for McEvans school sign out of pocket to replace an old, decrepit one, and the board moved slowly on other Shaw priorities. 
Communities adjust to playing on the same team 
Zalia Sanders, a Benoit native and a senior at Shaw High, was miles away from home at the Aug. 28 matchup between Leland and Shaw. But the rural community on a bayou has become a second home for her. She, along with three other students, said Shaw and Benoit have come together despite a tumultuous consolidation in 2014.
Leland cheerleaders perform on the sidelines during their school’s football game against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayLeland plays against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayShaw players celebrate a play during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Leland player runs the ball during their game against Shaw at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Shaw player runs the ball during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA Shaw player runs the ball during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayShaw High School cheerleaders pose for a photo before players take the field against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
At the game, she stood by the fence with her older sister, Ja’khyria Williams, who is a college freshman. They reflected on what became common in the wake of consolidation: student fights.
She said the rivalry between Rosedale and her native Benoit can be fierce — a  feud that stretches back to the 1980s, long before her time in school. 
There was an uptick in fighting between Rosedale and Shaw youth in the years after the consolidation in the late 2010s and in 2024, Rosedale Police Chief Aaron Malone recalled. But while he remembers some dispatches last year related to disputes, this year has been mostly quiet.
The catalyst can be as small as an unfriendly look or as big as allegations of romantic infidelity, Sanders said. 
Shaw fans cheer after a play during their game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Still, she said, she loves Shaw High. She got more comfortable at Shaw schools through joining the volleyball team, she says. 
“When you’re playing on the same team, you get to know each other as people.”
Shaw, the town miles down the country highway, no longer feels so foreign, she said. But between board members weighing another school closure and consolidation talk in Jackson, students like her might be sent to yet another community for school.
Shaw residents don’t want to reopen the wounds of consolidation
Arika Williams, a Benoit native, was wrapping up her shift in the concession stand.
By the fourth quarter, she was counting cash from the stand’s register beneath the hum of an electronic fan. Her brows knitted beneath her tortoiseshell-framed eyeglasses as she shifted to counting the remaining stock of chips and sodas.
Arika Williams works the concession stand during Shaw High School’s football game against Leland at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“If we can all work together and go in the direction we’re going, I think we can all be successful,” Williams said. Initially, she worried consolidation could mean her son would miss out on extracurricular opportunities in Shaw and spend too much time on a school bus.
The big Delta sky had gone black by the fourth quarter. The headlights of old Silverados lit up reflective workmans’ vests in the dark streets by the field. Some were trying to catch the game’s last moments after getting off work.
In the past, some of the Shaw Warriors’ biggest boosters were Ray Brooks Tigers. Ray Brooks alumni, Lajaruis Jaron among them, said they know the importance of community more than anyone in the county. They know how losing schools and football victories can fracture a community. 
During the football game, he leaned forward to watch a Warrior nab the ball. He cheered. The player ran the ball to the end zone. Two students sprinted school flags by the edges of the field. 
Shaw scored again.
Leland fans watch as players compete against Shaw High School at Shaw’s former high school football stadium on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Jarone said he attends each season’s game whether home or away. He owns multiple maroon and yellow T-shirts. He couldn’t imagine autumn without a Warriors football game. 
“When the bus moves, I move,” he said.
Jarone attended Ray Brooks School, not Shaw, but like Williams and Phillips and Sanders, he said he’s found a new home. He’d hate for another district consolidation to force students to find another one.
“I hope consolidation doesn’t happen to these kids like it did to us because it will take a toll,” he said. “This is how it’s always been for small communities. The odds have always been stacked against us.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The cost of healthcare is hitting America where it hurts: The wallet
authors: Renuka Rayasam, KFF Health News, Sam Whitehead, KFF Health News
text:
Lynn Ludaway was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2023 and since then the
medical bills haven't stopped. The resident of Evanston, Illinois, says she has racked up tens of thousands of dollars in healthcare bills. (Photo by Hannah Norman/KFF Health News)This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here with permission. 
Bill McAdams, a 45-year-old travel nurse from Holiday, Florida, was uninsured last year when he experienced a stroke. He hadn’t been able to afford his agency’s health plan, which would have cost $3,600 monthly to cover him and his wife. The hospital that treated him sent him a bill for $93,000.
Janet Marx, 56, of Milford, Connecticut, has doubled up on insurance coverage through her husband’s employer and Medicare because she has lupus and fibromyalgia, disabling chronic conditions. Still the couple sold their home, the house where Marx grew up, to afford the costs of their medical care.
Sheila Robinson, 61, in District Heights, Maryland, has a $10,000 deductible on her Affordable Care Act plan, so she tries to negotiate cheaper self-pay options when she sees a doctor. She puts the $659 monthly premium on her credit card, even though she knows not paying the bill in full means she must pay interest.
“I am just afraid to even go to the doctor,” said Robinson, who has arthritis, a pinched nerve in her neck, and high blood pressure. “Every month, I am in the hole.”
This year, KFF Health News has chronicled how rising healthcare costs are upending the lives of Americans. Reporters have heard from more than 130 people across the U.S. who are trying to afford their premiums, copayments, prescriptions, and medical bills even as housing, energy, and food costs swell. People told us they are forgoing health insurance coverage, rationing their medications, cutting back on doctor visits, and putting off health procedures.
“We’re not talking about the uninsured or those who are low-income who are struggling now,” said Rebecca Kirch, executive vice president at the National Patient Advocate Foundation. “Now it’s become an all-of-us issue.”
While healthcare costs have largely grown faster than the overall economy for decades, they’ve escalated at a dizzying pace recently. In 2023 and 2024, health spending hit its highest growth rates in two decades excluding 2020’s COVID-fueled surge.
The prices that hospitals, doctors, and other clinicians charge have increased, along with how much care people are getting. Overall health spending hit nearly $5.3 trillion in 2024, up from $3 trillion a decade earlier, according to federal data.
American health costs, expected to continue growing faster than the overall economy and help fuel it, are projected to hit 20% of the nation’s gross domestic product by 2032, up from just under 19% today.
At the same time, Americans are shouldering higher insurance premium payments and other out-of-pocket costs. Low-income and middle-class people with health conditions are feeling the brunt.
The GOP-led Congress decided against extending COVID pandemic-era subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans and cut billions from other federal health programs to offset the costs of tax cuts for wealthy Americans and heightened immigration enforcement, arguing that government insurance programs are rife with fraud and waste.
Despite $500 rebate checks sent by President Donald Trump to fewer than 5% of higher-income ACA marketplace enrollees, his administration has been expanding access to insurance plans with higher deductibles and lower premiums that push more costs to patients if they need care. Employers are passing along rising healthcare costs to employees, and clinicians are charging patients up front.
It’s not all bad news for consumers: Prescription drugs recorded their biggest price drop in decades this year. The Biden and Trump administrations both worked to help lower them amid consumer pressure.
But many say they’re still feeling the pain of rising prices. Ahead of the November congressional midterm elections, healthcare costs continue to top a list of the public’s worries about affordability, according to polling conducted in mid-September by KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. Nine in 10 Democratic respondents and three-quarters of Republican ones said the U.S. healthcare system needs either a complete overhaul or major changes.
‘Profit margins everywhere’
The typical American family spends about $5,600 a year, or 9% of their income, on health insurance premiums, out-of-pocket healthcare costs, and taxes that fund health programs, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker. But overall, the nation’s annual healthcare spending comes to the equivalent of more than $15,400 per person.
The reason behind those high U.S. healthcare costs is straightforward: The prices that clinicians, hospitals, drugmakers, and other players in the health system charge are high. For example, while doctors in the U.S. perform about a third as many inpatient knee replacements as in other wealthy nations, the cost per surgery is higher than in most of those countries, according to the Peterson-KFF tracker.
More recently, multiple trends have driven that price growth in the U.S., health economists and policy researchers said. Hospitals are merging and using their consolidated market power to charge more. New technologies and therapeutics, such as GLP-1s for weight loss and diabetes, have high price tags. Inflation and the Trump administration’s tariffs are layering costs onto everything from latex gloves to medical devices. And higher numbers of uninsured Americans means fewer people to bear more of the costs.
“It’s really everything all together at once,” said Christopher Whaley, a Brown University health policy researcher.



Why the U.S. has high healthcare prices, however, is more complicated. Whaley and other health economists point to how the American healthcare system is structured and financed. Clinician charges and administrative costs are higher in the U.S. than in other countries. The U.S. doesn’t centrally set all prices for services, ration care, or control for quality.
In most local American markets, insurers negotiate prices with hospitals, clinicians, and drugmakers, which then charge for every test, procedure, or medicine regardless of its outcome. More than half of all healthcare payments were based on this fee-for-service model, according to a 2022 research brief published in the journal Health Affairs. Under this model, hospitals and doctors make more as they bill more.
The complexity of different billing systems, rates, insurers, and networks adds to the price tag. The cost of sending out bills and managing paperwork can be hundreds of billions of dollars. Insurers try to keep medical costs in check, in part by limiting what they’ll reimburse. They also take their own cut along the way.
“There’s profit margins everywhere, and there are varying degrees of financial incentives throughout the healthcare system,” Whaley said.
The incentives, however, don’t necessarily promote better health.
Steven Ullmann, director of the Center for Health Management and Policy at the University of Miami Business School, where he’s a professor, said that the country’s health system encourages expensive treatments over low-cost preventive care. He said that keeps people locked into seeing clinicians because they’re in their insurance networks, not necessarily because they produce better outcomes.
Even though people in the U.S. pay more for care than in other countries, Ullmann said higher prices don’t always mean better quality. For example, he said the prices for prenatal ultrasounds in Orlando vary widely with no obvious difference in quality.
“Same city, same procedure,” Ullmann said. “That is a reflection of a broken system.”
And those high prices can keep people from seeking needed services.
In 2025, a health system garnished the wages of Carmilla Collins, 52, of Omaha, Nebraska.
Collins, a single mother, said she didn’t question the tests or medicines doctors ordered when she got diagnosed with thyroid disease or received regular preventive procedures such as a colonoscopy — until she found herself in debt. The hospital hired a collection agency to sue her for unpaid medical bills that she accrued when she was both insured and uninsured. Then a court allowed the debt collector to take hundreds of dollars out of her paycheck.
Collins remembered being “spitting mad.” She almost couldn’t make rent.
“I’m working two jobs,” she said. “And I’m going to be homeless because of this noose that’s around my neck.”
Collins eventually qualified for financial assistance from the hospital, but she said she put off thyroid surgery for four months even as a goiter swelled against her throat, making it hard for her to eat. She had health coverage through her employer at that point but was worried about affording the costs of her deductible and other fees. Eventually, she said, her health declined until she could no longer put off the surgery.
“I equated taking care of my health with debt that I couldn’t afford,” she said.
No quick fixes
How to slow rising costs — and overall U.S. health spending — has long vexed elected leaders and policymakers.
That’s because reducing overall healthcare costs for patients means doctors, hospitals, drug companies, insurers, or other players across the health system would get paid less.
“For the most part, health spending for us is income to someone else,” said Zack Cooper, a health economist at Yale University.
Eliminating administrative complexity or setting price caps — which is how some countries lower overall costs — faces steep odds at the federal level. Since 1998, the health sector has spent more than $14 billion lobbying members of Congress in both parties, according to OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks money in U.S. politics.
After Lynn Ludaway, 40, was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis three years ago, she said, she considered divorcing her husband just to make her eligible for aid to cover medical costs, even though they wanted to stay together.
She initially had coverage through her husband’s job but still faced large out-of-pocket bills. Ludaway, who lives in Evanston, Illinois, also racked up expenses from navigating life with a disabling health condition, such as paying for Uber rides and a cane as her mobility declined. Her medical bills stretched into the tens of thousands of dollars.
“I thought I was well prepared for an emergency,” said Ludaway, who gave up her consulting business and raided her savings and retirement accounts to pay for tests and treatment. “Nobody can prepare for this.”
She now pays a $500 monthly premium for coverage through Illinois’ ACA marketplace. But because of her husband’s job, the couple makes too much to qualify for state or federal assistance.
“I am in this weird in-between,” she said. “I need to rest to heal, but I need to work to live.”
Instead Ludaway relies on private financial aid programs, through foundations and the hospital system where she gets her care. She forgoes what she can’t afford, including dental and mental healthcare. She said she must be even more budget-conscious than she was in college.
“Broke undergrad has nothing on chronic illness,” she said.
Shifting costs
Many current federal healthcare proposals focus on shifting costs rather than lowering them, and ideological differences about who should bear those costs deeply divide lawmakers.
The GOP has prioritized tax and spending cuts, which put the cost more on patients than taxpayers and are expected to boost the number of uninsured, to eliminate what they claim is pervasive fraud in government health programs. Last year, Democrats fought to extend enhanced subsidies for marketplace plans, which would buffer patients somewhat from premium hikes by pushing the bill to taxpayers.
Some progressive Democrats, including candidates winning primaries in battleground states, are reviving calls for “Medicare for All,” versions of which would create one centralized public insurer. Such a system could end out-of-pocket costs and provide major relief for patients such as Ludaway, but not necessarily cut overall health spending. Clinicians, hospitals, drugmakers, and other groups could still lobby for high prices, which taxpayers would then be on the hook to pay.
And some ideas with broad bipartisan support, such as forcing hospitals and doctors to publicly post medical prices, have had little effect on costs.
Policy debates about increasing access to coverage and improving quality of care should also focus on overall health spending, not just who’s picking up the tab, said Michael Chernew, a professor of healthcare policy at Harvard Medical School.
“We don’t have some rich uncle that’s coming and just paying for all of our care. One way or another, collectively we are paying,” Chernew said. “It’s just we’re shifting who is paying, how much we’re paying, and through which mechanisms we pay.”
Despite trillions in health spending, the nation’s system leaves millions of uninsured and underinsured people unable to afford care. About 27 million people — nearly 10% of the population under age 65 — didn’t have health insurance in 2024, according to KFF. And the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office projects that number to grow by 10 million or more by 2034 because of policy and funding changes.
Melody Stephens in Berryville, Arkansas, became uninsured when she dropped her ACA marketplace coverage for this year after the monthly premium payments for her and her younger daughter jumped from just over $200 to more than $2,000. Stephens, 55, a geriatric nurse at an assisted living facility, said she also couldn’t afford the $1,000 monthly premium payment for her employer-sponsored plan.
“There was just no way I could do that,” Stephens said. “That was just not feasible.”
Stephens first got an ACA plan after she was diagnosed with anal cancer about a decade ago. Even with coverage, she filed for bankruptcy two years ago. While her plan largely covered cancer care, it left her with big bills for treatment of the side effects of radiation.
Now she and her daughter are relying on financial assistance and cutting back on care. When her daughter, a college student, had some surgeries, the hospitals wrote off the bills, Stephens said. But they still owe money for tests and treatments.
Stephens also stopped taking a GLP-1 that she was prescribed for diabetes and a medication for nerve pain because of the cost. Stephens can’t afford a colostomy, so she lives with incontinence, she said.
She said she wishes lawmakers in Washington would fix the healthcare system. “They just seem to fight,” she said.
A tipping point?
Next year, insurers say they expect to hike premiums for ACA marketplace plans by 15%, the second year in a row of double-digit premium increases. Employer health costs are expected to rise 9.5%, likely increasing the burden on workers.
Policy researchers and economists who have studied health costs say they are skeptical that federal lawmakers are ready to tackle overall health spending, even as the midterm elections loom.
But pressures are building, said Michael Cannon, a health policy analyst at the libertarian Cato Institute. “We cannot stay on this path forever,” he said.



The pain of high costs is felt throughout the economy, including by employers and state governments that help foot the bill for medical care. That reality is giving way to policy proposals that buck some past political positions.
Last year, the GOP-led legislature in Indiana capped how much some nonprofit hospitals can charge patients covered by employer health plans. Starting in 2029, five of the state’s largest nonprofit hospitals risk losing their tax-exempt status if they charge those patients more than the price limits. And this year, Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott proposed capping certain drug prices. Both cost-control efforts, along with Trump’s plans to lower prescription drug prices, are traditionally more the domain of left-leaning politicians.
For McAdams, the nurse in Florida, dealing with high health costs took a physical toll. He believes a subsequent stroke he experienced was caused by the stress of haggling over his hospital bill.
After his first stroke in September 2025, McAdams bought insurance, but it didn’t cover preexisting conditions. In March, he started experiencing problems with his vision and balance. He went to an urgent care center, instead of the emergency room.
“I was so afraid of dealing with the billing issues again that I did not want to go to the emergency room,” he said.
Then, after talking with the hospital regarding his stroke bill later that month, he said, he experienced problems again and landed back in the ER anyway — with the second stroke.
Now he is applying for Social Security Disability Insurance because he can no longer work as a nurse. The health system eventually lowered his total bill to $50,436 — but that’s still more than he can afford without a steady salary. He and his wife are also expecting a baby this fall.
McAdams was once proud to be part of the nation’s healthcare system, which saved his life and those of so many others. But the financial stress has changed his view. Now, McAdams said, his trust in it is gone.
Are you struggling to afford your health insurance? Have you decided to forgo coverage? Click here to contact KFF Health News and share your story.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.



Here are some stories of Americans struggling with the cost of healthcare and health insurance.
Bill McAdams, 45
Holiday, Florida
In March, Bill McAdams started experiencing problems with his vision and balance and went to an urgent care center, instead of the emergency room. He said he feared getting saddled with medical bills on top of one he already had from a stroke he had experienced while uninsured months earlier. Later that month, after getting upset while talking with the hospital regarding the bill from his stroke, he said, he experienced problems again and landed back in the ER — with a second stroke. Now he owes even more money.
“Due to all the stress, it delayed me in seeking care,” he said. “I didn’t want to deal with the stress of more hospital bills.”
— Sam Whitehead and Renuka Rayasama
Shayna Sanders, 45
New Haven, Connecticut
Shayna Sanders, a marriage and family therapist, has bought health insurance through her state’s Obamacare marketplace for more than a decade. In that time, her monthly premium payments have climbed to close to $1,000. She said she has a “love-hate” relationship with insurance companies: They help her make her living by covering her patients’ appointments, but their coverage feels increasingly out of reach for her.
“Some of the health insurance plans that they have, I probably couldn’t afford them myself due to the cost.”
— Sam Whitehead
Janet Marx, 56
Milford, Connecticut
Janet Marx is on Medicare and has health insurance through her husband’s employer plan. She also receives Social Security disability income because she has fibromyalgia and the disabling autoimmune condition lupus. But she and her husband still struggle to afford their out-of-pocket medical costs. She’s so frustrated about high healthcare costs that she was a guest speaker at an online event for the National Patient Advocate Foundation. Having to scrounge to cover a recent string of $80 copayments for in-home physical therapy led her to an “aha moment,” she said. She sold her home, the place where she grew up, and the couple moved into an apartment.
“Things are just getting too expensive to afford the house and health problems,” she said.
— Renuka Rayasam and Sam Whitehead
Damien Waikoloa, 35
Honolulu, Hawai‘i 
Damien Waikoloa wanted to keep health insurance to manage several chronic conditions, even though premium payments for his ACA plan went up to more than $400 a month, from around $240 a month last year. But keeping his coverage meant the small-business owner in Honolulu had to cut back on other spending. He’s trying to reduce the costs of running his business, including considering lowering his own pay. And he’s cutting back on dining out and traveling to visit friends and family in Seattle and California.
“Things like saving for a down payment for a house or even starting a family have completely gone out the window,” he said.
— Renuka Rayasam

name: Washington State Standard
title: Bird flu spreads to Washington dairy farms
text:
(Photo by Kirsten Strough/USDA)Bird flu is hitting Washington dairy farms and it’s spreading fast. 
The Washington State Department of Agriculture confirmed the first detections in two Yakima County dairy herds in early October. On Oct. 26, the agency reported the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Benton County. 
In the span of three weeks, 27 dairy farms tested positive for bird flu. 
“The virus is moving fast … despite all the efforts that we’ve done within containment,” said Amber Itle, state veterinarian. “Right now, the risk for humans is very low.”
Milk from an infected dairy cow does not pose a risk for human consumption, Itle said. However, the department recommends drinking pasteurized milk because the virus will be killed during processing. The virus has not been found in meat, Itle said. 
Containing the spread will be challenging because researchers don’t fully understand how HPAI transmission occurs, Itle said. Transferring sick dairy cows and contaminated equipment from one farm to another are known causes, but there’s likely many more. 
“There’s been some studies that even suggest that flies can move this virus, the wind can move this virus, and possibly even … birds that maybe move from one farm to another,” Itle said. 
Washington is the 20th state in the country to detect avian influenza in dairy cattle. 
In the last two years, the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory conducted more than 7,000 bird flu tests on individual farms. Until three weeks ago, all tests came back negative, Itle said. 
In response, “every farm in the targeted milkshed where we’re seeing spread is being tested on a weekly basis,” Itle added. 
Symptoms of the disease include decreased milk production, changes in milk appearance, loss of appetite, fever, respiratory issues and changes in manure. When properly treated, most infected cattle recover within six weeks, according to the agency. 
The Washington State Department of Agriculture recommends isolating animals suspected of carrying the disease and reporting the symptoms to the state by emailing ahealth@agr.wa.gov or by calling (360) 902-1878.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri passed a law to compensate the wrongfully convicted. Now it doesn’t want to pay.
text:
Dale Helmig is seeking compensation for the more than 14 years he spent wrongfully incarcerated in Missouri (Katie Moore/Marshall Project).After Missouri lawmakers expanded eligibility for wrongfully convicted people to receive compensation last year, Dale Helmig thought he could get nearly $1 million for the more than 14 years he spent in prison. And Darryl Burton hoped to obtain more than $1.5 million for the 24-plus years he was incarcerated.
But today, they are back in the legal system that put them away. The state attorney general is arguing in court that the two men aren’t innocent, setting aside judges’ prior decisions — and that even if they were, the new law isn’t retroactive.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s effort to fight their compensation requests — the first two under the new compensation law — is part of a long history of the office vigorously opposing innocence claims. Under her predecessors, attorneys there have kept people in prison even after a judge has ordered their release and continued to fight cases in the face of overwhelming evidence of innocence.

This article was published in partnership with The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Subscribe to their St. Louis email list, and follow The Marshall Project on Instagram, Reddit and YouTube.

Peter Joy, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Attorney General’s Office “has opposed claims of innocence on a very consistent basis, even though there have been times when the local prosecutor’s offices have recognized that the person had a valid claim of innocence.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean they aren’t examining each case on its merits, Joy said. But if they were opposing these without a “good faith basis,” it would be a violation of prosecutors’ ethical obligation to seek justice, he said. A spokesperson for Hanaway declined to comment, citing the pending cases.
When Helmig and Burton were released from prison, only those exonerated through DNA evidence qualified for state compensation — not people like them, whose convictions were overturned based on recantations or other types of newly discovered evidence.
Then, last year, the Missouri legislature expanded eligibility and increased the amount of money exonerees can collect. The measure was approved by Gov. Mike Kehoe.
The law allocates about $65,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration. That amount is paid on an annual basis, not as a lump sum.
In Helmig’s case, a judge in DeKalb County, about an hour north of Kansas City, ruled in 2010 that there was clear and convincing evidence that he was innocent. 
Helmig had been convicted in the 1993 murder of his mother, Norma, whose body was found in a river in central Missouri, near where she lived. Prosecutors said his motive was a dispute over a phone bill, and that he’d thrown her purse from the bridge he would have traveled on from her home on the night of the murder. 
But uncovered evidence implicated Helmig’s father, court records show. The couple were in divorce proceedings. Helmig’s father had access to her mail at a local post office, including a canceled check that was dated after her death and later found in the purse. That undermined the prosecution’s theory about when the purse had been discarded — a key detail in their case against Helmig.
A state trooper also recanted his testimony. During the trial, he had told jurors that Helmig had not denied killing his mother when, in fact, he had. 
“This case presents the rare circumstance in which no credible evidence remains from the first trial,” the DeKalb County judge wrote in overturning Helmig’s conviction.
Helmig was released from prison in December 2010. He moved in with his brother and began rebuilding his life. It took him a while to find a job, but he eventually began driving a cab and painting decks. Sometimes he made extra money speaking to law classes about his arduous journey through the justice system, which wasn’t over because the Attorney General’s Office appealed his case.
Months later, the Western District Court of Appeals decided that two of Helmig’s six arguments were enough to establish “a fundamental miscarriage of justice” and upheld the decision to vacate his conviction. The other four issues — including more direct claims about his innocence — were set aside.
That would have unforeseen consequences. 
Since 1989, 56 people have been exonerated in Missouri. DNA evidence played a role in 15 of the cases, according to the National Registry of Exonerations.
Previously, those exonerated through DNA evidence could request $100 for every day they were incarcerated, paid up to a maximum of $36,500 annually. Six people have received the payments since 2015, according to state records, costing the state about $80,000 on average each fiscal year.
State Rep. LaKeySha Bosley, a Democrat from St. Louis who sponsored an earlier version of the bill, said the expanded measure was intended to be retroactive, meaning people like Helmig and Burton could petition for the money. 
“I don’t believe that we should put a limit or timeline on those who lost years of their life,” Bosley told The Marshall Project. “It is our fault as the government, and we should rectify that, regardless of when they were exonerated.”
But Jeffrey Gutman, professor emeritus at George Washington University School of Law and an expert in wrongful conviction compensation, said parts of Missouri’s new statute weren’t clear. It does not expressly say whether the law applies to past exonerations, and it doesn’t entirely lay out the procedure for proving innocence. It’s not surprising, he said, that the Attorney General’s Office is fighting the cases based on the statute’s language.
Three-quarters of states have some type of compensation law, though the amount and process for obtaining compensation varies widely. Gutman pointed to Louisiana and Oregon as other states where it’s been difficult for exonerees to get compensation. 
State officials have dragged people back into court, sometimes in yearslong legal battles where officials questioned their eligibility and innocence. On the other hand, Illinois this year increased its compensation rate, and California has made it easier by streamlining the process for those exonerated under a particular statute.
Gutman said compensation statutes are important because there’s no other remedy, like filing a lawsuit, in cases where no government agency or official is at fault. 
And regardless of who is to blame, he said, “Society owes them compensation for their enormous suffering.”
In September, Helmig found himself back in the courtroom where he was wrongfully convicted for a hearing on his compensation request. His attorney, Sean O’Brien, argued that the law was retroactive because many relevant parts are written in the past tense. He also said a judge had determined his client was innocent, pointing to the DeKalb County judge’s decision.
During a September 2026 hearing, Assistant Attorney General Andrew Clarke argues against granting compensation to Helmig (Katie Moore/Marshall Project).
Assistant Attorney General Andrew Clarke argued that most laws passed in Missouri are prospective. He then said that Helmig did not have a case for compensation because of that Western District opinion. That court found that prosecutors had withheld evidence about Helmig’s father and that an unauthorized map was introduced during jury deliberations. 
It went on to conclude it did not need to address the other issues, including claims of Helmig’s actual innocence. The court added that Helmig was not “in any way impaired by our determination to address no more than that which is necessary.” 
At the time, the prosecutor could still seek a retrial. She chose not to.
“I think that that is the final legal determination,” O’Brien told Gasconade Circuit Judge Craig Hellmann. 
But Hellmann dismissed Helmig’s petition for compensation, writing in a judgment that Helmig was not eligible because he could not establish actual innocence. 
O’Brien has since filed a motion asking the Western District to recall its 2011 opinion. At the time, there was no harm in only taking up two of the claims, he said. But in light of the new law, that’s changed. A decision remains pending.
“Frustrating doesn’t begin to cover it,” O’Brien said of the roadblocks that Helmig has faced in requesting the compensation. “Dale is unquestionably innocent, the statute was written with people just like him in mind, and the State is invoking every conceivable legal technicality to obstruct his recovery.”
Helmig said he’s not surprised the AG’s office is opposing his compensation request, given its track record on wrongful conviction claims.
“They don’t care, it doesn’t matter if you’re innocent,” he said. But the lack of accountability in his case still gnaws at him, he said. “It’s really unbelievable.”
Helmig said receiving the compensation would help give him a retirement. Now 70, he’s had to slow down his work painting decks due to his age and high blood pressure. He said he lives on about $530 per month in Social Security. He spends his days simply: fishing with his brother at Lake of the Ozarks and chopping wood to keep his trailer warm in the winter months. If he gets the money, Helmig said he’d like to move somewhere outside of Missouri.
In the other restitution case, a St. Louis judge held an initial hearing in early October. Darryl Burton’s attorney, Burton Haigh, provided a sweeping overview of his client’s history: Burton was exonerated in 2008 after spending 24 years behind bars and a long appeals process that concluded when a judge in Cole County granted him reprieve.
He’d been convicted in a 1984 fatal shooting at a St. Louis gas station. At trial, prosecutors relied on two witnesses, one who later recanted and one whose account was said to be unreliable, court records show.
Michael Spillane, with the Attorney General’s Office, said this case differed from Helmig’s and he will be raising different arguments, though he didn’t elaborate.
After the hearing, Haigh told The Marshall Project he believes the Legislature’s intent was to help people like Burton and that he meets the requirements for receiving compensation.
“When violations of people’s due process are recognized, it’s foundational in our system to make wrongs right,” he said.
Spillane declined to comment. The sides are expected to present arguments next year.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Why Missouri’s doctors and lawyers hide burnout until it breaks
text:
(Getty Images).Burnout among Missouri’s doctors, lawyers and executives rarely announces itself. It shows up as a surgeon in Kansas City who stops sleeping through the night, a litigator in Clayton who adds a second drink most evenings, a hospital administrator in Springfield who snaps at a staff meeting and spends the drive home replaying it. Their work stays excellent. That is exactly the problem.
I am a licensed clinical social worker, and the people I see most often in this situation are not short on money, insurance or information. They are short on one thing: a way to get help that nobody at work will ever hear about.
The research on attorneys makes that point more clearly than anything else I know. The largest study of lawyer mental health, published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine in 2016, screened 12,825 licensed, employed attorneys. When the authors asked why people had not sought help, the two most common answers were not wanting others to find out and concerns about privacy or confidentiality. Among attorneys who had been in treatment, about half named the first reason.
That finding has held up. A 2026 research paper by my firm, CEREVITY, works through the decade of studies that followed and notes that the headline numbers vary with the method used. The fear of exposure is the one finding that shows up every time someone asks the question, in attorneys and in law students alike.
Doctors and senior executives carry the same calculation. A physician wonders who at the hospital will see the claim. A chief financial officer pictures the board hearing about it. A partner thinks about origination credit and what the firm did the last time someone admitted they were struggling. Each person decides, usually quickly and usually alone, that the safer move is to wait.
Here is what that waiting looks like in practice, in a composite drawn from common patterns rather than any one person. A Kansas City executive notices in January that she is lying awake at 3 a.m. By spring she is canceling lunches and rereading emails four times before sending them. By late summer a colleague asks if she is OK, and she says she is just busy. She finally calls someone in the fall, after a panic attack in a parking garage. The care she gets then is harder and slower than it would have been in January.
Missouri already has a piece of the answer, and it deserves more attention. The Missouri Bar’s lawyers’ assistance program offers counseling and referrals to every lawyer and judge in the state at no cost, and the Bar states plainly that its services are confidential and that reaching out does not affect a lawyer’s license. That last sentence matters more than any brochure. It answers the exact question that keeps people away.
Three changes would extend that logic beyond the bar.
First, employers should say the confidentiality promise out loud, in writing and from the top. A benefit nobody trusts is a benefit nobody uses. If a hospital system, law firm or company in St. Louis or Kansas City offers counseling, its leaders should spell out who can see what, and who cannot.
Second, boards and managing partners should stop treating a request for help as a performance signal. The people most likely to hide strain are the ones whose standing depends on looking unshakable. If the first person to admit difficulty gets quietly passed over, everyone else learns the lesson.
Third, professionals themselves should stop waiting for a crisis to make the decision for them. Early signs are ordinary: broken sleep, short temper, more alcohol, less patience with family. Help works best at that stage, before the panic attack in the parking garage. Confidential options exist, including burnout therapy for leaders delivered by video, and many people never need to tell their employer anything at all.
Missouri asks a lot of the people who run its hospitals, courtrooms and companies. The least the state’s institutions can do is make sure the help they offer is help those people will actually use. That starts with taking the fear of being found out as seriously as the people feeling it do.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Mom of 10 wins $11.3M verdict after insurer denied husband’s COVID death claim
text:
Vaneza Ramos, husband Jose Gaytan and one of their children at a ribbon cutting ceremony for their second La Michoacana store along the South Omaha 24th Street corridor. (Courtesy of Pesek Law)OMAHA  — Vaneza Ramos said she felt a sense of peace and vindication upon hearing a jury verdict that awarded her $11.3 million in a case against an insurance company that denied a claim after her husband died of COVID-19.
Beyond the dollar value, she and the couple’s 10 children are happy to see their dad’s reputation affirmed, as she said he was portrayed as a liar.
La Michoacana at 4002 S. 24th St. in South Omaha was Jose Gaytan’s first paleta store. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“It was really difficult,” Ramos said of the loss of her husband during a pandemic and with a house filled with children asking for their father. “Physically and emotionally, we’re now more stable,” though the economy has made times tough, she added.
Her husband, Jose Gaytan, died May 31, 2020 — just 20 days after Ramos gave birth to their last baby. Farmers New World Life Insurance rejected their $350,000 life insurance claim, saying Gaytan had a history of a heart attack and that a post-death investigation showed he failed to disclose the medical condition on his application. 
The company instead tried to send a $17,360 check, the amount Gaytan had paid into the policy.
Not only did a Douglas County jury side earlier this year with Ramos on the value of the policy — but a second jury on Oct. 16 said Farmers should pay the $11.3 million for bad-faith damages. 
Her lawyer, Ross Pesek, said the award should provide some material relief to the South Omaha family that managed without the life insurance benefit to keep afloat their La Michoacana frozen dessert and diner businesses following the death of owner and head of household Gaytan.
Pesek said the jury factored in emotional distress and financial hardship when determining an amount. The family’s truck was repossessed. She fell behind on vendor bills, impacting their business reputation. Her mother moved in to help; an 18-year-old son set his plans aside to work at the business. They borrowed money.
Pesek called the case — believed to be a state rarity as a life insurance jury case involving a COVID death — a win also for “civil justice.”
He referenced the biblical story of David and Goliath to emphasize an imbalance of power between a widow raising 10 children, two with special needs, and one of the nation’s largest multiline insurance groups that has resources to “delay, deny, defend” for years.
“It shows there can be justice in our community and justice in our world,” Pesek said.
Expanding business, family
Raised in Coahuila, Mexico, Gaytan arrived in the U.S. seeking a better future and in 2008 opened his first ice cream shop, which operates mobile paleta carts as well, on the South Omaha commercial corridor.
Inside La Michoacana Nevería y Paleta at 4924 S. 24th St. This is the second location opened by Jose Gaytan, along with wife, Vaneza Ramos. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
He and his wife, Vaneza, blended a family, each bringing two children to their 2009 marriage before having six more children together. The couple opened a second store in the area and also distributed their frozen treats to other merchants. Ramos told friends her husband wanted a big family. He lived to see their youngest son born on May 11, 2020.
Gaytan had not been feeling well and died May 31 after being hospitalized for a few days. He was 55  years old. COVID-19 was the cause, according to the death certificate. 
In September 2020, Farmers declined to pay the $350,000 policy. 
Ramos’ team argued that the information Farmers identified as faulty on the application was provided by its own agent, Michael Powers. Pesek said Powers had previously sold Gaytan a life insurance policy from another company, then approached him about changing to Farmers. 
Ramos produced a text message chain between her and Powers, which showed the agent knew Gaytan was hospitalized for his heart in August 2018. According to court transcripts, Powers said he thought Gaytan had “heartburn,” not a heart attack. 
Attorneys for Ramos argued further that Farmers had conducted a medical history exam as part of her husband’s application, and that his medication and conditions were disclosed. 
“Anyone with Google knows that lisinopril is used to improve survival after a heart attack,” Ramos said in court records. “Farmers cannot say they didn’t know my husband had a heart attack.”
The attack happened a few months before the Farmers life insurance policy took effect and about two years before Gaytan died of COVID. 
The Farmers legal team did not respond to a request for comment, or to say whether the insurance provider would appeal. Powers could not be reached for comment.
Long, twisty road
The case has gone through a number of court actions. Initially, District Court Judge Katie Benson granted summary judgment in favor of Farmers and Powers. A state appeals court, however, returned the case to Douglas County District Court for further proceedings.
Pesek Law attorneys Ross Pesek and Alejandra Ayotitla represented an Omaha mother of 10 in a life insurance trial case against Farmers Insurance. (Courtesy of Pesek Law)
The first jury in March subsequently found that Farmers breached the insurance contract, rejecting the allegation of fraudulent misrepresentation. The second jury this month considered whether the insurer acted in bad faith and put a monetary figure on harm caused, said Pesek, who represented Ramos along with Alejandra Ayotitla, both of South Omaha-based Pesek Law.
Other attorneys represented Ramos earlier.
Pesek, who represents many Spanish-speaking clients, said the verdict confirmed his faith in peer juries “delivering high-quality justice that is free from racial prejudice and bias.”
He said Wednesday that Ramos has not yet been paid and that he admires his client’s strength.
The family business was challenged during the pandemic and later amid general community apprehension about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in South Omaha, Ramos said. She said ICE activities have led to reduced shopping and commercial activity in the area. 
At one point in 2023, Ramos testified before a Nebraska legislative committee on pandemic-related relief for North and South Omaha. She teared up then as she spoke about her husband and his death, which she said set back plans for their future.
Family ‘recovering’ 
Pesek said the jury decision was “validating and restorative” for the family but that it continues to recover from the loss of Gaytan.
Omaha’s South 24th Street corridor includes two La Michoacana stores featuring frozen treats. This is the exterior of 4924 S. 24th St., which Vaneza Ramos has continued operating after the 2020 death of her husband and business partner. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Isaac, born just before his dad’s death, is now six years old Bryan, at 24, continues to help with the family business but testified that someday he’d like to open his own business in a skilled trade such as plumbing. 
Wednesday afternoon, both La Michoacana locations were open, with customers trickling in and throughout the South Omaha business corridor.
Ramos said she plans to continue the family business and keep life as normal as possible for her children.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ hospitals gave $7.8 billion in free care, services, report says
text:
Hospitals in New Jersey provided $7.8 billion in community services in 2024, a new report shows, things like free care, donated time, and community screenings. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor.)Hospitals in New Jersey provided $7.8 billion in free care, no-cost screenings, research, and other community benefits in 2024, according to the latest annual report released by their trade group.
The New Jersey Hospital Association’s community benefit report, which covered 59 nonprofit acute care facilities, shows these providers committed 21% of every dollar spent to programs like free mammograms, heart-disease screenings, mental health clinics, healthy food, and more. In all, they funded more than 90,000 community events and 42 million individual interactions with New Jerseyans.
Cathy Bennett, the group’s president and CEO, said the real measure of the benefit is the lives that were improved.
“This commitment is demonstrated every single day – in a free health screening that identifies a serious health condition before it becomes a crisis; in school-based programming that sparks a career pathway for students; in research that provides new hope for current and future patients; and free and discounted healthcare services for those in need,” she said.
New Jersey is home to some 70 hospitals that received more than $3.2 billion in public funding in the current state budget. According to the new report, the 59 facilities surveyed generated $37.4 billion in economic impact overall and employed some 172,000 residents. That’s up from $31.4 billion and 160,000 jobs in 2023, per their previous report. 
In 2024, community benefit spending included more than $5 billion in unpaid care and nearly $1.5 billion in subsidized health services, or care provided at a loss to the hospital, the report notes. Nearly $602 million went to educating health professionals— for scholarships, internships, and training —  and more than $100 million was spent on community health programs, like blood-pressure clinics. Another $472 million was allocated for supplies, equipment, or donated staff time, it says.
The work includes a program run by Hackensack Meridian Health to help people identify and lower their heart-disease risk. RWJ Barnabas runs a healthy communities program that uses community health workers to connect people to services. Atlantic Health hosts a free mental health program for veterans, University Hospital in Newark operates a mobile mammogram clinic, and Inspira works with local pharmacies to provide free meds to people who can’t afford their prescriptions.
“Each of these contributions is an investment in good health, with the potential to change the lives of the individual and strengthen health across New Jersey,” the report notes.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: A legitimate independent contractor should actually be independent
text:
A company should not be able to make someone an independent contractor simply by putting those words on a piece of paper, argues Charles Wowkanech of the New Jersey State AFL-CIO. (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)Working people in New Jersey are getting squeezed from every direction.
The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, utilities, and almost everything else remains too high. Federal policies are pulling back investments working families depend on. New Jersey is fortunate to have recently elected a pro-worker governor who cares about these issues, but there are limits to what any state can do when federal policy is moving in the opposite direction.
At the same time, something quieter but just as consequential is happening in the workplace: more corporations are trying to turn jobs into gigs.
For generations, a job came with certain basic understandings. If you worked for a company, that company had responsibilities to you. It followed wage-and-hour laws. It paid into unemployment and disability systems. It carried workers’ compensation. Workers had protections if they were hurt, lost a job, or were denied wages they had earned.
Increasingly, some corporations and business lobbyists want a different arrangement: the company gets the work, while the worker carries the risk.
No employee. No employer. Just an ever-growing universe of so-called “independent contractors.”
That should concern every working person in New Jersey — and every taxpayer.
This debate is often discussed in connection with ride-share and delivery work, where abuse of workers is widespread.  But it is much bigger than those industries. Worker classification affects construction, trucking, nursing, healthcare, cleaning services, logistics, and many other corners of the economy.
The app-based transportation industry is one of the nation’s biggest offenders of classification laws. Here in New Jersey, Uber paid a $100 million fine in 2022, but admitted no guilt, so they continue to operate using the same labor model. Lyft paid the state of New Jersey $19.4 million in 2025 to resolve allegations that the company misclassified its drivers. Via, the state’s largest micro-transit contractor, was investigated and audited by the New Jersey Department of Labor and was subsequently fined over $1.5 million in April of this year for misclassifying their drivers and for failing to pay into essential worker protection programs, including unemployment and temporary disability funds. 
The New Jersey Department of Labor and Attorney General’s Office are currently in the process of auditing Amazon Flex, which began in 2025. These are massive, multimillion-dollar businesses that could easily afford to follow the law and not exploit their workers. But they chose not to, simply to further increase profits.
New Jersey has an important protection against that race to the bottom: the ABC test.
The principle is straightforward. A legitimate independent contractor should actually be independent. A company should not be able to make someone an independent contractor simply by putting those words on a piece of paper.
The principle behind New Jersey’s employment protections is as necessary as ever: Businesses should not be able to avoid basic responsibilities to workers simply by changing the label attached to the work.
There is a reason classification matters. Employee status is connected to real responsibilities and real protections — minimum wage and overtime, unemployment insurance, temporary disability, earned sick leave, workers’ compensation, and other safeguards.
When companies improperly push those responsibilities off their books, the costs do not disappear.
They move.
They move onto workers and their families. They move onto responsible employers that continue playing by the rules. And eventually they move onto taxpayers and public programs.
Working families are already being boxed in by high costs, economic uncertainty, shrinking public investment, and an increasingly precarious labor market. The answer cannot be to make stable jobs and basic workplace protections even harder to find.
New Jersey’s employment protections were built over generations because working people understood what happens when the balance of power in the workplace becomes too lopsided.
Technology changes. Business models change. The economy changes.
But some principles endure.
When someone is truly running an independent business, the law should recognize that independence.
And when a company is using classification simply to shed responsibilities to workers and the public, New Jersey should be enforcing the important laws it already has on the books, while also expanding and protecting the freedom of workers to join unions for a better life.
A job should still be a job in New Jersey.

name: WyoFile
title: Proposition 1 will test Wyoming’s tax relief appetite. Here’s what you need to know.
text:
Wyoming’s first citizens initiative to land on the ballot in 30 years has stirred up a contentious fight, pitting property tax relief against local government funding for essential services. 
Proposition 1, also known as The People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption, landed on the Nov. 3 general election ballot with the backing of more than 30,000 valid signatures collected around the state. If passed, it will exempt 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value from property taxation, causing Wyoming’s annual property tax revenues to decrease by an estimated $92.6 million to $124.8 million.
The initiative was among a raft of efforts to relieve property owners after COVID-era real estate trends inflated residential values and associated taxes. Some of those efforts have already borne fruit, including a 2025 bill to create a 25% exemption on the first $1 million of a primary residence’s fair market value.
That measure shrank 2025 revenue pools for public education, municipalities and special districts such as hospitals. Some county governments implemented hiring freezes and mandated departmental budget cuts. Other entities closed libraries and stopped maintaining parks. Many dipped into reserves. 
These impacts have been cast as cautionary tales — examples of painful consequences brought on by tax cuts. Over the last year, a chorus of opposition has swelled against Proposition 1 — voices that include county treasurers, fire chiefs, education advocates and perhaps most notably, prominent Republicans. If Proposition 1 passes, they say, the damages will spiral out of control. 
“The reduction by 50% would have an immediate and devastating effect on the services most Wyoming citizens rely upon in their communities,” Gov. Mark Gordon wrote in an op-ed opposing Proposition 1. Calling it “tax reform” is inaccurate, he wrote. “Tax reform is fundamentally different from destroying a tax base or relying on the legislature to fund essential services.”
Basin Library Manager Jen Lindgren shelves a book in September 2025. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
Proposition 1’s supporters, including many who align with the far-right Wyoming Freedom Caucus, say misinformation capitalizing on fear has blown the impact of the tax reduction out of proportion.
Opponents are leaving out important nuances such as the fact that the residential property tax cut won’t apply to property tax categories like mineral, industrial, agricultural and commercial, former state representative and Proposition 1 advocate Marti Halverson said. As for the predictions of hardships, she said, they don’t ring true. 
“When you look at all the revenues that have been hoarded by counties and special districts and cities and towns all over the state since 2019, I am not buying it that anyone has cut anything to the bone,” she said. 
Heightened rhetoric on both sides of the issue has many voters curious about where the truth lies and what’s at stake. Tax systems are complicated, and factors like assessment fluctuations and owner opt-in rates make it impossible to pin down Proposition 1’s exact implications. 
That said, understanding the context around both sides’ arguments can help voters decide whether to vote yes or no. Here are three things to know about Proposition 1 before you go to the polls. 
Tax bills spiked, then came reform efforts.
Wyoming residents have a relatively low tax burden and no income tax, due largely to the state’s reliance on severance taxes on mineral extraction. 
Homeowners do pay residential property taxes. Those residential taxes are pooled with property taxes from minerals, industrial sites, agricultural land and more, and the generated revenues help fund K-12 public schools, county government, special districts, community colleges, along with cities and towns. 
During the COVID pandemic, so-called “Zoomers” — newly untethered from their offices — flooded into the Mountain West, snapping up homes, creating more demand and fueling home price increases. That resulted in spiking tax bills for some Wyoming homeowners; increases varied by county. In Park County, the average homeowner saw their tax bills jump over 60% in three years.
The sticker shock that ensued helped trigger a wide-ranging relief effort. In October of 2023, two-time gubernatorial candidate Brent Bien, along with his former campaign manager Rich Weber and former Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar, secured approval to begin collecting signatures to get a 50% exemption on the ballot, with no cap on the value.
Some condominiums at Teton Village, the base of the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, are valued at more than $7 million and subject to annual property taxes of almost $50,000. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Bien did not respond to WyoFile’s request for an interview, but in a recent conversation with The Talk Shop radio host Eric Henderson, Weber said the measure intends to protect homeowners on fixed incomes who cannot afford ever-mounting tax bills. Weber likened claims of service cuts and closures to “crying wolf,” calling those warnings “phony baloney.”
Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative in January 2025 after verifying more than 30,000 signatures. More than 50% of voters will need to vote yes for it to pass. 
The numbers indicate high interest — at least when the signature collecting was happening between late 2023 and early 2025. Wyoming lawmakers also passed several property tax relief measures after signature collecting began, including a 25% homeowner exemption and a 50% long-term homeowner exemption.
The latter efforts have already achieved property tax relief, Proposition 1 opponents argue. Further cuts Proposition 1 would impose, they say, are reckless. In his op-ed, Gordon likened it to cutting “the legs out from under communities and counties.”
County and special district officials are scared. Proponents say this is a ‘chicken little’ tactic.
Residential property tax collections dropped from $656 million in 2024 to $535 million in 2025, according to the Wyoming Taxpayers Association. 
That amounted to smaller revenues for county administrators, hospital districts and others. Cities reduced park maintenance, libraries closed, agencies charged more for subsidized childcare, smaller crews reduced weed spraying and department heads implemented hiring freezes. 


In Fremont County, administrators cut $2.5 million from the budget, which entailed trimming costs for courthouse security, increasing fees and slashing the library budget — an action that angered many locals.
During fraught budget discussions, county officials warned that Proposition 1 would only exacerbate the situation and lead to outcomes like library branch closures. If it passes, Commission Chair Larry Allen said in a meeting, “we’re looking at over a third of our budget just disappearing.” 
That became a common refrain among county treasurers, fire chiefs and education advocates. Consequences, they warned, will include fire station closures, less manpower for emergency responses and smaller budgets for road and bridge infrastructure, community colleges and public schools. 
“If Prop 1 passes, nearly every county in Wyoming, except mineral-rich counties and counties with wealthy homeowners, will face serious reductions in funding for police, fire, EMS, hospitals, and road and sewer infrastructure,” according to the Wyoming Taxpayers Association.
This kind of rhetoric does not sway proponents like Halverson, who argue that county officials are capable of finding responsible cuts without having to axe critical services and that both state and local governments have flush reserves. 
“The sky is not falling,” she said. 
Wyoming’s 23 counties vary in their reserve amounts; mineral-rich counties generally have healthier savings. The state, meanwhile, has a robust “rainy day fund” of more than $1 billion, but its function is not to backfill local tax shortfalls, opponents say. 
Anti-Proposition 1 messaging has ignored the measure’s nuances, Halverson said, such as the fact that homeowners would have to opt in to get the exemption, they must prove primary-residence status and that it only applies to the residential property structure, not the land it sits on. 
In a video posted to the Wyoming Freedom Caucus Facebook page, Wheatland Republican Rep. Jeremy Haroldson clarified many of those facts. 
“Prop 1 is simply a targeted property tax exemption for qualified homeowners, not a 50% government cut,” Haroldson said. 
The opposition movement has grown and includes many Republicans.
The Wyoming Education Association, Wyoming Hospital Association, Wyoming Association of Community College Trustees, Wyoming Realtors and Wyoming Taxpayers Association all oppose Proposition 1, creating a formidable alliance.
The measure “is not justified and not fiscally prudent,” the taxpayers association wrote in an op-ed, and it stands to hobble counties by slashing revenue with no plan to replace the losses. 
The “Vote No on Prop 1” PAC is well-resourced. Campaign finance filings show nearly $2 million in contributions; the National Education Association has donated $1.4 million. Bien, Weber and Aguiar’s PAC, BCR Voter Initiatives, meanwhile, reported contributions of less than $4,000. 
The Wyoming Republican Party endorsed Proposition 1. But prominent Republicans have joined the opposition. Long-serving lawmakers like Sen. Ogden Driskill, R-Devils Tower, and Rep. Lloyd Larsen, R-Lander, signed an op-ed against it. Gubernatorial candidate Eric Barlow and Steve Harshman, who is running for Superintendent of Public Instruction, also expressed opposition. 
In this way, Proposition 1 has become another arena in the Wyoming Republican Party’s fracture, with the Freedom Caucus bloc splintering from more moderately conservative Republicans.
A man leaves the patient entrance of Ivinson Memorial Hospital in Laramie in March 2020. Albany County Hospital District owns and operates the facility. (Andrew Graham/WyoFile)
After years of consolidating power in Wyoming’s Legislature, the Freedom Caucus in August lost majority control of the House and backslid in the Senate, which many say indicates a backlash. 
In a newsletter that elaborated on her reasons for opposing Proposition 1, Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, posited that the tax measure is “the last relic of a failed agenda.
“The Freedom Caucus used the COVID-era spike in home values to push for slashing property taxes,” wrote Storer, a member of the Legislature’s Revenue Committee. “In August, Republican voters rejected these extremists. Proposition One belongs on the trash heap with the rest of that agenda.”
(Storer is the president and CEO of the George B. Storer Foundation, a financial supporter of WyoFile. The foundation has no role in WyoFile’s editorial content.)
