title: Who is responsible for Yellowstone’s water quality? After whiplash between Biden and Trump, EPA says Wyoming.
text:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Gov. Mark Gordon have struck a deal over Clean Water Act enforcement in America’s first national park. But what led up to the deal unfolded largely out of public view.
A new era of “concurrent jurisdiction” where Wyoming takes the lead in Yellowstone National Park was announced last week alongside a photo of Burgum and Gordon shaking hands. 
“This is a proper and practical acknowledgement of the exceptional partnership of Wyoming’s DEQ and the National Park Service,” Gordon said in a statement. 
Burgum tipped his hat to his boss. President Donald Trump has prioritized “cutting red tape and putting decisions closer to the people they impact,” the Interior secretary said. 
“The people of Wyoming know its land and water better than Washington ever could,” Burgum said, “and the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality has proven it has the expertise and commitment to protect its own water resources.” 

Gov. Mark Gordon and U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum congratulate themselves on a deal struck to let the state Department of Environmental Quality administer the Clean Water Act in Yellowstone National Park. (Office of Gov. Mark Gordon)

Not included in the press release were details about several years of regulatory changes and disputes that preceded the deal. For over a half century leading up until 2023, the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality took the lead on regulating water quality matters in Yellowstone National Park. That year, the Biden administration’s Environmental Protection Agency asserted that Yellowstone and 15 other national parks were “lands of exclusive federal jurisdiction” where the EPA ought to instead have the reins. The other national parks included Denali, Mount Rainier, Olympic, Hot Springs, Hawai’i Volcanoes, Yosemite, Sequoia, Crater Lake, Glacier, Rocky Mountain, Mesa Verde, Lassen Volcanic, Great Smoky Mountains, Mammoth Cave and Isle Royale.
The changes centered on sections 401 and 402 of the act, which concern point-source pollutants and discharges such as wastewater. In 2025, EPA also extended its jurisdiction in Yellowstone to include surface water quality standards.
Three industry groups and affected states, including Wyoming, weren’t happy about losing jurisdiction. In December 2023, they sued, asking a federal judge out of Louisiana’s Western District for an injunction that would prevent the change from happening.
“States, such as Wyoming, have a longstanding history of issuing 401 certifications for discharges originating within national parks located within the state’s boundaries,” the lawsuit stated. “Wyoming, for example, has issued 401 certifications in Yellowstone National Park since 1973 when Congress specifically gave States the authority to issue certifications within state boundaries.” 
The states’ injunction request was denied. U.S. District Court Judge James Cain, a Trump appointee, agreed with the EPA that the “public interest is best served” by allowing the changes to remain in effect while the court weighed the case. 
A final ruling never happened. In early 2025, the case was suspended to let the EPA review the issue early in the second Trump administration. This year the administration proposed and finalized regulatory changes to section 401 of the Clean Water Act, which was at the center of the legal dispute. 
Although the Trump administration’s recent rule changes did not address national parks of “exclusive federal jurisdiction” such as Yellowstone, Burgum and Gordon’s agreement marks at least a temporary resolution to the issue in Wyoming. 
The plan to hand authority back to Wyoming is being welcomed by the state’s Department of Environmental Quality, federal the Environmental Protection Agency and water quality watchdog groups. Jennifer Zygmunt, DEQ’s water quality division administrator, pointed out that there has never been any deficiencies identified with the job the state agency was doing in Yellowstone. 
Wyoming’s standards sometimes even extended beyond those imposed by the EPA, Zygmunt said. Under the state system, for example, all surface waters in Yellowstone and other national parks are managed as “outstanding resource waters” (formerly class 1), she said, whereas the EPA did not have the same classification.
For that reason, the Wyoming Outdoor Council’s Lindsey Washkoviak called the planned resumption of Wyoming authority over Yellowstone waters a “good move.”
“DEQ has historically managed water quality in the park, and their rules are much more clearly defined than the federal government’s,” Washkoviak said in a statement. “The state classifies all of Yellowstone’s waters as ‘outstanding resources waters’ — meaning they are pristine and cannot be polluted past a certain level. When the federal government took over management of Yellowstone’s water quality last year, it was not clear whether EPA would honor that designation.” 
Under EPA’s jurisdiction, there was a “worrisome loophole” that could have led to Yellowstone waters becoming more polluted, she said. 

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 8 Administrator Cyrus Western. (EPA)

EPA Region 8 Administrator Cyrus Western, a former state lawmaker, told WyoFile that the agreement with Wyoming is an example of “cooperative federalism” that the Trump administration has emphasized. 
“The state has done it, they know how to do it and they’ve got the staff on hand that have the skills and competency to handle it,” Western said. “So let’s figure out a way to do it — and ultimately, that’s exactly what happened.” 
The EPA and DEQ’s draft agreement about the administration of Yellowstone waters has not been made public, but was submitted to Congress for a 60-day review on Oct. 16. Public input is not part of the process. 
Congress does not vote on or approve the decision, but the two-month window allows lawmakers to raise any questions or concerns. After that, the Interior Department will finalize it. 
The agreement calls for “concurrent jurisdiction.” But Wyoming will be taking the lead in terms of on-the-ground work and permitting, Western said. 
“Wyoming is the permit writer for these discharge permits,” he said. “All the kind of quality checks that happen throughout the permit writing process, that’s all DEQ.”
The post Who is responsible for Yellowstone’s water quality? After whiplash between Biden and Trump, EPA says Wyoming.  appeared first on WyoFile .

title: What’s in a hat?
text:
Opinion

We’re in the final stretch of this election season, thank God. It’s a hallowed and important part of life in a republic like ours. I think you can make the argument that it’s even more important in a thinly populated state like ours. That said, it ain’t always pretty. Sometimes it is, as my old friend Jack Streeter used to say, “uglier than nine miles of muddy road.” 
Since Democrats are somewhat scarce in the Cowboy State, the Republican primary election is a big deal here. And if the spending of the candidates and their supporters is any indication, it’s also an expensive deal. But I’ll leave that to the political pundits and focus instead on something that caught my attention: hats.
Somewhere along the line, advisors to the trust fund babies and political refugees seeking public office in Wyoming got the idea that if you sent an AI-generated image of the candidate wearing a western hat to the voters, they would reciprocate with a vote on Aug. 18. If you sent the voters one of those every day for a month, that vote would be a sure thing. It was a strategy born inside the Beltway and destined to fail. 
Nothing looks worse than some pilgrim running for office in an ill-fitting hat. It reeks of artifice at best, cheap manipulation at worst. What’s next? Rodeo buckles? Bull cutter knives?  Woolly chaps? But at least for now, it’s hats. Always a hat. And that started me thinking. 
As near as I can tell, the men in my family have always been men with hats. Part of it, no doubt, comes from being caught between a genetic rock and a climatic hard spot. We are outdoor men in a sunny climate who still bear the fair skin of our German and English ancestors. Consequently, in order to avoid being burned to a cinder from the top down, we wear hats. Let me illustrate:
The elder Walt Gasson on horseback, who came to Wyoming as a young boy from Iowa in the late 1800s. (Photo courtesy of Walt Gasson)
Above is my grandfather Walt Gasson, born in Iowa in 1875 and transplanted to Wyoming as a little tyke. He was a ‘stockman” who summered his sheep in the Wyoming Range near Commissary Ridge and wintered them in the high desert country south of Rock Springs. It called for a lot of time in the saddle, riding from camp to camp, bringing supplies to the herders. He wore a hat that was the real article — weather-beaten and battered, with a low crown and a wide brim to shelter him from the sun and ever-present wind. 
If you look very closely, you can see that he’s also wearing a neckerchief to protect his neck and gloves to protect his hands. No skin cancer for old Walt Gasson. Like all the stockmen of the time, he covered every square inch of skin with something. It was a pity all that protective gear couldn’t shield him from the influenza epidemic of 1918 that killed him. 
My dad is in the picture below, fishing in the Wind Rivers in 1960. Gus, the son of Walt Gasson the sheep rancher, was never very far from his stockman’s roots. And he was never very far from his hat. This one was his favorite. It was a Resistol with a flat crown and a tightly curled brim, in the style of the day. He wore it for years, and like all favorite hats, it grew battered and sweat-stained. My mother tried to get him to buy a new one, but he loved that hat. Like his father, he died young. A heart attack killed him seven years after this photo was taken. I remember coming home once to find my mom sitting in the big chair by the bay window. She was holding that hat and silently crying. 
Gus, the son of Walt Gasson the sheep rancher and father of the author, fishing in the Wind Rivers in the 1960s wearing hig signature Resistol hat. (Photo courtesy of Walt Gasson)
And the third picture is me this past summer. And sure enough, I’m wearing a hat. Being a Gasson male, I never go out without one.  That one is a twelve-year-old Stetson straw with a wide brim and a Gus crease in the crown. Like me, it’s got a lot of miles on it. And I think it’s legit. Like the previous generations, there’s no artifice, no agenda — the hat is simply a part of who I am. 

The author, Walt Gasson, and Goose out for a ride this past summer. (Photo courtesy of Walt Gasson)

If you look at the photos of my grandfather, my father and me, you’ll notice something much more important than the hats we wear. All three photos are taken in the outdoors, in the mountains and deserts of Wyoming that we call home. We’re Wyoming guys — guys who hunt and fish and ride and feel best when we’re with family and friends in the great wide open, and sometimes when we’re all alone. 
Whenever I open the mailbox and see one of those campaign mailers that features some Wyoming wannabe in an ill-fitting lid that looks like it was purchased under the grandstands at Frontier Park, I mentally delete them as a serious candidate. In this era of artificial intelligence and media influence, your hat says a lot about you. If it’s an expression of who you are, then that comes through clearly. Think Mike Sullivan, JD Williams or Jim Byrd. If it’s just playing dress-up, that comes through clearly as well.  To borrow a line from The Lion King, “You must never go there, Simba.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Trump administration to send election monitors to Idaho’s largest county
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Cathedral of the Rockies in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The Trump administration is sending election monitors to Idaho’s largest county on Election Day next week, the state’s top election official confirmed Wednesday.
The decision comes as the Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors — who the DOJ says are meant to assess local compliance with federal voting rights laws — to all 50 states. That would make for a significantly expanded presence than under the Biden administration, which sent election monitors to 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections, States Newsroom reported. 
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, an elected Republican, said the U.S. Justice Department notified him and the Ada County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, that there will be two teams in Ada County on Election Day. Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, also a Republican, said around six election monitors who are local to Idaho will be stationed near polling places — but not inside.
In a statement, the Justice Department said its election monitors in Idaho and elsewhere will be “doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.”
“All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” a spokesperson for the federal agency told the Idaho Capital Sun.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho’s top election official called deployment ‘routine’

The federal election monitors in Idaho, McGrane said, will be ensuring that voters have access to voting and assisting the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, such as by ensuring polling places are abiding by disability access requirements under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or ADA. McGrane called it a routine measure. He said he last remembered election monitors sent to Idaho under the Obama administration.
In this file photo, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“I’m fairly sure we’ve had it under all (presidential) administrations in some form. I can most clearly remember ADA conversations when Obama was president. But it has been routine in the past,” McGrane said in an interview.
The Trump administration’s decision to expand election monitors in states for the midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, follows recent attempts by the administration to intervene in state election processes, such as to restrict mail-in voting and obtain state voter rolls. That history has left some officials across the country concerned about the expanded election monitoring efforts. But McGrane said he isn’t worried.
“I’ve seen the concerns among my peers and others nationally,” he said. “Initially, I wanted to understand and make sure what their mission was. After talking to … the new U.S. Attorney John Shirts … I feel reassured that this is something fairly routine. This is something that we’ve experienced before. And I don’t expect that voters will really even notice that it’s happening.”
Tripple said he isn’t worried either.
“They’ve done this before. It’s happened during multiple different administrations over the last couple of decades,” he said. “ Obviously, with the temperature around elections and a little bit of friction between states and the (Justice Department), I’m sure some will probably try to make hay out of this in terms of you know political wins on one side or the other. But it doesn’t bother us at all. … This will be a good opportunity for them to kind of see how elections should be run.”
McGrane said the election monitor teams in Idaho will be in plain clothes, and staffed by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho, which is a part of the Justice Department that oversees federal law enforcement in Idaho. The agency directed questions about the deployment to the Justice Department. 
Ada County, Idaho’s most populated county that is home to Boise, has the highest share of Democratic registered voters in the state. The county has more than a third, or 54,000, of the state’s 123,000 registered Democrats, according to VoteIdaho, a website run by the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office. Idaho is a Republican controlled state, with nearly 650,000 Republican voters and 251,000 unaffiliated voters. 
In the Nov. 3 election in Idaho, all Republican incumbents in statewide offices and congressional seats are facing challengers. 
 Idaho sent out more absentee ballots than in last midterm election, state data show

In the 2026 election, Idaho election officials have sent out more absentee ballots than during the last midterm election, in 2022, state data show. Midterm elections are when the president is not on the ballot, and midterms often have lower turnout than presidential elections.
Idaho election officials have issued 156,794 absentee ballots for the 2026 general election, according to data on VoteIdaho. That’s more than the state sent out in the 2022 general election, when nearly 138,500 absentee ballots were issued. This year’s absentee turnout is still lower than the last presidential election, in 2024, when more than 188,000 absentee ballots were issued.
The recent uptick in Idaho follows a national trend of a surge of early and absentee voting, States Newsroom reported. 
McGrane, Idaho’s top election official, said some election officials believe the turnout might be driven by a ballot initiative that seeks to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. But he cautioned that it isn’t clear yet whether the higher absentee ballot numbers will translate into higher than usual turnout for a midterm election. 
So far, more than 98,000 absentee ballots in Idaho have been returned. To count, absentee ballots are due to election offices by the time polls close on Election Day. More than 94,000 ballots have also been cast in Idaho through early voting.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Buttigieg, Colorado Democrats rally in Boulder ahead of pivotal midterm elections
text:
U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, left, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg rally Democratic voters at the Boulder Theater on Wednesday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)After an unprecedented eight years in full control of state government, Colorado Democrats are confident they’re days away from not just keeping their grip on power, but turning the state a deeper shade of blue than ever.

On stage at the Boulder Theater Wednesday night, the state’s top Democratic leaders rallied the party faithful in a series of speeches that doubled as a line of succession for the state’s highest offices: Outgoing Attorney General Phil Weiser was introduced by the candidate hoping to succeed him as attorney general, Secretary of State Jena Griswold, who was in turn introduced by Jefferson County Clerk Amanda Gonzalez, the candidate hoping to succeed Griswold as the state’s top elections official.
All three, along with Democratic treasurer candidate Jeff Bridges, are favored to win their races on Election Day, Nov. 3. Democrats in the state Legislature, meanwhile, are eyeing a two-thirds supermajority in both houses. And Colorado Democratic Party Chair Shad Murib said a once-unthinkable 8-0 split of the state’s seats in the U.S. House of Representatives is in the party’s grasp.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Every single Republican-held congressional district (in Colorado) is on the priority list to flip,” Murib said to cheers at the rally. “We are the only state in the country that gets to say that, and it’s because of what you all have done. That means we can win the majority in the House right here in Colorado.”
“We have the opportunity to put this country on a better path forward — to not only do that, but to hold Donald Trump accountable, and then go on to win the White House in 2028,” Murib added.
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, widely considered a likely contender for Democrats’ 2028 presidential nomination, headlined the rally, hosted by Rep. Joe Neguse, whose 2nd Congressional District includes Boulder.
“We can have better leadership in this country,” Buttigieg said. “We can have nice things in the United States of America, and Colorado has some great candidates showing us what that leadership looks like.”
Neguse and Buttigieg made stops earlier in the day in Thornton, where former state legislator Manny Rutinel is challenging incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in one of the country’s top House battlegrounds, and in Douglas County, where Democrat Eileen Laubacher hopes to pull off an upset over Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s most heavily Republican district.



Quotation







We can have better leadership in this country ... We can have nice things in the United States of America, and Colorado has some great candidates showing us what that leadership looks like.


– Pete Buttigieg, former Transportation secretary


Nationally, pollsters and election forecasters rate the Democrats as strong favorites to win back control of the House — and a surprising number of competitive races in traditionally deep-red states like Texas, Alaska and Kansas have put the Senate in play, too, as voters turn sharply against the Trump administration over cost of living concerns, the war in Iran and other issues.
“You deserve better than the likes of Gabe Evans and Lauren Boebert and (5th District Rep.) Jeff Crank, and whoever this guy is they found to run against Phil Weiser,” Buttigieg told the crowd, referring to Republican governor candidate Victor Marx. “You deserve better, and you’re going to get better.”
Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a candidate for attorney general, and Jefferson County Clerk Amanda Gonzalez, a candidate for secretary of state, appeared on stage at the Boulder Theater on Wednesday to rally Democratic voters ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Boulder residents Nancy Portnoy and Joel Silverman left Wednesday’s rally feeling energized.
“I’m just hoping every single person up there wins, and we’re doing everything we can to make sure that happens,” said Portnoy, who is phone-banking for Rutinel in the home stretch of the campaign. “I show up at all the meetings. My wish is to get more people off their butt.”
“What (Trump) is doing to this country, and how he and his friends — people who can get money off of him — what they are doing to enrich themselves at the expense of this country, it’s a crime,” Silverman said.
No ‘back to normal’
Colorado Democrats haven’t lost a statewide election since President Donald Trump first won the presidency in 2016, and they’ve had total control of state executive offices and the Legislature since the 2018 midterms — the longest sustained period of one-party rule in state history. In recent elections they’ve made inroads in traditionally conservative areas like Douglas County and Colorado Springs, where Crank faces a tough challenge from Democrat Jessica Killin in a race that the national party has prioritized.
In an interview, Buttigieg said the balance that Colorado Democrats have struck between “civic equality, economic opportunity and personal liberty” is a model that the party can follow nationally to bring independents and former Republicans into the fold.
“The message I’m going to have in Boulder is not that different from the message I’m sharing in Mississippi,” Buttigieg said. “You can see how people from very different communities can respond to the same message, because people are up against the same problems. Especially when it comes to the cost of living.”
Buttigieg, a former mayor of South Bend, Indiana, placed fifth in the 2020 Democratic presidential primary before serving as Transportation Secretary during the Biden administration. In the aftermath of Trump’s first term, Democrats made a mistake, he said, in trying to go “back to normal.”
“It’s very important for Democrats to make clear that our project is not to restore some old status quo,” said Buttigieg. “It’s to move us into a different future that is better than the cruelty and the chaos of the Trump years — and also better than what we were dealing with before, which helped lead to the Trump years.”
Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democratic candidate for Colorado governor, rallies Democratic voters at the Boulder Theater on Wednesday ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Neguse, first elected in 2018 and now the fourth-ranking Democrat in the House, said that Democrats had pursued policies at the national level that were “unmoored from the daily concerns of most Americans,” while failing to pass anti-corruption measures, like a ban on congressional stock trading, that have a high degree of popular support.
“Passing an agenda that is very focused on tackling entrenched corruption, and then being able to advance some policies that make life easier for most Americans — that’s our our task,” Neguse said.
In the view of many loyal Democrats hoping to see their party take back Congress next week, aggressive oversight of the Trump administration should be firmly atop that anti-corruption agenda.
“I know they’ve said the first 100 hours is about affordability and gas prices and all that,” Silverman said. “But then they’ve got to start bringing in (Defense Secretary) Pete Hegseth. They’ve got to start bringing in all the all the people below Trump — to face Congress, and answer questions, and be held accountable.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee congressional candidate responds to allegations he sent unsolicited nude pics
text:
Sen. Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee for the 9th Congressional District, said allegations he sent nude pictures in the past were "youthful indiscretions." (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Republican congressional candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump dismissed accusations he sent nude pictures as “youthful indiscretions.”
In a story published Tuesday by the Nashville Scene, Sen. Brent Taylor stopped short of admitting to sending the pictures after more than one anonymous source said they had received or seen nude photos from him, including as recently as 2021. Taylor said he had been forgiven by his wife, Kimberly.
Asked Wednesday whether he sent nude pictures to anyone and, if so, whether they were unsolicited or consensual, Taylor told the Lookout by text he had “nothing relevant” to add to what he said in previous interviews.
But a Tennessee Democratic senator says she’s not surprised by allegations.
Sen. Charlane Oliver of Nashville, who sits behind Taylor on the Senate floor, said the accusations in the Nashville Scene report didn’t catch her off guard, considering how “crass” he is during meetings. 
The Scene published the article with only a week left before the Nov. 3 election in which Taylor is running against Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson of Memphis for the newly-drawn 9th Congressional District seat.
Out-of-state Dem govs with 2028 ambitions are working to boost TN US House candidates

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker’s Ready for the Fight PAC, which has already spent $1.6 million supporting Pearson, started running an attack ad against Taylor on Wednesday using the Scene article as its basis.
State Senate candidate David Weatherspoon, a Democrat running against Taylor in a separate state race, and state House candidate Jesse Huseth said Wednesday, if elected, they would file legislation to make “cyberflashing” a crime. Huseth, a Democrat, faces Republican Rep. John Gillespie in the House District 97 race. Tennessee has no punishment for sending unsolicited nude photos by text.
“Sending unwanted, sexually explicit photos is despicable, but especially so if it comes from a public servant,” Weatherspoon said in a release.
Taylor, a first-term senator from Eads in Shelby County, is known for making what he considers comical idioms on the Senate floor such as, “hanging in like a crackhead’s last tooth” and “working harder than an ugly stripper,” a comment that upset Oliver.
“His character is unbecoming of a congressperson,” she told the Lookout Wednesday.
Oliver said Taylor has been a “bully” toward her but hasn’t made any sexual comments. She said he also “doxxed” her on the Internet, which led to death threats. Taylor said Wednesday night he didn’t know what she was talking about.
“He would compliment me a lot, but also it would be coupled with micro-aggression,” Oliver said. “But no, I’ve never been made to feel uncomfortable around him.”
Senate Republican leaders declined to comment on the matter Wednesday, and other Democratic senators were tight-lipped.
Taylor said in the Scene article he was at one time a “rounder,” someone who hangs out at bars and gets into immoral activity, after an individual who requested anonymity out of concern about retaliation told the publication they got unsolicited nude photos from Taylor in 2021, before he won the state Senate seat. Another eyewitness confirmed the Taylor photo, according to the Scene report.
Sen. Charlane Oliver, a Nashville Democrat, said the accusations toward Sen. Brent Taylor didn’t catch her off guard, describing him as “crass.” (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Taylor has held himself out as a Christian while in the legislature, in addition to pushing legislation to remove Democratic District Attorney Steven Mulroy from office in Memphis, passing a state takeover of the Memphis City School Board and supporting the Memphis Safe Task Force, which has split the community.
His opponent, Pearson, issued a statement this week saying, “Men of faith — let alone men who are married, in their fifties, and in public office — have no business sending unsolicited nude photos to women.” Pearson said the news “reflects very disturbing behavior” from someone who has held public office since 1995. 
Taylor has served on the Memphis City Council, Shelby County Commission and Shelby County Election Commission.
Taylor told conservative radio talk show host Matt Murphy Tuesday that it was a consensual text communication, though he admitted it was “with somebody that I shouldn’t have been communicating with, and this is a result of it.”
Asked by Murphy if he would describe the matter as an extramarital affair, Taylor said, “Anytime you have a relationship with someone outside your marriage, that is problematic, and I’ve acknowledged that, and I’ve acknowledged it to my wife, and I regret that.”
Taylor said one of his biggest regrets is that his wife and two children have to deal with the matter.
The Southern Christian Coalition, a collection of progressive ministers, is calling for Taylor to say whether he would use a congressional seat to demand the release of the Epstein files and investigate allegations involving Trump. 
“If Brent Taylor is so casually dismissive of his own predatory conduct, can Tennesseans trust him to hold all of Epstein’s enablers accountable — even if the investigation leads to Trump?” the Rev. Gordon Myers said in a release.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: How would Tommy Tuberville govern Alabama?
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville recently released his plan for his first term, should he be elected, and it reflects the broader back-and-forth messaging of his campaign from the beginning. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


Key Points

U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican nominee for Alabama’s governor, is widely considered the favorite in Tuesday’s election against Democratic nominee Doug Jones, his predecessor in the U.S. Senate. 
Tuberville’s recently released “Playbook” – his first term agenda – sets ambitious goals for the Republican-controlled Legislature to achieve while maintaining fiscal responsibility.
While there is limited polling in the state, two Republican-leaning polls released last week show Tuberville up by more than 12 points, while a Democratic-leaning poll released Wednesday shows the race as a toss-up. 




U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican nominee for Alabama’s governor, embraced data centers earlier this year, calling community concerns “bull crap.” Then as opposition to the facilities mounted, he unveiled a plan to give communities more power and promised regulations. 
Earlier this month, he reaffirmed his support for the facilities, citing economic opportunity. In his recently-released policy plan, called the “Playbook,” he went back to the community-controlled model that he wrote about in his September column. 
“I’m changing how Alabama treats data centers. No more tax breaks. They go in the highest property tax class, pay the full cost of the power lines, substations, and water systems they need, and replace the power and water capacity they take,” the playbook says. “Local communities decide whether a data center is right for them, and if your community says no, my answer is no.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The data center issue reflects broader trends in the campaign: ambitious plans on a host of issues — including healthcare, education and sweeping audits of state government — often paired with back-and-forth messaging, all of which face the possibility of fiscal difficulties in Alabama’s budgets next year.  
Multiple messages seeking an interview with Tuberville, or a member of his staff, were left unanswered over the last two weeks. 
Tuberville remains the favorite to win the governor’s mansion in his contest with Democratic nominee Doug Jones, his predecessor in the U.S. Senate. Tuberville beat Jones in 2020 by 20 points after Jones was the first Democrat to win statewide office in two decades in 2017. 
Tuberville has maintained a financial edge over Jones throughout the race. Through Wednesday, Tuberville had raised $17.3 million since his campaign launch in May 2025 to Jones’ $6.8 million since his launch in December. Tuberville had about $2.3 million on hand to Jones’ $523,000. 
While Jones outraised and outspent Tuberville at the beginning of the month, the Republican nominee is catching up as Election Day grows near. In the third weekly report of October – the last before the campaigns began filing daily reports – Tuberville raised $704,000 and spent $2.2 million. Jones raised $219,000 and spent about $700,000. 
Campaigning around Alabama, Doug Jones tries to open a path for Democrats

Two recent polls showed a closing gap, but still predicted a comfortable Tuberville win. Both The Alabama Poll, run by Michael Lowry, a former aide to U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, and a poll conducted by the right-leaning Cygnal for Alabama Daily News and Gray Television found 51% of respondents said they would likely vote for Tuberville, and 39% for Jones, leaving about 9% undecided. The margin of error for each was 4% and 4.38%, respectively.
A poll released Wednesday by Democratic-leaning firm Blueprint Polling showed the race as a toss-up. It surveyed 695 likely Alabama voters between Oct. 22 and 24, 48% of whom indicated support for Tuberville and 45% for Jones, with 7% undecided. The poll has a 3.72% margin of error. 
David Hughes, a political science professor at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who previously spent time at Auburn University at Montgomery, said in a recent phone interview that a win for Tuberville will likely depend on turnout in rural counties and in the 2nd Congressional District, the state’s most competitive.
The district was redrawn after the Supreme Court weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in the Louisiana v. Callais decision this spring. 
The new district was rated R+7 and was expected to be a fairly easy Republican pick-up. But incumbent U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, has managed to outraise state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, and the Center for Politics moved the district from “Lean Republican” to “Toss-up” on Tuesday. 
“I’m really interested in what turnout is going to look like in Shomari Figures’ district. That, I think, will be pretty telling come election night of who’s turning out or not because that shouldn’t be a particularly competitive district, but it’s beginning to look very competitive,” Hughes said. 
Hughes said other important areas for Tuberville will be Madison, Shelby, Lee and Tuscaloosa counties. 
The Center for Politics also shifted its rating for the governor’s race from “Safe Republican” to “Likely Republican” last week. While most races between the U.S. House and Senate, and open governorships seem to be shifting towards Democrats, the center changed its rating for the Oregon governor’s race from “Likely Democratic” to “Leans Democratic” on Oct. 6. 
J. Miles Coleman, associate editor of the Center for Politics, said in a phone interview Tuesday that many of the center’s shifts, especially in governors’ races, are shifting away from the party in power.
“I think kind of one-party fatigue could be playing into this election as well,” Coleman said.
Gov. Kay Ivey won reelection in 2022 with 66% of votes to Democratic nominee Yolanda Flowers’ 29%. He also said that shifting Alabama’s race to “Likely Republican” does not mean that they think Jones will win, but it does reflect the polls and the closing gap.
“We have had polling that Tuberville is up, but he’s up by like 10 or 11 points, which is still comfortable. But in 2022, I think Gov. Ivey won by closer to 30 points, probably even more,” he said. “It’s probably not going to change hands, but it could get a little interesting.”
The campaign trail
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama (left), the Republican nominee for governor of Alabama, shakes hands with President Donald Trump at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
Tuberville has limited many of his campaign stops to friendly territory, and often closed them to the media despite being marketed as “open to the public.” In at least one instance, that distinction was not communicated to a Mobile-based reporter who was escorted out of an event last week after asking a question. 
Most of the events are hosted by the local Republican Party, and marketed as “meet-and-greets.” 
He also made an appearance at a rally in Mobile on Oct. 2 with President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Tuberville.
“Tommy was a great coach, and he was a great senator. He’s going to be a fantastic governor, and he’s been my friend,” Trump said at the rally.
During the 2020 campaign, Tuberville and Trump’s relationship was rocky at the start, with Tuberville expressing frustration over the lack of healthcare access for veterans’ during the president’s first term. The president ultimately endorsed Tuberville over former U.S. Sen. and Attorney General Jeff Sessions in the 2020 primary. 
Donald Trump tells Mobile rally to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’

Tuberville repeatedly praised Trump during his time in the U.S. Senate. In February, he suggested in a social media posting that Presidents Day should be named “President Donald J. Trump Day.” Now Tuberville touts his endorsement and relationship with the president, but has largely left Trump out of his advertising. 
“We’re going to win in November this year. I’m not running to have a governor in front of my name. I’m running to help. I’m not running for another job,” Tuberville said at the rally. “I want to come home and help this state get bigger and better. We got industry jobs. So buckle up.”
Rep. Scott Stadthagen, R-Hartselle, chair of the Alabama Republican Party, said in a phone interview Wednesday that Tuberville was the best candidate for the state’s high office. 
“I think having a strong conservative for our Republican nominee is extremely crucial moving forward for the state,” Stadthagen said. “I think some of the stuff that he plans on doing for the state is going to be a generational change for my daughter and for everybody else’s kids moving forward.”
With those values comes a laundry list of policy priorities, many of which would require additional or new funding, but Stadthagen thinks a Gov. Tuberville will be able to achieve everything he hopes to in his first term. 
Preparing for a new administration
Construction of the new Alabama Statehouse as seen on July 29, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. Legislators are expected to occupy the new building in time to verify November’s election results. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Tuberville’s playbook covers everything he wants to accomplish in his first term. He plans to reduce taxes, expand the CHOOSE Act, the state’s voucher program; reduce the state workforce, bring more private jobs to Alabama, protect rural hospitals and audit every government agency, and more. 
The 22-page document has every aspect of his agenda, including an accountability system for his own administration. After the first year, Tuberville pledges to have a “full efficiency review,” and after the first 90 days, the administration will publish a public “scoreboard.” 
The scoreboard will include a measurement, like the state income tax, what it is today (5%), the administration’s target, “lower,” and a timeline. For that measure, it’s by the end of the first term. 
Lowering the income tax is part of his “Family Affordability Act,” which includes eliminating the state grocery tax, extending a utility rate freeze, a freeze on property tax rates for seniors and lowering the cost of childcare. 
“And too many families are working harder and still falling behind. Groceries, power bills, insurance, and child care keep climbing, and paychecks haven’t kept pace,” he writes in an introductory letter. “I’ll eliminate the state tax on groceries, cut the state income tax in my first term, and make sure no family’s power bill goes up so a big company can plug in.”
Stadthagen said Tuberville’s agenda will be “generational change” for Alabama. But most of Tuberville’s proposals will need approval from lawmakers. The governor of Alabama is weak relative to the Legislature, which can override gubernatorial vetoes with simple majority votes and effectively has the last word on policy.  
The elimination of the grocery tax is broadly popular across both parties. Republican leaders earlier this month announced they have a bill ready to file after the election to do so. Jones has called for repeal for months, and Democratic lawmakers on Monday reaffirmed their support for the elimination of the sales tax on food. 
Some of Tuberville’s proposals require funding – like widening I-65 to three lanes from Mobile to Huntsville – while others, like the elimination of the grocery tax and the reduction of the income tax, reduce state revenue. Stadthagen is not concerned about Tuberville’s ability to balance the state’s budget, though.
“Yes, things are going to cost a little bit more, but he’s for smaller government. He’s for saving money and cutting and being fiscally responsible with our tax dollars,” Stadthagen said. 
Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, outgoing chair of the General Fund Committee, said in a recent interview that he thinks Tuberville has put in the time to learn the limits of the governor’s office.
“Tuberville is working hard to get a grasp of the job already,” Albritton said. “I hear questions coming from many of them, asking and trying to get a grasp of what’s going on and what can happen. So, I think he will be as prepared as any person that comes into the governorship will be, at least academically.” 
Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, chair of Senate Education Trust Fund Committee, said in an interview Wednesday that some of Tuberville’s proposals that will impact the ETF – the reduction of the income tax and expansion of the CHOOSE Act – need to be done responsibly.
As public splits over CHOOSE Act, so do Alabama political candidates

“That’s the bread and butter of the ETF,” Orr said. “With the mobility of society today, we’ve got to be careful. We’ve got to at least look at it and see if it’s something that we can address again without wrecking the budgets and our responsibility to educate children and provide higher education services and all the other things we do in the ETF. We’ve just got to move cautiously. It’s a noble goal to have.”
The winner of next month’s election are likely to face challenges from the get-go. Former Finance Director Bill Poole and Legislative Fiscal Officer Kirk Fulford have repeatedly warned state agencies that fiscal year 2028 will be “challenging” and budgets will need to be conservative. The state’s two public employee insurance boards are seeking more funding and increasing premiums or direct costs amid rising healthcare costs. 
Orr said both of the agencies’ expected requests are part of the national issue, and the Legislature will have to “figure it out” in conjunction with Tuberville. 
“We’re going to have to deal with that at the state level, just like ordinary citizens are having to deal with it as they write their checks for their healthcare premiums via their employer,” Orr said. 
Although bipartisan efforts would not be required should Republicans maintain their supermajorities in the Legislature, many bipartisan and Democratic-led efforts have prevailed during Gov. Kay Ivey’s tenure. Some bills like a ban on Glock switches failed under Democratic sponsorship, but became law with Ivey’s support after a few years; or legislation guaranteeing paid parental leave for educators that took a bipartisan effort across both chambers.
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, the chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, said in a recent interview that he hopes that the teamwork will continue under a Tuberville administration. 
“As long as the Tuberville administration is bringing things to move the state forward, and not trying to carry the state backwards, then we can sit down at the table and we can come to some agreements on how to move Alabama forward,” Singleton said. 
Stadthagen echoed that sentiment. 
“We in the Alabama State House are completely different than DC. Of course, we stand strong on our policies for our party, but we have a really good working relationship within the chambers of the State House,” he said. “It’s completely different because we all know that we have to move and do what’s best for the state of Alabama.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Commentary: Why I believe in voting
text:
Voters use touch screens to fill out their ballots during early voting at the Bismarck Event Center on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)I think everyone should vote, but not for the aggravating script we’ve heard over the last two decades. I think people should vote because they matter, their lives matter, their voice matters, and they deserve to be heard. 
I say this as someone who isn’t partisan and has spent my adult life being disappointed in a political system that continues to grow more toxic and divisive every year. With each election cycle asking us to vote for the lesser of two evils and never the better of two goods. 
I cannot stress enough that people in their 30s and younger are disillusioned by a government that clearly doesn’t seem to work for us. And it’s difficult to believe things can get better when we’re exhausted working multiple jobs, taking care of our families, worried for our friends, and getting harassed by endless text messages, spam calls and attack ads. 
Politics is a mess, and it isn’t a surprise that our voter turnout in North Dakota for the 2022 midterm was 42.9%. Why waste a perfectly good night standing in line to vote for a system that treats you like a number, while life feels like it’s getting worse each day regardless of who is in charge?
So, why vote? Why participate in a system that is this awful? That’s the question a lot of younger folks think about all the time.  
The answer I would give is that voting isn’t about the system. It isn’t about the politician or issue. It’s about you. We’re a democracy, and that means you get a voice. This year there is a chance for people to choose if we give free school meals to kids or not, where your voice can change North Dakota for generations to come. 
A vote, by itself, is often not a particularly powerful thing. However, the act of voting is tremendously powerful as it sends the message that there are people who haven’t given up yet. That democracy is still alive. That people still believe in the potential for us to be better than we are now.
I think people should vote because it’s an act of resistance to fascism. I think they should vote because even if that vote doesn’t make tomorrow better, we feel better when we try, even if we end up losing. We feel more hopeful and resilient through the act of doing something than never trying or giving up.
The world does not change tomorrow because we voted, but the act of voting can change who we are and how we see ourselves.
When we invest in ourselves by paying attention to our democracy, participating in it, and demanding better before, during, and after elections than we do get somewhere different and hopefully better. Vote because you matter, vote to say that you matter, and hold the system to account afterwards.  
All information on voting, where to vote, how to vote, and where candidates stand can be found through the League of Women Voters’ Vote411 guide.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado officials prepare for Medicaid eligibility changes set for 2027
text:
(Getty Images)Colorado’s Medicaid program is preparing to implement new work requirements and shorter renewal periods for the program beginning next year.
Beginning Jan. 1, some Coloradans on Medicaid, known as Health First Colorado, will need to self-attest that they are meeting new requirements or are exempted. Otherwise, they will lose their health coverage.
“In many cases, we do expect that the changes will result in, or already have resulted in, coverage loss, additional administrative burden, like more paperwork or processing times, and impacts on statewide uncompensated care,” said Adela Flores-Brennan, the Medicaid director and director of the Health Policy Office at the state’s Department of Health Care Policy and Financing.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
When Arkansas implemented work requirements for its Medicaid program in 2018, about 18,000 adults lost coverage in one year, primarily because people did not report their work data to the state. The move didn’t meaningfully increase employment numbers.
The change is one of many due to new federal rules under the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” passed by Republicans and signed by President Donald Trump in 2025. About 5,900 people in Colorado have already lost Medicaid coverage because of a change related to which immigrants can receive Medicaid. Most of those people who lost coverage are refugees and people seeking asylum, Flores-Brennan said. She expects that around 3,800 more people will be removed from the program as her department manually works through people who get Supplemental Security Income and will remain qualified.
The work requirements will affect about 175,000 of the 1.2 million Coloradans on Medicaid, Flores-Brennan said. Those are people who qualify for Medicaid because of their lower income under the Affordable Care Act expansion. The department sent out notification letters to recipients in September, and it will send a second round at the end of October.
Verification comes in 2028
Colorado is one of many states that will rely on self-attestation for the first year of the new requirements, as well as data it already has. People will be able to fill out a form about their qualifying activities — a combination of 80 hours per month of work, volunteering or education. People also fulfill the work requirement if they earn $580 in a month.
Some people are excluded from the work requirements. That includes people who are incarcerated, pregnant people, young adults who were in foster care, people receiving treatment for a substance disorder, disabled veterans, caregivers and people deemed “medically frail.” Medical frailty would prevent a person from working or volunteering 80 hours per month, such as blindness, a disability, drug or alcohol disorder, serious health condition that requires regular treatment and disabling mental health disorder.



Quotation







In many cases, we do expect that the changes will result in, or already have resulted in, coverage loss, additional administrative burden, like more paperwork or processing times, and impacts on statewide uncompensated care.


– Adela Flores-Brennan, the state's Medicaid director


The department will use existing data when possible to identify Medicaid recipients who have medical frailty, but the state might need more information, and recipients will be able to self-attest.
Beginning in 2028, the department will have to verify everything that is self-attested. That will create a lot of administrative workload.
“Throughout the the next year, we are going to be working with our stakeholders to think about what the processes are and how we operationalize that verification process in a way that is minimally burdensome for both our eligibility workers, our members and also providers in the case of medical frailty,” Flores-Brennan said.
The department launched an online self-screener tool for Coloradans on Medicaid to determine if they are subject to the new requirements. It also offers a page that answers many frequently asked questions about the changes.
The Medicaid renewal timeline will shrink to six months starting next year. State officials said they are working to see if an auto-renewal system is feasible. If not, they will send renewal packets to individuals. The department urges recipients to make sure their mailing address, phone number and email are up to date in Colorado PEAK, the state benefit manager.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Can data center concerns help Democratic women win in deep-red West Virginia?
text:
Lucia Valentine walks a neighborhood, door-knocking for her campaign in a rural area of West Virginia. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th.  Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
EASTERN PANHANDLE, W.Va. — Over and over on a recent October Saturday, Jenny Thacker explained to voters in West Virginia’s Eastern Panhandle why the groundwater in the region is particularly susceptible to contamination from data centers.
“Basically, instead of having soil that the water goes down through evenly and filters all the bad stuff out, we have a broken bedrock, and so there’s cracks,” Thacker would begin.
Thacker was nine months into her campaign to flip a House of Delegates seat for Democrats in deeply conservative West Virginia. Data centers have been “the number one issue people have talked to me about,” she said. By that Saturday, with just over two weeks until the election, she had her explanation of the region’s groundwater issues down pat.
Thacker, an ocean cartographer who retired several years ago from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), navigated her Prius from a homecoming parade to a garden group lunch to a barbecue fundraiser for a local 4-H group. Her bumper stickers hinted at the priorities that have defined her life: “May The Forest Be With You,” “Tree Hugger,” “Save The Ash Trees,” and “Peace Corps: Proud To Have Served My Country.”

Jenny Thacker is campaigning to flip a House of Delegates seat for Democrats in deeply conservative West Virginia. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
At the 4-H fundraiser — where a plate of pork barbecue, baked beans and mac ‘n’ cheese was  $10 — Thacker used her hands to show Debbie Morris, 66, how cracks in the region’s bedrock act as chutes that carry water quickly from the surface to the underground water table.
If that surface water has the chemical pollutants in it that data centers use to cool their equipment, they end up in the groundwater, and boiling the water only concentrates the chemicals, Thacker explained. And as data centers extract groundwater to use for cooling systems, they can quickly use up entire pockets of water.
Thacker’s district is in Jefferson County, where as much as 90% of the population relies on municipal or private wells. Voters have told Thacker that some of their wells are already running dry. Drilling a new one — assuming they can locate a water pocket in the bedrock — can come with a $25,000 price tag.
As Thacker ate a plate of barbecue, Morris nodded along, periodically stopping to accept treats for safekeeping from her tutu-attired granddaughter. Morris met Thacker months earlier and said she has been impressed by her campaign, which has included hundreds of drop-ins to speak with voters at community events like this one.
“She’s everywhere … and this is not the easiest crowd. It’s a smart crowd, and they’ve supported her with open arms,” Morris said.

Jenny Thacker, who is running for election to represent District 100 in the West Virginia House of Delegates, speaks with organizers of a pork barbecue fundraiser for the Kabletown Mountaineers 4-H Club at Uvilla United Methodist Church in Jefferson County, West Virginia, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
The two women discussed a law enacted last year that, as GOP Gov. Patrick Morrisey put it, took away local oversight and created a state-level “one-stop shop” for data-center permitting. West Virginia’s counties and municipalities are now legally barred from enforcing local ordinances and land-use rules related to microgrid sites or high-impact data centers. When the state legislature, which has a GOP supermajority, voted on the legislation, only three Republicans in the House of Delegates defected from their party to vote against it. In the Senate, one did. Thacker’s opponent, Del. Bill Ridenour, voted yes. Thacker’s pitch to voters focuses on why localities, and not the legislature, are best positioned to oversee data centers, based on their specific geologies and community needs.
“I have my list for when I go to the polls to make sure I don’t vote for any of these people,” Morris told Thacker. “The fact that you can meaningfully discuss this is so important.”
“I’m a little scared that even if I get elected, I won’t be able to do it by myself,” Thacker responded.
“You’re planting a seed,” Morris said as her granddaughter brought over a Ziploc bag of Italian ricotta cookies covered in sprinkles.

West Virginia has not been fertile ground for Democrats for some time. The only state that has backed President Donald Trump by a higher margin than West Virginia is Wyoming. West Virginians haven’t voted for a Democrat for the White House since Bill Clinton’s reelection in 1996. They last picked a Democrat for governor in 2016, electing Jim Justice. Now a U.S. senator, Justice announced at a rally with Trump eight months into his gubernatorial tenure that he would switch parties.
The state’s last Democrat in the U.S. Senate, Joe Manchin, announced in his final year in office that he would become an independent. All of West Virginia’s current statewide officers are Republicans. In the House of Delegates, there are nine Democrats and 91 Republicans; in the state Senate, it’s two Democrats and 32 Republicans.
West Virginia also has the distinction of having the lowest percentage of women serving in its legislature, with women holding only about 11% of its 134 seats.

A sorority’s float travels down German Street during the Shepherd University Homecoming Parade on October 17, 2026, in downtown Shepherdstown, West Virginia. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
Lacey Connelly, a political director who started working with the West Virginia Democratic Party this cycle, said that when the party started to recruit candidates for this year’s legislative races, it became clear that the futures of Democrats and women in the Statehouse could be intertwined.
We “got more creative with our candidate recruitment, not just looking at candidates we thought could raise the money and would have the time to do the work, but people who were already enmeshed in their communities, already doing the work advocating for policies or laws they thought would make people’s lives better,” Connelly explained.
“It tends to fall on women to deal with the public school system; it tends to be women who are dealing with the healthcare system for their families; it tends to be women who are balancing the budget and making sure they have enough money for new shoes for school,” she continued. “These women [candidates] are really showing that it’s the women interacting with the systems in this state who need the most help.”
Polling released this month by the state’s Democratic Party showed that 57% of West Virginians believed the Mountain State was on the wrong track, and just 30% were happy with the direction it was heading. The Republicans in statewide office had lower approval ratings than Trump, and his was lower as compared with past surveys. Democratic voters were more enthusiastic about their candidates than Republican voters were. Del. Mike Pushkin, the state’s Democratic Party chair, said at the time of the poll’s release that “West Virginians are tired of watching their utility bills climb, their hospitals and their schools close, and their elected officials writing blank checks to AI data centers.”
These are the issues that the Democratic women trying for the Statehouse are focused on. Thacker also talks frequently to voters about locality pay for teachers, meaning that those in more expensive areas of the state, like the Eastern Panhandle, would earn more. At the 4-H fundraiser, she met a woman who is a public school teacher, as is her husband. The couple commutes to a district in neighboring Virginia to teach and earn significantly higher salaries.
Lucia Valentine, also in the Eastern Panhandle, is running a campaign focused on lowering costs, with local data center oversight, teacher pay and improving childcare accessibility as key components. Elizabeth Ferris, running for state Senate in the Eastern Panhandle, is focused on restoring local control over data centers, public school funding and government transparency (She was able to run in part due to income from a forthcoming debut novel imagining Charlotte Brontë’s writing of “Jane Eyre.”) Kim Hundley, a teacher, is trying to flip a Senate seat in the Charleston area with a campaign focused on improving public education and a broken healthcare system that she experienced directly during breast cancer treatment.

Lucia Valentine lost her first campaign for the House of Delegates to Republican Del. S. Chris Anders by about 700 votes in 2024. Anders is a staunch abortion opponent known for his anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric who voted yes on the data center bill. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
“I don’t think anybody expects to get rid of the Republican supermajority this cycle, but I think that there’s going to be a significant number of Democratic candidates who will win, and I think a lot of them are going to be women,” said Kendra Sullivan, who was recently elected to Harrison County’s Democratic executive committee.
Democrats even believe that one of their candidates has a chance to flip a House of Delegates seat in Mingo County, which Trump won in 2024 by more than 70 points. Tara “BabyT” Sexton, a self-made environmental activist, has used her creative social media posts to highlight the drinking water crisis in the Central Appalachian Coalfield, prompting an August visit from the Republican governor.
“From stem to stern we have really strong women leading these races and I think we’ll win a lot of them,” said Sam Petsonk, an attorney who serves as one of the state’s delegates on the Democratic National Committee.
Del. Kayla Young, one of the two Democratic women in the House, where there are just 12 women total, said even if only some of these women prevail, it will considerably improve her ability to talk about “women’s issues” like schools and childcare at the Statehouse.
“A lot of times they don’t get the time of day because people consider them women’s issues, but they’re economic issues,” Young explained. “I realized also that for two whole years I was the only mom in the legislature that had kids who are under 18 years old, so when we’re talking about childcare or public education or paid leave, I’m literally the only person in the room who has any experience with that, and it’s terrifying. Women are the majority of the population in West Virginia.”

Valentine, a managing director at the “cross-partisan” West Virginia Women’s Alliance, is running in a district adjacent to Thacker’s that extends west from Shepherdstown to Martinsburg into Berkeley County. As you drive the area’s country roads, one side is often Valentine’s district, the other is Thacker’s. Many yards feature both women’s campaign signs.
Valentine began that same Saturday at the homecoming parade in Shepherdstown with Thacker. Then, she went to Martinsburg to march in another parade. Afterward, she met up with The 19th to do some door-knocking in a rural area between the two cities that Valentine described as “winnable turf” with a mix of “red persuadable, high-turnout independents and middle-to-high turnout moderate Republicans.”
It is the second time Valentine has tried for the House of Delegates. In 2024, it was an open seat, and she lost to Republican Del. S. Chris Anders by about 700 votes. Anders is a staunch abortion opponent known for his anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric who voted yes on the data center bill. School choice, ending the income tax and stopping “woke ideology” are among the issues featured on his campaign website. He helped relaunch the far-right West Virginia Freedom Caucus and serves as its chair.
Valentine said Anders’ focus on social issues and national debates has left a “big opportunity for me to try to appeal to that middle and moderate Republican group who are willing to look at people over party; I want to focus on the local issues we all agree on.”

In West Virginia’s Eastern Panhandle, Democrat candidates Jenny Thacker (left) and Lucia Valentine (right) are campaigning on data centers, teacher pay, childcare and healthcare. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
A main way that Valentine has communicated with voters about these local issues is through a robust door-knocking campaign. She explained that in 2024, she didn’t start door-knocking until September. This time around, she hired a field consultant and began in May. She estimates that she had already knocked on about 4,000 doors that reached about 8,000 people — or about two-thirds of the total voters in her district. There were still two weeks and change to do more ahead of Election Day.
The second house on Valentine’s list to knock that day was a registered Republican, a man — his wife answered the door.
“Hi, I’m Lucia. I’m running for local office. I’m just checking in with neighbors today because I want to see if there’s any issues that y’all are concerned about,” Valentine began.
“You’re a Democrat, am I right?” the woman asked.
“Yeah,” Valentine replied.
“You’ve got it,” the woman said of her vote.

Lucia Valentine, who is running for election to represent District 97 in the West Virginia House of Delegates, speaks to a resident while canvassing door-to-door in Shepherdstown, West Virginia, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
The two women laughed, and Valentine explained the issues that had come up as she knocked on doors around the district: growth, infrastructure, roads, data centers. “Get ‘em out of here,” the woman replied as she took campaign literature. “If you have any questions, feel free to reach out,” Valentine said, writing her cell phone number on a purple Post-it note.
“I almost came out and volunteered!” her husband, the registered Republican, shouted as the women wrapped up their conversation.
After a couple more hours of door-knocking, Valentine went home to change for the 30th birthday party her parents were hosting for her that evening at their home overlooking the Potomac River. Statehouse campaigns in West Virginia are mostly fueled by volunteers, friends and family, and many in Valentine’s inner circle who have powered her campaign would be there.
By 6 o’clock, the taco bar was set up, the bourbon apple cider slushy machine was spinning, and the Frank Sinatra impersonator who sang at Valentine’s father and stepmother’s wedding was testing his microphone. As the room filled with toddlers, octogenarians, friends from college, and a chaotic mix of dogs and cats, Valentine’s stepmother made a birthday toast.

Lucia Valentine attends a 30th birthday celebration hosted by her parents at their home in Shepherdstown, West Virginia, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. (Moriah Ratner for The 19th)
“We’re super proud of Lucia. We’re super excited for her, and most of all, we’re just really happy that we get to be her parents. So happy 30th birthday!” she said.
The Frank Sinatra impersonator started to sing: Fly me to the moon, let me play among the stars.
People began to dance.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: West Virginia stewardship is key to our prosperous future
text:
The author holds a basket cranberries foraged in Tucker County, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of Paula Kaufman)This October I picked cranberries in the West Virginia bogs. It was a banner year with fields full of red. I could have picked more, but just harvested enough for myself.
The profusion of berries left me wonder-struck with the thought that if we sustainably harvested Appalachia instead of ravaging it, we’d be immensely prosperous. Such abundance. What would West Virginia look like if we fed the golden geese of our resources instead of killing the flock for a one-time prize?
Our history is a relentless teacher. Take timber for instance — the boom and bust cycles created frenetic towns now empty. And only a few old growth tree groves remain such as at Cathedral State Park in Aurora, West Virginia, evidence of our rapacious hunger and insatiability.
And so I tread carefully over the sphagnum moss in the bog which supports rare pink orchids and pitcher plants, their hairy mouth traps open for insects. If we are not mindful we may once again become a “place of ugliness, a monotonous panorama of destruction,” as one writer put it in 1900, amid our clearcut forests on fire and smoking from the destruction.
But there’s hope. Nature regenerates. Can it come back from mountain top removal mining? Usually not. Mine reclamation (the idea of returning mountains to their original contour before they were blasted, or spraying them with grass seed in lieu of a forest) is laughable. A despicable coal company ruse.
And reclaiming land after a future abandoned data center sounds impossible. Some damage is too Herculean to be undone. So we must be purposeful and highly circumspect in our land use plans.
West Virginia Agriculture Commissioner Kent Leonhardt echoed this point in a statement on the Department of Agriculture’s website writing, “When it comes to data centers and other large-scale developments, I strongly encourage developers to consider land that is less suitable for agricultural production. We should not be cutting ourselves short on the prospect of agricultural development by taking farmland out of production.”
This is particularly notable because some of our largest high-impact data centers are being built along prime Ohio River farming lands. We have little flat land in West Virginia. These developments undermine generations of future farming potential. Leonhardt writes that our agriculture annually has a $5 billion impact.
Healthy land is inextricably bound to West Virginia’s prosperity. Full stop. And our woods are slowly recovering from the late 1800s when about 30 billion board feet of lumber were cut in West Virginia. (So much that if laid side by side it is estimated to be enough to build a boardwalk 2 inches thick and 13 feet wide from the earth to the moon.)
And now West Virginia is the third most forested state with over 12 million acres of trees, writes the West Virginia Division of Forestry.
Such positive statistics are buoyed by human efforts such as red spruce restoration projects spearheaded by groups like the Central Appalachian Spruce Restoration Initiative (CASRI) and the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy.
Spruce trees matter in West Virginia because they anchor a high-elevation ecosystem that shelters native wildlife, stores carbon and purifies water. Red spruce are regrowing in areas like Canaan Valley State Park, Kumbrabow State Forest, Cranesville Swamp and the Mower Tract in the Monongahela National Forest.
I saw progress in action this year when I volunteered with a group planting seedlings in Pocahontas County. We planted hundreds of 3-year-old seedlings. A senior wetlands scientist volunteer said: “If you remove the stress, the land will heal itself.”
Indeed, plants that were dormant generations are making comebacks, albeit slowly in human time — as it takes 1,000 years to create 1 meter of peat. But progress nonetheless.
Do not despair. Let’s re-calibrate our definition of an ecological victory. Small victories matter as much as big ones. Healthy land is sacrosanct and integral to a viable West Virginia future. Fixating on short-term gains is the antithesis of prosperity. We have a sacred compact with our land to be in reciprocity with it and to shift the power imbalance. Change is possible.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas amendment aims to prohibit noncitizens from voting in local elections
text:
Union County residents cast votes during the last days of early voting at the El Dorado Municipal Auditorium on Oct. 30, 2024. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Sponsors of a proposed constitutional amendment that would only allow United States citizens to vote in Arkansas elections say it’s a preventative measure, but critics argue it’s unnecessary and sends immigrants an unwelcoming message. 
Issue 1, also known as “The Citizens Only Voting Amendment,” proposes amending the state’s constitution to prohibit noncitizens from voting in state or local elections held in Arkansas. It’s one of four ballot measures being considered by Arkansas voters in this year’s election.
State lawmakers referred the measure to voters by approving a 2025 resolution sponsored by Republicans Rep. David Ray and Sen. John Payton. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Last month, Ray and other Issue 1 supporters held a press conference at the state Capitol where they cited examples of places where noncitizens are allowed to vote in local elections such as Washington, D.C.
“Americans should decide the future of America,” Ray said. “That’s what I believe, and that’s what the vast majority of Arkansans believe.”
Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The Trump administration has campaigned against noncitizens voting in elections, but research shows it’s exceedingly rare.
Arkansas’ constitution already states that “any person” who is a U.S. citizen, an Arkansas resident, at least 18 years old and legally registered to vote is eligible to cast a ballot in an election in the state. 
The nonpartisan League of Women Voters of Arkansas said it opposes the measure because there’s already a requirement that voters be a U.S. citizen, executive director Kristin Foster said. 
“This is adding in unnecessary language to the constitution where protections already exist,” Foster said.
Ray said the state constitution’s current phrasing is “a floor rather than a ceiling,” meaning it would not prevent noncitizens from being added to the list of eligible voters.
“Arkansas’ constitution protects the rights of all U.S. citizens to vote, but it doesn’t preclude a city or another local government from granting eligibility to noncitizens,” he said. “That is primarily what Issue 1 aims to address.”
Ray acknowledged there aren’t any local governments in Arkansas trying to allow noncitizens to vote, and said the proposal is a preventative measure.
In 6 states, ballots include bans on noncitizen voting

Arkansas is one of six states considering this type of constitutional amendment or law change in November’s election. 
In addition to Washington, nearly two dozen municipalities in California, Maryland and Vermont have permitted noncitizens to vote in certain local elections, such as school board elections. This allows all citizen children to have a voice — through their parents and guardians — about the elected officials who approve their school district’s policies, according to Stateline.
In Arkansas, allowing noncitizens to vote in school board elections could affect children who were born in the U.S. and have parents who immigrated from another country, such as the Marshall Islands. 
Arkansas has the largest Marshallese population in the country. A compact agreed to following years of nuclear weapons testing by the U.S. near the islands allows Marshallese migrants to legally live and work in the U.S., but does not provide an automatic path to citizenship.
Holly Dickson, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Arkansas, said the state’s constitution has been clear for more than a century that only U.S. citizens can vote in Arkansas. 
“Issue 1 is about whether Arkansas will send a hateful, un-American message that immigrants aren’t welcome here,” Dickson said in an email. 
Arkansas was settled by and continues to be inhabited by people of various cultural backgrounds, including Indigenous people, and immigrants from Germany, Italy, Vietnam, Latin America and India, she said. 
“Immigrants helped build Arkansas and still make our communities stronger,” Dickson said. “Issue 1 will be a litmus test for Arkansans’ character and values.”
Critics of Issue 1 have also argued its approval could spur lawmakers to pass proof of citizenship laws during the 2027 legislative session and establish requirements many qualified voters could not meet, according to the Public Policy Center at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. 
Proponents of the measure have said it’s a way to address voters’ concerns about illegal immigration, according to the center.
If voters approve Issue 1 at the polls, it would be effective Jan. 1. 
You can read the proposed constitutional amendment in its entirety here. 
Editor-in-Chief Andrew DeMillo contributed to this report.
