name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis immigrant food pantry says need remains high a year after federal task force entered city
text:
The Collective Good Immigrant Pantry, a project of Indivisible Memphis, has seen a spike in requests for food since a federal law enforcement task force arrived in the city. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) After her two adult daughters were arrested while working at a Memphis nightclub during a sweeping U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raid in late August, a grandmother suddenly found herself responsible for the care of her eight grandchildren.
It’s families like this that The Collective Good Immigrant Pantry — a food pantry run by volunteers out of garages and spare rooms — has provided with food and necessities for more than a year as immigration enforcement surged with the deployment of the Trump administration’s “Memphis Safe Task Force.”
On Aug. 30, ICE arrested 121 people from El Corralón night club, marking one of the agency’s largest raids since President Donald Trump began his second term in office. Five of those people had criminal convictions or charges, according to a U.S. Department of Homeland Security news release. It’s not clear if the other 116 people arrested had criminal histories.
“It’s easy to think about the individuals as a number, but every one of those people had a life outside of that club,” said Jessica Miller, co-founder of The Collective Good. “Some had children, spouses, and parents who depend on them, and the impact didn’t end with the people that were taken into custody. It ripples throughout the entire community and their families.”
Since the pantry started in July 2025, volunteers have made more than 3,200 deliveries to families in need, including those experiencing financial distress after a primary provider was detained or deported, or immigrant families who are afraid to leave their homes to get groceries, Miller said. 
The average household they help has at least five people, including adults and children. Diapers, baby formula and snacks for children continue to be among the pantry’s most pressing needs.
Jessica Miller, a spokesperson for The Collective Good Immigrant Food Pantry, speaks about the grassroots initiative on Oct. 8, 2025 in Shelby County, Tennessee. (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)
Miller said the pantry’s 1-year anniversary was a somber one. Need for the pantry had decreased over the summer before spiking in September after the nightclub raid. In the weeks that followed, weekly delivery counts ballooned from 23 households to 74. The week of Oct. 11, pantry volunteers made 57 deliveries.
In the pantry’s early days, many of the families they helped were first-time recipients. Now, the pantry helps some families consistently. On an anonymous message board, volunteers post short accounts of their deliveries and interactions with recipients. They describe children overjoyed to receive small toys, books and craft supplies — extra gifts from volunteers — and tight hugs and tears from grateful parents. 
“When we started the pantry, we were doing crisis response,” Miller said. “What we didn’t know was that we were building an emergency response system that families were still going to desperately need more than a year later, and the crisis didn’t end when the headlines stopped. For those families, there’s been no return to normal.”
The Memphis Safe Task Force, a multi-agency law enforcement operation, has made 13,825 arrests between its start in September 2025 and Oct. 22 of this year, according to the U.S. Marshals Service. Of those, 848 were ICE-related administrative arrests made as part of the task force’s activity. Administrative ICE warrants are not criminal warrants and are not signed by a judge or magistrate. They only indicate that an ICE official determined a person is “removable from the United States,” according to federal law enforcement training materials.
Federal data shows ICE made 1,575 arrests between Sept. 29, 2025 and Aug. 5 of this year, and nearly 60% of those arrested had no criminal conviction and no pending criminal charges, according to a recent analysis from The Institute for Public Service Reporting in Memphis. Of those 1,575 arrests, 249 people had criminal convictions, and only 10 (0.6%) arrestees had been convicted of violent felonies including rape, aggravated assault, robbery and homicide.
The Institute for Public Service Reporting analyzed national ICE arrest data provided by the agency after the Deportation Data Project filed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. The data runs through Aug. 5, 2026. Arrests at El Corralón were not included in the data set.


“It’s so easy for people to say, ‘oh, well, they need to do it the right way, and they need to go back to their country,’” Miller said. But the people that the pantry serves are experiencing a wide variety of situations. 
Some are families with children that lost their sole providers, Miller said. Some people have been detained and released with ankle monitors, and have limits on what they can and can’t do. Some people have Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, status, meaning they were brought to the United States without legal status as children and have a permit from the federal government to live and work in the United States.
Tennessee recently began rejecting driver’s license applications and renewals for immigrants with work permits, which until now, had been accepted as sufficient proof that an individual is authorized by the federal government to live and work in the United States for the purpose of obtaining a Tennessee license. Among those expected to be impacted are the state’s 6,000 DACA residents. 
Without valid driver’s licenses, immigrants who are legally allowed to live and work in the United States risk arrest, detention and deportation if they drive anywhere, including to work, school, or the grocery store, Miller said.



Quotation







When we started the pantry, we were doing crisis response. What we didn’t know was that we were building an emergency response system that families were still going to desperately need more than a year later, and the crisis didn’t end when the headlines stopped.


– Jessica Miller, Collective Good Immigrant Pantry


The pantry collects donations of nonperishable food and hygiene items like shampoo and deodorant through its Amazon wishlist. The Collective Good also accepts cash donations, which are used to purchase fresh dairy, meat and produce for deliveries and fill in for shortages in nonperishable items.
The rising cost of groceries is hurting the pantry’s supply, too, as donations decline and prices for basics increase, Miller said. Vegetable oil was just over $2 when Miller first added it to the pantry’s Amazon wishlist. Now, it’s more than $4. Choosing how to allocate funds when nonperishable donations wane has become a challenging balancing act.
But, she said, the existence of The Collective Good is proof that similar pantries can be started anywhere. None of the pantry’s founders had professional experience in this work, and its more than 100 volunteers are community members who took it upon themselves to help.
Above all, Miller said she hopes that people do not “become accustomed to suffering.”
“Back when we first started sharing the stories, people were shocked,” Miller said. “But a year later, I’m afraid some people have started to accept this as normal, and there’s nothing normal about families being afraid to leave their homes to buy food.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee Gov. Lee questions state rules denying licenses to immigrants legally able to work in U.S.
text:
Gov. Bill Lee, pictured taking questions from reporters earlier this month, on Wednesday questioned the state's implementation of new rules denying driver's licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in the United States. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Gov. Bill Lee said Wednesday he is seeking more information about new rules imposed by state driver’s license administrators that have prevented immigrants legally authorized to work in the United States — including so-called “Dreamers” — from obtaining or renewing a Tennessee driver’s license.
Questioned by reporters, Lee said he had “just become aware of that.” The governor said he was trying to determine “what impact it actually does have and are there changes we need to make.” He questioned whether an interaction between state and federal laws has created “unintended consequences potentially.”
“That’s kind of what we’re trying to figure out right now,” Lee said.
Hundreds of individuals, among them long-time Tennessee license holders, have recently been blocked from obtaining or renewing licenses despite producing valid employment authorization cards issued by the federal government. Thousands more in Tennessee could be blocked when trying to renew their licenses, placing immigrants permitted to work in the United States at risk for arrest, detention and deportation if caught driving to work, school or the grocery store without a license. 
Until recently, the work permits were accepted as proof of valid immigration status for the purposes of obtaining a license. For many immigrants who are not permanent residents with Green Cards, the work permits serve as a primary document to demonstrate they are authorized to be in the United States.
Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits

A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security, which administers driver’s licenses, said last week the state’s change to a list of acceptable documents to obtain a license was prompted by one of the provisions of a 2025 law that took effect Jan. 1.  The spokesperson did not provide a response to fresh questions Wednesday about whether the department was reviewing the changes.
The law says temporary licenses may be issued to immigrants who have been “authorized by the federal government for a specific purpose and for a specified period of authorized stay.” 
Jason Pack, the department’s spokesperson, said the state’s position is that the work permit “does not provide sufficient information to verify an applicant’s lawful status.”
Immigrant advocates said they believe the state has only newly interpreted the state law to deny licenses in recent weeks. A state website listed the work permits as acceptable documentation as late as August, according to an online website archive. The legislation does not name acceptable or unacceptable documents.
Among those affected are so-called Dreamers, who belong to a federal immigration category known as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA. DACA recipients were brought here without legal status as children and are now protected from deportation. Immigration attorneys and advocates say multiple other categories of immigrants, including some asylum seekers, are also impacted.
Rep. John Ray Clemmons, chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, questioned the state’s interpretation of the 2025 law and warned a large-scale denial of licenses would be “devastating” to tens of thousands of immigrant families in Tennessee, and to the local economy.  He urged business owners to advocate for impacted workers.
“These are individuals who are fully complying with the letter of the law, positively contributing to our communities and paying taxes just like everyone else,” Clemmons said in a statement. 
“It would appear that our state is attempting to put these legal residents in a situation where they either drive to work, risk getting cited and jeopardize their legal status or they stay home, get terminated by their employer and contribute little to nothing to our economy while their family struggles to find food and keep a roof over their head,” Clemmons said.
Reporter Sam Stockard contributed.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Phillip Ensler, John Wahl meet in lieutenant governor debate
text:
Voters will choose between Republican John Wahl and Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, for lieutenant governor on Nov. 3, 2026. On Wednesday night, the candidates took part in a debate in Huntsville. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The state’s Democratic and Republican nominees for lieutenant governor took the stage Wednesday night in Huntsville for the first, and likely only, debate between candidates for state office in this year’s election cycle.
During the hour-long debate, Democratic nominee Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery and former Republican Party Chairman John Wahl, fielded questions about education, affordability and data centers.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has called for a debate with Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville, who has declined.
 Big Office, Big Ideas, Little Power 
Ensler took the debate’s first question, which focused on how to keep the position relevant with the limited power it has, highlighting his time in the Legislature.
“In my four years in the legislature, now I’ve worked across the aisle,” Ensler said, citing relationships with Democratic and Republican leaders in the Legislature. 
Last year, Gov. Kay Ivey signed SB 116, sponsored by Sen. Will Barfoot, R-Pike Road, which banned the usage of glock switches or devices that turn semi-automatic handguns like pistols into fully automatic weapons, which were used in a mass shooting at a nightclub in Birmingham. Ensler had pushed for a for a state-level ban on glock switches for years prior to the ban. 
He also carried SB 361, sponsored by Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, and signed by Ivey in April, in the House of Representatives. The legislation makes it illegal to tether a dog to a stationary object, including trees and poles, without providing adequate shelter, food or water.
In February, Ensler filed two bills to establish a lottery in the state. Neither bill made it to committee.
Later in the debate, Wahl, a former Alabama Republican Party chair, suggested that the fact some of Ensler’s bills did not come out of committee undermined claims to work across the aisle.
“If you’re not able to even get a bill through a committee or onto a committee agenda, how are you going to be effective as lieutenant governor?” he said. Most legislation does not advance out of committee.
Jones and Ensler have been campaigning together for a large majority of this year’s election cycle. In September, Jones said if both were elected, he would work to expand the lieutenant governor’s power and give Ensler a portfolio to work on. The candidates also said they would support legislation to allow the governor and lieutenant governor to be elected as a ticket like president and vice president of the United States.
Wahl said during the debate he opposes the idea of using a ticket to elect the governor and lieutenant governor.  
“I think the people of Alabama deserve a chance to vote on the people for their positions for their leadership, and I think lieutenant governor is a very important position, and it’s important voters have a chance to vote there because it’s the bridge between the legislative and executive branch,” Wahl said.
Wahl did not mention if Tuberville had offered him a place in his administration.
 Affordability 
On the topic of affordability, Wahl said working to eliminate the grocery tax should be at the top of the next Legislative agenda and that Republicans would be able to get it done.
“It was only once Republicans got control of the state house that we were able to go in, balance the budgets, pay off some of the debt, and then actually start providing genuine tax cuts for the people of Alabama,” he said.
Alabama’s constitution, enacted in 1901, requires state budgets to be balanced each year and caps property taxes. The state’s income tax rates and thresholds are set by a 1933 constitutional amendment. 
Former Rep. John Knight, D-Montgomery, a former chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund committee, joined Ensler and other Democratic candidates in the state at a press conference Monday that highlighted the party’s decades-long efforts to lower the tax. 
In 2023, the Republican-controlled Legislature reduced the grocery tax from 4% to 3% and reduced the tax again to 2% in 2025. During the 2026 regular session, the Legislature approved a two-month grocery tax holiday in May and June which coincided with the primary election and the runoff.
One way to recoup the revenue loss if the grocery tax is eliminated, Ensler said, is to have a state lottery.
“I hear from Alabamians all over, Democrat, Republican, independent, they know people that are crossing state lines to all the surrounding states to buy lottery tickets. We’re missing out on hundreds of millions of dollars right here in Alabama,” he said.
In 2024, a lottery bill was passed in the Alabama House but stalled in the Senate.
Ensler also said he would work to cut taxes for Alabamians and sharply criticized the Trump administration for how affordability has been handled.
“The biggest reason (Alabamians) are hurting is because of Trump’s war overseas, from an agenda that John, that you support, and that’s an agenda that is raising gas prices,” Ensler said. “It is raising prices of fertilizer and diesel on our farmers. The tariffs and the trade wars supported by the president that got you in this race that you have stood by that is hurting Alabamians.”
 Data Centers 
Data centers have become a major focus in this election cycle. Earlier this month, the Lowndes County Commission approved a $1.15 billion tax break for Alabama’s largest planned data center, shocking residents who had been protesting the data center for months.
Wahl called data centers “a necessary evil” but said they need to have strict regulations as well.
“We have to make sure that those communities are protected,” he said. “Closed-loop water systems. Make sure that you know they’re not going to raise consumer rates. I want to see these data centers actually putting money up to make sure that they’re paying for their own power. They’re not affecting power rates on citizens.”
Ensler, like Jones, has called for a one-year moratorium on data centers for the Legislature to approve a review process for them.
“There are residents all over our state who are very concerned about the lack of transparency. They’re concerned about data centers being forced on their communities. They’re concerned that Alabama Power is (hiking) up their prices, so I have stood with residents,” he said.
 Healthcare 
When asked how to eliminate healthcare deserts in the state, Ensler said he wants to expand Medicaid.
“That is free money that we can get from the federal government, 90% of it,” he said. “Then the 10% that the state would be on the hook for, that would pay for itself because if hospitals stay open, people stay employed. That’s good for the local economy. That’s good for the state economy. So it is a moral failure. It is wrong and cruel that we have not expanded Medicaid.”
Wahl said that instead of expanding Medicaid, the focus should be on ensuring that rural hospitals remain open and working with local doctors to provide healthcare.
“We could create triage centers where people can go and have somewhere, small emergency rooms across the state where they can go and get immediate care, especially get stabilized in the case of serious injury,” he said.
According to the University of North Carolina’s Sheps Center, nine rural hospitals have closed since 2009 and only 30% of rual hospitals have labor and delivery units.
 Education 
When asked what should be done about the CHOOSE Act, Ensler said while he doesn’t agree with money being diverted from public schools, the voucher program is likely here to stay and should be remodeled to include an income cap for eligibility.
“I would want it to go to those who most need it because there are low-income families now who have been eligible for the CHOOSE Act, but then can’t afford the difference between what a private school charges and what they’re getting from the government,” he said.
Wahl said he supports the CHOOSE Act. Wahl, who as chair of the Alabama Public Library Service board worked to restrict library content that critics said targeted LGBTQ+ characters and themes, said he wanted to “take the social agendas out of the classroom.”
“As a state party chairman for the last few years, the number one call I got were from teachers, from any profession, and talking about the material that is being put into her curriculum, whether it’s sexually explicit, whether it’s you know pushing transgender ideologies, whatever it is,” he said. “And I think we have to go back to the basics.”
Wahl did not say what schools were using the material.
 Criminal Justice 
One thing both candidates agreed on was that Alabama’s prison system needs to be re-evaluated. Ensler said one way to address concerns with Alabama’s prison system is to revamp the parole process and look at strengthening re-entry programs.
“We have people that are older and they’re not a public safety threat, and we should look at a parole process that will help reduce prison overcrowding,” he said. “We should have stronger reentry and rehabilitation programs, and make sure that there are adequate mental health and healthcare services.”
Wahl also said he would be supportive of re-evaluating the re-entry process.
“If there are opportunities to look at nonviolent offenders and try to get them through rehab or other situations, I’m absolutely supportive of that. I think we have a lot of opportunities to try to get people out of our prison system and back as productive members of society. And that’s my goal, especially when it comes to drug crimes and some other things where you don’t have a victim,” he said.
Wahl’s residency also came up during the debate. He said he has a second residence in Tenneesee and criticizing him for that is “foolish.”
“I’m a farmer. I live near the Tennessee border. I have you know, I farm in different areas,” he said. “I have consistently been a citizen of Alabama. I have always voted in Alabama, and I’ve always paid my taxes in Alabama.”
The Alabama Republican party dismissed a challenge to Whal’s residency in February. Documentation for the challenge, submitted by former Rep. Gil Isbell, R-Gadsden, included a traffic citation in which Wahl submitted a Tennessee driver’s license and evidence that he allegedly was registered to vote in the state.
After Ensler pushed back by saying Wahl was registered to vote in Tennessee and had a driver’s license for the state, Wahl accused Ensler of being registered to vote in his home state of New York.
“You moved to Alabama in 2012, yet you continued to vote in New York City until 2016, and you actually have been a registered voter in New York until last year, so I think look, this is a pot calling the kettle black,” Wahl said.
The candidates were also given the chance to ask each other one question. When asked by Wahl if he would support eliminating the state income tax, Ensler said it would be “fiscally irresponsible to cut it for wealthy families who already can afford to pay their fair share.” 
“If we completely cut the income tax, what would happen is that we would have to reduce services, potentially things like public safety or funds for roads and bridges or funds for hospitals,” he said. “So I wouldn’t want to take that revenue completely away, but certainly give that tax break, though, to working and middle class families.”
Ensler then asked Whal what he’d like to work with Democrats to achieve, Wahl said he wants to work to maintain civil rights and said the Republican Party has been a part of the fight before.
“Republicans don’t always get the recognition we deserve because we are the party of civil rights,” Wahl said. “We are the party who opposed slavery. We are the party who fought for the civil rights movement, and I think that’s something we don’t always get the credit we deserve.”
Ensler pushed back, noting that the Republican-controlled Legislature this spring voted to use a map previously struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court as racially discriminatory, effectively redrawing four U.S. Congressional Districts.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Young Boozer, Rosilyn Houston face off in Alabama State Treasurer race
text:
The Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery, Alabama, as seen on Nov. 14, 2025. Republican incumbent Young Boozer will face Democratic nominee Rosilyn Houston in next Tuesday’s election for Alabama state treasurer. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)Alabama voters next week will choose whether to retain one of the state’s longest-serving state treasurers or elect a retired banker in his place. 
Republican incumbent Young Boozer will face Democratic nominee Rosilyn Houston in next Tuesday’s election to the position, which manages and protects the state’s finances.
Boozer served as Alabama state treasurer from 2011 to 2019. Gov. Kay Ivey appointed Boozer to the office in 2021 to finish the term of State Treasurer John McMillan, who became executive director of the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission.
Multiple messages seeking comment were left with Boozer. His campaign website touts his accomplishments in office, including rebuilding the Alabama Prepaid Affordable College Tuition (PACT) Program fund, being fiscally conservative and returning unclaimed property funds back to taxpayers.
Houston said in a recent interview her priorities include protecting taxpayer dollars and more transparency from the office.
“I envision under that transparency model a citizen to come to the treasurer’s website and to be able to click on a dashboard and see all the buckets of money that the treasurer is responsible for, and then drill down in that, and to see how those dollars are performing and how those dollars are coming back into the communities across or the counties, even across Alabama,” Houston said.
Houston also wants to help teach financial literacy across the state through engaging with the community.
“Helping to foster connectivity, alignment, and partnerships with, say, our schools. I really believe that we need to teach (financial literacy) in school,” Houston said. “Financial education (needs) to be a regular part of our curriculum, and churches, community centers, organizations can come together and work on these strategies as well. And I think the state could be a major partner in ensuring that we help to connect these organizations to our citizens, so that we have a more competent state as it relates to managing money.”
According to campaign finance reports, Boozer has raised $144,100 and spent $270,000 as of Wednesday morning. Houston has raised $76,400 and spent $64,800 as of Wednesday morning.
The general election is on Nov. 3.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: As Trump threatens election interference, Colorado clerks prepare like never before
text:
Election workers inside Boulder County's ballot processing facility handle ballots on Tuesday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)During the June 30 primary election in Colorado, Lori Mitchell, the Chaffee County clerk, planned with other local officials for disaster scenarios as the threat of wildfire loomed. It turns out the planning they did is useful now for the general election, she said, as another potential disaster approaches, the source of which is entirely human: the Trump administration.
That a disaster like a wildfire is comparable to the administration’s efforts to undermine the election says a lot about the state of democracy in America.
“Election officials are always thinking about the worst possible thing that could happen,” Molly Fitzpatrick, the clerk in Boulder County, said Tuesday. “Historically, that has been flood, fire, mass protest scenarios — we have added federal interference to the list.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Fitzpatrick was speaking during a media tour of a ballot processing facility, and her message echoed recent assurances from both Democratic and Republican election officials in the state. It might be hard to swallow that an American president is one of the worst possible things that could happen to an American election, but those officials are telling voters that despite federal malfeasance, they’re confident they can defend democracy. 
Warnings of disaster are everywhere. The Trump administration last year sued Colorado to obtain sensitive voter data, a move state officials viewed as election interference and which they successfully rebuffed. Trump’s executive order that would have allowed him to meddle with mail ballot systems threatened to severely hurt the handful of universal mail-ballot states like Colorado before the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in. 
Colorado was 1 of 15 states flagged by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for “election integrity” monitoring ahead of the June primary, which Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold said was part of the administration’s “hostility” to the state. The administration plans to send election monitors into a toss-up district in Colorado, an encroachment the state’s top Democrats view as a “bad-faith” form of interference. 
Earlier this year, Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said ominously in a letter to Griswold about ICE at polling places that the agency plays “an important role in investigating voter fraud, and will continue to perform this vital mission.”
Beyond Colorado, Trump and MAGA-world rhetoric suggests other ways Trump could meddle with elections, such as deployment of military members to polling places, invocation of the Insurrection Act, and seizure of ballots and election machines.
Mitchell, a Democrat, has worked with her county attorney to prepare in case federal agents attempt to seize election material.
“We know that the threat is out there. We’ve prepared for it the best we could, about how if they show up we have a protocol for checking the credentials, checking what they’re asking for, this and that, and just make sure we’re following the law.”
Mitchell was first elected clerk in 2014. Threats to elections this year raise concerns like never before, she said.
“It’s very concerning,” she said. “Because some of our most dangerous times are not during the election time, it’s right after … Some of the scarier times are right after the election.”
She has shared this insight with local emergency personnel and law enforcement, who have talked to Chaffee election judges this year for the first time, to help provide some comfort.
“This is a whole new ball game,” Mitchell said. “This is a whole level of desperation that is, I think, very scary.”



Quotation







This is a whole level of desperation that is, I think, very scary.


– Lori Mitchell, Chaffee County clerk


Bobbie Gross, the Republican clerk in Mesa County, took the extra step this year of hiring third-party security services to be deployed at the county’s main elections facility, a precaution she also took for the 2024 election.
Gross is confident the rule of law will prevail.
“We do hear the talk out on the streets, and I’m thankful that the judicial system has worked very well, and I think that the federal government doesn’t have the authority to do a lot of things they’re contemplating or putting out there that they might do. The law’s not really on their side for that,” Gross said.
Election denier Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk who went to prison for her role in an election security breach in her own office, met with Trump earlier this month to discuss “election integrity” plans. Her lawyer, Peter Ticktin, later suggested those plans could involve the seizure of ballots, and he gameplanned “civil war.”
“That wouldn’t be too successful in Weld County,” said Carly Koppes, a Republican who serves as clerk in conservative Weld County and is the president of the Colorado County Clerks Association. She monitors administration election rhetoric.
“At this point they’re throwing anything and everything at the wall, and they’re just trying to see what’s going to stick and what’s going to cause the most noise in this election,” she said. “I don’t think there’s a whole lot of oomph behind it.”
But she and other clerks around the state are preparing for contingencies. They’ve had training on what an FBI badge looks like, and what a subpoena and warrant looks like. They’ve coordinated with Griswold’s office and local law enforcement to respond to emergencies.
“This is all about, at the end of the day, communication, and that’s one of the greatest strengths of the clerks here in Colorado, is we communicate. We talk to each other.” she said. “That’s what makes us so strong.”
Election administration in Colorado is spread across offices in the state’s 64 counties. Whatever attempts Trump makes next week to reverse results he doesn’t like, the clerks in those offices will be on the front lines. They’ve prepared for disasters before. Now they’re preparing for whatever disaster the country’s own president might throw at them.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Let’s be clear-eyed about what federal election monitors on the ground in KY really mean
text:
A polling location is open for early voting at Paristown Hall in Louisville on Saturday in May, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Tensions are high during the last week of the election season. But that reality requires us to be even more clear-eyed on what the law requires and what will happen on the ground on Election Day. 
This week brought a flurry of news stories generating concern about the federal Department of Justice sending election monitors to polling places in Kentucky. But those stories often lacked vital context: this is nothing new but is a normal part of election administration. The Biden DOJ also sent federal monitors to Kentucky polls in 2024. And there are strict rules about what these monitors may do. 
The DOJ’s letter regarding its plans in Kentucky is not contrary to any of these rules. It explains that the monitors will only “observe and take notes.” They cannot “intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process.” They are not law enforcement officials, will not be in uniform, and cannot be armed. 
As the Brennan Center for Justice explains, “The purpose of staff monitors is to observe, document, and report on compliance with civil rights laws. Because there is no specific grant of special privileges for monitors, in many states, monitors may only enter polling places with state or local officials’ permission; otherwise, they must observe outside.”
Kentucky election officials have already explained that the federal monitors may not enter polling places. That is consistent with Kentucky law, which limits who can be inside the voting location. There is no suggestion that they will try to enter polling places, and election officials will tell them they are not allowed if they try.
In an upcoming episode of my radio show and podcast, Democracy Optimist, a series on the WEKU program “Eastern Standard,” Secretary of State Michael Adams said that he has assurances from the highest level of the federal government that “there will not be federal government law enforcement at the polls. There won’t be ICE. There won’t be FBI.”
Importantly, these DOJ monitors are not law enforcement. They have no authority beyond observing what is happening — which is exactly what the letter says they will do. 
Given the political climate, people are understandably concerned about the Trump administration meddling in election administration. The U.S. Constitution gives the president no authority to dictate election rules. But sending civilian federal monitors to watch the process, from outside the polling place, is not as concerning as some are making it out to be. 
Of course, there’s likely a political motivation here. Trump is sending more federal monitors across the country than did previous administrations. There’s also an open question as to whether these monitors are going only to counties with more Democratic voters. But a press release or a DOJ letter saying that the federal government is watching the election does not mean that there are problems with how the election is run. So long as the monitors follow the law, it also does not mean that the DOJ is improperly interfering with the state’s election administration.  
All that said, Trump’s goal has been to sow confusion and concern, which could potentially cause people not to show up to vote or question the legitimacy of the election. We should not let him be successful in that by playing into his hand.
Instead, let’s focus on the facts: millions of people across the country will validly cast their ballots. Thousands of election officials will count the ballots. The winners will take office. 
The bottom line is that federal monitors being sent to Kentucky is neither concerning nor unprecedented. Our jobs are to go out to vote (and bring a friend!) and avoid speculation about voting problems that are unlikely to occur.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: What if you hold an election and candidates don’t show up?
text:
A recent photo of Herbie Hardin by the Fairfield, Kentucky sign. (Courtesy of Herbie Hardin)It started as an idea years ago among his buddies: Why not be the mayor? 
Thirty-year-old Herbie Hardin has lived near Nelson County’s city of Fairfield his entire life, riding his bike as a kid down the street to visit his aunt. It was an easy decision for him to move there, a city with a little more than 100 people, when a friend wanted to sell a home in 2021. 
“I kind of always liked the vibe that it gives off. You know, it’s just a little one-caution light town. It’s got a little gas station,” Hardin said. “I just knew it was a place that I wanted to live.” 
On the last day to do so this summer, he decided to try to make the youthful idea a reality by filing to run for mayor. But he’s taken on the role even sooner: when the longtime mayor of Fairfield died in July and the city clerk asked him to step in as interim mayor, he accepted. 
Hardin said he hasn’t really done any campaigning or put out any yard signs; he’s unopposed in this fall’s general election. But he said word-of-mouth spreads quickly in a small town — especially at the local gas station and deli, Fairfield Grocery. 
“I think that’s where a lot of people found out that I was the mayor,” Hardin said. “I go in there quite a bit, and, you know, it’s a small town. People talk. People know what goes on.” 
On Kentuckians’ ballots this fall are not only highly watched races for U.S. Senate and Congressional seats but also races for city mayor, city council and city commission — including several incorporated cities across the state with around 200 people or fewer. 
Herbie Hardin stands in a road sign for Fairfield, Kentucky with a t-shirt in 2022. (Courtesy Herbie Hardin)
Some of the leaders of these very small towns say politics is nowhere near akin to the politics of larger races, with people voting for who they know in town, and some local officials having served for a long time. But it can also be difficult to find people to run for local office. 
Two people have filed as write-in candidates for the four-person city commission in Fairfield, meaning that Hardin would have to appoint local residents to the commission. Under state law, the governor would have the power to make appointments if the city doesn’t take action within 30 days of a vacancy. 
Since becoming mayor, he’s had to deal with calls of “little goofy stuff” such as people complaining about barking dogs or cars blocking the road. But he finds it rewarding.
“This also makes me feel good about myself knowing that people know, ‘Hey I have a problem, I’m gonna call Herbie and I know he can get it taken care of,’” he said. 
A community identity
Fairfield isn’t the only small city with few or no candidates having filed to run for office. 
In the Owen County city of Gratz, with around 70 people, only one candidate for mayor is also on the ballot. In the Muhlenberg County city of South Carrollton, with about 140 people, no one has signed up to run for office. 
The Webster County community of Slaughters, with about 190 people, has only Mayor Chris Winstead on the ballot. Winstead told the Lantern the entire city commission is running as write-in candidates because the former city clerk forgot to remind the commission about the filing deadline to appear on the ballot. 
“There’s no drama involved in it,” Winstead said about his local elections. “We don’t have a lot of money for people to mismanage, or we don’t get a lot of attention or anything like that.” 
He said it can be hard to encourage people to run for local office given the population loss small, rural cities are already dealing with; the local elementary school closed in 2012. 
But he believes maintaining a city government, with people dedicated to solving local issues, is key to the community’s identity and cohesion. He said one of those issues is frequent flooding from the East Fork of Deer Creek that floods the main road in town. 
“We’re trying to keep the town from just going away, and you know, just being a part of history. We want to make it better,” Winstead said. 
On the other side of Webster County, the city of Wheatcroft, with about 90 residents, is asking its residents to vote on whether to dissolve the city entirely and become a part of the county after more than a century as an incorporated community. No one is on the ballot for mayor or city council in Wheatcroft. 
Republican Webster County Judge-Executive Steve Henry told the Lantern he has mixed feelings about the dissolution vote after discussing the possibility with Wheatcroft leadership in past months. Every couple of months, he has a meeting with the various mayors of small cities in his county of about 13,000 people, each city having somewhat different needs and its “own culture.” 
He said Wheatcroft was potentially looking at raising property taxes to meet the requirements of a state law passed in 2022, leading to the dissolution vote being put on the ballot. 
“They’ve always had trouble getting people to serve on the city council,” Henry said about Wheatcroft. “When you lose the interests of the government within the city, that’s when you start seeing the overall decline.”
Even with the pending vote on dissolution, Henry said Wheatcroft’s identity will still remain. 
“I know there were some people concerned that it wasn’t going to be Wheatcroft anymore. It will always be Wheatcroft,” Henry said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: From ‘Dopesick’ to the campaign trail: Beth Macy takes on Ben Cline in Virginia’s 6th District
text:
Democrat Beth Macy (left) introduces herself to people at the Clarke County Fair in Berryville in August. (Photo courtesy of campaign)Beth Macy never expected to trade journalism for politics. But when protesters outside U.S. Rep. Ben Cline’s Roanoke office began urging her to challenge the Republican incumbent from Botetourt County, she found herself reconsidering her plans for the future. 
“I’m like, no, I’m a journalist,” Macy recalled in a recent phone interview with The Mercury. “I want to write another book or two, become a master gardener and retire. I have a really nice life.” 
But the author of “Dopesick,” whose reporting on the opioid epidemic inspired an award-winning television series, eventually changed her mind. 
Now she is the Democratic nominee running against Cline in Virginia’s 6th Congressional District, hoping to turn a career spent documenting addiction, poverty and economic hardship into a seat in Congress. 
Cline, a four-term incumbent and former state lawmaker, was unavailable for an interview for this story. He is running in a district that long favored Republicans, although national Democrats have added the race to their list of targets.  
For Macy, the move into politics followed years of reporting and a more recent turn toward advocacy. 
She joined activists pressing the U.S. Justice Department and a bankruptcy court to hold members of the Sackler family, the former owners of OxyContin maker Purdue Pharma, accountable for their role in the opioid crisis. 
A separate, yearslong legal battle resulted in a $7.4 billion national settlement that took effect in May, ending the Sacklers’ ownership of Purdue and permanently barring them from selling opioids in the United States. Virginia, which helped negotiate the agreement, stands to receive up to $103.8 million over 15 years for addiction prevention, treatment and recovery programs. 
After President Donald Trump won reelection nearly two years ago, Macy began attending protests outside Cline’s office. She initially resisted calls to run, but said passage of Trump’s sweeping tax and spending law, which he dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill, made her reconsider. 
“My husband and I just looked at each other, and we’re like, let’s just take him down,” she said. 
Macy feared the law’s Medicaid changes would make addiction treatment harder to obtain. Cline voted for the legislation, which Republicans have defended as a way to extend tax cuts and reduce federal spending. 
 From the newsroom to the campaign trail

Macy grew up in Urbana, Ohio, in a family that struggled to make ends meet. She has written about receiving utility shutoff notices and food assistance, and credits a federal Pell Grant with helping her attend college. 
“I came from nothing,” she said. “And every day I wake up and I go, ‘Damn, this is me.’”
She spent 25 years at the Roanoke Times before becoming a best-selling author. Her first book, “Factory Man,” followed a Virginia furniture maker fighting to preserve American manufacturing jobs. “Truevine” told the story of two Black brothers and their mother in Jim Crow-era Virginia. 
“Dopesick” examined the opioid epidemic, while “Raising Lazarus” focused on efforts to address it. Macy’s latest book, “Paper Girl,” is a memoir about her upbringing. 
Macy said the people she met during those years of reporting still shape how she thinks about public policy. She carries a reporter’s notebook on the campaign trail, writing down what voters tell her about their lives.
“I think Congress could use an investigative journalist right now,” she said. 
Macy’s healthcare agenda includes restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act premium subsidies and reversing Medicaid changes in Trump’s spending law, which she calls the “One Ugly Bill.” She supports Medicare for All but said her immediate priority would be protecting existing coverage. 
Macy also wants to expand addiction treatment in prisons and improve access to care for people leaving incarceration.
Her interest in veterans’ care is personal, she said. Her father served in World War II and never received treatment for post-traumatic stress after returning home. 



Quotation







I think Congress could use an investigative journalist right now.


– Beth Macy


On energy policy, Macy has called for a moratorium on data center development while federal officials craft rules addressing land use, water consumption and jobs. She argues the industry is expanding too quickly and communities need more protection. 
 A steep climb in the 6th

Virginia’s 6th District follows the Interstate 81 corridor from the northern Shenandoah Valley to Roanoke. Cline won reelection in 2024 with 63% of the vote, defeating Democrat Ken Mitchell by roughly 28 percentage points. 
However, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently put the district “in play,” although Cline adviser Tim Murtaugh dismissed the designation as an attempt to manufacture enthusiasm. 
Independent election analysts remain skeptical of Democrats’ changes. The Cook Political Report rates the race solidly Republican, while the University of Virginia’s Sabato’s Crystal Ball classifies it as safe Republican. 
Both ratings are less competitive than those for the neighboring 5th District, where analysts have moved the contest toward Democrats. 
Macy argues her fundraising and conversations with voters show she can make the race competitive. She said internal campaign polling has her gaining on Cline, although those results have not been independently verified. 
“I tell people, flat out, that we will not win this race unless we reach out to the middle,” she said. 
Through Sept. 30, Macy has raised about $2.6 million, compared with about $1.9 million for Cline, according to the nonpartisan Virginia Public Access Project. 
Her campaign said it raised more than $1 million between July and September, combining two federal spending reporting periods, and does not accept corporate PAC donations. 
More recent Federal Election Commission records show Macy had raised about $2.93 million through Oct. 14. Figures compiled by Ballotpedia put Cline’s receipts at approximately $1.91 million through the same date. 
Cline, however, had more money left to spend, with about $527,000 cash on hand compared to Macy’s $363,000. 
David Richards, a political science professor at the University of Lynchburg, said Macy’s fundraising, name recognition and support from energized Democrats have made the race more competitive than Cline’s previous contests. 
Still, Richards said he expects Cline to win, although the margin could narrow to the low single digits. The district’s Republican electorate, he said, remains a substantial obstacle for Macy. 
“Money matters, but money doesn’t vote,” Richards said. 
He said dissatisfaction with Trump, Congress and the economy could hurt Cline, but Macy would likely need a significant number of Republicans to break ranks or stay home to win.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Dominion asks SCC to recoup RGGI costs from customers, adding up to $13 to bills monthly
text:
State Corporation Commission building in downtown Richmond. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)This summer, Dominion Energy rejoined the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a carbon market designed to offset carbon emissions. Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin yanked Virginia from RGGI in 2023 and in her first speech to lawmakers in January, Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced the state’s imminent return to the program, a move cemented by legislation that took effect earlier this year. 
At the State Corporation Commission headquarters on Wednesday, the utility debated how to recover the cost of the carbon allowances from customers and how to implement the bill credit lawmakers allocated to offset the impact on ratepayers.
Ten states are part of the RGGI agreement to limit carbon and purchase permits for emissions. Virginia received over $800 million over the three years the state was in the program before the removal. State law previously required 50% of the funds go to low-income efficiency programs, 45% to the Community Flood Preparedness Fund, and the remainder to administrative costs.
Dominion was directed to rejoin the RGGI agreement by July 2026, forcing the company to participate in the September allowance auction before the cost recovery mechanism has been reimplemented. The costs of the program have been stacking up since then. 
The company projects for the next year, with the addition of the eight months the company has been back in the agreement, RGGI fees will total $1,179,089,492. According to SCC filings, Dominion will need approximately 35.5 million CO2 allowances for the period of July 1, 2026 though Feb. 28, 2028.
The so-called RGGI rider, the portion of customers’ monthly bills that are allocated to the cost recovery of these allowance purchases, is not anticipated to begin until March 2027. The amount is approved annually by the SCC.
The utility has offered two methods of how payments can be allocated to customers’ bills. One way is to add all 20 months of costs to bills without mitigation, which would mean a jump of about $13 a month for the average residential customer. 
A mitigation plan has been developed as the other method, to spread out the eight months that have not yet been recovered over a period of two years. That would make the monthly bill increase about $10. 
But environmental groups like Appalachian Voices, who are intervenors in the RGGI rider case, said at Wednesday’s SCC hearing that financing costs would add up with the delayed payment plan and tack on up to $17 million.
The carbon dioxide trading program is part of the commonwealth’s push to get public utilities to move away from fossil fuels as a key source of power generation. The cost of the carbon allowances has increased since the last auction the state participated in. Dominion projects carbon prices to be $37.04 to $38.32 per CO2 allowance over the July 2026 through December 2028 period.
With the spike in carbon allowance prices and with affordability a priority for the Spanberger administration, an amendment to address those challenges was tacked on to the state budget that was settled in late June. 
The amendment directs 45% of the funds that the state brings in from the RGGI agreement to be dispersed back to residential, small business, and church customers in the form of a bill credit, which energy officials estimate will almost totally offset the RGGI costs on bills.
The change will mean less money for the low-income energy efficiency, flood preparedness and climate change planning programs that it fueled in previous years.
Debates about exactly how the money from the state will be calculated and reinstated to customers through the credit bubbled up during Wednesday’s hearing. 
“It’s the companies’ understanding that a process has not been finalized at this point. But the current thinking by the Department of Environmental Quality is that they will use the prior quarter’s actual emissions as reported on the state’s website to determine that allocation,” Lisa Crabtree, the director of strategic planning for Dominion, testified.
Appalachian Voices and the Sierra Club’s attorneys argued that Dominion has continued to build out their fossil fuel portfolio despite the mandate to phase out carbon emitting energy sources. 
The utility has defended its resource plan that includes natural gas and renewable energy sources, dubbing both critical to “maintain grid reliability”.
The SCC will consider the methodology of reinstating the RGGI Rider to bills and implementing the bill credits that are mandated by the legislature in the coming months. The commission has until Feb. 5 to make a determination.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Are sales taxes the fairest way to fund improved schools? 47 localities are asking voters to decide.
text:
A view from outside the newly renovated Gloucester County High School, which opened last September. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Amid lingering inflation from high fuel prices, 47 Virginia localities are about to ask their residents to vote on Tuesday for a ballot question that will make every retail purchase they make near their homes costlier.
Interesting timing to say the least. But that doesn’t make it wrong.
If voters approve the proposed tax increases, which are capped at 1%, their proceeds would by law be directed toward capital improvements for public schools in those localities. That’s a worthy purpose, ranking right up there with public safety and healthcare.
Yet the decision is not easy. Voters are being asked to weigh their current financial situations against their children’s futures. There are valid points on either side of this argument that warrant respect.
Still, it’s hard not to feel it’s a shame that it’s come to this.
Virginia localities weigh 1% sales tax for school construction as voters decide on expansion

The sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation there is, burdening most those who have the least. 
The person who works all day then moonlights as a rideshare driver to cover rent, grocery and utility bills with no capacity to save anything pays as much tax on a new refrigerator as a Fortune 500 CEO with a summer house on Martha’s Vineyard and a fleet of Teslas.
It’s a shame because as a commonwealth, our state leaders have preened and posed and positioned themselves as champions of making our schools — in affluent communities and poor ones — safe, modern and excellent, turning out graduates who can hold their own anywhere. You know, the literal definition of a “commonwealth.”
But in the end, the full measure of K-12 educational excellence was tossed back into the laps of Virginia’s 133 localities. 
Because Virginia is a Dillon Rule state — meaning local governments are strictly limited in the tax rates they can raise without legislative approval — the General Assembly empowered the 95 counties and 38 independent cities to ask their voters if they will shoulder a sales tax boost. Thirty-five percent of those localities are doing that in this election.
State approval didn’t happen through the more transparent regular legislative process. A stand-alone bill that would have authorized the extra penny of tax on every dollar’s worth of retail spending passed the House of Delegates this year, but the Senate carried it over to the 2027 session.
The authorization was buried in small type and dense legislative jargon on page 723 of the 887-page state budget enacted on June 29, one day ahead of the deadline for averting a state government shutdown.
Eight Virginia localities — Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania counties and the city of Danville — got state permission to ask their voters to approve the sales tax increase before it was extended to all localities this year.
As the Mercury’s Nathaniel Cline explained in his reporting on Oct. 5, those eight localities have generated a combined $119 million through those higher taxes since 2019, but results are mixed and satisfaction is not universal.
In Halifax, the first locality to receive authorization, students enjoy a new high school and remodeled elementary and middle schools that wouldn’t have been affordable without the $20.8 million the county has taken in over the past five years.
Danville took in nearly $31 million from 2023 through last year, giving the city ample bonding authority for impressive upgrades to its facilities.
That’s not bringing much comfort, however, to voters in York County, which would see its combined sales tax rate reach 8% — the highest in Virginia — if the measure passes. Already, York is tied with two of its Peninsula neighbors, James City County and Williamsburg, for the state’s highest rate at 7%.
By no stretch is York County struggling economically. According to the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, its median annual household income is just under $110,000, or about $16,800 greater than the statewide median. 
But that doesn’t translate to York residents gladly paying significantly more in taxes on their purchases than the statewide average of just under 6%.
York County Supervisor G. Stephen Roane Jr. opposed putting the sales tax increase measure on the countywide ballot with so little time to weigh the political and economic consequences against the benefits.
“I thought we needed time to study other options to seek money to provide for school infrastructure projects. I thought we moved too quickly,” he said in an interview.
Particularly, he said, he was concerned about the effect the state’s highest sales tax could have on merchants in his county. Within reason, consumers will travel to save money, and retailers in the cities of Poquoson and Hampton — both sharing York’s eastern boundary — could beckon frugal York shoppers to make the short drive and exploit a tax rate two percentage points lower, especially on big-ticket items.
As incomes go, York’s ranking among the top 10% of the state’s most affluent localities can be quite misleading, Roane noted.
“Affluence is an average across the board, so there are people below that average who are going to struggle,” he said. “You’ve got to be mindful of everybody in the county.”
Virginia as a whole compares favorably to neighboring states when it comes to sales tax burdens. Our average combined state and local rates are about even with those of every adjacent state but Tennessee — a state that proudly eschews an income tax yet forces consumers to pay almost an extra dime on every retail dollar spent except for groceries, which are taxed at a lower rate.
Even with the additional penny of sales taxes for schools, Virginia would still be a bargain compared to Tennessee and wouldn’t make the commonwealth inherently uncompetitive with any other nextdoor state.
The greater question for Virginians heading to the polls, however, is whether this is the most equitable way to invest in our local public schools and, by extension, the commonwealth’s future.
Fortunately, these are the most meaningful and productive questions that we as a commonwealth can and should ask ourselves — at all levels of government. And in the end, there are good answers and better answers, but no wrong ones.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Data centers tighten county executive battle in Frederick
text:
Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater speaks to a resident while campaigning in the Hillcrest neighborhood outside the city of Frederick in late October. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)With just days left in the campaign, Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater (D) finds herself in an unlikely dogfight with an underfunded GOP challenger who is now the subject of attack ads produced by a super PAC.
Voter anger over data centers may, at least in part, be responsible.
“Without the data center issue, she would be cruising to an easy, guaranteed, no-doubt-about-it reelection,” said Kai Hagen, a Democrat and former Frederick County Councilmember who lost to Fitzwater in the 2022 primary.
Just across the Potomac from Loudoun County, Virginia — which hosts one of the largest concentrations of hyperscale data centers in the world — Frederick County’s Adamstown is Maryland’s ground zero for data center development.
Of late, it’s been a rocky road. There’s been outcry from residents, who sought to bring data center zoning onto the ballot, but who saw a 20,000-signature petition quashed by Maryland’s highest court.
Fitzwater says she’s listening. She imposed a pause on new data centers and, after initially singing its praises, she rejected a September deal that would have granted data center developers new rights in the county in exchange for $110 million for school renovations, a community center and a new fire truck.
But her reversal brought the county’s data center quandary back to the courts, this time with data center campus developer Catellus crying foul.
A data center under construction in Frederick County’s Adamstown in late September. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Had the issue been handled differently, Hagen said, Fitzwater likely would not be in so tight a race.
“Clearly, the issue has made a difference,” he said.
So much so that Republican nominee Jeff Holtzinger, who served one term as Frederick mayor nearly two decades ago, is making an unlikely run despite an array of political disadvantages.
He’s running in a year when Democrats are predicting a “blue wave” over voter disapproval of President Donald Trump (R), in a county where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than 11,500 voters. On campaign funding, he’s been outraised by Fitzwater 32-1, and outspent by nearly 40-1.
Mike Hough, a Republican former state senator who lost the 2022 executive’s race to Fitzwater by less than 1,000 votes, said the Fitzwater-Holzinger contest is one that “we shouldn’t be talking about.”
“I don’t think Jeff has hardly any money, so on paper it shouldn’t be a race…. I think the data centers are part of the issue for sure,” Hough said.
Hough also thinks Fitzwater, whom he describes as “very aggressively pro-growth,” is hurt by the fact that “data centers … fit part and parcel with the growth that people don’t like” in Frederick County.
A recent poll by the Institute for Politics at the University of Maryland Baltimore County found nearly 8 in 10 Maryland voters opposed the construction of data centers: 83% of Democrats, 91% of unaffiliated voters and 55% of Republicans.
In Frederick, a county of roughly 210,000 people, 39% are registered Democrats, about a third are Republicans and 28% are unaffiliated voters, up 3 percentage points from four years ago, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections.
The data center issue seemingly reared its head in the June primary, when County Council President Brad Young, a Democrat, lost his seat, while candidates preaching “data center sanity” largely won out. It came after the council, with Fitzwater’s support, expanded an existing zone for data centers near Adamstown, but barred them from elsewhere in the county.
Then came United Frederick, a super PAC that has so far reported pumping more than $400,000 into Fitzwater’s race. The group’s ads target Holtzinger, linking him to the Make America Great Again movement and President Donald Trump (R), as well as ICE and unpopular immigration enforcement activities.
The group’s funding, about $550,000, comes from Maryland State Education Association, AFSCME and Total Wine and Food Supply, a company co-founded by former Rep. David Trone, a Democrat.
A sign opposing “data center suck-up” candidates sits outside ahome in Adamstown, where a data center campus is under construction. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
The race has attracted other outside attention. Gov. Wes Moore (D) stopped in Frederick to rally with Democrats including Fitzwater during a barnstorming tour of Western Maryland. On Friday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D) and Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-8th) and April McClain Delaney (D-6th) will make campaign stops in the county.
Fitzwater, a former music teacher, who first entered politics 12 years ago as a county council member, says she’s feeling optimistic.
During canvassing efforts focused largely on Democrats and the county’s growing number of unaffiliated voters, she said she does not hear about data centers terribly often.
“People are not asking me about this at the doors. They’re talking about ICE. They’re talking about affordability,” Fitzwater said. “They want to vote against Trump. It’s not the first thing that is on people’s minds.”
Knocking on doors in a Frederick suburb on a recent sunny afternoon, Fitzwater led with her experience as a teacher, and the fact that she’s a mom with two children enrolled in the county public school system. She argued she would continue to bolster investment in Frederick schools. But she also pitched herself as an “antidote to what we’re seeing in Washington.”
The responses to data centers may change depending on which door is knocked and who answers.
In rural places along the county’s southwestern border with Virginia, such as Adamstown, Jefferson and Middletown, the issue hits close to home, said Frank Hollewa, a Republican candidate for Frederick County Council.
“It’s probably the issue in certain sections of the county, like in Jefferson and Middletown, and here in Point of Rocks and Adamstown,” Hollewa said. “Yeah, it is a huge issue, but you know maybe somewhere else they might think naively: ‘That’s their problem.’ But like I said, the tentacles — this is far-reaching.”
When data centers do come up, Fitzwater said the concerns she hears while canvassing are often national in scope.
“It’s not usually about some specific thing the county has or hasn’t done,” Fitzwater said. “It’s more of an overarching concern about data centers, AI, what’s going to happen — not wanting to see them kind of taking over.”
Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater campaigns in the Hillcrest neighborhood outside of the city of Frederick in late October. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Still, Fitzwater admits that data centers have “shifted the temperature” of the race — and her last year or so as county executive.
What began as a data center campus on a polluted brownfield — a shuttered aluminum smelting facility — expanded to 2,600 acres in late 2025, when the council approved zoning changes, roping in former agricultural land. But the county also banned data centers in all other industrial areas for the first time.
“There really was an effort to represent that action as an expansion of data centers, which it just wasn’t,” Fitzwater said. “What it did was actually restrict where data centers can go.
“We heard very loudly and clearly from folks they didn’t want to see data center sprawl — pockets of it all over the county,” Fitzwater said.
She worries some of her constituents have become lost in a national anti-data center furor, and caught up in the potential negative side effects of data center proposals in other states. She believes the solution lies in educating voters about the county’s efforts to centralize — and police — the hyperscalers.
“One of my challenges has been: How do you communicate that, while also recognizing these larger concerns and fears that people have that are well beyond anything that’s happening here?” Fitzwater said.
She’s committed to working with the next county council to reduce the zoning expansion approved in 2025.
Thomas Slater, a Frederick attorney and longtime Democratic activist, argues that Fitzwater’s recent reversals, including on the zoning decision and the $110 million agreement, will work in her favor.
“My assessment is that she has turned it around, and is likely to win because of the fact that she is trying to distance herself from being considered pro-data center — and the weakness of her opponent,” Slater said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
But he acknowledges some voters could see it as flip-flopping.
“Some people think they don’t trust her, because it seems obvious that she is reversing what seems to be her position. But other people say she’s reading the public and reacting to the voters,” Slater said.
It wasn’t data centers that drew Holtzinger to reenter the political fray to oppose Fitzwater, but rising property taxes and poorly planned growth.
True to his civil engineering background — which helped him defeat local political heavyweight Ron Young for mayor in 2005, following a water crisis — Holtzinger said he’s concerned that the county lacks the water resources to feed the data centers, and that local roads are ill prepared for associated truck traffic.
He argues that the county has so far bungled its handling of the hyperscale developers interested in Frederick, spurring a potentially costly lawsuit from data center developer Catellus, filed earlier this month.
“The secrecy, the flip-flopping,” Holtzinger said. “Her political maneuvering has put the entire county in a very difficult position.”
Holtzinger is quick to criticize the effort to brand him as a MAGA Republican and tie him to an unpopular president.
“They’re trying to deflect to national politics and identity politics,” Holtzinger said in response. “It’s disingenuous and it’s lazy.”
Holtzinger said he, like outspoken Frederick Sheriff Chuck Jenkins, a Republican, supports 287(g) agreements, which up until this year let local law enforcement transfer detainees to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, arguing that it kept immigrant detention in controlled environments rather than out on the streets. But as county executive, he said he wouldn’t focus on that issue — or other national talking points.
A view of data center construction in Frederick County’s Adamstown in late September. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
“I have no control over ICE. My focus is going to be on core local government issues, things that people rely on every day to go about their lives,” Holtzinger said.
He draws a sharp contrast to Fitzwater on school funding, arguing that the school system has been spending wastefully, and must be scrutinized more closely.
“I strongly believe in a strong public education system,” he said. “But there has to be accountability.”
The United Frederick ads also argue that Holtzinger is hiding his true record on data centers, pointing in particular to one comment he gave the Frederick News-Post: “I am not against data centers.”
One election flyer “leads people to believe that I — along with Donald Trump and Elon Musk — turbo-charged the development of hyperscale data centers,” Holtzinger said. “That’s ridiculous.”
“You would think I’m the county executive and I’m the one making all the bad decisions. I’m not in office. She is,” Holtzinger said.
Nevertheless, Holtzinger’s message on data centers has seemingly resonated with voters of varying political stripes in and around Adamstown, where data center construction continues unabated even amid a temporary moratorium on new proposals.
“The average Frederick County voter will go: ‘Isn’t it great? She’s doing a moratorium,’” said Adamstown resident Elyse Wilson, an independent voter who supports Holzinger. “People think a moratorium is stopping.”
Numerous large warehouses already appear amid a sprawling construction site, attracting concerns about polluting dust, contaminated groundwater and eventual air toxins from diesel generator use. And on Oct. 14, the county’s planning commission approved three new data centers on a parcel to which a developer already had development rights.
Some say they’ve lost faith in Fitzwater, and a change is needed.
That includes Adamstown resident Hope Green, whose front yard once overlooked farm fields but now sits face-to-face with one of several data center warehouses — hardly blocked by a smattering of recently planted trees.
“Everything’s been destroyed here. Our environment, our health and wellbeing. They’ve just decimated it,” Green said.
Frederick County resident Hope Green (at right) looks out at the view of data center construction from her front yard. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
