name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: New report shows there were 2,529 oil and gas incidents in Ohio in a decade
text:
Anti-fracking advocates hung up signs before an Oil and Gas Land Management Commission meeting. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal)There were more than 2,500 oil and gas incidents reported in Ohio from 2015 through 2025, according to a new report. 
The number of incidents are generally increasing, going from 103 in 2015 to 268 in 2025, according to a new report published last week by FracTracker Alliance in partnership with Buckeye Environmental Network. 
FracTracker Alliance analyzed ODNR records from 2015 to 2025 for the report. 
“That’s much more (total incidents) than I would expect,” said Gwen Klenke, the report’s author. There were 2,529 incidents recorded in Ohio from 2015 to 2025. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Obviously everyone’s human. Everyone makes mistakes, so there’s always going to be some amount of things going wrong, but 2,500 is a pretty massive number for 10 years. … It just feels like it’s more than it should be.”
The Ohio Department of Natural Resources did not respond to the Ohio Capital Journal’s questions by deadline.
The Ohio Oil and Gas Association said the report was not “an objective assessment of Ohio’s energy industry.”
“FracTracker’s conclusions should be viewed for what they are: advocacy, not a comprehensive assessment of the safety, environmental performance and regulatory oversight of Ohio’s oil and natural gas operations,” Ohio Oil and Gas Association Director of External Affairs Mike Chadsey said in an email.
“Ohio’s energy producers remain focused on responsible development, protecting our communities and delivering the reliable energy that powers our state.”
Bev Reed with Buckeye Environmental Network said the findings from this new report are alarming. 
“It’s incredibly important that ODNR and the legislature get their act together,” she said in an email.
“We also received documents showing that an injection well company in Washington County requested that ODNR not suspend its injection well near Marietta, despite the fact that the state had grounds to immediately suspend the well.”
The yearly total of oil and gas incidents in Ohio according to a report published from FracTracker Alliance in partnership with Buckeye Environmental Network. (Screenshot)
The report showed incident classifications are often unclear. 
“There’s this really pervasive lack of good data throughout the whole data set, which is concerning considering its incidents and spills, things that we would want good details about, and related to that was the characterization of the incidents,” said Klenke, FracTracker’s Midwest Program Coordinator. 
A 2016 incident in Columbiana County was categorized as a “minor” incident, but was described as “static electricity from overhead power lines caused a conventional well’s tank to explode,” according to the report. 
Another incident categorized as “minor” in Gallia County involved an unknown quantity of oil and gas wastewater was released from a well while it was being plugged. ODNR’s records reveal the well had been “flowing overnight with no well control in place.” 
“I pointed out major explosions being categorized as minor incidents, and that just doesn’t seem good for public understanding of these types of events,” Klenke said. 
ODNR has about 25 inspectors who are responsible for Ohio’s 96,000 wells, according to the report. This means one inspector is responsible for 1,500 wells in Harrison County while another inspector is responsible for about 24,000 wells in 26 counties, according to the report. 
“Really any increase, I think I’d be happy with,” Klenke said when asked how many inspectors she wishes ODNR had. 
“If they got 26 inspectors in Ohio, I’d be celebrating.”


More than 1,200 of the incidents were categorized as release/discharge. There 615 gas releases, 108 fires, 94 explosions or fires, and six injuries, according to the report. 
Of Ohio’s 88 counties, there were incidents in 73. Most of the incidents are in the eastern part of Ohio. 
Stark County had the most incidents with 133, followed by Noble County with 129, and Trumbull and Guernsey counties both had 114, according to the report. 
“Residents in those counties should be especially vigilant when they are doing things like going on hikes or walking more rural lanes,” Klenke said.  
“I would hope that residents in those counties would just really keep their eyes peeled for anything that doesn’t seem right. If they see something, they should definitely call emergency services to get them out there to at least check things out.”
Klenke said she hopes to see more oversight and accountability with Ohio’s oil and gas wells.
“It can happen with more inspectors,” she said. 
“It can also happen with just better tracking of the incidents, better follow through, just generally with well owners who may be concerned that something’s wrong with their well.”

title: Domestic violence noted as ‘most prevalent violent crime in Ohio’ as state boosts funding
text:
A domestic violence awareness ribbon. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)With data showing domestic violence as the “most prevalent violent crime in Ohio,” state officials recently announced boosts to domestic violence programs, including survivor services and law enforcement training.
The Ohio Department of Public Safety’s Office of Criminal Justice Services found that more than half of all violent crime arrests in Ohio had a domestic violence charge as part of the case, with 70% of the arrests conducted on repeat offenders.
The researchers studied half a century of criminal history data in the state, including about 2 million violent crime arrests from 1974 to 2023, according to a release about the research.
The study also found that from 2014 to 2023, 54% of violent crime arrests involved domestic violence. That statistic went up to 56% in the last five years.
“Anecdotally, we suspected that domestic violence was among the most frequent violent crimes in the state, and this data confirms it,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement.
“The data also reinforces the fact that Ohio must continue to be innovative in its work to protect both domestic violence survivors and the law enforcement officers who respond to calls for help.”
Ohio had its second highest amount of deaths from domestic violence-related incidents in 2025, according to data released this month from the Ohio Domestic Violence Network. The report showed 134 deaths in 101 cases.
The year before was the highest amount of deaths since the network began collecting fatality statistics 11 years ago. In 2024, Ohio had 157 deaths in 108 cases. Over the last two years of data, the network found that in 49% of cases, the victim was attempting to leave the situation.
“These homicides are not random,” said Maria York, the network’s director of policy and communications, when the report was announced. “They are the final act of control.”
As part of a recent announcement of funding set aside for “specific domestic-violence-related projects,” the governor’s office said an additional $1 million will be directed toward the state’s domestic violence shelters recognized by the Office of Criminal Justice Services.
The 55 shelters across the state will each receive a one-time grant of $18,000 for “immediate shelter and meeting the critical needs of family violence victims and their dependents,” according to the governor’s office.
The Office of Criminal Justice Services announced another $4 million in “federal emergency shelter and supportive services grants for domestic violence victims and their dependents,” in an Oct. 27 press release.
The funding is from the Family Violence Prevention and Services Act Formula Grant to States and Territories, administered through the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services.
The state office said 64 projects in 46 counties will be funded for one year, from July 2026 through June 2027.
The grant amounts ranged from $115,000 going to Stark County’s Domestic Violence Project, Inc., to $30,000 awards for Greene County’s Violence Free Futures, Geauga County’s Womensafe, and Summit County’s Asian Services in Action, Inc.
Law enforcement will also be receiving state funding meant for programs related to domestic violence, like one to provide training on “lethality assessments,” which are used to decide how much a survivor risks future domestic violence based on the situation to which law enforcement are responding.
The funding announced by the governor’s office is also set to help establish “co-responder partnership models.”
Those models would partner victim services advocates with law enforcement “to help ensure that trauma-informed support is immediately available on-scene for survivors after law enforcement responds to a domestic violence incident,” according to the governor’s office.
A separate grant is also set aside to fund “ballistic shields,” which would be used by law enforcement when responding to “high-risk calls like domestic violence incidents.”
In addition, DeWine tasked the Ohio Collaborative Community-Police Advisory Board to develop standards for responses to domestic violence, and investigations of it, using the Ohio Domestic Violence Network’s handbook for law enforcement working with domestic violence survivors.
The network praised the new grant funding and the work to set law enforcement standards.
“We are especially pleased to work with the Ohio Collaborative to provide law enforcement with more guidance about responding to domestic violence calls, which can be the most dangerous calls police get,” said ODVN’s senior director for survivor services, Alicia Williamson, in a statement.
The network worked with the Office of Criminal Justice Services on a training initiative to offer seven regional, in-person trainings, and seven virtual trainings for law enforcement in Ohio.
According to a press release from ODVN, topics in the trainings will include trauma-informed investigations, lethality assessments, strangulation and brain injuries, protection order enforcement, and victims’ rights.
The first of the trainings is scheduled for Nov. 18 in Columbus.

title: Ohio economists split on gas tax replacement
text:
An interstate freeway in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
Ohio has paused its gasoline tax in an attempt to bring down high fuel prices, but some are debating whether to replace it altogether. In a recent survey, Ohio economists weighed the options.
Revenue from the gas tax is mostly used to build and maintain roads and bridges. And as electric vehicles and hybrids proliferate, a “vehicle miles traveled fee” would ensure a stable source of funding, the thinking goes.
When asked whether that would be more efficient than a gas tax, a panel of Ohio economists divided, according to a survey conducted last week by Scioto Analysis. Sixteen said it would be, 11 said it would not be, and four were uncertain.
In the comments section of the survey, Lucas Englehardt of Kent State University agreed that a miles-traveled fee makes sense in terms of funding road maintenance. But he said policymakers need to be cognizant of other expenses created by gas-burning cars.
“In as far as the goal is funding roads, it makes sense to proportion the fee to the use of roads — miles traveled being a reasonable approach, and much more representative of the benefit than ‘fuel used’ is,” he wrote. 
“The one wrinkle here: the gas tax is part road user fee but also part emissions charge. So, for the question of road funding, a per-mile charge is more efficient — but that doesn’t mean that it’s more efficient overall.”
David Brasington of the University of Cincinnati disagreed that a miles-traveled fee would be more efficient for a practical reason. He said people probably wouldn’t go along with its implementation.
“If you use GPS tracking of Ohio drivers, it would be feasible, but people would probably have big privacy concerns,” he wrote. “Other ways of implementing a miles-driven system have high costs of administering the system compared to a gas tax.”
Ali Enami of the University of Akron said he thought a miles-traveled tax would be more efficient than a gas tax. But he said that if the purpose is to maintain roads, vehicle weight should also be taken into account.
Research has shown that a loaded, five-axle truck does as much damage to a road as hundreds or even thousands of cars, depending on the road’s condition.
“I would add that other factors, such as vehicle weight, should be included in the calculation of the fee,” Enami wrote. “That is, holding vehicle miles traveled constant, a road used by heavier vehicles would require more frequent repairs.”
When it comes to fairness, Ohio already digs a little deeper into the pockets of those who drive the most fuel-efficient vehicles. Owners of hybrids pay a $100 annual fee while those who have plug-in hybrids pay $150 and owners of full EVs pay $200.
Kevin Egan of the University of Toledo said that means that those driving fully electric vehicles are already paying more than the average gas-powered motorist is paying in gas tax.
“Ohio’s $200 annual registration fee on electric vehicles (vs. $35 for a gas car) is already a little more than the average gas car driver pays in state gas tax so this change already makes-up for lost state gas tax revenue from an electric car,” he wrote. 
“The advantage is it is easy to implement as it is just a higher annual registration fee. Yes, a vehicle-miles-traveled fee would be more efficient as those driving electric cars more would then pay more, but it would require tracking each vehicle’s annual mileage, which is not currently done.”

title: Commentary: Patients first? Putting the OSMA Ohio governor endorsement in perspective
text:
(Stock photo by Wichayada Suwanachun/Getty Images)In mid-September, the Ohio State Medical Association’s Political Action Committee (OSMAPAC) endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy for governor over Dr. Amy Acton, a physician and Ohio’s former health director whom many credit with saving lives during the pandemic. Ramaswamy is a billionaire biotech investor.
Physicians took notice. More than 1,000 signed an open letter backing Acton, warning that Ramaswamy’s positions, including calling Medicare and Medicaid “a mistake,” threaten patients’ access to care. Many signers belong to OSMA.
Anyone who has studied the history of American health reform will recognize the pattern. The most powerful physicians’ organization, the American Medical Association, has repeatedly stood in the way of patient-centered reform. That is not a fluke. 
Organized medicine exists to advance the professional and economic interests of physicians. Benefits to patients are sometimes real, but they are more often incidental.
The record is long. In 1920, after initial openness, the AMA’s House of Delegates came out against compulsory health insurance. In the 1920s it fought the Sheppard-Towner Act, which funded state maternal and child health programs, as a threat to fee-for-service medicine. 
In 1943, the Supreme Court upheld the AMA’s conviction for conspiring to cripple a Washington, D.C., prepaid group practice that threatened fee-for-service medicine. After World War II, the AMA assessed members $25 each to fund a campaign against Truman’s national health insurance plan, branding it “socialized medicine.”
In 1961, it enlisted Ronald Reagan for “Operation Coffee Cup,” recorded messages warning that Medicare would end American freedom.
As we know, Medicare passed and became a dependable and integral source of physician income. 
By 2009, the AMA was backing the health reform push that became the Affordable Care Act, which put millions of newly insured patients in physicians’ waiting rooms. The through-line is not political partisanship, but members’ interests: resist what threatens them, welcome what helps them.
We saw this dynamic at work during the COVID-19 pandemic, when, as the Ohio Capital Journal reported in 2021, the Ohio Hospital Association and Ohio Osteopathic Association publicly – and rightly – opposed dangerous anti-public health bills being pushed through the General Assembly. 
The problem is they did this at the same time as their PACs contributed to the sponsors of that very bill. 
The formal explanation for such hypocrisy is that these organizations’ political action committees operate independently of the main organizations. But voters can fairly ask why they should trust these organizations’ public statements when their campaign contributions point the other way.
I say this not to criticize organized medicine. Representing members is a legitimate function for trade associations. 
The error is ours, the voters, when we mistake a political endorsement for a verdict on patients’ welfare. Professional interests, not Hippocratic fidelity, drives these decisions.
In announcing its endorsement, OSMAPAC cited Ramaswamy’s backing of physician-led care, efforts to grow the physician workforce, and plans to reduce administrative obstacles for physicians. 
OSMA President Dr. Gary Katz explained that Ramaswamy believes physicians, not insurers, should make medical decisions, and noted that OSMA’s members span the political spectrum. 
Fewer prior authorizations and less insurer interference are reasonable positions for health professionals to take — and anybody who listens to Dr. Acton talk about health care access and public health knows that she supports reducing the administrative burden and other barriers that undermine patient care.
But instead of support for patients, OSMA offered a litany of physician-centric practice conditions. 
Missing was any mention of improving our approach to chronic disease, Ohio’s unacceptable disparities in infant mortality, private-equity raids on rural hospitals, or the coverage losses Ohioans face as major Medicaid and ACA changes arrive in 2027.
The comparison with other health-sector groups is instructive. In April, the Ohio Nurses Association, a union representing more than 10,000 nurses and other health professionals, endorsed Acton, citing health care costs and union values. 
The Columbus Medical Association did not make an endorsement. Three health-sector organizations made three different choices, each reflecting its constituency. The nurses’ union is also an interest group, and it said so by naming its values. 
Even within physician ranks, there is no single “physician” position. The more than 1,000 doctors backing Acton are as much physicians as the small panel of board members that made the OSMAPAC endorsement.
We should read the endorsement for what it is: one governing board’s judgment about what serves its profession. It tells you something about physicians’ interests, about which thoughtful physicians can and do disagree. 
But it cannot tell you what is best for Ohioans, more generally, and it certainly is not a marker of which candidate will put patients first. 
For that, look at the candidates’ records on coverage, public health, and the hospitals and clinics Ohioans depend on. And remember history, which counsels some skepticism whenever organized medicine claims to speak for the public.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.

 Catching Our Eye

• JD Vance-founded donor network. The Washington Post reports, “Brazilian judge orders investigation into JD Vance donor network.”
A Brazilian Supreme Court justice on Tuesday ordered a police investigation into alleged ties between a donor network co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and the presidential campaign of Flávio Bolsonaro in the run-up to Sunday’s election.
Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino directed the Brazilian federal police to investigate the “nature” of the contacts between the Rockbridge Network, which was founded in 2019, and any Brazilian companies or political operatives to aid or finance Bolsonaro’s run.
It’s a crime in Brazil for a political candidate to accept funding or other campaign assistance from a foreign source.
• Too late to mail ballot back. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “Why it’s almost too late to vote by mail in Ohio in this November’s election.”
If you want to vote on a mail-in ballot, your request must be at your local board of elections by 8 p.m. tonight (Tuesday Oct. 27). But Ohio’s top elections official says it will be too late to mail it back.
If you submit your request for a mail-in ballot, you might get one mailed to you by Election Day. But Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said if you do, it might be a good idea not to mail it back.
• Accelerating extreme climate change. The Associated Press reports, “Trump says he’s ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling.”
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is “terminating” a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling…
The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.
Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Obama rallies with Georgia Democratic candidates as early voting winds down
text:
Former President Barack Obama speaks at a rally with former Sen. Jon Ossoff and Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderWith a U.S. Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and a slew of other statewide races on the ballot, former President Barack Obama visited Georgia Wednesday to fire up supporters to elect a slate of Democrats and send a message to the White House. 
The former president joined U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is up for reelection, and Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in a jam-packed arena in Morrow, which is just south of Atlanta. 
The rally also featured other Democratic candidates running for statewide office, including state Rep. Tanya Miller, who is running for attorney general, Penny Brown Reynolds, who is running for secretary of state, and state Sen. Josh McLaurin, who is running for lieutenant governor.
Already, 2.2 million Georgians have cast a ballot as of Wednesday, with just two more days to vote early. Election Day is Tuesday.
At the rally, Obama railed against President Donald Trump, describing the previous “two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence” under the Trump administration and Republicans. He said that voters are “so ready for something new” and that “it feels like change is in the air.”
“I don’t have to tell you how tough things are out there. You’re living it,” Obama said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Obama argued that many voters who helped get Trump elected in 2024 were frustrated with post-pandemic inflation and thought that he might turn things around, but instead, Obama said that prices have continued to go up because of Trump policies. He pointed to Trump’s tariffs that have destabilized long-standing trade agreements and the war in Iran that he described as “an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for.”
Former President Barack Obama speaks at a rally with former Sen. Jon Ossoff and Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“These are not serious people, and we’re all paying a price for their lack of seriousness,” Obama said.
But Obama ended his speech on a positive and optimistic note, saying that “this election can be a start” of change.
Democrats are feeling bullish about their chances of seeing a “blue wave” in a year that Republicans are struggling to hold on to seats that would normally be considered safe for Republicans. Obama has been traveling the country targeting a few races that are considered competitive and could be a toss-up, holding rallies in Michigan and Ohio. 
Ossoff, who is the only Democratic senator running for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024, was initially seen as a top target for Republicans. But Ossoff has maintained a lead in polls against Republican Congressman Mike Collins. In the governor’s race, polling averages show that Bottoms is deadlocked with billionaire healthcare executive Rick Jackson.
Ossoff used the moment to try to boost Bottoms and other Democrats on the ballot.
Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama and Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“Georgia, with just six days to go, I’m here to tell you I have no doubt our victory is near at hand,” Ossoff said. “In six days, our juggernaut coordinated campaign will have turned out the vote like never before to elect Josh McLaurin, Penny Brown Reynolds, Tanya Miller and Democrats up and down the ballot. In six days, we’ll elect a Medicaid-expanding governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms.
“And in six days, Georgia, we’ll rebuke the crook President Donald Trump with such clarity and power that no president will ever dare such abuses again for centuries,” he added, to which the crowd erupted with chants of “yes, we can.” 
Before Ossoff took the stage, Bottoms promoted her platform that includes providing more funding toward education and pre-K, along with raising teacher pay. Bottoms received major applause and cheers when she said she would pause construction on new data center development, work to abolish Georgia’s six-week abortion ban and stand up to Trump.  
She also took the opportunity to continue to tie Jackson to Trump, saying that Jackson supports Trump policies because he personally and financially benefits from them. She pointed to Trump’s lax stances on data centers and pointed to Jackson’s investment in a Texas data center project. Jackson is endorsed by Trump and has campaigned at two of the president’s rallies this month, but he has also taken steps to distance himself from the White House.
Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama and Sen. Jon Ossoff in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“Slick Rick has made it clear that his number one priority will be to do whatever his big daddy Donald Trump tells him to do,” Bottoms said.
Republicans raced to downplay Obama’s visit, with Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, saying in a statement before the rally that Bottoms and Ossoff needed Obama “because they can’t stand on their own records of coddling criminal illegals, defunding the police and putting Georgia last.”
Jackson’s campaign called Obama’s rally a life raft for Bottoms. Spokesperson Garrison Douglas said that “Obama can’t cover up the fact that Keisha Lance Bottoms is a failed mayor who abandoned her city after making it less affordable and less safe.”
Janelle Monáe performs at a rally headlined by former President Barack Obama, Sen. Jon Ossoff and Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
But the rally felt like anything but a rescue mission. Instead, the rally had the hallmarks of a celebration. In between speakers, Clark Atlanta University’s marching band the Mighty Marching Panthers and artist Janelle Monae performed, and at other times, rally goers danced and sang along to loud music as if they were in a concert.
Nell Robison, a 44-year-old actor who attended the rally with his family, said he was excited to show his sons the importance of casting their vote.
“I wanted them to see our first Black president, and I want them to understand how important politics is, not just at the presidential level, but also at the governor level, senate level, things like that,” he said.
Obama’s endorsement of Ossoff and Bottoms, he added, would likely serve to energize Georgia voters in the midterms.
“Whoever that man supports, they get a strong turnout,” he said. “Just the fact that he’s putting his name on the line for these people shows a lot, and a lot of people came out here for him.”
Jessica Novas, a 49-year-old retired Navy veteran, said she was honored to see Obama speak, calling him her “forever president.”
She expressed skepticism, though, that visits from political figures were an effective way to reach undecided voters, arguing that rally attendees were more motivated than the general public.
But Novas’ mood illustrates another goal of these spirited political rallies: to energize attendees to encourage other Georgians to turn out and cast their ballots.
“It’s about getting what we get in the room to edify the people outside of the room, and I’m just up for the challenge in the next six days,” she said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee Brewers win first World Series title in franchise history
text:
Brewers fans at the game four watch party react to the end of an inning. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)The Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in game five of the World Series Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, clinching the first World Series title in Brewers history.
Wisconsinites enthusiastically cheered for the team at watch parties, including at American Family Field, which packed in a sold out crowd of 31,000 fans three nights in a row. Big crowds also watched the game in the Deer District outside of Fiserv Forum in downtown Milwaukee, at Tropicana Field in Tampa, and in bars and livingrooms all over Wisconsin.
“Thank you. That’s it,” Jacob Misiorowski, the Brewers starting pitcher, said when asked about what the win would mean for Wisconsin and Milwaukee in an interview on Fox Sports after the game. “They’ve been nothing but support for us this whole year and years prior,” he said of the fans, tearing up as he spoke.
“I think about the state of Wisconsin, they pushed us through for sure,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. 
The Brewers lost just twice in the playoffs and along the way swept the mighty Los Angeles Dodgers, who boast the highest payroll in Major League Baseball.
The Brewers won the first three games in the series, but lost in the fourth game on Tuesday in Tampa after blowing a 12th inning lead.
On Thursday during the fifth game, the Brewers came back strong, keeping a lead on the Rays during the whole game and only allowing the team to squeak in one score during the ninth inning.
The World Series game four watch party at American Family Field sold out, with fans packing into the stands along the first and third base sides. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
The team, and its huge win, represents a point of unity in a state sometimes riven by political divisions and a 50-50 partisan split. The World Series provided a respite from politics , especially with less than a week to go before the midterm elections.
The Brewers have been based in Wisconsin’s largest city, but the MLB’s smallest market, since 1970, when they moved to Milwaukee from Seattle. The team last appeared in the World Series over 40 years ago in 1982 where they faced the St. Louis Cardinals and lost in seven games.
A Marquette Law School poll released Wednesday found that 77% of Wisconsinites are supporters of the Brewers with 49% identifying as fans and 28% identifying as casual supporters. Only 1% said they actively root against the team. The Brewers had the second largest professional sports fanbase in the state, behind the Green Bay Packers.
Fans were happy to soak up the statewide joy the team could offer including during the game four watch party at American Family Field. 
Sarah Coleman, a Brookfield native who now lives in Milwaukee, said the Brewers’ underdog story was part of the team’s appeal. 
“It says a lot that a small market team swept the highest paid team in Major League Baseball,” she said. “It’s cool to talk about the underdog.” 
Milwaukee resident Joe Santiago, alter ego Super Cervecero, attends the World Series game four watch party in a lucha libre costume. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
“It’s nice to enjoy something so positive,” Christal Glynn-Skipini said. 
The win was celebrated by Wisconsinites across the political spectrum. 
Gov. Tony Evers, a lifelong Brewers fan, reacted to the win in a post on X, writing in all caps, “JAZZED AS HELL IS AN UNDERSTATEMENT”.
The candidates for governor also celebrated the Brewers (the team at times has played a role in the race). 
Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate running in the open race for governor, reacted to the win online: “FOR THE FIRST TIME EVER, THE MILWAUKEE BREWERS ARE WORLD SERIES CHAMPIONS!!!” 
Crowley and members of his party have pointed to his role in negotiating the stadium deal that kept the team in Milwaukee through 2050. Republican state Rep. Rob Brooks recently told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Crowley was “big part” and “true partner” in getting the deal done.
Supporters of the deal, including Evers, said the state and local government investment was important because of the economic activity that the Brewers bring to the state. According to the Milwaukee Business Journal, the Brewers’ World Series appearance was estimated to generate between $10 million to $12 million in economic impact per home game. 
Republican candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany said in a post that “Ueck is smiling down on us tonight,” referring to the late Bob Uecker, who was the legendary Hall of Fame radio broadcaster for the team. 
“What a moment for Wisconsin,” Tiffany said. “GO BREWERS!” 
Milwaukee Mayor Cavalier Johnson said in a post that “this special team represented what this city is all about and the entire state of Wisconsin is proud of them.” 
“Congratulations guys — you deserve every bit of this victory,” Johnson said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: Florida wildlife agency put a homebound dementia patient under surveillance
text:
A bear wanders through one of the pastures on the Olsen family cattle ranch in Davie. The natural beauty of Ben Olsen's family property motivated him to become an environmental activist, which has led to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission putting him and his parents under surveillance. (Photo via Ben Olsen)Growing up, I watched a lot of Bugs Bunny cartoons. I always cracked up when inept hunter Elmer Fudd would turn to the camera, put a finger to his lips and tell viewers, “Be vewwy vewwy quiet — I’m hunting wabbits!”
So, when I was talking to Ben Olsen last week, naturally the image that popped into my mind was Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Chairman Rodney Barreto saying, “Be very very quiet! I’m hunting CRITICS!”
Ben Olsen in an FWC T-shirt, via subject
You’ve probably never heard of Olsen, a law firm employee whose family owns a ranch in Davie. He’s not a name-in-lights Florida environmental champion, leader of a big organization, or someone who makes a lot of headlines. He’s just one of those people who gets important things done in the background.
Among the organizations he has volunteered to help: The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
Turns out he’s also one of the people the FWC has been spying on.
You can imagine, he said, how this discovery blew his mind. “Hey,” he thought, “you’re tracking a guy who’s HELPING you guys!”
Then he discovered that the list of people the FWC had put under surveillance included his mom, then 67.
“They did a search on me, my father, and my mother 50 times in one day,” Olsen told me. “This is clearly a bigger issue than we thought. … They were going after a woman with dementia.”
Yes, you read that right. At the time that the FWC decided her activities merited a criminal investigation, Olsen’s mom was living with Alzheimer’s disease.
In her declining years, Sallie Olsen never left the house, much less showed up at FWC meetings to comment on environmental issues, Olsen said.
Yet the FWC classified this frail, elderly lady as a major threat to the agency and its leadership.
 A bogus investigation
I first wrote about the FWC’s surveillance in July.
A documentary filmmaker named Brent Fannin had discovered that people who criticized the wildlife agency — many of them opponents of its anti-science bear hunt — had had their driving records pulled.
The FWC’s declared reason for doing this? An ongoing criminal investigation that didn’t actually exist. It was as big a bunch of humbug as anything P.T. Barnum put on display.
Brent Fannin via subject
In July, the known number of critics the FWC had been keeping an eagle eye on totaled 16 — more than a dozen but fewer than a score.
Fannin has continued digging into this and encouraging others to file their own public records requests. He told me last week that the number of souls the FWC snoops scrutinized had now climbed to 49.
The words “driving records” don’t adequately describe what the J. Edgar Hoovers of the FWC were hoovering up concerning these 49 folks.
“The records were in the Driver and Vehicle Information Database, known as DAVID,” the Miami Herald reported in July: “The system contains people’s driving records and other sensitive information like their Social Security numbers, medical disability records, addresses, signatures and emergency contacts.”
The suspicion, the Orlando Sentinel reported then, is that the FWC used those DAVID records to trace its critics’ travel patterns. How? By employing the system of Flock cameras that dot our highways and read passing license plates. That way, the state agency could keep tabs on where their critics go and who they meet.
So many Florida cops have abused the DAVID system to track their ex-wives and ex-girlfriends that five years ago the Legislature boosted the penalties for misusing it. To me, it sounds like the FWC’s silly searches ought to trigger those enhanced penalties for our wildlife cops, too.
I asked Fannin this week if the FWC has ever apologized for pulling his records under false pretenses.
“Haha hell no. they haven’t apologized,” he told me via e-mail. “In fact, they tried to make us seem like violent criminals.”
 Strictly routine
When the Herald ran the whole situation by Baretto, the politically influential Miami developer who chairs the wildlife commission, he didn’t deny his agency was pulling the records.
Rodney Barreto via screen grab
But Barreto, an ex-cop, tried to make it sound like it was no big deal, everybody settle down, this is strictly routine!
He told the Herald that during the bear hunt debate, he and the other commissioners had received threats. That’s why, he said, FWC officers checked out those extremely violent environmental sickos: “When people sign up to speak, their names are checked. That’s all.”
However, Barreto was — well, let’s be kind and say he was misinformed.
FWC spokeswoman Shannon Knowles told me in July that the agency’s law enforcement officers were not vetting speakers at the agency’s meetings. They were tracking potential threats, a much more serious endeavor indeed.
“Claims that the FWC misuses or weaponizes its law enforcement authority are false,” she said three months ago. “Threats concerning the harming of officers, staff, and commissioners are taken seriously and is why it’s imperative that law enforcement works to ensure public safety by monitoring, preventing, and assessing potential security risks to maintain safe public spaces.”
Why, this is clearly the most important criminal investigation since the Justice Department probe of former FBI director James Comey for taking a picture of seashells arranged to spell “86 47”.
The FWC’s reasoning for its First Amendment violations fell apart when the agency — in response to public records requests — released unredacted copies of the threats. The records clearly showed that none of the threats came from the people being investigated.
Needless to say, a homebound woman with dementia was never any threat to the FWC.
 A majestic paradise
Olsen told me he has never sent any threats to state officials in any agency. He doesn’t need to.
When he’s got something to say to the wildlife commissioners, he’ll show up at one of their meetings to speak to them in person.
After all, he volunteers with five programs the agency runs, including deer management and python removal.
He has met Barreto and shaken his hand, although not since he learned about the FWC pulling his parents’ files. He has not had much direct interaction with FWC executive director Roger Young, who came from the agency’s law enforcement side.
Olsen (and his parents) never took a position for or against the bear hunt, he told me, although they have seen bears on their property. What pushed him to become an environmental activist was his discovery of a threat to his family’s 608-acre ranch from the federal government.
“We’ve been on the land for 100 years and owned it for 75,” he told me. “It’s a beautiful, majestic paradise.”
To his dismay, he learned of a plan by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to seize the ranch via eminent domain and flood it as part of the joint federal-state billion-dollar Everglades restoration program.
Using historical land records, Olsen put together a 68-page report that challenged the Corps’ assumption that the ranch had been part of the vast Glades marsh. Nope, he said, this was always dry land. (He’s suing the U.S. Department of Interior over its failure to promptly hand over public records about the issue.)
Olsen also pointed out that his family’s land was prime Florida panther habitat. Motion-sensor cameras have snapped more than a few photos of the endangered cats stalking across the grassland.
Flooding the ranch, he said, would eliminate that exceedingly scarce habitat, which is rapidly being eroded by rampant development.
When he sought assistance in resistance from the FWC, Olsen encountered a very cold shoulder.
‘I was begging them to help me and the leadership of the FWC kept saying, ‘We can’t do anything,’” Olsen said. The state agency had signed onto the federal plans to flood the property and wouldn’t change its stance, despite Olsen’s evidence.
That’s what led to him becoming the subject of this phony investigation, he said.
“I was living with my parents at the time, taking care of my mother through the end stages of early-onset dementia,” he told me. Because of where he lived, and the fact that he drove a truck registered to his parents, the investigators pulled their DAVID records as well as his.
“I was tracked because I exposed how the state was not protecting panthers,” he told me. His only crime was “advocating in public meetings for private property rights and endangered species habitat.”
Panthers on Ben Olsen’s family ranch via Ben Olsen
 A Flock-ing mess
After talking to Olsen, I was keenly interested in hearing how the FWC could justify putting Olsen’s mother under a microscope.
I tried reaching Barreto. He never returned my calls.
Knowles, the FWC spokeswoman, said she couldn’t comment on the Olsen situation. Turns out there’s now a REAL investigation of the phony investigation.
“A formal complaint has been filed with our Inspector General’s Office, and therefore we are unable to address any further questions,” she told me.
However, she added, the FWC “maintains that we complied with all applicable user agreements and all legal requirements governing access to and use of DAVID records.”
Sen. Carlos Guillermo Smith (Photo viaFlorida Senate)
The guy who filed the complaint is Sen. Carlos Guilllermo Smith. He’s from Orlando, so he’s used to dealing with people stuck in Fantasyland.
In an interview with the “Florida Matters” radio show, Smith said news about what the FWC was doing “was throwing up all kinds of alarm bells.”
Smith pointed out that Gov. Ron DeSantis, who appointed all seven of the wildlife commissioners, had yet to make any comment about what the agency had done.
Except he kind of did, in a roundabout way.
On Aug. 25, Olsen spoke to the Everglades Restoration Joint Working Group about the use of Flock cameras to track FWC critics. He also talked to several state employees at the meeting and gave them details about the tracking of his mom and dad. They promised to pass the word up the chain of command.
The very next day, DeSantis announced that he wanted legislators to tighten regulations on the use of Flock cameras, explaining, “I don’t want to have this become a surveillance state.”
Five days later, he issued an executive order banning Flock cameras from all state highways.
Yet he said not a word about the wildlife commission’s use of them.
 Desperately seeking something
When the story about the FWC’s investigation first broke, two of the victims, Bear Warriors United founder Katrina Shadix and Speak Up Wekiva founder Chuck O’Neal, told me they planned to sue the agency for violating their privacy.
Katrina Shadix via screengrab
Chuck O’Neal via subject
So far, neither has filed suit, but both say legal action is on the way. Shadix promised me that her suit would include more than two dozen plaintiffs.
Olsen, meanwhile, is planning a legal strategy for forcing the FWC to hand over all its records and acknowledge its wrongdoing. It helps that he works at a law firm run by family members.
While it’s tempting to just pop a batch of popcorn and munch it while we watch this all play out, I have a suggestion for a more constructive activity. I see by the calendar that Halloween is this weekend, so I think everyone reading this column should celebrate that spooky holiday in a particular costume.
I think we should pay tribute — yeah, that’s the right term! — to Chairman Barreto.
We should all cosplay as him dressed as Elmer Fudd. And when we’re knocking on people’s doors, instead of shouting, “Trick or treat!” we should say, “Be verrrrry verrrrrry quiet! I’m hunting … EXCUSES!”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Did Trump’s shipping waiver lower diesel prices?
text:
The Trump Administration is frantically searching for ways to bring diesel prices under control, and the search is landing just as New England households start buying heating oil for winter.
The White House has considered everything from encouraging refiners to limit exports, allowing broader use of tax-exempt dyed diesel and pressing European allies to release emergency diesel stocks. The president’s threat of a diesel export ban has dominated headlines. Those are extraordinary measures, but so are diesel prices, which recently reached record levels above $6 a gallon.
This has a particularly pronounced impact on Connecticut, where about one in three homes relies on heating oil. If current prices hold, those households could pay roughly $1,700 more to heat their homes this winter.
One measure the Trump Administration has repeatedly pointed to as a success in taming high energy prices is its waiver of the Jones Act, which requires waterborne goods shipped between U.S. ports to use vessels that are built, owned, and operated by Americans.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in August that allowing foreign vessels to move petroleum between U.S. ports had kept energy prices in California and on the East Coast “lower than they would otherwise be.”
Maybe. But that is a counterfactual. There is no pump displaying what diesel would cost in an alternate world without the waiver, just as there is no gas station selling gasoline at pre-Iran war prices.
We can, however, look at what actually moved and put those barrels in perspective.
The Cato Institute, which favors the outright repeal of the Jones Act, has counted 997,000 barrels of petroleum products delivered into New England over 115 days, or about 8,700 barrels a day. Cato shows exactly why a Jones Act waiver would not solve New England’s upcoming fuel problems. 
Cato is now touting the supply aspects of the waiver, where before their refrain was that foreign tankers would move product for three or more times less than U.S. flag tankers. The fact that foreign tankers with waivers are getting rates above U.S. flag tanker rates has temporarily silenced that subterfuge.
For perspective, the six New England states consumed roughly 259.4 million barrels of petroleum products in 2024 – over 700,000 barrels every day. Connecticut’s total diesel consumption alone was about 17 million barrels, of which a little more than half was for home heating oil. 
Put the numbers next to each other, and the waiver volumes Cato identified were equal to roughly 1.2 percent of the region’s normal consumption rate.
How much did the Jones Act waiver do for New England’s fuel supply? There is little evidence the waiver helped shore up the region’s supply of distillate, which includes diesel and home heating oil. Just 2.5 million barrels were in storage by late September, according to the Energy Information Administration. That’s a record low and about two weeks of ordinary supply.
For reference, in 2020, the region had 12.6 million barrels of distillate stored for winter. 
Connecticut’s own distillate stocks, held at bulk terminals in New Haven, Bridgeport, and Groton, are about 85 percent lower than in 2020, according to the latest Energy Information Administration data.
The other question is, what is the cost impact of the Jones Act waiver on the East Coast? Previous analysis published by the NBER suggests that eliminating the Jones Act would reduce average East Coast diesel prices by less than 2 cents per gallon. In Connecticut — using the NBER’s New England figure — it is only about half a cent per gallon for diesel.
My own estimates put the waiver’s effect at about 2/100 of a cent per gallon of gasoline nationwide.
That is a very different scale from the problem Chris Wright and the Trump Administration are trying to solve.
This should not be surprising. Freight is only one part of the delivered price. Fuel prices track crude oil and refinery margins much more closely than the cost of a ship. 
The crack-spread pricing and windfall profits of oil majors have received significant attention from the Administration for this reason. In the second quarter of 2026, Valero earned $3.7 billion – more than five times the prior year’s earnings – and Phillips 66 earned $3.8 billion, its strongest quarter since 2022, with refining profits of about $3.1 billion. 
Ultimately, Connecticut buys fuel in a global market. Refinery outages, crude prices, international diesel demand, exports, storage economics and the cost of tanker capacity all matter.
The search for a diesel fix has been frantic, and winter is not waiting. As politicians look for someone to blame, it’s been demonstrated that the Jones Act is not the right scapegoat.
John D. McCown is Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Center for Maritime Strategy and author of the 2020 book Giants of the Sea.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Zach Lahn joins HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for MAHA rally
text:
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke alongside Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn at a rally hosted by the MAHA PAC in Clive Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn emphasized his opposition to the COVID-19 vaccine Wednesday at his “Make America Healthy Again” rally with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Lahn has long highlighted his support for the MAHA movement spearheaded by Kennedy at the federal level, which he says centers around his positions on healthy food, clean water and safe medications. The candidate, who is running against Iowa Auditor of State Rob Sand in the Nov. 3, 2026, general election, said his top priority as governor “is to clean up our water and to stop the cancer crisis in the state of Iowa.” But he also said there are many other health-related proposals he supports as a candidate — including restrictions on the availability of certain vaccines.
“Even with fake news here, I’m going to say this: The fight to pull the COVID vaccine off the market is a pro-life issue,” Lahn said,
Lahn has brought up several policies related to vaccines on the campaign trail — including his pledge to ban the COVID-19 vaccine if elected governor. He has also said he would scale back vaccine requirements for children to attend school. During a primary-season a debate hosted by Moms for Liberty, Lahn said he would ban mRNA vaccines in Iowa.
The ban discussed in January was about gene-based vaccines that use nucleic acids like messenger RNA — mRNA — to create proteins and trigger an immune response. There has been ongoing research on mRNA vaccines for decades, but the COVID-19 vaccines developed by Pfizer and Moderna were the first mRNA vaccines to receive U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval. While reviews of the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines have found the doses were safe and effective, there has been persistent skepticism about the effectiveness and potential adverse health risks caused by these vaccines.
The Iowa Democratic Party held a news conference Wednesday where Dana Drochner, a breast cancer survivor, said addressing Iowa’s cancer crisis requires leaders to continue research and development on mRNA vaccines and other medical treatments.
“I benefited from new medical treatments, and there’s more and more that are being developed every day, such as the mRNA vaccines,” Drochner said. “I feel like all treatments should be up for consideration to fight this disease because it’s a very difficult issue, and we should not leave any possible option untouched in this fight.”
Speaking to reporters, Lahn said his comment during the primary season was specifically about the COVID-19 vaccine. Speaking with reporters at the rally, Lahn did not clarify whether he would support banning other mRNA vaccines that could receive FDA approval in the future — but he did say he would support Iowans accessing mRNA therapies developed to treat cancer, genetic disorders and infectious diseases.
“Now they’re looking at other interventions — which are therapies — that could help treat cancer,” Lahn said. “I think those are great. If they’re promising, great. We need them in the state for sure. But those are very individualized interventions. It’s not a mass-produced product like a vaccine would be. It’s a therapy, and I support them.”
But Lahn said during his speech that he believes there is reason to mistrust medical experts.
“I believe wholeheartedly that during COVID the veil was lifted, that we saw firsthand what the medical establishment was willing to do to collude with the government to gain power,” Lahn said. “And let me just be very clear about this: The medical establishment has completely lost our trust and has done nothing to earn it back. They have not.”
There were several speakers who spoke before Lahn and Kennedy that brought up their concerns about vaccinations. Iowa Rep. Bill Gustoff, R-Des Moines, said he joined the “medical freedom movement” after his child had an adverse reaction to the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella (known as MMR vaccine), before going on to help the group Informed Choice Iowa, a group founded in 2017 in opposition to vaccine requirements and health mandates.
Former state lawmaker Joe Mitchell, the Republican running for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, said “the story of MAHA is personal to me,” sharing a story about his 93-year-old grandmother died two weeks after receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, which he said was given “without anybody’s consent” after she became a nursing home resident.
Mitchell also said he was “not a big fan” of former Chief Medical Advisor Anthony Fauci, who served from 2021 to 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic. If elected to Congress, the Iowa Republican said he would want to serve on the House Oversight Committee “because I want to investigate the hell out of Anthony Fauci.”
In May, Kennedy announced the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will no longer recommend COVID-19 vaccines for healthy children and pregnant women. The HHS secretary did not speak about vaccinations at the rally, but instead focused on water quality — another top issue for Lahn’s campaign and in other races across the state.
Kennedy spoke about his long history in environmental protection work as a lawyer and through his work at nonprofits, including the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) and the Waterkeeper Alliance, which he founded.
He said during this work in the 1980s and 1990s, he spoke with many people who believed they could not turn to government officials for help in combatting companies that were polluting local waterways.
“They had come to the conclusion that many Americans have now come to: that government was in cahoots with the polluters, and that our government had been captured by profit interests, and we’re stealing something fundamental from the American people,” Kennedy said.
He said he believed Lahn embodied the values needed to address these problems by focusing on ways to improve water and air quality, and to ensure Iowa children are eating healthy — he said “to me is the most important election going on in this country today.”
“We have to figure out a way to grow food without poisoning our kids, without  giving ourselves cancer, without destroying the soils that enrich us and enrich our microbiome … and we need somebody who is really smart, who understands these issues, who is rooted in those soils, who has credibility with everybody in the political landscapes,” Kennedy said. “… There are very, very few people in this country who fill that bill. And I can think of one of them, the most important one — it’s the person that we’re here tonight to support.”
Lahn told the crowd, “you’ll notice that not everybody up here believes all of the same things.” Though he did not say where he disagreed with other speakers, he said the fact that there were there were different positions being expressed at the rally showed attendees, “you are in the presence right now of people who are not for sale, who are not able to be bought off, who are going to do the bidding of the people.”
“This is not a monolith,” Lahn said. “This is not what it’s supposed to be. It’s not supposed to be where everybody’s thinking the same thing all of the time.”

name: California
title: Judge rejects Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
text:
In summary
A federal judge refused to order California to set aside 20,000 ballots, citing a ‘pattern of attempted election interference’ by the Trump administration


Saying the Trump administration had embarked on “a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference,” a federal judge on Wednesday refused to order California election officials to set aside 20,000 ballots over claims those voters might not be citizens.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton.
“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” the judge wrote, saying if he granted the Trump administration’s last-minute request “either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process. Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”
The ruling is the latest legal defeat for the Trump administration as it has sought to find evidence that would validate President Donald Trump’s longstanding claims that Democrats win because of rigged elections.Carter said he declined to be a party to a process that could disenfranchise voters.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” he wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the executive (branch) can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
Carter also slammed the federal government for not providing a clear accounting of its methodology in creating the list of 20,000 possible noncitizens, saying prosecutors provided vague explanations “and raised multiple questions regarding reliability.”
Federal officials insist their list is mostly accurate and came from investigators correlating public voter files, government data and commercial databases, but prosecutors have acknowledged that some of the people on the list are likely citizens.
State and county officials and civil rights groups have said that the list appears to be riddled with inaccuracies and it often omits key data such as Social Security and driver’s license numbers that would allow county officials to confirm who the people are.
In a briefing with reporters Wednesday before Carter’s ruling, California Democratic Attorney General Rob Bonta said the federal government’s case was little more than an “amateur hour” political stunt to validate Trump’s conspiracy theory that elections are rigged for Democrats.“It’s a joke. It’s embarrassing, but it is dangerous,” Bonta said. “They are trying to attack the fundamental right to vote with trash data.”
In a Fox News interview on Wednesday before the ruling, Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, said the administration would appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and possibly to the U.S. Supreme Court.“We’re moving at a lightning pace because the way California does elections, everyone already has a ballot,” Essayli said. “Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been returned, and the counties already started processing those ballots. … That’s why we need an order now to separate and segregate these ballots — not to cancel any vote — just to sequester them so we can figure this out.”  
Higher court declined to intervene
A 9th Circuit panel already rejected one attempt by Essayli’s office to get an emergency order. A three-judge panel ruled 2-1 Monday to reject an urgent appeal to bypass Carter’s courtroom.  The federal government claimed the district judge didn’t schedule a hearing fast enough.
Meanwhile on Wednesday, a group of civil rights organizations, including California’s chapters of the American Civil Liberties Union, sued the Trump administration and urged a federal court to block the administration’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative.” 
The groups claim the initiative has been targeting and intimidating naturalized U.S. citizens, former green card holders who have gone through the citizenship process. The initiative directed immigration officials to generate target lists of possible noncitizen voters and to coordinate with ICE field offices to interrogate individuals it identified.
The civil rights groups contend the federal government is using illegal tactics and faulty data to harass innocent legal voters.  
“These allegations are putting eligible voters — including naturalized U.S. citizens — at risk of disenfranchisement,” Theresa Lee, an attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, said in a statement. “The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like.”Carter noted in Wednesday’s ruling that those most at risk of being disenfranchised are naturalized citizens.“Individuals that the federal government recently identified as noncitizens on voter rolls in different states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalized citizens,” Carter wrote.The ACLU’s and other groups’ suit came a week after a federal judge in California issued an order blocking the Department of Homeland Security from doing in-person interrogations of people investigators suspect may be noncitizens. 
The judge in that case, Araceli Martínez-Olguín, who was appointed by President Joe Biden, ruled that the federal government was relying on “faulty data sources that sweep in U.S. citizens” and was likely violating the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits voter intimidation. 
Martínez-Olguín’s order is in effect through Election Day.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump calls for Peltola to be criminally charged, removed from Alaska’s U.S. Senate race
text:
Mary Peltola listens to a question posed by moderator Michelle Egan at a candidate forum held by the Alaska Oii and Gas Association on Aug. 27, 2026. Next to Peltola is i Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola, a Democrat and former U.S. House member, is challenging Sullivan.  (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)President Donald Trump on Wednesday called for Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola to be criminally charged and drop out or be removed from the ballot.
His comments followed the publication of a New York Times article revealing that her campaign worked with the national Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit spoiler candidates that could dilute votes for her principal opponent, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
The U.S. Department of Justice has already filed a Trump-directed but legally dubious lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from declaring anyone but Sen. Dan S. Sullivan the winner of the election.
Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins

Alaska’s U.S. Senate race is one of a handful of “toss-up” races nationally that could be won by either a Democrat or Republican and thus decide which party controls the U.S. Senate.
Peltola has consistently been polling ahead of Sullivan, and the Times article was published less than a week before Election Day, in the middle of early voting, with more than 58,000 Alaskans already having cast ballots.
Third-party Republican and Democratic groups have already spent millions of dollars in all three of Alaska’s statewide races in attempts to boost spoiler candidates. In the U.S. House race, Democratic candidate Eric Hafner — a felon who has never lived in Alaska — is being boosted by Republican groups.
The Times article alleges that early on in the Senate race, Democrats sought to recruit people with the same name as the incumbent — including Petersburg’s Dan J. Sullivan, who is on the general election ballot alongside Peltola, Sen. Sullivan and Palmer Republican Gerald Heikes. The article is based in large part on internal text messages provided by a former Peltola aide. 
Dan J. Sullivan did not return emails and phone calls seeking comment on Wednesday.
The Alaska Beacon has not independently confirmed the Times reporting.
Legal experts, including some in Alaska, said the actions described in the article are not illegal but do amount to a dirty trick. 
Fairbanks political writer Dermot Cole, a Peltola supporter, wrote online, “What Peltola and her backers did was juvenile and stupid. The Peltola campaign lied to Alaskans about this and should come clean. There’s no excuse for how Peltola has handled this.”
Republican U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski supported Peltola in her 2022 and 2024 campaigns for U.S. House but endorsed Sullivan this year. After the publication of the Times article, she issued a statement criticizing what she called “a pattern of lies and coverups.”
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process. Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong. Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign,” Murkowski said in a statement.

Peltola and her campaign had denied any relationship with Dan J. Sullivan.
The Peltola campaign issued a statement implying that she will stay in the race, and she has not canceled any scheduled appearances before Election Day.
“Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight. The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign,” wrote a campaign spokesperson. 
Alaskans for Mary is a political group formed earlier this year; most of the allegations in the article appear to predate its creation.
At a campaign event Wednesday on the Kenai Peninsula, Peltola did not answer questions from reporters asking about the Times article but alluded to it in public remarks.
“Nobody’s waking up worried about ballot composition,” she said, according to local public radio station KDLL-FM. “Not even me. I’m worried about my bills. I’m worried about affordability in health care.”
Alaska Division of Elections says Petersburg Sullivan is likely ineligible to run for U.S. Senate

Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice, following instructions from Trump, filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections, asking a judge to prevent the state from certifying a victory by anyone other than Dan S. Sullivan from being declared the winner of the ongoing Senate election.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have asked to intervene in the lawsuit, and the federal government opposed that intervention until the Times article published.
Now, the DOJ is urging Judge Sharon Gleason to allow Peltola to be part of the lawsuit so it can “seek expedited discovery from the campaign regarding the reported conspiracy.”
The DOJ lawsuit is legally tenuous — under the U.S. Constitution, states and not the federal government have principal jurisdiction over elections — but the Times reporting nevertheless supportsRepublicans who have repeatedly referred to Dan J. Sullivan as “Decoy Dan”, suggesting he was recruited and supported by Democrats.
“Alaskans deserve to know the truth. Mary Peltola, her campaign, and her senior advisors colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers, and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit a candidate to deliberately deceive and confuse voters, and then repeatedly lied about it,” said Nate Adams, spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign. “Not one player in this operation has acted in good faith with Alaska voters. Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along. We always knew this was a concerted effort to deceive voters, and Mary Peltola was hoping it would stay hidden until after the election.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Green and Pinkston speak after gubernatorial forum. Here are the biggest takeaways
text:
Tennessee gubernatorial candidates Lauren Pinkston (left), David Hatley (middle) and Jerri Green (right) listen to a question during the Tennessee Press Association gubernatorial forum hosted by Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: Ephraim Rodenbach, MTSU Seigenthaler News Service)
Three out of four gubernatorial candidates in Tennessee participated Tuesday night in a forum held at Middle Tennessee State University a week before voters elect a new official to the state’s highest office.  
​Democratic nominee Jerri Green and independent candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston attended the event, hosted by the Tennessee Press Association. The candidates answered questions about solutions to voters’ biggest concerns — including affordability, Tennessee vouchers, healthcare system and the decrease of rural hospitals.
The forum marked the only nonpartisan event between candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election. Republican nominee and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not respond to an invitation to participate. Blackburn, the projected favorite to win the governor’s race, is yet to debate her political opponents in the gubernatorial race. 
The forum took place in a studio at MTSU’s Scott Borchetta College of Media and Entertainment department and aired live on the Tennessee Press Association’s YouTube channel, among other platforms.
​Following the forum, Pinkston and Green answered press questions. Hatley declined the invitation. 
Here are the biggest takeaways from a post-forum availability with the candidates. 
Green and Hatley call out Blackburn
During the forum and press conference, Green repeatedly called out the Tennessee senator for not attending. Green has invited Blackburn at least four times to debate during the gubernatorial race, though Blackburn has repeatedly declined. 
“She won’t even take your questions,” Green said to members of the press. “If you can’t answer your questions, you don’t have the answers. That’s why she wouldn’t be on this debate stage with me tonight.” 
During the forum, Hately also criticized Blackburn for her absence.
“She’s been in Washington for over 20 years, but didn’t think it was important to show up to a job interview for the highest job in the state of Tennessee,” Hatley said.  
Blackburn hosted a rally in Hendersville at the same time as the debate, according to her X account.
MTSU junior journalism student Jaeda Jackson asks an affordability question during the Tennessee Press Association gubernatorial forum hosted by Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: Ephraim Rodenbach/MTSU Seigenthaler News Service)
Green says Tennesseans will face ‘facism’ if she isn’t elected
When asked what Tennesseans would miss if she was not elected as governor, Green said she believes the state is nearing authoritarianism. 
“We are the front lines of fascism, and I’m not extracting,” Green said. In reference to the far right political movement, she continued, “Every space and place they can, they are testing out what democracy will tolerate,” she said in reference to far-right movements.   In closing, Green said Tennesseans need someone who will push back against policies that could threaten American democracy. 
 “It is important to choose someone who is going to push back,” Green said. “Our government works best when there are people that have a give and take, a push and a pull.”
Pinkston believes Tennesseans are ready for an independent governor  
Despite Tennessee never electing an independent for governor, Pinkston believes the state is ready for a governor not from one of the major parties. 
“I believe Tennessee has what it takes to set the tone for the rest of the country to show them what it looks like to actually move out of the two-party system and into something new and modern,” Pinkston told media members after the forum. 
 As of 2026, 43% of Americans identify as independents, higher than Democrats or Republicans, according to U.S. polling data.
During the broadcast, Hatley agreed Tennessee is ready for an independent governor.
“Tennessee has a great opportunity right now to elect something outside of a politician and see what can be changed in the government from the outside and in,” Hatley said. 
While Pinkston and Hatley believe the state could see its first independent governor, the race presents an upward climb, as Blackburn and Green maintain ownership in the polls, as both Pinkston and Hatley trail.  
“I’m sure they loved their 15 minutes of fame, but they do not have the numbers to win this race,” Green said. 
Early voting ends in Tennessee on Oct. 29. The general election takes place Nov. 3. If elected, Blackburn, Green or Pinkston would become Tennessee’s first female governor. 
Gary Davis is a student journalist at Middle Tennessee State University. This story was reported in partnership with the MTSU Seigenthaler News Service.
