name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska candidates for governor vary on approaches to outmigration, state support for families
text:
Voters walk across the map of Alaska on the floor of the Alaska State Library, Archives and Museum on Tuesday, Aug. 20, 2024. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)With affordability top of mind this election, Alaska candidates for governor offered varying perspectives on how their administrations would support working families and cap the ongoing tide of outmigration from the state, if elected. 
Alaska has seen a steady exodus of people leaving the state. Last year, state demographers reported more people left than moved to Alaska —  the 13th consecutive year of net outmigration. The median household income in 2024 was nearly $94,000 according to the U.S. Census Bureau. And a recent study by the non-profit United Way estimates nearly 40% of Alaskans do not earn enough to cover basic expenses like for food, housing, child care and healthcare. 
Coupled with fuel prices at a record high this year, driven by the U.S. war on Iran, Alaskans have seen rising costs of groceries and transportation, as well as housing, healthcare, and child care. Families and officials also point to school districts facing severe budget shortfalls forcing cuts, larger class sizes and some closures as a driver of families leaving the state. 
Three of the four candidates — Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — participated in an online forum on Monday with the Alaska Children’s Trust, a non-profit advocacy group that focuses on supporting children and families and preventing child abuse and neglect.     

Three of the four Alaska gubernatorial candidates, Republican Dave Bronson (left) Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican Treg Taylor participate in a forum hosted by the Alaska Children’s Trust on Oct. 26, 2026. (Screenshot of Facebook livestream)
 

The fourth candidate in the running for governor, Republican Bernadette Wilson, did not participate due to a scheduling conflict, organizers said. 
Trevor Storrs, executive director of the Alaska Children’s Trust, moderated the forum and noted that Alaska’s economy “depends on families, not just resource development” and asked the candidates how they would support working families and stem the tide of outmigration. 
Kreiss-Tomkins said his priority would be the supply side, and boosting state investments across sectors. “There should just be more housing, more abundant energy, more availability of childcare,” he said. “And the scarcity of all of those things is driving up costs in a big way in Alaska, and around the country, and it’s working families that feel that squeeze.” 
On housing, Kreiss-Tomkins said his administration would focus on accelerating construction: finding appropriate state lands to make available, and reducing permitting and regulations for all types of housing. Similarly for child care providers, he said he would seek to reduce state regulations hindering new facilities and available space. 
Taylor said he also supports reducing regulations on new housing projects and on childcare providers. He said his main focus in reducing costs for families and businesses would be reducing the cost of energy. 
“It’s all about energy,” he said. “I would pursue an all of the above approach to energy, (and) reducing energy costs. Whether it be dams, whether it be solar, whether it be the AKLNG line, which I think is absolutely critical for Alaskans to reduce long-term costs for Alaskan families.”[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
He said he would also pursue making more state lands available for housing development and reducing regulations in order to build. “I also want to do a modern day Homestead Act where families are able to build a home and create an environment where they can grow and grow their families,” he said.
Bronson said he would work to reduce costs by opposing tax increases on families and businesses. “Adding those on is an expense burden to the people of Alaska. That’s not how you move forward,” he said. 
He said he also opposes imposing family and medical leave as an “interruption to the private enterprise process.”
Widening gap between need and access to Medicaid and SNAP
Candidates were asked how they would address delays and errors in state public assistance programs, including Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program, or SNAP.
Nearly 60,000 Alaskans have lost Medicaid coverage since Jan. 2025, including over 20,000 children according to data collected by the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families. Some of those children lost coverage due to paperwork rather than ineligibility, Storrs noted. Thousands more are expected to lose coverage with new eligibility requirements enacted by the Trump administration’s Big Beautiful Bill Act that go into effect in January.
Alaska also has had the highest SNAP error rate in the country for four consecutive years, and some residents face months-long delays in food assistance. But state officials say modernization efforts to improve administration of the program and processing times are underway.
All three candidates agreed the state assistance programs have major problems that need more state investment and focused attention. Kreiss-Tomkins and Taylor said they would publish the backlog numbers so that the public can monitor the progress to reduce it, and hold officials accountable. 
“It’s going to be brutal at the beginning because those numbers are going to be ugly as all heck, but it needs to be out there, and then the numbers need to go in the right direction,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Taylor cited his experience as attorney general working on reducing the backlog in processing sexual assault examination kits. He called the SNAP backlog “unacceptable” and pledged to fund technology improvements for the system and improve access to benefits. “This should not be happening,” he said. 
Bronson said he would boost pay for state workers in the Division of Public Assistance to help reduce the backlog in SNAP and Medicaid processing. “We don’t have enough people because we don’t pay enough. I’m a fiscal conservative, a strident fiscal conservative, and I just look at it this way: if we’re going to do certain things in government, if we decide we’re going to do them, we better do them well,” he said.
He criticized Dunleavy for underfunding the state’s social assistance programs and said he supports boosting funding for social services. “We have to smartly, efficiently and economically add money to the pot because if not, this failing is just going to keep going on,” he said. 
All three candidates said they support increased funding for the state’s foster care system, run by the Office of Children’s Services, which has been a focus of lawsuits and legislative scrutiny after an audit showed the agency has failed to implement reforms.  
“Some of that may be resources, I think there’s also potentially a management leadership restructuring question,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Youth mental health and suicide prevention
The candidates presented varying approaches to supporting youth mental health and suicide prevention. Last year, Alaska youth suicides hit a 10-year high — a rate that is six times higher than the national average.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he supports expanding access to mental health providers, including through telehealth and easing licensing requirements. He noted that supporting Native cultural activities, particularly in rural Alaska, can help support a sense of cultural identity and belonging, including subsistence activities and language learning.  
Taylor said he would “supercharge” the Alaska Mental Health Trust Authority, a state corporation that manages roughly one million acres of state lands and a trust that generates revenue for mental health services each year. 
“Right now they feel like just handing out a few checks every year to charities is what their duty is. No, their duty is to create a comprehensive system of mental health in the state of Alaska,” Taylor said. 
He said he would also seek to improve the K-12 education system to create more opportunities and pathways for viable jobs for youth: “You have to have economic opportunity for these kids, and they need a sense of purpose, they need a sense of opportunity, they need a sense of hope, and they need a sense of pride.”
Bronson agreed the state needs more mental health providers. He described meeting a woman who is working on suicide prevention in communities along the Yukon River, where salmon runs have crashed dramatically altering residents’ ways of life.
“That’s a trigger,” Bronson said. “And in the immediate, you’ve got to have someone right there in front of them, whether it’s a hotline or a person, so they can call and get to help in the immediate. But then, long term, systemically, you’re going to have to spend money to deal with this. We just are.”
All three candidates expressed support for boosting state spending on K-12 schools, which has been a major topic of discussion this election season. 
Early voting is underway in Alaska, and continues through Election Day at 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New Legacy Fund website makes investments more accessible but transparency issue lingers
text:
The new Legacy Fund website is presented during a joint meeting of the State Investment Board and the Legacy Fund advisory board on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota has launched a new website aiming to make Legacy Fund investments more transparent to the public. 
The long-awaited website allows users to see where and how the state has invested taxpayer money through the Legacy Fund, a sovereign wealth fund fueled by oil taxes, which is valued at $15 billion. 
“We’re creating the transparency we’re looking for,” said Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, who chairs the Legacy Fund advisory board. 
State officials who sit on the two boards responsible for overseeing the Legacy Fund hailed the website as a major step forward during a presentation Wednesday. Some praised how easy it is for a typical person to navigate. 
“I’m pretty excited about this,” said Gov. Kelly Armstrong. “I was really, really impressed, and I can barely turn on an iPad.”
Bill requiring Legacy Fund disclosure website sees support in North Dakota Legislature

But Rep. Bernie Satrom, R-Jamestown, one of the sponsors of the 2025 law requiring the website’s creation, said the intent was to improve the transparency around investments state officials have declined to disclose. He said the website falls short.
“It’s a beautiful website, but transparency means more than putting information on a website,” Satrom said. “My goal was to have transparency, not just making information more accessible.”
The lawmaker said no information has been made available to North Dakotans that wasn’t already public in some form. Satrom would like more disclosure related to investments known as commingled funds.
“I’d like to see a complete accounting of the portfolio, including the underlying holdings of those commingled funds; a clear explanation of what information is being withheld and why,” Satrom said.
What the website includes
The website highlights the fund’s history and how the earnings have been spent by the Legislature. 
It also has a page dedicated to explaining what role different arms of government have in managing the fund’s investments. Jodi Smith, executive director of the Retirement and Investment Office, said she hopes it will cut down on the number of questions staff get about how the earnings are spent, which they have no control over. 
Jodi Smith, executive director of the Retirement and Investment Office, presents the new Legacy Fund website to a joint meeting of the State Investment Board and the Legacy Fund advisory board on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
State officials hope it will be easy to understand and allow members of the public to browse for information. 
State Treasurer Thomas Beadle said he frequently hears questions from the public about why the Legacy Fund isn’t being used for one initiative or another. He said the information on the website about the fund’s history includes a helpful reminder that the fund exists to provide a safety net for the state down the road. 
“This is the one-time harvest. This is the retirement account for after oil is done producing. After you’re done working, after oil is done producing, then you can touch your retirement account more,” Beadle said. “This was set aside, so we don’t relive the bust of the ’80s.”
The Legacy Fund was established by a constitutional amendment approved by voters in 2010. Earnings from the Legacy Fund have been used by the Legislature since 2019 for property tax credits and other purposes. 
Investment details can be found on the holdings page. The investments can be sorted by country, region, economic sector or investment type.
Limitations
Satrom’s criticism focuses on pooled funds, sometimes known as commingled funds, that pool money from multiple entities and invest it in a variety of ventures. Those underlying investments are not made public.
The website includes 75 line items totaling $6.4 billion, or 42% of the Legacy Fund, for investments that are not listed individually. These include both pooled funds and cash.
Those underlying investments are not available on the website because they are considered “proprietary” and confidential under North Dakota’s open records laws. 
“If we provide that to the public, we’re giving up the external manager’s strategy. So that’s where it becomes trademarked confidential information,” said Sarah Mudder, communications director for the Retirement and Investment Office that oversees the Legacy Fund’s investments. 
New Legacy Fund website will launch Nov. 1, aiming to improve investment transparency

Satrom is skeptical there isn’t a way to disclose those investments without compromising the external manager’s strategy. 
The lawmaker said he may propose legislation in the session that begins in January addressing commingled funds and open records laws.
“There’s information they should be providing, and if they don’t feel like they can under our laws, then we need to change the laws,” Satrom said. 
Satrom is worried the Legacy Fund may be invested in what he considers risky ventures, or in countries or companies that may be working against the United States’ national interests, like Russia. He said the key is transparency so the public can have confidence in how it is invested.
“Would the people of North Dakota approve of these investments if they knew what they were? I don’t think so,” Satrom said, but he can’t be sure and that’s the point. “It’s more than just making a return on the investments. Money can do good when we invest in good things.”
Not all of his legislative colleagues share his level of concern. Rep. Jonathan Warrey, R-Casselton, vice chair of the Legacy Fund advisory board, said it is a “minor concern” in his eyes. He said the website “is a huge step forward for clarity on where the investments are” and he hasn’t seen any evidence that the state’s money is being invested into any “nefarious” companies or projects that aren’t visible to the public. 
“We’ve got professional fund managers managing this. We’ve given them the charge to eliminate direct investments into adverse countries,” Warrey said. 
What’s next
State officials plan to continue improving the website. Smith said they plan to add information about how much is deposited into the fund from oil taxes by the end of the year. 
The investment data will only be updated annually. Smith hopes to improve that, but real-time reporting isn’t on the table. 
“This is a long-term investment for the state of North Dakota. I’m far less concerned about what happened last Tuesday as I am about what happened last fiscal year,” Armstrong said. 
The website cost roughly $500,000 to develop in one-time costs, not including licensing, maintenance and other fees. Members of the public with requests or suggestions are invited to reach out to state officials via the Contact Us form on the website. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Supreme Court denies attempt to overturn potential wins of 4 legislative candidates
text:
North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Mark Friese asks a question during a hearing on Oct. 2, 2026. In a Wednesday opinion authored by Friese, the Supreme Court denied a petition that challenged the eligibility of four legislative candidates.
(Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Supreme Court on Wednesday denied an effort by GOP officials to overturn potential election victories of four legislative candidates whose paperwork they challenged, saying the court case came too late.
The three challengers filed a petition with the court asking the seats be declared vacant and filled by appointment should any of the four challenged candidates win. Two of the challengers lost their primaries to three of the candidates they allege are ineligible due to primary paperwork errors they said Secretary of State Michael Howe’s office wrongly allowed to be corrected without the original petition signers’ consent.
The challengers were District 25 GOP Chair Matt Evans, Rep. Jeff Hoverson, R-Minot, and District 7 GOP executive committee member Douglas Pearson. They challenged the eligibility of candidates Blaine DesLauriers and Tim Mihalick of Minot-area District 3, Steve Sauter in Bismarck-area District 7 and Terry Goerger in Richland County’s District 25. Appointments would have favored Evans and Hoverson, who lost their primaries to Goerger, DesLauriers and Mihalick.
In the court’s unanimous opinion, Justice Mark Friese said the challengers filed their court case a month after the Aug. 31 deadline for candidates to correct their nominating petitions. The timing of the challengers’ case “disrupts an ongoing election, potentially confusing voters,” he said.
Friese said the challengers by their own account knew of the paperwork problems they alleged in late July. Citizens Alliance of North Dakota Executive Director Brandon Prichard asked Secretary of State Michael Howe to investigate and reject the candidates’ petition signatures. In late August, Howe told him state law allows corrections to candidate filings, according to emails in court papers.
North Dakota Supreme Court justices ask why they should upend voters’ will in candidacy dispute

Had the challengers pursued their case “with the diligence the statutory timeline required, any insufficiency could have been met with notice and an opportunity to correct,” Friese wrote. “Instead, (the challengers) ask this Court to declare the petitions insufficient when no correction is possible, an inequitable and harsher result than the statute they invoke contemplates, and after the voters in the affected districts have selected their preferred candidates.”
The court heard arguments last week, during which justices asked about the timing of the challengers’ case and how they could possibly overturn the will of voters.
The challengers filed their petition with the court days after absentee voting began for North Dakota’s Nov. 3 general election. The case showed the divide in the state’s dominant Republican Party over how candidates opt to get on the June primary ballot, by GOP endorsement or with petition signatures.
Prichard said he respects the court and the justices, but called the decision “odd” and “convenient.”
He said he believes the court erred in its reasoning because it applied state law in challenging petitions with a different statute that deals with correcting petitions.
“I think that this is just one that got away from them, respectfully,” said Prichard, a law student and former lawmaker. “I think the decision of the court is going to create a really bad precedent of limiting when challenges can be brought.”
In a text message statement, Howe said he appreciates the court “seeing this effort to thwart the votes of thousands of North Dakotans for what it is. Elections are decided at the ballot box, not in a courtroom. Our office and excellent staff for decades has been consistent in applying the law and processing candidate paperwork.”
Sauter called the opinion “the right decision.”
“I know we followed the rules, and I have the utmost faith in North Dakota and our processes,” Sauter said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Secretary of State confirms DOJ election monitors will be in Iowa
text:
A table hosted "I voted" stickers for voters to pick up after casting their ballots at the Polk County Election Office in Des Moines on the first day of early voting, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Election monitors for the U.S. Department of Justice will be deployed to some Iowa polling locations on Election Day, Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate confirmed Wednesday.
The Justice Department regularly deploys monitors to election sites nationwide. Under President Joe Biden, monitors were sent to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states to observe the 2022 elections, but the monitoring program has expanded significantly under President Donald Trump. As DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels announced Monday, the department intends to deploy 1,000 monitors across all 50 states.
This will include Iowa polling locations. It is still unknown which specific locations will have monitors, and the DOJ said Monday the full list of locations will not be released until Election Day, Nov. 3.
At a news conference at the State Emergency Operations Center in Johnston on Wednesday, Pate confirmed monitors are expected to be in Iowa. He did not share further details on locations, but said the monitors will not have an impact on Iowans’ ability to vote or the election process.
“They are there strictly as a monitor,” Pate said. “They can (have) no contact with our election workers, nor do they consult or advise or have any direct impact in that respect at all. They will let the county auditors know if they’re coming in. They will (send) to those county auditors their credentials to make sure, but they’re not in uniform, and they’re not imposing themselves on the process in any manner.”
The event was a chance for members of the Iowa Election Security Team — which includes the Secretary of State’s office as well as the Iowa National Guard and state departments of Public Safety, Homeland Security and Emergency Management — to assure voters of the integrity of the upcoming election and talk about the steps taken to address cybersecurity and other potential threats.
While Pate answered questions about DOJ monitors, he also emphasized Iowa’s “strong” election system, saying, “when you cast your ballot in the upcoming general election, it will be counted fairly, accurately and securely,” and he noted that Iowans have expressed “high confidence in our election results” in recent years.
He expressed concerns that focusing on the DOJ monitors could discourage people from voting.
“I just want to underscore again — this is what can cause disenfranchising of voters,” Pate said. “Because this kind of stuff goes out, and then people think ‘big brother’ is trying to impact them in their voting opportunities.”
Pate said the DOJ is choosing to exercise their ability to monitor elections “for certain civil rights issues, and they have certain criteria they have to follow.” He said the federal department is working with his office as well as with county auditors to ensure they are following guidelines, and said the monitors plan to submit reports after the election that focus on disability issues and provisional ballots.
Pate’s opponent in the 2026 election, Democrat Ryan Peterman, who is running for Iowa Secretary of State, said there were reasons for Iowans to be concerned about the presence of DOJ monitors at polling places.
“The Department of Justice has a longstanding role in protecting voting rights, most notably the use of poll observers in the 1960s to ensure states were abiding by the Voting Rights Act,” Peterman said in a statement. “However, the current leadership has made numerous representations that have turned out not to be factual about elections this year and we must ensure the observers here in Iowa do not interfere with our election workers and voters.”
Peterman said Pate “owes Iowans answers” about the federal monitors.
“Where in Iowa are these federal monitors going to be deployed? Why are they being sent here? What is the Secretary of State doing to ensure they do not interfere with Iowa voters?” Peterman said. “At this moment, it is critical that we have a Secretary of State who is honest and transparent with voters.”
But Pate said this response to the DOJ monitors could promote distrust in the state’s election process and in sources of information, such as the his own office, among voters who are trying to find reliable voting information.
“It’s worth pointing out that this job is about being nonpartisan and wearing a referee jersey,” Pate said in a statement. “Political statements like this are why this office continually urges voters to turn to trusted sources for election information — the Iowa Secretary of State’s Office and Iowa’s 99 county auditors.”
Pate emphasized federal election observers will be required to “follow the same rules as every other election observer and poll watcher – including the Democratic and Republican observers regularly sent by the parties, candidates, and the U.S. Congress. They are simply observers, dressed in plain clothes, and are not permitted to interfere with the voting process in any way.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Whitmer tags in to rally Democrats in some of Michigan’s most competitive congressional districts
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer stumps for Democratic candidates in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)With just days remaining in the 2026 election season, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer hit the road to help rally support for Democratic candidates running in fierce political battlegrounds.
Whitmer joined former prosecutor Christina Hines in Rochester, part of Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, Wednesday afternoon, stumping for Democrats up and down the ballot alongside outgoing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) and Theresa Brooks, who is running for Michigan’s 9th Senate District, another key battleground, trying to unseat incumbent Sen. Michael Webber (R-Rochester Hills).
Hines faces U.S. Army Capt. Mike Bouchard Jr., who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump. He is the son of  Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard.
Michigan’s 10th Congressional District encompasses southern Macomb County and a portion of eastern Oakland County, including Rochester and Rochester Hills. The district is currently represented by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor.
While the nonpartisan Cook Political Report previously rated the district as “lean Republican” it adjusted its rating in August to “toss-up” meaning either party has a strong chance of winning the district.
Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/ Michigan Advance)Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/ Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines, Michigan Senate candidate Theresa Brooks and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/ Michigan Advance)Former prosecutor and Democratic congressional candidate Christina Hines in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines take questions from the press following a campaign launch in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo Kyle Davidson/Advance)
Over the past month, Whitmer has campaigned alongside Democrats across the country through her role as vice chair of the Democratic Governor’s Association, telling reporters Wednesday that people across the nation are feeling the squeeze from Trump’s tariff policies and high fuel prices due to the war in Iran. 
“Whether I am talking to a sugar beet farmer in Saginaw, Michigan, or I am in Arizona with Katie Hobbs or Ohio with Dr. Amy Acton, people are all feeling the stress of how expensive everything is,” Whitmer said. “And that’s why, as you heard me talking with my fellow Michiganders here, you know we’ve got to make sure that we are listening and plotting a way to help people keep more money in their pockets because all the stress in Washington, D.C., is going to continue for the next two years, unfortunately.”
Hines emphasized that as a 36-year-old mother of three, she has felt the impact from the Trump administration’s policies, drawing a contrast between herself, James and her opponent.
“The reality is that people don’t want another version of John James, another rubber stamp, which is all that Michael Bouchard Jr. is. He has explicitly said that there’s not a single thing that he disagrees with Donald Trump over,” Hines said, citing a Feb. 19 Inside Elections article.
“He wants to continue Trump’s policies when he’s in Washington and be his ally. That is not what we need. That would hurt Michiganders. It would hurt the people in our district,” Hines continued, noting she would vote to get the U.S. out of the war in Iran to end the Trump administration’s tariffs and to fight back against corruption.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bouchard’s Communications Director Jon Shiner said that the Republican candidate had been clear in his intent to work with and stand up to anyone on behalf of the district.
“He has called for the trade conflicts to end and will vote to end the war in Iran. He has the experience to deliver on both of these. All Hines does is play partisan politics,” Shiner said in an emailed statement.
Later in the afternoon, Whitmer joined Democratic nominee William Lawrence who is campaigning against the incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in the highly competitive 7th Congressional District.
“I say he’s their representative because he’s certainly not our representative. He doesn’t represent our interests. He does what Trump wants, and he does what his corporate donors want every single time it matters,” Lawrence said, while kicking off a canvass launch in Brighton, which Whitmer also attended.
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer rallies canvassers in Brighton on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Democratic Congressional Candidate and political organizer William Lawrence in Brighton, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Barrett campaign strategist Jason Roe told Michigan Advance that anyone who has paid attention to Barrett has recognized that he’s willing to break with Trump on a number of issues. 
“What Tom has done is represent the district,” Roe said, noting that Barrett had secured $146 million in federal funding for critical infrastructure, Michigan State University and the Lansing regional airport and helped return $6.5 million to constituents.
Roe said Barrett has also distinguished himself in Congress by proposing bills to prevent the federal government from overruling local officials on data centers, barring elected officials from signing nondisclosure agreements for data centers and legislation to reform campaign finances and the healthcare system.
Lawrence has campaigned heavily on data centers, calling for a one-year moratorium in order to develop regulations. He has also opposed corporate spending in politics and supported a single-payer healthcare system.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Some Georgia Republicans try to distance themselves from national politics as Election Day nears
text:
Rick Jackson rallies supporters in Roswell Oct. 27, 2026. Polls show the race in a statistical tie as Jackson travels the state campaigning with Gov. Brian Kemp. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThey say all politics is local, and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp seems to hope that holds true next week.
Rick Jackson and Brian Kemp at a Jackson campaign rally in Canton Oct. 24, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Kemp has been traveling the state singing the praises of the man he hopes will take over his job after this year, Republican businessman Rick Jackson. Kemp is set to complete his second and final term in January, and Jackson is locked in a tight race with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms to succeed him.
At a campaign stop in DeKalb County Tuesday, Kemp urged supporters to focus their closing message on Republican results in Georgia rather than what is coming out of Washington.
“We can’t let the Democrats nationalize this election,” Kemp said at the DeKalb-Peachtree Airport. “This is about you. This is about us. This is about your community, this county and this state, and the things that we have achieved under great leadership now for almost 24 years.”
Kemp’s comment came just before former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris were scheduled to campaign in Georgia, though Republican national figures have also visited the state to stump for GOP candidates. President Donald Trump visited the state twice this month, and high-profile politicians like Texas Sen. Ted Cruz have also hit the campaign trail in the final stretch of the campaign.
The shift also comes as Republicans have openly expressed alarm over Democratic turnout during early voting.
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks in Roswell on Oct. 27, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republicans have occupied the governor’s mansion in Georgia since 2003 when Sonny Perdue became the first Republican governor in Georgia since Reconstruction.
Kemp, the state’s third consecutive two-term Republican leader, is set to leave office on a high note. An Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll released this month found nearly 70% of Georgians approve of his performance and 52% say Georgia is moving in the right direction.
The same poll suggests Georgians lack those warm feelings for Republicans at the federal level. Only 42% of respondents said they approved of Trump’s performance, and only 33% feel the nation is headed in the right direction.
Much of that displeasure with Trump, who won Georgia in two of the last three presidential elections, comes down to inflation. Voters attribute rising prices for gasoline and other goods to Trump’s war in Iran and tariff policy.
And those low numbers could make the typical midterm election slump even more pronounced, said Emory University political science professor Andra Gillespie.
“The national mood is anti-Republican in this cycle, which is customary given which party that is in power, but it’s exacerbated by the fact that Donald Trump has a particularly low approval rating in this particular cycle,” she said.
In that kind of environment, campaigning alongside Kemp makes sense, Gillespie said. But in addition to overcoming the drag of running as a member of the party in power during a midterm, Jackson has to overcome a lack of name recognition.
“He’s trying to attach himself to a record of success, but the challenge in terms of believability is whether or not he can actually lay claim to somebody else’s track record and be taken seriously,” she said.
“He’s basically trying to buy some of Brian Kemp’s incumbency advantage, but he’s not the incumbent, and there is the rub,” she added.
President Donald Trump and GOP governor candidate Rick Jackson share the stage at a White House event at Cobb County’s Wheeler High School. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson and Trump are both wealthy men, and Jackson welcomed comparisons between himself and the president during the primary. Even though Trump endorsed Jackson’s Republican opponent initially, Jackson told primary voters he would be Trump’s favorite governor and pledged to govern like Trump but with a Southern tone. The president has since endorsed Jackson.
But speaking with the press after the DeKalb event, Jackson was quick to correct a reporter who asked about him campaigning with Trump over the weekend.
“I didn’t campaign, I visited the rally,” Jackson said.
Jackson visited Trump on stage at a rally in Perry Saturday after initially saying he would skip the event. Jackson also shared the stage with Trump in Dalton the week before.
Jackson told reporters in DeKalb that he thinks Georgians will make the distinction between Georgia Republicans and the national party.
“I think everybody understands that’s a federal issue,” Jackson told reporters in DeKalb, speaking about his association with the president. “In the Senate race, they push a yes or no button. But what a governor does every (day), just like Gov. Kemp has done, it doesn’t matter what happens in DC and who’s president. You have to get along with everybody, and that’s what I’ll do from that standpoint. You have to solve the problems for Georgians, because every decision a governor makes every day affects everybody in Georgia, and that’s why we need to keep it going the same way it’s been doing.”
From left, Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor, and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff at a rally in Atlanta on May 31, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Bottoms and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat who is running for reelection against Republican Congressman Mike Collins, have both eagerly sought to associate their opponents with Trump in Georgia voters’ minds.
That’s pretty much par for the course in a midterm election with an unpopular president in power, said Jason Shepherd, Kennesaw State University political science professor and former chair of the Cobb County Republican Party, and while the president may get the headlines, state and local leaders often have a greater impact on the life of the average citizen.
“If I was a Democrat running with an unpopular Democrat president like Joe Biden four years ago, then I’d be reminding voters the same thing,” he said. “It’s how we govern and manage our affairs in this state that matters more than what’s happening in Washington D.C.”
“It’s not the White House or Congress that’s going to fix potholes in your neighborhood,” he added. “It’s not the White House or Congress that’s going to make a determination on how successful your schools are. That’s all going to be governed at the state and local level, and not liking what’s going on in Washington doesn’t translate to how best to govern the state.”
But speaking to reporters Tuesday in Atlanta, Bottoms said nationalizing the race is fair play.
“The nation’s paying attention,” she said. “This race is about Georgia, but Georgia is an important part of what happens across this country. I’ve said repeatedly, so goes Georgia goes the South, so goes the South goes America. We know that when we sent two senators in Senators Ossoff and Warnock to D.C., that it changed the landscape of America. So it’s about who shows up to vote in Georgia, but we’re going to take all the energy and support we can get.”
Early voting ends this Friday, with more than 2 million ballots already cast. Election Day is Tuesday.
Georgia Recorder reporter Alander Rocha contributed to this report.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Gov. Lee extends off-road diesel enforcement relief for farmers, loggers through Dec. 31
text:
Gov. Bill Lee has singed an order extending the use of tax-exempt dyed diesel by Tennessee farmers through the end of 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee farmers and loggers will be allowed to use tax-exempt diesel — usually limited to off-road vehicles — on public roads through the end of the year, Gov. Bill Lee announced Tuesday.
The move is meant to offer some relief during harvest season from high diesel fuel prices amid the war in Iran.
The red-colored diesel is the same as normal diesel but is not taxed because it is typically limited to off-road use and thus does not put wear and tear on public roadways.
Lee first directed state departments to suspend enforcement of the state laws that prohibit using the untaxed diesel on public roads in early October. The suspension was initially limited through the end of the month, but now matches the timeframe of President Donald Trump’s executive order temporarily deferring federal taxes on dyed diesel through Dec. 31.
Normal diesel fuel is subject to a federal tax of 24.4 cents per gallon and a state tax of 27 cents per gallon, meaning those purchasing dyed diesel for on-road use during the relief period could save around 51.4 cents per gallon. 
Tennessee governor lets farmers use untaxed diesel on roads after Trump defers federal enforcement

The Internal Revenue Service, IRS, stated it would not “impose a penalty when dyed diesel fuel is sold for use or used on highways nationwide” from Oct. 1 through Dec. 31, according to guidance issued on Oct. 14. The IRS also stated that it will pause fuel inspections during that time period, and will not require taxpayers to keep records of dyed diesel distribution, sale or purchase during the relief period.
In a “Frequently Asked Questions” document published Oct. 23, the IRS stated it is “considering a grace period or other measures to address residual red dye in tanks” and will issue further guidance.
Federal guidance has not, however, eliminated the federal tax obligation, meaning taxes could still be due at a later date. Trump instructed federal departments to explore ways to fully eliminate the tax liability.
Lee’s directive does not specify whether the state will require documentation.
Trump announced a separate fuel relief program for farmers totaling $8 billion on Oct. 21, but details on payment rates and timeline have yet to be released. The expense may also require Congressional approval.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Democratic lawmakers highlight affordability as first legislative priority in ‘27
text:
The Montana state capitol pictured after a late-night Senate vote on Jan. 9, 2025. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)Many facets of everyday life, from flipping on the lights as days grow darker to running weekly errands, are getting more expensive for Montanans, and Democratic lawmakers hope to address those issues in the 2027 legislative session.
During a Tuesday press conference at the state Capitol, Democratic legislative leaders shared three proposed bills they hope will help ease the climbing prices of groceries, housing and energy.
“Costs have continued to grow out of reach for anyone of the average income,” state Rep. Kelly Kortum, who is running for state Senate representing part of Bozeman. “Families need to afford the basics without worrying where they will have to trade off in their budget, or if they will have the money to afford it at all.”
Kortum acknowledged that many costs are tied to national and international policies, supply chains and corporations, “aspects of these are all far out of reach for the Montana legislature,” but said his colleagues planned to take whatever steps possible to fight “for a Montana we can all afford.”
Sen. Laura Smith, who is likely to be a part of Senate minority leadership next session, introduced a proposal aimed at stopping grocery stores from using personal data and AI algorithms to fix prices differently for different people. 
Large grocery chains have begun replacing in-store paper price tags with digital shelf tags, which make it easier for employees to change prices on individual items. 
But in many cases, the move has driven concerns that prices could be altered based on who is purchasing an item. For shoppers who purchase groceries online, there are concerns that personal data could be used to cater prices to individuals — similar to how airlines use “dynamic pricing” based on someone’s search history or ride-share apps will surge prices when services are in high demand. 
“Montanans deserve to be protected from algorithms controlled by large businesses with no accountability to the average shopper,” said Smith, D-Helena. “Montanans should not be charged different prices depending on the time of day, their purchasing history, and even their projected income.”
Similar pieces of legislation have been pushed in states around the country. 
Two states — Connecticut and Maryland — have enacted laws prohibiting the use of personaldata in grocery pricing, while a similar bill advanced through the New York legislature this year. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis vetoed his state’s proposed legislation, saying it was overly broad and could prevent lowering  prices in some instances. 
Local legislation has also been passed, with Seattle adopting a ban on so-called “surveillance pricing” earlier this month. 
“It’s a phrase I never thought that I would have to say in regular life or as a legislator: I do not want robots choosing the price of your groceries,” Smith said. 
 Localizing housing ownership

In a state where housing prices have outstripped wage growth — especially in popular areas such as the Flathead Valley and Bozeman — affordability of renting or owning a home is top of mind. 
Sen. Jacinda Morigeau, D-Arlee, shared proposed legislation that would focus on just one facet of the affordable housing situation, the “scourge” of private equity firms and corporations buying homes, apartments and mobile home parks in the state. 
“Nationally, it’s estimated that private equity firms own 13% of all apartment units,” Morigeau said, citing reporting by Lee Enterprises that 30 mobile home parks in the state are owned by private equity — about 3,900 homes. 
“To these faceless corporations, Montanans are just numbers on a spreadsheet, and their homes are assets to extract money from to the detriment of the people who live in them,” she said.
A proposed bill Democrats plan to bring next session would ban private equity firms and institutional investors from owning residential real estate property, including mobile home parks. 
Federally, Congress passed legislation this year aimed at slowing corporate ownership of single-family homes by prohibiting large private equity firms from buying additional single-family homes with some exceptions. 
Montana’s proposed legislation would pair with additional Democrats’ efforts in 2027 to bolster new construction and focus on keeping homes in the hands of Montanans, Morigeau said. 
“It reinforces the thought that Montana money should stay in Montana, keeping our local economy strong instead of being funneled to the coffers of out-of-state investors,” Morigeau said. 
 Lights on, bills low

The lawmakers also outlined a proposed bill that would focus on addressing rising energy costs across the state. 
Rep. Peter Strand of Bozeman said that energy bills for Montanans have jumped around 44% in the last four years for customers of Northwestern Energy, the state’s monopoly utility company. 
Strand said a new Efficiency First Act would be a public-private partnership that would require utilities to prioritize investments in Montana’s energy grid, incentivize modernization of substations, and expand weatherization programs. It would also provide for investments in technologies for homes and businesses such as smart thermostats and heat pumps to address energy demand within buildings. 
“Each of these investments improves the resiliency and function of the grid, which, bottom line, means lower costs for everyone along the line,” Strand said. “As a teacher, I saw what it meant for my students to be able to return each night to a healthy and warm home, not one where parents have to choose between paying rent, getting groceries, or paying for utilities.”
Montana’s next legislative session will begin on Jan. 4 and Republicans are projected be hold majorities in both chambers. 
“We’re very interested to hear Democrats’ ideas and to engage in honest and good-faith discussions about what’s possible this session on affordability policy and many more topics,” a spokesperson for Senate Republicans told the Daily Montanan by text message.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. says feds looking for ways to fund faith-based recovery programs
text:
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., spoke to reporters after touring Sheepgate, a Christian recovery and treatment program in Colfax Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Wednesday he supports finding new ways to provide federal funding for faith-based recovery programs.
The secretary visited Sheepgate, a Christian recovery and treatment program located in Colfax, to speak about the Great American Recovery Initiative, a federal program launched by President Donald Trump through an executive order issued in January. The federal program is an effort to provide more national resources and coordination for services that focus on addiction and substance abuse disorders across the country.
Part of the increased funding effort comes through the Safety Through Recovery, Engagement, and Evidence-based Treatment and Support (STREETS) program — a $96 million funding initiative within the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) to provide up to eight communities with $3 million annually for four years to develop care systems for people who are homeless and have substance abuse disorders or serious mental illnesses.
Kennedy visited Detroit on Tuesday to discuss the Detroit Health Department’s receipt of STREETS program funding for long-term services to assist people struggling with homelessness, serious mental illnesses and substance abuse disorders.
At the Michigan event, Kennedy said the program will have a “new emphasis on faith-based recovery.”
Though Sheepgate — nor any Iowa facilities — received federal dollars through the STREETS program, Kennedy said the Colfax recovery center was a “exemplar” facility showcasing the type of care encouraged through the Great American Recovery Initiative — long-term programs that offer a year of “in-house recovery and reintegration into the community,” he said.
“Our plan of Great American Recovery is to reorient recovery towards value-based recovery in this country,” Kennedy said. “We follow the addict comprehensively over the lifetime, from detox to rehab to housing to jobs and stability. And that’s value-based care — but also to include more and more faith-based care, and that’s one of the reasons we came here to Sheepgate.”
But programs like Sheepgate are not currently receiving federal funding, Kennedy said, because of a policy enacted by the Biden administration “to stop all assistance to faith-based recovery programs and to discourage the state from supporting them.” 
Regulations enacted in April 2024 by nine federal departments overseeing social service grants including drug rehabilitation services placed restrictions on partnerships with faith-based organizations to ensure funding did not go toward “explicitly religious” purposes, but some churches and faith-based services said the regulations made their programs ineligible for federal assistance. Kennedy said this policy has been changed during the Trump administration, but that problems remain.
“We’ve changed that policy at the top, but there are still impediments to us getting the money to these kind of programs,” Kennedy said. “This program is entirely funded by private donors, and that’s getting harder and harder for them to do. And we want to make sure that these kind of programs — they serve such a critical role — we want to make sure that they continue to function.”
He said HHS is “looking for ways to make sure that they can get federally funded” moving forward.
Kennedy is also set to appear — in his personal capacity — alongside Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and 2nd Congressional District candidate Joe Mitchell at an event hosted by the MAHA PAC Wednesday evening.

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevadans pay tribute to civil rights and labor trailblazer Dolores Huerta
text:
Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the United Farm Workers, speaks at the 30th AFL-CIO Constitutional Convention on June 8, 2026, in Minneapolis where she named the first recipient of the Si Se Puede Award. (Photo courtesy AFL-CIO)In an outpouring of messages expressing condolences, Nevada lawmakers and organizers praised civil rights and labor activist Dolores Huerta, who died Wednesday, as an inspirational trailblazer. 
“She was a voice for the voiceless, a fighter for working families, and a powerful reminder that our communities have the strength to create change,” said Democratic Assemblywoman Cecelia González, who serves as the Chair of the Nevada Latino Legislative Caucus.  “Her words, ‘Sí se puede,’ were never just a slogan. They were a call to action that inspired generations of Latinos, women, workers, and community leaders to stand up and demand a seat at the table.”
Huerta, 96, was known for her work as a co-founder of the United Farm Workers in the 1960s, where she aided in mobilizing migrant farm workers working on large grape farms in California.
Earlier this year, Huerta revealed she had been sexually assaulted by Cesar Chavez, who she co-led in the farm workers movement.
“The formation of a union was the only vehicle to accomplish and secure those rights and I wasn’t going to let Cesar or anyone else get in the way,” she said in a statement at the time. “I channeled everything I had into advocating on behalf of millions of farmworkers and others who were suffering and deserved equal rights.”
Her activism and influence stretched beyond California leading her to be recognized nationally and garner notable accolades such as the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which was awarded to her by President Barack Obama in 2012.
Some Nevada labor leaders were only able to get to where they are “because of the foundation Dolores Huerta created,” said Susie Martinez, the executive secretary-treasurer for the Nevada state AFL-CIO.
“She helped pave the way for generations of organizers, and her courage will continue to inspire us to speak up, stand together, and never stop fighting for working people,” she said. “We honor her life by carrying that work forward.”
Democratic. U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen said Huerta’s ability to engage and energize the community was unmatched. 
“She touched so many lives throughout her decades of service, fighting to advance the rights of immigrants, women, and farm workers,” Rosen said.
In addition to visiting Nevada to join various campaigns, Huerta also spoke on behalf of Nevada legislative initiatives, including efforts to abolish the death penalty in 2021.
“To all the Nevada legislators, I am calling on you to join in getting rid of the death penalty,” Huerta said in a video at the time, adding that “in Nevada 40% of the people on death row are persons of color, most of them Black.”
The legislation passed the Assembly in a partyline vote before being killed in a Democratically controlled Senate without getting a hearing.
In 2025, the City of North Las Vegas honored the civil rights activist by opening the Dolores Huerta Resource Center, a facility that offers bilingual support services, workforce development, and mental health resources.
Democratic Assemblymember Cinthia Zermeño Moore, along with other lawmakers, attempted to enshrine Huerta’s legacy in Nevada by sponsoring legislation in 2025 that required the governor to proclaim April 10 Dolores Huerta Day. 
Assembly Bill 98, which passed with bipartisan support, was vetoed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who wrote in a veto message “there is no need to codify additional days into law.”
Huerta “taught us that our voices matter, that everyone deserves a seat at the table, and that we belong in spaces of power,” Moore said in a statement. “Although that legislation was vetoed, no veto can diminish her contributions to our country and the generations she inspired.”

name: California
title: Lawsuit claims lawmaker retaliated against employee for reporting misconduct
text:
In summary
A former staffer for Democratic Assemblymember Anamarie Ávila Farías accuses the lawmaker of whistleblower retaliation and racial discrimination in a recently filed lawsuit.


A former staffer to Assemblymember Anamarie Ávila Farías has sued the first-term Democratic lawmaker and the California Assembly over allegations of racial discrimination and whistleblower retaliation.
Pa’tanisha Davis Pierson, who worked as a district director for Ávila Farías’ Concord office, alleges in a lawsuit filed on Oct. 21 in Contra Costa Superior Court that the assemblymember retaliated against her after she told the Assembly human resources department that she believed a staff member was doing campaign work on state time. 
Davis Pierson, who is Black, said Ávila Farías stripped her responsibilities after she reported that the lawmaker allowed a staffer to conduct campaign duties for Ávila Farías from the district office. The complaint also accuses Ávila Farías of racial discrimination for yelling at Black staff and interns and giving them less desirable work than other employees. Davis Pierson said she received an “unwanted hug” in the months leading up to her resignation letter in April.
The employee still works for Ávila Farías.
“I vigorously deny the allegations and will defend against them through the appropriate legal process,” Ávila Farías said in an emailed statement. “I am proud to have one of the most diverse staffs in the Legislature, reflecting the diversity of the Contra Costa County community.” 
On Nov. 3, the Assembly’s Workplace Conduct Unit opened an investigation into Davis Pierson’s allegations. Ten days later, the employee Davis Pierson reported “body-checked” her in the hallway of their district office, according to the lawsuit.
Davis Pierson also claims the Assembly human resources department retaliated shortly after she made her report when it refused to accommodate her requests for time off and a hybrid schedule following a medical procedure.
The Assembly Rules Committee, which oversees labor disputes among lawmakers and staff, is aware of the lawsuit but declined to comment, citing personnel issues and pending litigation, according to Chief Administrative Officer Lia Lopez.
Davis Pierson and her attorneys, David Pearson and Stefano Abbasciano, did not immediately return phone calls and voice messages seeking comment Wednesday.
The Workplace Conduct Unit did not immediately return a phone call and message inquiring about the status of the investigation. 
Davis Pierson was on the job for less than nine months when she made her whistleblower report, according to the lawsuit. She began working for Ávila Farías’ office in January 2025, just a few weeks after the freshman lawmaker joined the Assembly after nearly a decade on the board of directors of the California Housing Finance Agency.
Ávila Farías is up for reelection in her heavily Democratic district in November.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Social Security, Medicare top of mind for Montanans heading into Election Day
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.A high portion of Montanans are 65 and older, but those who receive Social Security benefits are facing a 22% cut in 2032 without action from Congress.
That’s according to data from the Social Security Administration.
The topic is a question from voters, and it was a rallying point for at least one political candidate on the ballot in Montana this year.
Sam Forstag, running for the U.S. House, puts on a pair of gloves in front of the Missoula County Courthouse to show he is ready to fight for Social Security and Medicare. Tula Thompson, with the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare PAC, said her organization supports Forstag in the 2026 election. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)
Sam Forstag, running for the western U.S. House district, recently received a pair of boxing gloves at a rally to represent his ability to fight for Social Security and Medicare.
Forstag, a Democrat, is running against Republican Aaron Flint in a competitive race.
At an event last week, four organizations that advocate for Social Security and Medicare announced their support for Forstag.
“He (Forstag) submitted one of the best completed questionnaires we’ve ever received with regard to his positions on Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and drug prices,” said Social Security Works PAC President Jon “Bowzer” Bauman in an email. “His opponent, Aaron Flint, never even bothered to return the questionnaire. The contrast is stark.”
A spokesperson for Flint did not respond to requests for comment about his stance on Social Security. His campaign site said seniors should not pay more income taxes on Social Security, and Flint would protect it.
More than 22% of Montanans are 65 and older compared to 18% nationally, according to the U.S. Census.
In Montana, an estimated 226,293 people 65 and older receive Social Security benefits out of 270,750 in all, according to the Social Security Administration.
Montanans receive $6.07 billion a year in Social Security benefits, largely dollars that go directly into the economy, according to the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.
The fund is projected to be depleted by 2032 without action from Congress, according to a 2026 Social Security Administration report. That means the fund wouldn’t have enough money to pay all scheduled benefits “in full and on time,” the report said. It estimates funds could cover 78% of people’s Social Security checks.
Focus on western House
Social Security Works PAC did not endorse in the U.S. Senate race or eastern House district; it typically endorses only in competitive races, said Linda Benesch, vice president for communications.
Two other organizations that recently announced support for Forstag also did not endorse in the other federal races in Montana.
The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare PAC endorsed Forstag, and Chairman Max Richtman said it’s the only race in Montana the organization has weighed in on.
“It’s the one we think has a realistic chance of success,” Richtman said.
Richtman said his organization likes Seth Bodnar, the independent candidate in the U.S. Senate race, but having the Democratic nominee, Alani Bankhead, stay in the race makes a win by Bodnar difficult.
Political analysts consider Republican Kurt Alme the favorite for the Senate race in Montana.
Incumbent Republican U.S. House Rep. Troy Downing is expected to win in the eastern district.
In the eastern district, Big Sky 55+ endorsed the independent in the race, Michael Eisenhauer. Democrat Brian Miller is also running.
Senate candidates on Social Security
At a recent debate, Bodnar said the person elected to the U.S. Senate will help decide what happens as people face a 22% cut in their benefits, and “the stakes are incredibly high.”
But he said the solution is easy.
He said raising the cap on income that’s taxable for Social Security from $184,000 would create a system that is both more fair and “more solvent for the long run.”
For example, for someone earning $100,000 a year, 100% of their income is taxable for Social Security purposes, Bodnar said. But he said that means for someone earning $2 million a year, less than 10% is taxable for Social Security.
“This is a simple fix, folks,” Bodnar said. “We just need leaders in D.C. who stand up and advocate and fight for this. I can be that leader.”
Bankhead’s campaign website describes Social Security as “the most successful anti-poverty program in our history.”
At the debate, she agreed on the fix and accused Bodnar of parroting her plan. She said Congress needs to “tax the wealthy their fair share.”
“You do that by removing the income limit on Social Security so that we can fund Social Security in perpetuity,” Bankhead said.
Alme addressed Social Security at a later debate.
He said he used to be budget director for the state and knows how to pay off debt, and he would focus on eliminating waste to help bolster Social Security funding.
He said he would strengthen the program and “will never support a cut in benefits for seniors.”
Rally for Forstag
On the steps of the Missoula County Courthouse, advocates for Social Security and Medicare announced last week their endorsements of Forstag, a smokejumper and union leader.
Many older Montanans are struggling, and Rep. Connie Keogh said senior homelessness is on track to triple by 2030.
“This is a result of a system that is failing us, and it’s certainly not the future that we should be demanding for our children and grandchildren,” said Keogh, a Missoula Democrat. “Sam is about solutions.”
Keogh represented the Montana Chapter of the Alliance for Retired Americans, which endorsed Forstag.
Trent Bolger, with Big Sky 55+, said Forstag demonstrated he understands the issues by earning the endorsements of his organization and the three others focused on Social Security and Medicare.
Tula Thompson, with the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, said Social Security checks from the western district add more than $3.1 billion to Montana’s economy every year.
But Thompson said the benefit reduction would mean a $500 loss every month for the average senior in Montana if nothing changes.
At the rally, Thompson presented Forstag with boxing gloves so he could “continue to fight for seniors.”
Forstag said he’ll fight to expand Social Security and Medicare and fight to be sure all earners carry their own weight, to lift the payroll tax cap so the top 6% are paying the same rate as the bottom 94%.
In Montana, he said, 11% of the people living on the streets are older than 55, and 19 rural hospitals are at risk of closure.
“We are so much better than that, and we can fix those things,” Forstag said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Anne Arundel schools amended gender policy, DOJ still files a lawsuit
text:
Two months after Anne Arundel County schools amended a gender policy after a threat from the federal government, the Justice Department filed suit anyway, claiming schools facilitated the "secret transitioning" of children without telling parents. (Photo by Unai Huizi Photography/Getty stock images)Slightly more than two months after Anne Arundel County public schools amended a gender policy due to a threat from the federal government, the school district got sued anyway.
In a 31-page complaint filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Maryland, the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division charges the county’s Board of Education with “facilitating the secret ‘transitioning’ of children’s ‘gender identity’ at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent.”
The suit seeks a court injunction to not only prevent Anne Arundel schools from enforcing its “Safe and Inclusive Environments for LGBTQ+ Students” policy, but also to allow parents to review and challenge any errors in their child’s educational records. The policy, the suit says, violates the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
The suit represents two parents, identified as John and Jane Doe, who are practicing Christians with a daughter, identified as Mary, who was a senior in an Anne Arundel County high school. It said the parents learned by accident that school district staff has been calling the daughter a male name, at her request, and concealed the fact from them.
The parents believe “using pronouns inconsistent with that person’s sex is false and harmful,” the suit says.
Supreme Court ruling on transgender athletes revives debate in Maryland

“Schools should not discuss preferred pronouns or ‘gender identity’ with a student without parental notification and consent,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a statement on the lawsuit. “Parents should not be lied to, stonewalled, or branded as ‘safety concerns’ when they ask to see the education records that reveal what schools are secretly doing to their children. This Department will end illegal school policies that keep parents in the dark.”
The school district said it was notified of the lawsuit Tuesday afternoon and “is reviewing it closely.”
“AACPS disagrees with the allegations and stands by its compliance with FERPA and PPRA (Protection of Pupils Rights Amendment). Moreover, the school system has been in regular contact with the Department of Justice in a good faith effort to resolve their concerns while adhering to our obligations to all students, parents and staff,” school district spokesperson Bob Mosier said in an email.
“It’s regrettable that the Department chose to pursue litigation rather than continuing constructive dialogue,” his email said. “Because the case is now before a federal court, AACPS will address the claims in its court filings and will have no further comment at this time.”
The suit comes after America First Legal of Washington, D.C., filed a suit against the county schools on July 8 in U.S. District Court of Maryland, also on behalf of John and Jane Doe parents with a daughter in high school. They alleged the district secretly facilitated their minor child’s social “gender transition” at school without their notice or consent.
According to the complaint, the school district began in 2019 to adopt policies that include a guidance document for staff “to conceal gender identity information from parents of high school students.”
The U.S. Department of Education’s Student Privacy Policy Office and the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division announced July 27 they were taking enforcement action against Anne Arundel County after the district classified a student’s gender identity as “confidential medical information” that couldn’t be shared with parents.
More than three weeks later, on Aug. 19, and several days before the first day of school, Anne Arundel County Superintendent Mark Bedell wrote a letter to the school community that the policy had been amended.
It reads, in part, “Nothing in this regulation shall be construed to limit or otherwise interfere with parents’/guardians’ rights under FERPA, including the right to inspect and review their student’s complete education record. Under FERPA, education records generally include all records, files, documents, and other materials maintained by AACPS that contain information directly related to a student.”
As for the latest suit, it also wants the school district to receive written parental consent before a minor student responds to any surveys or evaluations that includes any political affiliations, sex behavior and attitudes or religious practices.
