name: National
title: College students in swing states rally against off-campus voting sites, student ID bans
text:
Students at North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro, N.C., begin a 40-minute walk to the nearest off-campus early polling site on Oct. 22, 2026. Election officials declined to put an early campus voting location at the school despite protests. (Photo by Elisha Brown/Stateline)GREENSBORO, N.C. — Led by members of the marching band and Aggie and Aggietha, the North Carolina A&T State University mascots, hundreds of students at the nation’s largest historically Black university walked 40 minutes from campus to the nearest early polling site on a recent afternoon. 
They started the journey with a pep rally, watched over by 15-foot bronze statues of the four students who led sit-ins at the Woolworth’s Counter in downtown Greensboro to protest segregation during the civil rights movement.  
“There’s a legacy that’s set out before us, with the A&T Four, with Jesse Jackson, and all of them being Aggies. When a fight comes, it’s a matter of how, and not if, we’re going to take up the fights,” said Shia Rozier, a 22-year-old senior who has led efforts to get a polling site on campus. 
Rozier and other student leaders around the country are pushing to make voting more accessible to college students. Students have protested against laws and decisions from local election officials that they say could make casting ballots harder, including off-campus polling sites and bans on student IDs when voting.
US Supreme Court ruling restores NH ban on use of student IDs at polls

In Greensboro, nearly 370 voters cast ballots at the early polling location students visited Oct. 22, according to Guilford County election data. It’s also the nearest early location for thousands of other students at University of North Carolina-Greensboro and Bennett College. 
“Not having a voting poll on site is obviously not ideal, but like we got to make a change some way, so we worked through hardship and voted,” said Lathan Nance, an 18-year-old A&T student who voted for the first time last week. 
Stateline spoke with college students from three swing states — New Hampshire, North Carolina and Texas — who are rallying against barriers to voting during the midterm elections. 
They are marching to the polls, organizing rides to polling sites and canvassing on Election Day. Several said they are looking to break misconceptions about Gen Z. 
“They think we don’t have a voice, so we just have to prove them wrong,” Nance said. 
Calls for more midterm polling sites in North Carolina 
Students at three North Carolina universities — NC A&T, Western Carolina University and the University of North Carolina, Greensboro — and a college Democrats group filed a federal lawsuit in January against state and county election officials over a lack of early voting sites at their campuses for the midterm primaries.
The plaintiffs said off-campus early polling locations burden those who lack transportation, have disabilities or limited financial resources. They accused the defendants of violating the First, 14th and 26th amendments, the latter of which lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 and said voting rights should not be “denied or abridged” based on age. 
A GOP county elections board member said he was warned against voting for a campus polling site

A federal judge in February denied their request for a temporary injunction against moving early voting sites, noting in an order that federal courts have a precedent to stray away from intervening in state election laws near an election.
Jason Tyson, the director of external affairs at the North Carolina State Board of Elections, said those schools did not host midterm early voting sites in previous years, and the county election boards decided polling locations were not needed on those campuses.
“There’s a lot of confusion and probably misinformation regarding this topic,” said Tyson.
“The correct thing is that during every midterm and general election, voting sites expand and contract,” he said. “The general election is a much bigger contest and bigger event to handle, so of course there are going to be more voting sites and more interest during a presidential year.” 
Rozier said the denial of an on-campus early polling site after protests and lawsuits was difficult, but she’s proud of her peers and the marches. “I think it shows the Board of Elections doesn’t get to decide whether we get to vote, whether they’re deciding where we’re going to vote,” she said. 
UNC-G and NC A&T have on-campus precincts for Election Day. 
Rides to the polls in key Texas county
Last year, local election officials removed the University of Texas, Arlington as a polling site. Now, students have to walk about 20 minutes to a courthouse to cast a ballot during the early voting period and on Election Day, according to Andres Morales, the university’s student body president. The city has an on-demand rideshare service but lacks public transit. 
“UTA has frequently hosted voting since 2012 and is equipped to provide a secure voting location that meets all state and county requirements,” Jeff Caplan, a spokesperson for the school, wrote in a statement to Stateline. 
The Tarrant County Election Administration did not respond to requests for comment. 
The county is considered a battleground because voters in the Republican-leaning area have supported Democratic candidates in recent elections. 
Morales said there was little protest when the polling site was taken away ahead of an election on constitutional amendments in November 2025, but added that students are more passionate about voting during the midterms. 
“I think it’s started a fire in the students, a movement for students to go out and start voting more and work with other organizations to help students vote,” said Morales, 28. 
He said student leaders are working with various organizations and the city to shuttle students from campus to the closest election site during the early voting period and on Election Day. Students are also planning to march to the polls Friday, the last day of early voting in Texas. 
Student ID ban in New Hampshire 
In August, the voting rights group Open Democracy sued New Hampshire election officials in federal court over a new law that banned student IDs as proof of identity at the polls. The case was fast-tracked to the U.S. Supreme Court after a district judge enacted a temporary injunction on the ban’s enforcement. 
The court upheld New Hampshire’s law, writing in an unsigned order that lower courts shouldn’t alter election rules on the eve of an election. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
Federal judge blocks Indiana’s ban on use of student IDs for voting

“The Supreme Court’s decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials,” New Hampshire Republican Attorney General John Formella said in a statement. 
Raevan Granfield, a 19-year-old at Keene State College, said the Supreme Court decision “heavily disenfranchises a group of people that already are facing a lot of blows in New Hampshire.” 
The state is one of just three, alongside Alabama and Mississippi, that do not allow early voting. 
Granfield is voting absentee because they plan to canvas on Election Day with New Hampshire Youth Movement, a progressive advocacy group. But they said a lot of students don’t know about that option and cannot get to the polls because of classes. 
Three states — Florida, Indiana and New Hampshire — have explicit bans on student IDs, but the Indiana law is blocked by the courts and the Florida statute does not take effect until January. About a dozen states do not consider student ID as a valid way to prove identity when voting, according to the Campus Vote Project, a nonprofit organization that encourages voting. 
Yael Bromberg, an American University adjunct law professor and expert on youth voting rights, said the rise of student ID bans creates voter confusion. 
“In some of these states, it’s very clear that the rollbacks are simply to target and disenfranchise youth voters,” she said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma lawmakers consider strategies to counter student absenteeism
text:
A student writes on a worksheet at Adelaide Lee Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 11. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Addressing student absenteeism will take two things, school district and court officials said Wednesday: money and manpower.
Speakers at an interim study at the state Capitol agreed Oklahoma could help improve school attendance by funding more full-time staff dedicated to meeting with families and connecting them to resources, overseeing court diversion programs and prosecuting truancy cases.
Oklahoma House lawmakers held the study to examine how certain schools, district attorneys and court systems tackle truancy and chronic absenteeism amid a rise in rates nationwide.
“We cannot legislate good parenting,” said Charity Eakens, of Ada City Schools. “We cannot force families to value education, but we can create systems that provide meaningful support, remove barriers and hold people accountable. And we have to stop expecting schools alone to carry that responsibility.”
Students can’t learn if they’re not in school, she said, but getting them to attend consistently is “anything but simple.”
The Ada district, which sits within the Chickasaw Nation and where almost half of all students are Native American, handles many of its truancy cases in partnership with tribal nations and their court systems, said Eakens, the district’s director of First American programs.
Over the past three years, Ada schools have referred more than 250 students with five or more absences to the Chickasaw Nation’s family advocacy program, and the vast majority of these cases reached a positive resolution, she said. About 7% ended up in tribal court.
But, court is not the first step, Eakens said. First is a meeting that brings a family, school and tribal nation together to discuss the cause of a student’s absences.
In many cases, the underlying issue is homelessness or poverty, and the family is connected with tribal or community services, Eakens said. Other families simply need guidance on ways to get their children to school regularly. 
She said Oklahoma should implement similar restorative attendance support programs statewide. Doing so would take more staffing across the state.
“Even in a small district, it takes someone who can do that full time,” Eakens said.
A parent walks her daughter into Adelaide Lee Elementary on the first day of school Aug. 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Buchanan Elementary in Oklahoma City takes a committee approach. Its front office staff meets weekly to review which children had absences, Principal Monserrat Randolph said. 
School staff call these students’ families to check in and then send a letter home after the child’s fourth absence. 
The next step is a text message from the principal. Randolph said she makes sure to include in her message the text of a state law requiring parents to ensure their children attend school.
“That’s what actually pushes them to (realize), ‘Oh, this is a real thing. It’s a big issue. It’s the law,’” Randolph said.
The situation sometimes progresses to an in-person meeting to discuss with parents what resources they might need. If the absences continue, the school refers the matter to the Oklahoma Department of Human Services, which she said is “the end of the line for us.”
Buchanan has improved from a D grade for absenteeism in the 2022-23 school year to a B the past two years on state evaluations, Randolph said.
The Oklahoma State Report Cards, which evaluate the performance of each public school, gave the state as a whole a D for chronic absenteeism, with just under 81% of students in good attendance. Chronic absenteeism is defined as missing 10% or more of the school year for any reason.
Elevated absenteeism rates have been a persistent issue nationwide since the COVID-19 pandemic, national data shows.
Chronically absent students have a 77.8% high school graduation rate, said Dennis Williams, senior director of accountability at the Oklahoma State Department of Education. Those who aren’t have a graduation rate of 94.4%, he said during the interim study.
A student walks into the Freshman Academy attendance office in Jenks Public Schools on Nov. 13, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
While acknowledging student attendance isn’t entirely within a school’s control, the Oklahoma Legislature passed a bill in 2025 to change the state report cards, shifting chronic absenteeism to an opportunity for bonus points toward a school’s grade rather than counting against it. The state is still waiting on final approval from the U.S. Department of Education to make the report card change, Williams said.
Absenteeism begins to worsen in sixth grade and reaches its peak at the high school level, Oklahoma City Public Schools administrators told lawmakers. Some Oklahoma City high schools have half of their students who are chronically absent.
“What we’ve seen again and again is that the reasons are so broad and so complex that as a district, this is not going to be a problem that we’re going to be able to solve alone,” said Alisha Suffield, the district’s chief of schools. “We recognize that attendance will not improve through a single initiative or by asking schools to work harder without support. It requires intentional investment and, bigger than that, a shared responsibility.”
Oklahoma City Public Schools Chief of Schools Alisha Suffield speaks to the Oklahoma State Board of Education during a meeting Jan. 28, 2025, at the state Department of Education in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Every district attorney’s office in the state should have a truancy program, said Erik Johnson, the district attorney for Pontotoc, Hughes and Seminole counties. That requires “the want-to and the availability of manpower to make it happen,” he said.
Students with 10 absences are referred to Johnson’s office, which prosecutes parents who refuse to take the issue seriously, he said. Anyone found guilty of state truancy laws could be subject to a fine or imprisonment in a county jail.
Johnson said his office tries a different tactic for high school students refusing to attend school. These students are encouraged to earn their high school diploma through the General Education Development (GED) test and to enroll in a job skill program at a local career technology center.
“We put them through welding programs, (commercial driver’s license) programs, cosmetology programs and demonstrate a pathway to these kids so that they can see, ‘Well, you know, I don’t have to just be a screw-up the rest of my life,’” he said.
Grady County District Judge Kory Kirkland encouraged more courts to implement “graduated sanctions,” which allows students to complete agreed-upon terms to avoid juvenile charges for truancy or other offenses. That could involve the completion of a drug treatment program or other requirements.
Kirkland said he’s seen this approach succeed in his courtroom, but it’s time-consuming. It would take funding for a full-time program coordinator and a prosecutor dedicating half of each week to these cases, he said.
Finding a solution to student absenteeism “is something we’ve got to do,” said Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber, as the study concluded.
“We’ve got to figure it out,” said Lowe, the head of the House Common Education Committee.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: MAP: Data center rules enacted in Arkansas’ most populous county after judge’s veto overridden
text:
An audience member attending a Pulaski County Quorum Court agenda-setting meeting holds a sign opposing data centers on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Data center opponents notched a hard-fought win Tuesday night after the Pulaski County Quorum Court voted to override the outgoing county judge’s veto of land-use regulations for the facilities.
The 10-4 vote comes a month after Pulaski County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the regulations that the panel passed in September. 
Two data centers are planned in Pulaski County, one within Little Rock city limits and another in an unincorporated area just off 145th Street. The latter, being built by AVAIO, will have to comply with the regulations, the ordinance’s sponsor said last month.
Hyde — defeated in March’s Democratic primary by former circuit and appeals Judge Wendell Griffen, who authored the regulations — cited legal concerns when making the veto.
Since the quorum court first considered data center regulations for Arkansas’ most populous county in May, the opposition to the power-hungry computing hubs has grown, with polling showing increasingly bipartisan opposition.
That unpopularity has pitted pro-data center interests such as the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce against Pulaski County residents opposed to the AVAIO data center project in the unincorporated part of the county. 
‘They own it’: A split-screen view of data centers comes to central Arkansas

The new regulations require prospective data center projects to submit to the county electrical load analyses, water and wastewater plans, land-use suitability studies and a decommissioning plan, among other requirements. 
Hyde, in vetoing the regulations last month, raised questions about the legal risks of enacting the new limits.
Prospective data center projects would also be required to demonstrate that the development won’t “materially impair” utilities and other public infrastructure that serve surrounding properties under the new regulations, but do not limit the amount of water or power a project can use.
The override came the day after the city of Van Buren approved regulations of its own. The Arkansas River Valley community has received some preliminary inquiries from data center companies, according to Talk Business and Politics, but has not fielded anything beyond that.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: DOE to loan up to $5.1 billion to Alliant Energy for Iowa and Wisconsin energy projects
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy agreed to an up to $5.1 billion loan to Alliant Energy.  (Photo by Robert Zullo/ States Newsroom)Alliant Energy Corporation has closed a $5.1 billion loan package with the U.S. Department of Energy to fund power generation and energy storage projects in Wisconsin and Iowa. 
A news release from the DOE said the loan would help to “strengthen grid reliability in Iowa and Wisconsin” by adding more than 2.6 gigawatts of power generation capacity and delivering electricity cost savings of more than $1 billion to ratepayers in both states. 
A spokesperson for Alliant said if the company accesses the full lower-interest loan package from DOE, the projected lifetime-adjusted interest savings would result in Iowa customer savings of $800 million and Wisconsin customer savings of $400 million. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alliant said with the 30-year loans, the company may pursue: 1.6 GW of new natural gas generation; 240 megawatts, or MW, of increased capacity at existing natural gas facilities; 1 GW of energy storage; and 2 billion cubic feet of liquified natural gas storage. The news release notes the company is not limited to pursuing only those projects. 
Lisa Barton, the company’s president and CEO, said Alliant is making “smart, forward-looking investments to deliver safe, reliable and cost-effective energy.”
“This federally backed financing helps lower the cost of building the generation and critical energy infrastructure our customers depend on, while strengthening the grid and supporting long-term savings,” Barton said in a news release. “We are focused on meeting growth responsibly, maintaining affordability and creating lasting value for customers and communities across Iowa and Wisconsin.”
Alliant’s earnings reports show the company anticipates 60% load growth by 2031, and that it has contracted at least 3.4 gigawatts of demand from data centers. 
Alliant has planned several new natural gas generating plants in Iowa, including the Bobcat Energy Center in Marshalltown which a spokesperson for Alliant said is one of the projects the company may pursue, but is not limited to, with the DOE loan. 
On its website pages for the Bobcat, Riverhawk and Morgan Valley Energy Centers, Alliant specifies that the additional generation is not being built to serve data centers. A clean energy group and a group fighting the Morgan Valley plant, however, allege the utility is using data centers – and their anticipated energy load demands – as an excuse to build the plants. 
The Morgan Valley plant is slated for Linn County, where data centers from Google and QTS are in the works and where Alliant has existing investments. Linn County supervisors voted recently to deny a rezoning request from Alliant to build the natural gas plant, though the decision could be overruled by the Iowa Utilities Commission. 
The Department of Energy has also agreed to loan up to $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to help restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, a nuclear energy plant in Linn County. Google has contracted with NextEra to purchase more than 90% of the energy generated at the nuclear plant.
A spokesperson with Alliant said the company may also use the loan to support battery energy storage system, or BESS, projects including one in the works in Lansing and two BESS projects underway in Wisconsin. The lithium-ion battery storage facilities charge when energy is plentiful and can help supplement energy when demand is high. 
The spokesperson also noted the liquefied natural gas storage facility being built in Rock County, Wisconsin, as a potential project supported by the loan.
DOE said the loan to Alliant would help advance President Donald Trump’s directive to “safeguard the reliability and security of the United States’ electric grid.” 
The executive order notes that the nation is experiencing an “unprecedented” surge in electricity demands that is driven by “artificial intelligence data centers and an increase in domestic manufacturing.”
Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said the loans through the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing are “delivering” on the president’s promise to lower energy costs and “unleash the full potential of American energy.”
“These investments will drive down energy costs for families and businesses in Iowa and Wisconsin, strengthen our nation’s electric grid, and fuel American prosperity for decades to come,” Wright said in the news release.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico immigrant advocates, police to propose streamlined visa process for undocumented victims
text:
Santa Fe Dreamers Project Legal Director Deshawnda Chaparro, left, New Mexico Immigrant Law Center Associate Managing Attorney Valeria Garcia Tavarez, middle, and Albuquerque Police Department Commander Paul Haugh, right, speak before the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Oct. 28, 2026, about their legislative proposal to streamline the process under which undocumented crime victims can obtain visas. (Photo courtesy of Felipe Vásquez and New Mexico Immigrant Law Center)New Mexico immigrant advocates and law enforcement leaders on Wednesday told state lawmakers they plan to reintroduce a bill in the upcoming legislative session in January that would streamline the process for undocumented crime victims to obtain visas.
Under current federal guidelines, undocumented immigrants who survive certain violent crimes and then cooperate with a police department’s investigation or a district attorney’s prosecution are eligible for a U Visa, which provides lawful status for four years. Typically, an official within the police department or prosecutor’s office handling the crime has to certify the victim’s eligibility for the visa.
However, advocates and law enforcement leaders told state lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee that New Mexico lacks uniform standards for how police and prosecutors should certify U Visa eligibility. In some cases, the victim’s attorneys don’t even know who the certifying official is within a police department.
Local DA says immigrant crime victims are going silent amid deportation fears, letting abusers free

That jeopardizes a victim’s ability to stay in the country, and can also jeopardize a police department’s ability to investigate the crime and refer charges to a prosecutor, Albuquerque Police Department Commander Paul Haugh said.
“Victims need to know that they can come forward,” he said, adding that their cooperation is “fundamental to us as an agency being able to prosecute crimes.”
Haugh spoke alongside New Mexico Immigrant Law Center Associate Managing Attorney Valeria Garcia Tavarez and Santa Fe Dreamers Project Legal Director Deshawnda Chaparro. The three said they plan to introduce a bill in next year’s legislative session that would require law enforcement agencies to make decisions on whether to certify an undocumented victim’s U Visa eligibility within a specific timeframe, which would be expedited if the victim was simultaneously undergoing deportation proceedings.
They said they’re also considering how to add penalties for law enforcement agencies that don’t comply with the proposed requirements.
“Rarely are we having to argue with law enforcement agencies on the actual merits,” Garcia Tavarez said. “What we are seeing more uniformly — and the major reason why we’re hoping to enact this piece of legislation — is the vast majority of time, there’s just no response.”
Garcia Tavarez added that this proposal would mark the fourth time a similar bill has come before the Legislature.
Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez (D-Albuquerque), who has sponsored previous iterations of the proposal, said she’ll support it in the 2027 legislative session because she’s heard of too many undocumented victims receiving “uneven treatment between jurisdictions.”
Senate Majority Whip Cindy Nava (D-Bernalillo) similarly supported the bill, saying that her family has undergone the burdensome process of obtaining a U Visa.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
She said that Santa Fe police helped her sister, a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient, certify her eligibility as she sought a U Visa after being attacked outside Santa Fe’s Target store. Enshrining stronger guidelines and timeline requirements in state law would help to streamline the process, she said.
“This is something nobody actually wants to do,” she said. “It is not an easy process in any way, shape or form.”
Garcia Tavarez, the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center attorney, told Source NM after the committee hearing that she and other advocates are still examining whether an undocumented victim could expose themselves to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents by cooperating with a local police department’s investigation. She said recent immigration arrests in New Mexico are partly why the bill will include an expedited U Visa certification timeline for victims who are in deportation proceedings.
“If one victim doesn’t feel safe, none of us do,” she said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Kearney senator preparing legislation to bring state into regulations for Head Start programs
text:
State Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney. April 8, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — State Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney said he is hoping to bring legislation next year that would officially bring Nebraska’s Head Start programs into state statute amid growing uncertainty about long-term federal support.
Clouse introduced Legislative Resolution 472 earlier this year to examine the state’s existing programs and lay the groundwork for future legislation. The resolution was discussed at a public hearing Wednesday before the Nebraska Legislature’s Education Committee.
Head Start is a federal program for children in low-income families that began in 1965. It currently serves about 5,500 Nebraska children across 37 programs statewide, according to Clouse and other testifiers.
The program serves expectant mothers and children through age 5.
Multiple testifiers spoke to the range of benefits offered by the program, including family support, developmental screenings and access to medical and dental services.
Currently, Head Start is not referenced in Nebraska statutes, Clouse said. The program is funded 80% by the federal government, with local governments contributing the remaining 20%.
Jill Bomberger, Head Start director for Lancaster and Saunders counties, said local partnerships are a critical component of the program, as individual programs adjust their services based on consultations with parent leaders on present needs.
However, Bomberger said, there would be some benefit to defining the program in state law as concerns grow about the continuation of federal aid. In recent years, the Trump administration has expressed interest in eliminating all federal funding for the program, but those proposals have not been approved by Congress. Multiple testifiers said establishing the program in statute would ease some concerns and provide stability for participating families and staff.
“This is to try and provide some of that stability, get it defined,” said Mitchell Clark, policy adviser for First Five Nebraska. “And then going forward in future years, if the state Legislature would consider anything else to support Head Start, it’ll make it a little easier, because state statute recognizes it and knows what it is.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Clouse said his office first learned about the issues with Head Start after concerns were raised about fingerprinting requirements for new hires.
Under federal law, new Head Start employees are required to complete a fingerprint-based background check. In Nebraska, that is done through the state Department of Health and Human Services, but Bomberger said some programs don’t have the necessary childcare licensing to access that resource. Clark said this leaves those programs in “limbo” when bringing in new staff, as they lack the authority to request a fingerprint check.
He said he will likely introduce a bill to address these concerns, but is considering other areas that may need addressing.
Bomberger said there are other opportunities for the state to support Head Start by helping the program retain its educators. She said working for Head Start alone is not enough to maintain a teaching certificate in Nebraska, which forces certified teachers to choose among taking graduate classes, leaving their job for a position in a school system or giving up their certificate.
“Allowing that teaching practice within Head Start to fulfill those requirements would help keep those key professionals in our programs,” Bomberger said.

name: VTDigger
title: FBI investigates former Burlington school administrator in alleged $1.8 million fraud
text:
The Burlington School District central office building as seen on Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Charlotte Oliver/VTDigger

BURLINGTON — Federal investigators are probing whether former Burlington School District administrator Stephanie Phillips defrauded the district in a scheme involving at least $1.8 million over 13 years.  
Phillips worked for the district starting in 1988 until she retired in May. She most recently served as the district’s director of teaching and learning. The FBI is looking into whether Phillips created a fake company called the Leading and Learning Consultants of VT to fraudulently take money from the school district, court documents stated. 
“I think it is fair to say that they were funds earmarked for professional learning,” said Russ Elek, a district spokesperson, in an email to VTDigger. 
Phillips has not been charged with a crime and did not immediately respond to requests for comment Wednesday. 
Superintendent Tom Flanagan emailed parents and community members Tuesday night responding to news of the investigation. 
“If these allegations are proven true, our district and community are victims, and we will seek to recover all funds and bring them back to our students,” Flanagan wrote, referring to the situation as “possible embezzlement.”  
“Shortly after Ms. Phillips left the District this spring, we identified concerning financial discrepancies. We reported them immediately and have been fully cooperating with both local and federal investigating agencies,” Flanagan added in his email. 
Federal agents executed a search warrant of Phillips’s house in Colchester on Oct. 16, regarding records and information about her company, according to court documents. The search was conducted “in connection with an ongoing federal investigation,” according to Sarah Ruane, a spokesperson for the FBI in Albany. Ruane declined to provide additional information. 
Agents had probable cause to believe Phillips “defrauded BSD by creating a false company — Leading and Learning Consultants of VT, LLC — and using that company in at least two fraudulent ways,” wrote Special Agent Eric Boyce in an affidavit. 
Phillips submitted invoices from her consulting company for her regular work at the school district, “allowing her to be paid twice for the same work,” Boyce wrote. She also generated invoices for work that was never done, according to Boyce. 
Investigators believe the company may be fake because agents have no evidence the company did any work with other school districts, although Phillips claimed the company had other clients, court records stated. 
Business filings with Vermont’s secretary of state’s office list Don Collins, a former state senator who chaired the Senate Education Committee, as the company’s manager. Reached on Wednesday, Collins, who is Phillips’s father, initially said he had no recollection of the company. He declined to comment further on the investigation. 
Since March 2013, agents believe Phillips fraudulently obtained at least $1,769,000 from the school district, according to court records.
Agents are investigating whether Phillips committed wire fraud, mail fraud and theft from school programs that receive federal funding, according to federal court documents. 
Phillips held positions of authority during her time at the district, working as an acting superintendent in 2014 and as an assistant principal at one point, according to Elek. 
Federal agents started their probe after the current superintendent filed a complaint with the Burlington Police Department in June, saying Phillips was paid by the district for work that was never completed, court documents show. 
Since discovering the information, Flanagan wrote in the community email, the district has strengthened its invoicing procedures and put tighter limits on individual spending. 
“We will continue to strengthen our financial controls with an outside expert who will review our system and provide us with additional steps we can take to ensure we are protected moving forward,” he said.  
News of the investigation was first reported by Vermont News First.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  FBI investigates former Burlington school administrator in alleged $1.8 million fraud.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hartford coalition will help residents navigate Medicaid changes
text:
A new citywide task force will help Hartford residents navigate upcoming changes to the Medicaid program, Mayor Arunan Arulampalam announced Wednesday.
“The message to Hartford residents is really simple: if you rely on HUSKY D for your healthcare coverage, you may be losing it,” Arulampalam said in a press conference at Hartford City Hall. “We want to make sure you know about resources that are there if you do lose your coverage, because of frankly stupid and cruel cuts from the federal government.”
HUSKY D is the part of Connecticut’s Medicaid program that provides coverage to low-income adults who don’t have dependents. Starting Jan. 1, enrollees will have to prove they are complying with new work and community engagement requirements to maintain their coverage. The requirements state that residents must prove they work at least 80 hours or earn a minimum of $580 per month. Or, residents have to show they do at least 80 hours of community service a month or participate in a qualified training program. There are various exemptions, though, like being declared “medically frail.”
State leaders have been scrambling to protect Connecticut residents’ Medicaid coverage. The Hartford HUSKY D Response Coalition is a collaboration between several institutions that operate citywide, including city government agencies, local health centers, employment access groups and religious institutions. Task force members said they will work together to help residents learn more about the Medicaid changes, navigate how to maintain their coverage and providing information about job training and community engagement opportunities.
“The sooner people seek information and assistance, the more prepared they will be when the changes actually take place,” Ebony Jackson-Shaheed, director of the city’s health and human services department, said.
In Hartford, around 13,000 residents will be affected by the changes, according to city officials.
Arulampalam did not say how much money is going into the task force. “I think we’re still trying to figure that out, and it’s going to take some time,” he said.
Officials emphasized that there are actions Hartford residents can take now to be prepared before the changes to HUSKY D are implemented.
These include:

Contacting the Connecticut Department of Social Services to find official information about eligibility, benefits and coverage options.
Making sure the information available to the state Department of Social Services and any Access Health CT account information is up-to-date.

DSS has created a website to help residents learn more about the HUSKY D changes. Residents can also fill out an online questionnaire to find out if their eligibility will be impacted.
Task force member Angela Harris, chair of Phillips Health Ministry and Phillips Metropolitan CME Church, said that residents should make sure their phone number, email address and mailing address are updated and accurate. DSS will be reaching out to HUSKY D enrollees with information about the program changes.
“So if you see an alert on your phone, it’s DSS, not spam,” Harris said.
In Hartford, there are also several federally qualified health centers that offer services to residents regardless of insurance status. One of those is Wheeler Health on Woodland Street.
“Our charge is to serve all individuals that reside within our targeted community, and that’s what we do, and that’s what we will continue to do,” Sabrina Trocchi, president and CEO of Wheeler Health, said. “We do not, as health centers, are not asked to collect any information regarding documentation status, and that is not something that we will begin at this point.”
The coalition is still in its beginning stages. More information will be provided in the coming months on how Hartford residents can reach out to the task force.
The local United Way will serve as a “project management lead” for the coalition.
“As the backbone organization for the North Hartford Triple Aim Collaborative, United Way, together with collaborative members, is well positioned to connect residents to employment, job training, and volunteer opportunities to help them meet new requirements and maintain health coverage,” said Eric Harrison, president and CEO of United Way of Central and Northeastern Connecticut.

name: Nevada Current
title: Ponder ‘a prolific sexual predator’ says prosecutor as judge lowers bail
text:
Jon Ponder, Hope for Prisoners founder, at an earlier court hearing in early October. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)Jon Ponder, the felon embraced by President Donald Trump, Gov. Joe Lombardo, and most of Southern Nevada’s elected officials, used his powerful connections to prey on female inmates, Clark County Deputy District Attorney Michelle Fleck alleged Wednesday during a hearing to lower Ponder’s $1 million bail. 
“The stark reality is that Jon Ponder is a prolific sexual predator,” Fleck said, noting he used his position at Hope for Prisoners, a respected prison reentry program, to gain trust of public officials and access to women. 
“He cultivated relationships with some of the most powerful people in this community and in this state while smoking methamphetamine behind closed doors,” Fleck said, adding that police found meth and paraphernalia while searching Ponder’s home.  
“That is a person who is deeply, deeply entrenched in a life of crime. There was no setting and there was no relationship that was too sacred for Mr. Ponder to exploit.” 
The Current reported in August that the Hope for Prisoners board of directors was advised in 2020 to terminate Ponder, following an investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct raised by participants and employees. 
Following Trump’s pardon of Ponder, a three-time bank robber, at the Republican National Convention in 2020 and a tide of good will from national supporters, the board, which included then-Undersheriff Kevin McMahill and District Attorney Steve Wolfson, did not terminate Ponder. 
Gov. Joe Lombardo, who was sheriff at the time and formed a partnership with Ponder and HFP, will not say whether Metro conducted its own investigation into the allegations. 
Lombardo also refused to comment in 2024, when a resignation letter from board member Kristina Wildeveld about the allegations against Ponder surfaced in a lawsuit against him and the organization. 
The Dept. of Corrections denied the Current’s request for correspondence between NDOC and Lombardo’s office, citing the potential that it may be used as evidence. Lombardo’s office will not comment. 
Wolfson appeared in campaign ads with Ponder and launched a diversion program that allowed non-violent felons to avoid prison by completing Ponder’s program. 
“Ponder used his authority and his position with all of these women who were dependent on his program, dependent on him in order to get out of the system,” Fleck said. 
The charges in the indictment involve seven victims and span 11 years, from 2015 to 2026. 
“There is a particular dangerousness to a person who can sustain that level of deception for so long with so many different people,” Fleck said.  “He used access, he used his credibility, and he used his power to obtain submission.”
Fleck asked Judge Ron Israel to leave Pardon’s $1 million bail in place or increase it. 
“He has demonstrated that his ability to appear trustworthy while repeatedly betraying the people who trusted him the most is something he is very comfortable and confident with,” she said.
Ponder, according to Fleck, “engaged in an insidious pattern of sexual harassment with female inmates. He had unfettered access to them. He was able to go into Jean in an unprecedented manner. He was able to access women through Casa Grande,” Fleck said, referring to the minimum custody camp for women offenders and a halfway house in Las Vegas operated by the Nevada Department of Corrections.
Ponder’s alleged victims are all mothers, Fleck told Israel, adding that Ponder “used their children and families to hang over their heads in order to get them to submit sexually.” 
His approach to the women was consistent, Fleck said. “The sexual requests that he had for them were the same. The fantasies that he asked them to act out were the same. And the ones that ultimately engaged in sexual relationships with him, it was similar and same acts. This court has got to evaluate the danger that he is to the community.”
The Current was first to report in April that Ponder was under investigation. His attorney, Robert Draskovich, said the investigation began in March and that Ponder expected to be arrested, and hired a defense attorney early on. 
“He is going to fight this case,” Draskovich said Wednesday, noting the presence of Ponder’s supporters in the court. 
Fleck countered that police found a ‘go bag’ in Ponder’s home when he was arrested. 
Ponder, she said, did not rehabilitate himself after serving time in prison. 
“Instead he reinvented himself, and he became somebody that this community believed that they could trust. Somebody who was given privilege and access, and who became a beacon of hope for other prisoners,” she said. “Behind that public identity, Your Honor, there was somebody and is somebody today that is much more cunning and much more calculated and much more dangerous.”
Ponder “used ‘church’ services at Jean Conservation Camp as an opportunity to prey on women,” Fleck alleged. “During baptisms he would prey on women for sexual satisfaction.” 
Grand jury testimony indicates Ponder used HFP Christmas parties as a means of reuniting women with their children, only to extort sexual favors. 
“Certainly, the charges are some of the most serious I’ve seen,” Israel said of the 26-count indictment that includes four counts of sexual assault, which each carry a life term. 
Draskovich argued Ponder’s bail should be lowered because he initially faced 19 counts, including one count of sexual assault that carries a life sentence, and was released on $200,000 bail.
Ponder told Israel he had not been treated recently for addiction or mental health issues and was not under the influence of any drugs or medication, and that no one had ever suggested he be treated for a mental health or emotional condition. 
In June, his wife filed for divorce, claiming he put his hands on her neck. She later filed to dismiss the divorce complaint. 
Justice of the Peace Suzan Baucum released Ponder to house arrest on $200,000 bail in August to the home he shares with his wife. He was arrested and detained following his indictment on Sept. 30 and has remained incarcerated since on $1 million bail set by Judge Carli Kierney. 
Israel decreased Ponder’s bail to $400,000 cash only, meaning he cannot post a percentage and obtain a bail bond. He remained in custody as of Wednesday afternoon. 
Ponder entered a plea of not guilty, relinquished his right to a speedy trial and a status check is scheduled in mid-November, at which time a date for trial is expected to be scheduled.

name: National
title: Caring for aging parents is getting more expensive
text:
Tennessee resident George Raines works on mobility issues with physical therapist Brad Ellis, standing, in Chattanooga, Tenn., in March 2024. A new study details soaring costs for people who care for their older parents and other family members. (Photo by Anna Claire Vollers/Stateline)Costs are soaring for people who care for their older parents and other family members, according to a new study.
Out-of-pocket expenses are nearly 60% higher than they were just five years ago for family caregivers, who now spend an average of $11,508 a year on caregiving, according to a report released this week by AARP, a nonprofit that advocates for people aged 50 and older.
“Whether they’re paying for groceries, housing or medical care, family caregivers are marking a significant financial commitment that can affect their own economic security,” said Debra Whitman, AARP executive vice president and chief public policy officer, in a statement.
Across the U.S., 63 million people care for family members, preparing meals, managing medications, attending medical appointments and performing other daily tasks for their loved ones. The report found a 50% increase in the number of adults providing such care over the past decade.
Family caregivers provide about $1 trillion in mostly unpaid labor each year, the AARP reports.
They also spend thousands out of their own pockets: That $11,508 in annual caregiving spending eats up 31% of the average household income.
And the burden is much heavier on low-income families. Caregivers with annual household incomes under $40,000 spend an average of 76% of their household income on caregiving, according to the report. At the other end of the economic spectrum, those with incomes above $85,000 a year spend between 9% and 19% on caregiving.
Most of those caregiving dollars go toward housing and medical care, the report found. More than a third of the money spent on medical care goes toward insurance premiums, copays and direct payments to providers.
Those caring for someone living with Alzheimer’s disease or another form of dementia spend more — an average of $15,846 annually.
Nearly two-thirds of working caregivers reported experiencing at least one work-related disruption because of caregiving, such as having to alter work hours or take time off for caregiving responsibilities.
Caregiving costs also vary depending on where a person lives. Caregivers who live in states such as New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania spend the most, an average of $15,845 per year. That’s nearly twice what those who live in midwestern states such as Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota and Missouri, who spend $7,955.
The costs also vary by race and ethnicity. Asian American and Pacific Islander caregivers report the highest average spending at $16,716 (31% of average household income). Black caregivers spend an average of $13,565 annually – 52% of their household income, the highest percentage of any group.  Hispanic and Latino caregivers spend an average of $10,684 per year (29%), and white caregivers reported the lowest average spending, at $9,806 per year (24%).
The report’s authors recommend policy changes including tax credits, grants, paid leave for working caregivers, expanded home care options and help navigating the health care system.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Uthmeier: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids
text:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier speaking at the Cuban Club in Ybor City on April 17, 2026. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)An artificial intelligence company allows users to generate sexually explicit pictures and videos of minors, or “nudify” them, Attorney General James Uthmeier alleged in a legal complaint Wednesday.
Filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County, Uthmeier’s suit alleges A2E, an artificial intelligence image platform, committed “unconscionable,” “deceptive,” and “unfair” practices under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
“If Defendant’s business practices are not ‘deceptive,’ ‘unfair,’ or–above all–despicably and utterly ‘unconscionable’ under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, what is? They must be stopped,” Uthmeier wrote.
The defendant is Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm that owns A2E. The first allegation in the 26-page suit is that Rengstorff’s product lets “predators” “nudify non-consenting Floridians,” including children, and allows users to alter images of adults to feature child-like appearances.
“Just because you create the vehicle, it doesn’t give you exemption from liability. So while users might be providing images, at the end of the day, this AI software, this is the manufacturing hub that is actually churning out the child porn content. So we want to make them pay. We want to shut them down,” Uthmeier said during a news conference announcing the suit in Orlando. 
Uthmeier said his office is investigating possible criminal offenses, too. 
In 2025, Florida lawmakers approved a measure that requires social media companies to delete deepfakes, or AI-generated sexual depictions of people created without their consent.
DeSantis signs Brooke’s Law targeting deepfakes

That law is in play, Uthmeier says.
The suit brings a few specific examples, including a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than “100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year stepson, some with images of the two children performing oral and other sexual acts with him.”
A2E did not respond to a Phoenix request for comment. 
The attorney general complains the software warns users it is “strictly prohibited” to apply it to nonconsensual sexual uses but “Defendant attempts to shift all responsibility for compliance to users.”
Also during the news conference Wednesday, Uthmeier announced that the Office of Statewide Prosecution charged a 26-year-old from Kissimmee with 100 felony counts. Uthmeier said Jerry Jesus Reyes was investigated after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children reported a tip. 
Of those counts, one alleged transmission of child pornography and 86 allegations of unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual performance by a child. Thirteen counts alleged unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual activity with animals.
“Disgusting, disturbing, depraved — it’s inhumane,” Uthmeier said. 
Uthmeier faces his first election in less than a week. He was appointed to the his post year last year by Gov. Ron DeSantis.
Although Uthmeier has been showing up for Republican political events running up to the election, his public appearances mostly have involve official news conferences. Since his August primary election, he has hosted 26 news conferences.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Gulfport moves forward with $54M road project amid environmental concerns
authors: McKenna Klamm, RHCJC and Justin Glowacki, RHCJC
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
GULFPORT — Gulfport plans to break ground this month on a $54 million road project that would give drivers another way across Interstate 10. City officials say it would improve traffic flow and emergency access, while environmental advocates raise concerns about wetlands and flooding. 
The Interconnecting Gulfport project would build an overpass west of U.S. Highway 49, connecting the Airport Road area south of I-10 with Daniel Boulevard to the north. The route would also provide another entrance and exit for Gulfport Premium Outlets. 
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality approved two state-level authorizations in May. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also lists a federal permit issued with special conditions June 12. 
The city awarded Cotton Creek Transport Inc. a construction contract in September, with completion required by May 2029. 
What will change for drivers 
Plans include two roundabouts, connecting roads, drainage improvements, lighting, sidewalks and access for bicyclists and pedestrians.
City officials say the road would improve emergency response and provide another evacuation route during hurricanes. 
Engineers considered several routes before selecting the current alignment. According to a 2022 environmental assessment, an earlier option was eliminated because of conflicts with existing infrastructure, right-of-way limitations and environmental restrictions. 
Some residents hope the project will ease congestion around Highway 49 and I-10. 
“It’s honestly a good idea. It’d probably clear up a lot of the congestion in that area,” said Quintana, who has lived in the Gulfport-Biloxi area for 14 years. 
Vehicles travel through an intersection along U.S. Highway 49 in Gulfport. The city’s $54 millionInterconnecting Gulfport project aims to reduce traffic congestion and improve emergencyaccess by providing another route across Interstate 10.  Credit: RHCJC News
Gulfport resident J.E. Lawrence said afternoon traffic can make travel difficult.
“It’d be beneficial for all of our residents if we could do this from the 49 to I-10 aspect. Putting an (overpass) in could alleviate a lot of the traffic problems that we see, especially from Airport Road to, say, around the Crossroads Mall area. It’s very congested there during the day, especially at 5 o’clock when everybody’s getting off work,” Lawrence said. 
What the traffic study shows 
A traffic analysis by engineering firm Neel-Schaffer compared projected conditions in 2045 with and without the new road. 
The study projected improvements in some areas but found that certain intersections could still experience significant delays. 
At Highway 49 and Airport Road, traffic conditions were projected to worsen by 2045 whether or not the project is built. 
It has not been confirmed whether the projections were updated following subsequent design changes.
Wetlands and flooding concerns 
The project’s potential effects on wetlands and nearby neighborhoods have drawn opposition from the Education, Economics, Environmental, Climate and Health Organization, known as EEECHO. 
Katherine Egland, the organization’s co-founder and deputy executive director, said the group favors another route and has concerns about flooding. 
“I’m all about economic advancement, but this does not have to be at the expense of the environment,” Egland said. 
Egland said EEECHO has also sought an explanation from city leaders about their choice of route. 
“We’ve asked the former mayor and the current mayor for a meeting to help better understand why they would select this road over much better alternatives, and they have declined to meet with us to explain why,” Egland said. 
A sign directs drivers to Gulfport Premium Outlets, which would gain an additional entrance and exit through the proposed Interconnecting Gulfport road project.  Credit: RHCJC News
The project’s 2022 environmental assessment documents public concerns about flooding and effects on nearby communities, including Forest Heights. 
The Federal Highway Administration issued a finding of no significant impact for the selected route in 2022, determining that a more extensive environmental impact statement was not required. 
In May, the city said it had enlarged a planned detention pond to manage heavy rainfall, increasing the estimated wetlands impact from 66 acres to 98.3 acres. 
City officials said engineering analyses projected improved drainage and reduced flooding risks from rainfall runoff. The detention system is not intended to protect against coastal storm surge. 
The city provided information about the construction contract and planned groundbreaking but has not responded to follow-up questions, including whether drainage projections were updated following the design changes.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Minogue highlights sheriffs’ concerns with PROTECT Act
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
text:
THE PROTECT ACT has made its way even further into the gubernatorial race, as 12 sheriffs have asked Gov. Maura Healey to consider addressing what they’re calling “an unintended public safety consequence” of a law intended to guard against overzealous immigration law enforcement by ICE.
On the State House steps, GOP gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue on Tuesday accused Healey of “ignoring” the sheriffs’ request. Healey later called US Immigrations and Customs Enforcement “a rogue agency,” aligned Minogue with President Donald Trump and ICE, and said she’d “continue to talk with the sheriffs” about the concerns.
In an Oct. 22 letter to Healey, a bipartisan group of sheriffs wrote that the law passed in August with the intent to protect immigrants is hindering their ability to communicate with federal law enforcement when pretrial detainees subject to an immigration detainer and facing “violent, dangerous or drug-related charges” are released.
“I’m not here to try and make this into something political because I believe it is very dangerous when you mix politics with public safety,” Plymouth County Sheriff Joseph McDonald, one of two Republicans who signed the letter, told reporters at Minogue’s press conference. 
“The big problem that I am here to talk about with the PROTECT Act is the fact that it precludes communication between local law enforcement, here in particular the sheriffs and our employees, and our federal law enforcement partners, specifically those at ICE,” McDonald said. “It takes away perhaps what is the strongest and best tool that we have to fight crime and keep the public safe, and that is communication.”
Hours after Minogue spoke to the press, the Healey campaign announced that the 12 Democratic sheriffs endorsed Healey. They wrote in a release that “While the PROTECT Act presents some challenges for our Sheriffs’ offices, we are confident that through continued collaboration with Governor Healey and Lt. Governor Driscoll, we can work together to refine the legislation, address our concerns, and find practical solutions that protect the rights and dignity of individuals while ensuring the safety and security of our correctional facilities, staff, and the communities we serve.”
The sheriffs wrote in their October 22 letter that there are pretrial detainees in their custody who are subject to immigration detainers, are charged with qualifying violent or dangerous offenses, and have bail set below $1,000. 
“These individuals may be released without advance notification to relevant federal law-enforcement partners, potentially, posing a threat to our communities,” they wrote. “If federal authorities do not receive notice while an individual remains in custody, they may instead seek to locate that person in the community. This can create avoidable risks for the public, law-enforcement personnel, families, and others who may be present during those encounters.”
McDonald was the only sheriff with Minogue Tuesday, but the letter that Minogue held in the air at his press conference was also signed by Sheriffs Thomas Bowler of Berkshire County, Paul Heroux of Bristol County, Robert Ogden of Dukes County, Kevin Coppinger of Essex County, Lori Streeter of Franklin County, Nicholas Cocchi of Hampden County, Patrick Cahillane of Hampshire County, James Perelman of Nantucket County, Patrick McDermott of Norfolk County, Steve Tompkins of Suffolk County, and Lew Evangelidis of Worcester County. 
The sheriffs requested that the administration “review this issue and consider a legislative, regulatory, or administrative solution that permits limited, public safety-based notification when a pretrial detainee is subject to a detainer and is charged with a qualifying violent and dangerous offense.” 
The law has been a point of contention between Healey and Minogue, the latter of whom has said he thinks state and local authorities should coordinate with federal officials to target violent criminals and drug dealers. Healey has defended her administration’s tactics meant to protect immigrants.
Of the clause in the PROTECT Act, Minogue said it’s “something that does not keep our people safe. It’s the lowest element of party politics, and it shows that the one-party system has lost common sense, doesn’t care about the safety of our people, and is doing whatever they can to cause fear and chaos.”
Minogue called on Healey and lawmakers to “listen to our sheriffs, work with them immediately on these concerns before creating potential gaps in public safety.”
McDonald drew a line between his comments and Minogue’s.
“I want to be very clear. I think the Legislature had the best of intentions when they did this. I’m not going to say that there was corruption. That was Michael’s take on his other stuff,” McDonald said, referring to Minogue’s allegations about the State Police union’s endorsement of Healey. 
“With reference to this, I think the Legislature engaged in a very thoughtful process, a very deliberative process,” McDonald continued. “For some reason, the legislation in its final form didn’t necessarily reflect all of what I think was contained within that deliberative process. So what the problem was, was this limitation on communications.”
Healey signed the PROTECT Act on August 5 after months of private negotiations amongst lawmakers and escalating concern about violent federal enforcement in Massachusetts and across the country. 
“The most important thing we can do as law enforcement is communicate with each other. And when we can’t do that, that’s when you end up with situations where ICE agents are going into the communities, not notifying us,” McDonald said. “We get a call that someone’s under attack or perhaps being kidnapped. We end up with a situation where our officers respond, the locals, and are unable to know until they get there that someone else with a gun is there as well.”
“I think we have inadvertently further victimized those otherwise law-abiding immigrants who come to this country that may not have legal status, but we have further terrorized them,” McDonald said. 
He suggested that if state and local law enforcement can’t notify ICE about someone with an immigration detainer and violent charges once they exit their facilities, “that individual who could be subject to an orderly transfer of custody without going into the community is now going to be released into the community to disappear, to God knows where, to force those ICE officers to go out into the community. And we’ve seen it so many times, to face protesters, and inadvertently innocent people can oftentimes get hurt. What we’ve done here is not simply enabled that scenario to occur, we have essentially required that scenario to occur.”
Asked at a scrum in Weymouth Tuesday if the sheriffs’ letter lends credibility to the idea that the PROTECT Act needs to be looked at, Healey referred to her time as attorney general and pitted her immigration policies against Minogue’s.
“The bottom line is I’m going to do everything I can to keep people safe here, and I’m going to continue to do everything I can to work with public safety officials, with law enforcement, as I’ve done throughout my career, and my administration will continue to do that,” Healey told reporters. 
“Right now, we wouldn’t need the PROTECT Act if ICE wasn’t doing what it’s doing throughout communities in Massachusetts and in states around this country, and it’s part of a failed agenda by Donald Trump,” she said. “My opponent will repeal the PROTECT Act and wants to double down on ICE’s involvement in Massachusetts. That doesn’t make us safe.”
Asked whether Minogue would repeal the PROTECT Act if elected, his campaign spokeswoman Elizabeth Hopkins said, “Mike’s position is that because the PROTECT Act contains a provision preventing sheriffs from cooperating with other agencies, it creates serious public safety issues. Mike has made clear that, as governor, he would listen to law enforcement, public safety experts, and sheriffs, and work to address those grave concerns.”
Sheriffs are also dealing with remaining fiscal 2026 budget deficiencies and scrutiny of their spending. The House on Oct. 21 passed a $2.35 billion supplemental budget that did not address sheriffs’ budget gaps, as lawmakers historically have in closeout bills. 
Asked how he’s feeling about that and if it’s related to “tension” between law enforcement and the State House, McDonald said, “I hope it isn’t related to any of this tension. I think a cynical person would feel that way, and I try not to be a cynical person.” 
“I have every confidence that the Legislature and the governor value what it is that the sheriffs do. And I think we’ll come out of this okay, because we have to. You know, the sheriffs play a vital role, county corrections plays a vital role,” McDonald said. “I think this latest bump in the road is just that — it’s a bump in the road, and we’ll get through it. But I think you’re perceptive to ask that question.”
House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz told the News Service last week that “we are still having dialogue with the sheriffs.” He pointed to a House proposal that would change how sheriffs’ departments are funded and said the House has asked for more information related to past deficiencies. 
“We are still working through that process with them, but have not got the entirety of the needed answers on that, and so we’re still working through that. And until we work through that, I think we’ve made it clear that we weren’t gonna be doing any further deficiencies budgeting going forward,” Michlewitz said. 
[Colin A. Young and Sam Drysdale contributed reporting.]

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ municipal judge admonished for wearing Palestinian attire to training
text:
An East Orange municipal judge who wore a keffiyeh and a baseball cap embroidered with the Palestinian flag admitted to "insensitivity." (Photo by Dana DiFilippo|New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s top judge has publicly admonished an East Orange municipal judge for wearing a traditional Palestinian scarf and a baseball cap embroidered with the Palestinian flag to a judicial training conference.
Judge Steven Brister’s hat and black-and-white checkered scarf, known as a keffiyeh, violated a state judicial conduct rule that requires judges to uphold the independence, integrity, and impartiality of the court, New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Stuart Rabner said in an order filed Wednesday.
Rabner dismissed two other charges the court’s Advisory Committee on Judicial Conduct had filed against Brister in March, including that he violated rules barring political speech and requiring judges to observe high standards of conduct and avoid the appearance of impropriety. The court’s six other justices unanimously joined Rabner’s order.
Brister originally had declined to remove the cap when asked and said he wore the scarf for religious reasons and the hat because it matched his outfit and was raining.
But in an affidavit he filed earlier this month, Brister acknowledged his garb “may have displayed an insensitivity to some attendees” of the conference, which was held in June 2025 at a Bergen County hotel and drew more than 400 judges and court staff. He requested public admonishment as his punishment.
“Given my position as a Municipal Judge, and given the nature of the event, it was of paramount importance that the integrity and independence of the judiciary be upheld. My failure to recognize the potential impact of my attire fell short of the high standards and expectations of my office,” Brister wrote. “Regardless of intent, better choices could have and should have been made, particularly in the face of communicated offense by some attendees of the conference.”
The public admonishment comes five years after Brister was suspended for 30 days for making misogynistic comments to a man facing domestic violence charges.
In that case, he told investigators his remarks were “well-meaning but undeniably misguided” and were rooted in his religious beliefs in the biblical story that Eve was created from Adam’s rib.
