name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT leaders tout efforts to train workforce in AI
text:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont is trumpeting the state’s efforts to equip its workforce with AI skills and expertise, even as some economists and labor leaders raise broad concerns about its potential to upend the nature of employment.
At a press conference in East Hartford Wednesday, the governor joined university leaders, state officials and members of the business community to lay out state workforce development programs aimed at easing the AI transition and supporting workers. 
“We’re putting our employers first and helping pull students through that process in order to build the skills, knowledge and abilities that they need to be successful,” said Kelli-Marie Vallieres, the state’s chief workforce officer.
Much of the event focused on highlighting the importance of Connecticut’s “Tech Talent Accelerator,” a four-year-old workforce development program that facilitates partnerships between higher education institutions and businesses.
In February, the state announced that it was launching the Tech Talent Accelerator 3.0, a more artificial intelligence-oriented version of the program. The Office of Workforce Strategy is supporting several AI pilot programs, including an AI accounting and entrepreneurship course at Connecticut College, an AI for Cybersecurity program at the University of New Haven, and an online course on AI in healthcare business innovation at Quinnipiac University.  
The goal, Vallieres and others said, is to work collaboratively with businesses in the state to connect students and companies well before graduation day. 
Nicholas Schilling, a software engineer at IT and business consulting firm CGI, shared his experience of how that sort of relationship helped him. 
Schilling entered the University of St. Joseph with few ideas of the career he wanted to enter after school. But that changed when he was connected with CGI at an event. Schilling went on to study computer and data science, later completing an internship with CGI. After graduation, he went to work for the company full-time, and he now provides mentorship to students.
“Because I had spent so much time with CGI as a student, the transition to full-time employment was seamless,” he said. “I was able to focus on growth rather than trying to find my footing.”
[RELATED: CT redoubles efforts to equip workforce for AI economy]
In the hopeful eyes of Lamont, AI brings the potential for new opportunities and increased economic opportunity — and it fits into a broader push from state leaders to shift CT’s economy in a tech-oriented direction. 
“I’m pretty bullish because I think the world is moving in our favor in the sense that much more knowledge-based, skilled-based is where our future is,” Lamont said. “A lot of that will be better directed, better guided, and much more effective for people learning how to use artificial intelligence.” 
A multifaceted approach
The scene that unfolded Wednesday has become a familiar one: Lamont, surrounded by state officials and university leaders, describing the state’s unlimited potential and early success in various AI or technology initiatives and workforce development efforts.
Over the summer, the state celebrated a grant award from the National Science Foundation that will help build out its quantum computing sector. The project is also slated to receive $121 million in funding from the state. 
Around the same time, Lamont’s office announced that it was entering a partnership with RAISE US, a nonpartisan organization that offers workers displaced by AI a mix of retraining and upskilling. As part of the collaboration, Connecticut will pilot programs training workers to interact with AI. The lessons from Connecticut and other partner states will inform a national workforce strategy. 
Gov. Ned Lamont signs the Connecticut Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency (CART) ACT during a ceremony on June 2, 2026.  Credit: P.R. Lockhart / CT Mirror
State officials framed the partnership as a chance for Connecticut to provide leadership on a national issue. 
“States are where the rubber really hits the road,” Dan O’Keefe, commissioner of the Department of Economic and Community Development, told CT Mirror in July. “I think the federal government has been a bit hands-off on things, and we felt the need to fill the gap.”
The state has also launched other efforts, including the Connecticut AI Academy, a free online school that offers certificate programs in AI literacy and AI fluency. The academy is expected to expand to offer AI learning for teens, teachers and small businesses. 
And in August, DECD announced a $20 million investment into an applied AI workforce center in Hartford, a project that will help train workers in new AI skills and technologies. 
The relationship between workforce development and artificial intelligence is also being closely examined in the work of the state’s Career Pathways Commission, which is currently developing a plan for work-based learning and career exposure to create pathway opportunities beginning in kindergarten through adulthood.
“AI is not a major by itself, but it tends to be a minor in all the things you’re doing,” Lamont said. “So you learn how to apply it. That’s where Connecticut’s lead and its strength is going to be.” 
States are figuring out how to prepare workers for AI
Connecticut is far from the only state rushing to prepare workers for the AI transition. In recent months, several states have announced efforts to brace workers for the potential impacts of AI and what those impacts might mean for the future of work. 
Many of these efforts, like Connecticut’s, have revolved around helping the workers most likely to be displaced by AI develop new skills that will allow them to find roles working with the technology. In New York for example, Gov. Kathy Hochul recently announced the Pursuit AI Jobs Institute, a Queens-based workforce center that aims to train 40,000 workers in work-relevant AI skills by 2032. 
The center, which is expected to be completed in 2027, is being supported by $10 million in public investment. The effort is being supported by the launch of a National Advisory Council which will be chaired by former U.S, Education Secretary and previous Connecticut education commissioner Miguel Cardona. Cardona also currently serves as chair of Connecticut’s Career Pathways Commission.  
Other states are also launching efforts. In Arkansas for example, the state is partnering with RAISE US on a career navigation program called ArkansasLAUNCH. In Maryland, RAISE US is supporting career transition programming and other support for displaced workers.
The variety of state efforts being launched suggests that there are numerous ways to approach workforce development and skill training as AI technology develops. In the coming months and years, the question will be which efforts are most fruitful and what insights those initiatives provide about the best strategies to help students and those already in the workforce. 
Matthew Pugliese, deputy commissioner and chief investment officer of the state Department of Economic and Community Development , speaks during an event announcing a 100,000-square-foot flagship campus for the Hartford Innovation Center at State House Square on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. The $20 million investment comes from the Connecticut Innovation Clusters Program, which is administered by the Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
As the event at Goodwin came to a close on Wednesday, Lamont argued that Connecticut’s initiatives, while multifaceted, will all support the same goal: good jobs and economic stability for workers. 
“We’re not going to be the R&D for AI, that’s happening elsewhere” Lamont said.  “But we are going to be leaders when it comes to how to apply AI in the next generation of professions.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Supreme Court upholds dismissal of former Dordt student appeal in religious discrimination case
text:
The Iowa Supreme Court has upheld the dismissal of a case in which a Dordt University student was denied a religious exemption from the COVID-19 vaccine. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Iowa Supreme Court has upheld a lower court’s dismissal of a Dordt University student’s claim of religious discrimination that stemmed from a request for a COVID-19 vaccination exception.
Andrew Perry, a former nursing student at the Sioux Center private university, sued Dordt for religious discrimination in 2022 after the university denied his exemption request for receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, which Dordt’s clinical partners in 2021 began requiring for students completing clinical rotations in healthcare settings.
His lawsuit was dismissed in district court “primarily because the student did not have a sincerely held religious objection to the vaccine,” the Iowa Supreme Court’s opinion on the case stated. Iowa Supreme Court Justice David May said in the opinion that the justices found “no grounds for reversal,” agreeing with the district court’s ruling.
“Ultimately, the court found that the student’s claim was not credible. It was really his parents who opposed the vaccine, not the student,” May said in the opinion.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the court opinion, Perry’s mother, Gayln, expressed greater issues with the vaccine mandate than Perry had expressed himself, and was “adamantly opposed to Andrew getting the vaccine” while Perry volunteered and trained in how to administer the vaccine to patients.
She emailed back and forth with Dordt nursing program chair Deb Bomgaars about the requirement from Dordt’s partners for clinical rotations, the opinion stated. When asked by Perry about getting the vaccine to continue his studies, she allegedly threatened to cut off all of his financial assistance — including money for tuition, room and board.
Perry sent an email to Bomgaars stating he didn’t have a personal problem with the COVID-19 vaccine but wanted to respect his parent’s wishes, testifying later that he sent it “out of fear” rather than financial threats from his parents, but the district court found his testimony lacked credibility as to his true intentions behind the email.
The student discussed getting the vaccine behind his mother’s back with Bomgaars and others in the fall 2021 semester, the opinion stated, but submitted an exemption request based on his belief that “his body is a temple of God and that he must be a steward of his own body.” Three days before Perry put in his request, his parents sent a letter to the institution supporting his ask.
Perry’s request was denied on the basis that he didn’t submit a statement from his denomination opposing the vaccine or provide evidence of previous religious exemptions during his time in primary and secondary school.
No longer able to participate in Dordt’s clinical rotations as a student, Perry applied for other programs and was accepted into Palm Beach Atlantic University and started there in spring 2022.
The district court found that Perry wasn’t credible in his claimed opposition to knowingly introducing anything in his body that would put him at risk, noting that during cross examination it was disclosed that he vaped and had consumed alcohol to excess. It was also shown that Perry was more motivated by “pleasing his parents and financing his continued education” than by his religious beliefs, the court found.
In cases where a student claims religious discrimination through the Iowa Civil Rights Act, the court opinion stated the must student must demonstrate a “bona fide belief” that complying with the institution’s requirements would go against their religious beliefs or practices, that they told the institution about this issue, and that they were penalized for not complying.
While Perry fulfills two of the three criteria, the opinion stated it agrees with the district court’s finding that the request “was not sincere and cannot form the basis for a claim of religious discrimination in this matter.”
“Ultimately, the court’s sincerity determination was based on facts relating to Andrew’s credibility, not his performance or observance. Those facts showed that although Andrew was personally willing to take the vaccine, he was also well aware of the financial repercussions of defying his mother’s prohibition,” the opinion stated. “We find no error in the court’s approach.”

title: ‘Anything could happen’: Oklahomans wait in lines to vote early ahead of Nov. 3 election
text:
Voters line up to vote early on Wednesday at the MAC Center, 2733 Marilyn Williams Drive, in Edmond. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Nercissa Newberry didn’t want to leave anything to chance.
So on Wednesday, the first day of early voting, she cast her ballot in Edmond on her day off. 
“I didn’t want anything to stand in my way on voting day,” Newberry said. “I didn’t want some emergency to pop up.”
She waited about an hour.
“It was very smooth,” she said.
Nercissa Newberry cast her vote early at the MAC Center, 2733 Marilyn Williams Drive, in Edmond. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
She voted early in a presidential election where the line was very long, she said.
“I feel like they saw what happened last time and they made more days available for us, which is great,” she said.
She said she did her research and brought a cheat sheet. She didn’t vote a straight party ticket, but did vote for Democrat gubernatorial nominee Cyndi Munson.
“I feel like she cares about people,” Newberry said. “She wants to listen to the people.”
Like Newberry, Linda Barnett cast an early vote at the Oklahoma County Election Board.
“Anything could happen,” Barnett said. “I wanted to make sure I had my voice heard.”
Like the site in Edmond, the Oklahoma County Election Board had a short line. Voters came with spouses. Some pushed walkers. Others lingered outside the polling place chatting with each other. Security was on hand at both locations, where signs directed voters. 
For the first time, Oklahoma County had three early voting locations in an effort to make it easier to vote and cut down on lines. 
Barnett said it was a “piece of cake” compared to the lines to vote in the presidential election.
“It was really quick, easy and painless,” said Hope Wilson, who cast her ballot at the Oklahoma County Election Board.
Hope Wilson cast her vote early at the Oklahoma County Election Board, 4201 N. Lincoln Boulevard, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
She voted for Munson because she agrees with her views.
She believes the policies of President Donald Trump, who has been campaigning for Republicans across the country and stopped Oct. 1 in Durant, are pushing people to vote for Democrats.
Across the country, people are grappling with increased costs for things ranging from groceries to gas.  
Geary and Diane West cast their ballots in Edmond after waiting about 50 minutes.
The couple voted for a Republican ticket “because we can’t stand the direction Democrats are going in,” Geary West said.
The couple supports Donald Trump.
“He’s just a normal, goofy guy and we love him,” Geary West said.
Jayden Jarvis cast his ballot in Edmond and voted for Munson because he supports her policies.
He thinks Trump, or any president, will have an impact on the elections.
“Especially in the state of Oklahoma,” Jarvis said. “We are a big red state, so I know for sure it might impact a little bit more.”
David Suter voted in Edmond, selecting mostly Democrats because he doesn’t like what is going on in the government.
“I don’t care for a lot of the Democrats, but they’re better than what we got,” he said.
Early voting continues from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Thursday and Friday and from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday. 
The general election is Tuesday. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Unknown amount of liquid fertilizer ended up in ditch leading to Mississippi River
text:
Fertilizer storage tanks at the Merschman Fertilizer facility in Fort Madison, which leaked an unknown amount into a nearby ditch. (Photo courtesy of DNR) A leak in a liquid fertilizer tank in Lee County has led to an unknown amount of the fertilizer, mixed with rainwater, to enter a drainage ditch leading to a tributary of the Mississippi River, according to the Iowa Department of Natural Resources. 
DNR staff responded to the incident and are investigating the spill. According to a news release from the department, no dead fish have been observed, although residents are asked to avoid the area near Fort Madison.
In early October, staff at a Merschman Fertilizer facility in Fort Madison reported a leak in a liquid fertilizer tank. Staff then pumped the fertilizer into a different storage tank. Both tanks sit in a lined containment berm, according to the DNR, along with roughly six inches of gravel. 
Following rain in the area, staff at the facility operated a sump pump to remove liquid from the containment berm, which led to an unknown amount of the fertilizer product and collected rainwater to be pumped into a nearby drainage ditch. 
According to the DNR, the released liquid fertilizer was urea ammonium nitrate, or UAN, with 32% nitrogen. 
The ditch where the water was pumped empties into an unnamed tributary that empties into the Mississippi River. 
The news release from the DNR said cleanup operations are underway as the facility staff pump “the remaining product and rainwater mixture” to a different on-site tank. Temporary dams have been placed along the tributary to stop the mixture from moving downstream.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Red-tape cuts’: Morrisey announces ‘One Stop Shop’ online portal to speed up permitting process
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey celebrates the One Stop Shop Permitting Portal, an initiative of his administration, at the State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Oct. 28, 2026.(Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s push to cut red-tape in an effort to boost business growth took a step forward Wednesday with the official launch of a new online permitting tool.
The One Stop Shop Permitting Portal allows businesses to apply for permits, pay fees and track applications through a single account. It handles 330 different types of permit types used by 13 state agencies. 
The portal can reduce the processing deadline for oversized hauling permits from five to two days and timber license renewals from 14 calendar days to seven business days.
“We have to cut red tape faster than any state around us,” said Gov. Patrick Morrisey at the State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Wednesday.
“I know when I talk to companies trying to convince them to come to West Virginia, I could say, ‘What if we could get you up and running three months earlier, six months earlier? How valuable is that?’ And they all say, ‘Sign me up.’ That’s a selling point that’s very, very significant,” he said. 
A 2025 piece of legislation, requested by Morrisey, required the state Department of Administration to establish a public permitting dashboard for multiple state agencies. 
The portal had a soft opening on Oct. 1, three months ahead of the Jan. 1, 2027, deadline in the legislation. 
“As of yesterday, we’re at 8,001 permits with 15 that have gone through this new system with 1,536 new users,” said Eric Householder, cabinet secretary of the West Virginia Department of Administration.
Chad Shamblin, general manager of All Crane and Equipment Rental in Hurricane, said using the new portal reduced his permit application time from a couple of days to three minutes.
“This portal will make our permit application more speedy, efficient and allow us to spend more time dealing with our customers,” Shamblin said.
Jason Pizatella, chief executive officer of the Contractors Association of West Virginia, called it a “game changer for the industry.”
“The quicker we get a permit approved, it means we can get shovels in the ground and we can work faster,” he said. 
The governor said that the expedited process will follow state law and extra resources will go to compliance since they’re accelerating approval times. 
If a state agency misses its processing deadline on a completed application submitted through the portal, the agency is required to refund the applicant’s permit fees. 
“There’s going to be accountability too,” Morrisey said. 
Lawmakers budgeted $5 million for the portal, and the state worked with IT consulting company Delasoft in creating the online portal.
“Their total contract is $655,000,” Householder said.
Use of the portal remains optional until July 1, 2027, allowing businesses to continue using paper applications or existing agency systems without penalty.
Businesses and individuals can access the portal at SpeedToBuild.wv.gov. Questions about individual permits should be directed to the issuing agency through the portal’s resource guide.
According to Morrisey, his administration has announced $96 billion in private-sector investment since last fall, with more than 19,000 projected jobs.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As healthcare costs spike for Pa. employers and employees, state House Dems pitch universal coverage
text:
Healthcare costs are rising (again) in 2027 — and some people think it's time to start considering universal healthcare as an option. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)As millions of Pennsylvanians navigate their health insurance options during open enrollment, many could face double-digit premium increases over last year’s costs. The growth is reviving debates over universal healthcare and the government’s role in price-setting. 
Employers across the nation expect prices to increase by 8.2% in 2027, the biggest recorded hike since 2003, according to consulting firm Marsh. More than one-third of the 1,800 surveyed employers anticipated increases over 10%. 
“Many of our businesses are at their breaking point … but with every year that passes, it seems like we’re hearing more and more from our business owners that they believe it’s just simply unsustainable for them,” said Greg Moreland, the Pennsylvania State Director for the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB). 
According to KFF, job-based plans for workers are 9% higher this year than they were in 2025, with an annual cost of $7,471 for a family. For employees at businesses with less than 200 staff, it’s even more expensive. 
(Graphic from KFF)
For Rep. Greg Scott (D-Montgomery) and a select number of other liberal lawmakers, the continued cost burden signals a need to shift to a single payer system that covers all Pennsylvanians. 
“In my household, I believe healthcare should be a right. I don’t believe it should be a privilege reserved for those that can afford it,” Scott stated during an Oct. 5 press conference. 
Under House Bill 2763, which mirrors Senate Bill 1465, employers would pay a 7.5% payroll tax and employees would pay 2.5% — though employers can pay both — to replace “previous spending … on health premiums and out-of-pocket expenses.”
The coverage would also come without deductibles or copays.
Notably, Canada’s universal healthcare system started with a provincial plan in Saskatchewan and in the U.S., Oregon is exploring the option — potentially setting a precedent for a state-based version to advance. 
Adopting such a policy, however, is no easy task. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
A RAND Corporation analysis in New York state concluded that a single-payer plan could cover every resident, but would require “significant” new tax revenue, projecting that costs would decrease slightly over time. A proposed structure would decrease costs for most households and place the burden on high-income earners. 
“The estimated effects of the New York Health Act are highly dependent on assumptions about provider payments, administrative costs, and drug prices,” said Christine Eibner, co-author of the study and the Paul O’Neill Alcoa Chair in Policy Analysis at RAND. “The actual cost of a single-payer health plan in New York would be sensitive to the extent to which state officials would negotiate or set price levels and generate efficiencies that would curb health care spending.”
States would also need to negotiate with the federal government, which currently uses tax dollars to fund insurance programs like Medicare and Medicaid. 
 Role of commercial insurance

In 2024, the United States as a whole spent $5.3 trillion on healthcare, or an average of $15,474 per person. But KFF also reports that Americans have “half as many in-person doctor consultations per person as peer countries.” 
Hospitals make up the biggest portion of spending, and much of their revenue comes from commercial insurance, which pays higher rates than government-sponsored plans like Medicare and Medicaid. 
The Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council reports that for each commercial patient discharged in 2025, a commonwealth hospital can expect to make $31,800, on average. That’s almost twice the revenue earned on a Medicare patient ($16,990) and 30% more than a Medicaid patient ($21,658). 
Urban, rural hospitals closing at similar rates, study finds

Aside from hospitals, increasing drug prices have also pushed up spending, especially for those plans that cover GLP-1s. More than half of large employers who offer GLP-1 coverage for weight loss say that it’s had either a significant or moderate impact on their prescription drug spending, according to KFF. 
One frustration for employers, Moreland added, is the inability to compare prices between plans, limiting competition. According to the KFF employer poll, 29% of large companies reported difficulty getting information. 
“We don’t do a good enough job here in the United States of being transparent about what those medical costs are,” he said. “And then when you involve insurance, it becomes really, really confusing to the average person. It’s really confusing to me, and I live in this world every day.” 
Getting more cost clarity wouldn’t solve all problems, he continued, but “would really, really make a difference in the long run.” 
Moreland pointed to a few state-level efforts that NFIB supported, likening one to “a band-aid on a hemorrhage, but at least it’s something.” Options include creating a tax credit for businesses with 50 or fewer employees, allowing for association-level healthcare plans and another gives medium-sized companies access to their own aggregate claims data.
Only the first got any traction this year. But Moreland added that there’s a limit to what Pennsylvania’s lawmakers can do.
“I think it is a national crisis, and I think the only real solution for the entire country is going to come from the federal level,” he said. “The states — all they can do is nibble around the edges.” 
Universal healthcare isn’t the only option. Healthcare policy researchers at Georgetown University floated other possibilities for Congress, including:

Capping annual deductibles at $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a family, lowering the maximum out-of-pocket limit to $4,000 for a single person and $8,000 for a family. 
Limiting hospital prices with a Medicare-referenced hospital price cap — a method pursued by lawmakers in Indiana and Vermont. 
Requiring commercial health plans to cover certain services — like primary care, urgent care or behavioral health — and medications pre-deductible with no cost-sharing.
Taking the negotiated drug prices for Medicare into the private sector. 
Prohibiting hospitals from billing for facility fees for routine office visits or in outpatient settings alongside other site-neutral billing.

 Universal healthcare not universally loved

Still, Scott and other supporters say that their proposal would “help level the playing field” and make it easier for small businesses to opt into employee coverage. 
“Businesses with fewer than 50 employees generally aren’t required to offer health insurance, yet many do because they want to take care of their employees. That’s becoming harder to sustain,” Scott told the Capital-Star.
In addition to the employee benefit, Moreland said offering healthcare coverage is a competitive advantage for businesses.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Drew Whiting, the CEO of Erie Downtown Development Corporation who also employs roughly 50 people with another small business, spoke at the same early October event as Scott in favor of universal healthcare — the system available in 25 of America’s peer industrialized countries.
Likening the nation’s health system to a company, he said the United States was doing something different from competitors that cost twice as much but got worse results. Continuing the analogy, he added that any business leader responsible for that decision “would be fired.” 
“That’s what we’re doing with our healthcare system in the United States,” he concluded, even when other industrialized countries “have figured out there may be a better way to go.” 
And costs aren’t likely to let up, he continued, pointing to anticipated federal changes cutting Medicaid funding and limiting public coverage options. 
But not everyone is sold on the idea. 
Moreland, a veteran, pointed to systemic frustrations with his coverage under the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs as an example of poor delivery. 
“I think anytime you look at putting the government in charge of anything and taking it out of the hands of the private sector, I think we have concerns,” Moreland continued. “Provide me another example of where the government just took something over and did it just flawlessly perfect. I don’t know that that’s where we want to go.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: FCC moving forward on rule to allow prison cellphone jamming
text:
Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr during an Oct. 28, 2026 press conference in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The Federal Communications Commission said Wednesday it is moving forward with a rule change that will allow local and state correctional facilities to jam cellphone signals.
The commission will vote in three weeks on the final rule change, FCC Chair Brendan Carr told reporters at a press conference in Little Rock. 
He was joined by U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin — both Republicans — as well as state Corrections Secretary Lindsay Wallace, Division of Correction Director Dexter Payne, South Carolina Department of Corrections Director Joel Anderson and a representative of the Federal Bureau of Prisons.
The announcement came just over a year after Carr, Cotton and Griffin first announced the effort. While federal prisons are able to use jamming within their facilities, state and local prisons have not been allowed to do so under a federal law that prohibits states or individuals from “willfully or maliciously” interfering with “licensed or authorized” radio communications, which include cellphones.
Cellphones that state officials said were seized from people incarcerated in state prisons on display at the Arkansas attorney general’s office on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
The rule change will allow the jamming technology to be deployed by deauthorizing the use of cellphones within prison facilities. Carr said last year that the longstanding ban was due to a “misreading” of the law.
Once the rule change is in place, “corrections officials can apply to the FCC, outline how they’re going to do their jamming. They’ll get approval from the agency and they’ll be able to get going,” Carr said.
Cotton, who is running for reelection against Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, has been an advocate for allowing state and local prison officials the ability to jam cellphones. Cotton has at least twice introduced a bill to prohibit the FCC from disallowing state and local corrections agencies from jamming — though neither time has the measure advanced to a vote in its assigned Senate committee. 
Standing behind a table displaying cellphones they said were confiscated from people incarcerated in state prisons, Cotton, Griffin and Carr called contraband cellphones a public safety threat.
“A major prison drug ring in Georgia moved 14 kilograms of meth and nearly a kilogram of heroin into the Atlanta area using contraband cellphones behind bars,” Cotton said. “Also, in South Carolina, prisoners used contraband cellphones to run a sextortion scheme that targeted hundreds of our troops and tragically led to the suicide of several victims.”
He did not cite specific examples of cellphones being used for similar purposes in Arkansas, though he said sheriffs and correctional officers told him last year that finding and disposing of contraband cellphones was “one of the most dangerous parts of their jobs.” 
Cellphones are common in prisons around the country, and have been used to coordinate hits, drug smuggling and other crimes within prison walls. But they are also used in other ways. 
Incarcerated people have used them to stay connected with family and friends in the outside world. One person used one to take virtual college classes. Contraband cellphones were also used in the making of The Alabama Solution, an Oscar-nominated documentary shining further light on the dangerous conditions inside Alabama’s prisons.
Kaleem Nazeem, a co-director of decARcerate who was previously incarcerated in state prison, said in a text message that the changes would do little to address what drives most incarcerated people to use the cellphones in the first place.
“If the prices on using the (prison) phones wasn’t so high, then I don’t think you’ll have this problem where they’re running into problems with individuals having cellphones,” Nazeem said. “The majority of the individuals who are using these cellphones are only trying to, basically, stay in contact with their loved ones or try to stay up to date with technology and information.”
Attorney General Tim Griffin and U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton at a press conference in Little Rock, Arkansas on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
Cotton said state and local corrections officials would not be required to use cellphone jamming, and that the use of the technology would be “targeted” and would not “interrupt with lawful communications outside of prisons or jails.”
State prison officials said last year that increased gang violence in Arkansas’ prisons coincided with an increase in cellphone confiscations.
Carr said there could be legal challenges to the new rule if it’s approved by the commission, but expressed confidence that it would be upheld in the courts. He also denied that jamming cellphones in prisons opens the door to doing so in other places.
“That’s not something that’s been under consideration by the FCC at all,” Carr said. “Our view is that the jamming authorization is unique as to prisons and jails.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Pharmacy worker’s license revoked due to alleged theft of drugs
text:
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy oversees state-licensed pharmacies, pharmacists and pharmacy technicians in Iowa. (Photo by Getty Images; logo courtesy the State of Iowa)State regulators have revoked the license of a Dubuque pharmacy employee for the suspected theft of hundreds of pills.
The Iowa Board of Pharmacy recently charged pharmacist technician trainee Akasha Brown with obtaining or attempting to unlawfully obtain prescription drugs; stealing prescription drugs from a pharmacy for personal use or for distribution to others; and knowingly making misleading or deceptive representations in the practice of pharmacy or engaging in unethical conduct that is harmful to the public.
According to the board, Brown was employed at Hartig Drug Company in Dubuque in 2025 when the board staff learned the pharmacy had submitted a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration form indicating an employee had stolen controlled substances from the business.
The drugs listed in the form consisted of 168 tablets of alprazolam, commonly known by the brand name Xanax, a prescription drug used to treat anxiety disorders. The form also listed 100 capsules of methylphenidate ER, a stimulant commonly used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
The suspect named in the form was Brown, board records show.
The pharmacy then provided state officials with photos culled from a surveillance video, allegedly showing Brown, wearing a coat, taking medications from a pharmacy shelf and placing them into her coat pocket. They also show Brown leaving the pharmacy with her coat on and returning nine minutes later without the coat, the board alleges.
The pharmacy allegedly reported the matter to Dubuque police. According to the board, Brown told a board investigator she had not intentionally taken the drugs from the pharmacy, indicating she had forgotten placing the medications in her pocket and only discovered them later after retrieving the coat from her washer at home.
“I contacted (Hartig) and told them, ‘Hey, I found (the medication). I have it. It was in my laundry,’” Brown allegedly told the board staff. “I kept the bottle ’cause I had a feeling I would need proof … So do I throw it away now, or should I give it to the cops?”
Later, the board alleges, Brown told investigators she did not keep the medications or the bottles in which they were stored.
In its recent written decision revoking Brown’s license, the board said that although Brown claimed “she accidently took the prescription medication, Brown did not return either the medication or the medication bottles to Hartig. Brown also provided conflicting statements regarding what happened to the medication.”
Court records indicate no criminal charges were filed in the case.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Brown for comment.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Dolores Huerta, Chicana activist and defender of farmworker rights, dies at 96
text:
AUSTIN, TEXAS - AUGUST 16: Co-founder of the United Farm Workers Association, Dolores Huerta speaks during the "Stop the Trump takeover" demonstration outside of the State Capitol on August 16, 2025 in Austin, Texas. Over 200 nationwide demonstrations occurred today against the Trump administration's newly introduced redistricting plans. Earlier last week, Texas Democratic lawmakers fled to Illinois in an attempt to protest and deny quorum for votes on the proposed Republican redistricting plan, which would secure five additional GOP seats in the U.S. House. The Democratic lawmakers are preparing to return to Texas early next week after the special legislative session called by Gov. Greg Abbott came to an end yesterday. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
This story was originally reported by The 19th.
Dolores Huerta, who rose to national prominence as the co-founder of the National Farm Workers Association, and was known for her advocacy for women farmworkers, died on Wednesday. She was 96.
Huerta was born in New Mexico but spent most of her life in California’s Central Valley, an agricultural hub where a quarter of the country’s food is grown.
After graduating college, she became an elementary school teacher. A majority of her students were the children of migrant farmworkers. She left teaching when she realized that she could better use her talents to help their parents fight issues like wage theft and poor working and living conditions. She is widely quoted as saying: “I couldn’t tolerate seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes. I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”
She left the school to work at the Community Service Organization, a Latino civil rights group.  In 1955 she helped start the Stockton chapter of the organization, which is where she met César Chávez, a rising Chicano leader. The two went on to create the National Farm Workers Association.
One of the first major actions she undertook was helping organize the Delano Grape Strike in 1965, a five-year strike that was started by Filipino workers who were fighting for higher wages. About a week into the strike, NFWA joined the movement with 1,200 Mexican laborers. The two groups representing the strikers eventually merged to become the United Farm Workers (UFW), a labor union.
As part of the UFW’s work to fight for better working conditions and union contracts, Huerta went to New York to organize a national boycott against table grapes. There she met the feminist leader Gloria Steinem, who in 1968 flew out to California to march with the striking farmworkers.
While Huerta was the lead negotiator for the grape worker contracts that resulted from the organizing, her contributions and leadership during the strikes and subsequent boycotts were often overshadowed by Chávez. It was Huerta who coined the ¡Sí Se Puede! chant, which means “yes, it can be done” and came to define the farmworker movement – but the phrase has been erroneously credited to him over the years. The phrase continues to be a rallying cry of activists across the country, and more recently has been used by politicians like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former President Barack Obama.
Over the years, Huerta began to focus more on the women farmworkers in the movement, and in 1974 she helped found the Coalition of Labor Union Women. She worked to raise awareness about the specific dangers they faced in the fields, including an epidemic of sexual assault. In a 2013 interview with “Frontline” she talked about how farmworker women were often subject to threats and assault in the fields and were scared to speak up due to their immigration status or threats to their employment. She worked to elevate these and other women’s issues, including access to child care, through UFW, where she served as vice-president from its founding until 1999.
In March of 2026, Huerta revealed to the New York Times that she herself was a victim of sexual assault, detailing two encounters with Chávez, one of which she says was rape. The bombshell revelation came as part of a an investigation conducted by the Times that revealed a pattern of sexual assault by Chavez against women and girls in the movement.
Huerta said she kept the assaults she endured secret to protect the work they were doing. “I never talked about it to anybody and the reason I didn’t is because I just didn’t want to hurt the movement.”
Huerta also worked to change the culture within the union itself. In the same “Frontline” interview, she describes how she would take note of every time someone made a sexist comment in board meetings. The first time she did this, she noted 58 sexist remarks. “They were all shocked, and then the next meeting, I got them down to 30, then 20, then eventually two and pretty soon zero,” she said.
“I believe that’s why it’s so important to have women involved,” she said. “In the farmworkers’ union, we had a lot of women on the front lines, we had a lot of women in our departments. The best way to curb this type of macho sexist culture is to make sure that women are involved.”
In her later years, she became involved in the broader women’s rights movement, working for the Feminist Majority Foundation on its Feminization of Power campaign, where she advocated for more Latinas to run for office.
While in her early labor organizing years she was outspoken against abortion, she would later change her view on the issue. In an interview published in 2018 by Signs, a feminist journal based at the University of Chicago, she described how her stance was rooted in her Catholic upbringing and shifted as she learned from feminist leaders like Steinem and Eleanor Smeal, cofounder of the Feminist Majority Foundation.
“I’m glad I went through that because it helps me to be able to transfer that transition to other women, especially to Latina women, to make them understand that this is a basic right that women need to have. And access to abortion is a human right that women need to have because if you cannot have control over your body, it’s very hard to control anything else,” she said at the time.
Huerta herself had 11 children, whom she raised mostly as a single mother.
Throughout her life she received numerous accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom from then-President Barack Obama in 2012 and the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Award in 1998. She also was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame.
Her legacy continues through the Dolores Huerta Foundation, which she cofounded with her daughter Camila Chavez in 2003 to promote grassroots organizing for social justice; her daughter continues to serve as its executive director.
Several schools around the country, including four elementary schools in California, have been named in her honor. Three states — California, Washington and Nevada —  celebrate Dolores Huerta Day.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Providence City Councilor Miguel Sanchez wins free speech lawsuit against McKee staffers
text:
Providence City Councilman Miguel Sanchez, shown speaking at a City Council Meeting on Oct. 5, 2023, prevailed in a free speech lawsuit against Gov. Dan McKee's administration. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Fresh off a Democratic primary victory and poised to become the next president of the Providence City Council, Miguel Sanchez has also prevailed in a federal free speech lawsuit against Gov. Dan McKee’s advisors. 
Rhode Island District Court Chief Judge John McConnell Jr. affirmed that McKee’s advisors, Joseph Almond and Antonio Afonso, violated Sanchez’ constitutional speech protections when they fired him from his government job because of pro-Palestine statements Sanchez posted on his personal social media account.
“Both the Chief of Staff and the Deputy Chief of Staff of the Governor knew or should have known that they should not retaliate against Mr. Sanchez for exercising his constitutional right,” McConnell wrote in the 25-page ruling, first reported by GoLocalProv. “Yet the following day Mr. Sanchez was terminated from his employment right after Mr. Afonso acknowledged that Mr. Sanchez had a right to express himself.”
Sanchez did not immediately respond to requests for comment Wednesday.
Olivia DaRocha, a spokesperson for McKee’s office, said the governor’s office disagreed with the decision, and was “reviewing all options with legal counsel.”
First elected to the Providence City Council in 2022, the 28-year-old Democratic socialist has been outspoken about his support for Palestinians since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023. In the weeks immediately following the war, Sanchez called for a ceasefire and shared videos on X — formerly known as Twitter — from a pro-Palestine rally outside the State House.
Sanchez, who worked as a junior staffer in McKee’s Office of Constituent Services, was initially cautioned by supervisors about his personal social media content. On Nov. 1, 2023, after the Providence Journal published an article about Sanchez’ activism, he was fired from his $50,000-a-year state job.
In August 2024, Sanchez sued McKee, Almond, and Afonso, alleging they violated free speech protections under the First and 14th Amendments of the U.S. Constitution. His complaint also sought back pay and other monetary compensation, and his old job back.
McConnell does not address the request for damages or reemployment, leaving those questions outstanding. 
But McConnell firmly concludes that Sanchez’ social media account was clearly connected to his elected position on the city council, not McKee’s office, and that his day job in constituent services had little to no influence on public policy or communications.
McConnell also notes that two other members of McKee’s staff had posted personal views on social media that conflicted with the governor — one proposing to abolish the Law Enforcement Officers’ Bill of Rights and the other in support of a different presidential candidate in the 2024 election — yet were not fired nor asked to remove their posts.
McKee’s staff told Sanchez that his social media posts were disruptive, according to court documents. But the attention on Sanchez’ firing drew far more attention, prompting questions from 17 reporters, along with 63 emails and 38 calls to the constituent services offices within a day of the news being reported, according to court filings.
“The alleged distraction caused by his post pales in comparison to the inquiries after the firing,” McConnell wrote. 
McKee’s administrators, represented by the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office, claimed qualified immunity — a legal doctrine that shields government officials from lawsuits for monetary damages without clear proof they violated a law or constitutional right. But McConnell denied the defendants’ motion, pointing to their stated acknowledgement that they were firing Sanchez for self-expression.
Sanchez listed two  jobs —  a case manager for Better Lives Rhode Island, a Providence social services agency, and a community outreach coordinator for the Rhode Island Community Food Bank – on his 2025 financial form with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission.  He also reported income of more than $1,000 from Whatnot, an online platform for live auctions of collectible diecast cars.
Almond and Afonso still work for McKee, whose term ends in January,  DaRocha confirmed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Sherrill administration boasts of big reductions to permit backlogs
text:
More staff and centralized reviews have cut some permit backlogs by as much as 83%, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Wednesday. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s administration boasted of large reductions in permitting backlogs Tuesday after the governor said state departments expanded staffing and siloed permitters to more efficiently complete reviews that sometimes drag for months or even years.
The changes had so far cut nearly three-quarters of backlogged requests for environmental reviews that indicate the presence of wetlands and other protected waterways and reduced the backlog of permits to connect or alter low-traffic driveways that touch state highways by 83%, Sherrill and department heads said during a press conference Wednesday.
“It’s not just speed for speed’s sake. It’s realistically assessing how quickly we can get through these permits while at the same time upholding our strong standards,” the governor said at a Department of Transportation training site in Bordentown.
NJ’s low-cost health clinics see rising demand as insurance gaps widen

Permitting reform is the cornerstone of Sherrill’s pitch to private sector employers. On the campaign trail last year, she pledged to cut permit clearance times to prevent the government from holding businesses in limbo.
The administration in April launched a website to centralize permitting across three departments — those that oversee transportation, environmental protection, and community affairs — in a single place and has since added about 50 staff members to review permits within the Department of Environmental Protection alone.
“Permitting has a direct impact on how quickly projects move forward, businesses expand, and investments take shape in New Jersey,” said Transportation Commissioner Priya Jain. “I think I’m stating the obvious that when a business, developer, or municipality applies for a permit, timely decisions can make a real difference in project planning, cost, and schedules.”
Different types of permits require different levels of review, and some are far more expansive than others, and the amount of time a permit could sit before being marked as backlogged varied, said Jain.
Still, some applications before the Department of Environmental Protection sat without action for more than a year.
“We process about 20,000 permits a year at the Department of Environmental Protection. There were so many that were over 18 months, waiting to start a process, waiting to decide where I can and how I should design a project,” said Environmental Commissioner Ed Potosnak. “They can’t even get started. My heart sank. I thought, ‘This is unacceptable.’”
His department has sought to bring permit wait times below a year, Potosnak said, adding that reduced delays could help speed housing and other production in New Jersey.
While some classes of permits have seen massive reductions in backlogs, gains have been smaller and slower for more complicated applications.
The backlog for major access permits, which are needed to connect driveways with at least 500 daily trips to state highways, has fallen by 19%, and the backlog for remedial action permits issued by state environmental regulators has declined by 25%, officials said.
The governor’s push to speed permitting has drawn praise from the state’s business community, even among some who admitted doubts about her campaign trail promises.
“My members and others here today have heard all the promises before and are naturally skeptical,” Dan Kennedy, CEO of the New Jersey Commercial Real Estate Development Association, said at Wednesday’s press conference. “You have turned a lot of that pessimism into optimism already.”
The permitting progress made so far has sped commercial real estate projects in the state, allowing faster environmental cleanups that cut overall production times, Kennedy said.
Business groups have noted the shift in posture from the prior administration under Gov. Phil Murphy, even if it materialized in more frequent communication with business groups.
“To have everybody there at the table to talk, honestly, we didn’t really have that in the last go-around,” said Mike Egenton, executive vice president for government relations at the New Jersey Chamber of Commerce.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Federal election monitors won’t enter Indiana polling sites, officials say
text:
Voters cast their ballots for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Fox Hollow Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Two-dozen federal Department of Justice monitors will observe Election Day voting in two Indiana counties from outside the polling locations, election officials said Wednesday.
Up to 12 are expected to come to central Indiana’s Marion County, with another dozen going to Lake County near Chicago — heavily blue areas that host the state’s only Democratic representatives in Congress.
Marion County Clerk Kate Sweeney Bell said the observers will remain at least 50 feet from the entrance to the polls, just like people passing out campaign literature. This banned zone is the “chute.”
“Outside of every vote center or early vote center, there is a placard that is affixed either to the wall, to a window, to a stake outside that says ‘No campaigning beyond this point,'” she said. “… Well, same with federal election monitors. You can’t do anything past this point.”
DOJ sending election observers to Indianapolis, Lake County

She and Marion County Election Board attorneys spoke with DOJ representatives on Wednesday over the phone after receiving written notice last week of the impending visit.
That physical separation is in line with the Indiana Election Division’s take.
“Their default position is to remain outside and not enter the voting location unless state law otherwise permits their entry. In our agency’s view, our state law does not give federal monitors access to enter any voting location,” an Indiana Election Division official said.
Lake County’s Election Board didn’t respond to a request for comment by publication time.
The DOJ has for decades deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process.
But its plans to dispatch 1,000 observers to all 50 states are more ambitious than usual: just 289 were sent out for the 2022 midterms, and 714 for the 2024 presidential election, CBS News has reported.
Questioning to center on voting rights laws
Sweeney Bell said she was told the monitors in Indianapolis will work in teams of two, visiting an expected six or seven of the city’s 182 vote centers.
“Their intention is to talk to voters after they vote,” she said. But they can’t make someone speak.
Marion County Clerk Kate Sweeney Bell testifies during a House committee hearing on Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“A voter doesn’t have to answer a question if they don’t want to, and they will not be penalized in any way, shape or form for ignoring anyone they encounter on their way into or out of a vote center in Marion County,” she added. “… If they want to tell somebody trying to talk to them to pound sand, that’s their right. They will not get in trouble for it.”
The monitors will be in plain clothes, not DOJ uniforms, according to Sweeney Bell and the Indiana Election Division. They won’t be law enforcement officers and they won’t be carrying firearms.
Not all of them actually work for DOJ; the agency’s Civil Rights Division is also using observers from other federal entities. But all will have temporary credentials from DOJ, according to Sweeney Bell.
 They are supposed to provide that ID upon request.
DOJ representatives indicated the observers would be interested in polling accessibility, as part of the Americans with Disabilities Act, and provisional ballots, as related to the Help America Vote Act.
They also emphasized language assistance required in certain jurisdictions by the Voting Rights Act, Sweeney Bell recounted. But neither county is subject to that mandate.
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
She said they did not mention alleged noncitizen voting.
That’s despite an emphasis on election security from other Hoosier officials cheering on the DOJ.
Attorney General Todd Rokita said he “welcome(s)” the agency’s decision, citing the charges his office has filed against an alleged noncitizen accused of voting illegally in Indiana elections.
“It does happen, and we know there are more out there. That’s why it’s critical to ensure the laws are being followed,” Rokita said in a Monday news release. “Federal monitors who observe and report simply add another layer of accountability to the work our great state already does to protect the integrity of every legal vote.”
Asked why the DOJ selected Marion and Lake Counties for monitoring, and if observers have previously been sent to Indiana, the agency repurposed a statement it appears to be using nationally:
“We will be in all 50 states, including Indiana, doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades. All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process,” the statement reads. “Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
Sweeney Bell said she is encouraging everyone to follow the rule of law.
“They’ve got a right to be there, just as our voters have a right to vote free from harassment, intimidation, or any sort of coercion,” she said. “So I’m not going to say the sky is falling until I see it with my own eyes.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Bill McKibben sees a nation at a crossroads as he barnstorms battleground states
text:
Bill McKibben speaking to  a Sierra Club meeting in Montpelier in December 2024. Photo David Goodman/VTDigger
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Bill McKibben says that “elections should not be this important.”
They should not “be the deciding factor between continued stability and whatever kind of creeping fascism we’re playing with,” he writes. “And they certainly shouldn’t be determining questions of planetary survival. But they are.”
McKibben, founder of Third Act, which organizes Americans over age 60 “to safeguard our climate and democracy,” has been barnstorming the country in recent weeks to get out the vote and his message. He has traveled through battleground states including Pennsylvania, Kansas, Maine, Montana, Iowa and Texas listening to and speaking with residents about what matters to them and why their vote matters to the world.
McKibben says he has encountered a country grappling with economic anxiety, political division and growing concern about the future of democracy.
“We tell ourselves that this is the richest country on Earth,” he told me. “But man, for the most part in this country, there are a lot of people just barely getting by.”
McKibben is the author of some 20 books and a regular contributor to The New Yorker, The New York Times, Rolling Stone and his Substack, The Crucial Years. He is the Schumann Distinguished Scholar in Environmental Studies at Middlebury College and has won the Gandhi Peace Prize. His latest book is “Here Comes the Sun: A Last Chance for the Climate and a Fresh Chance for Civilization.”
In the political swing districts he has visited, McKibben said, frustration over the rising cost of living was nearly universal. Concerns about gas prices, groceries and housing surfaced repeatedly at doorsteps. Yet he also encountered a deeper sentiment among voters.
“People are really hurting, really feeling it,” he said, “and finally starting to understand in a way that I haven’t quite felt before that it’s not their fault that there’s some kind of corruption and collusion at the highest levels of our society that are making it extraordinarily difficult for anyone to manage to live out anything that even resembles the American dream.”

READ MORE

Although the campaign issues varied by region, McKibben said, concerns about President Donald Trump and the direction of the Republican Party were common themes.
In northern New York and Michigan, for example, he said voters were troubled by hostility toward Canada, a critical economic and cultural partner for border communities.
“Everybody apprehends and everybody understands that it’s insane,” McKibben said. “Canada is an ally and has been forever. We have no real beef with them in any way.”
He also expressed concern about the growing influence of wealthy donors in American elections, singling out billionaire Elon Musk’s spending as a sign of a democratic system under strain.
“When you have one man able to spend 15 or 20% of all the money that’s going to get spent in these elections himself, you have the kind of world that is so far from a working democracy that it’s hard to imagine,” he said.
Despite the political turbulence, McKibben, founder of 350.org, remains focused on climate change, the issue that has defined much of his career. Returning to Vermont, he warned that the effects of global warming are already unavoidable and accelerating.
“Let’s be honest: The ship is not going to be entirely righted,” he said. “Climate change is now advanced and advancing much further, even as we speak.”
Still, he argued that technological advances offer reason for optimism. Falling costs for renewable energy, particularly solar and wind power and battery storage, have created opportunities that did not exist a decade ago.
“We now do have the tools: cheap solar, cheap wind, cheap batteries, to finally at least start not stopping global warming — too late for that — but shaving tenths of a degree off how hot the planet eventually gets,” he said.
McKibben described the challenge ahead as “the biggest rescue mission in human history,” noting that even small increases in global temperature affect hundreds of millions of people worldwide.
At the same time, he said, Americans are increasingly exhausted by the intensity of modern politics.
But amid widespread voter frustration, McKibben said he found hope in the volunteers and activists he met across the country, especially older Americans reconnecting with the activism of their youth.
Many are “hearkening back to their first act, to the days of the civil rights movement and the peace movement and the first Earth Day,” he said.
For McKibben, those grassroots efforts remain the country’s best path forward.
“It is a struggle between democracy and money,” he said. “Not at all clear which side is going to win. But we will do what we can, and we will do it in the best possible spirit that we can.”
Disclosure: Bill McKibben is the husband of writer and journalist Sue Halpern, a board member of the Vermont Journalism Trust, VTDigger’s parent organization.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Bill McKibben sees a nation at a crossroads as he barnstorms battleground states.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Pipeline projects booming in the US while federal regulations ease, report notes
text:
Map of pipeline expansions across the country. A new report positions a boom in projects alongside rollback of environmental and safety regulations.  (Environmental Integrity Project)New pipeline projects are booming across the United States at the same time the Trump administration rolls back federal environmental and safety regulations, according to a new report. 
A new analysis from the Environmental Integrity Project, a policy nonprofit based in Washington, D.C., looked at public records from federal and state agencies as well as publicly available information from company websites to determine there were 193 new pipeline projects either proposed or under construction as of Aug. 1. 
The report said recent growth in U.S. pipeline capacity, expected to build 17,000 miles of new pipelines, is the largest in almost 20 years, when hydraulic fracturing technology expanded oil and gas drilling across the globe. 
Of the 193 pending projects, 151 would transport natural gas, and 81 will cross through more than 19,000 acres of federally protected wetlands, according to the report’s analysis.
In Louisiana, the buildout of new pipeline infrastructure is mostly to service the booming liquefied natural gas export industry along the Gulf Coast. The largest in the works by export capacity is the Driftwood Line 200 and 300 project. It would travel 71 miles from Beauregard Parish to Calcasieu Parish, crossing 151 acres of wetlands to carry 5.7 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day to the expanding LNG terminals. 
Jen Duggan, executive director with the Environmental Integrity Project, said during an online news conference Wednesday that these pipeline projects require thoughtful evaluation before they are built, something the report argues is not happening under the Trump administration. 
“Major pipeline projects that threaten public safety and our environment should undergo rigorous scrutiny with full transparency, meaningful public input, and comprehensive public hearings,” Duggan said. 
Of the 193 pipeline projects proposed or being built, 52 have requested or received expedited or streamlined reviews from federal agencies such as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and Army Corps of Engineers, according to the report. At least 30% of the 81 projects impacting wetlands have either requested or received accelerated reviews of wetlands permits under the Trump administration’s energy emergency policy. 
Enforcement actions against pipeline companies have also dramatically decreased under the Trump administration, the report found. The Federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration has the ability to issue warnings, order corrective actions and place fines on violators. Last year, the agency recorded 112 actions in response to pipeline infractions, about half its annual average of 217 over the past two decades and the fewest on record. 
“Cutting back on these pipeline safety rules and enforcement is a serious issue,” Duggan said. “Given the number and scale of proposed pipeline projects, the Trump administration should tighten pipeline safety rules and increase inspections enforcement and funding for safety research, not the opposite.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Right-wing influencer James O’Keefe charged with voter fraud after impersonating registered voters
text:
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announces felony charges for right-wing influencers James O'Keefe and Cam Higby for impersonating registered voters during Minnesota's primary election, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)Right-wing influencers James O’Keefe and Cam Higby have been charged by Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty for unlawful voting and identity theft after they pulled a dress-up stunt during the Aug. 11 statewide primary election, unsuccessfully trying to show that Minnesota’s defense against voter fraud is insufficient.
The men posted videos in August in which they went into different Minnesota polling places to attempt to register to vote using Minnesota’s vouching process, through which a registered voter can confirm up to eight voters’ addresses so that they can also be registered to vote. The two donned clothes traditionally worn by Muslims — Higby wore a niqab, a garment traditionally worn by Muslim women — and put on fake foreign accents.
The men used names of registered voters, some deceased, to begin the vouching process, Moriarty said at a Wednesday press conference. They stopped short of signing an oath under penalty of perjury, which Moriarty said is a major deterrent against people misusing the vouching option.
Still, Moriarty’s office is charging the two for violating a state law that forbids people from misrepresenting their identities when applying for a ballot, because the application is a “multi-step process” that they began, Moriarty said.
The charges come less than a week away from Minnesota’s Nov. 3 general election.
In recent months, Minnesota has faced heightened federal scrutiny regarding its elections. In September, federal prosecutors charged 10 people with illegally voting or registering to vote in Minnesota elections. Moriarty said she’s unaware of any federal investigation into O’Keefe and Higby’s voting registration attempt.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to discredit the election process, which is administered by states under the Constitution, and his administration has, largely unsuccessfully, tried to gain more control over elections, for example by attempting to acquire Minnesota’s unredacted voting roll.
The videos claimed to expose Minnesota’s vouching process as vulnerable to fraud, but did not show O’Keefe and Higby leaving before signing the oath, Moriarty noted.
“In fact, when they were at the polling place, they made excuses to leave as soon as the election judge asked them to sign the oath,” Moriarty said.
Right-wing provocateur O’Keefe, 42, is known for making secretly recorded and often selectively edited undercover videos with Project Veritas, the far-right activist group he founded and from which he was later fired — stunts that have resulted in prior encounters with law enforcement.
In 2010, along with other Project Veritas activists, he pled guilty to a misdemeanor for entering former Democratic Sen. Mary Landrieu’s office while posing as a telephone repairman. He paid a $1,500 fine and was placed on three years probation. In 2013, he was investigated by New Hampshire’s attorney general for giving names of dead people to election officials, though that investigation was dropped.
Higby, 26, is a conservative influencer who is known for organizing a college debates tour in honor of Charlie Kirk. Higby came to Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge and claimed to have “infiltrated” Signal groups of ICE observers, whom First Amendment lawyers said were protected by Constitution in their efforts to follow and document federal agents’ activities.
Higby posted on X within an hour of the charges being announced: “They want me in PRISON for exposing election vulnerabilities in their state.” He shared a fundraiser titled “Support Cam Higby (Minnesota Burqa Lawfare)” with a fundraising goal of $20,000.
Moriarty said that her office had enough evidence to charge the men without the video, since they knew the two registered to vote using other people’s names. Police also interviewed election judges in different polling places, who noted the “strange behavior” of O’Keefe and Higby, Moriarty said.
Minnesota’s vouching system is over 50 years old, though is sparsely used — less than 0.6% of votes cast in the 2024 general election used the vouching process, Moriarty said. The process is most commonly used by residents of senior living facilities or those who have recently moved. People registering through vouching still need to provide a Minnesota driver’s license number, Minnesota ID card number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number. If they attest to not having those numbers, they are assigned a unique voter number for identification by the state, to enable tracking and prevent duplicate voting.
Moriarty said that O’Keefe and Higby’s intentions to not vote and their derogatory comments did not factor into the charges.
“It is not against the law to be performative. It is not against the law to be offensive, it’s not against the law to say the things that they said if you’re standing outside the polling place,” Moriarty said.
“The fundamental issue here is you cannot go into a polling place and misidentify yourself, use other people’s identity, and say that to our election judges as you apply for the ballot, whether or not you intend to vote.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Auto seat maker opening $30M manufacturing plant at Scout Motors site
text:
Construction continues at Scout Motors $2 billion electric vehicle assembly plant located on 1,600 acres in Blythewood, South Carolina, on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A seat maker for cars is the latest Scout Motors supplier to announce a South Carolina location.
Brose Sitech, which makes car seats and interior parts, plans to open in the supplier park on the site of Scout’s Blythewood electric vehicle assembly plant.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“When we announced we would build an on-site Supplier Park at the Scout Motors Production Center last year, we promised it would lead to even more jobs, investment and economic prosperity in South Carolina,” Scout’s CEO Scott Keogh said in a statement. “This announcement represents the beginning of that promise being fulfilled.”
The Polish company, which has a regional headquarters in Detroit, pledged to hire some 330 new workers for its $30 million, 140,000-square-foot facility. The Blythewood location joins the company’s fleet of 22 global manufacturing plants internationally.
The company did not give an average wage or any other details on what it plans to pay employees.
Juan-Carlos Kieler, Executive Vice President of Brose Sitech Columbia Inc. (Photo courtesy of Brose Sitech)
“Establishing our first manufacturing location in Blythewood is an important milestone for Brose Sitech,” Executive Vice President Juan-Carlos Kieler said in a statement.
“The U.S. is a significant automotive market with strong opportunities for future growth. With our new production facility, we are bringing our expertise in complete seating systems closer to our customer Scout while laying the foundation for Brose Sitech’s long-term development in North America,” Kieler added.
The company expects to begin operations in 2027.
The announcement comes just two weeks after seven existing Upstate auto parts makers pledged to hire 200 South Carolinians as they expand production to meet the needs of Scout.
“The decision by Brose Sitech to establish its first U.S. manufacturing facility in South Carolina is a testament to the momentum created by Scout Motors’ historic investment in the Midlands,” U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., said in a statement. “This announcement is another important step in the growth of South Carolina’s automotive industry, and I look forward to the jobs, investment and long-term economic opportunities it will create for communities across our state.”
Other announcements
It also marks the second new jobs announcement in Richland County in two days.
SteelFab Inc. announced Tuesday it planned to invest $30 million and hire 100 people in Richland County.
The company will move into an existing manufacturing plant, previously occupied by Metso Minerals, which makes equipment for mining and processing minerals.
Upstate car parts manufacturers investing $82M to supply Scout Motors

In exchange, the state offered SteelFab income tax credits, worth $1,500 for each new job created.
The plant marks Charlotte-headquartered SteelFab’s fifth South Carolina location. Operations are expected to begin by the end of the year.
Headquartered in Charlotte, SteelFab engineers, manufactures and supplies fabricated structural steel and steel products.
The company has 18 facilities in the U.S., including four existing locations in South Carolina.
“This investment represents another significant milestone in SteelFab’s continued growth and commitment to South Carolina,” Chief Operating Officer Rob Rutherford said in a statement. “For nearly four decades, we have been proud to be part of South Carolina’s manufacturing community, and the establishment of our new Columbia facility builds on that strong foundation.”
