name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson business leaders urged to base data center opinions ‘on the facts’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Economic development officials on Wednesday urged Jackson business leaders to craft informed opinions about data centers and consider their impact on Mississippi’s infrastructure, economy and communities.
“You are entitled to all of your own opinions,” said Jeff Rent, president and CEO of the Greater Jackson Partnership, which organized the panel, “We are a nation of varying opinions. But I hope you will learn something today and base your opinion of data centers on the facts.”
Data centers are facing increasing pushback from residents in Mississippi and across the country as companies are rushing to meet the expected artificial intelligence demand for computing power. Residents are concerned about the impact on electricity rates, noise, water and the surrounding environment. There are seven data centers being built in Mississippi, with more potentially in the pipeline. In the Jackson Metro area, there are two in Madison County, one in Clinton and one in Rankin. 
State and local officials are eyeing more regulations. The Jackson City Council passed the state’s first data center moratorium and other cities have passed zoning regulations. Earlier this year, a legislative task force on artificial intelligence expressed concerns about the potential impact of data centers.
“There’s a lot of misinformation out there on social media, a lot of things that happen in other communities that are not relevant to our communities,” said Garrett Wright, director of Rankin First Economic Development Authority, “It is incumbent on everyone in this room, everyone on this stage, to make sure that the local population is fully informed of reality, not just what they are reading in the media.” 
Haley Fisackerly, president and CEO of Entergy Mississippi, said that it is important to understand what data centers are because they will be the new infrastructure, similar to railroads and the internet.
“I’ll tell you why I’m excited about it, “ Fisackerly said, “It’s not just about the growth and the jobs and investment. How is it going to transform the services we provide our communities and our customers?”
Fisackerly said that before Amazon Web Services decided to build a data center in Madison County, Entergy was concerned about the impact that rising costs, aging infrastructure, severe weather and a lack of sales growth would have on electricity costs for customers. 
Entergy, the state’s largest electricity provider, knew that it needed to build two new power plants by 2030, Fisackerly said, and having Amazon as a customer is now helping to pay for them and will lessen the increased costs for Entergy’s other’s customers. A report commissioned by environmental groups said that data centers have already increased rates for Entergy’s Mississippi residential customers by around $10 a month. Entergy has pushed back against these claims and emphasized that customers are benefiting from, not subsidizing data center costs.
Amazon has continued to expand its presence in Mississippi since the announcement of its first data center in 2024. It plans to invest $25 billion in Mississippi data centers in Clinton, Madison County and Warren County. 
“We have never seen an economic development opportunity like this in our state’s history,” Fisackerly said. 
Beyond the corporate investment, speakers on Wednesday highlighted data centers’ broader economic impact, including taxes directed towards public schools and job creation. Amazon recently tried to challenge Madison County’s property valuation which would reduce the amount it pays in property taxes. However, the county upheld the assessor’s valuation.
“When you think about data centers, it is not just the direct jobs. They are impacting every level of our education system. So, I’m so proud of what this entire region is doing to support the ecosystem for the data center industry,” Wright said.
“The jobs obviously are an important part, but what’s happening with the taxes? What’s happening with the wages? What’s happening with the home prices? What’s happening with the overall investment in the community,” said Andrea Hutchins, a project manager with Amazon Web Services.
The panelists emphasized the importance of partnerships between data centers, local businesses, government officials and the communities they’re building in. They encouraged people to ask questions and get engaged in the process.
“My advice is, it’s OK to say no. If you don’t want a data center, say no. Let your voice be heard,” said Joey Deason, Executive Director of the Madison County Economic Development Authority. But he cautioned against relying on misinformation and encouraged people to go to Amazon’s data centers in Canton to see and hear what they’re like. 
Panelists agreed that data centers are here to stay. Hutchins said that Amazon is projecting demand for at least the next decade, but there are ways data centers can be better partners. Deason said that there have been car wash gift cards given to people living close to the Amazon data centers and regular street cleaning in an effort to be good neighbors.
“I don’t think we can ignore the fact there have been some bad players or some some projects that have been detrimental to some local neighbors in the broader Southeast or even in the U.S. region. But there are a lot of ways to mitigate that,” Wright said, “ I think it’s incumbent on us as our developers to make sure that what we bring to our community is only going to increase the overall value of the region.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Campaign finance reports detail Guckian’s cash flow woes; ad war between Block and Foulkes escalates
text:
Republican Aaron Guckian is shown on stage during the last gubernatorial debate before the Nov. 3 general election on Tuesday night, Oct. 20, 2026, at Rhode Island College. (Photo by Corey Welch/WPRI 12)
Nearly one month after Republican Aaron Guckian boarded a private plane to Florida in search of donors for his dwindling campaign account, he still hasn’t submitted the requisite paperwork showing his travel expenses.
Meanwhile, the GOP nominee has less than $3,000 cash on hand — a tiny fraction of what Democratic nominee and frontrunner Helena Buonanno Foulkes has available — in the final week before the Nov. 3 general election, according to campaign finance reports filed with the Rhode Island Board of Elections. 
Candidates for state and local office were required to submit reports detailing campaign donations and expenditures for the 21-day period that ended Oct. 26 by midnight Tuesday — the last snapshot of campaign finances before the election.
Guckian submitted his report early Wednesday — nine hours after the midnight deadline. And the value of this ride on a private plane owned by Henry Mellon, cousin of billionaire and GOP donor Timothy Mellon, is not in his latest submission.
Mike Fahey, a spokesperson for Guckian’s campaign, said in an interview Wednesday that Guckian is working with the state elections board to submit the documentation for the private plane he took from Delaware to Florida on Sept. 30. He flew commercial on the way home, with a rental car snafu delaying his arrival in Rhode Island and forcing him to miss two gubernatorial forums. 
The cost for the private plane should have been reported as an in-kind donation in an earlier campaign finance report due Oct. 6. 
Guckian’s GOP primary opponent, Elaine Pelino, filed a complaint with the elections board over Guckian’s failure to report the cost of the plane ride and other travel expenses associated with his three-day trip to West Palm Beach for a private fundraiser.
In an Oct. 20 Facebook post announcing her complaint, Pelino alleged Guckian’s omission was intentional. 
“What concerns me most is that Guckian continues raising money from Republicans, including seniors on fixed incomes, without disclosing whether their contributions could ultimately be used to pay off expenses associated with his private jet travel,” she wrote.
Pelino is endorsing Block in the governor’s race.
Guckian defended his delayed accounting during an Oct. 20 debate — hours after Pelino announced the complaint — explaining that reporting of in-kind travel-related donations requires calculating total miles traveled divided by the number of people on the plane.
“It was an administrative thing,” Guckian said during the debate. “People don’t really want to talk about administrative things.”
The complaint against Guckian remains confidential, pending an audit or investigation that ends with evidence of a campaign finance violation, said Chris Hunter, a spokesperson for the board of elections. The elections board is scheduled to meet on Election Day morning, but it’s unclear whether the meeting will include any details about Pelino’s complaint or a resulting investigation. There is no meeting agenda posted as of Wednesday.
What is clear: Guckian’s cash flow woes have deepened since his last-minute trip to Florida to rub elbows with deep-pocketed GOP donors. Guckian reported one, $2,000 donation from a Clearwater, Florida, resident in his latest campaign filing, but it was unrelated to his trip to West Palm Beach earlier this month, Fahey confirmed.
In total, Guckian raised $5,400 from individual donors in the 21-day period that ended Oct. 26, boosting his campaign with a $7,000 personal loan. He spent nearly $17,000, mostly on consulting services and Facebook ads. 
Foulkes leads in donations
In contrast, Foulkes raked in more than $452,000 in donations during the same time frame, including nearly $30,000 from political action committees, with another $237,000 from in-kind contributions. She spent more than $541,000 to end the reporting period with just over $120,000 cash on hand.
Independent Ken Block, who trails Foulkes by 11 points in the latest public poll, reported $14,700 in individual donations, supplemented by a $20,000 personal loan. He spent a little over $234,000, leaving a $64,000 balance in his account.
The two have taken their fight to the airwaves with a series of increasingly contentious attack ads, the latest of which hit local broadcast stations on Tuesday.
Foulkes links Block, a former Republican, to President Donald Trump, describing the two men’s opposition to the Affordable Care Act as “horrible.” Block calls Foulkes a “puppet” based on her support from powerful labor unions and party officials.
Foulkes has spent more than $1.2 million on TV ads since the primary, with another $198,000 in broadcast ads on her behalf via the Alliance for a Better Rhode Island, a political group backed by the Democratic Governors Association, according to filings with federal regulators.
Block has spent over $127,000 on TV ads during the general election cycle, federal filings show.
Guckian, meanwhile, has not appeared on public broadcast networks at all, though he aired commercials on the New England Sports Network during the Boston Red Sox home opener in early April along with $3,600 worth of radio spots in the final week of the September primary. 
Foulkes has a $1.8 million outstanding loan from her 2022 primary run against Gov. Dan McKee. Block has a $1.2 million loan balance dating back to his first gubernatorial campaign in 2010.
Early voting continues through Monday, Nov. 2. The race also includes independents Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds, neither of whom filed the pre-election campaign finance report as of Wednesday afternoon.
Reporter Christopher Shea contributed to this story.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Lawmakers urge DCFS to revive expired psychiatric care contract for foster kids
text:
State lawmakers are urging the Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services to reach terms with the Tulane Institute of Infant and Early Childhood Mental Health to resume its services for the state's foster care program. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Mental healthcare for Louisiana’s foster children in crisis faces an uncertain future after the state’s child welfare agency could not reach terms to renew a contract that’s been in place for more than 30 years. In response, state lawmakers have pleaded with the leader of the Department of Children and Family Services to work through the impasse.    
Psychiatrists with Tulane University’s medical school have provided services to children in the state’s foster care system and their families since 1994, with a focus on complex cases. Its Institute of Infant and Early Childhood Mental Health has been recognized nationally and internationally by practitioners and scholars for its groundbreaking work with very young children who’ve been through abuse, trauma and neglect.
The state’s contract with Tulane lapsed at the end of September after more than a year of negotiations, DCFS Secretary Rebecca Harris told the state Senate Health and Welfare Committee at its Oct. 12 meeting. 
At the heart of the dispute is Tulane’s refusal to get approval from the state before providing services. Harris said this process would ensure the state doesn’t have to pay for care that qualifies for federal Medicaid coverage.
But Dr. Charles Zeanah, the psychiatrist who co-founded and leads Tulane’s Infant Institute, told lawmakers that requiring DCFS pre-clearance doesn’t take into account the real-time needs of his team.
“Either we can be trusted by DCFS to make good clinical decisions on the fly, or they should not contract with us,” Zeanah said.
The state relies on the institute staff to assess the mental health of children who experience abuse and provide them with needed care. Tulane also provides special support for drug- and alcohol-affected infants, and they assist foster families and caregiver relatives when children have to be housed away from their biological parents.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A copy of Tulane’s DCFS contract, obtained through a public records request, shows it was paid more than $400,000 for its services in the fiscal year that ended June 30. It was given a three-month extension worth nearly $134,000 to provide care through September.
Contract documents show the money goes toward Zeanah’s salary as well as seven psychologists who all allocate 100% of their time to the program. Language in Tulane’s contract says the state justifiably pays for these outside services because “DCFS staff [is] unable to fulfill this work responsibility. DCFS does not have programmatic capacity to service this client population.” 
The money paid to Tulane comes from a federal grant, specifically the $7 million provided in 2024 from the MaryLee Allen Promoting Safe and Stable Families program under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 
Tulane also puts up 25% in matching funds required for such federal grants, Zeanah said. 
It’s not evident how many foster children or families receive psychiatric care annually through Tulane’s team, but Zeanah told the Senate committee his staff will continue to serve the 15 families who are currently under their care. They won’t take any new cases unless the contract dispute is resolved. 
Zeanah declined an interview after the hearing through a Tulane spokesman, and DCFS has not provided an update when asked whether contract negotiations have resumed with Tulane. 
At the hearing, Harris said if Tulane continues to bill DCFS directly for its service, it could negatively impact the calculations Medicaid uses to determine its reimbursement rates for care providers. 
She also cited a Legislative Auditor’s report that found DCFS spent more than $20 million to provide services that Medicaid would have been covered, though the report from April states “it is unclear” whether some of the services should have been paid through the federal program.
Harris also pushed back against suggestions that her stance on the Tulane contract is financially motivated.
“We have been having conversations for over a year, and where the conversations started had nothing to do with efficiency but more to do with what is right,” Harris said.
Harris has implemented an overhaul of the DCFS child welfare division since Gov. Jeff Landry put her in charge of the agency in August 2025. It has included the reassignment of office-based supervisors to casework in the field and replacing a remote-staffed abuse hotline staff with an in-house call center. Both moves prompted dozens of retirements and resignations. 
Harris and her predecessors have been faced with persistently high levels of child abuse and neglect, including child fatalaties involving households who have had prior contact with DCFS.
Bipartisan frustration with the agency from lawmakers reached a peak in the spring when two measures were proposed to dismantle DCFS and hand off its responsibilities to other state departments. The governor stepped in to sideline those plans.
Some of that discontent remained evident at the Senate committee hearing, where lawmakers took turns pressing Harris for an explanation on why the Tulane contract was allowed to expire.
“As hard as it’s been to climb the hill, this knocks us back because we’re spending a lot of time and energy on something that’s been so positive for over 30 years,” Sen. Gerald Boudreaux, D-Lafayette, told her.
State Rep. Kim Carver, R-Mandeville, who joined senators for the hearing, also recommended Harris work to revive the Tulane contract. He acknowledged the DCFS child welfare staff holds perhaps the most difficult jobs in state government but said the decision to let the contract end will make things worse.
“I feel like I’m in an alternate universe,” Carver said.

name: VTDigger
title: Why Proposal 4 matters to LGBTQ+ youth
text:
This commentary is by Dana Kaplan, executive director of Outright Vermont.
Every day at Outright Vermont, we work alongside young people who are worried. They’re worried about their safety, the rollback of their rights, and their futures. With over 530 anti-LGBTQ+ bills across the country, their very existence is being debated among adults, and their access to healthcare, education, sports and other opportunities is shrinking. For queer and transgender young people, these are not theoretical threats or concerns; they are very real and impact their lives today. 
That is why Proposal 4 matters.
On Nov. 3, Proposal 4 will be on the ballot, and Vermonters will decide whether to amend our state constitution to permanently protect against discrimination based on characteristics including race, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and national origin. Proposal 4 would put these equal rights protections into Vermont’s constitution, making our commitment to equal rights more lasting.
It’s important to recognize that we have laws in place to protect Vermonters, but as we bear witness to what is happening across the country, laws alone can be tenuous protections and can change as political leadership changes.
With today’s reality as the backdrop, imagine being a young person planning for your future. Will you be treated equally when you attend school or search for a job or housing? Will you be able to live in a community where you know you are safe? 

READ MORE

Nobody should have to wonder whether their rights will be protected. And they should not have to be exceptional or endlessly resilient to be treated equally. Everyone deserves to know that they belong, that they matter, and that Vermont’s commitment to equality is more than a promise; it’s codified in our state’s constitution. 
Proposal 4 would send a strong message to LGBTQ+ young people and to all Vermonters who have experienced discrimination: You belong. You matter. Your rights will not depend on the goodwill of others — they are in the Vermont Constitution.  
And let’s be clear: This is not symbolic, and equality is not a limited resource. It’s about making permanent protections against discrimination for people across communities who have experienced unequal treatment. No one loses, and there are no trade-offs here. Making our commitment to equality clear is good for all Vermonters, and it’s staying true to our values as a state. It says to young people: Your future is not a political bargaining chip. You deserve a state that puts its commitment to your dignity, safety and equal treatment in its most fundamental governing document.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why Proposal 4 matters to LGBTQ+ youth.

name: Delaware
title: UD Technology Helps Ford Push Lower-Cost Electric Trucks Toward Two-Way Power
text:
Photo – Researchers at UD, including Willett Kempton and Rodney McGee, helped make this technology more affordable and practical.
University of Delaware professor Willett Kempton helped pioneer vehicle-to-grid technology nearly 30 years ago. Now Ford says a UD-developed communications standard is part of its new affordable electric truck platform.
NEWARK, Del. — Technology developed at the University of Delaware is playing a role in Ford Motor Co.’s effort to bring bidirectional power — the ability for an electric vehicle to send electricity back to a home or the electric grid — to a new generation of lower-cost electric trucks.
Ford said Tuesday, Oct. 27, that its 2027 Fathom electric truck will use SAE J3068 with LIN-CP, a communications technology standard developed at the University of Delaware, as part of an electrical architecture intended to make bidirectional charging less expensive.
The connection puts decades of Delaware research led in part by University of Delaware professor Willett Kempton into a vehicle Ford expects to sell for a starting manufacturer’s suggested retail price of $28,350.
Ford says the truck will be capable of supplying a projected 10 kilowatts or more of alternating-current power to a home without requiring the separate wall-mounted inverter used by some earlier systems.
Delaware professor helped pioneer the technology
Kempton and University of Delaware colleagues pioneered vehicle-to-grid, or V2G, technology nearly three decades ago. The idea is relatively simple: Instead of an electric vehicle battery only drawing power from the grid, a properly equipped vehicle can also return power when electricity is needed.
The technology could turn millions of parked vehicles into distributed energy-storage resources.
“Whether it could scale cost-effectively was an open question, and we’ve proven that it can — with the right combination of policies, standards and technology,” Kempton said earlier this year after completion of a Delaware V2G pilot project.
Kempton is a professor of marine science and policy and electrical and computer engineering at UD and is nationally recognized for his work on electric vehicles and vehicle-to-grid systems.
Ford’s announcement provides one of the clearest indications yet that some of the technology developed in Delaware could move beyond research projects and limited demonstrations toward mass-market vehicles.
Ford develops lower-cost system
Ford said cost has been one of the primary barriers preventing bidirectional power from becoming widely available.
Electric vehicle batteries store electricity as direct current, while homes typically use alternating current. Earlier systems often depended on additional external equipment to convert and manage that electricity.
Ford says the Fathom will instead incorporate its inverter into the vehicle’s electrical system, allowing the truck to produce AC power without a separate wall-mounted inverter.
The company said the approach uses fewer multifunctional components and is designed to lower the cost of the vehicle and supporting home equipment.
The truck’s communications architecture is where Delaware enters the picture directly.
Ford said Fathom uses SAE J3068 with LIN-CP, describing it as an existing communications technology developed at the University of Delaware that also helps reduce the cost of the vehicle’s charger.
That distinction is important: UD did not design Ford’s new truck or its entire bidirectional electrical system. Ford says it developed the Fathom hardware and software architecture after acquiring startup Auto Motive Power in 2023.
But the automaker is incorporating a communications approach developed through UD’s work into a production vehicle designed specifically around lower cost.
Delaware research moves from laboratory to electric grid
The Ford announcement follows years of cooperation involving UD, Ford, Delmarva Power and PJM Interconnection.
In 2024, the partners demonstrated vehicle-to-grid technology in Newark using Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles from Delmarva Power’s fleet.
The vehicles could continue performing their normal utility work while also providing grid services when they were parked and plugged in. Multiple vehicle batteries could be connected electronically and managed as a single resource known as a virtual power plant.
UD researchers also helped develop standards needed for vehicles, chargers and utilities to communicate safely and inexpensively.
Rodney McGee, director of UD’s Center for Transportation Electrification, previously led an SAE committee working on standards that incorporate LIN-CP signaling for low-cost AC charging, V2G operation and vehicle backup power.
Research suggests financial benefits for vehicle owners
The research reached another milestone this year.
A University of Delaware and Exelon/Delmarva Power report released in April found that the V2G-equipped vehicles used in the pilot successfully provided services in actual electricity markets.
Researchers calculated that, based on electricity-market prices from 2021 through 2025, a V2G-enabled passenger electric vehicle could potentially earn as much as $3,359 annually by providing grid services.
Heavier vehicles such as delivery trucks, fleet vehicles and school buses could potentially earn more than $9,000 per year because of their larger batteries.
Those figures are research estimates based on historical market conditions, not guaranteed payments for consumers.
The pilot also found no measured reduction in battery health after a year of market operation, according to UD.
The potential financial benefits are particularly significant for commercial fleet operators, school districts and utilities that could eventually use parked electric trucks and buses to generate revenue while helping stabilize the electrical grid.
A truck becomes more than transportation
For consumers, Ford is initially emphasizing two applications.
Its Home Power Management system is intended to allow customers to charge a truck when electricity is less expensive and then use some of the battery’s energy to power their homes when rates are higher.
The truck can also provide backup electricity during an outage.
Both applications require additional Ford home equipment, although Ford says its new Home Power Station is expected to cost roughly half as much as the company’s first-generation bidirectional charger. Backup operation will require an additional Home Backup Power Panel.
For Delaware homeowners concerned about rising electricity costs and reliability, the technology could eventually offer another way to manage household energy expenses.
However, actual savings will depend on electricity rates, equipment costs, vehicle usage and the availability of utility programs.
Delaware could play a role in national expansion
The larger opportunity — sending power into the electric grid and being compensated for grid services — remains more complicated.
Utilities and regulators must establish interconnection rules governing how vehicles operating as power resources connect safely to the grid.
Ford formed a working group in July with five major utilities, including Exelon, the parent company of Delmarva Power, to develop more standardized interconnection procedures before Fathom reaches customers in 2027.
That puts Delaware in an unusual position.
UD researchers helped pioneer V2G technology. Delaware was the first state to change its laws to permit electric vehicles to provide services to the electric grid. Ford vehicles have already been used in a Delmarva Power V2G demonstration, and Exelon is now participating in Ford’s effort to prepare utilities for broader deployment.
The next question: When will Delaware drivers benefit?
What remains uncertain is how soon ordinary Delaware customers will be able to use a vehicle such as the Fathom not only to power their homes but also to sell services into the electric grid.
Although Delaware has helped lead the research, broader consumer participation will depend on utility interconnection requirements, regulatory approvals, available compensation programs and the cost of compatible equipment.
Ford says Fathom arrives in 2027.
For Kempton and the University of Delaware, the launch could mark an important transition for an idea that began as university research decades ago: from proving that electric vehicles could support the electric grid to helping make the technology affordable enough to reach everyday drivers



TO GO BOX

What: Ford Fathom electric truck with bidirectional power capability.
When: Expected to launch in 2027.
Starting price: $28,350 MSRP, according to Ford.
Delaware connection: Ford says the truck uses SAE J3068 with LIN-CP, a communications technology developed at the University of Delaware.
What it can do: Supply electricity to a home, provide backup power during outages and potentially support electric grid services where utility programs allow.
Why it matters: UD researchers, Delmarva Power, Ford and PJM have demonstrated V2G technology in Delaware. Ford’s new truck could help bring some of that technology into broader consumer use.

name: Mississippi Today
title: How MVSU lost and regained a star basketball recruit from ICE detention
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
International student Qingfang Pang had barely touched down on his new campus in Itta Bena last month when he learned his expired visa could thwart his hopes of finally breaking into the highest ranks of college basketball, according to his new school, Mississippi Valley State University.
MVSU spokesperson Donnell Maxie remembered that day: The 6-foot-9-inch junior forward from China hadn’t been in Delta Devils territory for long, but he quickly caught students’ attention at the small, historically Black institution nestled in the fields ringing the tiny Delta college town.
“You walk around, and you’re a 7-foot or 6-9 Asian kid here,” Maxie said. “Everybody wants to talk to you.”
The semester was already in full swing — classes were a couple weeks in, and basketball season was due to kick off in less than two months — when Maxie said MVSU secured Pang as a late admit. As a player, he was different from the Delta Devils’ usual picks as the worst-ranked team in NCAA Division I basketball for the last three years in a row.
Mississippi Valley State University is seen on Wednesday, March 4, 2026, in Itta Bena. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Delta Devils are a basketball team with such a storied losing streak that they rake in funding for MVSU’s whole athletic department by traveling the country to get demolished in “buy games” against powerhouse schools — taking home a payout of up to $100,000 a match. The team hasn’t won a nonconference game against a Division I opponent in 20 years, but it did earn nearly $1 million in buy games in 2024.
The news of Pang’s addition ignited the hopes of fans of the underdog team such as Oliver Fell, who opened a fan account on X to find humor in the Delta Devils’ many losses. He has accrued over 10 times more followers than the team’s actual account.
Pang was taller than the usual MVSU baller, and more sought after. Coming out of high school in Queens in 2024, he garnered over 10 offers, including multiple bids from top-ranked Division I teams, like the University of Illinois and University of Michigan.
He ended up cutting his teeth on junior college basketball at Monroe University in New York for the last two years. This fall at MVSU marked his break into Division I basketball. 
Mississippi Valley State University basketball forward Qingfang Pang plays for his previous team, the Monroe University Mustangs. He played for the New York team during the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Credit: Monroe College Athletics
Pang stood out as an unconventional Delta Devils player for new head coach Mike Davis’ equally unconventional lineup — one that was filled with taller and more diverse talent than past teams at the HBCU. He was one of three ballers with an international background and two non-Black players, along with 7-foot center Tianhao “Howie” Wu, who also hailed from China.
“Pang is a guy who is frankly a caliber of player MVSU doesn’t get all that often,” Fell said. “A player who is excited to be a part of this team, who is certainly going to be one of the centerpieces on the squad and who brings a different kind of player and personality than Valley has seen before.
“Athletically, missing Pang would be a huge blow to the squad.”
Then, after Pang’s one day on campus, he was gone.
Three weeks in ICE detention
Pang hadn’t gotten the chance to play on the Delta Devils’ court when his new school realized his visa had expired, Maxie said. Pang and MVSU realized his transition wouldn’t run as smoothly as they had hoped.
Pang had been busy running through a checklist of first-day duties on campus. Maxie said he sat for a player photoshoot and met with the school’s international student services, which is in charge of making sure MVSU’s small contingent of 60 international students follows immigration requirements. 
The staff reviewed his documentation. Things quickly derailed from there, according to Maxie.
“Within 10 minutes of him being there, they told him, ‘Hey, man, you know your visa has expired?’” Maxie said.
Mississippi Valley State University’s Delta Devils basketball team announced the addition of forward Qingfang Pang in a September 14, 2026, social media post, two weeks before he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement after his visa apparently expired. “A FRESH START,” the post’s caption read. Credit: Via Instagram
Up to that point, Pang wasn’t aware his visa had expired, as he mistakenly believed that Monroe had arranged for it to be reinstated, according to his attorney, Marcus Session, a former professional basketball player. Monroe spokesperson Jacqueline Ruegger said the school warned Pang two years ago to reinstate his visa and that he had met with an attorney to discuss the issue at the university’s recommendation.
Because Monroe had already issued him the necessary immigration documents, Ruegger said, he was allowed to remain in the U.S. as long as he was maintaining a full course load at the school. But ultimately, he never reinstated his visa, and he graduated from Monroe in April with his associate degree in sports management.
In an effort to resolve his visa issues at MVSU, Pang decided to get a flight to New York to meet with his sponsor, a family friend, Session told WJTV. 
But in the process, Session said, he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the Greenville airport on Sept. 29, amid what immigration attorneys say is an increasing wave of immigration arrests at airports.
Aminata “Amina” Seck, a center on Kentucky State University’s basketball team from Senegal, is among the international student athletes who have been detained by immigration authorities in 2026 in high-profile detention cases for what the Department of Homeland Security has characterized as illegal overstays.  Credit: Kentucky State University Athletics
Pang’s case follows a string of high-profile detentions of college student athletes in recent months, including fellow HBCU basketball player Aminata “Amina” Seck, over what the Department of Homeland Security has said are illegal overstays. Immigration law experts said these issues have traditionally been resolved by simply filing paperwork to reinstate the students’ visas. But the Trump administration has had an unprecedented approach: detention.
“Making an example of high-profile people is a very strong way to send a message,” said Adam Cohen, a Memphis-based immigration attorney who specializes in representing universities and international students. “It discourages and makes people fearful.”
ICE held Pang in detention at Richwood Correctional Center in rural Louisiana. Federal inspectors have uncovered a history of violations at the facility, including unsanitary conditions and restricting detainees’ access to their attorneys without any justification. 
The day ICE arrested Pang, an immigrant from Peru who was being held at the detention center died of a heart attack from septic shock.
DHS wrote in a statement after his arrest that Pang “accepted voluntary departure” — an agreement to leave the U.S. — and would remain in ICE custody until his “removal.” But Pang didn’t know what he was agreeing to and was “tired” of being treated like a “criminal,” Session said.
Federal inspectors cited Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana for housing detainees in unsanitary conditions in a 2023 report, including these stained and discolored showers. Credit: Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General
Pang wanted to return to basketball and classes, but Session said authorities told him to sign a removal order and failed to provide him with an interpreter — a violation for which federal inspectors have previously cited the detention center.
Pang was gone just weeks before the Delta Devils’ basketball season was about to kick off, with MVSU not knowing when — or if — he could return.
“No one thought this would happen here,” Maxie said. “Yet we’re still doing everything we can to make sure we help this student, like we would do for any of our students.”
Fans rallied around the Delta Devils’ new recruit as his detention garnered national attention. Fell launched an online petition calling for his release that racked up over 500 signatures.
“He’s been gone since the 29th of September,” Fell said, “in a facility meant to house violent criminals that doesn’t seem to treat these detainees as if they are anything more than that.”


A detainee at Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana, holds up a burned shirt. After a surprise inspection, federal inspectors in 2023 found the detention center violated standards by providing detainees with burned, rusted and foul-smelling clothes. Credit: Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General


A detainee at Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana, shows a ragged, dirty sock. Federal inspectors found in a 2023 report that the detention center failed to provide suitable living conditions for detainees by giving them torn and damaged clothes. Credit: Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General


Pang’s case reminded international student Israel Makoka of his time in a cell at another immigration detention center in Louisiana, after ICE arrested him and his younger brother Max in April while they were waiting for their school bus in Hancock County. Their arrests marked some of Mississippi’s highest profile immigration cases this year.
“You can’t do anything,” Makoka said, “You’re just in a room.
“You start questioning everything: Why did I even come to America?”
Makoka, who is from the Republic of Congo, spent nine days in ICE custody. Since then, he’s tried to resume life as any other 18-year-old, by graduating high school, moving away from his host family, starting his freshman year at Hinds Community College and playing for the basketball team there.
But Pang’s case hit close to home for Makoka and his host mother, Gail Baptiste. Like Pang, Makoka found support in the basketball community when he was detained after he and his brother unknowingly violated their student visas by transferring to a school closer to their host family.
Max Makoka, Gail Baptiste and Israel Makoka pose for a photo in Houston, Texas, on Thursday, April 30, 2026, after the teens were released from nine days of ICE detention. Gail and her husband, Cliff Baptiste, are host parents for the teenage brothers from the Republic of Congo. Credit: Courtesy of Gail Baptiste
What started as a mistake set off an immigration case that the Makoka brothers and their host family are still navigating. As Makoka awaits a decision in immigration court on whether his visa can be reinstated, he has to wear an ankle monitor everywhere as a condition of his release. 
“I feel a little connected to him,” Baptiste said of Pang’s case. “When it’s a kid, and they have the language barrier, and they’re trusting other people to understand the process.”
After three weeks in ICE custody, Session said, the removal order Pang signed was rescinded, and he was released from detention on Oct. 20 on a $12,000 bond. His return came just in time for the Delta Devils’ season opener on Nov. 6: a matchup against the Oklahoma Sooners. 
His attorney applied for his visa to be reinstated, and it could take 15 months for his application to be processed, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ current estimates. As he awaits a decision, he may return to classes and the basketball court. 
Nichole Francis Reynolds, Coach Davis’ cousin and a Washington-area attorney who assisted with Pang’s case, said the forward would play before the school Saturday in MVSU’s Halloween basketball game.
Israel Makoka, a senior at Hancock High School, looks for some working room in a basketball game versus Long Beach High School, Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, in Pascagoula.  Credit: Bobby McDuffie/South Miss 6 Sports
Upon his release, Pang thanked Mississippi’s U.S. senators, Republicans Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, for helping to move his case forward. Despite their track record as Trump allies who support the president’s immigration policies, the senators’ intervention also proved pivotal in securing the Makokas’ release from detention, after the brothers’ largely conservative Gulf Coast community advocated for their return. Neither senator’s office responded to Mississippi Today’s request for comment.
But most of all, Pang was excited to return to the court.
“Thank you to Coach Mike Davis and the assistant coaches, who believed in me and never stopped supporting me, and to my teammates for standing by me,” he said in a statement. “I am looking forward to going back to school, catching up on my classes, and playing basketball again for Mississippi Valley State.”
What went wrong? 
MVSU maintains that as an international student, Pang bears sole responsibility to ensure he maintains a proper immigration status. On MVSU’s part, Maxie said the school fulfilled its responsibility to manage his international student records and help him navigate immigration requirements.
“It is on the student to then follow through, and he did not follow through,” Maxie said. “So this is all of his own doing, unfortunately.”
Mississippi Valley State University is seen on Wednesday, March 4, 2026, in Itta Bena. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
While Pang is legally responsible for ensuring his status, immigration law experts said, based on the available information, MVSU also bears some responsibility.
Cohen said MVSU was “late” in fulfilling the requirements that came with Pang’s transfer as an international student. Before Pang even came to campus, according to Cohen, the university should have reviewed his documentation and noticed his visa had expired. It should have obtained his international student records from Monroe and issued him a key document called a Form I-20, which would confirm his enrollment to immigration authorities and allow him to apply for his visa to be reinstated.
But MVSU didn’t fulfill those responsibilities until after Pang was already on campus or even later, when ICE had already detained him.
“It’s late in the game to be just seeing this file and the student’s there on campus,” Cohen said. “It’s like basically going to a university and taking classes before that university even has jurisdiction over your student record.”
It wasn’t until Pang was in ICE custody that MVSU moved to obtain his international student records from Monroe and issue him a Form I-20, according to Maxie. But he said MVSU didn’t cause any “paperwork delay,” saying the school’s international student services notified Pang about his expired visa as soon as they noticed it.
Qingfang Pang played basketball in the junior college league for the Monroe University Mustangs in New York during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, before joining Mississippi Valley State University’s Delta Devils during the fall 2026 semester. Credit: Monroe College Athletics
“Our people, they are on top of this stuff. They don’t play about this stuff,” Maxie said. “They make sure that their documents and their paperwork is in line so that we don’t have issues, particularly in this political climate that we’re in.”
Pang’s case has also raised questions about the accuracy of the Department of Homeland Security’s public explanation for his arrest. The department wrote in a statement that Pang was arrested after he “legally” entered the country while in high school in 2023 on a “temporary basis not to exceed September 5, 2024, but illegally overstayed.”
That last day fell on his first week of classes as a freshman at Monroe. Ruegger said that while Pang’s visa had expired then, the school had already issued him a valid Form I-20, allowing him to legally remain in the country as long as he was taking classes at Monroe.
As a result, Cohen said he couldn’t see how it was in any way “accurate” for DHS to say that Pang had illegally overstayed his visa for the last two years. The department did not respond to Mississippi Today’s request for comment about the basis of its explanation.
“I think they are just embellishments and half truths or no truths,” Cohen said of DHS’ statement. “It’s amazing to see what is said and compare it to the actual truth of it.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Can Ron DeSantis push Amendment 3 over the top?
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking the USF Health Morsani Center for Advanced Healthcare in Tampa on June 25, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Ron DeSantis was in Crystal River Wednesday, ostensibly to announce that his administration was providing an additional $100 million to restore and protect Florida’s water resources across 45 projects.
However, he spent nearly half of his press conference making the case once again for Amendment 3, the proposal on the statewide ballot that would cut property taxes for Florida homeowners.
With six days to go before Election Day, polls indicate the proposal might be in danger of failing.
A St. Pete Polls survey released Wednesday shows the measure with 44% support, with 39% opposed and 17% unsure. A University of North Florida poll released last week found Amendment 3 getting 50% support. Both would fall far short of the 60% threshold required for passage.
Although the governor has been the main driving force for well over a year-and-a-half in placing the property tax cut proposal before the voters, he initially declined to campaign for it after the Republican-controlled Legislature in June enacted changes to his original language.
He has since reversed that stance and has been actively supporting it, although not in any campaign ads. On Monday, he held a roundtable discussion with U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody and Department of Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson to extoll the proposal’s virtues and praised it again Wednesday as his press conference aired on the Florida Channel.
A variety of organizations have strongly opposed the measure, fearing it would significantly reduce tax revenues for local governments, forcing them to make serious budget cuts. State economists have estimated Amendment 3 would reduce revenue by $5 billion in its first year and as much as $12 billion annually when fully implemented.
The governor made the case in Crystal River that local governments can afford to take a financial haircut, noting they took in $32 billion in property tax revenues in 2019 and now receive $62 billion, well above what he says the pace of inflation and population growth would justify.
“My question is for those who say that we won’t have any services if Amendment 3 passes, did we not have services in 2019?” DeSantis asked. “So, don’t tell me we can’t give our homesteaders a relief. We can do it. One hundred percent.”
Law enforcement agencies such as the Florida Police Chiefs Association, have come out against the measure. In Jacksonville Wednesday, Jennifer “Cookie” Pritt, executive director of the organization, said during a press conference, “Before you vote, ask yourself one question: Where will the money for your local police come from? If no one can give you a straight answer, that tells you what you need to know about Amendment 3.”
DeSantis insisted again that if Amendment 3 passes, he would work with the Legislature to create a fund for fiscally constrained and other “bedroom” communities in places like the Tampa Bay area where they could apply for grants if they need more revenue for “critical needs” — to hire more police officers, for example.
The Legislature killed a provision of the governor’s original proposal that would have created a state trust fund to help local governments cover revenue shortfalls. There is no guarantee lawmakers would agree to do that in the approximately two months DeSantis has left in office.
The governor expressed concern that the Republican turnout hasn’t “been as strong as we would like to see” in vote-by-mail and early voting numbers that have come in. More than 3.7 million Floridians have voted so far, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, with registered Republicans holding a 1.2% lead over registered Democrats, 40.2%-39% (independent and third party registered voters amount to 21% of the state’s vote total to date).
The Republican Party of Florida has endorsed Amendment 3, while the Florida Democratic Party has opposes the measure.
Campaign spending has been heavily titled towards the pro-Amendment 3 forces. A political committee formed by the Florida Realtors to support it has raised more than $21.5 million, according to state election records.  The two political committees opposing Amendment 3, Floridians for Shared Prosperity and Vote No on 3 Florida, have raised a combined $1.3 million.
“I think that we need to do a better job of early voting,” DeSantis said. “Republicans have some work to do, and you guys just got to get out there and vote and then let the people’s will carry the day.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado requests $65M in federal relief to help with Pagosa Springs area flooding
text:
A view of San Juan River flooding in downtown Pagosa Springs on Friday. (Photo courtesy of Jacque Aragon)The Colorado Department of Transportation on Tuesday asked for $65 million from the federal government to assist with significant road repairs in the southwest part of the state, which experienced immense flooding over the weekend.
The total is just an estimate of the damage, and the state wants $6.5 million released immediately to start work.
“Our team has already done incredible work to restore access, and will continue to do so,” Shoshana Lew, the department’s executive director, said in a statement. “We know from experience that the Federal Highway Administration are tremendous partners when we encounter emergencies, and we truly appreciate their quick engagement as we work in real time to determine damages and repair needs to keep Southwest Colorado moving.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department estimates the bulk of that money, around $45 million, would be for repairing the visible damage on roads. The rest would go toward fixing non-visible assumed damage, engineering costs, field preparation, maintenance crews and administration.
Houses near County Road 335 in Pagosa Springs were flooded after recent storms. (Photo Courtesy of Cheri Maxwell)
Storms between Oct. 22 and Oct. 25 brought up to 7 inches of rain in areas like Pagosa Springs, and the San Juan River reached 15.02 feet in Pagosa Springs — up from under 6 feet two days earlier — on Oct. 23, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It has since receded to around 7 feet as of Wednesday afternoon. As surrounding waterways overflowed, the flooding topped 4 feet on some roads and damaged significant thoroughfares in the area. Wolf Creek Pass along Highway 160, the main connector between Pagosa Springs and South Fork, closed at the start of the flooding and reopened Tuesday, though officials caution travelers to plan for delays as traffic narrows to single lanes in damaged areas.
“While (CDOT) continues to assess the full extent of structural damage to roads and bridges, it is clear that needs will be significant and immediate, especially in order to make as many repairs as possible before winter,” the request letter reads.
The department also reported damage on U.S. 160 west of Pagosa Springs, Red Mountain Pass on U.S. 550 and Colo. 151.
Gov. Jared Polis verbally declared a disaster emergency in response to the flooding in La Plata, Archuleta, Montezuma, Dolores, Hinsdale, San Miguel, Ouray, San Juan, Mineral, Alamosa and Rio Grande counties. That activated around 100 Colorado National Guard members to help with search and rescues. The state’s Transportation Commission approved $5 million on Monday to help with initial repair efforts.
Drivers can see real-time travel alerts and road conditions through CDOT’s COTrip website.

name: National
title: Voters with felony convictions face new rules in several states for the midterms
text:
Incarcerated people at the Cook County Jail in Chicago cast their votes in the 2020 Illinois primary election. This year, more than a handful of states across the country have enacted laws changing voting rules for people with felony convictions. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)A half-dozen states enacted laws this year changing voting rules for people with felony convictions, including when their rights can be restored and how they can register to vote — affecting voters in next week’s elections.
A couple other states advanced measures that will affect such voters in future elections. And Virginia voters will decide on Tuesday whether to approve a measure advanced by the legislature to automatically restore such rights.
Altogether, at least eight states — Alabama, Delaware, Idaho, Maryland, Missouri, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Virginia — advanced or enacted legislation addressing voting rights for people with felony convictions or people who are incarcerated, according to legislation tracked by Ballotpedia and the National Conference of State Legislatures.
States put criminal justice, marijuana policies before voters in 2026

Currently, 23 states automatically restore voting rights upon release from incarceration for a felony conviction, while 15 require people to complete additional conditions, typically probation or parole, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. In 10 states, certain felony convictions can result in indefinite disenfranchisement or require additional steps to restore voting rights, while Maine, Vermont and the District of Columbia allow people with felony convictions to vote even while incarcerated.
In Virginia, voters will decide whether to amend the state constitution to automatically restore voting rights to people with felony convictions upon release from incarceration. Currently, the state constitution requires the governor or another appropriate authority to restore the rights.
Lawmakers approved the proposed amendment earlier this year, along with legislation that would align state law with the change. But the statutory changes are contingent on voter approval of the amendment and would not take effect until January 2027.
Missouri enacted a law in July allowing people convicted of certain felonies to regain voting rights before completing probation or parole, while maintaining the requirement for people convicted of specified offenses to complete those terms. The measure went into effect in late August.
In Oklahoma, lawmakers revised voting eligibility requirements for people with felony convictions, allowing those who receive a pardon or commutation to regain voting rights, provided they are not incarcerated or serving probation, parole or supervision for another felony conviction. The law, which takes effect Nov. 1, also clarifies eligibility requirements for people who have completed their sentences.
Tennessee this spring revised its voting rights restoration requirements, replacing provisions requiring payment of court costs and current child support obligations with a requirement that applicants have complied with child support orders for the preceding 12 months.
New laws restore voting rights to residents with felony convictions

A new law in Alabama, which went into effect on Oct. 1, requires the state Board of Pardons and Paroles to publish voting rights restoration procedures and an application on its website. The law also requires the board to post identifying information for people on probation or parole whose voting rights have been restored.
Meanwhile, a new law in Idaho, which went into effect in July, prohibits people convicted of treason in another state or jurisdiction from registering or voting in Idaho, even after completing their sentences. The change brings voting restrictions for out-of-state treason convictions in line with those for people convicted of treason in Idaho.
Some measures would affect voters in future elections.
In Delaware, lawmakers advanced a proposed constitutional amendment that would automatically restore voting rights to people with felony convictions upon release from prison, rather than requiring them to complete their sentences, including probation and payment of fines. The measure would have to pass the legislature again in the next session before taking effect.
In Maryland, Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed into law a measure requiring state corrections officials by Jan. 1, 2028, to provide monthly information about people released from state correctional facilities to election officials, who must use the information to automatically restore their voter registrations. 
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Trump approves Hurricane Isaias disaster relief 12 days after it was made
text:
A tree from the neighboring lot fell on Darryl Sweet's home in Pensacola, Florida, during Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The Federal Emergency Management Agency has announced that President Donald Trump approved Florida’s request for a major disaster declaration authorizing public assistance funds to help Florida local governments recover from Hurricane Isaias.
The announcement, 12 days after Gov. Ron DeSantis submitted the request, doesn’t say how much money has been approved.
Florida Division of Emergency Management Director of Communications Stephanie Hartman told the Phoenix earlier this month the state sought roughly $237 million for “debris removal, public infrastructure, and emergency protective measures.”
The 15 counties approved for public assistance are Bay, Calhoun, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gulf, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Liberty, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Wakulla, Walton, and Washington.
The FEMA website indicates the state’s request for individual assistance for nearly 1,000 damaged residencies in eight counties still is under review. Those counties are Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Holmes, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton, and Washington.
12 Days later
Hurricane Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 Hurricane in Destin Oct. 9 with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph.

The DeSantis administration submitted a disaster request with FEMA on the evening of Oct. 15. During a press conference announcing the request, DeSantis said he expected a decision ” very, very, quickly.”
While the request was sent to FEMA, only the president was authorized to approve it.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
GAO FEMA report
Trump announced in the summer of 2025 that he wanted to phase out FEMA and put states more in control of their emergency responses. Since then, Trump has continue to approve disaster requests from states stemming from weather events.
FEMA, like other federal agencies, has made workforce reductions.
An August 2026 General Accounting Office report found that in fiscal year 2025 more than 4,300 employees “separated” from FEMA, a 55% increase in separations from fiscal year 2024.
“These separations have resulted in a loss of institutional knowledge and experienced personnel, according to FEMA officials, and have exacerbated longstanding workforce challenges,” the GAO report found.
FEMA rescinded its strategic work plan in 2025.
“As a result, the agency has no overall strategic direction on which to base workforce planning — a systematic and continuous process for identifying the size and composition of a workforce needed to achieve an agency’s mission,” the GAO report notes. “Without a strategic plan that outlines clear goals and objectives, FEMA cannot effectively determine its future workforce needs, potentially putting its mission at risk.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico leaders pay tribute to civil rights icon Dolores Huerta following her death at 96
text:
New Mexico-born civil rights activist Dolores Huerta, a celebrated labor leader who received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, died Oct. 28, 2026, at age 96, according to her family. Above: Huerta during a visit to Albuquerque in November 2021 to push for federal infrastructure spending. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Legendary civil rights activist and United Farm Workers co-founder Dolores Huerta, a native New Mexican, died Wednesday at her home in California.
“We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96,” her family wrote in a statement posted by the Dolores Huerta Foundation on Wednesday morning. “As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy.”

Erik Olvera, a spokesperson for Huerta’s foundation, told Source NM in an email that Huerta died Wednesday morning from cancer, “surrounded by her family.” 
Huerta was born in Dawson, a small mining town in Northeastern New Mexico before becoming an effective and celebrated activist for migrant farmworkers across the United States. She co-founded United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez in the early 1960s, where the pair first began mobilizing migrant farm workers working on large grape farms in California.
A mural of Dolores Huerta at Broadway Boulevard and Lead Avenue in Albuquerque, photographedMarch 18, 2026. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) pictured with Dolores Huerta at the National Hispanic Cultural Center in Albuquerque, wrote in a statement Oct. 28, 2026, that Huerta once told her, 'You should dance in your 20s so you can march in your 90s.' (With permission from U.S. Rep. Leger Fernández's office)State Sen. Leo Jaramillo (D-Española) left, poses with Dolores Huerta and House Speaker and state Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) during Huerta's visit to the New Mexico Legislature in 2023. (With permission from state Sen. Leo Jaramillo)In a statement on Oct. 28, 2026, U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) called civil rights icon Dolores Huerta "a friend. A mentor. A real life super hero." (With permission from U.S. Rep. Stansbury's office)New Mexico Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque), El Paso, first met Huerta in the 1960s.
New Mexico Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) and Dolores Huerta march at a United Farm Worker rally, in an undated photo. (Photo courtesy Patricia Roybal Caballero)New Mexico Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) and Dolores Huerta, in an undated photo. (Photo courtesy Patricia Roybal Caballero)
By the late 1960s, the organization had built a growing union through much of the West and began training college students in how to build union power. That’s where New Mexico Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque), then a student at the University of Texas at El Paso, first met Huerta in the 1960s.
The two struck up a relationship that grew closer in the six decades since, Roybal Caballero told Source NM on Wednesday. The longtime Latina leader cried during a phone interview as she described what she said felt like losing her mother. 
“Every bit of who I am and what I do is rooted in my relationship with Dolores,” she said. “If I had not joined the United Farm Worker movement as young as I did, 60-plus years ago, I don’t know if my life would have been shaped in the manner that it has. It’s just in my blood.”
Roybal Caballero said Huerta’s death has further deepened her resolve to continue “la lucha,” the struggle for Latino migrant worker rights, and cement Huerta’s legacy in New Mexico, including by designating her Dawson home as a state-designated historical site. 



Quotation







Every bit of who I am and what I do is rooted in my relationship with Dolores.


– NM Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque)


Earlier this year, Roybal Caballero and other elected Latina leaders expressed solidarity with Huerta after she disclosed sexual abuse allegations against Chavez, her longtime partner in the labor movement. Huerta disclosed two incidents that led to pregnancies and two children she arranged to have raised by other families.
“I carried this secret for as long as I did because building the movement and securing farmworker rights was my life’s work,” Huerta wrote in a statement. “The formation of a union was the only vehicle to accomplish and secure those rights and I wasn’t going to let Cesar or anyone else get in the way. I channeled everything I had into advocating on behalf of millions of farmworkers and others who were suffering and deserved equal rights.”
Huerta’s decades of advocacy for farm workers prompted former President Barack Obama to award her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. 
News of Huerta’s death prompted an outpouring of condolences from New Mexico leaders. Many of them shared selfies with Huerta at marches or in the Roundhouse in recent years. 
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) wrote in a statement that Huerta once told her, “‘You should dance in your 20s so you can march in your 90s.’ And march she did. For justice. For dignity. For those whose voices were too often ignored. She taught us that the fight for a better world should be filled with joy, that resistance can be a celebration, and that the rhythm of change lives in all of us. Today, we mourn a giant. But her footsteps will echo in every march, her spirit will live in every movement, and her words will carry us forward.”



Quotation







She taught us that the fight for a better world should be filled with joy, that resistance can be a celebration, and that the rhythm of change lives in all of us.


– U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.)


U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) also described Huerta as a mentor, friend and source of inspiration. 
 “For so many of us, she was a beacon of the strength, power, and generosity of a movement that changed lives and which continues to propel us forward,” she wrote in a social media post. “To everyone grieving—we are with you and send our prayers and love to every one touched by Dolores’s work and fight.”
Even in her 90s, Huerta made appearances across the country and endorsed candidates for New Mexico local offices, including state representative and county commissioner. 
State Sen. Leo Jaramillo (D-Española), posted a photo of Huerta with him and other state lawmakers and wrote, “I’ll always remember meeting her at the Legislature. I asked if we could take a selfie, and she smiled and said, “¡Sí se puede!” It was a small moment, but one I’ll carry with me. Thank you, Dolores, for a lifetime of courage and leadership and for reminding us that when we stand together, change is possible. ¡Sí se puede!”
New Mexico House Speaker Javíer Martínez (D-Albuquerque) issued a statement noting that Huerta “lived her long life with courage and compassion. In addition to being the godmother of the farm worker movement, she was a tireless champion for working people, immigrants, women, and children right up until the very end. Dolores was also a proud daughter of New Mexico and we were fortunate that she gave so generously of her time and talents to the people of our state. Her legacy will live on in the hearts of all who speak out against injustice, stand up for the most vulnerable among us, and help our communities find their voices and build collective power.” ¡Vaya con Dios, Dolores! ¡Sí, se puede!”



Quotation







Her legacy will live on in the hearts of all who speak out against injustice, stand up for the most vulnerable among us, and help our communities find their voices.


– New Mexico House Speaker Javier Martínez


The New Mexico Senate Democratic Caucus also issued the following statement that said, “New Mexico has lost one of its own. Dolores Huerta’s story began here, in a working community. Her father was a miner, a farmworker, and a union man who served in this Legislature. She carried that legacy from northern New Mexico to the fields of California and then to the entire nation.”
New Mexico’s Nov. 3 gubernatorial candidates both issued statements, with Republican Gregg Hull saying New Mexico “has lost one of its own,” and that while Huerta’s “work carried her across the country, she never stopped being a daughter of this state. To generations of New Mexicans, she was an icon, a woman who spent her life standing up for hardworking families and showed what one determined person can accomplish. Few New Mexicans have left a mark on our nation like she did. My prayers are with her family and with everyone whose life she touched.”
Former U.S. Interior Secretary and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland said in a statement that Huerta’s legacy will “never be forgotten or erased.” 
“True servants of humanity give selflessly to make the world better for generations to come,” she said. “Dolores Huerta was a true servant of the people. Her long life fighting for workers and civil rights put dignity and respect at the forefront of our long march toward justice. She inspired generations who came after her with both words and actions, showing us all that we have the power to change the future.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Looming Medicaid cuts will increase burden for Colorado patients, advocates say
text:
Healthcare executives, patients and family members who fear cuts to Medicaid coverage under federal policy changes talked at a roundtable that U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper hosted Tuesday at Tepeyac Community Health Center in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Oliver Giminaro became fully dependent on caregivers after a spinal cord injury in 1992. His parents acted as those caregivers when he was still living at home in Delta. 
Before the injury, he loved playing football, camping, hiking, skiing and mountain biking, he said.
Now, if he didn’t have access to caretakers with the specialized skills required to help him, he would die, he said. Medicaid has paid for those caregivers for decades.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Giminaro went to college in Pueblo and earned an engineering degree. He got a job working for a boilermaker and was excited to contribute to a workplace with his education. But since the only health insurance program that pays for the type of long-term care he needs is Medicaid, he had to quit his job so he would financially qualify.
He is unable to work and now spends his time advocating for patients like him. But if he didn’t have Medicaid, he wouldn’t be able to live independently at home. 
“Medicaid allows me to function … if I didn’t have it would just be devastating,” Giminaro said. “If I didn’t have in-home care, I would have to live in an institution. We’ve all heard the horror stories and we all know that people thrive in community.”
The administrative processes patients have to go through to receive coverage under Medicaid are not set up for people with disabilities to successfully navigate. Some would argue that the system is designed for disabled people to fail, Giminaro said.
Cuts to Medicaid and caps on care would drastically affect not only Giminaro, but the healthcare workers and hospitals who have helped him for so long, he said. 



Quotation







As these cuts take effect, Coloradans health, well-being, economic, security and indeed their very lives are being put at risk ... Medicaid is the foundation of our healthcare system, and H.R.1 is a direct attack on that foundation.


– Adam Fox, deputy director of the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative


Giminaro and other patients and family members who fear cuts to public healthcare coverage under federal policy changes talked at a roundtable that U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper hosted Tuesday at Tepeyac Community Health Center in Denver.
Adam Fox, deputy director of the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative, emphasized that Medicaid cuts are only just starting, with more coming in 2027. The Republican tax cut and spending bill known as H.R. 1 cuts $1 trillion from Medicaid over several years, making it the largest cut to the program in history, he said. Colorado is estimated to lose up to $2.5 billion annually until 2032 because of cuts the law made. 
“As these cuts take effect, Coloradans health, well-being, economic, security and indeed their very lives are being put at risk,” Fox said. “Medicaid is the foundation of our healthcare system, and H.R.1 is a direct attack on that foundation.”
More Coloradans will continue to be stuck deciding between paying rent, buying food and seeking healthcare, he said. The end of enhanced premium tax credits for people who purchase health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace continues to increase costs, too.
“This also comes at a time when we’re seeing large healthcare corporations, whether it’s the insurers, the hospitals, drug corporations, or the various middlemen in our healthcare system, drive costs even higher,” Fox said. 
Program changes that will start next year, like additional paperwork and verification requirements, are “designed to rip away” coverage, Fox said. 
“We know that Medicaid is complicated enough as it is … but these requirements are so onerous, and the state has not had enough time to develop the systems necessary, that we fully expect these changes to bog down our entire Medicaid system, regardless of whether these requirements apply to everybody or not,” Fox said. 
Colorado legislators this year had to make cuts to the state budget to close a $1.5 billion budget gap created largely as a result of H.R. 1, and state analysis projects more budget cuts next year, Fox said. Amendment 87, a ballot measure Coloradans will vote on next week that would create a graduated income tax structure, would help fund healthcare, childcare and education programs, Fox said. 
How to do more with less
Healthcare officials at the roundtable talked about their constant need to help more people with fewer resources, and that dynamic will worsen under upcoming cuts to Medicaid. Pablo Hester, an executive at Tepeyac, said health centers like Tepeyac will have to take on an increased administrative burden as they adjust to the changes to Medicaid such as work requirements, and they need more staff to do that. 
For many people, community health centers are the best option for preventive care that is affordable and accessible, Jim Garcia, Tepeyac CEO and founder, said. But the need continues to exceed the center’s capacity.
Hickenlooper said community health centers are the “last hope” for a national health system that works.
“Anti-government forces in Washington are constantly painting pictures of waste and fraud and abuse,” Hickenlooper said. “What I see is constant improvement of efficiency and trying to figure out how to do more with less to still deliver the care that the community needs, and there’s not enough money.”
A denial
Even without the upcoming requirements, Medicaid is hard to navigate and stresses families when their access to care changes. Kari Brauer’s 11-year-old daughter, who has a developmental disability, requires daily assistance from a caregiver. 
Since 2020, Medicaid authorized 5.5 hours of certified nursing assistant care each day — a role Brauer has filled. But funding for that care ends this week since the state denied her most recent request. 
The denial letter acknowledges that Brauer’s daughter requires daily caregiver assistance but says she does not need the specific skills a nursing assistant provides, citing a lack of injuries or complications. 
“Are we supposed to wait until my daughter gets hurt before the cure that prevents it is considered necessary? The absence of injury doesn’t mean there is no risk,” Brauer said. “It means someone was there to recognize the risk and intervene before something happened.”
Brauer will be able to find another in-home Medicaid program for her daughter to enroll in, but it won’t provide as much support as the long-term nursing assistant funding did. The logistics of coordinating changes in care is a major stressor for Brauer, who works a full-time job on top of caring for her daughter.
